‌



View 2 Images CPR can be learnt for free at home or through dedicated courses (stock) (Image: Getty Images)

How can I learn to perform CPR?

You can learn CPR in the UK through free online interactive tools or by booking a practical, in-person training course with a major national provider. For full, hands-on certification or workplace compliance, you can book formal basic life support or first aid courses through trusted national bodies such as St John Ambulance or the British Red Cross.

Article continues below

If you want to learn the basics immediately, the British Heart Foundation has a free interactive online session available here. All you need is your phone or tablet and a cushion to practice chest compressions. It guides you through recognising cardiac arrest, calling 999, and using a defibrillator.

The guidance for giving CPR to children and babies is different from that for adults. Learn more about that by clicking here. Save a Life for Scotland provides more advice and guidance on how to give CPR to an adult.

News.title: Online shoppers told 'do not' when offered 'safe place' option
News.content:
Online shoppers told 'do not' when offered 'safe place' option

Customers may be giving up some of their legal rights if they choose this

View 2 Images People should avoid giving this option unless they 'absolutely have to' (Image: Yimbly)

People who shop online a lot and have parcels arriving regularly should try to avoid selecting one of these delivery options online, an expert claims. Doing this without thinking could mean people lose out on their legal rights if something goes wrong with their delivery.

‌



‌



Speaking to Matt Allwright on Channel 5, consumer expert Kat Cereda said: "I could bang on about this all day, don't put a safe place or a nominated neighbour unless you really, really have to because your rights get reduced."

‌



She explained that retailers have a responsibility from the moment you place an order to "make sure that parcel gets put in your hands". The second homeowners say it'll be fine to leave the bin behind or hide it in an outbuilding, the legal responsibility shifts.

‌



In the event something goes missing or gets damaged, Kat claims that companies have an excuse to claim they've met their end of the delivery deal by using a person's nominated safe space.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

She said: "If [the shop] can say 'oh, well, we've left it where you've said' on the porch and [it] gets swiped, they've done what they need to do and it's your fault that you didn't collect it."

‌



People give up the same protection to make a claim if something goes wrong when nominating a safe or trusted neighbour to receive the package instead. The expert claims that it's always best to avoid putting anything down in the event you need to claim for lost or damaged items.

Under the Consumer Rights Act 2015, the retailer remains legally responsible for your order if a courier leaves it in an un-nominated safe space and it goes missing. A photo of the parcel on a doorstep or in a bin does not prove it reached your hands safely if you never gave permission for it to be left there.

‌



View 2 Images Choosing this could lead to consequences if something goes wrong (Image: John Lamb | Getty)

Ensure our latest headlines always appear at the top of your Google Search by making us a Preferred Source. Click here to activate or add us as a Preferred Source in your Google search settings.

‌



Many delivery companies and apps allow you to explicitly state that the parcel must be handed to a person, or it must be taken back to the depot if you are out. Homeowners could also consider investing in a video doorbell or similar camera system.

These provide clear footage of the exact moment a driver leaves a package, and may be the undeniable proof needed that any lost or damaged items were left in an unapproved location. These smart systems could also be visible security deterrents, which may discourage opportunistic thieves.

Article continues below

If you are regularly out when drivers arrive, avoid home delivery entirely by routing your orders to secure public pickup points. If you shop frequently on Amazon, choose a local Amazon Hub Locker during checkout or see if services like Collect+ or Post Office Local Collect could be chosen to ship your goods to nearby corner shops, supermarkets, or post offices where staff will hold them securely.

News.title: 'His clothes still smell of him so I will never get rid of them' - mum of murdered teen Harvey Willgoose
News.content:
'His clothes still smell of him so I will never get rid of them' - mum of murdered teen Harvey Willgoose

Harvey, aged 15, was stabbed to death during his lunch break at All Saints Catholic High School in Sheffield on February 3rd 2025

View 6 Images Harvey Willgoose was stabbed to death at school (Image: PA)

The mum of murdered Harvey Willgoose faces another heartbreaking birthday with her son's cagoule still hanging up and his football lying at the bottom of the garden.

‌



‌



Harvey, aged 15, was stabbed to death during his lunch break at All Saints Catholic High School in Sheffield on February 3rd 2025. Now almost two years since he died, Caroline Willgoose, 52, told. how she still can't bear to get rid of his belongings.

‌



She said: “On Sunday Harvey would have been 17 years old. It’s not great, I feel like it’s worse now than it’s ever been. Harvey’s cagoule is still hanging up, his school shoes are still here, his washing is still in the washing basket. The football nets and his ball is still at the bottom of the garden, it’s just horrendous.

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 6 Images Caroline Willgoose and son Harvey (Image: Caroline Willgoose / SWNS)

‌



Grieving dad says police must question Suffolk Strangler after daughter’s unsolved murder READ MORE :

Blast rips through school killing at least 10 with dozens injured READ MORE :

“I can’t bear to part with them. I can’t. His clothes still smell of him so I will never get rid of them. That would be like throwing him away and I want to remember him every minute of the day.

“It’s just so sad there’s nothing sadder. You watch things on telly and you think ‘that’s not sad’. I look at his photos all the time, it’s like he’s still there.”

‌



View 6 Images CCTV of Mohammed Umar Khan, 15, entering school before he killed fellow pupil Harvey (Image: PA)

Harvey was killed by his classmate Mohammed Umar Khan, who stabbed him with a hunting knife he'd smuggled into school. In October last year, Khan, also 15, was found guilty of murder and detained for a minimum of 16 years.

‌



Since his death Caroline has been concentrating on helping other children and fighting for knife arches in schools.

The mum recently opened Harvey’s Hub, a youth club in Sheffield at The Spires Centre in Arbourthorne, just over a mile away from where her son was killed.

‌



“His friends message me and they put things on TikTok, how must they feel about losing their friend like that? It just breaks my heart. “

View 6 Images Caroline has opened Harvey’s Hub, a youth club in Sheffield (Image: Supplied)

‌



Speaking to the Mirror she said: “This is my way of giving back. I am going to go there today and see smiles on their faces and it will cheer me up. It makes me cry but in a different way.

“Harvey was a social butterfly. He would be first in the queue and last one to leave. He was a manager of a football team of older children when he was just 11.”

‌



She explains how his grandparents run the tuck shop and his other gran is on the door while Caroline cooks them a hot meal.

“Now we’ve got a permanent place we can ask for funding, I want them popping up around Sheffield. Hopefully they will be popping up all over the country," she said.

‌



“A lad came up to me and said last week; ‘I didn' t know it was going to be like this!’ There was an 11 year old on DJ set last week, it’s a bit different, with rooms where they can chill out. We’ve got some of Harvey’s friends that help, one who was at school with him that day and another who has been doing the glitter and putting face masks on.

“Kids are very misunderstood, they don’t have a voice any more, they get tarnished with a name, but these kids are absolutely brilliant, if they know you care and respect them you’re half way there.

‌



“Every single kid was a credit to their parents, all came and said thank you. It’s a deprived area too, I’m feeding them, and it might be the only meal they’ve had that night, it was lovely. Girls were meeting up outside all giddy and screaming. We ‘ve got a playstation and it was hardly used, what does that tell you?"

View 6 Images Harvey Willgoose was stabbed to death at school by another pupil (Image: yoRKSHIRE LIVE/MEN MEDIA)

‌



She continued: "The reason why I'm doing Harvey's Hub is because Harvey was all about socialising. He used to get Sheffield Wednesday fans and Sheffield United fans together and go and watch a different team because he just wanted everybody to be together."

"They have that many things taken away from them. I'm giving them something back."

‌



The youth club has received funding thanks to the local mayor and has pool tables, games consoles and darts, with its facilities inspired by Harvey's interests.

She says concentrating on the fight against knives has helped give her hope.

‌



“I’ve seen a change on social media, people fighting knife crime. All the millions the Government has been putting in is making a difference. I can see hope at last.”

View 6 Images Harvey Willgoose and his father, Mark (Image: PA)

‌



Although she said she was appalled after the school where Harvey died found a knife when they were looking for a vape during a bag search recently. The weapon was recovered and no injuries were reported, South Yorkshire Police said.

“I get hundreds of messages from around the country that pupils have been threatened. I fear there could be another one but I do feel things are changing. I think since our Harvey, people have been more aware.”

Article continues below

South Yorkshire’s Mayor Oliver Coppard said: “The courage Caroline, Mark and their family have shown since Harvey’s death has been extraordinary. Harvey was someone who loved bringing people together, so it feels fitting that his name will live on through a place where young people can meet, have fun, learn and feel safe. It's a great example of not only how we can work to prevent violence, but of Harvey’s legacy and what community can look like.

“Through our Violence Prevention Partnership, we’ll be supporting the development of Harvey’s Hub with a community grant, helping Caroline and Mark build something special in memory of their son.”

News.title: 'My strained knee turned out to be life-changing illness'
News.content:
'My strained knee turned out to be life-changing illness'

Brittany Pay, 37, who has stage four metastatic breast cancer, is urging women to trust their instincts about their health and push for answers

View 3 Images Brittany Pay, 37, is a comedian from London (Image: Jam Press/@brittpay_)

A woman has told how what doctors initially thought was a "strained" knee turned out to be incurable cancer.

‌



‌



Brittany Pay, a 37-year-old comedian, went from walking normally to being unable to manage the 10-minute journey to her GP within just four days because of excruciating pain. "I kept trying to find a reasonable explanation, but there hadn't been an accident or injury," Brittany said. "I tried resting, stretching, heat and cold, but nothing made a difference."

‌



Brittany, an Australian who lives in London, said her doctor appeared reassured by the lack of swelling around her knee and did not initially believe anything was seriously wrong. She said: "When I could barely stand to leave, they questioned whether it was really that bad. I felt I hadn't explained just how dramatically my life had changed in four days. I could walk and run. Now I can barely take a few steps. I knew my body, and I knew this wasn't normal."

‌



To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and find them easily on Google, make us your preferred source. It's free and easy to do - just click here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 3 Images Brittany is determined not to let cancer define her life (Image: Jam Press/@brittpay_)

NATO fighter jets scrambled as Latvian airspace violated and Putin's attacks continue READ MORE :

Princess Kate seen for first time since Anmer Hall break-in READ MORE :

Months later, in December 2023, Brittany received the devastating diagnosis of stage four metastatic breast cancer.

‌



By then, the disease had spread extensively to her bones, including her spine, ribs, pelvis and femur. A tumour measuring around 11cm had developed in her right thigh bone.

Brittany had previously attended a breast clinic three times between January 2021 and May 2023 after discovering a lump. She said it was scanned during her first appointment but dismissed, while her right breast was not scanned during her subsequent two visits. Looking back, Brittany believes the lump should have been investigated further.

‌



Since her diagnosis, Brittany has undergone multiple rounds of treatment and radiotherapy and major surgeries on both legs.

Surgeons had to remove a significant part of her right femur and replace it, along with her knee, with a metal implant. In June 2026, she underwent surgery on her left femur, where surgeons inserted a metal nail to strengthen the bone after it was weakened by cancer.

‌



View 3 Images 'I don't know how many more treatments will be available to me, but I know I'll keep going for as long as there are options,' Brittany said (Image: Jam Press/@brittpay_)

Brittany said: "Becoming disabled has honestly been harder for me to process than I ever expected. But I don't want to minimise what living with stage four cancer is like either. Having both experiences happen together has been horrific.

‌



"You're trying to come to terms with the fact that you have an incurable illness, while also navigating an entirely new life in which you can't walk, travel independently, or do many of the things you previously took for granted. It's difficult to separate the two because they affect every part of each other."

She described living with incurable cancer as feeling like she was "existing somewhere between life and death". "I've had to grieve the life I thought I would have while simultaneously trying to build a new one," she said.

‌



The cancer has since spread to Brittany's bones, liver and brain, and she is preparing to begin her fifth line of treatment, Enhertu. Despite this, she is determined not to let cancer define her life and finds joy in beauty, comedy, outings and spending time with friends.

"I don't know how many more treatments will be available to me, but I know I'll keep going for as long as there are options. I have a life worth fighting for, and I want to keep building it," Brittany said.

Article continues below

She said she wants young women to understand that breast cancer doesn't only happen to older women. "If something doesn't feel right, keep pushing for answers. Ask questions, ask for things to be investigated properly and get a second opinion if you aren't satisfied. You know your own body, and you shouldn't feel that you're being difficult or dramatic by asking for help," she said.

News.title: UK tells Argentina to stop agitating over Falklands after UN court slaps it down
News.content:
UK tells Argentina to stop agitating over Falklands after UN court slaps it down

In a landmark ruling, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ruled against Argentine President Javier Milei's bid to block drilling in the Sea Lion oilfield

View 2 Images A UN court has delivered a hammer blow to the Argentine government (Image: Getty Images)

The UK has called on Argentina to end its economic agitation against the Falkland Islands after it was slapped down by a UN court.

‌



‌



In a landmark ruling, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea ruled against Argentine President Javier Milei as he attempted to block an oil drilling project in the British overseas territory.

‌



It comes as tensions ramp up around the Falklands, which Milei has repeatedly claimed belongs to his nation. In a joint statement, Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said: "Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt.

‌



"The UK has no doubt over our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders.

To see more of the stories you love from The Mirror and to find them easily in Google then make us your preferred source. Free and easy-to-do, just click on the link here to find more from The Mirror at the top of your feed.

View 2 Images The ruling is a hammer blow to Argentine president Javier Milei (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

‌



Lucy Powell unveils new target to halve reading disadvantage gap by 2035 READ MORE :

"We now call on Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future and urge Argentina to end its wider economic pressure against the Falkland Islands."

The South American nation continues to claim sovereignty over the British overseas territory, and has been seeking to block the oil project, worth billions of pounds.

‌



The tribunal voted 18 to three against Mr Milei's demand at a hearing in Hamburg, Germany. Milei has been incensed over plans for drilling in the Sea Lion oilfield, branding it a clear and present danger to his country's claim over the territory. But in a decision read out by ITLOS president Maurice Kamga, the court rejected Argentina's arguments.

He said there did not appear to be any basis for believing it had jurisdiction as the tribunal is unable to rule on questions of sovereignty.

‌



UK Attorney General Ellie Reeves has previously warned that blocking the drilling would have devastating consequences for Falkland Islanders. The move would prevent them from developing their natural resources as they are entitled to do so, she said.

The Sea Lion development is a joint venture in the South Atlantic Ocean between British and Israeli companies, and contains an estimated 1.7 billion barrels of oil.

‌



In September Andy Burnham said the UK would defend the right of islanders to remain British after Milei ramped up the rhetoric in the decades-long dispute.

‌



The PM said at the time: "I think it’s right for me to set out the position clearly, and the clear position is: we will stand firm in the face of any threats.

“We will defend the right of the Falkland Islanders to self-determination and to remain British." It came after Milei claimed the Falklands were "under illegal foreign occupation" by the UK and threatened to "to take matters into our own hands".

Article continues below

The islands lie around 300 miles from Argentina's coast. The UK has said drilling at the field will start in March next year - with extraction to begin a year later.

It means oil firms Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum are set to push ahead with the plan under licenses granted by the Falkland Islands government and backed by Britain.

News.title: Hitler lookalike sentenced for glorifying the former Nazi dictator
News.content:
Hitler lookalike sentenced for glorifying the former Nazi dictator

Stefan Wijkamp. nicknamed the Dutch Hitler, sports a side-parting and clipped mustache just like his hero, who ruthlessly murdered millions of Jews during World War Two

View 3 Images Stefan Wijkamp has been nicknamed the Dutch Hitler (Image: Jochen Tack/imageBROKER/Shutterstock)

An Adolf Hitler lookalike has been sentenced to eight months probation for incitement to hatred.

‌



‌



Stefan Wijkamp, who sports a side-parting and clipped moustache just like his hero, praised the Nazi Party dictator during an interview at a demonstration in Munster, Germany, in July last year. He arrived at Munster District Court wearing a long leather coat and a tie with an edelweiss insignia once used by Waffen-SS mountain troops.

‌



The court heard the Dutchman, 59, had declared: "My love for Germany is Adolf Hitler." He also described the man who ruthlessly murdered millions of Jews during the Second World War as a "world wonder without equal," "brilliant," and a "genius."

‌



View 3 Images Wijkamp pictured at a previous protest in Berlin, Germany (Image: Getty Images)

Denmark celebrates its oldest ever woman as she turns 112 – then discovers she was a Nazi READ MORE :

Politician with Mein Kampf copy signed by Hitler resigns and donates book READ MORE :

Wijkamp, who has been nicknamed The Dutch Hitler, appeared in court on Friday in a bid to appeal a penal order imposed over the comments at the same court four months ago. Video of Wijkamp's comments, which included him using the term "Heil Hitler", was played to the court.

According to German broadcaster WDR, he repeatedly nodded in court, as if in agreement, as the demonstration footage was played. Tim Jander, of the public prosecutor's office, said: "It is absolutely clear beyond doubt that the defendant publicly glorified Hitler and thereby disturbed the public peace. A prison sentence is absolutely necessary."

‌



Judge Antonia Buddenbäumer said: "There are limits to freedom of expression, and these have clearly been exceeded." The judge ruled that Wijkamp's claim that "if we had won the war, everyone would have been standing here today shouting 'Heil Hitler!'" constituted incitement to hatred.

‌



View 3 Images A hand-coloured photographic portrait of Nazi Leader Adolf Hitler in the uniform of the Sturmabteilung, the paramilitary wing of the Nazi Party, also known as the 'Brownshirts' (Image: Popperfoto via Getty Images)

She sentenced him to eight months in prison, suspended for three years because he had no prior convictions. He was also ordered to pay a €1,000 fine and court costs.

Article continues below

Wijkamp, who is from the Dutch village of Oosterbeek - scene of bitter fighting in 1944 where British Airborne troops valiantly battled Nazi forces after their attempt to capture the bridge at nearby Arnhem - had demanded he be acquitted claiming his remarks were protected by freedom of speech laws. In his final statement, he said: "We Dutch speak plainly. I admire Adolf Hitler, and I love the Führer."

He is reportedly appealing the verdict, which is not yet legally binding.

News.title: Pensions and benefits services still down after 'cyber incident'
News.content:
Online benefits and pensions services were still down on Saturday morning following a "cyber incident" which forced the government to take them offline.

The Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) has not specified what triggered it to shut down access late on Thursday but has not ruled out that it was hit by hackers.

The government has assured benefits recipients and pensioners that usual payments will continue to be made after some claimants reported delays. It is understood the department believes delays were not linked to the cyber incident.

The UK's former chief technology officer David Knott told BBC Newsnight his "strong suspicion" was that the department had been targeted by hackers.

He continued: "[The government has] taken down some of the citizen-facing services, which implies to me that there's some kind of attack could be mounted through the front door."

John Curry, a leading cyber security expert based at Bath Spa University, told BBC News the DWP had "almost certainly" detected hacking activity taking place and shut down its systems in an effort to stop data being stolen.

Curry said if the DWP had discovered hackers inside its computer systems, then the "best thing to do is slam the front door shut".

He also said the government may deliberately release limited information in order to "keep the enemy in the dark" and not give any possible hackers hints about ongoing work to secure sensitive systems.

On Friday, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden said there had been a "serious cyber incident" without offering further details, while the department said the move to close online services was a "precaution".

Downing Street would not be drawn on whether the DWP had been targeted by hackers but did say other departments had not been accessed by a "malicious actor".

The government said it was working with GCHQ's National Cyber Security Centre to investigate the incident, which indicates a hack has not been ruled out.

The incident has fuelled concerns about the vulnerability of state computer systems and whether security protocols are keeping pace with demand and advances in AI technology, which can be used to aid hackers.

Matthew Gould, former Cabinet Office head of cyber security, said: "There are hundreds and hundreds of legacy systems that are kept going with huge commitment and skill from the people doing it, but where frankly the system is relying on very old infrastructure."

He added: "What is needed a lot of the time is quite boring investment in upgrading what is already there, moving platforms on to more stable bases, making systems more resilient.

"It doesn't make for great headlines but there is an awful lot of investment that's required on a digital estate as large as the government's or the NHS's to keep it strong and resilient."

News.title: Woman, 21, dies in Staffordshire crash following police pursuit
News.content:
A 21-year-old woman has died in a crash following a police pursuit in Staffordshire.

The front-seat passenger of a Seat Ibiza, which had been followed by officers, died at the scene of the crash in Rugeley Road, Hednesford, just after 23:00 GMT on Friday, Staffordshire Police said.

The force said the Seat collided with an Vauxhall Astra, which was also being driven by members of the public, after the "short police pursuit".

A 23-year-old man from the Walsall area was arrested on suspicion of causing death by dangerous driving. The force said the Astra driver was helping with police inquiries.

The incident has been referred to the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) due to the police involvement before the collision.

West Midlands Ambulance Service took two other people from the scene to hospital with injuries not believed to be life-threatening or life-changing.

The woman's next-of-kin have been informed and are being supported by trained police officers.

The route has reopened to traffic after being cordoned off following the incident.

Staffordshire Police has appealed to witnesses who were in the area at the time or saw the vehicles beforehand to get in touch.

News.title: Catherine's emotional cancer documentary strips away the stiff upper lip
News.content:
The Princess of Wales's personal account of her experience of cancer has a soul-baring, emotionally candid tone never presented before in a royal documentary.

Discussing it at a private screening, she said it reflected the "fear, anxiety, uncertainty" shared by hundreds of thousands of people each year "who receive the words no one wants to hear" about having cancer.

The documentary, Heal, being shown on BBC One on Sunday, couldn't be further away from a stiff upper lip.

This is royal television without any palaces or carriages, it's an intense 30 minutes examining how "cancer strips everything away" and then a different kind of self-awareness emerges.

It reveals more of Catherine's inner thoughts than any of her previous speeches and we hear more from her children than ever before.

"Cancer does change you. It changes your body, it changes you physically. You have to go through treatment and surgeries and everything.

"But there's a much deeper part to what a cancer diagnosis shifts in you. I think when you've had to confront your own vulnerabilities, you know, when you're faced with your own mortality, you have to accept that life is not infinite and in those moments, yes, a shift does happen," she says.

News.title: 'I don't know what I'd do without it': Is this the end for Poundland?
News.content:
For Charlie Franklyn, a trip to Poundland is almost as routine as going to work.

The care worker from Teesside pops into her local branch nearly every day â it's where she buys cleaning products, beauty bargains and the budget-friendly finds she loves sharing online.

Charlie has been creating social media content for five years, and Poundland is one of her regular filming spots.

Her videos showcasing the store and its wares have proved popular, and although she's never been paid by the retailer, she's been gifted products over the years and built relationships with staff who invite her in to film.

"For me, Poundland is more than just a shopping stop. I buy so many things from there that are much cheaper than in other shops."

News.title: A clinic is offering to reassess ADHD and autism diagnoses - and hundreds of people are interested
News.content:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.

Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.

But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.

This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.

At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.

But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.

Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.

"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.

If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.

The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.

The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.

And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable â and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.

Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.

News.title: Carly Rae Jepsen's viral hit proves what fans knew all along
News.content:
For years, Carly Rae Jepsen's fans have been telling anyone, external who'll listen, external that she wrote the perfect pop song... and they don't mean Call Me Maybe.

No, it's Run Away With Me â three minutes of pure euphoria that captures the moment a crush snowballs into a full-blown love affair.

Released in 2015, it stalled at number 58 in the charts, but it has long been a highlight of Jepsenâs live shows. Then, last week, it made a surprise appearance in Grand Theft Auto VI.

It provides the soundtrack to a pivotal sequence where the game's protagonists get their first taste of the high life - zooming around on jet skis and shooting champagne bottles from the back of a yacht.

"Have I ever done that? I have not!" Jepsen laughs.

"My guilty admission is that I haven't even played the game yet, but I'm excited to try it. I'm gonna become a late-in-life gamer!"

The placement has given the song a new lease of life. Its daily streams rose from 20,000 to 281,000 overnight. On Friday, it re-entered the UK charts at a new peak of 28.

"It's wild," says Jepsen from her home in Los Angeles. "I love a plot twist, and this was exactly that."

News.title: The AI-powered race to get GTA 6 onto PC before Rockstar
News.content:
Hot off its record-breaking console launch, the developer of Grand Theft Auto 6 is facing a problem â and it's one that is increasingly affecting the wider games industry.

Rockstar is yet to announce an official PC version of GTA 6, but with the emergence of powerful AI tools, coders and gamers have taken matters into their own hands.

The developer has typically released Grand Theft Auto on PC long after its initial console launch â 19 months later in the case of GTA 5.

This time it may not have that luxury â in part because of an apparent leak of files from an Xbox development build of the game, but also due to the rapid advance of AI coding platforms.

These tools are being used to recreate or adapt existing games, sometimes within days, taking away the control developers have over their products.

News.title: Flu cases are rising - should you get a vaccine now?
News.content:
"If you're offered it, it's a good idea to have it," says Prof Nick Hopkinson, professor of respiratory medicine at Imperial College London.

"The main reason is to avoid serious complications in vulnerable groups â so as many as possible should have it in those groups.

"People don't understand it's a potentially life-threatening infection and that the vaccine is safe."

Flu is a viral infection which affects the nose, throat and lungs. Often it goes away on its own but it can make people seriously ill â complications can include pneumonia, heart attacks and other underlying illnesses getting worse.

It can also kill.

In England last winter, UKHSA estimated there were 3,798 deaths attributed to influenza.

Scientists have to predict which strains of influenza will be circulating before the vaccine is manufactured each year in time for winter.

The current one protects against three strains â two influenza A strains and one influenza B strain.

Even if these strains drift slightly, experts say getting vaccinated is still a good idea to lower the risk of severe illness.

News.title: Pharmacies get new powers to swap prescriptions during shortages
News.content:
Pharmacies are being given more freedom over the prescription medicines they can give to patients when items are out of stock.

Staff will be able to offer the same drug in a different strength or form â two 5mg tablets in the place of a 10mg pill, or a cream instead of an ointment, for example.

The change should help patients avoid repeat trips to their GP for an alternative prescription when the issue can be resolved safely and easily at the chemist.

And for the first time, children in England who miss their flu vaccination at school will be able to receive it at a pharmacy instead.

News.title: Set time aside for children to read for pleasure, schools to be told
News.content:
Schools in England will be expected to set aside regular time for students to read for pleasure under changes to the national curriculum.

Primary schools will have to allocate time every day for children to read and secondary students will be given time every week to focus on entire books, poems and literature, the Department for Education (DfE) said.

Education Secretary Lucy Powell is poised to unveil the plans in Parliament on Monday, framing them as part of a larger effort to address the "ticking time bomb" of declining literacy rates.

The push to boost reading rates will also help with the "battle for attention with mindless scrolling", the DfE said.

Schools are already facing stricter guidance on phone use, that means children will not be able to access their devices at all during the school day, in a bid to reduce screen time.

The DfE statement continued: "Reading enjoyment and daily reading levels remain too low, particularly among disadvantaged children and boys."

Year 8 students will undergo a mandatory reading check to identify students who need additional help.

The government will also unveil a new target to halve the reading disadvantage gap by 2035, with a new goal to see at least 80% of students meet their expected standard in reading.

Powell said reading would be placed at the centre of the curriculum shake-up.

Explaining the changes ahead of Monday, Powell said: "Across the world, we are seeing a ticking time bomb for our future generations, as reading and literacy levels are falling with too many children seeing reading as a chore or missing out altogether.

"Reading fluently is the gateway to lifelong learning, opening up every subject in school and creating opportunities throughout life."

Broader changes to the curriculum come after two reviews that found pupils were becoming increasingly disengaged in their early teenage years, impacting attendance and achievement, the Department for Education (DfE) said.

Secondary schools have been told not to teach GCSEs early, with the government seeking to promote a "richer, more engaging" experience at Key Stage 3.

The curriculum overhaul is the first to be introduced in more than a decade since former Conservative Education Secretary Michael Gove brought in reforms focused on encouraging students to engage with the "core knowledge" of facts and principles.

Children's author and former school librarian Sue Wallman said children need to be given time and space to discover the joy of reading.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I think it's very difficult and students who have never been read to just do not have the association between reading and relaxation and comfort.

"They find it very hard, they panic when they have to read out loud."

She said children need to be offered comfortable and relaxed spaces so they can "fine their books in their own time" over several years.

News.title: 'I wouldn't be here today without you': Student's praise for man who stopped train attacker
News.content:
Meeting after the guilty verdicts were delivered, the two train passengers hugged.

Astrid told the Nottingham Forest fan, who had been travelling home from a match: "It's brilliant to meet you... now we will know each other for a long time."

Crean said: "It means the world to me to meet her. Meeting her was the best thing, it was worth waiting for. I'm just so happy."

Astrid, who did not want to use her last name, said Crean was a hero for his actions that day.

"I just owe him everything," she said, before adding: "I wouldn't be here today without you, and to put your life on the line for someone else, a complete stranger, is just complete bravery."

She said Crean had a "split second to make a decision" and she owed him her life because of that.

"So I'd just like to say thank you," she said.

Crean praised her for alerting him to the danger of Williams as she ran past.

"You can be proud of yourself, and your parents will be proud of you," he added.

During the trial, Crean told the court he decided "to try to stop" the attack and "launched himself towards and at" Williams.

Crean and Astrid both faced terrifying moments as Williams rampaged down the train.

Crean said Williams asked, "Do you want to die?" as he stabbed him several times.

Crean then managed to lock himself in a toilet and call 999 telling them what had happened and that he was covered in blood and scared.

He said he remembered seeing Astrid crying with makeup running down her face.

The fashion student said she remembered seeing Crean throw himself at the attacker and put himself between her and Williams so she could escape.

"I was able to shut the door with the rest of the people behind me. If you hadn't been in between us... I have no idea what would have happened if you weren't there, literally in that second."

Astrid had seen an interview with the 62-year-old on the BBC two days after the attack and contacted the BBC to say he was the man on the train who had helped protect her and others.

Only now the trial has finished have they been able to meet.

Crean said he is pleased the jury found Williams guilty of attempting to murder him as he did not believe he should be allowed to get away with the vicious attacks on him and the other passengers.

On Thursday Cambridgeshire police apologised for failings in stopping Williams after another assault the month before the Huntingdon attack.

As well as the train attacks, Williams was found guilty of attempting to murder four other people in separate incidents and will be sentenced at Cambridge Crown Court on 4 and 5 February.

Crean believes more should have been done to prevent these further offences. "I think they should have had him before. He shouldn't have been allowed to go running around like this. And if they'd picked up on it, we'd have had him before."

Having survived the attack, Astrid is running the London marathon for Crimestoppers as part of her efforts to turn around the harrowing situation she found herself in.

She can, she says, because of Stephen Crean's actions. And he has promised to be there for her again: this time on the finish line.

Additional reporting by Rozina Sini

News.title: NHS boss warns of 'horrible spike' in flu as hospital admissions surge
News.content:
Sir Ciaran Devane, chief executive of the NHS Alliance, representing employers, said: "While the flu season is clearly hitting earlier this year and could add to the strain on NHS services heading into another difficult winter, we are yet to see how or when it will peak.

"The NHS has already had to deal with the challenge of heatwaves this summer, so this could pile yet more pressure on already squeezed services."

Suzanna McDonald urged people to get vaccinated, saying thousands of people die from the flu every year.

Flu levels are expected to increase further as Christmas approaches and people start socialising indoors more.

McDonald also called on those who are ill with respiratory symptoms to practise good hand hygiene by washing hands with warm soapy water, cough and sneeze into elbow or into a tissue, and to stay at home in bed and avoid anyone at much higher risk from catching diseases.

Meanwhile, it emerged that just a little over a third of toddlers in England have had a vaccine so far this autumn on the NHS.

Two and three-year-olds can have the vaccine, given as a nasal spray, for free at GP surgeries and some community pharmacies.

But the UKHSA said just 39% of those eligible had taken up the offer.

School age children usually have the vaccine at school, with a catch-up available in pharmacies from 1 December for those who missed it.

McDonald said: "Please don't dismiss the importance of a flu vaccine for your children.

"It will help keep them out of hospital and even save lives."

This time last year an early increase in flu cases caused real concern across the NHS.

The virus was spreading sooner than expected and the fear was that the numbers would continue climbing right through the always challenging Christmas and New Year period.

As it happened the outbreak peaked early and the bleakest predictions did not become reality.

This time hospital admissions with flu patients are a little higher than 12 months ago after another early surge materialised.

Once again, officials do not know when the peak might be reached.

Adding to the challenges is an increase over the last year in patient numbers with a range of illnesses and conditions, partly explained by the ageing population. That means even more pressure on hospitals and their staff.

A bad flu winter could create significant problems.

News.title: RAF apologises after jets flown low over Lockerbie near bombing anniversary
News.content:
The Royal Air Force has apologised to the residents of Lockerbie after military jets were flown over the area close to the anniversary of the deadly bombing.

A Pan-Am jumbo jet came down over the Dumfries and Galloway town in December 1988, killing all 259 people on board and 11 people on the ground.

Local MP David Mundell said there was an understanding in place after the attack that there would not be low flying over the community out of respect to residents, but reports suggest this was broken on several occasions earlier this month.

The RAF said it was sorry for any distress caused, and that it was investigating.

Nearly 40 years on, the Lockerbie bombing remains the deadliest terrorist attack in UK history.

The plane was flying from Heathrow to New York when the bomb exploded in its forward hold, breaking the plane apart at 31,000 feet (9,449m).

Victims were of 21 different nationalities, and 190 were American.

News.title: Stalker who moved house to be closer to his victim is jailed
News.content:
A stalker who moved house to be closer to his victim and waited outside her friend's house for almost eight hours while she was inside has been jailed.

Hamza El-Hay, 31, met his victim on social media and was hired to do construction work on her grandmother's house.

He began making inappropriate comments towards her, including asking her if she was a "virgin".

A sentencing hearing at Cardiff Crown Court on Wednesday heard the victim made it clear she had no interest in having a relationship with El-Hay, but his behaviour still escalated.

El-Hay, of no fixed abode, pleaded guilty to stalking and was sentenced to 20 months' imprisonment and made the subject of a restraining order.

Despite rejecting his advances, El-Hay continued contacting the victim, sending her gifts, turning up at her home, following her in his vehicle and even moving house to be closer to her.

On September 25 last year, the victim spotted El-Hay's vehicle while she was at Cardiff Shopping Park - he then parked next to her, got into the passenger seat of her car and refused to move.

On 31 December, the victim saw him following her in his car as she went to a friend's house then saw him near her home when she returned later.

On 12 January, El-Hay followed her along the M4 and the M50 as she drove to Scotland for a holiday and she was forced to pull on to the hard shoulder to escape him.

Eleven days later, he paced back and forth outside the home of one of her friends for seven-and-a-half hours while she was inside.

Prosecutor Ben Jones said the final incident took place on 24 January while the victim was travelling along Newport Road when El-Hay pulled up next to her car at speed.

Letters had also been left on the victim's car by El-Hay, as well as images and flowers.

In a statement read to the court by the prosecution, the victim said: "I am suffering from anxiety and depression, I haven't been sleeping well and I am suffering with panic attacks.

"My hands shake so often, my hands shake when I see him and when I tried to ring 999. When he approached me I pretended not to see him and if I saw a white van I panicked.

"I don't feel like myself anymore or recognise myself in the last year. I don't laugh or have fun anymore. I tried to help him as a friend and he used that against me."

Hannah Friedman, defending, said her client was born in Morocco and was sent as a young child to live with his aunt, where he was put to work as a labourer.

She said he had a difficult childhood and ran away from home at nine years old. He travelled to Barcelona aged 13, moved to the UK in 2011, and to Cardiff in 2016.

News.title: Police look for more than 100 gig-goers to help Co-op Live probe
News.content:
Police have said they are trying to contact more than 100 gig-goers to help their investigation after an unknown substance was released at a concert at Manchester's Co-op Live arena.

Detectives believe a "small group of organised criminals targeted people in the crowd to commit a series of robberies on the night".

More than 12,000 people were evacuated from the arena during a performance by US rapper Don Toliver on Sunday.

One woman was taken to hospital and 88 others were treated at the scene after concertgoers reported a "horrible smell" and some people "coughing up blood".

No arrests have been made and the substance has not yet been identified.

Assistant Chief Constable Tom Harding said: "We're working to identify those [robbery] suspects and the substance that we believe was released in the crowd as part of these incidents.

"All of this work is ongoing at pace.

He said there had been "similar incidents at two Don Toliver gigs in Europe that are also relevant to our enquiries".

Fans reported that a spray or gas was released into the crowd in Zurich and Paris.

News.title: Channel 4 executive defends Huw Edwards documentary
News.content:
A senior Channel 4 executive has said there is "clear public interest in confronting" Huw Edwards after it received criticism over an upcoming documentary about the former BBC newsreader.

The 65-year-old, who pleaded guilty to making indecent images of children in 2024, has spoken to Channel 4 as part of a documentary which follows the disgraced broadcaster after his conviction. The programme is due to air on Tuesday.

Louisa Compton, director of news, said "nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness" of the harm caused by Edwards' offending.

It comes after Downing Street said "we have no interest in hearing" from Edwards and that broadcasters must "act responsibly".

Victims campaigners, politicians and members of the public have criticised the decision to allow Edwards to give an account of his actions.

The Observer newspaper and Tortoise Media also interviewed Edwards for a podcast series to be released in the coming days.

It will be the first time Edwards has been publicly questioned about the events which led to him leaving the BBC and later receiving a suspended jail sentence.

Channel 4's Compton said Edwards "is not being allowed to tell his story unchallenged or on his own terms", adding he was not paid and had no control over the content of the film or questions he was asked.

She said he had "never publicly faced detailed questioning about his criminal behaviour or the complete collapse of his career and reputation", adding: "There is a clear public interest in confronting him with those questions rather than allowing them to remain unanswered."

Edwards, who was the BBC's most senior news presenter, pleaded guilty in July 2024 to three counts of making indecent images of children and was given a suspended six-month prison sentence.

He admitted having 41 images, which were sent to him on WhatsApp â including some showing a victim aged between seven and nine.

Compton said: "Nothing about making this film diminishes the seriousness of that harm, nor does Edwards' participation entitle him to sympathy, redemption or rehabilitation."

Duncan Craig, head of We Are Survivors, which supports male survivors of sexual abuse and rape, accused the media outlets who have interviewed Edwards of "not thinking about the victims".

He said giving a platform to sexual offenders "gives them the ability to nail themselves to the cross".

The interviews have also been criticised by three people who previously alleged Edwards behaved inappropriately towards them.

One anonymous accuser, who said in 2023 that Edwards had sent them threatening messages, said it was "incredibly bizarre that anyone, big names like Channel 4, are platforming him when he's a convicted sex offender".

Another who claimed Edwards sent them suggestive messages, while they were working at the BBC, said they were "disgusted", while a former junior BBC employee who previously said they had received inappropriate messages from him called it "strange and irresponsible".

News.title: Macy’s Thanksgiving parade gets underway after 2-day delay with lineup ‘90 to 95%’ intact’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Macy’s managed to keep about 95 percent of its Thanksgiving Day parade lineup intact despite a two-day weather delay, as the 100th-anniversary celebration finally got underway Saturday morning in New York City.

The parade kicked off at 8:30 a.m. from Manhattan’s Upper West Side and is expected to run until noon. It follows its usual 2.5-mile route through Midtown, ending at Macy’s flagship store in Herald Square.

British singer-songwriter RAYE opened the national broadcast with her song “Joy,” joined by her sisters, Amma and Absolutely. This year’s parade features a record 100 balloons and other inflatables, including several new additions. Newcomers include Bluey and Hello Kitty Big Apple, while longtime favorites such as Underdog and the Blue Hippo are returning.

Will Coss, vice president and executive producer of Macy’s Studios, said most performers, marching bands and other participants were able to rearrange their travel plans to make the new date.

“I’d say 90 to 95 percent of our bands, performance groups, celebrity talent, has been able to adjust plans, make accommodations to their existing travel and appearance plans, and will be with us on Saturday morning,” Coss said Friday as the parade balloons were being inflated, according to the Associated Press.

open image in gallery Will Coss, vice president and executive producer of Macy’s Studios, said 90 to 95 percent of the performers, marching bands and celebrity guests were able to rearrange their schedules and attend Saturday’s parade ( Reuters )

“The goal for the team over the last 48 hours was to just do a quick pivot. We looked at our plans, we readjusted a few things, but for the most part the parade that we will be delivering tomorrow is the parade we set out to deliver on Thursday.”

The lineup includes LL Cool J, Gloria Gaynor, Megan Moroney, Teddy Swims, Queen Latifah, Keke Palmer, Jimmy Fallon & The Roots, and JoJo. Other performers include Baha Men, Natasha Bedingfield, Blues Traveler, DEVO, Feid, Mckenna Grace, Icona Pop, Il Volo, Indigo Girls, Wyclef Jean, Natalie Merchant, Leslie Odom Jr. and Smash Mouth.

The parade also features a Dolly Parton tribute led by Megan Hilty, a performance by EJAE and appearances by Melissa Joan Hart, Jack McBrayer, Janet McTeer, Holly Robinson Peete and Rodney Peete. Cast members from Broadway shows including Wicked, Hamilton, Chicago and Rent are also taking part, along with the Radio City Rockettes.

open image in gallery The parade features a record 100 balloons and inflatables, including newcomers Bluey and Hello Kitty Big Apple, alongside returning favorites Underdog and the Blue Hippo ( Getty )

open image in gallery Thousands of spectators lined the streets of NYC to watch the delayed parade ( Reuters )

Still, some groups couldn't make the new date work. The University of Alabama’s Million Dollar Band was among those forced to drop out because of scheduling conflicts.

Other marching bands scrambled to raise money for extra hotel stays, meals and transportation. The Pride of Pearland Marching Band in Texas raised about $350,000 to cover the added expenses, while the University of Illinois’ Marching Illini raised money to cover an estimated $175,000 in additional costs.

“It’s been a long couple of days just working through some of the backend logistics, but the fact that everyone has been able to, and was eager to, adjust their plans speaks to the energy and the opportunity to get in front of a couple of million people and deliver this spectacle of joy,” Coss said.

News.title: England v New Zealand LIVE: All Blacks seek revenge in Nations Championship rematch
News.content:

Maro Itoje leads England against New Zealand again ( Getty )

England and New Zealand collide again on Nations Championship finals weekend as the All Blacks look to hit back after a record defeat.

The tourists were beaten 37-12 at Twickenham last week by an inspired England, with Dave Rennie’s side rather limping towards the end of a gruelling year of international action. Can they lift their level to avoid another defeat to their hosts? Rennie has freshened up his squad in search of a response, with Jordie Barrett following in the footsteps of brothers Scott and Beauden as captain.

England, meanwhile, will hope to match the emotional energy they found on a special day for the sport last Saturday. News.title: The UK supermarkets taking part in Black Friday 2026
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Supermarkets are no strangers to a good deal. Whether it's a £10 advent calendar worth £90 at Lidl or a multi-buy offer on wine at Waitrose, there's usually a bargain to be found in the aisles. But while supermarkets are great for everyday savings, they're not necessarily the first place you'd think to look for Black Friday deals. So, with the sales well underway, is it worth adding a few bargains to your weekly shop?

Black Friday officially falls on 27 November this year, although plenty of retailers have already kicked off their sales, some as early as October. While the biggest discounts tend to be reserved for more expensive purchases, such as TVs, laptops and household appliances, supermarkets are getting in on the action, too. That said, don't expect to see your usual groceries suddenly slashed in price, as Black Friday offers rarely extend to food and drink.

Of course, supermarkets sell far more than groceries these days. From clothing and beauty products to toys, homeware and tech, there's plenty worth keeping an eye on. But not every supermarket is taking part in Black Friday this year, so we've rounded up which ones are offering discounts and which ones are sitting it out.



Which supermarkets have started their Black Friday sales?

So far, Lidl, Tesco, Asda and Morrisons have all launched Black Friday sales. Waitrose, M&S, Sainsbury’s, and Co-op aren’t officially running Black Friday sales, but they’re running generic offers. M&S, for instance, has a big sale on across nearly every product category, including clothing, luggage and beauty gift sets.



What are the best Black Friday deals at supermarkets?

Asda

Asda’s deals are focused on home, electricals and beauty, from George at Asda, rather than food and drink. This year’s Black Friday sale has already started both in-store and online, with up to 40 per cent off hundreds of products, spanning LED face masks to duvets.

Expect top big-name brands like Lego, Tassimo and Salter, including Salter’s the chocolatier hot chocolate maker (was £39, now £30, Asda.com). IndyBest deputy editor Sabrina Sahota reviewed Salter’s answer to Hotel Chocolat’s velvetiser and said “it’s simply much more versatile than the velvetiser, with options to make frothed milk at different consistencies for cappuccinos, lattes and more.”

Lidl

Lidl has launched its Black Friday sale, which covers home, kitchen, beauty and more, and well-known brands including the likes of Gtech and Russell Hobbs. Now, in Lidl stores, Silentnight’s mattress topper is £29.99, down from £49.99 (Lidl.co.uk). From 19 November, more deals will land at the supermarket, such as on the Remington shine therapy pro hair dryer for £16.99 (usually around £24), and the Henry xtra vacuum cleaner (was £130, now £119, Lidl.co.uk) will have £30 off.

Tesco

Tesco hasn't announced any Black Friday deals on groceries, but it has launched what it’s calling its biggest deals of the year – up to 60 per cent off in-store and up to 40 per cent off online, across home, tech and beauty. Right now, you can get £55 off a BaByliss straightener (was £90, now £35, Tesco.com). In-store, there’s 38 per cent off a Tefal flex air fryer (was £159, now £99) and 40 per cent off a Joie i-pivot car seat (was £150, now £90). There are more offers to come as the official Black Friday date nears.



Morrisons

From 16 November, prices in-store and on selected items online will be slashed by up to 67 per cent, but you’ll need a More card to access the savings. The Oral-B Pro electric toothbrush will be down to £20, while there’ll be 30 per cent off Lego sets. If you’re after a bargain on toys, electricals, beauty, home essentials, the sale could be worth a browse.

Sainsbury’s

Sainsbury’s isn’t running Black Friday offers, but there are still deals to be found. There’s 25 per cent off six or more bottles of wine, including Perrier-Jouet grand brut champagne for Nectar Card holders, and half price crowdpleasers including 1l of Baileys for £10. Tu hasn’t announced Black Friday offers but there’s up to 50 per cent off clothing at the minute.

Waitrose

Waitrose isn't taking part in Black Friday per se, but its deals on food and drink look generous. Stock up for the festive season with three for two offer on chilled party food, two for £4 on frozen Christmas veg, as well as various offers on wine & beer.

M&S

You won't see Black Friday banners at the high street stalwart, which doesn’t, officially, take part in Black Friday. However, there are nearly always offers at M&S, and November is no exception. Right now, there's up to 50 per cent off sports brands, including Adidas and Sweaty Betty, and up to 40 per cent off luggage. Get beauty gift sets, like Clinique hydration skincare gift set for men (was £117, now £55, Marksandspencer.com).



Co-op

Co-op doesn't run Black Friday sales either, but if you’re doing your weekly shop, you’ll be able to secure some generic savings on groceries, which are usually only available for Co-op members.

For more, we’ve rounded up the best supermarket Christmas food 2026

News.title: Pakistani leader and army chief speak to first astronaut aboard Chinese craft
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Pakistan’s prime minister and army chief spoke Saturday with the country’s first astronaut, who is aboard China’s space station, hailing his flight as a national achievement and a milestone in Islamabad’s close ties with longtime ally Beijing.

Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif made his remarks days after Muhammad Zeeshan Ali flew alongside Chinese astronauts Tang Hongbo and Wu Yi on the craft that blasted off from the Jiuquan Satellite Launch Center in northwestern China.

Ali is the first foreign astronaut in the history of China’s crewed space program and his flight was part of an agreement signed between Pakistan and China in February 2025. The crew will conduct more than 90 scientific experiments and technology tests during the mission.

Shehbaz Sharif and army chief Field Marshal Asim Munir spoke with Ali by video link from the headquarters of Pakistan’s space agency. "Zeeshan (Ali), it is a great day for all of us sitting here and 240 million people of Pakistan,” Sharif said in his televised remarks, as Ali stood aboard the station with a Pakistani flag on his chest.

“I extend my warmest felicitations to you on becoming the first Pakistani astronaut to orbit the Earth,” he said.

A Pakistani adventurer, Namira Salim, paid for a ticket to fly on Virgin Galactic's commercial flight in 2023, but was only in space for a matter of minutes.

Sharif said the Chinese mission opened opportunities for Pakistan’s young people in science and technology and expressed hope it would pave the way for more Pakistanis to travel to space. He thanked Chinese President Xi Jinping for making Pakistan’s participation possible and noted that the mission coincided with the 75th anniversary of diplomatic relations between the countries.

Sharif said Ali’s journey demonstrated Pakistan’s belief that outer space should be used for peaceful purposes and the benefit of humanity. “The experiments you are conducting alongside your talented Chinese brothers are not just for Pakistan; they will enrich the collective scientific knowledge of the international community,” he said.

Sharif told Ali that the entire Pakistani nation was eagerly awaiting his safe return home. The mission is due to last up to 10 days.

Munir also congratulated Ali, saying “We are really proud of you and proud of the armed forces that one of us has gone into space and achieved this great accomplishment.”

Her twins lie on a tarpaulin, floppy and listless. Speaking haltingly, Nye Bel describes how her village was attacked at night. She doesn’t know by whom.

She explains how she fled, how her husband and eldest son, Nyat, vanished in the chaos. How she survived on the kindness of others but now relies on aid.

Living in a makeshift camp in Akobo, a South Sudanese town on the eastern border with Ethiopia, she cares for her three desperate children and yearns for her missing fourth, who is just seven years old.

Nye’s pain, fear, and even moments of hope, are hers alone. But in the miserable tale of the emergence of the world’s youngest nation of South Sudan, it is a story that has been repeated countless times.

open image in gallery Villagers in New Fangak, on the White Nile, burn dung to keep flies off their cattle herds ( The Independent )

Millions in South Sudan are currently on the brink of starvation, victims of a country corrupted before conception and reliant on a dwindling supply of international aid.

Fifteen years after independence, South Sudan has earned tens of billions of dollars from oil. It should be thriving.

Yet, with near constant conflict, more than half its people are hungry and government officials haven’t been paid for more than a year.

The country is now going through its third civil war. There’s a lull in the fighting at the moment because there’s no cash for soldiers who have wandered home, often selling their rifles for food and seeds en route to their farms.

The soldiers, gunmen and tribal militia, the internal refugees and starving people are all victims of what the United Nations says South Sudan has experienced – “state capture” – where the country acts a cash-cow for a tiny section of society.

Its recent damning report concluded that South Sudan’s government has been “captured by a predatory elite that has institutionalised the systematic looting of the nation’s wealth for private gain”.

Now humanitarian agencies are warning that out of a population of nearly 12 million, 7.8 million – including two million children – face acute hunger. International donors are being asked to find hundreds of millions of dollars for emergency food.

open image in gallery Nye Bel describes how her village was attacked and she fled with three of her four children, losing her eldest son in the chaos ( Sam Kiley/The Independent )

In Akobo, there are some vital supplies for the thousands of internally displaced. But rations have been reduced due to swingeing foreign aid cuts over the past two years.

Hundreds of desperate new arrivals pour into the town every day. There are deep fears that soon the government may strike here again – maybe with air raids.

“If people are attacked again, it's going to be difficult for this vulnerable community,” says Gadmai Maban, Oxfam’s representative.

Crowds of people wait patiently to be officially registered – a means used by the UN to stop food aid being stolen and used by armed groups.

The lucky few drag sacks of the cereal grain sorgum, jerry cans of cooking oil and bags of “plumpy nut” sachets for child malnutrition into small groups for sharing out.

With rations cut, tensions are only checked by a desperation that is also shared.

Further west, the city of Malakal sits on the White Nile. An inland port, it’s a central node for the World Food Programme’s (WFP) shipping operations – and offers an opportunity for the local authorities to gouge foreign aid donations.

open image in gallery A young boy and his mother struggle to lift a bag of maize into their wheelbarrow at a distribution centre in the Bentiu internally displaced persons camp ( AFP/Getty )

The government-appointed local governor is illegally demanding VAT of at least 10 per cent on all food being shipped along the route upriver. The UN, literally, will not budge and so vast barges groaning with food aid nuzzle the city’s river banks for weeks.

Three days’ travel further upstream lies the city of Paguir, seen as a relatively safe haven from the fighting.

Growing numbers of people gather here, patiently waiting to be registered and fingerprinted, but similarly there are no food stocks to feed them.

“We don’t have enough food to give them, but we’re expecting some from Malakal,” explains Regina Muchai, the local head of Norwegian People’s Aid.

But she doesn’t know the crucial supplies are being held for ransom by the governor downstream. These self-inflicted complications make an already tricky delivery of food even harder.

open image in gallery A wounded patient receives treatment in South Sudan ( ICRC )

“We’re making really, really difficult decisions on who gets assistance. It’s like between you and me, basically deciding who’s getting food,” says Mutinta Chimuka, head of WFP in South Sudan.

“This is really a difficult situation because we’re faced with the humanitarian needs of food insecurity, but also faced with a very difficult environment that we work in.”

Such is the breakdown between internal factions that the WFP operates a specialist unit, led by a veteran of aid operations in Yemen, Iraq and Afghanistan, to negotiate “access” to allow supplies to get through.

But a belief that fixing the mess they make of their own country, and dealing with the horrors they inflict on their own people is someone else’s problem, has been baked into the minds of leaders here, on all sides, during earlier wars for independence.

In New Fangak, further along the Nile, the ethnic Shilluk militia, Agwelek, rules this hinterland. It is allied with the central government (for now). One of its commanders says, “the foreigners, the Europeans, should come back and run this place”.

All along the river, they face a real risk of flooding as the low-lying fields may soon be inundated by rising water. Dikes need to be dug to protect the villages, but local officials say they are “waiting for the WFP” to organise the work.

open image in gallery Volunteers in Kadet, along the White Nile, dig mud from the flooded fields to build dikes to protect their villages ( The Independent )

“We have renovated the previous dike that was constructed by WFP. We are still working on it, but we don’t know what will happen next. We depend on WFP and other NGOs that are helping us,” says humanitarian worker Riek Gatjiak.

“But surely it would be better for South Sudan to have a government that can use the oil money and the other revenues to build a dike for Fangak?” I ask.

“It could be good, but I don’t know where the money is,” he replies, with a nervous laugh.

The UN and International Committee of the Red Cross are wise to the jostling between governments and rebels. Both humanitarian groups refuse to pay customs duty, allow no graft, but can do little to stop the fighting.

Until recently, foreign aid organisations kept out of politics and clung to the “humanitarian imperative” to help, no matter the cost.

Food and fuel, money for logistics and other aid sent into southern Sudan through the 1980s and 1990s was mostly “diverted” by the rebels and used to fund their independence war against the north.

Meanwhile, the rebel southern Sudanese forces, and various militia, also didn’t think about the consequences of their internecine wars for the general population. It was assumed these people were not the responsibility of their leaders.

Civilians, women and children, teachers, nurses, doctors, were the burden that should be, and was, carried by foreigners – the “international community”.

open image in gallery A woman carries a fish as she walks near Kadet, on the White Nile ( The Independent )

And this remains a core belief within the elite running South Sudan now. The Independent approached government authorities multiple times but received no response.

The excoriating report from the UN is clear about the impact of the wealthy skimming off resources.

It said: “While a small group of powerful actors pillage and loot the country’s wealth and resources, enriching themselves, the state has effectively abdicated its sovereign responsibilities to its population, outsourcing critical services — such as the provision of food, healthcare, and education to international donors.

“This abandonment of duty has left the population at the mercy of volatile and insufficient humanitarian aid.”

Britain and the US have concluded much the same. Both have cut back on aid worldwide in the last two years.

In the long term that may be one solution, but for now it is a disaster for the 7.8 million South Sudanese going dangerously hungry.

News.title: Clashes erupt in Albania's capital as protesters call for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Clashes broke out Saturday between police and protesters in the Albanian capital, Tirana, as thousands of people called for the resignation of Prime Minister Edi Rama, the latest in a long series of anti-government protests.

The protest began peacefully, but small groups of masked demonstrators broke away and began smashing the windows of ministry buildings along the march route. Some protesters hurled Molotov cocktails.

Police used tear gas and water cannons to push back groups of protesters throwing rocks and using wooden sticks to try to smash street cameras and windows on government buildings.

Clouds of tear gas billowed through the area as police attempted to disperse groups of protesters that spread out across several streets.

Albanians traveled to Tirana from across the country and abroad for the rally, which coincided with the 114th anniversary of the country's declaration of independence, a day normally marked by national celebrations and a public holiday. Police were deployed along the main roads leading in and out of the capital, conducting vehicle checks.

“I came here specifically for the protest,” said Arian Lleshi, a 33-year-old who traveled to Tirana from the United Kingdom. “Why? Because we have been suffering for far too long. We have spread ourselves across Europe and around the world, and it is almost as if we are citizens without a state. We are like stateless citizens.”

The political parties that have been around in Albania since the fall of communism in the 1990s “no longer represent anyone,” Lleshi said. “They need to make way for a new generation of intellectuals and people who have a greater stake in the country’s future.”

Saturday’s protest was part of a series of demonstrations that began in late May, initially sparked by opposition to a major luxury tourism development on Albania’s southern coast that is linked to an investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, U.S. President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

The protests became known as the Flamingo movement and were later followed by student demonstrations in September, many of which turned violent, with students calling for better education and living standards. The demonstrators' main demand has since broadened to include calls for Rama's resignation.

Protesters chanted “Resignation!” as they gathered in Tirana’s main Skanderbeg Square.

“We have come out to demand our rights. We have had enough. Life has become very difficult. We are calling for a change to the entire system,” student Juna Vasili said.

Resident Suzana Gjeta, a retiree, said that she was demonstrating both on behalf of young people and those like herself “who are living on just 120 euros a month. We hope this system will go, that Edi Rama will go, and that this corruption will end,” she said.

___

Elena Becatoros contributed to this report from Athens, Greece.
