Sports.title: Remarkable moment ashamed Southampton boss Tonda Eckert removes a box of tissues from his press conference: Manager left furious at his own club for lack of 'class' in bitter win over Spygate rivals Middlesbrough
Sports.content:
Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has insisted taunts aimed at Middlesbrough 'don't come from me' after the Championship club targeted their rivals in their first meeting since the Spygate saga.

The club conducted themselves disgracefully in a bitter reunion six months on from their ejection from last season’s play-off final.

Daily Mail Sport asked Eckert about a series of provocative gestures around the fixture and whether he needed to remind the club to keep it classy ahead of future matches with Middlesbrough.

A mortified Eckert removed a box of tissues from the press conference podium when they were highlighted by Daily Mail Sport.

The tissues were an apparent reference to Middlesbrough boss Kim Hellberg crying in his press conference at Southampton last season when Boro lost in the play-offs semi-final before being reinstated.

‘I hope everyone who came here from the Middlesbrough staff knows that these things don't come from me,' Eckert said after removing the box of tissues, having stared at them for 20 seconds.

#SaintsFC boss Tonda Eckert removes a box of tissues from the desk during his post-match press conference 🤧



After their 2-0 win over leaders Middlesbrough, Eckert insists he just wants to focus on the football ⚽️



Get more recation on BBC sounds 😇👇https://t.co/StIk7i3ZGg pic.twitter.com/eo6BRETKeW — BBC Radio Solent Sport (@solentsport) November 28, 2026

Southampton head coach Tonda Eckert has insisted taunts aimed at Middlesbrough 'don't come from me' after the Championship club targeted their rivals over the Spygate saga

Hellberg cried in his press conference at Southampton last season and a box of tissues were shamelessly added to the podium in the press conference room after Friday's match

‘Everything you do in defeat and if you win you do in class and I try to do that. I hope that there's an appreciation that this doesn't come from me.’

Saints beat Middlesbrough in last season’s play-off semi-final but were booted out by the EFL four days before the final after Daily Mail Sport revealed Southampton had sent their very own Johnny English to spy on Boro’s training sessions.

Both managers called for an armistice before the match but that memo clearly hadn't reached the Southampton marketing team, who posted an inflammatory video on social media.

The uncouth 79-second film mocked Boro, with the narrator declaring, ‘they got another go, their story continued’ over footage of Oli McBurnie’s winning goal for Hull City in the play-off final was also projected onto the big screen just eight minutes before kick-off.

'I didn't like the video this morning,’ Eckert said. If we look back a couple of months, the reality is both clubs have lost.

‘One club has lost off the pitch, and the other club has lost on the pitch. It’s an episode that is good to close for both clubs to move forward.

‘It’s time to move on at one point. For me, that episode from last year is closed. I've apologised. I've apologised to Kim (Hellberg). I've invited him for a drink. I just hope that we can do everything we do with class.'

Southampton won their first meeting since the Spygate scandal by earning a 2-0 win over their rivals, which included an on-pitch flare up between the sides.

Even Tonda Eckert is genuinely fed up of Southampton Football Club. pic.twitter.com/NjKZyQvDTi — Boropolis (@Boropolis) November 28, 2026

Southampton's Finn Azaz mocked Middlesbrough's fans by pretending to cry after scoring

His celebration - in their first meeting since last season's 'Spygate' - sparked a brawl, with Azaz being booked

Southampton's Ryan Manning was seen celebrating their second goal with a pair of binoculars

Manning appeared to have picked up binoculars that had been thrown onto the pitch

Ryan Manning tucked James Bree’s cutback past Radek Vitek on 59 minutes to open the scoring for Saints before attacker Finn Azaz brought the contest to boiling point.

The former Boro forward scored Southampton’s second goal late on and then ran the length of the pitch to goad the away supporters by pretending to cry.

It sparked a fracas as Azaz and Will Lankshear – who wasn’t even at Boro last season when tensions were at their highest between the clubs – squared up, while travelling fans tried to get over the barricade.

Speaking after the match, Azaz said: 'They sang about me home and away last season, so I was just waiting for my moment to get one back. I have no regrets whatsoever.'

Manning was also pictured celebrating Southampton's second goal by looking through a pair of binoculars that appeared to have been thrown onto the pitch.

Binoculars had been handed out to Middlesbrough supporters prior to the match.

In a bitter reunion, Manning tucked James Bree’s neat cutback past Radek Vitek on 58 minutes before Azaz added a second as Southampton remained unbeaten at home in ten months. Saints, though, were needlessly provocative throughout.

The scenes calmed post-match but Southampton’s off-field operation humiliated the club – taking their celebration too far.

Binoculars had been handed out to Middlesbrough fans prior to the match at St Mary's

The Spygate saga was referenced by fans of both clubs around Friday night's clash

Southampton also reminded Hellberg of his tears following their play-off by playing Oasis' Stop Crying Your Heart Out over the speakers. Throughout the match, the Saints fans sang: 'We saw you cry on the telly.'

Hellberg added: 'In general, those who show more emotions and stand up for what is right are brave people. Hiding behind people and being afraid of emotions, that's the problem we have in the world a little bit.

'We have to hide from everything, how people are feeling, mental health and everything. It’s important we stand up for that – I'm not afraid of showing feelings.'

Considering Southampton started this season on minus four points for the breaches, their supporters’ staggering endorsement of the cheating was as indiscreet as the espionage itself.

‘We’ll spy when we want,’ sang the Southampton fans – a reminder of when their spy kid tried to conceal himself behind a tree near Middlesbrough’s training ground to film their training session. The EFL discovered three further spying missions on investigation.

Southampton fully embraced their cheats tag as they claimed three points, responding to chants of ‘you cheating b*******, you know what you are’ with sarcastic applause.

Victory moves Saints within four points of Middlesbrough, who remain top of the table going into the weekend but could slip down as far as fifth. Sadly, that was overshadowed by their crass conduct.

Sports.title: The Premier League's great shinpad scourge: How rise in footballers using 'sim card' size guards has left fans fuming and youngsters at risk of serious injury
Sports.content:
Is it woke nonsense that footballers wear shin pads with the size and protective capacity of a custard cream? Forget VAR, forget half-and-half scarfs, forget thirsty Gianni Infantino's drinks breaks, forget teenage tacticos lecturing you about 'pausa' on TikTok - the great shin pad debate has struck 'The Game's Gone' chord and divided fans. Recent footage of Newcastle's Matias Fernandez-Pardo pulling down his socks to reveal a thin pink foam disk, caused a stir. 'It's a sim card! It's a sanitary product! He's on £100,000-a-week, the club shouldn't pay him if he snaps his leg in half! - The complaints poured in but Fernandez-Pardo is not alone. In fact he's in the majority, with 6ft 7in Dan Burn one of the few team-mates to wear old school shin guards or 'cricket pads', as he's called them. Burn does not lack for shin. Peter Crouch was another with proportions from the Cretaceous period to choose a bulkier protector but most current forwards, wingers in particular, favour the barely-there pads and those of a certain generation wince at the sight. Matias Fernandez-Pardo shows his tiny shin pads (left) - The modern trend is in stark contrast to Peter Crouch's heavy duty option when he played (right) For most who have played the game at an amateur standard, those medieval battle-ready Sondico shin pads with ankle protectors were the norm. When the village meathead with the turning circle of Pavarotti is making it his mission to fill the local A&E department on a Sunday, that makes sense. Brave? Stupid? Complacent? Or all in the aid of performance? Plenty of the criticism of modern pros centres on the supposedly heightened risk of a horrific injury. The number of broken legs in the Premier League has declined over the past 15 years. Eduardo, Aaron Ramsey, Hatem Ben Arfa and Bobby Zamora all suffered agonising lower-leg fractures between 2006-2010. Crucially, the officiating since then has evolved. Two-footed lunges, studs-up challenges and sliding in from behind will get you sent off and even if the referee doesn't pull the trigger, VAR is primed to jump in. Leg breaks, from a direct impact on the shin at least, are a rarity now and damage is more likely to be cosmetic. Players are happy to risk cuts and scrapes to avoid wearing cumbersome pads that they feel are limiting. Top orthopedic sport surgeon, Dr David Abbasi, who runs his own clinic Prime Ortho Center and works cageside for UFC fights, told the Daily Mail: 'The problem with miniature shin pads is that they leave a significant portion of the leg’s tibia bone exposed to direct impact. 'Properly sized firmer shin pads provide greater coverage and help absorb forces from kicks, reducing the risk of painful bone contusions, lacerations and potentially fractures. 'From an orthopedic standpoint, smaller pads compromise protection for comfort. For youth players with less kick accuracy, I would definitely recommend the regular shin pads.' The miniature ones are perfectly legal. The official rule (4.2) gives plenty of wiggle room - failing to specify a certain size, shape or material shin pads have to conform to. And referees are only obliged to check that 'something' is being worn. Even that low-level of scrutiny can be tricky for officials, with Hull's Sorba Thomas seen on Sky Sports last weekend trying to convince the fourth official he was wearing protection. He gestured to his low-cut socks, incredulously pointing at an outline akin to a communion wafer. "They're almost like sim card size!" Sorba Thomas was held back from coming on for an issue with his socks! pic.twitter.com/kqR6wXnK0b — Sky Sports Premier League (@SkySportsPL) November 22, 2026 Tackles like this one from James Tarkowski on Yehor Yarmolyuk, for which he received a red card, are more severely punished now Phi Foden is one of many players to have personalised shin pads worn in sock sleeves Increasingly, the safety element has taken a backseat to aesthetic. Shin pads have become customised, monetised and personalised. If the traditionalists were annoyed before, wait until Chloe Kelly shows them the dog photo on hers. Aston Villa and Germany midfielder Leon Goretzka chose a topless picture of himself, flexing with the Champions League trophy during his Bayern Munich days. Phil Foden has a cartoon impression of a family photo, while others have sponsors, religious iconography or inspirational messages written on theirs. Some players have even pulled them out as a prop for goal celebrations. Shin pads have been around since 1874, when Sam Weller Widdowson cut down his cricket pads and stuck them down his socks while playing for Nottingham Forest. It quickly caught on but 152 years later, form is beating function. Top players viewing shin pads with a lofty level of disdain rather than useful safeguard can have dangerous consequences for young, impressionable players who want to mirror their heroes. David Platt holds up his shin pad alongside Gary Lineker after England beat Cameroon in 1990 Leon Goretzka (left) had a picture of himself topless on his own shin pads while on Germany duty Two years ago, a 15-year-old turning out for Penistone Church, a team from Barnsley in South Yorkshire, suffered a gruesome double leg break while wearing tiny 3cm by 9cm shin pads. He broke his tibular and fibula and later told the BBC: 'It’s not worth the extra bit of speed to have you knocked out of football for months and months. It’s not worth the risk. 'They were the most pathetic shin pads you've ever seen. Take a step back and look at the potential consequences of wearing them, and think, are they really worth it?' Alfie broke his leg in what the club described as a fair 50/50 duel with no malicious intent from the opponent. Top footballers playing in high stakes, strictly regulated games on the best surfaces with sports science behind them are clearly less exposed to risk than Sunday league players. Also, the need for marginal gains is so much greater as players and teams seek any conceivable edge to performance in the professional game. Trends inevitably filter downwards and grassroots players could heed the warning of Virgil van Dijk, one of the last of the dwindling 'proper' shin pad brigade. 'If you get kicked on your shin and your shin pad is that size of an AirPod, then obviously that's a big problem', the Liverpool skipper warned. Virgil van Dijk is one of the few players who still wear larger protective shin pads Luka Modric kisses the image of his children on his shin pad before coming on The science tends to back him up. A 2018 peer-reviewed study by the National Library of Medicine retrieved data over 25 years in Dutch hospital A&E departments, before and after the law to wear shin pads at all levels was brought in. They found: 'The incidence of lower leg football injuries decreased significantly following the introduction of the shin guard law (1996-2000: -20%; 2001-2005: -25%), whereas the incidence of all other football injuries did not.' But the severity of those injuries varies and there's dubious evidence that shin pads are effective at stopping broken legs. The bone tends to snap when studs are planted in the turf, rather than through a massive direct impact. Whether players reach for the carbon fiber or custard cream option is ultimately a personal decision. But those who hobble their way to the hospital waiting room having chosen the latter might find sympathy in short supply.

Sports.title: Inside Stoke City's turnaround under Mark Robins: How they cleansed 'toxic' dressing room, the medical guru who stopped their injury crisis, a transfer expert armed with Brighton's secrets - and why they won't fall away like last season
Sports.content:
Stoke City have been here before. They know how it feels to be among the pace-setters, striding towards the place where they once belonged. They know, too, how easy it is to fall away. At this stage last season, their first full campaign under Mark Robins, they sat second in the Championship. Would it be their year, a return to the top flight after seven years away, seven years in which they had finished in the bottom half of the Championship every season? It would not. They won three of their last 20 matches, none of their last six, and ended up 17th. Victory for Stoke – who finished in the top half of the Premier League for three seasons in a row in the 2010s, remember – over Millwall on Wednesday night, their fifth on the bounce, sees them second again. Beat West Ham this weekend, who haven't won in six, and it's time to dream. Will this be their year? Before a ball was kicked, Opta’s supercomputer had Stoke as the most likely team to be relegated. Robins, however, said things ‘felt different’. Speaking to those around the club this week, there’s a genuine belief they are. Not that anyone would have thought it three months ago, when a 4-1 thumping at Wolves – a third straight defeat to start the season – left them bottom. Club bosses wondered whether a change might be needed. The mood in the stands was starting to shift. There had been little appetite to sack Robins in the summer, but now the questions of whether they made the right call crossed a few minds. Despite a dismal end to last season, and a poor start to this, Stoke stuck with boss Mark Robins - a decision that is paying off Jack McGlynn leads the celebrations during Stoke's 2-1 victory over Millwall in midweek. They sit second in the Championship

Your browser does not support iframes.

After spending £30million on players over the summer, selling them the vision of what the club was building under Robins, it was felt sacking him before the window had even closed would be a dreadful look. Stoke stuck by Robins, beat Norwich on deadline day in a gutsy backs-to-the-wall performance, and haven’t looked back since. One thing that did change after the Wolves defeat, even if it wasn't the manager, was the formation. Sorba Thomas, the club’s leading scorer last season, was sold to Hull for £8million. Not only did it allow Robins to cash in on a player who made it clear he wanted to leave, but also to switch to a wing-back system that now gets the best out of the squad. Robins and sporting director, Jon Walters, the former Stoke striker who felt the brunt of fan frustration following their collapse last term, have gone about building a club and culture that can finally succeed. The past few seasons have been spent shipping out plenty of rubbish and bringing in players with the right character and mentality. Insiders talk about how ‘toxic’ the dressing room was just a couple of years ago, and how the standards set were ‘ridiculously low’. A staggering injury crisis helped wreck their promotion hopes last season, so this summer the club revamped the entire medical department. Damian Roden, the head of sports science during their Premier League days, returned as head of medical and performance. The club’s Premier League heroes of yesteryear, the likes of Ryan Shawcross and Robert Huth, have hailed Roden as one of the key factors in them finishing ninth three times on the spin under Mark Hughes. Roden’s periodisation model, which adjusts training volume and intensity to keep players at their freshest for match day, underpins Stoke’s weekly schedule. He’s been joined in the medical bay by Matt Ratcliffe and Mark Sertori, who spent more than a decade at Manchester City and was recently head performance for Roma. So far, Stoke have only had a couple of muscle injuries. John Coates, Stoke's owner (left), and sporting director Jon Walters have found a formula that is working as the club chase a return to the Premier League George Hirst scores the second of two goals against Millwall. The son of Sheffield Wednesday legend David has been working with Robins, a former striker, on his finishing The change in the Football League’s financial restrictions from the old-school Profit & Sustainability Rules, which capped losses over a rolling three-year period, to the new Squad Cost Ratio that allows clubs to spend a percentage of their revenue, has been a gamechanger for the Potters. Suddenly, the shackles are off. Stoke have an owner in John Coates who puts in as much money as they can. They recently opened a new £12m first-team building at their Clayton Wood training ground, which boasts a gym, swimming pool, hydrotherapy and cryotherapy suites and a tactics room for video analysis. Now, they can spend on the squad too without worrying about being hamstrung by losses from previous years. They hope to bring in more players in January. The squad value has soared from around £30m a few years ago to more than £100m now. Stoke are also finally starting to reap the rewards of their bespoke data-led recruitment model, following in the footsteps of Brighton and Brentford. Like those two clubs, Stoke’s owner Coates – son of Peter, who co-founded bet365 – has vast experience in the gambling industry. Their head of recruitment Ian Torrance helped set up Southampton’s ‘Black Box’ scouting database and used data from Tony Bloom’s Jamestown Analytics during his time at Italian side Como. Nearly all their signings this summer have hit the ground running. Ethan Galbraith, brought in from Swansea in a deal worth up to £10m, already looks like one of the best midfielders in the Championship. Jack McGlynn, one of two players signed from the MLS alongside Luca Bombino, has been another revelation in midfield and already has five league goals. Justin Devenny brings Premier League experience from Crystal Palace. Defender Luke Graham, snaffled from Dundee for £2m, has been a rock at the back and has earned his first Scotland call-up. Former captain and centre back Shawcross, one of Robins’ first-team coaches, has worked extensively with Graham, analysing video clips. Ethan Galbraith, brought in from Swansea in a deal worth up to £10m, already looks like one of the best midfielders in the Championship McGlynn, signed from the MLS, has been another revelation in midfield Robins, a former Manchester United front man, has been doing one-to-one work with striker George Hirst, who joined for an initial £6m from Ipswich. That’s paying off, too. Hirst scored the winner against Birmingham last weekend and both goals against Millwall in midweek. Stoke paid compensation to hire Arsenal Under 21s coach Max Porter, who helped bring through Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri and Max Dowman with the Gunners. He is in charge of how Stoke move the ball in possession – and appears to be doing a fine job. The big question, especially after last season’s tail-off, is whether they can sustain this form. Stoke are, on the face of it, overperforming their underlying numbers. Opta’s expected table, which calculates where a side should be based on their expected goals (xG), has Stoke 16th. The feeling inside the club, however, is that in games where Stoke took an early lead and looked to defend it, it was always likely their opponents would rack up shots and xG. If you look at Stoke’s rolling xG average, too, Robins’ side are starting to consistently create more than their opponents. Even if they were getting lucky earlier in the season, they aren’t anymore. Their first-half performance against fellow promotion chasers Birmingham was hailed by those inside the club as the best Stoke have played in years.

Your browser does not support iframes.

No goalkeeper has kept as many clean sheets as Viktor Johansson, one of the most reliable stoppers in the division Insiders feel the squad now has the depth to deal with any injuries that do come their way. Midfielder Djibril Soumare came off against Birmingham and is expected to be out for a while but they have plenty of cover. Galbraith missed two games and Stoke won them both. Fans, for the first time in years, are going into matches expecting to win. They have one of the meanest defences in the Championship. No goalkeeper has kept as many clean sheets as Viktor Johansson, one of the most reliable stoppers in the division. Stoke’s realistic aim is to finish in the play-offs. They have 35 points so far and know the average to finish in the top eight is around 69. It would need near-relegation form not to achieve that from their last 29 games. Stoke have been here before. This time it feels different.

Sports.title: Cruel Xabi Alonso threw poor Wesley Fofana to the lions by starting him: Chelsea boss was as much at fault as his liability of a defender - and he is risking losing the fans with his baffling decisions, writes KIERAN GILL
Sports.content:
We know what Chelsea’s fans thought of Wesley Fofana starting. Whenever he had the ball, boos spilled out of the away end, and a few times, there was one song filling the City Ground.

‘F*** off Fofana, you’re not wanted here,’ it went. It started from the first minute, but was at its loudest when he bundled over Liam Delap for Nottingham Forest's penalty for 2-0 and then when he was put out of his misery after 56 minutes, substituted for Levi Colwill.

As much as it was on Fofana – after that unauthorised interview in which he laughed off his penalty miss which confirmed their Carabao Cup exit to Liverpool, showing nowhere near the winning mentality these fans expect within their club – it was also on his manager Xabi Alonso.

It was the easy decision to drop Fofana. It was there, staring at Alonso. Poor performances have become the norm from the 25-year-old Frenchman this season. Against Leeds. Against Liverpool. Against Manchester United. Chelsea’s £75million defender was a liability against them all.

Then he handed his manager another reason to leave him out of his starting line-up with that interview conducted behind his club’s back. Fofana made a few faux pas in it, not least by mentioning how he was advised that he still had so much money to make out of his £200,000-per-week contract when he considered quitting football. But had Alonso listened to it, he would have also heard how Fofana’s mental health suffered while he was trying to battle back from his injury hell.

Xabi Alonso's decision to start Wesley Fofana was cruel - and the defender returned a mistake-addled performance

Fofana fouled Liam Delap to give away a penalty on another night of chaos for Chelsea

Yet Chelsea’s manager exposed him here. Cruelly, we could even say, after what turned into an excruciating experience for Fofana. Alonso must have known he might be subjected to such abuse. It was surely flagged by someone inside of the club as a risk.

Alonso cannot blame starting Fofana on having no other options at centre back. The very fact he used Moises Caicedo in central defence in the place of Colwill showed it could be done. That was a problem in itself, taking Chelsea’s best midfielder out of where they needed him most.

And so, Fofana started, struggled, heard the abuse, made a mess of one long ball and then tripped Delap. With that, Chelsea were two goals down, and on their way to a fourth defeat in five league games. Alonso was noncommittal when asked how on earth he could use Fofana again after this, but it is hard to see how he can start when Crystal Palace visit Stamford Bridge on Wednesday.

Alonso has now overseen the same number of Premier League losses as the sacked Liam Rosenior – six – but in fewer games managed – 12 to his predecessor’s 13.

Chelsea’s manager is making problems for himself amid it all. By starting Fofana. By selecting Danny Welbeck over Emmanuel Emegha. By not bringing on Estevao when the away end were singing the substitute’s name while Chelsea were already trailing by two goals.

Alonso was wrong to start Danny Welbeck and wrong to put Moises Caicedo at centre-back

Alonso’s decisions and his declining to explain them afterwards brought to mind that scene from Moneyball. The one where Billy Beane (played by Brad Pitt) is telling Peter Brand (Jonah Hill): ‘It's a problem that you think we need to explain ourselves. Don't. To anyone.’

Yet sometimes, an explanation would help. Alonso was asked at his post-match press conference to tell us his tactical thinking behind Fofana over Colwill. He did not, instead saying: ‘It's always the best tactical decisions approaching each game and today that was my decision.’

It is not the first time he has been unwilling or unable to articulate the reasoning behind one of his bold calls, and that is an issue for the fans who are quickly losing their faith.

After full-time, Alonso stood in front of the away end at the City Ground and stared, presumably to take his medicine after orchestrating this latest Premier League loss.

Imagine you are Delap, Igor Jesus or Morgan Gibbs-White. You see Chelsea have named their centre backs as Fofana and Caicedo. You are happy with that.

Then imagine you are James McAtee or Xaver Schlager. You see Chelsea have taken Caicedo out of their midfield and added in Jordan Henderson next to Romeo Lavia. You are happy with that.

Then imagine you are Jair Cunha, Nikola Milenkovic or Murillo. You see Chelsea have selected Welbeck, 36, rather than the unpredictable and enthusiastic Emegha, 23. You are happy with that.

Emmanuel Emegha was a bright spot for Chelsea, coming off the bench to score twice

Forest's players can only have fancied their chances from the moment they saw what the opposition was putting up, and Alonso’s selections facilitated that optimism. The fact that Welbeck was hooked at half-time told us he knew he got it wrong. Emegha was introduced and scored twice, becoming the first substitute to be involved in a goal for Chelsea this season and adding to the goal he scored in their 4-1 loss to Leeds from last weekend.

It was Emegha who gave his side a fighting chance while Cole Palmer put in yet another anonymous performance and with Morgan Rogers joining him on this occasion.

Tactically, Alonso cannot hide from these bad showings. We see clearer patterns in Jackson Pollock paintings. Chelsea tried three different set-piece routines from the training ground here, as if they needed an alternative way to try to get a goal because they have been so unthreatening from open play of late. None of Austin MacPhee’s wacky ideas worked here.

But Palmer is letting his club down especially, having only signed his new contract until 2034 last month. Perhaps he is now too comfortable with that tidy bump.

Sports.title: There's a convenient ignorance in the new Tyson Fury documentary. This is what they've chosen to hide, and what it reveals about Netflix's cynical relationship with reality, writes OLIVER HOLT
Sports.content:
There's a convenient ignorance in the new Tyson Fury documentary. This is what they've chosen to hide, and what it reveals about Netflix's cynical relationship with reality, writes OLIVER HOLT

Oliver Holt Chief Sports Writer

There are some affecting and moving moments in Tyson Fury, the documentary about a part of the fighter’s career which, conveniently, does not include any defeats, does not mention the fact that he served a backdated two-year drugs ban after he first won the world heavyweight title in 2015 and skims quickly over his predilection for homophobia and misogyny.

Fury’s wife, Paris, emerges from the 103-minute film as the hero of the piece, a strong, funny, clever, caring, emotionally intelligent woman who held her family together as her husband struggled with mental health issues and she tried to cope with the trauma of giving birth to a stillborn child.

Her relationship with Fury is everything that is good about the film, which was released on Netflix on Friday morning.

It is a fascinating study of the fighter, too. Or at least of the parts we are allowed to see. We are not allowed to see wrongdoing or cruelty or ridicule or bullying but we are allowed to see vulnerability.

We are allowed to see a fighting man who has a recurring dream about seeing a slow-motion plane crash and realising too late that the plane is heading straight for him and that there is nothing he can do to escape the fireball.

Any analysis of Tyson Fury – or what was left of it after some feverish last-minute editing removed all references to a diagnosis of schizophrenia that had been eagerly trailed in the build-up to its release – has to begin and end with the fact that it is more of an exercise in public relations and promotion for his fight against Anthony Joshua next month than an examination of a career in full. It is a long, long way from the unvarnished truth and that makes it average.

The Tyson Fury documentary is a fascinating study of the fighter. Or at least of the parts we are allowed to see

Fury’s wife, Paris, emerges from the 103-minute film as the hero of the piece, a strong, funny, clever, caring, emotionally intelligent woman who held her family together

Its most chilling episode is the aftermath of Fury's victory over Wladimir Klitschko in Dusseldorf in November 2015 when Fury falls into an agony of self-loathing.

He sits on a stage promoting a rematch that never happened, taking off his shirt and parading his bloated body to the cameras, saying that he hates everything about boxing and wondering aloud whether Klitschko will do him a favour by ‘knocking me into next week’.

‘I do not care about anything or anybody,’ he says in that clip.

And on the stage beside him and in the audience in front of him, people laugh heartily and people smile nervously and by then Fury knows he may face drugs charges because he has tested positive for the anabolic steroid nandrolone.

But the film does not tell us that. It does not explore what effect that might have had on Fury’s mental state. It does not explore quite how much of an advantage using the drug gave him over opponents.

The film's ethos raises more questions about just how far companies like Netflix are prepared to go to manipulate the image of sportsmen and women whose stories they are telling and selling. Partly because of the late panic about the mention of a schizophrenia diagnosis and its subsequent excision from the film, the line between where truth begins and ends feels thoroughly blurred by the time the credits roll.

Let’s be honest about this: the film was partly sold to the public on the back of that claim that Fury had been diagnosed with schizophrenia – as well as bipolar disorder, anxiety, depression, ADHD and OCD – some months after the 2015 world title victory over Klitschko in Germany.

That was how it was trailed. That was what garnered many of the headlines. It was not until Daily Mail Sport’s Jeff Powell MBE broke the story that the British Boxing Board of Control might not let the fight go ahead if it believed Fury was suffering from the illness or any lingering psychosis that the mention of schizophrenia was edited out of the scenes.

Fury will finally step into a ring with Anthony Joshua next month. And the primary purpose of the documentary is to advertise the fight

'Only one thing is certain,' Board general secretary Robert Smith had said on Thursday afternoon. 'That Tyson will not be allowed to enter the ring unless our doctors are satisfied there is no risk to his health.

'We are reviewing all the information about his mental condition and will come to a decision about authorising the fight in the next few days.'

Netflix, whose broadcast of the Joshua-Fury fight represents a leap forward in their move into boxing and live sport in general, sensed a clear and present danger to their investment, a danger that they had brought upon themselves.

It was not long before there was a statement. There had been a mistake. Fury had never been diagnosed with schizophrenia after all and everything was fine now. Nothing to see here.

And so, on Friday morning, once Tyson Fury had been aired without any mention of schizophrenia at all, the BBBofC released a statement, too. ‘Tyson Fury has been cleared to box on December 11,’ it said. Sighs of relief all round. Whatever you do, don’t mention the schizophrenia.

It may have been a blip in the promotion, which will ramp up as the fight gets closer, but the episode shone a light on Netflix and its coverage of sport as it seeks to move further and further into the arena. At the heart of its coverage, there is a contradiction that is also a flaw.

Much of its selling point is to show the viewer things they have not seen before, to take them behind the scenes of a sport and allow them to get to know the combatants more closely than ever. It is part of what has made Drive to Survive, their F1 behind-the-scenes documentary, so stunningly successful.

But Drive to Survive only shows you what F1 wants you to see. It’s an official version. It’s varnished.

The Netflix cameras chase Adrian Newey and Christian Horner through the paddock in filming for an episode of Drive to Survive

The inconvenient stuff, the anabolic steroids, the stuff that might harm the product? That is nowhere. That does not even get a mention in the Fury documentary

And the Tyson Fury documentary carries exactly the same vibe. The inconvenient stuff, the anabolic steroids, the stuff that might harm the product? That is nowhere. That does not even get a mention.

‘People in the boxing world just wanted to use me,’ Fury says in the documentary as he looks back at the time of his gravest battle with mental illness.

Until late on Thursday night, schizophrenia was being used to plug one of his fights. Boxing has always been a dark trade so cynicism is greeted with a shrug.

Some things have changed since Fury fought Klitschko in 2015, some faces are different and there is a new broadcaster, or streamer, in town. But some things remain the same.

Sports.title: Tyson Fury's warning to son Prince, 15, as teenager begins boxing career TONIGHT - as heavyweight star reveals why he will 'NEVER' coach his kids
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury's warning to son Prince, 15, as teenager begins boxing career TONIGHT - as heavyweight star reveals why he will 'NEVER' coach his kids

Tyson Fury has warned his son Prince that he must be prepared to make enormous sacrifices if they are serious about following him into boxing.

Prince, 15, as well as his younger brother Tyson Jr, 10, will both step into the ring for the first time on Saturday, with the former two-time heavyweight world champion admitting there will inevitably be added scrutiny on the pair because of their famous surname.

But Fury, who is currently training for his December showdown with Anthony Joshua, will be watching from afar and is determined that his sons understand the sacrifices required to succeed, having dedicated almost four decades of his own life to boxing.

'It's definitely a job of sacrifice, dedication and commitment, and years upon years upon years of doing the same old stuff,' told the Daily Mail in an interview with Netflix ahead of the release of his new documentary, TYSON FURY.

'I'm necking on 40 years old. I've been doing it since I've been a child. I had no childhood. I had no teenage years. I had no early adult years.

'It is a lonely sport, and if it doesn't go well for you, then you do feel like you've been mistreated sometimes. For all these like boxers that I've known who haven't really done that that well, but committed a full lifetime to it anyway it's really hard.

Prince Fury, 15, (pictured above) and his younger brother Tyson Jr, 10, will both step into the ring for the first time on Saturday

View this post on Instagram

'So my boys need to really want it if they're going to be in this game, and I have told them that. They've said they're sure this is what they want at the moment, so I am just supporting that.'

The Gypsy King also knows better than most the expectations that come with being a member of the Fury family.

He has previously spoken about wanting his children to forge their own identities rather than feel obliged to replicate his achievements. But with two of his sons now preparing to make their amateur debuts, the spotlight is already beginning to find them.

'Prince is boxing on Saturday, and so is my other son, Tyson is boxing too,' he said. 'There will no doubt be a lot of eyes and opinions on them because they are my sons.

'At the end of the day, it's an amateur boxing match. I just told them to enjoy it, do the best you can, and that's it. And if you're meant to win, you win. If you don't, no problem. Dust yourself off and try again.

'They shouldn't have the pressure of the Gypsy King's crown on them now.'

The boys' interest in boxing has already featured in Netflix's At Home With The Furys, with viewers given an insight into Prince's early ambitions and the family's relationship with the sport.

The brothers have been training alongside their father since 2023, but their first competitive outings will come under the guidance of Manx ABC head coach Peter Roberts.

View this post on Instagram

Tyson Fury says he has no interest in overseeing his sons' boxing careers as a coach

Prince, who recently turned 15, will compete in the 13th bout of a 17-fight show at the Villa Marina in Douglas, Isle of Man. He is matched against an opponent representing the Merseyside and Cheshire team, with the individual opponent yet to be publicly named. His younger brother, known as Tutty, will take part in an unscored skills bout.

Fury, meanwhile, is preparing for his December 11 showdown with Joshua and is currently training in Miami, meaning he is unlikely to be ringside for his sons' first appearances.

After almost a decade of failed negotiations, it was Saudi Arabia's Turki Alalshikh who finally helped turn the long-discussed prospect of Fury facing Joshua into a reality.

Alalshikh has also ensured the blockbuster showdown will take place on British soil, bringing the two heavyweight rivals to Cardiff in front of their home fans.

The blockbuster showdown will be broadcast live globally on Netflix, marking another major moment in the streaming giant's growing investment in live boxing.

And while the former world champion has spent years mastering the art of boxing, he has no intention of becoming his children's trainer.

'I don't really train the boys, and I never want to. I'm not a boxing trainer. And I don't think that father-son training dynamic works,' he explained.

'I'm a boxing performer, not a boxing trainer. I think people underestimate the job of a boxing trainer. It's like babysitting. It's a full-time job, and you've got to be a jobsworth and take it home with you because a lot of these fighters need adult supervision.

After almost a decade of failed negotiations, it was Saudi Arabia's Turki Alalshikh (middle) who finally helped turn the long-discussed prospect of Fury facing Joshua into a reality

'I've got enough children to look after without taking on any more through my job.'

Instead, Fury leaves the work to the coaches at their local gyms, insisting they deserve the credit for developing his sons. His own involvement is deliberately limited to the school-run-style routine of getting them to training and collecting them afterwards.

'Do you know what I do? I drop the boys off at the gym because they can't drive at the moment, then I go for a walk, go for a run, have a coffee, and come back to pick them up. That's it. I honestly don't get involved.

'People think I'm training the boys on the pads and doing all that sort of stuff, but I don't. The only thing they might do when they're in camp with me is come to the gym, punch the bag in the corner, do a bit of shadow boxing or go for a run down the road.

I'm not physically hands-on with their boxing training, nor do I ever want to be, because there's a special relationship between a boxer and their trainer. If you build that relationship from the beginning and maintain it over a long period, you develop a special bond, like the one Sugar and I have.

'I'm their dad. I can't be that too.'

The blockbuster showdown between Tyson Fury and Anthony Joshua will be streamed live globally on Netflix, while Fury's brand-new documentary, TYSON FURY, is available to watch now.

Sports.title: Bayern Munich are at war with themselves over 'unacceptable' treatment of Jamal Musiala, writes CRAIG HOPE - now the £20m-a-year star faces a bitter fight for his future after seizure and injury hell
Sports.content:
Bayern Munich are at war with themselves over 'unacceptable' treatment of Jamal Musiala, writes CRAIG HOPE - now the £20m-a-year star faces a bitter fight for his future after seizure and injury hell

It was four years ago this week that I spoke to Lothar Matthaus - and all he wanted to talk about was Jamal Musiala.

The Bayern Munich midfielder was 19 and the poster boy of Germany's impending World Cup campaign in Qatar. Indeed, quite literally, there were posters and shirts bearing Musiala's face and name in Matthaus' Bavarian apartment.

My plan was for the Germany legend to open up on his own World Cup stories, but he enjoyed more slapping me down on Musiala, who had spent much of his childhood in London and played for England Under-21s.

'I like to provoke you again,' he said, having already crowed, playfully, over penalty shootouts. 'You gave the best player from the young English generation to Germany - Jamal Musiala. I have a son who is eight years old. I have to buy the Bayern Munich shirts with No.42 on the back, and I have to buy the Germany shirt with No.14 - my son is crazy about Musiala.

'So, thank you, England, for giving us Musiala. I do not know why you did not fight more to keep this player in the English shirt. We are so happy to have him. When he is on the field, this is like Messi three years ago. He has everything. Fast, good dribbling, the last pass, he can score. He is becoming the complete player. In the future, he will be one of the very best players in the world.'

Today, you wonder which shirt adorns the wall of his son's bedroom. If it is still Musiala, it will be because of loyalty and hope that his father's belief can still be true. That, however, would contrast with the loyalty and belief of Musiala's paymasters at Bayern Munich.

Jamal Musiala has been the subject of a huge row engulfing Bayern Munich this week

The German club's hierarchy have undermined their star and the terms of his contract

For what is playing out in Bavaria right now is an unedifying and divisive debate centred, fundamentally, on the health of a 23-year-old. Musiala has, since April of last year, been under the care of neurological experts after experiencing 'absence-like' symptoms. This only became apparent to the public in August of this year when he collapsed twice in the space of four days during pre-season friendlies.

He revealed a neurological dysfunction but described it as treatable. Last week, away from the cameras, there was another seizure. And then, on Friday of this week, confirmation of a thigh injury that will keep him sidelined for several weeks.

There have been other injuries too, including a broken leg at the 2025 World Club Cup, and a 120mph car accident in April of 2025, for which Musiala lost his license. But also, two months prior, there was a new contract signed until 2030, said to be worth upwards of £20million per year. This, for Bayern, is the complication.

To put it bluntly, Musiala is now paid too much money for what the club gets in return. Since the start of last season, there have been just 14 starts, 16 substitute appearances and seven goals.

'We are in a dilemma,' said Uli Hoeness, Bayern's honorary president, earlier this month. 'He has an illness that cannot easily be cured, but can be managed reasonably well with medication. But whether he will ever again have the level of performance he once had…'

Fellow board member Karl-Heinz Rummenigge added his opinion, with all the subtlety of the goals he used to hammer for Bayern and West Germany.

'It's also well known that he has a contract that involves very substantial sums of money,' he said. 'I think it's responsible and completely normal for a club to consider how to handle this. Because then these sums are, of course – sorry, with all due respect – no longer feasible. Unfortunately, what we know suggests that it will be difficult for him to get back to the level he so often showed.'

I was at Bayern's training ground in May. Everywhere, from the club shop to the fencing around the pitches to the messaging in the media suite, are the words - 'Mia san mia'. Translated, the Bayern motto means, 'We are who we are'. At its core is an essence of family, a bond uniting players, staff and supporters. When Vincent Kompany collapsed on the training ground last month, the exhausted head coach was afforded rest and support.

Only, these past couple of weeks have not felt very 'Mia san mia', especially not for Musiala and his family. Nor, it would seem, for his team-mates.

Musiala was viewed as a future star when he first broke onto the scene with the German club

On Wednesday night, after Musiala played the final 14 minutes of Bayern's 2-1 defeat at Lille, captain Joshua Kimmich said: 'The club is always paramount and greater than any individual player - but not greater than the person. That's absolutely unacceptable and not in the spirit of Bayern, which stands for being a family and sticking together. This (Musiala's situation) is something that should have been discussed and resolved together at a table.

'Jamal has our full support 100 per cent, and I'm convinced that he has the club's support as well, even if one or two people have expressed different opinions.'

A truce, of sorts, has since been called.

'FC Bayern and Jamal Musiala's management have agreed to continue their discussions in a spirit of partnership and confidentiality,' said a club statement. 'The player's health is the top priority for both parties. Jamal Musiala will receive full support throughout his recovery.'

At 11am on Tuesday, Musiala's representatives had entered the Sabener Strabe training ground for crisis talks and the above statement was the outcome. It still leaves many more questions than answers, for Musiala and Bayern.

For starters, the treatment of the player risks unsettling and unnerving others in the dressing-room. What if Harry Kane had damaged his ankle ligaments before his new contract was signed, rather than two weeks after? Would Hoeness and Rummenigge have advised against committing to the Ballon d'Or winner? Facetious that may sound, but the thought of contracts being revisited in the event of illness or injury is a dangerous seed to plant.

Since Hoeness' comments surfaced, Bayern have drawn at home to Cologne and lost at Lille. Revelations about goalkeeper Manuel Neuer's private life have hardly helped, either. 'Cheating on pregnant women is a whole different level of evil,' posted his estranged wife. The club is unaccustomed to the headlines of late.

Christian Falk is the head of football at leading tabloid Bild and he has followed Musiala's career, and recent events, as close as anyone. So, what happens now for Musiala?

'That is the biggest question,' he says. 'There are two Bayern Munichs right now. The one Musiala has trust in on the sporting side, including Vincent Kompany and director of sport Max Eberl. Then, on the other side, the big bosses, the elder statesmen (Hoeness and Rummenigge). But at Bayern, this is where the decisions are made.

But the diagnosis of a neurological health condition has been a major setback for the star

Insiders say he has not been the same player since his long-term injury owing to a leg break

But his team-mates are rallying around him, with captain Joshua Kimmich branding his bosses' comments as 'unacceptable'

'So while everything now is calm, and Bayern have 'back-pedalled in the boat' and are offering support and help for Musiala, if there is no improvement in the next four to six months, the bosses will talk again. Everyone knows this.'

I was at Bayern's Champions League semi-final second leg against Paris Saint-Germain last season and have revisited my match report, noting the sole comment concerning Musiala, 'one run apart, he struggled'. He was, from memory, peripheral. The game was quicker than him.

Does Falk, then, believe we will ever see Musiala regain or exceed his previous level?

'Kompany has said he was at his very best in training recently,' he says. 'But everyone else is not so sure. It is not just the illness, but also the broken leg. That injury alone would have been enough to impact his level. After that, we have seen that he is not dribbling the same, he does not have the trust in his skills. A lot of the doubt is in his head. If he can remove that, he can be a very, very good player. But the same or better? Maybe not.

'Musiala always had the plan that the next step could be Real Madrid or Manchester City and winning the Ballon d'Or. If he is to be the player he wants to be, the chances are he cannot stay at Bayern, because I don't think he will forget this situation.'

Matthaus has also had his say this week, defending Kimmich.

'I think it was a fantastic interview,' he said. 'Perhaps it didn't sit well with the Bayern bosses, but it should serve as a wake-up call for them to handle situations like this differently in the future. Maybe he will be fined, but you don't resolve things by handing out fines. That would only open up another can of worms. He showed that he is a true captain because he is not only standing up for Musiala, but wants to protect all his players.'

For now, Musiala must protect himself. When he was nine years old at Corpus Christi Catholic Primary School in London, he wrote a poem, 'Moment', which won a competition. One line from that feels very poignant today.

'Suddenly the car stops,' he wrote, referencing his arrival at Chelsea's academy. 'I close my eyes. I take a deep breath. I'm not nervous anymore. I'm happy. I know what I've to do.'

This time, the challenge for Musiala is not to prove how good he can be, but to rediscover how good he was.

Sports.title: Parrott fires Republic of Ireland into Nations League play-offs
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott fired the Republic of Ireland into a Nations League play-off berth with two penalties in their 3-0 victory over 10-man Kosovo at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The result ensured the Republic finished runners-up in group B3, and also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month's qualifying draw for that competition.

Tuesday night's contest turned on its head in the 26th minute, when Kreshnik Hajrizi was sent off for handling the ball off the line, and Parrott took advantage with a top-corner finish.

The Real Betis striker doubled the Republic's lead from the spot five minutes after the restart, and Jack Moylan added a 75th-minute cushion to keep alive the hosts' hopes of booking a place in League A for the first time through the March play-off.

Image: Parrot struck twice from the penalty spot

Heimir Hallgrimsson's lone change from Saturday's defeat to group winners Austria was the insertion of John Egan into the line-up, replacing injured captain Nathan Collins.

How Ireland finished as group runners-up...

It was a contest that lacked fluidity in the opening 10 minutes, before the Republic found a foothold and Finn Azaz looked to pick out Parrott, but was blocked.

Kosovo then twice missed chances to take the lead. Lindon Emerllahu fired just wide in the 17th minute, and Caoimhin Kelleher was called into action for the first time a minute later to deny Vedat Muriqi.

What had been a largely uneventful encounter suddenly took a dramatic twist in the 26th minute, a red-card incident sparked by Moylan's cross, glanced on by Liam Scales to Parrott.

His effort - clearly goalbound - was cleared off the line by Hajrizi, who extended his arm like a goalkeeper, and was immediately shown a red card by Latvian referee Edgars Malcevs.

Parrott stepped up and gave Arijanet Muric no chance when he rifled into the top right corner to set the Republic on their way.

It remained just a one-goal advantage at the break despite a handful of chances falling the Republic's way, while the visitors created one when Kelleher denied Ilir Krasniqi with 10 minutes remaining to ensure there would be no first-half equaliser.

There was a flurry of Republic chances immediately after the second half kicked off before Parrott added his second penalty.

Muric had just denied Jayson Molumby's effort from range and Parrott was rushing forward to meet the loose ball when he was taken down by the Kosovo keeper.

This time he dove in the right direction, but failed to stop Parrott from doubling the hosts' lead.

The Republic were less successful from open play, unable to put the game away from a string of subsequent chances despite finding themselves in plenty of space, and should have added a third before the hour.

Moylan's persistence finally paid off with 15 minutes remaining, nodding home substitute Liam Kitching's cross in off the post.

The Republic nearly added a late fourth when Adam Idah stung the palms of Muric with two minutes left.

Parrott dreaming of home Euros

Republic of Ireland striker Troy Parrott speaking to RTÉ about the 2028 Euros:

"I've been thinking about it since I was a kid, I think everyone has.

"Look, it's not a guarantee that we are going to qualify for that tournament, so I think tonight was very important to get into pot two so that we have a better draw.

"We'll be going into the qualifiers now, trying to make sure that we qualify for the tournament.

"A tournament that's one of the host nations being Ireland, without Ireland it would be heartbreaking for all of us, so I think it's a mission now to make sure that we're there.

"It was disappointing that we didn't win the group because that's what we all wanted to do at the start.

"There's been so many nearly matches where we've nearly won, we've played really well and haven't won, and I think tonight we went out there with the mindset that no matter what we have to win.

"Obviously the red card helped us, but I have no doubt in my mind that group of players who were out on that pitch would have won that game."

'We want to play the top teams'

Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson speaking at his post-match press conference:

"Everybody, and especially us, likes to play the top teams. To compare yourself with the best teams, that's one thing.

"Second is those teams will expose your weaknesses, and that helps you in your growth to play these teams, so we can continue our growth.

"We're already looking forward to March. Tough teams in the pot. Whoever we draw is going to be a tough two games, and it's good for this team at this time to play these matches instead of friendlies.

"We're really excited for March, and looking forward to meeting the players again."

Sports.title: Kalajdzic scores late as Republic of Ireland taste defeat in Austria
Sports.content:
Sasa Kalajdzic dealt the Republic of Ireland a late blow in Linz with the only goal in Austria's 1-0 Nations League victory at the Raiffeisen Arena.

The result ensured that, no matter how the closing contests in Group B play out, Austria sealed promotion to League A.

Ireland enter Tuesday's critical home clash at the Aviva Stadium in third place, with one point fewer than their final opponents, Kosovo.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men were not without chances, but only Kalajdzic made one count when he broke the deadlock in the 79th minute.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson urges UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in a behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; there were allegations of spitting by an Israeli player at half-time, while the Israeli government criticised the Irish players for bowing their heads during the national anthem

Republic of Ireland: Heimir Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future after tense draw

Ireland's head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson has called for UEFA to keep his team and Israel separate in future

Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

The Ireland boss was speaking following his side's 1-1 UEFA Nations League draw with Israel behind closed doors in Serbia.

The games between the two nations this international break were overshadowed by politics, with the Football Association of Ireland (FAI) urged to boycott the internationals amid ongoing conflict in the Israel-Gaza War.

This continued in Serbia, as Ireland fitness coach Damien Doyle was allegedly spat on by an Israeli player at half-time, according to reports in the stadium.

Irish media reported that the incident took place as the teams went down the tunnel. Ireland boss Hallgrimsson confirmed there was an allegation, but he admitted he didn't see it and declined to comment further on it.

However, when asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Israeli Government accuses ROI of 'moral blindness'

The Israeli Government have accused the Ireland football team of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during their national anthem.

For the second time in a week, the Irish players, coaching team and FAI all bowed their heads while the Israeli national anthem was played pre-match.

Image: Republic of Ireland players bowed their heads during the national anthem

The official Israeli Government X account posted: "While some use the football field as their political theatre, for us this is personal.

"1939: Irish players raised their arms in salute to Nazi Germany.

"2026: Irish players bowed their heads during Israel's anthem.

"Different generations. The same moral blindness.

"Today, Israel's players wear black armbands to remember those brutally massacred by Hamas on October 7 - including former professional footballer Lior Asulin.

"Some of us have skin in the game. Others just make a show of it."

Sky Sports News has contacted the FAI for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged that a derogatory term had been used, which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. The term is not associated with antisemitic or anti-Israeli abuse.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying: "That's completely untrue," before bringing the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called following an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist, who said a microphone had been taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands that no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland draw with Israel in second Nations League meeting
Sports.content:
Match report and reaction as Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in behind-closed-doors contest in Serbia; Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out after the break; sides clashed at half-time

Republic of Ireland 1-1 Israel: Troy Parrott scores again as sides draw second controversial Nations League meeting

The Republic of Ireland drew 1-1 with Israel in the second controversial Nations League fixture between the sides.

Troy Parrott's first-half penalty was cancelled out by Dor Peretz after the break in the behind-closed-doors game in Serbia.

The Republic's 'home' fixture was held on neutral territory at the 4,500-seat TSC arena in Backa Topola, due to "operational challenges that could impact on the delivery of the game on home soil" according to a June Football Association of Ireland (FAI) statement.

Both sides wore black armbands. The Republic's, the same as in Hungary to acknowledge - as the Football Association of Ireland chief David Courrell explained before that contest - "all lives lost" in the ongoing Israel-Hamas conflict.

Israel's armbands - which read "7.10" - were to commemorate the October 7, 2023 Hamas-led attack on southern Israel, their official X account confirmed.

The pitch featured no sponsored content or branding, just UEFA graphics with slogans like "football for all", a decision taken by the FAI.

Image: The referee pleads with the benches in Serbia

Tensions rose at half-time after a fracas broke out in front of the tunnel and players from both sides engaged in a heated argument, with the Israeli Government later accusing Irish players of "moral blindness" for bowing their heads during Israel's national anthem, as they did in Monday's first match.

Officials broke up a second altercation in three minutes of added time, and there were more heated words exchanged after the final whistle.

On the pitch Parrott, who has now scored 10 times in his last seven competitive internationals, fired the Republic in front from the spot in the 39th minute before Dor Peretz drew the sides level two minutes after the restart.

The result puts Ireland third in Nations League Group B3, level on points with second-placed Kosovo.

Hallgrimsson calls on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future

Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson has called on UEFA to keep Ireland and Israel apart in future.

Speaking after the 1-1 draw, Hallgrimsson also declined to comment on the half-time fracas between the two sides.

When asked if the two countries should be playing each other again, he told RTE Sport: "No, they shouldn't. That's not ours to decide - that's UEFA who decides that. Obviously, there's a big support for Palestine in Ireland. There's not many countries that support Palestine as much as Ireland does.

"I wouldn't wish any national team to go through what we've gone through in these two weeks, so maybe UEFA just needs to step in and do something."

On the half-time incident, he said in his post-match press conference: "I was there. I'm not going to comment on it. It's something that a disciplinary committee is probably going to look at."

Sky Sports News has contacted UEFA for comment.

Two Israeli journalists banned for post-match press conferences

Meanwhile, prior to the match, UEFA confirmed that two Israeli journalists were banned from the post-match press conferences, after Saturday's pre-match Ireland press conference descended into chaos.

The media access for Ireland was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed Irish players had racially abused them during the match in Hungary last weekend.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close.

After the press conference ended abruptly, Serbian police were called due to an allegation of assault by an Israeli journalist who had the microphone taken from them by an FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there was no further action was taken by police.

Sports.title: Ireland news conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media
Sports.content:
Republic of Ireland vs Israel is being played in Serbia as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott; protests briefly halted Ireland's draw with Austria on Thursday over opposition to Sunday's Israel fixture

Republic of Ireland vs Israel: Heimir Hallgrimsson's press conference cut short after tense exchanges with Israeli media

Republic of Ireland head coach Heimir Hallgrimsson's pre-match press conference ahead of Sunday's match against Israel in Serbia ended abruptly after a tense exchange with Israeli media.

The media access was cut short after an Israeli journalist alleged that Israeli players had claimed they were racially abused by Irish players during their match in Hungary last Sunday.

The journalist alleged a derogatory term was used - which Sky Sports has chosen not to repeat. It is not a term associated with being antisemitic or anti-Israeli.

An Irish press officer refuted the allegation, saying "that's completely untrue", and brought the news conference to a premature close as one of his colleagues remonstrated with the reporter.

Image: Ireland's players bowed their heads before facing Israel in the reverse fixture last week

Hallgrimsson later labelled the accusation a "verbal attack" during a separate briefing for members of the Irish press.

The exchange in the main press conference took place after Hallgrimsson was also asked a question about a co-pilot who attacked a pilot and tried to hijack a flight travelling from Dubai to Tel Aviv earlier this week.

The reporter's question was shut down by the FAI press officer.

Sky Sports News understands there are no open UEFA investigations at this stage from the previous meeting between Israel and Ireland last weekend.

The FAI are conducting their own investigation into whether striker Adam Idah was racially abused by Israeli supporters during their 3-0 UEFA Nations League win but have yet to make an official complaint to UEFA.

Image: Protesters interrupted Ireland's draw with Austria by throwing tennis balls onto the pitch with Palestine flags on them

Despite the high-profile nature of the fixture, members of the Irish media later reported that there was no UEFA delegate present at the news conference.

Sky Sports News was told a UEFA match delegate does not have to attend press conferences. The duty is left to the venue media manager, whose job it is to report anything if there is an incident.

Sunday's match is being played in Backa Topola, Serbia, as the FAI moved the game to a neutral venue for "operational reasons" in June following widespread calls for a boycott.

Sky Sports News has approached the FAI for comment.

Sports.title: Ireland held by Austria despite Parrott double as protests interrupt game
Sports.content:
Troy Parrott scored twice but the Republic of Ireland were forced to settle for a 2-2 draw after Austria came back in the second half of their Nations League encounter at the Aviva Stadium in Dublin.

The contest was twice interrupted in the opening 45 minutes, first due to what campaign group Stop the Game later referred to in a statement as a "limited tennis ball protest", when - around the 20th minute - tennis balls wrapped in stickers featuring the Palestinian flag and the text '#StopTheGame' were launched onto the pitch.

The match paused a second time when an invader carrying what appeared to be a Palestine flag entered the pitch and was promptly tackled and carried off by security.

The protests came after Ireland's decision not to boycott their game against Israel last week - although goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu did make himself unavailable.

Ireland are due to face Israel again on Sunday.

Image: Tennis balls with Palestine flags were throw onto the pitch

Before the protests, Parrott scored a sensational 12th-minute opener, and then added a penalty on the stroke of half-time.

A pair of substitutes proved Ireland's undoing after Alexander Prass halved the deficit in the 71st minute and Michael Gregoritsch drew the sides level six minutes later.

Heimir Hallgrimsson's men had a chance to top Group B3 with a victory, but they sit third behind Austria and Kosovo at the halfway point of the group stage.

Hallgrimsson made three changes, including the reintroduction of Finn Azaz, who was greeted warmly when his name was announced over the PA system before the match.

Bazunu was back in the squad, while Liam Scales and John Egan were awarded starts.

There was a significant security and police presence outside the stadium, where a small group of protesters also gathered before kick-off.

There was an audacious early effort from Sasa Kalajdzic, who tried to catch Caoimhin Kelleher off his line with a lob from midfield, before Ireland enjoyed a couple of attacking spells deep in the visitors' half.

Image: Parrott is congratulated after scoring his second goal against Austria

It was a brilliant opener from Parrott, who realised he was on his own after bringing down Adam Idah's glanced-on header from a goal kick.

The Real Betis striker was sandwiched in a triangle of white shirts, before nutmegging Philipp Lienhardt and evading every other challenger with a mazy run before planting the ball past Florian Wiegele and into the bottom corner.

Image: A protestor was carried off the pitch during the game

Kelleher denied Patrick Wimmer and there were a few more promising spells for Austria before Parrott doubled their lead.

Ryan Manning won the penalty after he was clipped in the box by Nicolas Seiwald. Parrott stepped up after a VAR check and blasted it past the Austria 'keeper.

Austria cut the deficit after Liam Kitching was caught out and Austria worked the ball to the unmarked Prass, who blasted the ball beyond Kelleher. The offside flag was initially raised, but the decision was reversed after a VAR check.

The Brentford goalkeeper then failed to stop Gregoritsch's free-kick as Ralf Rangnick's side fought back for a point.

Ireland captain Dara O'Shea was denied by an excellent leaping Wiegele save, Gregoritsch directed a shot over the crossbar and both sides fended off attempts at a late winner.

Sports.title: Hallgrimsson admits 'toughest days' of career after Ireland beat Israel
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland beat Israel 3-0 in their controversial Nations League fixture at a neutral venue in Hungary.

Players did not shake hands with each other before their meeting at the Nagyerdei Stadion in Debrecen and there was no exchange between Ireland captain Dara O'Shea and Israel's Manor Solomon.

Ireland players also appeared to bow their heads while Israel's national anthem was played out before kick-off.

Black armbands were worn by Ireland players, which Football Association of Ireland (FAI) chief executive David Courell said was a gesture to recognise "all lives lost" in the Israel-Gaza conflict.

Goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu was the only player who chose not to play after the squad voted to proceed with the match on Saturday amid calls for the game not to go ahead.

Goals from Troy Parrott, Adam Idah and Jack Moylan sealed the victory for Heimir Hallgrimsson's side.

Moylan celebrated his goal by kissing and raising his black armband before kissing his badge.

Hallgrimsson: I couldn't be more proud of the players

Republic of Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson:

"It has been some of the toughest days of my coaching career, but its not about me.

"The game, the desire the players showed to make a statement on the pitch - they are football players, they wanted to show on the pitch, make that talking with their feet.

"What they did was impressive. In tough times that's when you find your leaders, there were so many players that stepped up in these tough times. The energy levels they showed was impressive.

"The performance was good given all the preparation, the lack of training, all of our meetings were about something other than football.

"I couldn't be more proud of the players.

"By playing I know we are making some people unhappy. By playing we are making others happy. Winning probably pleases everyone, but there will still be people angry that we played the game.

"I hope we can settle that slowly down and stay together as a team. I wish people in Ireland continue supporting these boys, because they certainly deserve it."

Sports.title: Republic of Ireland slip to deserved defeat in Kosovo
Sports.content:
The Republic of Ireland slipped to a 1-0 defeat away to Kosovo in their Nations League opener in Pristina.

The build-up to the League B3 encounter had been overshadowed by the controversy around upcoming fixtures against Israel, which Republic boss Heimir Hallgrimsson had admitted many of his squad members were uncomfortable about playing.

Chiedozie Ogbene had fired an early chance over before Kosovo responded to finish the first half strongly at the Fadil Vokrri Stadium.

The home side saw two shots cleared off the line and Ireland goalkeeper Caoimhin Kelleher then clawed away a header from Vedat Muriqi as Hallgrimsson's side got to the break on level terms.

Ireland - who are scheduled to play Israel in Hungary on Sunday and then again in a 'home' tie at another neutral venue in Serbia seven days later - dug in for the second half but were eventually undone with seven minutes left when Kosovo captain Muriqi bundled the ball in from close range.

Udinese defender James Abankwah was handed a first competitive start as part of a back five, with in-form Real Betis striker Troy Parrott the lone forward and Dara O'Shea taking the captain's armband.

Image: The Republic of Ireland have won two of their six games in 2026 so far

Ireland created what ended up being their only real clear chance in the 22nd minute. Abankwah got away down the right and ran into the Kosovo penalty area before cutting the ball back to Ogbene, who sent a curling effort over the crossbar.

Kosovo, who are in League B for the first time, went close on the half-hour mark when a cross from the left found its way through to Muriqi, whose angled shot was cleared off the line by Jayson Molumby.

Veldin Hodza then saw his 10-yard strike blocked in front of goal by O'Shea before Kelleher got up to claw away a looping header from Muriqi, which was set for the top corner.

Ireland made a positive start to the second half, with a deep cross from the right by Abankwah finding Parrott at the far post and his header was gathered by Kosovo goalkeeper Arijanet Muric.

Image: Vedat Muriqi scored the winner for Kosovo

Kosovo, though, continued to carry a threat themselves. Baton Zabergja sent a 20-yard effort just wide of the top corner, which again got the home supporters into full voice.

Muriqi forced Kelleher into another smart reaction save from an angled shot at the near post before Kosovo eventually made the breakthrough in the 83rd minute.

Ermal Krasniqi's shot was deflected onto the crossbar and Muriqi reacted quickest in a crowded six-yard box to nod the ball over the line.

Kosovo should have got a second late on when substitute Krasniqi dragged his shot wide after being set up by Muriqi following a break onto a long ball.

Ireland pay price for 'off day'

Ireland manager Heimir Hallgrimsson told RTE:

"[Kosovo are] a good team, momentum with them, crowd with them, and to be honest they deserve the win.

"There was nothing that we didn't know about how they would play, where their threats would be, but [it was] an off day for a lot of our players and [it is] a tough place to come to if you have an off day, so a deserved win for Kosovo."

Hallgrimsson added: "We were the team that needed to defend today and didn't connect in possession or passes, not as sharp as we have done.

"We have to quickly find out the reason that we had an off day. We can all do better than we did today.

"It is a two-day turnaround for the next one, so we better be quick…and do better than this versus Israel. They are probably in the same position as us [having lost to Austria]."

Asked if the controversy from playing the fixtures against Israel had impacted on his team's performance against Kosovo, Hallgrimsson said: "I couldn't say now. It is difficult to measure that one."

He added: "This is the situation, we have to cope with it. And like I said before the game, this camp is a test of character.

"We need to do better in that area than we did here today. We knew that we needed to win the duels, win the one-vs-ones, but sadly they had the upper hand on all the basics."

What it means and next fixtures

Sports.title: Tyson Fury is CLEARED to fight Anthony Joshua: Gypsy King clears medical checks after Netflix schizophrenia claim threw $150m bout into jeopardy
Sports.content:
Tyson Fury has been given the medical all clear for his British bonanza fight against Anthony Joshua.

The mega millions world heavyweight title battle at Cardiff's Principality Stadium on December 11 was in jeopardy following claims that the Gypsy King is suffering from schizophrenia.
