Ghana News.title: ‘Is Ghana’s internet banking system down?’ – Users report widespread bank app and digital payment service disruptions
Ghana News.content:
Ghanaians have taken to social media to report disruptions to banking apps and digital payment services, raising concerns about the reliability of the country's electronic financial channels.

The complaints, which circulated on Saturday, November 28, 2026, involved reports of difficulties accessing banking services and completing transactions across different platforms.

While the reports have prompted questions about whether the disruptions are connected, there is no confirmation that all the affected services are experiencing a common technical problem.

Fidelity Bank Ghana on X, however, confirmed that some of its digital services are unavailable because of a technical issue.

We're aware of the disruption and working to restore affected services as quickly as possible. Thank you for your patience. https://t.co/kB9tdXoSqn — Fidelity Bank Ghana (@fidelitybankgh) November 27, 2026

In a notice issued on Friday, November 27, the bank said account-to-wallet transfers, instant transfers to other banks and GhQR transactions had been affected. Customers had reported difficulties with the services since Wednesday, November 25.

On X, several users expressed frustration over what they described as disruptions across multiple banks.

"It seems users of various banks are reporting service downtimes. What is going on?" one user asked.

Another wrote:

Is that why there are so many maintenance messages from the banks. Every minute bia dear customer — Seyram (@__theSeyram) November 28, 2026

A third questioned whether the disruption extended across the banking system, writing:

Is the whole internet banking system in Ghana down or what??? Cos all these banks can’t be doing maintenance today….. — Afi T (@afitsegah) November 28, 2026

"Ghanaian banking apps are down ‼️"

Concerns over national security

One social media user described the reported disruptions as a national security concern, arguing that the absence of information from relevant institutions was adding to public anxiety.

What is happening with the Ghanaian banks is a national security threat. The silence is not forward-looking. A lot of the digital channels are down — Daniel Oduro (@Daniel_Oduro) November 28, 2026

However, there is currently no verified evidence linking the reported disruptions to a cyberattack or a wider compromise of Ghana's banking infrastructure.

Similar disruptions in the UK and US

The complaints in Ghana come days after banking customers in the United Kingdom experienced difficulties accessing some digital services.

On Friday, November 27, Lloyds Banking Group and Bank of Scotland experienced intermittent problems with their mobile apps and online banking platforms, leaving some customers unable to log in or complete transactions.

The disruption affected a banking group with approximately 28 million customers. Lloyds later confirmed that its services had been restored and apologised for the inconvenience.

Earlier in November, customers of major US banks, including JPMorgan Chase, Bank of America and U.S. Bank, also reported difficulties with some banking services.

JPMorgan Chase attributed its transaction delays to a software bug in its on-premises hardware systems, saying there was no evidence that the incident was cyber-related.

The bank also clarified that the issue was not systemic, although other financial institutions could experience delays involving transactions with JPMorgan.

The incidents in the UK and US are separate from the reports in Ghana, and there is no evidence linking them.

While several banks have acknowledged disruptions to some of their services via SMS to their respective users, the extent of the wider complaints remains unclear.

The Bank of Ghana and other affected financial institutions are yet to provide a comprehensive explanation of the reports circulating on social media.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.

World.title: Suspected Chinese spy balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing
World.content:
Washington —

The Chinese spy balloon that transited the US earlier this year was able to capture imagery and collect some signals intelligence from US military sites, a source familiar with the matter tells CNN.

The balloon was able to transmit information back to Beijing in real time, the source said, and the US government still does not know for sure whether the Chinese government could wipe the balloon’s data as it received it. That raises questions about whether there is intelligence the balloon was able to gather that the US still doesn’t know about.

Still, the intelligence community has not been overly concerned about the information the balloon was able to gather, the person said, because it is not much more sophisticated than what Chinese satellites are able to glean as they orbit over similar locations.

A US intelligence official told CNN on Monday that “although analysis of the wreckage of the High Altitude Balloon remains ongoing, thus far, its flight over the United States does not appear to have provided critical new insights to the People’s Republic of China.”

The US also knew what the balloon’s path would be and was able to protect sensitive sites and censor some signals before the balloon was able to pick them up, officials have said.

As CNN has reported, the US intelligence community last year developed a method of tracking what it says is a fleet of these Chinese balloons operating across the globe, controlled by the Chinese military.

The FBI is still examining the balloon, but so far officials have been able to glean additional information about how the device worked, including the algorithms used for the balloon’s software and how it is powered and designed.

CNN has reached out to the National Security Council at the White House and the Pentagon for comment. NBC was first to report on the new intelligence.

Video Ad Feedback Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33 • Source: CNN Justin Trudeau on what the world needs to do to handle China's threats 1:33

The balloon first crossed into US airspace over Alaska in late January before passing through Canada and down into Montana, where it hovered for a few days, leading the US to believe it was trying to surveil sensitive military sites, like Malmstrom Air Force Base in Montana. It was eventually shot down by the US off the East Coast on February 4, and the incident further escalated tensions between Washington and Beijing, including the postponement of a diplomatic visit by US Secretary of State Antony Blinken to China.

A senior State Department official said in February that, as the balloon floated across the US, it “was capable of conducting signals intelligence collection operations.”

Gen. Glen VanHerck, the commander of US Northern Command and NORAD, said at the time that the US “did not assess” that the balloon “presented a significant collection hazard beyond what already exists in actionable technical means from the Chinese.”

The surveillance program, which includes a number of similar balloons, is in part run out of the small Chinese province of Hainan, officials told CNN. The US does not know the precise size of the fleet of Chinese surveillance balloons, but sources tell CNN that the program has conducted at least two dozen missions over at least five continents in recent years.

Roughly half a dozen of those flights have been within US airspace, although not necessarily over US territory, according to one official familiar with the intelligence.

China has maintained that the balloon was actually just a weather balloon thrown off course, and the US has been assessing the possibility that it was not deliberately maneuvered into the continental US by the Chinese government, CNN has reported.

Still, China did maintain some ability to maneuver the balloon, officials believe. And once the balloon was over Montana, China appeared to take advantage of its position to loiter over sensitive sites and try to collect intelligence.

This story has been updated with additional reporting.

World.title: Beijing promised to 'fight back' over Taiwan leader's US visit. But this time it has more to lose
World.content:
Hong Kong —

An anticipated meeting between Taiwan’s President Tsai Ing-wen and US House Speaker Kevin McCarthy in California this week has sparked concerns of a repeat of the pressure campaign China launched last year when then-Speaker Nancy Pelosi visited Taipei.

At that time, Beijing encircled the island democracy with unprecedented military drills – firing multiple missiles into its surrounding waters and sending dozens of warplanes speeding across a sensitive median line dividing the Taiwan Strait.

It also cut off contact with the United States over a number of issues from military matters to combating climate change, in retaliation for what it viewed as a violation of its sovereignty.

This time, Beijing has already threatened to “resolutely fight back” if a Tsai-McCarthy meeting goes ahead.

Video Ad Feedback See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32 • Source: CNN See why tensions are rising between US and China over Taiwan 2:32

It also slammed Washington for allowing Tsai to stopover in the US while en route to and from official visits in Central America, warning it could lead to “serious” confrontation between the two powers.

A defiant Tsai staked out her own ground, pledging as she took off on her 10-day trip not to let “external pressure” stop Taiwan from connecting with the world and like-minded democracies.

But the optics of the meeting, taking place in California and not Taiwan, and its timing – at a particularly thorny moment in China’s foreign relations and ahead of a presidential election in Taiwan that could reset the tone of its relationship with Beijing – may see Beijing tread more carefully this time, or at least not escalate further, analysts say.

“This puts the burden on China not to overreact, because any overreaction is only going to push China further away from the world,” said Yun Sun, director of the China Program at the Stimson Center think tank in Washington.

That doesn’t mean, however, that Beijing won’t be closely watching Tsai’s movements as it calibrates its response – and decides how much military might to flex over her meeting with an American lawmaker on American soil.

The opacity of China’s system – and the potential for competing interests within its vast bureaucracy – also make it difficult to accurately predict its response.

“Every time Taiwan does anything that China doesn’t like, the Chinese react with their own military coercion,” Sun said. But in the current situation, “they have to consider the consequences of overreaction,” she added.

House Speaker Kevin McCarthy talks to reporters at the Capitol in Washington on March 24, 2023. J. Scott Applewhite/AP

Rising pressure

The expected meeting, which McCarthy’s office announced earlier this week would take place on Wednesday, also comes at a precarious moment in US-China relations.

Washington and Beijing are struggling to stabilize their communication amid flaring tensions over issues from a downed suspected Chinese surveillance balloon to semiconductor supply chains – raising the stakes of potential damage to that relationship if Beijing lashes out as it did when Tsai met Pelosi.

Taiwan is still feeling the fallout of that response last August, with Chinese military forces now regularly making incursions over what had previously been an informal but largely respected border of control between Beijing and Taipei in the Taiwan Strait. Taiwan’s official Central News Agency also reported Monday that Tsai would meet with McCarthy, citing Tsai’s presidential office.

Video Ad Feedback See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05 • Source: CNN See image of a Chinese balloon hovering over Taiwan 3:05

But a meeting between Tsai and the leader of the Republican majority in the US House of Representatives, who ranks second in line to the Presidency, would mark another symbolic moment for Taiwan and the US, which only maintain unofficial ties.

For Tsai, who is entering the final year of her two-term presidency, “it’s clearly a capstone event,” according to Wen-Ti Sung, a political scientist at the Australian National University’s Taiwan Studies Program. “She has this image as the Taiwanese president who has taken US-Taiwan relations to new heights, and who … has been able to give Taiwan almost unprecedented international visibility,” he said.

That increased visibility – and enhanced cooperation with the US – has followed China’s mounting pressure on the island, which sits fewer than 110 miles (177 kilometers) from the mainland coast.

China’s Communist Party claims the self-governing island democracy as its own despite never having controlled it, and has vowed to take the island, by force if necessary.

The party has undertaken a sweeping expansion of its military capabilities over the past decade under leader Xi Jinping – and ramped up its pervasive economic, diplomatic and military pressure on Taiwan.

That’s driven concerns, among some in Washington, that Beijing is preparing for an invasion, though China’s official language still suggests that scenario is not its preferred option for achieving the claimed goal of “reunification.”

It is those pressures – and how to support Taiwan against unilateral actions by Beijing – that are likely to be on the table when Tsai, McCarthy and a bipartisan group of US lawmakers sit down on Wednesday.

Congress has been a pillar of increasing American support for Taiwan in recent years. Lawmakers regularly visit the island and drive bipartisan legislation enhancing support and cooperation.

While the US switched its diplomatic relations to Beijing decades ago, it maintains unofficial ties with Taiwan and is bound by law to provide the democratic island with the means to defend itself.

Under Washington’s longstanding “One China” policy, the US acknowledges China’s position that Taiwan is part of China, but has never officially recognized Beijing’s claim to the island of 23 million.

Though McCarthy does not have Pelosi’s decades-long record of advocacy regarding China, the California Republican is now a leading voice pushing for closer scrutiny of Beijing, and meeting Tsai could help him to burnish that image.

Last month, McCarthy told reporters that meeting Tsai in the US would not impact whether he travels to Taiwan in the future – something he had earlier said he wanted to do.

Fighter jets of the Chinese People's Liberation Army Eastern Theater Command conduct joint combat training exercises around Taiwan on August 7, 2022 in this photo released by Xinhua News Agency. Gong Yulong/Xinhua/AP

Beijing watching

A meeting in California, on US soil, is widely seen as less likely to provoke Beijing than a McCarthy visit to Taiwan.

Pelosi’s trip – the first from a lawmaker of that rank to the island in 25 years – generated a fever pitch of nationalist and anti-US rhetoric in mainland China.

This time, so far, domestic conversation in China’s heavily controlled media sphere has been significantly muted.

But the stakes remain high – including for Beijing itself – over how it responds, analysts say.

As Taiwan prepares for a presidential election in January, a fierce response could push voters away from Taiwan’s main opposition party Kuomintang (KMT), widely seen as more friendly toward Beijing.

It could also jar with another high profile trip happening now: a tour of mainland China from former Taiwan president and senior KMT member Ma Ying-jeou, the first visit from a current or former Taiwan leader since the end of the Chinese Civil War in 1949.

Ma’s tour is a “once in a half a century opportunity to send a conciliatory message between the two sides, Beijing shouldn’t want to tank that,” said Sung, the political scientist.

China is also acutely aware that its actions toward Taiwan are under a significantly brighter global spotlight following the invasion of Ukraine by Russian President Vladimir Putin, a close diplomatic partner of Xi. Putin’s rhetoric over Ukraine has echoes of how Xi speaks of Taiwan.

Beijing has recently sought to position itself as an agent of peace in that conflict – especially as it aims to repair frayed ties with Europe.

This week, as Tsai is expected to meet with McCarthy, French President Emmanuel Macron and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen will head to China – an important opportunity that Xi may not want to overshadow with military posturing.

An aggressive response also risks stoking confrontation with the US, not yet six months after Xi and US President Joe Biden called to enhance communication during a face-to-face meeting in Bali.

“(A less overtly aggressive response) would imply that Beijing does not wish to escalate tension with the US to a level that can risk getting out of hand,” said Steve Tsang, director of the SOAS China Institute in London.

“A reset in US-China ties is not on the agenda, but an easing of tension is not beyond the realm of possibility.”

World.title: Court rejects Argentina’s request to stop UK oil activity near Falklands
World.content:
An international tribunal refuses Buenos Aires’s application, giving green light for the project off the disputed region.

An international court has rejected Argentina’s request for provisional measures to halt United Kingdom-authorised oil drilling near the Falkland Islands.

Saturday’s ruling by the United Nations-backed International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea is a setback to Buenos Aires’s latest effort to challenge economic activity around the disputed territory.

Argentina’s request marks the latest spat between the two countries, which fought a brief but bitter 74-day war in 1982 over the UK-administered islands in the South Atlantic.

In September, Argentina launched an arbitration process against London over the Sea Lion project off the Falklands, which is led by the UK’s Rockhopper company and Israel’s Navitas.

Buenos Aires has argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.

It has asked the court to impose emergency measures and order the UK to take the necessary steps “to ensure that no new drilling for exploitation, and no installation of production infrastructure” takes place in the North Malvinas Basin.

It further urged the Hamburg-based court, an independent court set up under UN auspices, to order the UK to “refrain from using the information obtained in the exploration of the natural resources of the disputed maritime areas”.

The Sea Lion oil field is located about 220km (135 miles) from the islands, which lie 600km (372 miles) off Argentina’s Patagonian coast and almost 13,000km (8,077 miles) from the UK.



Argentinian President Javier Milei has doubled down on his country’s claim over the Falklands – known in Argentina as Las Malvinas – since US President Donald Trump said he was open to reviewing Washington’s stance on the territory.

The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain part of the UK.

But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by the UK after 1833.

London’s argument

The UK, meanwhile, has urged the court to reject the case, saying it was rooted in Argentina’s claims to sovereignty.

London argues the sovereignty claim falls outside the UN Convention on the Law of the Sea’s arbitration process aimed at settling maritime disputes.

The UK government’s chief legal adviser, Ellie Reeves, told the judges in a two-day hearing earlier this month that the order sought by Argentina “would prevent the people of the Falkland Islands from developing their natural resources, as they are entitled to do so”.

This could have “devastating” economic consequences for the islanders, she said, adding that what Argentina “wants is to take control of those resources for itself”.

Britain’s Prime Minister Andy Burnham also raised the Sea Lion project with Trump in a call in late October.

“The prime minister raised the economic consequences of Argentina’s coercive measures for the UK and US and reiterated the importance of respecting the islanders’ right to develop their natural resources,” Burnham’s office said in a statement.

The tribunal was set up under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS), which came into force in 1994 and which sets out a “regime of law and order in the world’s oceans and seas, establishing rules governing all uses of the oceans and their resources”.

If the court orders provisional emergency measures, these would be legally binding on both parties.

World.title: Bootleg alcohol poisonings in Iran see dozens dead and badly injured
World.content:
A spate of alcohol poisonings in Iran has led to deaths and serious injuries including blindness.

Two years after four people were executed for distributing contaminated alcoholic beverages – causing the deaths of 17 people and leaving 199 with injuries, including blindness – another spate of mass alcohol poisoning has swept through Iran.

Since mid-November, more than 20 people have died and at least 500 have been poisoned from consuming methanol-contaminated alcohol, the same substance used in medical disinfectants and wound care, and potentially fatal if consumed.

The first death was reported on November 16 in Marvdasht, in Fars Province, central Iran. By Friday, 66 people in Fars Province, 126 in Hormozgan Province in southern Iran, 230 in Razavi Khorasan Province and 15 in West Azerbaijan Province had been poisoned.

Police have launched a crackdown on bootleg alcohol sellers since then and by Friday, about 10 people were arrested across Iran in connection with the cases.

On Friday, the prosecutor of Razavi Khorasan Province said that the poisoning cases in Razavi Khorasan, Fars and Hormozgan provinces were connected. But several individuals had been arrested in connection with a “contaminated alcohol distribution network”.

Banned

A former Tehran police detective, speaking on condition of anonymity, said that any investigation into these incidents will have to look at the wider bootleg alcohol industry to avoid repeat poisoning incidents.

“In cases such as methanol poisoning affecting several cities or provinces, investigators need to look beyond the distribution network and examine the production network as well,” he said.



“Sometimes distributors may not even know that the alcohol they are selling to the public is contaminated. In such cases, investigations usually continue until those responsible for producing the contaminated drinks are identified and apprehended.”

Laws in effect banning alcohol were established in 1980, shortly after the Islamic Revolution, although religious minorities such as Christians and Jews can still access beverages such as wine.

The sale and purchase of alcohol is illegal in Iran, with drinkers potentially facing punishments of 80 lashes and jail, while repeat offenders have been executed.

Despite the strict laws, Hossein Kermanpour, spokesperson for Iran’s Ministry of Health, recently repeated the government’s advice that people should avoid consuming alcohol – but if they do and experience unusual symptoms, they should seek immediate medical attention.

The use of cheap medical-grade alcohol as the base of their products has made the consumption of illicit alcoholic beverages highly risky, the former police detective said.

“They typically buy medical-grade ethanol and mix it with a certain percentage of grape or date-based alcohol before selling it. Some use tea or acorn extracts to alter the colour and taste, while others add tequila or whisky-like flavourings to imitate the taste and appearance of commercial spirits,” he said.

“The problem is that medical alcohol, which is supposed to be ethanol, can sometimes contain traces or higher concentrations of methanol due to various factors. If the ethanol used in production is contaminated with methanol, the resulting product can become extremely toxic. In such cases, even the producers themselves may be unaware that the alcohol they purchased was contaminated, potentially exposing consumers to serious poisoning.”

Medical issues

Iranians say that alcohol is said to be available in major cities, and two official studies conducted in the early 2010s found an increase in alcohol consumption among Iranians aged between 15 and 64.

The National Mental Health Survey commissioned by the Ministry of Health in 2011 estimated that 830 per 100,000 people (approximately 623,000 individuals) had alcohol dependence, while 2,800 per 100,000 were recreational drinkers. A second survey also reported that there was a particular increase in alcohol consumption among people aged under 18 and women. A more recent study by the Ministry of Health in 2021 gave a more mixed assessment about any rise in alcohol use in Iran.

Dr Shadi Hassanzadeh, a general practitioner in Mashhad, told Al Jazeera that only when patients experience extreme medical issues – such as blurred vision, progressive loss of consciousness, and seizures – do they realise this is not ordinary intoxication and seek help, although by then it might be too late to save their eyesight.



“Methanol, or industrial alcohol, is extremely dangerous when used in homemade alcoholic drinks because consumers have no way of detecting its presence. By the time its effects become apparent, serious damage may already have been done to the body,” said Hassanzadeh.

Maryam, a nurse at an ophthalmology hospital in Tehran, told Al Jazeera that despite the law, she does not see people admitted with alcohol-related incidents afraid to reveal consumption of illicit alcohol.

“Since there is a widespread belief that consuming industrial alcohol causes blindness, ophthalmology hospitals are among the first places people turn to for treatment. The most common symptoms they present with are vision problems,” she said.

“Most people do not realise that seeking medical attention soon after consuming industrial alcohol increases their chances of saving their eyesight. Because they often do not know they have been poisoned, they delay seeking treatment until it is too late for doctors to do anything.”

Most cases of alcohol poisoning happen during weekends and national celebrations, she said, when Iranians have a respite from gruelling work and education schedules.

“During the first 24 hours after consuming methanol, the symptoms can resemble those of an ordinary hangover, making it difficult for people to recognise the danger,” she said. “They may only realise something is seriously wrong around 72 hours after consumption, when the symptoms become more severe,” she said.

World.title: Norse Atlantic ends flights: How Iran war continues to batter aviation
World.content:
The Norwegian budget carrier is the latest airline to fold under ‘eyewatering’ fuel costs driven by the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

The Norwegian airline Norse Atlantic has filed for bankruptcy for its main operating unit, cancelling all flights and halting ticket sales, as soaring jet fuel prices triggered by the United States-Israel war on Iran claim another operator.

The long-haul, low-cost carrier said on Friday that it had failed to secure the short-term financing it needs to keep flying.

It joins a growing list of carriers that have collapsed, entered restructuring or cut routes since the US-Israel war on Iran began in late February and disrupted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key artery for Gulf oil and refined fuel exports.

Here is what we know.

Why has Norse Atlantic stopped flying?

The board of the airline’s Norwegian operating subsidiary, Norse Atlantic Airways AS, filed a bankruptcy petition with the Agder District Court on Friday, after concluding there was “no longer a basis for continued operations”.

The filing came a day after the airline suspended all flights, and two days after it warned that its financial position was “critical”. Its shares closed 85 percent lower on Thursday.

“If a short-term financing solution is not secured urgently, it is the board’s intention to file for bankruptcy,” the company said as it grounded its fleet.

A day later, it confirmed that no rescue had materialised. “Despite extensive efforts, the company has so far not been able to secure sufficient funding to meet its short-term liquidity needs,” Norse Atlantic ASA said.

“We were unable to absorb the extra cost … Fuel is what toppled this company,” Chief Executive Officer Eivind Roald told Norwegian public broadcaster NRK.



The bankruptcy covers only the Norwegian operating unit. Roald said the listed parent company, Norse Atlantic ASA, and its UK subsidiary were still trying to find a solution for the remaining parts of the business.

“The Board of Norse Atlantic Airways AS has made the difficult decision to file for bankruptcy despite extensive efforts from the Company and the Group to find a solution,” Roald said in a statement.

“Many airlines hedge their fuel purchases and stockpile fuel to protect themselves against crises like this. Norse Atlantic did not hedge at all, so it had no protection against rising prices,” aviation analyst John Strickland told Al Jazeera.

As a result, the airline was left fully exposed to spot prices on routes that burn large quantities of fuel.

“Passengers are also unsure about booking flights at a time like this, and the airline faces stiff competition on transatlantic routes,” he said.

Operations at the airline had been shrinking for months. Roald said in May that Norse had cancelled more than 700 flights since the war began and cut 75 jobs that month in a bid to save $50m. It dropped its Los Angeles summer schedule in April and later announced it would pull its New York routes.

The final blow came when the lessors of its Boeing 787 fleet issued termination notices for all of its aircraft, a move Norse is contesting.

“It means Norse Atlantic is unlikely to continue operating because the lessors have terminated those contracts,” Strickland said. “Those lessors want to protect their finances, so if they doubt that Norse Atlantic will pay what it owes, they will terminate the contracts.”

He added that Norse “had favourable contracts before they were terminated”, terms it is unlikely to secure again.

Which other airlines have collapsed or cut back?

The first major casualty after the start of the US-Iran war, which has triggered oil shortages, was Spirit Airlines. The US ultra-low-cost carrier ceased operations on May 2 after talks for a $500m federal rescue failed, citing a spike in fuel prices as a key factor. Spirit, which had filed for bankruptcy twice since 2024, had been flying for 34 years.

“It is with great disappointment that on May 2, 2026, Spirit Airlines started an orderly wind-down of our operations, effective immediately,” the carrier said in a statement.

In Europe, Latvia’s national carrier airBaltic abandoned expansion plans in August and entered Chapter 11 restructuring in the US, citing fuel costs and disruption tied to the Iran war. On October 5, it said it would cut 500 to 700 of its roughly 3,000 jobs and fly a smaller fleet to fewer destinations.



The airline said the redundancies would ensure the “company’s structure and cost base are aligned with the future scale of the carrier”.

In Spain, the Barcelona-based low-cost airline Volotea began formal negotiations with creditors on September 29 under the country’s pre-insolvency procedure. It puts the cost of higher fuel prices since March at about 150 million euros ($174m) and plans to shrink its fleet from 44 aircraft to 30-35, although its flights continue to operate.

“The impact of the war this year will be around 150 million euros, despite everyone’s efforts and decent fuel hedging for the first months,” Volotea’s chief executive told staff, according to the French travel trade outlet TourMaG.

Spanish long-haul carrier Plus Ultra suspended flights to Colombia in June, blaming an “unprecedented increase” in fuel costs. On November 17, it indefinitely suspended its Madrid routes to Buenos Aires and Lima as part of a financial and operational restructuring, leaving Venezuela as its only remaining market.

Larger airlines have also trimmed their networks. United Airlines said in March that it would cut capacity by 5 percent on less profitable routes, while several European carriers, including KLM and Finnair, have extended suspensions of flights to Gulf hubs into 2027.

“The impact has been huge,” Strickland said. “We have already seen a number of bankruptcies, especially among small, privately owned airlines in Europe. We have also seen midsize and regional European carriers struggling and restructuring their debt.”

He warned that the squeeze “will affect the market for low-cost, long-haul flights”.

Why are airlines struggling?

“The main challenge is the fallout from the war involving the United States, Israel and Iran,” Strickland said. “The crisis is affecting oil supplies from the Gulf, and that has driven up the price of fuel.”

Global jet fuel averaged about $99 a barrel on February 27, the day before the war began, according to the International Air Transport Association (IATA). It more than doubled to $209 in April. After easing in early summer, prices climbed again, averaging about $190 a barrel in early October and more than $200 in Europe.

The rise is not only for crude. Refineries in the Gulf supplied about one-fifth of the world’s jet fuel and kerosene exports before the war, and disruption to that supply has pushed the “crack spread” – the premium of jet fuel over crude oil – to record levels. As a result, jet fuel has risen in price far faster than oil itself.

The IATA expects the industry’s fuel bill to rise to about $350bn this year from $252bn in 2025, with fuel accounting for 31.4 percent of operating costs, up from about 25 percent. For some low-cost carriers, fuel can account for as much as 60 percent of costs.

It forecasts that global airline profits will halve to $23bn, with net margins of just 2 percent.

“War-related disruptions in the Middle East and rising fuel costs have shifted the outlook for airlines to the worse,” IATA Director General Willie Walsh said when the forecast was released in June.



IATA’s chief economist, Marie Owens Thomsen, said: “This is eye-watering stuff,” according to Aviation Week. “It will affect absolutely everyone in the global economy.”

Airlines have passed part of the extra cost on to travellers. US airfares were 23.4 percent higher in August than a year earlier, and the five biggest US carriers earned 18 percent more passenger revenue in the third quarter even as traffic grew by less than 1 percent.

“Even when airlines hedge against crises like this, the higher costs will still be passed on to passengers,” Strickland said.

Budget long-haul carriers are the most exposed, however, because their customers will not pay much more for a ticket. “They depend on price-sensitive travellers, and with fuel costing more, they haven’t been able to sell many seats at prices that work for them,” Strickland said.

“They don’t have the same market power as Qatar Airways and other carriers,” he added.

How have Middle East airlines fared?

They were hit hardest by the start of the US-Israel war on Iran at first. Emirates, Qatar Airways and Etihad all halted operations during the most intense, earlier phase of the war, and have flown reduced schedules since.

The damage shows in the numbers. Emirates reported a 68 percent drop in half-year profits before tax to $1bn for the six months to September 30, with capacity down 17 percent and passenger traffic down 25 percent.

But the Gulf carriers have remained profitable while others have failed, and several factors are now working in their favour.

Their first advantage is having fuel on their doorstep. Emirates, Qatar Airways, Etihad and Saudia operate close to some of the world’s largest refining centres and, with Gulf refiners unable to export normally, local stocks have grown. Qatar’s reserve cover has risen by more than five months and the UAE’s by about 15 days, according to Bloomberg.

Gulf governments are also working to cut their exposure to the strait. Thani bin Ahmed Al Zeyoudi, the UAE minister of state for foreign trade, said he expected a plan to reduce reliance on the Strait of Hormuz, particularly for oil, to zero by the end of this year, the Emirati daily Emarat Al Youm reported.

While still much more expensive than before the war, jet fuel is cheaper in the region than in the rest of the world. In early October, jet fuel averaged about $165 a barrel in the Middle East, compared with more than $200 in Europe, IATA data shows.

The Gulf carriers also have deeper pockets and better protection than airlines like Norse. Emirates’ fuel costs before hedging rose 60 percent, but $1.9bn in hedging gains cut the net rise to 13 percent, and the region’s big airlines entered the crisis with large cash reserves to absorb the rest.

Competition has thinned, too. Many foreign airlines have stayed away from Gulf airports, with Finnair suspending flights to Dubai and Doha until March 27, 2027, and KLM’s Dubai service suspended until March 2027. That leaves more of the market to home carriers.

Strickland pointed to that market power as the key difference between Gulf carriers such as Qatar Airways and budget operators such as Norse, which have had to compete on price alone.

The advantage has limits, however. Qatar Airways has trimmed its departures by about 7 percent for the northern winter schedule, and the Gulf carriers remain exposed to any renewed fighting in the region.

What is the outlook for 2027?

Airline executives expect little relief.

Panellists at an IATA energy forum this month warned that jet fuel prices could spike again in 2027 as inventories shrink and spare refining capacity remains limited.



Some airlines are testing whether they could withstand $200-a-barrel jet fuel in 2027, according to the Reuters news agency.

Raising fares has limits. “Fares are really determined by demand rather than the cost inputs,” Oliver Wyman consultant Scott Laurence told Reuters, warning about the risks of deeper capacity cuts.

Many are heading into next year less protected. Ryanair has hedged only about 25 percent of its fuel for the year from April 2027, and Turkish Airlines just 12 percent. Air France-KLM is modelling a 2027 fuel bill, after hedging, of 10.4 billion euros ($12bn), up from 9.2 billion euros this year.

Airlines are also wary of locking in today’s prices. “The risk is that oil prices might roll off and we catch ourselves on the wrong side of the market,” Ryanair chief executive Michael O’Leary told analysts this month.

That points to higher fares and further capacity cuts, particularly on marginal routes.

World.title: Taiwan opposition party wins re-election in Taipei mayoral race
World.content:
Voters across Taiwan have cast ballots for mayors, council members and other local leaders.

The candidate for Taiwan’s opposition Kuomintang party (KMT) has secured re-election in the mayoral race for the capital, Taipei, after his main rival conceded defeat.

Voters on Saturday cast ballots for some 11,000 positions across Taiwan’s 16 counties and “six municipalities”, or largest cities, in local elections closely watched by China, which considers the self-ruling island to be a part of its territory and has pledged reunification by force if necessary.

The DPP looked set to clinch half of the municipalities, taking back Taichung – the island’s second most populous city – along with Tainan and Kaohsiung.

But its Taipei candidate, academic Puma Shen, conceded defeat late on Saturday to incumbent Chiang Wan-an of the KMT. Chiang won by a double-digit margin in the previous election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate.

In addition to the capital, the KMT is likely to win the other two municipalities: New Taipei City, the most populous of the six municipalities, and Taoyuan.

Election campaigns ahead of the vote centred on domestic issues including transport, childcare and the environment, rather than disputed ties with China.

The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the ruling DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims. KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April.

Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defence said 33 Chinese warplanes encircled Taiwan on Friday, including bombers and fighter jets, along with eight warships.



The KMT dominated the last local elections, winning across 14 cities and counties. The DPP managed only 5, while other parties and independents took 3.

Preparations and campaigns for the 2028 presidential and parliamentary elections are expected to start after Saturday’s election results.

President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP is likely to run again, while outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen could be the KMT’s frontrunner.

World.title: Tarantulas, scorpions and more found in luggage at Peru airport
World.content:
Tarantulas, scorpions and more found in luggage at Peru airport

NewsFeed Tarantulas, scorpions and more found in luggage at Peru airport

Peruvian authorities have intercepted two Chinese nationals at Lima’s international airport as they attempted to smuggle 677 wildlife specimens to China in their luggage. The haul, including hundreds of tarantulas, centipedes and scorpions, was valued at $100,000.

World.title: India fumble chances as New Zealand finish day two on top in Christchurch
World.content:
India limp to 116-6 at stumps on day two of the second Test, in reply to the Black Caps’ first innings 356.

Share India fumble chances as New Zealand finish day two on top in Christchurch on social media

India fumbled their chances with bat and ball as a clinical New Zealand finished day two of the second Test well on top, with their pace bowlers shining in the Christchurch sun on Saturday.

India ⁠were 116-6 at stumps in reply to the Black Caps’ first innings 356, with Dhruv Jurel on seven not out and tailender Akash Deep next in the line of fire after Washington Sundar’s dismissal for 10 wrapped up play.

It was ⁠a formidable display by the home quicks, who shared the wickets around and had the ball swinging wildly on a tricky Hagley Oval pitch.

Kyle Jamieson and Jacob Duffy grabbed two wickets apiece, with Nathan Smith and Matt Henry each chipping in another.

Smith landed a hammer blow with the final ball of the day, having Sundar edge a short ball to captain Tom Latham in the slips, ending ‌a tortured, 60-ball knock.

India’s hopes of remaining in contention for the World Test Championship final were already on a knife-edge. They may now be doomed.

Only victory will keep them in the hunt, and that looks far-fetched after a day of poor fielding and squandered starts with the bat.

After dropping Latham on 29 on day one and seeing the opener go on to score 59, India spilled another four catches in the innings after winning the toss and sending the Black Caps in to bat.

Wicketkeeper Tom Blundell, dropped on 49 in the gully, finished with his team’s top score of 89 before ⁠top-edging a Gurnoor Brar delivery to be caught at long leg.

India pacer Akash Deep saw three ⁠chances grassed before he could finally celebrate a five-wicket haul when tailender Henry was caught slogging.



Deep’s 5-99 was a rare highlight for India in the field, with pace spearhead Jasprit Bumrah frustrated and wicketless.

India piled on 720-9 in one innings in the drawn first test in Wellington but their top-order batters squandered their starts in Christchurch.

Henry struck with the sixth ball to remove opener Yashasvi Jaiswal for a duck before towering quick Jamieson had number three Devdutt Padikkal caught behind for 21.

Jamieson’s ⁠steepling bounce also knocked over captain Shubman Gill, who edged to the slips ⁠to be out for 17.

A charging Pant tried to seize back control from the bowlers with typical aggression but threw his wicket away for 23 with a big swing at Duffy.

KL Rahul then suffered a moment of madness as he got down on one knee and sliced a drive straight to Devon Conway at ‌point to be out for 25.

Jurel, whose seven runs were eked out of 45 deliveries, and Sundar held on for some 90 minutes in the final session but could barely nudge the score forward.

With New Zealand’s tail-end batters contributing a handy 66 ‌runs ‌between them, Gill will desperately hope for the same lower-order starch from India on day three.

It may still do little to prevent a big New Zealand lead and a platform for the hosts to take a series-sealing victory.

World.title: Security tries to remove Palestinian flag at Selfridges on Black Friday
World.content:
Security tries to remove Palestinian flag at Selfridges on Black Friday

NewsFeed Security tries to remove Palestinian flag at Selfridges on Black Friday

Pro-Palestinian protesters demonstrated in a Selfridges department store in London on Black Friday. They unfurled a Palestinian flag and urged shoppers to boycott brands linked to Israel as security tried to intervene.

World.title: Israel unity government talks stall: What happens now?
World.content:
Eisenkot struggles to form a government as talks with Netanyahu stall over rotation deal and coalition compromises.

The future of Israel’s government remains unclear following October elections that produced no clear winner.

The leader of the centrist Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, and his main rival, caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s Likud party, have been convening for rounds of talks in a bid to establish a “unity government”.

But the talks ended on Sunday without a conclusive deal, with the two parties announcing that a “follow-up” meeting will be held soon.

So, what is the latest on the talks? And what happens if they fail to reach an agreement?

Here’s what we know.

Why are Eisenkot and Netanyahu in talks?

Following the October 27 general election, Israeli President Isaac Herzog held consultations with political parties to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority. Eisenkot and his presumed partners won 48 seats between them, while Netanyahu’s alliance won 53.

Some 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot to form the next government, while only 46 backed Netanyahu.

In November, Eisenkot was instructed by Israel’s president to form a new government by December 6, with a deadline that can be extended by 14 days.

In order to form a government, one party, alliance or coalition requires a minimum 61 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. This means Eisenkot must ally with other parties or lawmakers to make up the seat numbers.

Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats in the election. But Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with them, which would have given him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over Israel’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats.



He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote.

Until this week, Eisenkot had struck firm coalition deals with only the Democrats and Yisrael Beiteinu, bringing his total to 36 seats out of a potential 48 – still far from any majority.

Eisenkot has, therefore, been talking to Netanyahu’s right-wing Likud party in hopes of establishing a unity government, but Likud wants a rotation deal that would go against Eisenkot’s promise to replace Netanyahu.

The talks have caused other complications as well. The left-wing Democrats party, which won eight parliament seats, separately said it was suspending talks with Eisenkot this week in protest at the prospect of Netanyahu’s party remaining in government.

What’s the latest on the talks?

On Tuesday, the Yashar party announced that it agreed to sign a coalition pact with the Yisrael Beiteinu party, after meeting with leader Avigdor Lieberman, marking the first confirmed alliance since the election.

Israeli media also reported on Friday that Netanyahu is “preparing” to announce that he is willing to serve second in a prime minister rotation with Eisenkot under a unity government deal.

Israel’s public broadcaster Kan reported that the offer had already been proposed unofficially, so Likud could assume “plausible deniability”, as the party remains conflicted on the terms of the offer.

The rotation deal would mean that Eisenkot would serve for the first two years as prime minister, and Netanyahu would serve the final two years.

But in a statement on Friday, Eisenkot accused the Likud party of stalling coalition talks in a bid to bring about new elections. He claimed that Likud was “unwilling to compromise, and, over two weeks, refused to put a single concrete proposal on the table”.

Eisenkot said the two sides are “approaching a moment of decision”, but the question is “whether Likud will engage in serious negotiations and commit to a partnership that requires compromise or keep up appearances and continue to stall”.

Meanwhile, Eisenkot is grappling with division among his own side as the options of forging alliances with ultra-Orthodox parties or the Arab-majority parties, who are willing to back him, have proved controversial.

The Arab-led parties could give Yashar 19 seats, but Lieberman has said he will not support any government that includes those parties.

Why is Eisenkot accusing Netanyahu of ‘stalling’?

Eisenkot said Likud’s negotiating team had refused to meet more frequently over the past two weeks. The two sides have met five times.



He added that their team was uncooperative and had rejected three proposals, including one for a state inquiry into the “failures” of October 7, the removal of “extremists” from government and a law making military or national service mandatory for all.

Instead, Eisenkot claimed that Likud proposed “the worst” proposal for a unity government with “the same government, the same partners, no change, no conscription law”.

Eisenkot said Netanyahu’s strategy is to “run down the clock until the mandate expires”, attempting to “drag Israel into another election under the outgoing government”.

“I do not intend to cooperate with such a charade,” he added.

What happens if no agreement is reached?

One of Eisenkot’s options is to reach a deal with the country’s two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas. But if talks with them fail, analysts say Eisenkot could ask his allies to choose between keeping Netanyahu in office or accepting support from the Arab-led parties.

The Joint List, an alliance of three Arab parties, holds 11 seats in the Knesset, while Ra’am holds eight.

Daniel Levy, a former Israeli peace negotiator and president of the US/Middle East Project, told Al Jazeera that if this were to happen, Eisenkot could tell his allies to “form a government for a few months, just to get Bibi [Netanyahu] out of power and prepare for new elections”.

Analysts say that if Eisenkot reaches his deadline of December 6 to form a government without a decision, Israeli President Herzog could assign the task to another member of the Knesset, including Netanyahu, and give them a 28-day period to form a government with no extensions.

If still no government is formed, Israel could move towards a new round of elections, with Netanyahu remaining caretaker prime minister until a government is formed.

This happened in 2019, after the April election, when Netanyahu was unable to form a government. As a result, the Knesset was dissolved and a second election took place in September that year. Again, no majority was reached, leading to a third vote in March 2020. A government was finally formed later that month when Netanyahu struck a unity government deal with Benny Gantz’s Blue and White alliance.

World.title: Argentina's bid to stop Falklands oil drilling rejected
World.content:
Argentina's bid to block an oil exploration project near the Falkland Islands has been rejected by a UN-backed international tribunal.

The Argentinian government had called for the Sea Lion venture to be halted as it claimed there was an ongoing dispute over the sovereignty of the Falklands, a British overseas territory. The UK has repeatedly rejected that claim.

Speaking on Saturday, the president of the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea said it was the wrong court to rule on questions of sovereignty.The decision was upheld in a vote 18-3.

After the ruling, Argentina's President Javier Milei said "this decision is not the final word" and declared "the Falkland Islands are Argentine".

In a joint statement, UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves said that Buenos Aires must "respect the right of the Falkland Islanders to determine their own future."

"Argentina sought to stop the Falkland Islanders making their own sovereign decisions and failed in this attempt," they wrote, urging Argentina to "end its wider economic pressure" against the territory.

The case is the latest diplomatic row between the UK and Argentina, which fought a 74-day war over the islands in 1982.

Buenos Aires argued that while it believed there was a territorial dispute over the Falklands, nothing should be done that could change the situation - including the building of oil wells.

The UK responded that the Law of the Sea court had no jurisdiction over the issue, and that pausing the Sea Lion project could have huge economic consequences on the islands' local population and companies connected with the venture.

The tribunal's decision ultimately rested on its own powers - this was a territorial issue, and a maritime court was not the right place to hear the dispute.

Buenos Aires disagreed, writing in a statement after the decision that "Argentina did not ask the court to rule on sovereignty", but to apply the United Nation's sea laws to the UK over its "exploitation of our resources".

It also said that five individuals would face sanctions for their involvement in the oil drilling venture, something Milei had been threatening. The statement did not specify who the sanctions would be against.

"The message is clear: those who participate in the illegal exploitation of our resources will face the consequences," the statement said.

World.title: Two staff killed in Israeli strike on Gaza medical clinic, MSF says
World.content:
Two workers for the medical charity MÃ©decins Sans FrontiÃ¨res (MSF) have been killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza, according to the organisation.

MSF said the strike was a direct hit on one of the charity's clinics, the location of which was known by the Israeli military.

In a statement, the Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the two people were Hamas operatives "acting as security guards at a clinic operated by MSF". The IDF added the strike was "not directed at a hospital" and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.

The head of the World Health Organization (WHO) said that attacks on health facilities and health workers in Gaza were "outrageous and unacceptable".

In a post on X, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus wrote: "Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked."

In its statement, MSF - which is also known as Doctors Without Borders - said that the two workers who were killed were watchmen, and added that the strike brought the number of its colleagues killed in Gaza to 17.

The organisation said it was "devastated and outraged" and added: "âOur premises were clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military."

In its own post on X, the IDF said that the two men, who they named as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, were "terrorists in Hamas' military wing".

The Israeli military added it was another example of Hamas "embedding itself within international organizations".

It said that "precautionary measures were taken to minimize harm to civilians" before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had "advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops".

Witnesses told the BBC the two men were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended and fired a missile.

Video footage from the scene of the strike showed a small crater beside a plastic chair, with bloodstains and limited damage in a courtyard behind the medical clinic.

Hundreds of Palestinians have since attended the funeral of the MSF workers, carrying the two bodies, wrapped in white plastic bags and placed on stretchers, on their shoulders as they made their way through the streets of the city.

Mohammed Imad, a close friend of Abu Hasira, one of the men killed, said he had seen him just hours before the attack.

"He was a peaceful, kind-hearted man. His only concern was looking after his wife, his two children and his mother," he told the BBC.

He said Abu Hasira had no affiliation with any armed group and had worked at the clinic for a long time.

The two workers' deaths follow an increase in Israeli strikes across Gaza over the past week.

Gaza's civil defence spokesman said eight Palestinians were killed in Israeli attacks across the Strip during the day, including the two MSF workers.

Violence has continued in Gaza since Israel and Hamas agreed to a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

At least 1,705 people have been killed in Gaza over the past 13 months, according to the territory's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

The humanitarian situation also remains dire, with heavy rainfall earlier this month causing flooding and damage to tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

The UN and its partners have called on Israel - which controls Gaza's crossings - to allow in more supplies to help Palestinians prepare for the winter, including tents, heaters and water pumps, as well as vaccines and medicines to combat infectious diseases.

The Gaza war was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on southern Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 others were taken hostage.

Since then, more than 74,770 people have been killed in Israeli attacks in Gaza, the health ministry says.

World.title: Afghanistan explosion kills 10 students and injures more than 100, official says
World.content:
At least 10 students have been killed and 110 others have been injured following an explosion near a school in Afghanistan, a spokesperson has told the BBC.

The incident happened on Saturday morning in the Anderseir area of Asadabad, the capital of Kunar province, the spokesperson for the Taliban government's interior ministry said.

Posting on X, Abdul Mateen Qani said that according to initial investigations, the blast was caused by "negligence and carelessness" at an explosives depot belonging to nearby mining companies.

An investigation into the incident was ongoing, he added.

The province's culture and information director Sami ul Haq Bayan said the blast took place in a house near Shagai Middle School in Asadabad as explosives were being prepared for mining and blasting rock, reports AFP.

The Associated Press also cites the official saying up to 15 wounded people remain in hospital, while the rest have been discharged after treatment.

Pictures from inside a damaged classroom show shattered glass and debris surrounding abandoned shoes and school bags.

World.title: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
World.content:
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, SÃ¡nchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.

The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.

SÃ¡nchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.

FeijÃ³o sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.

Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, AragÃ³n, and Castilla y LeÃ³n.

FeijÃ³o has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.

"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.

One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by SÃ¡nchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".

World.title: OpenAI counter-sues Apple over alleged theft of trade secrets
World.content:
ChatGPT-maker OpenAI has counter-sued Apple, alleging that the iPhone maker stole trade secrets through a former employee.

In a federal lawsuit filed in July, Apple sued the artificial intelligence (AI) company and two of its employees who previously worked for Apple, claiming it had engaged in a "pattern of theft" of proprietary information.

A countersuit, filed in California on Friday, alleged that Apple gained confidential information through the hiring of a former OpenAI employee and accuses it of discouraging hardware suppliers from working on future OpenAI devices.

Apple denied the counterclaims, describing them as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own case.

OpenAI is developing AI-enabled personal devices, which it claims in the countersuit could threaten to "outcompete Apple on what Apple views as its own turf".

The filing alleged Apple had gained confidential information by rehiring a former employee who had worked at OpenAI for six months.

OpenAI accused the employee, who it said gained access to information on a new device and the company's roadmap for future physical products, of sending "dozens of OpenAI documents" to his personal phone numbers. It also said he presented OpenAI's plans to senior Apple staff "at Apple's request".

OpenAI said: "Given the timing, it now appears that stealing those documents may have been his reason for joining OpenAI in the first place."

The counterclaim also alleged Apple encourages employees to mix work files with their personal iCloud (Apple's cloud storage service) accounts so it could later accuse those who leave to work for competitors of theft.

A spokesperson for Apple said: "This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products - not about inadvertent retention of Apple information."

In its own lawsuit, the tech giant alleged that at least two long-time Apple workers who left the company to join OpenAI took part in a "pattern of theft" by emailing themselves internal Apple information.

Apple also accused the AI firm of undertaking a "strategy to extract Apple's confidential information".

A spokesperson for OpenAI previously denied the claims, telling the BBC: "We have no interest in other companies' trade secrets."

Along with OpenAI, and two former Apple employees, Apple is also suing io Products, the design startup founded by Sir Jony Ive, a long-time Apple executive who designed the iMac, iPod, iPhone and iPad.

OpenAI acquired the company last year in a $6.5bn (Â£4.7bn) deal.

World.title: Eight killed in Peruvian military helicopter crash
World.content:
Eight military personnel have been killed in a helicopter crash in a remote area of Peru known for growing and trafficking drugs.

Authorities say the aircraft came down near the town of Sanabamba during a mission to evacuate an army patrol in the valley of the Apurimac, Ene, and Mantaro rivers, known by its Spanish acronym VRAEM.

Often referred to as 'Cocaine Valley', the area is Peru's largest coca-growing valley where gangs and the remnants of the former Shining Path rebel group operate.

The Peruvian ministry of defence said the pilot was the sole survivor of the crash, the cause of which is still unknown.

In its statement, the ministry said "search and rescue operations located the aircraft and the nine military personnel who were on board".

It named the pilot as Enzo Espinoza Roque and said he was evacuated to Lima to "receive specialised medical treatment".

The aircraft was reported missing on Thursday night after rescuing three army personnel.

No further information was shared about why the group needed to be rescued, but it was confirmed that they were among those who were killed in the crash.

Joint Command of the Peruvian Armed Forces posted a tribute online extending "deepest condolences to the family members, friends, and comrades-in-arms of the members of our VRAEM Special Command who lost their lives while carrying out a military mission. May God keep them in His glory".

In February, a MI-17 helicopter crashed in southern Peru in February killing all 15 on board.

Peru, along with Colombia, is one of the world's largest producers of coca leaves and cocaine, according to the United Nations.

World.title: Australian wrestler Bronson Reed dies aged 38, WWE says
World.content:
Professional wrestler Bronson Reed has died aged 38, World Wrestling Entertainment (WWE) has announced.

The company said the wrestler, whose real name is Jermaine Haley, died on Friday due to medical complications but did not give further details.

Paying tribute, WWE added: "Jermaine was a larger-than-life figure in WWE, but more importantly, he was a phenomenal person, a devoted family man, and a beloved colleague."

They also offered condolences to the Australian's family, including his pregnant wife, Paige, and their daughter.

WWE has been contacted for further comment.

Haley was honoured at the WWE event at Akins Ford Arena in Athens, Georgia on Friday.

The show began with a 10-bell salute for Haley and in his match, Canadian wrestler Kevin Owens wore an armband that read "Bronson" and addressed the crowd.

Owens said Haley loved performing.

"I knew for a fact, beyond performing in this ring, he loved his family more than anything so tonight if there is anything to take away from a tragedy like that - it's take care of each other and love each other... Forgive each other," Owens said.

"Bronson, for me, we were lucky to have you and you will be extremely missed."

WWE greats posted tributes online including the retired 16-time world champion Ric Flair, who wrote: "another soldier in our business that left us way too early!"

WWE Hall of Famer Diamond Dallas Page said "I was deeply saddened to read about the passing of Bronson Reed. I couldn't help but think of Eddie. Such a shame. My heart goes out to his friends & family. RIP brother."

WWE wrestler Eddie Guerrero - known as Latino Heat - died of heart failure at age 38 in 2005.

World.title: 'Poison seller' Kenneth Law apologises in court to the families of his victims
World.content:
The Canadian man who sold toxic chemicals through online suicide forums in 40 countries apologised in court to the families of the victims, saying he deeply regrets his actions and will never repeat them.

Kenneth Law made the remarks on Friday during a sentencing hearing where prosecutors asked a judge to give him a 25-year prison term.

The 61-year-old pleaded guilty in May to 14 counts of aiding the suicide deaths of 14 people in Ontario, Canada, though he has admitted to causing the deaths of dozens of victims in England and Wales.

He will not face charges in the UK or over any British deaths under a plea deal which saw Canadian authorities withdraw more serious charges of murder.

During Friday's sentencing hearing in an Ontario court, prosecutors stressed that many of his victims were young and struggling with mental distress.

If Law receives the prosecution's recommended sentence, he would serve just under 20 years in prison, after accounting for credit for time served since his May 2023 arrest.

As she sought to make her case in court on Friday, Crown Attorney Kathleen Doherty described Law as a predator taking advantage of "vulnerable people".

"What they needed was help. But what they found was Mr Law and his products for death," Doherty said.

She also said Law's motives were financial.

"If people could pay, he sold it to them. There's no discussion or inquiries or anything going on whereby Mr Law would have any ability to appreciate the circumstances of the individual he was dealing with," she said.

Law's defence lawyer, Matthew Gourlay, countered those claims, arguing that his client was not responsible for any of their battles with mental illness..

"Each of these incidents is its own unique tragedy," Gourlay said. "Mr Law may be a common denominator between them, but Mr Law was not the cause of the struggles and hardships that caused all these victims to seek out his products in the first place."

He said Law held a "misguided belief" he was helping his victims

Law's defence attorney has asked the court to give him a 12-year sentence.

At the end of the hearing, Law told the court that he had deep regret for aiding in the suicide deaths of his victims.

"To the families of the victims, words can never replace the loss of your loved ones. I convey my deepest condolences. I remain remorseful. I'm sorry."

The sentencing hearing followed an emotional few days of testimony in September, when grieving family members and friends told the court of the pain Law had caused.

Those impact statements will be taken into account at sentencing, which is due at a later date.

Authorities said the former chef sold about 1,200 packages of toxic substances to recipients - who he met in online suicide forums - in 40 countries, roughly a quarter of which were sent to the UK.

If you or anyone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this article, details of organisations offering information are available at BBC Action Line

World.title: Tinubu tasks Energy Commission with accelerating Nigeria’s bioenergy industry
World.content:
President Bola Tinubu has directed the Energy Commission of Nigeria (ECN) to accelerate the development of the country’s bioenergy industry as part of his administration’s efforts to reduce dependence on petrol and diesel, lower energy costs and create jobs.

The president gave the directive following Nigeria’s admission as a Partner Country of the Global Bioenergy Partnership (GBEP), an international initiative hosted by the Food and Agriculture Organisation of the United Nations (FAO).

According to a statement issued by the president’s spokesperson, Bayo Onanuga, on Saturday, Nigeria was admitted into the partnership on 5 November in Rome, Italy.

The statement said the development followed the Federal Executive Council’s approval of the Strategic Plan of the Nigeria Bioenergy Partnership.

Bioenergy refers to energy derived from biomass, including organic materials of plant and animal origin, as well as their waste and by-products. These materials can be converted into electricity, heat and fuels through various processes.

Diversifying Nigeria’s energy sources

Since assuming office in 2023, Mr Tinubu has introduced several initiatives aimed at diversifying Nigeria’s energy sources and reducing energy costs.

These include the Presidential Initiative on Compressed Natural Gas (Pi-CNG), whose mandate was later expanded to include electric vehicles, and the establishment of the Presidential Committee on Green Economic Initiatives.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Nigeria’s participation in the Global Bioenergy Partnership is expected to build on these efforts by creating opportunities to harness the country’s agricultural resources and biomass potential.

The president said Nigeria had no reason to overlook the economic benefits of converting agricultural waste and other organic materials into commercially viable energy products.

“Developing a domestic biofuel industry will open new markets for Nigerian farmers, create employment opportunities and stimulate manufacturing, particularly in rural communities,” Mr Tinubu said.

“I expect the Commission to translate Nigeria’s membership of the Partnership into investments, new industries and more affordable energy for Nigerians.”

He commended the Director-General of the Energy Commission of Nigeria, Mustapha Abdullahi, and his team for securing the country’s admission into the partnership and advancing the federal government’s energy diversification policy.

Mr Tinubu also urged the commission to work with the private sector to establish biofuel production facilities across the country without compromising national food security.

Nigeria seeks investment in bioenergy sector

In a separate statement issued on 24 November, the Energy Commission said Nigeria’s admission into the partnership marked a significant milestone in the country’s sustainable energy development efforts.

It said Mr Abdullahi represented the federal government at the 32nd GBEP Steering Committee Meeting in Rome, where he formally endorsed the partnership’s Terms of Reference on behalf of Nigeria.

In his acceptance speech, Mr Abdullahi expressed the country’s appreciation to the partnership and reaffirmed Nigeria’s commitment to contributing to global efforts towards sustainable bioenergy development, energy security and climate action.

He also presented Nigeria as a potential destination for sustainable bioenergy investments, highlighting its abundant agricultural resources, biomass potential and opportunities across several areas.
