These include bioethanol, biodiesel, biogas, biomass-based electricity generation, sustainable aviation fuel and waste-to-energy.

The commission said Mr Abdullahi called on GBEP partners and international investors to deepen collaboration with Nigeria, emphasising the need for strategic partnerships, investment mobilisation and an enabling policy environment to unlock the sector’s economic and environmental benefits.

As Nigeria’s designated focal point to the partnership, the Energy Commission will coordinate the country’s participation in its programmes, including those focused on sustainability, capacity building and international knowledge exchange.

The commission said membership would provide Nigeria with a stronger platform for international cooperation, investment opportunities and technology and knowledge transfer, positioning the country to play a greater role in sustainable bioenergy development in Africa and beyond.

World.title: Two MSF workers killed in Israeli strike on Gaza
World.content:
Two workers for the medical charity, Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF), were killed in an Israeli strike in Gaza on Friday.

This brings the total number of MSF officials killed in Gaza to 17, according to MSF.

The organisation reported that the strike directly hit one of the charity’s clinics, which was clearly marked with its logo. The Israeli military knew the clinic’s location.

“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight. This is a direct hit on MSF, bringing the total number of MSF colleagues killed in Gaza to 17,” it wrote on X.

The BBC reported that the two men, identified as Muhammad Hasira and Moaz Alitsbach, were sitting at the clinic entrance when an Israeli drone descended.

The World Health Organisation (WHO) described the attack as “outrageous and unacceptable.”

In a post on X, Director-General Tedros Ghebreyesus wrote: “Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

But the Israeli military said the two MSF workers killed were members of Hamas and accused them of planning attacks against Israeli forces.

Israel said the case was another example of Hamas “embedding itself within international organisations.”

It also stated the strike was “not directed at a hospital” and caused no damage to medical infrastructure.

It said, “precautionary measures were taken to minimise harm to civilians” before the strike on Gaza City, adding the men had “advanced plans to carry out attacks against Israeli civilians & IDF troops.”

Israel did not provide any evidence to support this claim.

READ ALSO: Ukraine denies expanding war with Russia after Libya attack

Since 2023, Israel has deliberately targeted humanitarian workers, journalists, and medical professionals in Gaza. It has justified its violence with allegations of Hamas infiltration. Israeli forces have also targeted civilian infrastructure and launched a genocide campaign against Palestinians in Gaza.

Violence in Gaza has also persisted despite a US-brokered ceasefire in October last year. Israeli strikes take place almost daily in areas under the control of Hamas, which are home to 2.1 million people, most of them displaced.

Gaza Health Ministry estimates that at least 1,705 people have been killed over the past 13 months,

The humanitarian situation also remains dire. Weeks ago, heavy rainfall caused flooding and damaged tens of thousands of shelters for displaced families.

World.title: Wanogho wins Nigeria’s first gold at World Para Powerlifting Championships
World.content:
Nigeria’s Cynthia Wanogho has won the country’s first gold medal at the 2026 World Para Powerlifting Championships in Bahrain, lifting 112kg to emerge champion in the women’s up to 50kg category.

The 29-year-old secured the title in her first international competition, delivering an impressive performance to beat her rivals and give Nigeria an early boost at the championships.

Wanogho lifted 112kg on her second attempt to clinch gold, finishing ahead of Alfiia Zimagullova, who lifted 105kg to win silver, while Kazakhstan’s Gulim Kurmanbayeva claimed bronze with 104kg.

Her victory marks a significant breakthrough for the Nigerian athlete, whose first appearance on the international stage ended with a gold medal against some of the world’s competitors.

Speaking after her remarkable feat, Wanogho expressed gratitude to God and described the victory as a memorable moment in her sporting career.

“I feel so great. I feel so happy. I give thanks to God Almighty. I feel so happy. This is my first time. I thank God that gave me victory. And I pray next I will do more than this. I pray for strength and more power next time,” she said.

She said she took up powerlifting after encouragement from her coach, who noticed her potential and persuaded her to give the sport a try.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to her, she began the sport in 2015 and has since dedicated her strength and commitment to pursuing success in powerlifting.

Wanogho’s victory comes as Nigeria seeks to maintain its status among the leading countries in para powerlifting, having finished second overall at the previous World Championships in Cairo, Egypt.

Nigeria sent 17 athletes to the 12th edition of the championships, which runs from 27 November to 2 December, with Paralympic champion and world record holder Folashade Oluwafemiayo leading the contingent.

The team is targeting another strong performance after its podium finish in Cairo, with Wanogho’s gold providing an early indication of Nigeria’s medal prospects in Bahrain.

The championships bring together some of the world’s best para powerlifters, with Nigeria seeking to consolidate its reputation in the sport and add to its growing list of international achievements.

World.title: Can Adeleke’s Tinubu campaign role resolve Osun’s political disputes amid APC resentment at home?
World.content:
Osun State Governor Ademola Adeleke’s emergence as coordinator of President Bola Tinubu’s re-election campaign in the state has stirred controversy within the All Progressives Congress (APC), with some party members in the state questioning the arrangement and its implications for their political interests ahead of the 2027 general elections.

The appointment has also raised questions about what the alliance could mean for the Accord Party, on which platform Mr Adeleke won re-election in August. The governor was inaugurated for second term on Friday.

While the governor is expected to mobilise support for Mr Tinubu’s presidential bid, candidates of the Accord Party will be competing against APC candidates for seats in the Senate and the House of Representatives in the elections to be held simultaneously with the presidential poll in January 2027. The Accord Party currently holds zero Senate seat and six seats in the House of Representatives from Osun State, while APC holds two and three seats, respectively.

However, beyond the political implications for both parties, the alliance has raised a bigger question about whether Mr Adeleke’s relationship with the president could help resolve some of Osun’s longstanding political and institutional disputes in the state.

These include the protracted crisis over control of local governments and the withholding of local government allocations, as well as violent disputes over control of transport unions and motor parks in the state.

The soft spots the two leaders – Mr Tinubu and Mr Adeleke – have for each other became increasingly visible in the run-up to the Osun’s August governorship election, when Mr Tinubu’s intervention helped to reverse the restriction the Economic and Financial Crimes Commission (EFCC) placed on the state government’s bank accounts.

On 5 August, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the EFCC had obtained a court order restricting bank accounts of the Osun State government, about 10 days before the governorship election in which Mr Adeleke was seeking re-election on the Accord platform against the APC candidate, Bola Oyebamiji.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

President Tinubu subsequently directed the EFCC to approach the court to vacate the order and discontinue the action against the state government. The president described the timing of the restriction as “embarrassing,” saying it could create the impression that a federal institution was being used to interfere with the electoral process. The account was subsequently unfrozen on 22 August.

Following Mr Adeleke’s victory in the election, defeating APC’s Mr Oyebamiji, the governor publicly reaffirmed his support for Mr Tinubu’s second-term bid, describing the president as a son of Osun State. He said he wanted the president to complete his development projects and reforms, particularly in the South-west in his second term.

The political significance of the alliance is underscored by Osun’s voting pattern in the 2023 presidential election where Mr Tinubu lost Osun to Atiku Abubakar, then of the People Democratic Party (PDP). Mr Adeleke belonged to the PDP as of the time of the 2023 elections. Atiku, a former Nigerian vice president, polled 354,366 votes against Mr Tinubu’s 343,945 to win Osun, the only state in the South-west region that fell into PDP’s electoral column in the 2023 poll.

Although Mr Adeleke said his support for Mr Tinubu was not based on any agreement with the president, he maintained that he was willing to work with APC members, including Mr Oyebamiji and former governor Gboyega Oyetola, the minister of Marine and Blue Economy, to secure the president’s re-election.

But his appointment as Osun coordinator of the APC presidential campaign council on 13 October took the relationship beyond public endorsements and into a formal campaign structure.

The appointment was followed by consultations and the inauguration of a 344-member campaign council in Osogbo on 22 October. The council comprised leaders and members of the APC including Mr Oyetola, Mr Oyebamiji, and party’s state chairman, Tajudeen Lawal, as well as members of Accord Party and PDP.

However, some prominent APC figures, including Mr Oyetola, Mr Oyebamiji and Mr Lawal, were absent from the inauguration.

The APC leadership said its members were not adequately consulted nor invited, alleging that Mr Adeleke had sidelined some of its party leaders. The development fuelled concerns among party members about their place in a campaign structure headed by a governor from another political party.

Ayodele Fanibe, an APC top figure in Osun, attributed the absence of some prominent party leaders from the inauguration to what he described as Mr Adeleke’s failure to consult the party’s state leadership.

“His failure to do the right thing must have resulted in what happened at the inauguration. The party chairman said he was not informed, and that is the duty of the DG to do,” he said.

However, Olawale Rasheed, spokesperson for Mr Adeleke, disputed claims that APC leaders were not invited. He said the governor had reached out to Mr Oyetola and Mr Oyebamiji by himself via phone, but they did not answer his calls.

He added that the governor also contacted other prominent party figures and mobilised their supporters, including the APC National Secretary, Ajibola Basiru, former Osun governor Adebisi Akande and his former deputy, Iyiola Omisore, who were listed as advisers to the campaign council.

“What has the governor done wrong? We are the outsiders, the governor is an outsider. Who owns the project? APC owns the project. The instruction to inaugurate the council came from Abuja. The governor complied, and this is why the short-notice arrangement went ahead,” Mr Rasheed said.

The arrangement has therefore created an unusual political situation in Osun where Accord is leading the presidential campaign for APC.

However, beyond the electoral calculations, the alliance is also being tested by the state’s unresolved political disputes. There have been questions whether Mr Adeleke alliance with APC can help resolve the wider disputes over political and institutional control in the state.

The unresolved local government crisis

One of the biggest tests of the relationship between Mr Adeleke and Mr Tinubu is the lingering dispute over control of Osun’s 30 local governments, which has resulted in prolonged withholding of council allocations and repeated confrontations over access to council secretariats.

The crisis dates back to the local government election conducted on 15 October 2022, during the administration of Mr Oyetola of the APC.

In November 2022, the Federal High Court nullified the election in a suit marked FHC/CS/OS/103/2022, which challenged the legality of the exercise. The decision was subsequently upheld by the Court of Appeal, according to court records cited in subsequent proceedings.

The dispute intensified after Mr Adeleke defeated Mr Oyetola in the November 2022 governorship election and the new administration removed the APC-elected council officials, who were already embroiled in legal challenges over the validity of their election.

On 21 February 2025, the Osun State High Court sitting in Ilesa ordered the Osun State Independent Electoral Commission (OSIEC) to proceed with a fresh election to fill the vacant positions across the 30 local government areas. The election had initially been scheduled for 22 February.

Following the re-run election, OSIEC declared PDP candidates winners of all the chairmanship and councillorship seats. Mr Adeleke, who was then a member of the PDP, subsequently swore in the elected officials.

The APC, however, maintained that its officials elected in October 2022 were entitled to remain in office, citing a separate Court of Appeal decision which it argued had reinstated them. The disagreement over the competing claims to the council positions further complicated the legal status of the two sets of officials.

The dispute subsequently escalated into a security crisis, with rival groups laying claim to council secretariats across the state.

In February 2025, attempts by APC members to take over some council secretariats triggered violent confrontations with supporters of the PDP-backed chairpersons.

PREMIUM TIMES reported that at least five people were reportedly killed in the clashes, prompting Mr Adeleke to direct the newly elected chairpersons to stay away from the secretariats to prevent further violence.

The disagreement over which officials were entitled to control the councils also affected access to their statutory allocations from the Federation Account.

Between March 2025 and June 2026, about N216 billion earmarked for Osun’s 30 local government councils was withheld by the federal government, according to a review of Federation Account revenue-sharing data reported by The Guardian.

The figure comprised N131.5 billion for March to December 2025 and another N85.3 billion between January and June 2026.

The dispute over the withheld funds later reached the Supreme Court after the Osun State Attorney General and Commissioner for Justice, Oluwole Jimi-Bada, on behalf of the state government sued the federal government over the withheld funds.

In December 2025, PREMIUM TIMES reported that the Supreme Court struck out the suit, ruling that the Osun State Attorney General lacked the legal standing to institute the case on behalf of the local governments.

Judge Mohammed Baba-Idris who delivered the lead majority judgement of the Supreme Court held that only duly elected and inaugurated local government officials were autonomous entities with the capacity to sue and be sued.

However, while declining to entertain the suit, the court faulted the federal government’s withholding of the councils’ allocations, describing the action as a “misuse of power,” and urged the government to ensure that the funds were paid directly into the local government accounts.

“Refusal to release the funds is a clear misuse of power by the defendant, and it is a clear disobedience to the court’s order that funds should be paid only to a democratically elected government,” the justice declared.

The legal contest over control of the councils continued into 2026. In June, the Federal High Court in Osogbo dismissed a suit filed by APC elected chairpersons and councillors seeking an extension of their tenure beyond October 2025.

The court held that the claim for tenure extension lacked legal foundation. The affected officials subsequently appealed the judgement.

Following the ruling, chairpersons and councillors elected in February 2025 resumed at some council secretariats, including those in Ede North, Ede South, Iwo, Boripe and Ila, despite resistance from APC members.

The struggle over the secretariats persisted after Mr Adeleke’s re-election in August 2026, with PDP-backed chairpersons making further attempts to occupy council offices and facing resistance from APC members.

The recurring confrontations further exposed the absence of a lasting settlement over the administration of the councils.

The prolonged dispute has also affected local government workers, whose welfare and salaries have become entangled in the disagreement over access to statutory allocations.

On 9 November, the Osun State chapter of the Nigeria Labour Congress (NLC) began a three-day sympathy strike in solidarity with local government workers over the continued withholding of council allocations.

The action, which followed the expiration of a seven-day ultimatum to the federal and Osun State governments, disrupted activities in government offices and public schools across the state.

The crisis has therefore evolved beyond a contest between the APC and the Adeleke-led administration. It has become a prolonged institutional and financial dispute, with implications for grassroots governance, workers’ welfare and the delivery of public services across the state.

A PREMIUM TIMES report documented the impacts of lack of local government governance and withheld funds.

Tinubu-Adeleke alliance towards resolving LG crisis

With the political relationship between Mr Adeleke and Mr Tinubu strengthening after the governor’s re-election, negotiations to resolve the local government crisis and address the withheld allocations have reportedly gathered momentum.

PUNCH reported in October that Mr Tinubu had initiated a peace process shortly after Mr Adeleke visited the Presidential Villa following his re-election. The president subsequently constituted a committee led by his Chief of Staff, Femi Gbajabiamila, to develop a framework for resolving the dispute.

Confirming the resolution, Mr Adeleke’s spokesperson, Olawale Rasheed, said the presidency and the state government are working towards a total resolution of the local government control crisis.

Mr Rasheed said the discussions involved the interests of the APC-backed council officials and the PDP chairpersons elected in February 2025, as well as questions surrounding the management of local government funds. He expressed optimism that the negotiations would produce a resolution before the 2027 general elections.

“What the governor and the Presidency are doing is to set up a negotiation team to iron out how best we can resolve it. In fact, the negotiation is almost reaching the final stage, and the negotiation continues to resolve the matter. All this will be over before the election,” he added.

Although Kola Olabisi, the Osun State APC spokesperson, said he was unaware of any committee set up to resolve the local government crisis.

“I am unaware of such an arrangement. The fellow who spoke about it is in a better position to explain. I don’t know anything about it,” he said.

However, experts said a political relationship between Mr Tinubu and Mr Adeleke would not, by itself, settle the legal questions surrounding the council leadership or secure the release of the outstanding allocations.

Adebola Bakare, a doctor of Political Science and director of the Institute of Legislative Studies at the University of Ilorin, described the Osun State local government control crisis as a complex issue requiring a careful review of the previous legal proceedings involving the contending parties.

He noted that the political alliance between Mr Adeleke and Mr Tinubu could provide an opportunity to resolve the crisis, but stressed that this would depend on the parties reaching a common ground and agreeing to settle the dispute out of court. Otherwise, he said, the protracted legal battle could continue to complicate efforts to restore local government administration in the state.

“If there is a resolution committee, as you mentioned, and it is able to settle the matter out of court with its framework, that would be the best approach. The case before the court arose from the crisis, so if both parties can find common ground and agree to an out-of-court settlement, the court has no option but to strike out the case,” he said.

Transport union crisis laced with politics

The struggle for control of motor parks has also exposed the limits of political influence in resolving Osun’s institutional disputes.

For months, rival factions within the National Union of Road Transport Workers (NURTW) have been embroiled in disputes over leadership and control of motor parks across the state, with the crisis also fuelling allegations of political favouritism.

The disputes have escalated into violent confrontations, shootings and deaths as rival factions battle for control of the parks.

In July 2026, the state government suspended NURTW activities in motor parks following a violent clash between rival factions.

The government maintained that the recognised state executive was the one led by Nurudeen Alowonle, while accusing a faction led by Kazeem Oyewale, popularly known as Asiri Eniba, of attempting to take control of parks and garages.

The NURTW national leadership rejected the suspension, arguing that the governor lacked the authority to halt the union’s activities. It subsequently inaugurated a seven-member caretaker committee for the Osun chapter, a move also rejected by the state government.

However, despite the interventions, violence continued. In August, two people were shot dead during a confrontation in the Naira and Kobo area of Ikire, in Irewole Local Government Area, reportedly amid an attempt by a faction to take control of a motor park following Mr Adeleke’s re-election.

The crisis escalated further in September when Olalekan Oyeyemi, popularly known as Emir Ajagungbade, an Accord Party top figure and associate of the governor, was shot dead at Mayfair motor park in Ile-Ife.

Mr Oyeyemi was also involved in the transport sector and had served on a government-appointed transport committee. Police later recovered another corpse from the park.

Reports linked the killing to the struggle over motor park leadership. The police said they were investigating the incident to establish the motive for the killing and identify those responsible.

Following the incident, Mr Adeleke again banned NURTW activities in the state, directed rival groups to vacate motor parks and garages, and ordered security agencies to arrest those allegedly involved in the killing.

He also announced plans to reintroduce a Park Management System, which he said would restore order and discipline to the transport sector.

The government subsequently pursued a legislative solution. The Osun State House of Assembly passed the Integrated Transport, Traffic and Park Management System Bill in September, which Mr Adeleke signed into law on 5 October.

The legislation, however, sparked another political dispute, with the state APC challenging the House of Assembly over the authority the legislation granted the state government to regulate and manage public motor parks.

The APC argued that the state government lacked the constitutional authority to take over the functions relating to public motor parks, citing Section 7(1) and the Fourth Schedule of the Nigerian constitution assigning responsibilities over motor parks to local government councils.

However, the assembly rejected the APC’s interpretation, arguing that the Nigerian constitution also recognises the role of state legislatures in providing the legal framework for local government administration. It challenged the party to approach the courts if it considered the legislation unconstitutional.

The disagreement is significant because the existing local government crisis has put the local governments and their finances under an unclear control.

Although the new law provides a framework for regulating parks, ticketing and revenue collection.

APC resentment, moves to rival Adeleke’s campaign role

Mr Adeleke’s Tinubu campaign role has also exposed divisions within the Osun APC.

The appointment was particularly sensitive because the governor belongs to the Accord Party, while the APC has its own political structure and leaders in the state.

Former governor Mr Oyetola has long been regarded as the party’s prominent figure in Osun and was not included in the list of campaign council members published by the APC.

The development unsettled some party members who had expected an APC chieftain to coordinate the president’s campaign in the state, claiming Mr Adeleke appointment to lead APC’s presidential campaign council could give the Accord party momentum in the political landscape of the state and could give it a potential to emerge victorious in legislative seats it is contesting against APC’s candidates.

The disagreement became more visible after Mr Adeleke announced a 344-member campaign council and invited members of the APC, PDP and Accord to participate in the presidential campaign, where Mr Oyetola and Mr Oyebamiji were absent.

APC forms competing campaign structure

The resentment within the APC soon resulted in the emergence of a rival presidential campaign structure by the state’s party.

On 2 November, the Osun APC unveiled a 168-member campaign council to mobilise support for Mr Tinubu’s re-election and other APC candidates in the 2027 elections. The party appointed Mr Oyebamiji as its director-general.

The move effectively created a parallel campaign structure to rival the party’s national campaign council list that appointed Mr Adeleke to lead the presidential campaign in the state.

The composition of the council was immediately triggered by four members of the party’s state executive committee, who accused the leadership of excluding officials they said should have been included.

They also questioned why the council appeared to disregard the earlier arrangement naming Mr Adeleke as the coordinator of the president’s campaign in the state.

Following backlash from its national body, the state chapter discontinued the parallel presidential campaign structure and renamed it the Osun State APC Parliamentary Campaign Council.

Its membership was expanded from 168 to 183 to accommodate all members of the state executive committee, while Mr Oyebamiji retained his position as director-general.

Although the change removed the immediate duplication of presidential campaign structures, it did not necessarily resolve the underlying disagreement over Mr Adeleke’s influence or the distribution of roles within the party’s campaign machinery.

It also raises questions about how much authority the governor will exercise over APC members who may be reluctant to take direction from Mr Adeleke in the course of campaigning for Mr Tinubu.

However, Mr Olabisi dismissed suggestions that the political alignment between Governor Adeleke and President Tinubu could affect the contest for legislative seats for APC, insisting that both parties were campaigning separately for their candidates.

He added that his party had established a separate campaign committee for its parliamentary candidates.

“The only nexus between Accord and the APC in this election is the presidential contest. We are campaigning for our own candidates, both at the presidential and legislative levels,” he said.

Mr Olabisi also noted that the party is prioritising voter education to ensure its supporters could identify and vote for its candidates. “Voter education is one of the things we are able to prioritise in order to ensure that potential voters are adequately educated.”

Mr Bakare said earlier indications suggested that Mr Tinubu had been willing to accommodate Mr Adeleke in the APC when the PDP was experiencing internal divisions that threatened to affect the governor’s re-election bid. However, he said opposition from the APC’s state leadership prevented the move.

“From the indications at the time, when the governor wanted to defect to the APC following the PDP crisis, he held several meetings with President Tinubu. From the president’s body language, it was clear that he was willing to accept the governor into the party.

“Unfortunately, local political considerations prevented that from happening because anyone joining a party has to do so through its structures at the grassroots,” he said.

Mr Bakare said Mr Tinubu’s subsequent appointment of Mr Adeleke to lead his presidential re-election campaign in Osun demonstrated the president’s confidence in the governor and reflected their existing political relationship.

He added that the appointment could compel APC leaders in the state who opposed Mr Adeleke’s emergence to align with the president’s decision.

“Now that the president has appointed him to lead his presidential campaign in the state, it shows the confidence he has in him and reflects their earlier relationship. Whatever disagreements or resentment APC members in the state may have, they will have to respect the president’s decision and follow Mr Adeleke’s direction because, whether they like it or not, he is the one calling the shots,” he said.

What is at stake for Adeleke and Accord?

For Mr Adeleke, the arrangement presents both an opportunity and a political risk.

His role in Mr Tinubu’s re-election campaign could strengthen his relationship with the federal government and provide a channel for resolving disputes between the state and federal governments. It could also help secure federal cooperation on issues affecting Osun, particularly the local government crisis and the release of council allocations.

But the governor must also protect the political interests of the Accord Party, the platform on which he secured re-election and which is fielding candidates for the 2027 state and national legislative elections.

The presidential and National Assembly elections are scheduled to be held on the same day, 16 January, according to the revised timetable released by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

This means Mr Adeleke will be campaigning for Mr Tinubu while Accord candidates contest against APC candidates for seats in the Senate and the House of Representatives.

The governor has sought to draw a clear boundary between the two contests, maintaining that his alliance with the APC is limited to the presidential election and that he will campaign for Accord candidates in the legislative polls.

“I urge all political parties to campaign for their candidates as I will do for Accord candidates. We have no deal on the National Assembly and the state assembly elections. All our candidates will face the electorate, who have the final say,” Mr Adeleke said in a statement signed by his spokesperson, Mr Rasheed.

Experts noted that arrangement could become increasingly difficult to manage as the campaign intensifies with both parties confronted with a delicate balancing act.

Mr Bakare expressed that both parties would need to educate their supporters on how to navigate the alliance at the polls, particularly by helping them distinguish between the presidential, senatorial and House of Representatives ballots.

“The major issue for both parties is how they educate their supporters so that the alliance will not hurt their parties. They have to examine how much their supporters can differentiate between the presidential ballot, senatorial ballot and House of Representatives ballot,” he said.

With voter education, Mr Bakare said he believes both parties won’t compromise their respective candidates’ chances in the legislative elections.

World.title: Nigeria’s Maria Wophill wins 2026 World Athletics Woman of the Year award
World.content:
Nigeria’s Maria Wophill has been named the 2026 World Athletics Woman of the Year in recognition of her decades-long efforts to promote gender equality and expand opportunities for women and girls in athletics, according to a press statement issued by World Athletics on Saturday.

The award recognises Ms Wophill’s contributions to sports administration, particularly her advocacy for greater female representation in leadership positions, mentorship of women in sports and initiatives aimed at encouraging girls to participate in athletics.

A veteran sports administrator, Wophill has held several positions in Nigeria’s sports administration, including serving as Secretary General of the Athletics Federation of Nigeria (AFN), as well as senior roles in the Federal Ministry of Youth and Sports Development.

Her work has focused on improving women’s access to leadership positions in sports federations, supporting female athletes and creating pathways for women to contribute to the administration and development of athletics.

Ms Wophill was instrumental in advocating increased female representation on the boards of Nigerian sports federations, supporting efforts that led to the approval of additional positions for women across the federations.

At continental level, she championed the establishment of the Confederation of African Athletics (CAA) Gender Leadership Task Force in 2024 and has helped organise leadership seminars aimed at strengthening women’s participation in sports administration across Africa.

She has also mentored female coaches and sports administrators, including through the Women’s Sport Leadership Academy (WISH), while supporting programmes designed to develop the next generation of women in athletics.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Her grassroots contributions include initiating and coordinating the Abuja Federal Capital Territory Girls Sprints and Relays, a programme designed to introduce girls in junior and senior secondary schools to athletics and encourage participation in track events.

Ms Wophill’s recognition by World Athletics adds to a career marked by sustained service to Nigerian athletics. In 2019, she received the World Athletics Veteran Pin Award in recognition of her longstanding contribution to the sport. She is also a former athlete and retired director in the Federal Ministry of Youth and Sports Development.

Reacting to the latest honour, Ms Wophill described it as humbling and said it had strengthened her resolve to continue contributing to athletics, particularly in gender leadership, safeguarding young athletes and mentorship.

“This has been a truly humbling year and I am very proud to be acknowledged for the work I have done,” she said.

She expressed appreciation to World Athletics leadership and several Nigerian and African sports institutions, including the Confederation of African Athletics, Nigerian Olympic Committee, National Sports Commission, Athletics Federation of Nigeria and Association of Former Female Athletes of Nigeria, for providing opportunities to serve.

“This award has energised me to keep giving my best in all positions in athletics, with particular focus on gender leadership, safeguarding young athletes and mentoring within the sport,” she added.

World Athletics President Sebastian Coe praised Wophill’s contribution, saying her efforts to improve female representation in sports leadership, alongside her mentorship and support for women, had made a lasting impact on athletics.

“Maria has devoted much of her career to creating greater opportunities for women and girls in athletics. Her commitment to improving female representation in sports leadership, alongside her work in mentoring and supporting others, has made a lasting contribution to our sport. She is a thoroughly deserving recipient of this award,” Mr Coe said.

Wophill previously served on the World Athletics Women’s Committee from 2010 to 2018 and remains involved in initiatives promoting women’s participation and leadership in sports administration.

The Woman of the Year Award is part of the World Athletics Awards, which recognise outstanding contributions to the sport beyond performances on the track and field. It honours individuals whose leadership, advocacy and work have helped advance gender equality and create opportunities for women and girls in athletics.

World.title: Court sentences two to death for murder of NYSC member
World.content:
The Federal Capital Territory (FCT) High Court in Zuba, Abuja, on Friday sentenced two persons to death by hanging for the murder of a National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) member in 2022.

​The International Centre for Investigative Reporting (ICIR) reported that Jennifer Tsembe and Solomon Abuh were convicted and sentenced for the death of Stephanie Terungwa, aged 26.

​Meanwhile, the court also sentenced the third defendant, Monday Simon, to 14 years’ imprisonment for conspiracy and abduction of Ms Terungwa.

​Since 2022, the Nigeria Police Force (NPF) has been prosecuting the trio after Ms Terungwa was reported missing in Abuja.

​Ms Terungwa’s remains were later found. The convicts who were arrested by the police confessed their involvement in her death.

​How Ms Terungwa was killed

Ms Tsembe confessed to luring the deceased to her residence in Maitama, tying her up and pouring acid on the victim.

The convicts later dumped the deceased on the roadside.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Ms Tsembe cited jealousy over Ms Terungwa having a child with her boyfriend as a motivation.

Details of trial

During the proceedings, the prosecution lawyer, Adama Musa, presented nine witnesses and 15 exhibits to prove his case.

Following a four-year trial, the judge found the trio guilty of the crime and convicted them.

​Ahmed Sanusi, the Commissioner of Police in the FCT, lauded the investigating team and legal unit for their effort, a police statement said.

This sentence comes amidst demands by right groups to revoke the death penalty.

On 9 October, the National Human Rights Commission (NHRC), Avocats Sans Frontieres, the Australian High Commission, the Embassy of the Federal Republic of Germany and the Spanish embassy in Nigeria called for the revocation of the death penalty in Nigeria.

By December, Nigeria would mark 10 consecutive years without a state execution, meeting the international standard for a de facto moratorium. However, over 3,000 persons are on prolonged death row detention.

Amnesty International reported that as of 2025, 145 countries have abolished the death penalty both in law and practice.

While Nigeria would become a de facto abolitionist state, by December, some laws allow for state pardon for those on death row.

Similarly, section 12(2)(c) of the Nigerian Correctional Service (NCoS) Act, 2019 allows the commutation of a death sentence to life imprisonment under specific conditions.

World.title: PREMIUM TIMES reporter wins 2026 Ray Ekpu Investigative Journalism Prize
World.content:
Ekemini Simon, a senior reporter at PREMIUM TIMES, has won the 2026 Ray Ekpu Prize for Investigative Journalism in Akwa Ibom State.

This is the fifth time he has won the first prize in the competition set up in 2021 by Inoyo Toro Foundation in honour of Ray Ekpu, the co-founder of Newswatch magazine and the 1987 International Editor of the Year.

Mr Simon emerged as the overall winner at the Inoyo Toro Foundation’s 2026 ceremonies for the 19th Teacher’s Award and sixth Ray Ekpu Awards for Investigative Journalism, held on Friday in Uyo, Akwa Ibom State.

He won the award for a two-part investigation exposing oil companies’ continued gas flaring in violation of Nigerian laws and the Nigerian Upstream Petroleum Regulatory Commission’s (NUPRC) failure to enforce the country’s anti-gas-flaring regulations.

The investigation, titled Oil companies violate Nigerian laws, flare gas, face no sanctions and NUPRC fails to enforce Nigeria’s anti-flaring law as methane emissions go unchecked, examined regulatory failures and the continued environmental consequences of gas flaring in the Niger Delta.

Mr Simon previously won the prize four times while working with TheMail newspaper before securing his latest recognition with PREMIUM TIMES.

He has featured in all six editions of the competition and was runner-up in 2024, when Assistant Editor at PREMIUM TIMES, Cletus Ukpong, emerged winner.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Joseph Atainyang of The Watchman Post came second in the 2026 edition with his four-part investigation, Stalling a Dream: Inside Struggles of University of Maritime Studies, Oron.

Screening committee raises concern over low entries

Announcing the results, the Chairman of the Screening Committee, Nsikak Essien, a former editor of the defunct National Concord newspaper and former Chairman of the Board of Pioneer Newspapers, said the 2026 competition received only five entries, down from 22 in 2025.

Mr Essien, however, said the quality of the entries had generally improved compared with the previous edition, when, according to him, one-third of the submissions did not qualify as investigative reports.

He expressed concern that no woman journalist submitted an entry this year, compared with two female participants in the 2025 edition.

“In intellectual engagement, women are always top. Why is it different for investigative journalism? I encourage women to take part in investigative journalism and apply,” he said.

Mr Essien said the committee had maintained a minimum score of 70 per cent for the first three positions, but only two entries met the benchmark this year, leaving the third position vacant.

He said the decision was meant to preserve the award’s credibility and standard rather than distribute prizes to entries that did not meet the required threshold.

Other members of the screening committee were Ini Uko, a professor of English and Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) of the University of Uyo; Nsibiet John, Chairman of the Nigeria Union of Journalists (NUJ), Akwa Ibom State Council; Akpandem James, a former managing editor of Daily Independent; Kayode Komolafe, Deputy Managing Director of ThisDay and a board member of the Inoyo Toro Foundation; and Umoh Joshua, Secretary of the Committee.

The overall winner received N1 million, while the first runner-up received ₦500,000. Although the 2026 edition increased the total prize money to ₦1.75 million, the ₦250,000 earmarked for the second runner-up was not awarded.

The award was initially introduced with a ₦500,000 prize for the overall winner. Its prize structure expanded in 2024 to accommodate two additional positions after Thompson and Grace Investment Limited joined as sponsors.

The 2026 edition recorded a further increase in the prize purse, with the Ibom Heritage Cultural Organisation and Umoh Joshua joining the Inoyo Toro Foundation as sponsors.

Simon pledges support for aspiring investigative journalists

In his remarks, Mr Simon thanked the Inoyo Toro Foundation and other sponsors for sustaining the award, saying their investment would encourage investigative journalism and motivate more journalists to pursue accountability reporting.

He described himself as the competition’s biggest beneficiary, having won it five times and also finished as runner-up in 2024.

He pledged to support other journalists interested in investigative journalism, particularly those willing to commit the time and resources required to produce impactful reports.

“The field is ripe, but the harvesters are few. We call on journalists to rethink their work and prioritise investigative journalism, because that is what really impacts society.

“Nothing gladdens the heart of a journalist as the result or impact he gets from his work. When we put in our best, we contribute significantly to making our society better. But when journalists go to sleep, the decay becomes aggravated, and the journalist who is part of the society is also affected,” he said.

The NUJ Chairman in Akwa Ibom, Mr John, said investigative journalism often demands considerable sacrifices from practitioners, sometimes at the expense of their personal and family comfort.

He said journalists who undertake such work deserve recognition and commended the Inoyo Toro Foundation for sustaining the award.

Ray Ekpu charges journalists to remain courageous

The sixth edition marked the first time veteran journalist Ray Ekpu attended the ceremony of the journalism prize named in his honour.

Mr Ekpu thanked Mr Inoyo and his family for establishing the award, describing the gesture as recognition of excellence beyond ethnic or local government affiliations.

He said he neither came from Mr Inoyo’s local government area nor shared his tribal background, adding that the foundation’s decision to honour him reflected an appreciation of professional excellence.

“Udom Inoyo is a man who understands the meaning of excellence. He sees a man and says this is excellence and celebrates him,” he said.

Mr Ekpu said he had nominated Mr Essien to serve on the screening committee because of his experience working with him and his reputation for being tough, diligent and professional.

Addressing the award winners and other journalists, he described journalism as a profession built on truth-telling and charged practitioners to remain prepared to face the consequences of speaking truth to power.

He encouraged the winners not to rest on their achievements but to continue working towards greater recognition, including international awards.

Mr Ekpu identified extensive reading and a strong sense of justice as essential qualities of a successful investigative journalist.

“The secret to being an outstanding investigative journalist is that you have to read well,” he said, disclosing that his personal collection contained up to 10,000 books.

He cautioned journalists against relying solely on online encyclopaedias such as Wikipedia, which he said could contain errors, and urged them to cultivate the habit of reading books.

He also advised journalists to let injustice disturb them, arguing that such sensitivity could drive them toward credible investigations with meaningful social impact.

Mr Ekpu further asked journalists to remain humble, dress appropriately, and avoid letting professional achievements make them arrogant.

Recounting his experience under military rule, he said he was detained six times for his courageous journalism but never abandoned the profession. “I was still publishing. Remain courageous,” he told the journalists.

READ ALSO: Four PREMIUM TIMES journalists emerge finalists for 2026 Wole Soyinka Investigative Reporting Award

The Ray Ekpu Prize was established by Mr Inoyo to promote journalistic excellence, strengthen accountability in public office, combat corruption and impunity, defend human rights, and encourage national unity and ethnic cohesion.

The competition is open to registered NUJ members of Akwa Ibom origin, including journalists practising outside the state.

PREMIUM TIMES had earlier reported the expansion of the prize money to ₦1.75 million for the 2026 edition and the history of the initiative.

The newspaper also previously reported the recognition of its journalists in the competition. In 2024, Assistant Editor at PREMIUM TIMES Cletus Ukpong won the top prize for an investigation exposing the wrongful dismissal of a University of Uyo lecturer, while Saviour Imukudo emerged first runner-up in 2025.

World.title: Is renaming ASCON necessary?, By MJ Balogun
World.content:
Assuming (without conceding) that these objectives are outdated, is changing ASCON’s name the solution? What prevents us from updating the objectives and aligning them with current realities? And shouldn’t the views of former Directors-General of ASCON be sought before proceeding on this adventure? Among these ex-DGs are Professor Adele Jinadu, former INEC commissioner and former member of the National Merit Awards Board; Professor Sheikh Abdullahi, former minister of Health and member of the Federal Executive Council; Mr Ajibade Peters; Mrs Cecilia Gayya; and my humble self. Even without being invited, the ex-DGs met informally and agreed that the proposed name change ought to be put on hold to allow for wider consultation.

A few days ago, on 24 November to be precise, the House of Representatives’ Committee on Public Service Matters held a public hearing in the Administrative Staff College of Nigeria (ASCON), Topo, Badagry. The aim was to solicit the opinions of a wide cross-section of Nigerian society on an Executive Bill which seeks to transform ASCON into the “National School of Government.” Living far away in Canada, I was understandably absent at the momentous event. However, the lack of prior notification notwithstanding, I, as a former director-general of the Staff College, sent an emissary to submit my memorandum to the august Committee. I shall return to the memorandum later.

For now, I am delighted to report that those present at the public hearing sent me clips of what transpired. I sat aghast as I watched and listened to assertions that were either patently false or were otherwise anchored on fallacious assumptions.

Let me start with the lies told at the public hearing. One speaker took the microphone and, without batting an eye, claimed that France and Singapore both have schools of government! This is a whopper! It was surprising that the speaker got away with the fabrication. What France has is not a school of government, but an “Institut National du Service Public/INSP,” as well as an “École Nationale d’Administration/ENA.” Singapore does not have a National School of Government either. What it has is the Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, a post-graduate school of the National University of Singapore.

Realising that her fib would sooner or later be exposed, the “National School of Government” promoter quickly moved from France and Singapore and landed in Africa. She told the audience how Kenya and South Africa embraced the National School of Government idea. She then went on to ask pointedly: if these fellow African countries have National Schools of Government (hereafter simply referred to as NSG), doesn’t Nigeria risk being “left behind” if it refuses to convert ASCON into its own NSG? The earlier Nigeria joined the NSG bandwagon the better, she argued. Better for whom or fit for what purpose? She didn’t say.

Which ‘bandwagon’ are we even talking about here? Besides Kenya and South Africa, which other African countries have “National Schools of Government/NSGs”? The popular designation for public service training institutes in Francophone African countries is not NSG, but “Ecole Nationale d’Administration/ENA” or “Ecole Nationale d’Administration et de Magistrature/ENAM.” Ghana has not replaced its “Ghana Institute of Management and Public Administration/GIMPA” with a new name since its inception. GIMPA kept its name while expanding its mandate and despite becoming a full-fledged, degree-awarding, university!

ASCON, whose name we wish to change, has been a model for other training institutions. The late Robert Mugabe came to the Staff College, circa 1983, and liked what he saw. On return to Harare, he directed that Zimbabwe’s own Institute of Public Administration and Management/ZIPAM be created in Darwendale, a village that rivalled Topo, Badagry in serenity and scenic beauty. Though established in 1984, ZIPAM has not ceased being ZIPAM. It has not transformed itself into Zimbabwe’s version of the NSG.

Botswana, Egypt, Eswatini, Mauritius, Namibia, Tanzania, Uganda, and many other countries are among countries that have stuck to the names by which their public service training institutes are known. If this is the case, where is the bandwagon that Nigeria is hastening to jump on? This reminds me of an article of mine that the Quarterly Journal of Administration published in 1981. Titled, “Social Science and the Myth of Modernization” (Vol. XV, No.3, April 1981), the article introduced a new concept, “selective imitation.” Roughly translated, selective imitation is the tendency to import, from abroad, practices deemed pleasant or convenient, and to dismiss as “alien” or “unrealistic” practices that entail making hard choices. This rush towards NSG is an elementary exercise in selective imitation. The aim is to portray the NSG as “trendy” and to leave pertinent but tough institution re-engineering questions unanswered. NSG is, without doubt, all hype, no substance.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

What benefits will a change of ASCON’s name bring, anyway? Going by the NSG hype, the ASCON Act of 1972 is obsolete. The enabling law is long overdue for amendment. The challenges facing Nigeria, and by implication, the Staff College, could not be effectively tackled without replacing the ASCON label with NSG.

Let us examine this argument. It will be recalled that ASCON was established as a corporate body with perpetual succession 0n 1 June 1972. Its objectives as outlined in Section 1 (2) of the 1972 Act are: (a) to provide higher management training for the development of senior executives for the public and private sectors of the Nigerian economy; (b) to provide and arrange for a comparative study and investigation of the principles and techniques of management and administration, and for the exchange of ideas and experiences and for promotion of a better understanding between persons connected with management and administration in the various spheres of national life; (c) to conduct research into problems of management and administration arising in different spheres of national life; (d) to award grants, scholarships or travel fellowships for research in public administration and allied subjects; (e) to establish and maintain a library; (f) to undertake, organise and facilitate study courses, conferences, lectures, seminars and the like, and to promote the aforesaid objects; and (g) to undertake and provide for the publication of journals and of research papers and books in furtherance of the aforesaid objects.

Assuming (without conceding) that these objectives are outdated, is changing ASCON’s name the solution? What prevents us from updating the objectives and aligning them with current realities? And shouldn’t the views of former Directors-General of ASCON be sought before proceeding on this adventure? Among these ex-DGs are Professor Adele Jinadu, former INEC commissioner and former member of the National Merit Awards Board; Professor Sheikh Abdullahi, former minister of Health and member of the Federal Executive Council; Mr Ajibade Peters; Mrs Cecilia Gayya; and my humble self. Even without being invited, the ex-DGs met informally and agreed that the proposed name change ought to be put on hold to allow for wider consultation.

In a memorandum addressed to the Chairman and Members of the House of Representatives Committee on Public Service Matters, I communicated the ex-DGs’ interim views on the proposed name change. I further noted that rather than introduce novel capacity-building concepts or outline new strategic directions, the draft NSG Bill is a rehash of the 1972 ASCON Act. The ex-DGs are of one mind on the lack of correlation between the durability and goal-attainment capacity of an institution, on one hand, and an occasional name change, on the other. To put it another way, an institution’s value is a function, not of the number of times it changes its name, but by its capacity to log in concrete achievements. Oxford University has not changed its name since it was established centuries ago; since 1096, to be precise. Cambridge University has stuck to its name and identity since coming into being in 1209. Harvard University has not been known by any other name since 1780. Then, what will dropping ASCON’s original name and replacing it with a new one accomplish?

What value is inherent in the label, “National School of Government”? The name by which an institution is known endures with its accomplishments over time, meaning, as the institution rolls with the good and the bad before finally maturing. “ASCON” is the name and the brand by which the Staff College has been known for over five decades. Dropping this identity is tantamount to starting over.

Without changing its name, ASCON can accomplish the mission that the NSG was expected to accomplish. What is needed is, therefore, not a change of name, but a comprehensive stock-taking, followed by an in-depth analysis of the Staff College’s strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and dominant challenges. The formulation of new strategic directions will actually yield greater dividends than any abrupt name change.

In the meantime, I have spotted a few areas where the 1972 Act needs to be reworked to reposition the Staff College for current and unfolding challenges, while simultaneously bringing it at par with similar institutions in different parts of the globe. Specifically, the objects of the School should be fine-tuned to read as follows: (a) serve as the apex public service institution in which policymakers and members of the Higher Civil Service can exchange ideas on national governance norms and principles, and the sharing of good practices in public service management; (b) provide a forum at which political officeholders, members of the higher civil service, heads of security and law enforcement agencies, captains of industry, and civic leaders will brainstorm on solutions to recurring national challenges; (c) serve as a beacon for the dissemination of impact-oriented public service reform strategies and for the promotion of ethical leadership and accountability in public administration; (d) constantly apply formal didactic and innovative adult-learning (including bootcamps and Man O’War) techniques for the express aim of developing the executive and managerial capacity of the public service and turning the service into a truly professional, world-class, and citizen-focused institution; (e) on request from state and local governments, conduct tailor-made senior-level capacity-building programmes for various classes of officials; (f) organise executive and management development programmes for senior officials in the private and non-profit sectors; and (g) serve as a centre of excellence for the conduct of public administration research and the provision of improvement-targeted consultancy services.

In line with the new objectives, the Staff College should endeavour to (a) organise thematic policy retreats for political officeholders, members of the higher civil service, captains of industry, and civic leaders; (b) organise workshops and conferences on public service core values, institution strengthening, ethics and accountability; (c) conduct mandatory training programmes for officers aspiring to be promoted to the Directorate Cadre, or to other positions of responsibility in the federal civil service; (d) design, develop, and deliver mandatory instructions, orientation, and foundation courses for all new entrants in to the Civil Service across all tiers government; (e) provide structured, competency-based training and continuous education programmes for senior officers in the Civil Service; (f) collaborate with the Career Development Department of the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation on the revision and implementation of Schemes of Service, with a view to imposing successful participation in graduated levels of training at the Staff College as a major condition for career advancement; (g) conduct and promote comparative studies of public administration, governance and management practices to improve public service performance; (h) publish journals, occasional papers, policy briefs and policy-oriented publications based on research undertaken either by the School or in collaboration with outside researchers; (i) establish and maintain libraries and digital knowledge systems; and; (j) perform such other functions as consistent with the objectives of this Act.

The Governing Board, for its part, should comprise the following: (a) a Chairman who shall be a seasoned administrator of recognised standing in public service, academia, or the private sector; (b) the Permanent Secretary responsible for career management in the Office of the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation; (c) one representative of the Federal Civil Service Commission; (d) two renowned public administration scholars; (e) one representative of the private sector (selected in turn from the Nigerian Chambers of Commerce and Industry, the Nigerian Employers Association, and the Manufacturers Association of Nigeria), and (f) the Director-General of the Staff College who shall also be the Secretary.

Another Section of the 1972 Act that needs updating is that concerning the appointment of the Staff College’s Director-General. The mode and terms of the appointment need to be spelt out clearly. Considering the important role of leadership in institutional re-engineering, the Act should be amended to provide for the  of the Staff College’s highest post in major national newspapers. The post should not be filled except based on open and fair competition. This may warrant the establishment of an Executive Selection Panel presided over by the Head of the Civil Service of the Federation or his/her representative, with members drawn from the Federal Civil Service Commission, institutions of higher learning, watchdog bodies, and the private sector. This recommendation accords not only with the federal character provisions of the Nigerian Constitution, but also with the president’s recent undertaking to bring about a “Nigeria that works for ALL”

I have a lot more to say on ASCON, but I have decided to stop here for now.

MJ Balogun is a former special adviser to the President of the United Nations General Assembly and Former ASCON Director-General.

World.title: Referee faces suspension after punching goalkeeper in post-match rawl
World.content:
A Bolivian referee, Jordy Aleman, might face be faced with strict suspension rules after punching Real Potosi goalkeeper Cristian Martinez during a post-match confrontation following the 2026 Copa Bolivia final.

The incident occurred on Wednesday after Always Ready secured the trophy with a 3-1 aggregate victory over Real Potosi. The second leg ended in a goalless draw at the Victor Agustin Ugarte Stadium in Potosi.

Tensions flared after the final whistle as Real Potosi players approached Aleman to protest decisions made during the match.

Television footage showed the referee punching Martinez in the face, triggering further disorder before police intervened to protect the officials.

Reports from Spanish-language media, including MARCA, said the confrontation followed an insult directed at Aleman by the goalkeeper. Martinez reportedly told the referee, “I hope your mother dies.”

Martinez later said the punch left his mouth bleeding. However, in a defiant response reported by El Diario, he remarked: “He should hit harder.”

The goalkeeper also questioned Aleman’s professionalism and called for an exemplary punishment. He subsequently announced that he would not pursue legal action or file a formal complaint over the incident.

In a statement shared by Spanish publication 20 Minutos, Martinez said: “My intention is to consider this episode over and avoid allowing this situation to continue generating conflict.”

Aleman could face disciplinary sanctions under the Bolivian Football Federation’s Disciplinary Code, which reportedly provides for fines of at least 20 national minimum monthly salaries and bans of between one and three years for physical assaults.

The incident also led to four Real Potosi players and three members of the club’s coaching staff reportedly receiving red cards.

According to Bolivian publication Vision 360, the federation’s refereeing authorities are expected to review the incident alongside the match reports. Aleman’s status as an international referee could also have further implications.

The referee has yet to make a public statement on the incident.

World.title: Meet Nigerian’s Maria Wophill named World Athletics’ Woman of the Year
World.content:
Veteran Nigerian sports administrator Maria Wophill has been named the World Athletics (WA) 2026 Woman of the Year in recognition of her decades-long contribution to gender equality and the development of women and girls in athletics.

World Athletics announced the honour as part of its 2026 awards, recognising Wophill’s efforts to create opportunities for women in track and field through leadership, advocacy and grassroots development.

Wophill previously served as secretary-general of the Athletics Federation of Nigeria (AFN) between 2005 and 2013. She has also held senior positions in the Federal Ministry of Youth and Sports Development and served on the World Athletics Women’s Committee from 2010 to 2018.

Her contributions to Nigerian sports administration include advocacy for increased female representation on the boards of national sports federations, which helped secure additional positions for women.

At the continental level, she championed the establishment of the Confederation of African Athletics (CAA) Gender Leadership Task Force in 2024.

She has also mentored female coaches and sports administrators through the Women’s Sport Leadership Academy (WISH), while supporting grassroots participation through the Abuja FCT Girls Sprints and Relays, an initiative aimed at encouraging secondary school girls to take part in athletics.

Reacting to the recognition, Wophill expressed gratitude to World Athletics and Nigerian sports organisations, describing the award as a motivation to continue contributing to the sport.

“This has been a truly humbling year and I am very proud to be acknowledged for the work I have done,” she said.

She added that the recognition had strengthened her commitment to promoting gender leadership, safeguarding young athletes and mentoring people within athletics.

“This award has energised me to keep giving my best in all positions in athletics, with particular focus on gender leadership, safeguarding young athletes and mentoring within the sport,” she said.

World Athletics President Sebastian Coe described Wophill as a deserving recipient, praising her efforts to improve female representation and mentor others in the sport.

Her recognition is part of the 2026 World Athletics Awards, with the World Athletes of the Year, Rising Stars and Moment of the Year scheduled to be announced on Sunday.

World.title: Low turnout, BVAS glitches mar INEC mock accreditation in Ondo
World.content:
By Dayo Johnson Akure

The ongoing mock accreditation and voting exercise conducted by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) ahead of the 2027 general elections has recorded low voter turnout in some polling units in Ondo State, alongside technical challenges with the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS).

As of the time of filing this report, findings showed that only two persons voted out of 470 registered voters at Tipper Garage, Ward 2, Unit 046.

Similarly, at Champion Junction, Ward 3, Unit 15, only six voters participated in the exercise.

At High Court, Ward 5, Unit 11, 11 persons were recorded as having voted out of 940 registered voters.

However, the situation was different at Ajipowo, Ward 2, Unit 17, where a large turnout of voters was observed.

Despite the turnout, the exercise experienced technical challenges as the BVAS reportedly failed to capture the faces of some elderly voters, causing difficulties during the accreditation process.

The mock exercise is part of INEC’s preparations to test its electoral equipment and processes ahead of the 2027 general elections.

World.title: Why Tinubu should stay in office for 10 years – Akande
World.content:
By Ayobami Okerinde

Former Osun State Governor, Bisi Akande, has called for President Bola Tinubu to remain in office for 10 years, saying the period would allow him to complete ongoing projects and deliver lasting reforms.

Akande made the call during an interview on the Frankly Speaking with Icon podcast, published on Friday.

“He should remain in office, if possible, for another 10 years; otherwise, we go back to the situation of ‘Ebinpawa’ because there has been a foundation for hunger,” Akande said.

He cited the Olubadan’s comments on road projects across the South-West, including routes linking Ijebu-Ode, Abeokuta, Oyo and Ikire, as evidence of the administration’s ongoing work.

Quoting the traditional ruler, Akande said: “If you are working like this, and this had not been done 50 years before you, what again do we still say you should do, and you have not done?

“But so that you will be able to complete this good job that you started, Ibadan people and Oyo State people are supporting you to do another four years.”

Akande also blamed successive military administrations for what he described as decades of neglect of agriculture, education and economic development, saying their policies contributed to the country’s present difficulties.

“Forty years before he came, since 1966, when the military started ruling you, you have been laying the foundation for hunger. You have abandoned your farms. You have abandoned the job. You have refused to be educated. You have refused to be modernised,” he said.

He expressed optimism that Tinubu’s policies would produce significant improvements in the coming years, particularly in electricity supply and modernisation.

“So in another 10 years there will be electricity everywhere. There will be modernisation,” he said.

“They liberalised electricity. If you have money today, you can create electricity in your home. You can create it in your city. You can create it around you,” he said.

Comparing the policy with the restrictions under previous military administrations, Akande said individuals were previously prevented from generating electricity independently.

“Unlike what the military did before, if you tried to create electricity, they would arrest you. They would make you a debtor. They wouldn’t let you do it. They said only the Federal Government could do it. Tinubu came and said everybody can do it,” he added.

On his own public engagements, the former governor attributed his reduced movement around the country to age, contrasting his present situation with when he was younger.

World.title: Low voter turnout mars INEC mock election in Bayelsa, as accreditation process runs smoothly
World.content:
•Reports across the state indicate a seamless exercise despite poor participation

By Samuel Oyadongha, Yenagoa

The mock election organised by the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) recorded a low voter turnout across Yenagoa, the Bayelsa State capital, on Saturday, despite reports of a smooth accreditation process.

The exercise, designed to test the commission’s preparedness and assess the performance of its electoral technology ahead of the 2027 general elections, was seamless at the polling units visited.

At the Kpansia Epie Community Town Hall, no fewer than nine voters had completed the accreditation process as of 11:15 a.m. when this reporter left the unit.

The Assistant Presiding Officer, Sampson Wale, confirmed that operations with the Bimodal Voter Accreditation System (BVAS) were seamless.

The story is not different at Epie II CPS Opolo II and others.

The BVAS is being tested as part of efforts to identify and address possible challenges before the general elections.

Though participation was relatively low, INEC officials expressed optimism that voter turnout would improve as the exercise progressed.

Reports from other parts of the state also described the mock exercise as smooth.

World.title: NPFL faces fresh scrutiny after Shooting Stars fans attack referee
World.content:
The Nigeria Premier Football League (NPFL) is facing renewed scrutiny over its efforts to curb crowd violence after Shooting Stars supporters invaded the pitch and attacked match officials and Rivers United players following Friday’s 1-1 draw in Ibadan.

The incident at the Lekan Salami Stadium has raised fresh concerns about the safety of players and officials in the domestic league, particularly as similar incidents have continued despite disciplinary measures imposed on offending clubs.

As of Saturday, the NPFL had yet to issue an official statement on the violence. Neither Shooting Stars nor Rivers United had publicly commented on the incident.

Videos circulating on social media showed supporters storming the pitch shortly after the final whistle, with one fan dressed in green striking centre referee Grema Muhammad on the head.

Several Rivers United players were also reportedly attacked as the situation escalated, forcing security personnel and officers of the Nigeria Police Force to intervene and escort the match officials away from the hostile crowd.

In another video from the incident, Rivers United players were seen assisting an injured match official.

The violence overshadowed the encounter, which ended in a 1-1 draw, with both teams sharing the points.

The latest incident has also revived concerns about previous cases of supporter violence at the Ibadan stadium.

On April 6, 2025, Shooting Stars supporters reportedly attacked members of the Ikorodu City delegation and match officials following a goalless draw between the two sides. The incident also involved damage to Ikorodu City’s team bus.

The attack comes amid a series of disciplinary actions by the NPFL against clubs over security breaches and misconduct during the ongoing 2026/27 season.

The repeated incidents have raised questions about the effectiveness of the league’s disciplinary measures in preventing violence at match venues.

Although the NPFL has previously imposed financial penalties, points deductions and stadium restrictions on clubs over security breaches, Friday’s attack in Ibadan represents another test of its efforts to protect players, match officials and other participants.

The league is expected to review available video footage and match reports before deciding whether to open disciplinary proceedings against Shooting Stars.

World.title: Gunmen kill 51-year-old man, two others in fresh Plateau attack
World.content:
By Golok Nanmwa, Jos

Gunmen have killed three persons in a fresh attack on Nkiedowro community in Teegbe District of Bassa Local Government Area of Plateau State, throwing residents into mourning.

The attack, which occurred on Friday night, claimed the lives of three Irigwe natives, bringing to 20 the number of Irigwe people reportedly killed within the week, according to the National Publicity Secretary of the Irigwe Youth Movement, Joseph Chudu Yonkpa.

Yonkpa, who confirmed the killings in a statement made available to newsmen on Saturday, said the attackers launched two separate ambushes on the community.

“Yesterday night, Fulani militias launched two separate ambushes at Nkiedowro, Teegbe District, killing three Irigwe natives,” he said.

He identified the victims as Ngudo Kura, 51; Hosea Ishaya, 26; and Naomi Izeh, 22.

“This makes it a total of 20 Irigwe people killed this week in an unprovoked manner,” Yonkpa added.

He expressed condolences to the families of the victims and the entire Irigwe community, praying for the repose of the souls of the deceased.

Our correspondent reports that the latest killings occurred barely two days after 17 persons were given a mass burial following an attack on the Tafi Gana community, also in Bassa Local Government Area.

The development has heightened concerns over the security situation in the area, with residents reportedly apprehensive about possible further attacks.

The Irigwe Youth Movement urged residents to remain vigilant and avoid movements that could expose them to danger.

“We call on our people to intensify vigilance, avoid late-night and isolated movements, and report suspicious movements to the relevant authorities,” Yonkpa said.

The group also appealed to security agencies to strengthen surveillance and take necessary measures to protect communities in the area.

Efforts to get the reaction of security operatives were unsuccessful as of the time of filing this report.

World.title: Omo-Agege attack: How I learned of my husband’s death – Wife of slain NDC member
World.content:
By Enitan Abdultawab

Gift Umokoro, wife of slain Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC) member Comrade Efemena Umokoro, has recounted how she learnt of her husband’s death following an attack on party members in Ughelli, Delta State.

In an interview with BBC News Pidgin, Gift said she initially became suspicious after receiving calls from her husband’s friend and relatives, who asked whether she had heard from him without telling her what had happened.

She said her husband’s friend first called to ask where she was before requesting that she contact her husband because she wanted to speak with him.

“I was surprised and I asked her why she could not call my husband herself if she indeed wanted to talk to him,” Gift said.

She explained that the situation became more suspicious when her husband’s aunt later called to ask whether she had heard from him. Her sister also called with the same question.

Gift said she subsequently checked social media and began seeing RIP messages but found it difficult to believe that her husband was dead.

“I did not know how he ended up in Ughelli because it was Abraka he told me he was going to,” she said.

Recounting her husband’s last movements, Gift said he left home that morning wearing a white jalabia, explaining that he wanted to visit a political party member and one of the House of Assembly members.

She said their last conversation was around 3:30pm.

Gift further disclosed that when she contacted her husband’s friends, they initially denied that he had died, telling her instead that he had sustained injuries and was receiving treatment at a hospital.

She said she waited for them to come and take her to see him, but nobody showed up that evening.

“The next morning, they told me they were with him in the hospital. I waited from 6am till whenever. When I noticed nobody was coming, that was when I knew something was up,” she recounted.

Describing her late husband as a devoted father, Gift said he was deeply committed to his children and appealed to authorities to ensure that those responsible for his killing were brought to justice.

“He does not joke with his children. He should get justice. They should find the people that killed him,” she said.

Comrade Umokoro was among the NDC members killed during an attack on party supporters in Ughelli, Delta State, during a political gathering involving former Deputy Senate President Ovie Omo-Agege.

World.title: Defence Minister Calls for Integration of Nigerian Universities into National Security Architecture
World.content:
Follow THISDAYLIVE on Google Add us as a preferred source to see more of our stories in Google 

Linus Aleke in Abuja
