National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula has ordered a fresh review of CCTV footage capturing a member of Parliament allegedly picking up a mobile phone during a confrontation in the House in June 2023, following renewed demands by nominated MP Sabina Chege to have her device returned.

Wetang’ula, who chairs the Powers and Privileges Committee, said he would recuse himself from the proceedings and appoint another MP to review the recordings and present findings to the House, in a move aimed at ensuring the matter is handled appropriately.

“As your Speaker, I will take the following action. Although I am the Chairperson of the Powers and Privileges Committee, I will recuse myself from chairing this matter. I will forward the CCTV footage to the Committee and appoint another Member to act on my behalf, review the footage and present a report to this House,” he said.

The decision follows fresh revelations by Chege, who told Parliament that she had never recovered her phone, which allegedly disappeared during the confrontation involving several female legislators on June 8, 2023.

Chege narrated how she realised the device was missing after her colleague, Rosa Buyu, picked up her handbag while coming to her rescue during the altercation.

She said the phone was a newly purchased iPhone 16, barely a week old, and that she immediately raised the alarm but was assured by officers from the Sergeant-at-Arms that it could not disappear within the parliamentary chamber.

“That phone was an iPhone 16, Mr Speaker. I had just bought it. It was actually one week old. I had colleagues who were around me, whom I even asked to give me back my phone,” she said.

Chege explained that she was advised to seek medical attention following the confrontation and subsequently tracked the phone from Nairobi Hospital, where its location initially showed that it was still within Parliament.

She said the device's location later shifted to an area around Protection House, near Bunge Towers, before it was eventually traced to Donholm.

“When I got to Nairobi Hospital, we tracked my phone and established that it was still within Parliament. An hour later, its location had changed to an area near Protection House and Bunge Towers. The next day it was tracked somewhere in Donholm and from that time I did not get my phone,” she said.

The nominated MP said she reported the incident to parliamentary police, the Clerk of the National Assembly and the House Powers and Privileges Committee but had yet to recover the device.

“I want to say, till today, I have never recovered my phone,” she told the House.

Chege appealed to Wetang’ula to identify the person captured in the CCTV footage or ask them to return the phone before the current parliamentary term ends.

“To save the image of this House, please name the person. At least my phone should be returned,” she said, adding that a colleague had previously claimed to know who took the device but declined to disclose the identity.

However, her remarks triggered sharp exchanges, with some legislators questioning the manner in which the matter was being presented and warning against damaging Parliament's reputation.

Homa Bay Town MP Millie Odhiambo dismissed the incident as an issue that should not be elevated into a question of institutional integrity, arguing that members could contribute towards replacing the device.

“You can make a WhatsApp group and donate a phone for her. Don't tarnish the name of Parliament because you are a crying baby. You make people think Parliament steals people's properties,” Odhiambo said.

Ruaraka MP TJ Kajwang expressed concern that the allegations risked further damaging the reputation of legislators, saying the House needed to address issues that had become associated with its members.

“I have been in this House for 15 years. I do not want to end my term and request a renewal of my term with a tag of a thief,” he said.

Kajwang added that allegations circulating about MPs, including claims of selling recruitment opportunities, were damaging public confidence and needed to be addressed.

Lamu East MP Ruweida Obo also weighed in, declaring that most legislators did not engage in stealing other people's property.

“Sisi wengi si wezi, sisi hatuibi cha mtu na chetu hatutaki kiibiwe,” she said.

Wetang’ula, in his defence of the decision to review the footage, maintained that the recordings would help establish what happened and clear members who may have been wrongly implicated.

He clarified that he had not declared any legislator a thief, but had only indicated that CCTV footage showed a male member picking up a phone from a seat after the altercation.

“The Speaker never said there was a thief. The Speaker said a member took the phone. It is not right and morally comprehensible for anyone to take another person's property without their consent,” he said.

He cautioned MPs against relying on social media speculation and artificial intelligence-generated images to accuse colleagues, saying the CCTV review would provide an opportunity to establish the facts.

“It is easy and juicy to go on social media and use AI and amplify things and call people names. The CCTV will absolve everybody,” he said.

World.title: Ledama Ole Kina court battle over Sh1.2m dispute takes new turn
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Narok Senator Ledama Ole Kina has been granted a stay of execution in a Sh1.2 million compensation dispute with former Narok County Assembly employee Zakayo Rotiken.

The court has given the senator an opportunity to raise funds and settle the outstanding amount.

The Employment and Labour Relations Court, sitting in Nairobi, issued the orders on Tuesday, November 24, 2026, and scheduled the matter for mention on February 18, 2027.

The development follows a protracted legal dispute arising from Rotiken's dismissal, in which the court awarded him Sh1,220,737.61 in compensation.

During Tuesday's proceedings, Ole Kina sought between 30 and 45 days to raise funds and settle the outstanding amount.

The court subsequently granted a stay of execution pending further proceedings in the matter.

In a statement, Rotiken's lawyer, Tonge Yoya, said the stay of execution did not invalidate, overturn or extinguish the original judgment, insisting that the senator remained legally obligated to settle the award.

The claimant's legal team also told the court that it intended to challenge pending applications by Ole Kina, arguing that some of the issues had already been determined in previous proceedings.

The lawyers said an application dated November 19, 2026, seeking to amend a preliminary objection filed on September 25, 2026, was directed to be served upon them.

Ole Kina was further directed to file and serve written submissions on the preliminary objection within 14 days.

The objection is anchored on the doctrine of res judicata, which bars parties from reopening matters that have already been conclusively determined by a competent court.

Rotiken's lawyers contend that a previous application by the senator seeking a stay of judgment was dismissed on April 24, 2026, and argue that subsequent applications touching on the same issues should not be entertained.

However, the Parliamentary Service Commission (PSC) is considering a request to release funds to settle a court-awarded compensation to Zakayo Rotiken, a former employee of Narok Senator Ledama Ole Kina, in a labour dispute that has resurfaced following a dramatic confrontation between the senator and auctioneers.

In a letter addressed to the parties in Employment and Labour Relations Court Cause E165 of 2021, Rotiken versus Ledama Ole Kina, the Commission confirmed that it had received a request seeking the release of funds to settle the decretal sum and costs awarded by the court.

The letter signed by the Commission's Director of Litigation and Compliance, Anthony Njoroge, states that the request has been placed before the Commission for consideration, with a decision expected once deliberations are concluded.

"The Commission's decision shall be communicated to you as soon as the Commission has concluded its deliberations on the matter," reads part of the letter.

The development comes against the backdrop of a viral video showing Senator Ole Kina threatening to shoot a female auctioneer who had gone to repossess a milk delivery lorry belonging to his Enkanasa Cow Milk Company over an outstanding financial obligation.

The confrontation sparked public outrage, with questions emerging over the circumstances surrounding the attempted repossession and the senator's conduct towards the auctioneers.

The dispute is linked to a labour case filed by Rotiken, who had been employed by Ole Kina before his dismissal. The former employee moved to court seeking redress over his termination, resulting in a monetary award against the senator.

The dispute stems from a court case filed by former Narok County Assembly employee Zakayo Rotiken against Senator Ledama Ole Kina at the Employment and Labour Relations Court in Nairobi. The court awarded Rotiken KSh 1,220,737.61 in compensation following his dismissal.

The latest communication from the Parliamentary Service Commission signals that the institution is considering facilitating settlement of the court award, although it has not yet made a final commitment to release the funds.

World.title: Ruto backs Didmus Barasa for Bungoma governor in 2027
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Kimilili MP Didmus Barasa with President Ruto at a political rally in Mt Elgon during the President’s development tour in the Western region. [PCS]

President William Ruto has thrown his weight behind Kimilili MP Didmus Barasa in the race to succeed Bungoma Governor Kenneth Lusaka in 2027, setting the stage for a contest over the county's political leadership.

During his ongoing tour of Western Kenya, the President rallied support for Barasa, signalling his preference for the legislator in the battle for control of Bungoma County after the next General Election.

Barasa has expressed confidence in securing the United Democratic Alliance (UDA) party nomination, citing his development record and grassroots mobilisation in Kimilili as the foundation of his gubernatorial bid.

The MP has urged Bungoma leaders aligned with Kenya Kwanza to unite behind his candidature, arguing that a common political front would strengthen the region's bargaining power within the national government.

He said he intends to replicate his development model in Kimilili across the county's 45 wards, prioritising healthcare, education and youth empowerment.

“I want to take the development model we have implemented in Kimilili and extend it to all the 45 wards in Bungoma. Our people deserve better healthcare, improved education infrastructure, functional vocational training centres and quality early childhood education facilities,” he said.

The legislator pledged to strengthen county hospitals, improve the availability of medicines and expand access to healthcare services at the grassroots.

He also promised to invest in vocational training centres to equip young people with practical skills for employment and entrepreneurship, while improving Early Childhood Development and Education (ECDE).

Barasa identified agriculture, trade, infrastructure and youth entrepreneurship as key sectors requiring investment to unlock Bungoma's economic potential. He said his proposed administration would prioritise accountability, efficient use of public resources and improved service delivery.

His bid has received backing from a section of county leaders, including Senator Wafula Wakoli of Ford Kenya and Webuye East MP Martin Pepela.

However, Ruto's apparent preference for Barasa has attracted opposition from Sirisia MP John Waluke, who has questioned the endorsement and instead declared support for Westlands MP Tim Wanyonyi, who is associated with the Linda Mwananchi Movement (LMM).

Waluke argued that Bungoma residents should determine their next governor without external political influence.

“Bungoma belongs to its people, and the people must decide who will lead them in 2027. We cannot allow the gubernatorial contest to be determined through political endorsements from outside. Residents must be given the freedom to choose a leader who represents their interests,” he said.

The contest is also unfolding amid political differences between Barasa and National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang'ula, adding to the competing interests shaping Bungoma's succession politics.

World.title: Shun leaders inciting you to cause chaos, PS Omollo tells youth
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Internal Security Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo. [File,Standard]

Internal Security Principal Secretary Raymond Omollo has warned young people against political violence, saying the destruction of public property costs lives and diverts resources meant for development.

The warning comes amid concerns over political violence in Embu following the September 12 incident at Nembure Stadium, where a meeting attended by Deputy President Kithure Kindiki was disrupted, leaving one person dead, six vehicles torched and three others vandalised.

Speaking during a Mass at St Thomas More Kairuri Parish in Embu County, Omollo challenged young people to question leaders who ask them to disrupt meetings, block roads or destroy property.

“Before you leave home to disrupt a meeting, ask that leader whether they would allow their own child to do what they are asking you to do,” he said.

“Ask them what they are doing to help you access education, training and employment.”

Omollo said young people should also question what political leaders were doing to improve their access to education, technical training and employment.

He said the Government was working to expand opportunities for young people through education, technical training and employment.

The PS welcomed efforts in the technical and vocational education and training (TVET) sector to equip young people in Embu with skills to pursue their ambitions.

At the same time, Omollo commended county leadership for working with the national government to combat illicit alcohol and drug abuse.

Omollo said proposed legislative changes targeting the sector had passed the first reading in Parliament and urged residents to participate in the next stages of the legislative process.

On security, the PS acknowledged calls for more police vehicles, saying the Government was investing in personnel, vehicles and equipment.

However, he challenged residents to help protect public investments, citing reports that 10 police vehicles had been burned in Embu.

“We use our taxes to buy police vehicles, build markets and construct roads. We cannot pay for development and then allow a few individuals to destroy what belongs to all of us,” he said.

Omollo warned that anyone suspected of destroying property would be taken to court in accordance with the law, where the judiciary would determine their cases.

He maintained that political differences should not be used to justify vandalism, endanger lives or disrupt public services.

“The Constitution protects the right to express ourselves peacefully and unarmed. Political differences cannot be an excuse to vandalise property, endanger lives or disrupt the services our communities depend on,” he said.

Those present included Public Service, Human Capital Development and Special Programmes Cabinet Secretary Geoffrey Ruku, Embu Governor Cecily Mbarire, Senator Alexander Munyi and Deputy Governor Kinyua Mugo, among others.

World.title: Narok Senator under fire after threatening to shoot auctioneers in Sh1.2m dispute
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Narok Senator Ledama ole Kina is at the centre of a national uproar after a viral video captured him threatening to shoot individuals during a volatile confrontation involving auctioneers and a former Senate office employee.

The dramatic standoff erupted when court-backed agents attempted to seize a milk delivery truck over an unresolved legal dispute and has since ignited intense public debate regarding political accountability and the rule of law.

The controversy surrounds long court battle after Zakayo Rotiken, who served sacked as Narok North Constituency Coordinator between 2017 and 2020, was sacked.

According to records, the claimant was illegally dismissed amidst unpaid salary arrears.

On October 31, 2023, the Employment and Labour Relations Court ruled in Rotiken's favour , a decision that was subsequently upheld when the Senator lost his appeal.

With accrued interest, the court decree now stands at Sh 1.2 million.

Consequently, when the debt remained unsatisfied, licensed auctioneers moved in to execute lawful warrants which in turn provoked a furious reaction from Senator Ole Kina, who fiercely framed the entire episode as a political witch-hunt.

The lawmaker argued that Rotiken was hired by the Narok Senate office rather than his personal capacity, maintaining that any resultant liabilities ought to be handled by the Parliamentary Service Commission (PSC) rather than attaching his private property.

Defending his harsh words in the widely circulated footage, the senator dismissed the agents as trespassers and asserted action against them.

"Anybody who trespasses will get a bullet in their head or leg because that is trespass," said Ole Kina.

“Nitakupiga Risasi!” Senator Ledama Ole Kina embroiled in confrontation with alleged auctioneers over unpaid car loan https://t.co/k4OSXpNsdi November 21, 2026

The claimant's legal team condemned the threats made against statutory court officers emphasizing that a court judgment is an enforceable command rather than a mere suggestion, calling upon the Inspector General of Police of Police and the Director of Criminal Investigatons to urgently investigate the alleged death threats.

Rotiken noted that he merely sought justice through proper judicial channels and should not be penalized or intimidated for pursuing his lawful entitlements.

"When I was illegally dismissed with unpaid salary arrears, I did not resort to violence or politics—I went to the Employment and Labour Relations Court. Nobody is above the law, and I appeal to the police to protect the officers doing their job so that justice can finally be served," he said.

Ultimately, as pressure mounts on security agencies to look into the firearm threats, the unfolding saga highlights a tense intersection between public office obligations and the absolute sanctity of judicial decrees.

While the senator maintains that his assets were unjustly targeted by political rivals, legal experts and the public continue to demand that the rule of law must prevail without exception.

World.title: Planning Minister to Bloomberg: Egypt aims to raise private sector share to 67%
World.content:
Minister of Planning and Economic Development Ahmed Rostom affirmed on Friday, November 27, 2026, that the Egyptian government is focusing on maximizing the resilience of the Egyptian economy amid global geopolitical conflicts and crises by proactively identifying and addressing potential risks.

This came during a television interview with Bloomberg anchor Francine Lacqua in London, following his participation in the eighth edition of the Ambition Africa forum.

Rostom added that Egypt achieved a growth rate of 5.1 percent at the end of the last fiscal year—among the highest recorded across the region and the African continent—in addition to recording a 4.9 percent growth rate during the first quarter of the current fiscal year.

Regarding the economic pressures resulting from the Iranian war, he explained that the energy crisis represents the primary source of pressure and one of the main drivers of uncertainty, not only for the Egyptian economy but for the entire global economy.

He noted the importance of adopting smart policies to address these challenges while identifying and capitalizing on available opportunities—an effort Egypt is actively pursuing by leveraging the diverse structure of its economy, which encompasses a broad mix of energy, productive activities and services sectors.

Turning to foreign direct investment (FDI), Rostom pointed out that Egypt recorded $18 billion in FDI during the last fiscal year, noting aspirations to maintain this positive trajectory and reach around $22 billion or more in the upcoming fiscal year.

The Planning Minister highlighted the sectors in which the government seeks to expand private sector participation, including tourism, information and communications technology (ICT) and logistics.

Addressing the private sector’s role in the economic transformation program, Rostom explained that the government is currently preparing the program, noting that private sector investments currently represent about 60 percent of total investments, with a target to raise this share to 67 percent over the next four years.

He explained that the private sector can play a larger role in the ICT sector—which represents one of the sectors of the future economy—alongside expanding its contribution to tourism and the services sector in general, as well as agriculture.

He affirmed that substantial opportunities exist for the private sector in manufacturing industries, particularly as Egypt seeks to deepen its industrial base.

Rostom stressed the need to view Egypt as an investment market that has proven its worth and resilience in facing various challenges, adding that investors can expect further facilitation and simplification of licensing procedures, alongside additional executive steps to implement the State Ownership Policy.

This will open further opportunities for private sector participation in the aforementioned sectors, including areas where the private sector already maintains a strong presence, particularly ICT, logistics and energy.

He added that Egypt is open to receiving investments across all sectors, foremost among them tourism, noting that tourism revenues reached around $18 billion during the last fiscal year and expressing expectations of attracting further investments in the field.

He also welcomed additional investments in logistics, given the pivotal importance of the Suez Canal as a main artery for global trade.

Regarding the Suez Canal and the outlook for its revenue recovery, Rostom explained that a rebound in the Suez Canal translates into broader economic recovery, as it provides a more efficient and faster corridor for trade movement and cargo transport.

He added that the canal accounts for about 25 percent of global container trade and 10 percent of global cargo trade, noting that Suez Canal revenues currently stand at around four billion, while witnessing increased transits of tonnages, vessels, and container ships, with expectations for continued recovery and a return of revenues to levels ranging between eight billion and nine billion annually or more.

World.title: Egypt’s Ambassador to Tanzania meets Zanzibar President
World.content:
Egypt’s Ambassador to Tanzania Rania Abdel Meguid met on Friday, November 27, 2026, Zanzibar President Hussein Ali Mwinyi.

The meeting addressed ways to advance and strengthen bilateral cooperation in several priority development sectors, particularly tourism, healthcare, infrastructure, energy and agriculture.

Zanzibar President Hussein Ali Mwinyi praised the existing investments of Egyptian companies in Zanzibar. Mwinyi highlighted promising opportunities for further Egyptian cooperation and investment in tourism and other development sectors.

He also expressed interest in strengthening tourism cooperation with Zanzibar by benefiting from Egypt’s extensive expertise in hotel services, hospitality and sustainable tourism. He also called for developing joint tourism programs linking Egyptian and Zanzibari tourist destinations with wildlife reserves on mainland Tanzania.

For her part, Ambassador Abdel Meguid reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to expanding bilateral cooperation in various fields, particularly healthcare. She highlighted the progress achieved through Egyptian medical convoys dispatched to Tanzania in various specialties, most recently in September

She said coordination was underway to establish comprehensive medical cooperation programs, including dispatching medical convoys, treating a number of critical Tanzanian cases in Egypt, sending Egyptian healthcare experts to Tanzania, and contributing to the establishment of hospitals and medical units needed in Zanzibar.

The ambassador also affirmed her readiness to work towards advancing bilateral cooperation in all the aforementioned fields, building on available opportunities and resources to strengthen Egypt’s presence in Zanzibar and contribute to its development efforts

World.title: FM reviews preparations for Egypt’s 2027–2031 human rights strategy
World.content:
Minister of Foreign Affairs, International Cooperation and Egyptians Abroad Badr Abdelatty chaired the eighth ministerial meeting of the Supreme Standing Committee for Human Rights (SSCHR) to review the implementation of Egypt’s National Human Rights Strategy and preparations for its second edition, covering 2027–2031.

The meeting, held on Thursday, November 26, 2026, began with a minute’s silence in memory of the victims of Wednesday’s accident in the Warraq district of Giza.

Abdelatty reviewed consultations on the new strategy with the National Council for Human Rights, civil society organizations and parliamentary human rights committees ahead of its expected adoption and launch.

He also reaffirmed Egypt’s commitment to strengthening cooperation with regional and international human rights mechanisms.

Social Solidarity Minister Maya Morsy reviewed programmes supporting economic empowerment, social protection and human development, while Justice Minister Mahmoud Helmy al-Sherif discussed legislative reforms aimed at protecting civil and political rights.

Prosecutor-General Mohamed Shawky Ayyad outlined efforts to review pretrial detention cases, conduct regular inspections of detention facilities and investigate complaints to safeguard legally guaranteed rights.

The meeting also discussed ongoing legislative reforms and efforts to strengthen political, economic, social and cultural rights in Egypt.

World.title: Military Production Minister attends main phase of Central Military Zone command post exercise
World.content:
Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces and Minister of Defense and Military Production Lt. Gen. Ashraf Salem Zaher witnessed on Friday, November 27, 2026, the main phase of the strategic-tactical command post exercise for the Central Military Zone and various specialized corps of the Armed Forces, which lasted several days as part of the combat training plan for Armed Forces formations and units.

The event was attended by Chief of Staff of the Armed Forces Lt. Gen. Ahmed Khalifa, commanders of the main branches and several Armed Forces commanders.

The main phase began with a presentation summarizing the tactical concept and the decisions made by commanders during the management of the exercise.

The Commander-in-Chief discussed with several commanders and officers the methods of executing their tasks and making optimal decisions to confront unforeseen situations during operations management, praising the distinguished level achieved by the participating personnel across all specializations.

Zaher also met with several Air Defence Forces personnel, conveying to them the greetings and appreciation of President Abdel Fattah El Sisi, President of the Republic and Supreme Commander of the Armed Forces, and his pride in their efforts to secure the state’s vital installations.

He affirmed that the Armed Forces prioritize upgrading the combat and technical capabilities of all corps and specializations to safeguard Egyptian national security across all strategic directions, particularly amid the major transformations and successive developments witnessing the world today.

He noted the importance of continuing to develop qualification and training programs to counter modern threats and smart weapons of all types, ensuring that Armed Forces personnel remain at the highest levels of readiness and preparedness to defend Egypt’s sacred soil.

In a related context, Khalifa witnessed one of the phases of the exercise, which included a presentation of decisions and cooperation organization procedures implemented by various specializations.

He also discussed the executed procedures with several exercise participants to ensure their ability to make sound decisions during the course of operations.

World.title: The case that illustrates how Trump’s retribution campaign is falling short
World.content:
Donald Trump has long sworn his second term in office would bring with it a campaign of retribution against his perceived political enemies.

But ultimately, those efforts have proven largely ineffective – and at times disastrous – for the administration and its Justice Department, despite an exceedingly loyal attorney general and an FBI director who long billed himself as a deep-state attack dog.

Few cases better exemplify the continued failure in prosecuting Trump’s perceived enemies than one brought against former FBI officials in October. In two weeks, a federal judge tossed the charges after an FBI agent testified the case was built at the behest of the president, with FBI leadership listing potential charges and demanding constant updates from agents.

In his written order released this week dismissing the case, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui ridiculed prosecutors for bringing a politically charged case with “rampant errors and misstatements stemming from the slapdash nature of this investigation and prosecution.”

“If a high-profile case like this is so poorly executed, what can the public expect in the run-of-the-mill case with far less resources and oversight,” Faruqui wrote.

An investigation to find a charge

In mid-October, two former FBI officials whose previous work focused on nefarious foreign influence were charged with making false statements to lawmakers in 2023, allegedly misleading members of Congress as to the extent of their knowledge of the FBI’s investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop years earlier.

The ultimate charges, however, did not stem from the origins of the investigation into the former officials, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, or the unit they worked for, the agency’s Foreign Influence Task Force, which focused in part on foreign efforts to interfere with US elections.

According to the agent, Bryan Witt, FBI Director Kash Patel ordered the agency’s Kansas City field office to investigate Floris and others on obstruction or conspiracy charges. That order, he said, came after Trump complained about Floris and other “rogue bureaucrats” during a primetime speech in July, claiming they buried intelligence showing China sought to help Joe Biden win the 2020 election, in part by manufacturing illegal ballots.

The president demanded the FBI and others investigate.

The next day, Patel gave the directive to start the probe, listing potential charges, Witt said.

FBI Director Kash Patel follows US Attorney General Todd Blanche into a news conference at the Department of Justice building on November 24. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images

Witt testified others at the FBI thought the investigation was a “witch hunt” and that he was concerned about the political nature of the case. The agent admitted that the evidence did not support the charges Patel listed nor the case Trump claimed. Instead, the agent said, during their search, investigators found claims around Hunter Biden’s laptop made by Floris and Benavides in two separate 2023 interviews the agents believed to be false.

“The takeaway for FBI staff is to be afraid,” Faruqui wrote in his order this week dismissing the case. “They are one tweet away from being prosecuted by their own government.”

Faruqui added: “The harm from this weaponization is metastasizing from current staff to future recruits. What sane person would join the FBI, particularly in the national security branch, under these circumstances? Starving the FBI of talented agents and analysts is a grave risk to our national security.”

Patel has overseen the firing of scores of agents who were assigned to investigations into Trump and his political enemies, as well as those seen to be acting in a way not sufficiently loyal to the president and his movement, lawsuits by fired agents have alleged.

Despite the victory for the former agents in the case, “the stain this prosecution leaves on the good names of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides is incalculable,” Faruqui wrote, noting the inherent cost of such prosecutions. “No matter what they do, they will never be able to escape their names being associated with this slapdash, politicized attack on them.”

‘Campaign of retribution’

The now-dismissed charges from October focused on statements Floris and Benavides made about their knowledge of the FBI’s investigation into Hunter Biden and his laptop. Prosecutors believed Floris and Benavides lied when they denied knowledge of certain facts records show they had been aware of years earlier.

Faruqui, however, found that several statements had been true and that other statements, made during roundabout, confusing questioning, were not knowingly false.

The judge noted FBI agent Witt made several errors in his own testimony about the investigation before the court, which “demonstrate how easy it is to forget something important.”

Magistrate Judge Zia M. Faruqui speaks, during an event where incarcerated students debated James Madison University students, at Prettyman Federal Courthouse in Washington, DC in November 2024. Craig Hudson for The Washington Post/Getty Images

“The Court chalks up (Witt’s) mistakes to confusion and bad memory, just as it does for Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides,” he added. “Just as (Witt) concluded about his own misstatements, any misstatement of Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides was ‘not an intentionally false statement.’”

Faruqui also found the government had not shown what motive the pair would have in lying to Congress by denying knowledge of a case and investigation that were already in full swing. Instead, Faruqi wrote that it was the government whose motivation “is clear” in their efforts to “appease President Trump.”

“Ms. Floris and Mr. Benavides did not have a reason to interfere with the already full-throttle Congressional investigation into Hunter Biden’s laptop,” he wrote. “There was no benefit Ms. Floris or Mr. Benavides received by making the allegedly false statements.”

Instead of fleshing out the case more fully, “getting to the truth interfered with the rush to charge,” the judge wrote of investigators’ efforts in the case.

“And the motive for that is clear: to appease President Trump in his campaign of retribution against the FBI and to score cheap political points to impact the midterm elections,” the judge wrote.

In a show of support, dozens of agents fired under Trump’s second term attended the hearing in early November when Faruqui first announced his decision to dismiss the case. Former acting FBI Director Brian Driscoll, who fought administration officials early in 2025 when they demanded lists of names of agents to purge and was subsequently fired, was also in attendance.

World.title: Putin’s biggest ally questions a key claim Russia uses to justify invasion of Ukraine
World.content:
Russia’s closest ally Belarus has questioned the logic behind Moscow’s claim over Ukrainian territory, likening it to Mongolia demanding to take over Russian lands.

Russian President Vladimir Putin has argued that Ukraine should be part of Russia because Kyiv was at the heart of the medieval federation known as the Ancient Rus.

Experts have long said this was – at best – an exercise in historical revisionism, but now even Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, who is usually hand in hand with Putin, has cast doubt on the claim.

Lukashenko told French magazine Le Point in an interview published Wednesday that, “to say that (Ukraine’s) lands were Russian from ancient times … well, Russian lands, if you look deeper, were once Mongol-Tatar. Remember? So then, according to that logic, all of Russia should be given to whom – Mongolia?”

In the wide-ranging interview laced with falsehoods and inaccuracies that was otherwise largely supportive of Russia, Lukashenko told the magazine he believed Putin understood the logic was flawed, calling him a “shrewd, clever politician.”

Speaking to the French magazine, Lukashenko celebrated his friendship with Putin and repeated the Russian leader’s false narratives about Ukraine starting the war by “killing and burning Russian people.”

Lukashenko’s convictions, and close relationship with Putin, go back a long time. He was the only member of the Belarusian parliament who voted against the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. And, during his 32 years as president, he has effectively turned Belarus into Russia’s vassal state.

Under his watch, Belarus has played a key role in the war in Ukraine. In February 2022, Lukashenko allowed Russia to use Belarus as a launching pad for Moscow’s full-scale invasion – even though he now denies knowing about it. Later, he agreed to host Russian tactical nuclear weapons.

“Putin and I can joke together, and we are all on informal, first-name terms with one another. He’s entirely approachable,” Lukashenko said, contrasting his relationship with Putin to that of US President Donald Trump’s relationship with the leaders of Western countries.

“You would never say such things to Trump. You sat around that table in Washington like parrots, afraid to say anything to him, sorry for putting it this way. He said whatever he wanted, even in a mocking manner. That is simply unacceptable among us,” he said.

Zelensky rejects Lukashenko offer

Lukashenko also suggested he would be open to taking Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky to see Putin. “I could board a plane together and fly to Moscow. The two of us. As the guarantor of his security, I could sit down with him and fly to Moscow,” he said.

Addressing that suggestion, Zelensky dismissed it as “not serious.”

“We are at war, we cannot meet in Moscow, we cannot meet in Kyiv. We all understand this perfectly well. When someone says such things, it is simply not a serious conversation,” he said.

Lukashenko also said he believed Russia would eventually take over the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, but he pushed back on some of Putin’s maximalist demands – such as the return of NATO’s borders to where they were in 1997.

“I am absolutely convinced that this is the start of negotiations. In any negotiations, both sides proceed from certain maximum conditions. But in the process of negotiations, one must sit at the table and negotiate,” Lukashenko told the publication.

World.title: Israel intensifies assassinations in Gaza as US urges Netanyahu to proceed with ceasefire plan
World.content:
Israel has intensified its campaign of targeted assassinations in Gaza, striking and killing Hamas commanders and political leaders, as the Trump administration urges Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to proceed with the US-brokered ceasefire plan.

On Thursday, the Israeli military killed Khaled Abu Nada, a senior member of Hamas’ Political Bureau and the organization’s Deputy Minister of Education, in a strike in central Gaza. According to a statement from Hamas, the strike on his residential apartment also killed his wife.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said the killing of Abu Nada would disrupt Hamas’ “financial operations and its ability to formulate economic policy.” Hamas said the attack was the result of Israel’s “policy of systematic assassinations” and warned that “targeting civilian homes constitutes a continuous breach of the ceasefire agreement in Gaza and a flagrant violation of all international and humanitarian laws, norms, and conventions.”

Since the nominal ceasefire was signed more than a year ago, Israel has carried out near-daily strikes on Gaza to target Hamas. According to the Palestinian Ministry of Health, more than 1,600 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza in Israeli strikes or military operations over that period.

In recent weeks, Israel has escalated those strikes. On Wednesday, Israel struck and killed Muhammad Abu al-Aouf, the head of Hamas’ internal security apparatus in northern Gaza. A day earlier, the IDF killed al-Aouf’s commander, Naeem Muhammad Abu Nahal, who led Hamas’ internal security across Gaza. In each of these cases, the IDF said the assassination was a “blow” to Hamas’ leadership capabilities, even as the militant organization has firmly entrenched its power in the half of Gaza not occupied by the Israeli military.

Mourners carry the bodies of Muhammad Abu al-Aouf, a Hamas internal security officer, and his family, killed in an Israeli strike according to the Hamas-run Health Minister, during their funeral in Gaza City, on Wednesday. Jehad Alshrafi/AP

The previous week, the IDF carried out strikes nearly every day targeting Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad, from platoon leaders to commanders of Nukhba, a special force within Hamas’ military wing.

In each case, the IDF issued virtually the same justification: “Throughout the war, and particularly recently, the terrorists advanced attacks against IDF troops and Israeli civilians and operated to restore the capabilities of terrorist organizations in the Gaza Strip, in systematic violation of the ceasefire.”

Hamas blamed both Israel and the US-backed Board of Peace for the ongoing attacks. The group said the board “bears political and moral responsibility for the continuation of these crimes as a result of its silence and failure to halt the aggression, and its continued provision of cover and support to the occupation.”

The board was established by the Trump administration and backed by a UN Security Council resolution to advance the Gaza ceasefire plan signed in October 2025. But the plan stalled within weeks of its implementation, and much of Gaza remains in ruins.

Globally isolated

On Tuesday, Netanyahu spoke by phone with Jared Kushner, Trump’s son-in-law, who played a crucial role in crafting the ceasefire deal, according to an Israeli source who said they discussed Gaza.

According to Axios, Kushner urged Netanyahu to carry out Israel’s obligations under the ceasefire plan, which would require Israel to stop striking Gaza and begin withdrawing forces that occupy more than half of the enclave’s territory.

But Netanyahu has refused to make progress on the 20-point plan until Hamas is completely disarmed. Last week, Defense Minister Israel Katz said that Israel “will not withdraw from the current lines of the security zones” until Hamas is “dismantled.” He also warned that Israel is ready to occupy more of Gaza.

Hamas has refused to unilaterally disarm, saying that it would only do so alongside a staged Israeli withdrawal from Gaza

In an extensive interview with New York magazine, Kushner warned that Israel was increasingly becoming globally isolated. “I feel like the fork in the road is Israel could rise from the tragedy of October 7, (and) be much more secure and much more integrated in the world, or they can go on the current trajectory, which is to trend toward global pariah status,” he said.

In another interview, with Mathias Döpfner, CEO of POLITICO’s parent company Axel Springer, Kushner called Netanyahu someone who “doesn’t always make it easy” to make progress in the Trump administration’s Gaza plan, and delivered his sharpest rebuke of Israel’s broader posture, arguing it should drop its “constant wartime mindset” and embrace economic diplomacy like Gulf Arab states do.

But Netanyahu has not shown any willingness to make concessions toward Gaza to advance the ceasefire agreement, particularly as his far-right allies have advocated for more strikes in Gaza and Palestinian emigration from the shattered territory.

On Wednesday, Kushner said in a podcast interview that Israel “needs to get out of the constant wartime mindset and focus on economic diplomacy.”

CNN’s Tal Shalev contributed to this article.

World.title: Houthis strike Saudi oil infrastructure as Riyadh intensifies attacks on Yemen
World.content:
Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis are trading increasingly intense strikes on strategic sites, including oil infrastructure and ports, marking a sharp escalation in fighting between the two sides.

A projectile struck an oil refinery in Saudi Arabia’s southwestern Jazan region on Thursday, killing a Nepalese worker and injuring several others, according to the Saudi Ministry of Energy. The strike sparked a fire and temporarily suspended some operations at the facility, the ministry said.

The attack came a day after the Houthis claimed to have struck Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil refinery at Ras Tanura. Satellite imagery taken Wednesday showed a huge plume of black smoke rising from the coastal peninsula following the attack.

The Houthi-controlled armed forces said the attack caused a fire at Ras Tanura, part of one of the world’s largest crude oil export terminals, in Saudi Arabia’s Eastern Province. A shipping source told CNN Thursday that oil loadings at the terminal were suspended after the attack, though it was unclear whether they have resumed.

The Saudi-led coalition said it intercepted and destroyed four drones over Ras Tanura, with falling debris but no reported injuries.

Ras Tanura has a refining capacity of 550,000 barrels per day and is part of a broader complex that housed Saudi Arabia’s main crude export terminal before the US-Iran war began.

Saudi state-owned oil company Aramco did not immediately respond to a request for comment from CNN.

The Houthis also claimed responsibility for a strike on Riyadh Wednesday that Saudi authorities said wounded 11 people. An eyewitness told CNN that Saudi Arabia’s trillion-dollar sovereign wealth fund, the Public Investment Fund, is headquartered inside the targeted skyscraper.

The Saudi-led coalition said in a later statement Wednesday that the strike was carried out by a Houthi drone and vowed a “firm response.”

The Public Investment Fund (PIF) tower in Riyadh’s financial district which the Saudi-led coalition said had been targeted by a “terrorist attack” on Tuesday. Saudi Press Agency

Strikes intensify in Yemen

Saudi-led forces meanwhile have stepped up attacks across Houthi-controlled areas of Yemen.

On Thursday, the coalition said it carried out a “precision military operation” against Houthi capabilities, destroying 50 targets it described as legitimate military targets across Sanaa, Hodeidah and Saada governorates.

A day earlier, the coalition said it attacked “operational capabilities” at the Houthi-controlled Hodeidah port and destroyed targets in Saada and Amran governorates.

The Houthi-controlled armed forces, meanwhile, said Saudi warplanes and missiles carried out 109 strikes over the previous 24 hours across Yemen including in Sanaa and Hodeidah.

The Houthi-controlled health ministry in Sanaa said Thursday that at least 19 civilians had been killed and 25 others wounded in Saudi strikes over the previous 48 hours across several parts of Yemen.

CNN has not been able to independently verify the claims about the strikes or casualties.

The International Committee of the Red Cross said Thursday it facilitated the transfer of human remains across front lines in Yemen between Tuesday and Thursday, at the request of the parties to the conflict. The ICRC did not specify how many remains were transferred or identify the forces to which they belonged.

Abdulqader al-Murtada, the head of the Houthi-controlled National Committee for Prisoners’ Affairs, said in a statement that 20 bodies of Houthi forces were transferred to Sanaa.

Crown prince’s US visit

The Houthis have repeatedly targeted infrastructure in Saudi Arabia in recent weeks, including Riyadh’s financial district. Riyadh’s international airport was also hit several times last month, killing more than a dozen people.

The escalating attacks come as Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman is planning his first trip to the United States since the Iran war began, where he is expected to attend next month’s G20 summit in Miami, Florida, according to a source familiar with the plans. Saudi officials have not yet publicly confirmed his attendance.

Saudi Arabia has sought US support in strengthening its defenses as it faces continued Houthi missile and drone attacks.

The planned visit would set up the first in person meeting between US President Donald Trump and Prince bin Salman since the outbreak of the war.

Smoke billows from the Yemeni capital Sanaa on Thursday after Houthi media reported a series of Saudi airstrikes against territories held by the Iran-backed group. AFP/Getty Images

Fighting between the Houthi group and the Saudi-led coalition reignited in July after years of relative calm brought about by a 2022 UN-brokered ceasefire. Clashes intensified in recent months after the militant group made an advance toward the critical Bab el-Mandeb Strait in September, threatening a new front in the Iran war.

This story has been updated to remove a reference to King Abdullah Economic City, which is in western Saudi Arabia.

World.title: Tubman University Graduates 256 at 13th Commencement, Highlights Academic and Infrastructure Gains
World.content:
The university’s 13th Commencement Convocation brought together government officials, international guests, education stakeholders and families as President Dr. Olu Q. Menjay outlined institutional progress, Founding President Dr. Elizabeth Davis-Russell urged graduates to provide worthy service, and Valedictorian Abraham Washington challenged them to uphold integrity and contribute to national development.

HARPER, Maryland County — William V.S. Tubman University has graduated 256 students from six colleges, with university officials highlighting developments in research, technology and infrastructure while challenging the graduates to use their education to address Liberia’s development needs.

By Peter P. Toe, Jr., [email protected]



The ceremony, held at the Tubman University Pavilion in Harper on Monday, November 23, 2026, brought together international guests, including representatives of partner institutions and donor organizations, national government officials, members of the university’s Board of Trustees, the Foundational Board, local authorities, education stakeholders, parents, guardians, faculty and staff.

Delivering his institutional message, TU President Dr. Olu Q. Menjay outlined developments in research, academic technology, student services and campus infrastructure, describing them as part of the university’s efforts to improve the quality of higher education.

Dr. Menjay said the university had been ranked first among Liberian universities in research publications by the Association of African Universities, of which TU is a full member.

He also announced that the university’s Institutional Review Board is operational, following Federalwide Assurance approval granted on January 28, 2026, and valid through January 28, 2030.



The President said TU’s digital library provides access to more than three million electronic books, journals and research documents. He also cited the introduction of plagiarism detection software as part of efforts to strengthen academic integrity and research standards.

The President further announced plans to introduce a paid campus vacation employment program in 2027. Under the initiative, sixty students, ten from each college, will be selected to gain practical work experience and develop professional skills.

On entrepreneurship, Dr. Menjay challenged graduates to become job creators rather than depend solely on the search for employment. He said the university plans to purchase liquid soap produced by its students for institutional use beginning next year.

The President also reported renovations to the College of Education, named after Dr. Elizabeth Davis-Russell, the academic complex and the capital housing complex. He said renovation work on the university’s College of Arts and Sciences building was continuing, with half of the building fully completed and already in use by students for classes, while the first phase of a new engineering complex was nearing completion.

He also acknowledged international support, including a donation of assorted university supplies from Howard Payne University in Brownwood, Texas, which he said was being shipped to Liberia.

For her part, Keynote speaker and TU Founding President Dr. Elizabeth Davis-Russell challenged graduates to use their education to provide what she described as “worthy service” that makes a meaningful difference in people’s lives.

Dr. Davis-Russell, 84, traveled from California, United States, to attend the ceremony. She also chairs the university’s Foundation Board.

She reminded graduates that TU was founded on values including excellence, integrity, civility, ethics, genuine care, professionalism, intellectual engagement, dependability and trustworthiness.

She said the university’s responsibility extends beyond its immediate surroundings, emphasizing that its focus must remain local, national and international.

“This university is not parochial,” she said, adding that its responsibility was to address local and national needs while maintaining an international outlook.

She urged the graduates to use artificial intelligence responsibly to address national challenges, including food insufficiency and diseases such as malaria.

“Are you going to become a passive participant or a diligent mover?” she asked, challenging graduates to use AI ethically to improve the human condition.

Dr. Davis-Russell called on graduates to build on practical projects and community initiatives undertaken by students who preceded them.

She urged graduates of the College of Education to advance earlier efforts in early childhood education that involved parents in children’s learning and care.

Business Administration graduates were challenged to help local business owners improve their practices, while Agriculture graduates were urged to contribute to making Liberia self-sufficient in rice production.

Graduates of Nursing and Health Sciences were reminded of earlier community health screening and public education efforts, including during the Ebola outbreak. She challenged them to continue promoting good health practices in communities.

She also urged Arts and Sciences graduates to preserve Liberia’s cultural heritage and work with health professionals to address infectious diseases and high maternal mortality.

As they enter the workforce or pursue further studies, Dr. Davis-Russell cautioned graduates against allowing rumors, popular opinion or the desire for power to influence their decisions.

“Know which lines you are unwilling to cross,” she told them, warning against compromising personal values to gain access to friendship or positions of power.

She urged the graduates to regularly examine their conduct and decisions by asking whether they could be proud of the person they see when they look in the mirror.

Valedictorian Abraham Washington used his address to reflect on his journey through poverty, hunger and financial hardship, saying determination and the support of others helped him reach graduation.

He paid tribute to his late mother, who raised and supported him throughout his education but died shortly before the ceremony.

Washington said her prayers, sacrifices and guidance would remain part of his success story.

Addressing his fellow graduates, he said the value of their education should not be measured only by the degrees they receive, but by how they use their knowledge to improve the lives of others.

He called on graduates to reject corruption, tribalism, political intolerance and the abuse of public resources, urging them to demonstrate integrity and accountability in their professional and personal lives.

Washington also acknowledged the contributions of the university’s international partners and sponsors, including the Boe Peace Foundation Africa, Waz Foundation, MOPP and other supporters.

He challenged graduates from the different colleges to apply their knowledge to national problems, including challenges in education, business, agriculture and healthcare.

“If our education cannot improve the lives of others, ask yourself, what greater purpose should my education serve?” he asked.

He concluded by reminding his classmates that while their academic journey at the university had ended, their responsibility to learn, serve and lead was only beginning.

With 256 graduates now entering the workforce and other areas of professional life, attention turns to how effectively their academic training will translate into practical solutions to Liberia’s longstanding challenges, from unemployment and food insecurity to poor healthcare, weak infrastructure and governance concerns.

Their contributions in the coming years will ultimately test the value of the education they have received and the university’s promise of producing graduates capable of making a difference.

World.title: Cummings Says Boakai’s US$5.7 Billion Gold-for-Infrastructure Deal Could Trade Away Liberia’s Birthright
World.content:
MONROVIA – A day after President Joseph Nyuma Boakai signed what his government calls the largest infrastructure program in Liberia’s history, the opposition’s most prominent economic voice has asked a pointed question: who pays?

By Rodney D Sieh

Addressing a news conference Thursday, Alternative National Congress (ANC) political leader Alexander B. Cummings compared the deal to the biblical Esau, who sold his birthright for a single meal. “We must not become an Esau Generation,” he said.



What Was Signed

Boakai promised to deliver four new power plants, a national transmission network and 14 major road and bridge projects within five years under the US$5.7 billion agreement he signed Wednesday with Bea Mountain Mining Corporation. Under the Master Infrastructure Development Agreement (MIDA), the deal would add 270 megawatts of electricity through four new power plants, more than three times the capacity of the Mount Coffee hydropower plant, and build a 146-kilometer highway.

The government’s case rests on how the deal is paid for. The President said the government would use higher gold prices to “ring-fence new revenue streams” from BMMC beginning in 2027 to fund the projects, and BMMC also agreed to a US$500 million bridge financing facility to keep construction on schedule. In other words, Liberia pays no cash up front. It pays with gold revenue it expects to collect in the future.

Two Speeches, Two Days



Set side by side, the President’s speech on Wednesday and Cummings’ remarks on Thursday agree on what Liberia needs. They part ways on the price.

Both start with the same hardship. Boakai spoke of ordinary people the deal would reach, saying “It will provide power for the welder, the tailor, the barber, and the shopkeeper,” and pointing to children studying at night and clinics keeping equipment running. Cummings opened on the same ground: roads that cannot be used in the rainy season, millions without reliable electricity, and farmers who cannot get their produce to market. “Liberia desperately needs roads. Liberia desperately needs energy,” he said. On the problem itself, there is no disagreement.

Both reach for a food metaphor. Boakai anticipated his critics in the language of the market: “I know some Liberians will ask, ‘Da What will we Eat?’ That is a legitimate concern.” Cummings answered with Esau’s meal: “His hunger was real. His need was genuine. But the price he paid was far greater than the temporary relief he received.” Boakai’s message is that Liberians will see real benefits from the deal. Cummings’ warning is that satisfying today’s hunger could cost the country something far more valuable.

Both speak for future generations, to opposite ends. Boakai called the signing “a historic day for Liberia as we lay the foundations for tomorrow.” Cummings warned that “in our urgency to solve today’s problems, we must not mortgage tomorrow’s possibilities.” To the President, the deal is a gift to future generations. To Cummings, it is a bill they may be left to pay.

They disagree on whether this is debt. The government insists the deal adds no borrowing. The President’s legal adviser, Keita, said “So we are not going to be adding to the government’s debt, and that is a big deal for all of us.” Cummings rejects the premise: “There is no such thing as free infrastructure. Someone ultimately pays.” His concern is precisely that pledging future revenue lets the government take on a debt-like obligation “outside traditional public debt transparency mechanisms.” The two sides are not arguing about the same numbers. They are arguing about whether committing future income counts as borrowing.

Both claim value for money. Boakai said “We wanted to make sure we got the best for our money and for the future.” Cummings’ closing line uses nearly the same words: infrastructure “at the right price, under the right conditions.” The difference is proof. The government points to safeguards it says are already written into the deal: audit rights and an owner’s engineer to monitor every stage and flag inferior materials or overcharging, and Keita added that “The company even agreed to be fined if they ever overcharge us.” Cummings wants independent valuation, independent certification and full publication of the documents. Both men are addressing the same risk, overcharging. The question is whether the government’s in-house safeguards are enough, or whether the checks must come from outside.

What the President left out. Published accounts of Wednesday’s speech do not mention competitive bidding, the Public Procurement and Concessions Commission, the role of the Legislature, or who will build the projects. Those gaps are exactly where Cummings focused on Thursday.

The Cummings Argument

Cummings went out of his way to say he is not against the deal itself. “We are not opposed to infrastructure development. We are not opposed to investment,” he said. “What we oppose is lack of transparency.”

He listed ten concerns. They include:

• possible breach of the Public Procurement and Concessions Act;

• no competitive bidding;

• no independent valuation or engineering assessment;

• possible overpricing;

• automatic deductions from future government revenue;

• conflict-of-interest risks.

He then set out ten conditions he says must be met before the deal proceeds. Among them: publication of all transaction documents, legislative hearings, an independent debt sustainability analysis, and independent certification of project costs and completed works.

Where the Criticism Lands

On several points, the public record supports him.

No competitive bidding. Reporting on the deal shows that MAPA İnşaat ve Ticaret A.Ş. is identified as the engineering and construction contractor. The Turkish Contractors Association identifies Mehmet Günal as MAPA’s chairman and Murathan Günal as deputy chairman, linking the family to both sides of the deal. In practical terms, the company financing the projects and the company building them appear to share the same family owners. The Liberian Observer found no description of a competitive tender for selecting MAPA, and noted that the government has not publicly released its independent financial due diligence or any comparative assessment of contractors. The paper was careful to add that common ownership is not, by itself, evidence of improper conduct, but it matters when judging how the contracts are priced and supervised.

That is also why the government’s owner’s engineer matters, and why Cummings is right to ask who appoints that engineer and who that engineer answers to. Cummings lists “governance and conflict-of-interest concerns” but never names MAPA or the Günal family. That was the most concrete point available to him, and he left it out.

The Legislature was not at the table. Senator Abe Darius Dillon has said the National Legislature had no role in negotiating or signing the deal. That supports Cummings’ call for legislative review and public hearings before ratification.

The final cost is unclear. Cummings warns that the real bill could be higher than US$5.7 billion. The published project list gives him some support. Alongside the power and road works, the government has announced a further US$1 billion for road networks across all regions, and it is not clear whether that is part of the US$5.7 billion or on top of it. Keita also defended the cost by saying the Via dam is designed to expand to at least 1,000 megawatts. If that expansion is part of the plan, its cost, and who pays for it, has not been disclosed.

Where It Falls Short

Cummings’ case is stronger on principle than on evidence.

His most serious charge is that royalties, income taxes, dividends and other government revenues from Liberia’s natural resources could be “redirected toward repayment — for decades.” But he supports this only with “indications.” He does not cite a clause, a figure or a document.

The government’s position is narrower. It says it will use extra revenue that higher gold prices make possible, while the company will also keep making its regular payments into the Consolidated Account. Who is right depends on how much that “extra” revenue is, how it is calculated, and what happens if gold prices fall. Neither the President on Wednesday nor Cummings on Thursday put those numbers before the public.

The scale is worth noting. LEITI’s FY2023 reconciliation report lists government revenues attributed to Bea Mountain at approximately $33.47 million for that fiscal year. Gold prices have risen sharply since then. Even so, paying off a US$5.7 billion program from one mine’s revenue would require gold earnings far above anything Liberia has recorded. Cummings could have made that point with hard figures. Instead, he leaned on the Esau story.

Nor does he say what he would do instead. He calls on the government to consider “alternative financing models” that could be cheaper, but he names none. For a former Coca-Cola executive who is expected to seek the presidency again in 2029, that is a missed opportunity to show how he would pay for 270 megawatts of electricity without the gold.

His description of the deal as “a human rights issue” may also strike some readers as overreach. His stronger points are the plainer ones: procurement, valuation and disclosure.

The Politics

Cummings insists this “is not a government-versus-opposition issue.” Even so, his remarks position him as the opposition’s guardian of the public purse, a role he has built since 2017.

That leaves two competing messages. The President promises the welder and the barber electricity and roads within five years. Cummings warns that the meal may cost the birthright. With much of the country still without reliable electricity, the President’s message may be the easier one for voters to accept.

What Comes Next

The deal now goes to the Legislature for ratification. That is where the two speeches will be tested against each other.

Dillon has said he wants the agreement scrutinized before any vote but has not said which way he leans. The questions lawmakers can fairly ask are the ones neither the President nor his critic fully answered:

• How much new revenue does the deal assume, and at what gold price?

• What happens to the repayment schedule if gold prices fall?

• Was MAPA’s pricing independently checked, and against what benchmark?

• Who appoints the owner’s engineer, and who does that engineer report to?

• Did the PPCC review the procurement?

• Is the US$1 billion road program inside or outside the US$5.7 billion?

On Wednesday, the President said the deal would lay “the foundations for tomorrow.” On Thursday, Cummings said history will judge the agreement not by “the speeches delivered on signing day,” but by what remains in 20, 30 and 40 years. Both men are appealing to the same future, and only the Legislature’s scrutiny of the deal will show which of them is right about it.

World.title: LRA Dashboard: Domestic Revenue Tops Us$1.2 Billion As Two Mining Giants Carry The Load
World.content:
ArcelorMittal, Bea Mountain pay more than a third of Liberia's domestic revenue as LRA beats FY2026 targets with five weeks left

MONROVIA – Liberia’s tax collector is on the verge of closing the books on its best year ever, but a closer look at who is paying shows how much of that success rests on a few companies.

By Rodney D Sieh

As of Thursday afternoon, the LRA’s live revenue dashboard showed a “balance to be collected” of US$13,177,571.81 against the government’s consolidated FY2026 target of US$1,301,728,411.15. The fiscal year runs to December 31.



A banner across the dashboard declared: “Congratulations, Domestic Tax! FY2026 target achieved!”

Taxes above target

According to the dashboard:

• Domestic tax collections stood at US$902.26 million against a target of US$895.79 million, about US$6.5 million over.



• Customs collected US$307.69 million against a budget of US$280.93 million, about US$26.8 million over.

• Combined domestic revenue reached US$1.21 billion against a target of US$1.18 billion, a surplus of about US$33.2 million.

That puts Liberia past the US$1 billion mark the LRA set for itself last year. In 2025, the LRA collected about US$818 million, exceeding the approved target of US$804.6 million by US$13.4 million, which it called the highest outturn in the country’s history. If the dashboard figures hold, FY2026 domestic revenue is up nearly 48 percent on that record.

Because domestic revenue is already over target, the remaining US$13 million gap sits in the US$120 million budgeted from external resources such as donor grants. The dashboard’s totals imply that about US$73.6 million of that has come in so far, leaving a shortfall of about US$46 million. The tax surplus covers most of it, but not all.

Two companies, a third of the revenue

LRA data on its top revenue contributors show how concentrated the base is.

ArcelorMittal Liberia leads with US$289.4 million, more than double the next payer. That figure likely includes a one-off payment. Under the iron ore company’s third Mineral Development Agreement, a US$200 million signature bonus was payable to the Government of Liberia within 30 days of the effective date, and the Senate passed the agreement on January 30, 2026. Without that bonus, ArcelorMittal’s ordinary contribution would be about US$89 million.

Bea Mountain Mining Corporation is second at US$134.1 million. That is a steep rise for the gold miner. LEITI’s FY2023 reconciliation report listed government revenues attributed to Bea Mountain at approximately $33.47 million for that fiscal year. Record gold prices are driving the jump.

Together, the two mining companies paid about US$423.5 million, roughly 35 percent of all domestic revenue collected this year.

The top ten together paid about US$608.3 million, just over half of all domestic revenue.

Two of the top ten are government bodies. The Civil Service Agency, in third place, appears largely because it remits income tax withheld from civil servants’ salaries. In effect, that is the government paying itself through its own payroll. The Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority is ninth.

Three of the top ten are fuel importers: Aminata & Sons, Conex Petroleum and West Oil. Orange Liberia is the only telecom company in the top ten. Its rival, Lonestar Cell MTN, is not on the list.

November snapshot

A separate LRA table shows the top contributors for what appears to be November alone. A European Union grant of US$17.8 million led the list. ArcelorMittal followed with US$13.5 million and Bea Mountain with US$9.3 million. Lonestar Cell MTN appears there at US$1.26 million, behind Orange at US$1.89 million.

Why it matters

The figures have a direct bearing on this week’s biggest economic story. On Wednesday, President Joseph Nyuma Boakai signed a US$5.7 billion infrastructure deal under which new revenue from Bea Mountain, driven by higher gold prices, would be “ring-fenced” from 2027 to pay for power plants and roads.

The LRA data show what is at stake. Bea Mountain is now the government’s second-largest source of domestic revenue. How much of its future payments go into the infrastructure deal, rather than into the national budget, will matter more than ever.

The data also point to a broader risk. When one iron ore company and one gold miner provide over a third of domestic revenue, a fall in iron ore or gold prices, or a disruption at either mine, would hit the budget hard. And ArcelorMittal’s US$200 million bonus will not recur next year. To match FY2026, the LRA would have to make up that money from other sources in FY2027.

A caution on the numbers

The dashboard describes itself as showing “unreconciled collections.” The figures may change once the LRA reconciles its accounts at year-end, and the agency has not yet published final FY2026 figures.

World.title: Liberia: LPRA Launches Five-Year Strategic Plan, Discloses US$13.8 Million Revenue Contribution
World.content:
LPRA Director General Marilyn T. Logan speaks the launch of five-years strategic plan at EJS Ministerial Complex in Monrovia/ 26/112026

The Liberia Petroleum Regulatory Authority (LPRA) has launched a five-year Strategic Plan covering 2026 to 2030, with a commitment to publish its first-ever State of the Petroleum Sector Report in 2027. The plan seeks to strengthen petroleum regulation, attract investment, develop local technical expertise and improve transparency and accountability in Liberia’s oil and gas industry.

The Strategic Plan, covering 2026 to 2030, was unveiled to stakeholders Thursday at the Ellen Johnson Sirleaf Ministerial Complex in Monrovia by LPRA Director General Hon. Marilyn T. Logan, who said the roadmap would position Liberia to compete more effectively for global petroleum exploration investment while ensuring that the country’s natural resources are managed in the national interest.

Speaking at the launch, Minister of State for Presidential Affairs Samuel Stevquoah commended the LPRA for developing the plan, emphasizing President Joseph Boakai’s expectation that Liberians must benefit fairly from the country’s petroleum resources.



He said the President wants to ensure that Liberians have a fair share when international oil companies begin operations in the country.

“Liberians really want to know whether they will have a fair share when oil companies begin operation in Liberia,” Stevquoah said, reflecting the President’s position.

He noted that the strategic plan comes at a time when Liberia has opportunities to attract serious investors into petroleum exploration and advance development aspirations that citizens have long awaited.Stevquoah also called for stronger coordination among institutions responsible for regulating and managing the petroleum sector, saying the President expects all stakeholders to work together, respect each other’s mandates and draw on one another’s expertise.

Guests Observe prayer at the LPRA five-year strategic plan launch in Monrovia l 26/112026

At the launch, Logan disclosed that the Authority has contributed US$13.8 million to the national budget over the past three years, following what she described as an inherited situation of tax arrears and almost no revenue contribution to government.



She said the LPRA now ranks among Liberia’s eleven highest revenue contributors and is the best-performing state-owned enterprise in terms of revenue contribution.

The Director General also highlighted progress in attracting petroleum investment, revealing that Liberia went more than a decade without signing a new Production Sharing Contract before the current leadership took office in March 2024.

“Within 18 months, we changed that story: we secured and signed eight production sharing contracts, and the Legislature has since ratified all eight,” Logan said.

She added that a reconnaissance programme is underway in the Harper Basin, while the Authority’s 2026 Direct Negotiation Licensing Round, launched last month, is expected to surpass the results achieved in 2025.

Providing an industry perspective, Bertrand Touze, TotalEnergies Vice President and Country Delegate responsible for launching the company’s exploration programme in Liberia, said the country was once again attracting attention on the international petroleum exploration scene.

He disclosed that TotalEnergies has opened a new office in Liberia and engaged skilled Liberian companies to support its exploration activities.

Touze said the company expects approximately half a dozen vessels to arrive in Liberian waters in early 2027 to support exploration activities in its offshore blocks.

He added that TotalEnergies would maintain transparency in its operations and implement health, safety and environmental measures as it pursues the possibility of discovering oil or gas in Liberia.

Logan noted that Liberia is competing for a limited share of global exploration investment as international petroleum companies become more selective about where they commit capital. Citing International Energy Agency estimates, she said global upstream investment stood at just under US$570 billion in 2025, approximately four percent below the previous year.Against this background, she stressed that Liberia’s ability to attract investment will depend not only on its geological potential but also on credible regulation, ethical conduct, competitive contract terms and timely decision-making.

Guests pose for group photo at after the launch of LPRA’s five-year strategic plan launch at EJS Ministerial Complex in Monrovia/ 26/112026

Under the new strategic plan, the LPRA has outlined six priority areas to guide its work through 2030. These include strengthening the management of petroleum rights and contracts, developing Liberian technical expertise, improving petroleum data management, protecting the environment and public safety, strengthening institutional governance and promoting transparency and local participation.

A major component of the plan is the development of local technical capacity. Logan announced that the Authority’s entire Technical Department will travel to France in January 2027 for practical training in petroleum data analysis. A second phase of training will be conducted in Monrovia, focusing on petroleum operations, safety and other technical areas. The programme will also be open to other actors in the petroleum sector.

She said the objective is to build a pool of Liberian specialists capable of independently assessing the country’s petroleum resources and effectively reviewing the technical activities of international operators, reducing reliance on external technical support.

On environmental protection and operational safety, the plan provides for joint regulatory protocols between the LPRA and the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA), alongside specialized training for inspectors in Health, Safety and Environment audits.

The Authority also intends to establish risk mitigation and emergency response frameworks and ensure that operators’ safety plans are reviewed before petroleum activities begin.
