World.title: Why Advent calendars are thriving in the ‘little treat’ economy
World.content:
The countdown to Christmas began in October — at least on social media.

Over the past few months, content creators have been getting a head start on the holidays by unboxing, reviewing and promoting an array of Advent calendars. The anticipation behind each cardboard flap has translated into millions of views, as consumers lean into the surge in popularity surrounding the product.

“Brands are bringing out their advent calendars earlier and earlier, and so they go faster every year,” said TikTok creator Courtney Cahoon, who said nowadays she’s purchasing the calendars as early as August and sharing highlights with her 1.7 million followers.

The calendars originated in Germany in the 20th century, where a printer took inspiration from the candies attached to cardboard he had used to count down to Christmas as a child, according to retail giant Williams Sonoma.

While the calendars are not a new holiday offering, demand for the product has increased in recent years — which explains why it might feel like there’s a calendar for just about everything and for just about everyone. Global market for such calendars could reach $2.47 billion by 2033, according to trade publication Retail Insider.

Nowadays, the calendars have evolved into a marketing vehicle for brands looking to showcase everything from everyday essentials like McCormick’s spices to luxury goods like a $1,020 set of mini perfumes from Maison Francis Kurkdijan.

Experts like Freddy Tran Nager, an associate professor of communication at the University of Southern California, attribute the popularity of the calendars to what’s called “the treat economy.”

“We’ve had a rough few years,” said Nager, the founder of the marketing consultancy Atomic Tango LLC, referring to the economic challenges facing the U.S. economy. “And so you know, some people indulge in what’s called the ‘treat economy.’ They can’t afford a car. They can’t afford a home, but they can certainly afford little treats for themselves.”

Creators who specialize in sharing product recommendations on their feeds — sometimes in exchange for a commission from the brands — have also encouraged users to lean into indulging in calendar deals earlier and earlier.

On platforms like TikTok, searches for “advent calendar” spiked from Nov. 2-8, with the app reporting that many of its creators have posted videos sharing which calendars are underrated and which offer the best value. Ahead of Black Friday, TikTok said in a recent weekly trends report that more “creators are sharing holiday gift guides and reviewing advent calendars. Shoppers are also turning to TikTok Shop for holiday finds.”

Faire, an online wholesale platform that tracks consumer habits, told NBC News in an email that “by the end of September, retailers had already spent more on advent calendars than in all of last season.”

Advent calendars. Papier

Hannah Wall, Faire’s trend expert, also attributed to the popularity of the advent calendar to “treat culture,” citing peak interest from Gen Z.

“Gen Z has made it an adult staple because it’s the ultimate small treat and they’re choosing squishies, tea, jam, and beauty countdowns over chocolate for a daily dose of holiday joy,” Wall wrote in an email statement.

Jintao Zhang, an assistant professor of marketing at Binghamton University, offered a similar observation.

“We know that the largest consumer group consuming social media is Gen Z,” he said, adding that the age group “determines the prevalence and also the attractiveness of advent calendar on social media.”

Social media users also tend to trust content creators, particularly those with smaller followings who are known as “micro” or “nano” influencers, according to Zhang. Still, he warned people to be cautious as some influencers post content that is sponsored without necessarily disclosing it in an obvious way.

Influencers typically approach their calendar videos in two different ways: Some do countdowns, going through each day of the calendar individually (as intended); while others open an entire calendar in one video, sharing its contents altogether.

Natalie Violette, a beauty and lifestyle influencer with more than 4 million followers on TikTok, said she either purchases or receives the calendars from brands in an effort to maintain authenticity in her reviews.

“They like seeing … the honest reactions and reviews on these calendars, and definitely … the surprise factor, no question, I think that’s what really brings them in,” said Violette, whose journey with this type of content began three years ago when a follower challenged her to do a complete makeup look just by using products from a calendar.

Her calendar videos have become so popular that they draw in new viewers every holiday season. The calendars she posts often sell out, she added.

Even calendars that she isn’t a fan of pick up traction online. For example, Violette was among the creators who criticized the Skims calendar, which, for $148, included hair ties and bobby pins. As a result of the online backlash, the Kim Kardashian-owned brand began offering refunds to customers who were unhappy with the product.

Sarah Lynn, who has built a following of more than 200,000 followers on TikTok for her calendar content, described it as “super fun” to show people what’s on the market. Sometimes, however, she said the offerings are hit or miss.

She particularly doesn’t appreciate when brands are “just filling it with random kinds of junk that they know are not really their best selling products.”

“If this was not my job and if this wasn’t what I was doing for work, I would not be spending all this money,” Lynn said. “But I never want people to feel like they have to buy anything or that they’re necessarily missing out.”

“Whatever people want to take from my content, they can definitely take from it,” she added. “Whether it’s entertainment or shopping inspiration or neither.”

World.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade kicks off after being postponed
World.content:
The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade is kicking off in New York City Saturday morning after it was postponed for the first time in its 100-year history due to weather.

The festivities stepped off at 8:30 a.m. and will last until noon.

New characters from Hello Kitty, the Minions, Harry Potter and Disney are among those joining the lineup along with 28 floats, 31 clown crews, 24 performers, nine marching bands, 17 performance groups and nine other specialty units.

The Tom Turkey float during the Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, on Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Participants prepare to march during the Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, on Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The parade will make its way along the 2 1/2-mile route from the Upper West Side to Macy's flagship store at Herald Square.

Parade organizers announced Wednesday they would be postponing the annual celebration to keep participants and spectators safe.

A powerful storm inundated the Tri-State Area Thursday with heavy rain, strong winds and coastal flooding.

"Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday," they said, in part.

An acrobat flips in front of the Tom Turkey float during the Macy's 100th Thanksgiving Day Parade in New York, on Saturday, Nov. 28, 2026. Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images

The Joe Cool Snoopy and Woodstock balloon during the 2026 Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Nov. 28, 2026, in New York City. Kevin Mazur/Getty Images

Days before, questions were looming as to whether the parade's iconic balloons would fly.

The threshold is 34 mph winds, and Thursday's forecasted winds were up to 60 mph.

But the balloons should be able to fly without a hitch on Saturday. The weather is looking much better, with mostly cloudy skies but dry. Gusts will be up to 25 mph, and highs are in the low 50s.

World.title: Argentina's bid to halt oil drilling off Falkland Islands rejected
World.content:
Argentina's bid to temporarily block oil drilling off the nearby U.K.-held Falkland Islands was rejected Saturday by an international tribunal that rules on maritime disputes.

At a special hearing in Hamburg, Germany, the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea voted 18-3 against Argentina's request to halt drilling at the Sea Lion offshore oil project in Falkland Islands waters, around 300 miles east of Argentina's southeastern coast.

The dispute over the planned drilling revived memories of the bitter war the two countries fought 44 years ago over the islands, which Argentina calls the Malvinas and which have been a British overseas territory since 1833.

In a joint statement, British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband and Attorney General Ellie Reeves welcomed the decision and urged Argentina to respect the right of the Falkland Islanders, who number around 3,500 people, to "determine their own future" and end its wider economic pressure.

"This outcome is a vindication of the U.K.'s robust legal defence and strategy," they said. "The U.K. has no doubt of our sovereignty of the Falkland Islands, our sovereignty and sovereign rights over the surrounding maritime areas, and the right of self-determination of the Falkland Islanders."

In its decision on Saturday, the judges ruled there did not appear to be any basis for believing Argentina had jurisdiction, as the tribunal is unable to make decisions based on questions of sovereignty, Agence France-Presse news agency reported.

Buenos Aires had argued the plan violates a UN resolution calling for both sides to desist from unilateral actions until their dispute over the sovereignty of the islands is resolved.

Argentine President Javier Milei has vowed to penalize companies working on oil production around the islands and argued that the joint U.K.-Israeli operation is a "clear and present danger" to his country's claims over the islands.

Milei has doubled down on his country's claim over the islands since President Trump said he was open to reviewing Washington's stance on the territory.

The Falkland Islanders themselves voted overwhelmingly in 2013 to remain British.

But Argentina rejects that outcome, arguing the principle of self-determination does not apply to a population it considers implanted by Britain after 1833.

Following Saturday's ruling, Rockhopper Exploration and Navitas Petroleum are expected to push ahead with the plan under licenses granted by the Falkland Islands government and backed by Britain.

The U.K. has said drilling at the field about 140 miles north of the islands won't commence until March 2027, with extraction expected to begin a year later. Argentina considers the project an illegal exploitation of resources in waters it claims as its own.

World.title: Charity honoring veteran who raised millions with walks to be disbanded
World.content:
A charity set up by the family of a British World War II veteran who raised tens of millions by walking laps of his garden during the coronavirus pandemic has applied to be disbanded, two years after the country's charity watchdog found "repeated" financial misconduct.

An application to have the charitable company created in honor of Capt. Tom Moore removed appeared Friday on the register of Companies House, the official U.K. government executive agency that maintains the public register of British companies, including charitable ones.

Moore, who died in 2021 at 100 years old, raised almost 39 million pounds, or $49 million, through his daily walks in his yard, inspiring people across the U.K. who followed his exploits in daily TV updates during the early weeks of the pandemic. All of the money he raised was donated to Britain's National Health Service.

Captain Tom Moore, 99, poses with his walker while walking a lap of his garden on April 16, 2020. JUSTIN TALLIS/AFP/Getty

"That's a lot of dollars — isn't it?" Moore told CBS News in 2021.

Moore was knighted by Queen Elizabeth II in July 2020 during an outdoor investiture ceremony at Windsor Castle, in recognition of his huge charity efforts. He also received about 125,000 cards from the public for his 100th birthday and participated in a charity music single that saw him become the oldest British No. 1 artist ever.

Following the success of his fundraising, his family established the Captain Tom Foundation to continue his fundraising efforts. However, the charity was soon embroiled in controversy and Britain's charity regulator concluded in November 2024 that Moore's daughter and son-in-law personally benefited from the charity.

The Charity Commission for England and Wales slammed them in a damning report that found they made almost 1.5 million pounds, or $1.9 million, from activities linked to the charity, including a book deal and an 18,000-pound fee to attend an awards ceremony.

Queen Elizabeth II knights Captain Sir Thomas Moore on July 17, 2020 in Windsor, England. Getty Images

It also barred Moore's daughter, Hannah Ingram-Moore, from serving as a trustee for any charity for 10 years and her husband, Colin, for a period of eight years.

The millions raised by the late Sir Tom and donated to NHS Charities Together before the foundation was formed were not part of the commission's inquiry.

The charity is now known as the 1189808 Foundation, having dropped Moore's name at the request of his family last year.

World.title: College student finds golf ball-sized brain tumor: "There's no way"
World.content:
Niko Pitinii, a communications major at the University of Pittsburgh, had been excited to celebrate his 21st birthday with family in Las Vegas. But when the trip finally came, all he could do was sleep.

It was the first sign that something was wrong. In the weeks that followed, Pitinii battled severe fatigue. He lost weight rapidly. One day, he fainted in the shower. When he went to the emergency room, bloodwork showed nothing alarming and he chalked the episode up to the steam and hot water.

He tried to focus on daily life: He was juggling classes and working as the student equipment manager for the Pittsburgh Panthers, his school's football team.

Then, during a Panthers practice, he fainted again. His boss told him to seek immediate medical attention. Pitinii went to his primary care provider, who sent him back to the emergency room. A doctor ordered a scan of his head, stomach and lungs.

"I think they thought it was my heart," Pitinii said. "Then the results of the CT scan came back, and they're like, 'Yeah, you have a big-ass brain tumor in your head.'"

A scan shows the tumor in Niko Pitinii's brain. Cleveland Clinic

"There's no way"

Pitinii was transferred to the Cleveland Clinic the next day. There, doctors found the tumor was so large that it was obstructing one of the ventricles in his brain, causing a buildup of spinal fluid. That fluid buildup, called hydrocephalus, was the cause of some of his symptoms, said Dr. Pranay Soni, a skull base surgeon who operated on Pitinii.

A tube was placed in Pitinii's head to drain the fluid. But that was just a stopgap measure: In a few days, Soni would need to do another operation to more permanently repair the obstruction. During that procedure, the tumor was biopsied. Doctors believed the golf ball-sized mass was benign, but needed to test it to be certain.

But hours before the procedure was set to begin, Pitinii received unexpected news from Dr. Amy Smith, who would become his oncologist.

"This doctor I had never seen before walks in ... and she starts talking about cancer, and we're like, 'What are you talking about? What do you mean, cancer?'" he recalled. "She's like, 'Yes, you have cancer.' I'm like, 'How do you know, you haven't even done the biopsy yet?' They had rerun my bloodwork, and I was pregnant!"

Niko Pitinii after completing treatment. Niko Pitinii

Pitinii wasn't actually pregnant — but he had high levels of beta-hCG, a hormone most frequently seen in pregnant female patients. Smith, a pediatric oncologist at the Cleveland Clinic, said the hormone is secreted by some tumors, including a rare kind of brain tumor called germinoma. Seeing it in Pitinii's bloodwork gave his care team an idea of what was going on.

Germinomas of the brain are rare, Smith said. They account for about 1% of brain cancers. Pitinii was told the cancer is very treatable — with a cure rate of 90% to 95% — but the news was still upsetting.

"It just freaked me out. Like, I'm going in to have brain surgery, and then they tell me I also have cancer on top of it all? It was just bad timing. It was a lot of information to process," Pitinii said. "I remember thinking: 'Nah, that's not real. There's no way.'"

Undergoing intensive treatment

Pitinii's surgery went smoothly. He was released from the hospital 24 hours later and was able to celebrate Christmas with his family. After the New Year, he began cancer treatment.

The biopsy had confirmed his tumor was a germinoma. Pitinii's care team recommended he begin with four rounds of chemotherapy, followed by a month of radiation.

The months that followed were exhausting. Pitinii decided to take a semester off from school so he didn't have to juggle classwork and cancer treatment. He had chemotherapy once a month from January to April. Then he had 24 targeted proton radiation sessions, ending on June 2. Throughout the process, he leaned on the clinic's social workers and other psychological staff members for emotional support.

Pitinii underwent an MRI on July 7. The next day, he was told he was cancer-free. On July 9, he rang the hospital's "Bravery Bell" to commemorate the end of his cancer treatment. A social worker on his care team surprised him with a small gift: a 3-D printed model of his tumor, which Pitinii said he still has.

Niko Pitinii and his family celebrate after he finishes cancer treatment. Cleveland Clinic

"Just trying to get there"

Pitinii returned to the University of Pittsburgh for the fall semester. In September, the Panthers nominated him for the Courage Award, a national honor that celebrates a person who overcomes adversity. The winner will be declared during the Capital One Orange Bowl in January.

Pitinii continues to see Smith regularly, and a recent MRI and round of bloodwork confirmed that he remains cancer-free. He will have regular check-ins with Smith, including scans, for the next 10 years. Pitinii's cancer has only a "7 to 10% chance of recurrence," Smith estimated. Even after he no longer sees Smith regularly, Pitinii will continue to follow up with Cleveland Clinic's survivorship team to stay on top of any side effects caused by his treatment.

For now, Pitinii is focusing on school again. Getting back into the swing of things hasn't been without its challenges. Pitinii lost around 60 pounds during his medical journey, and an appetite stimulant meant to help him regain weight has made it difficult to sleep. Focus and concentration are difficult sometimes, he said.

Niko Pitinii holds up a 3-D printed model of his tumor. Cleveland Clinic

"At cancer school, they don't tell you about these things," he joked.

Pitinii is set to graduate next year. He's considering getting a master's degree in social work, so he can help other young cancer patients. But for now, most of his energy is focused on recovery.

"There's an adage that for every one day of treatment, it takes three days to recover. So I know it's going to be a while, and I know it's not going to happen as fast as I want it to. But I'm just trying to get there."

World.title: Power being slowly restored as heavy Thanksgiving storm eases
World.content:
Heavy rain over flooded East Coast communities began easing Friday, and power was slowly restored to hundreds of thousands of customers as some places stayed on guard for high-tide flooding following a round of holiday storms.

The storms snarled travel and downed trees and power lines. The heavy weather led to water rescues from New York to Virginia. In New York City, preparations were underway to hold Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade on Saturday after an unprecedented postponement because of rain and high winds.

Elsewhere, wet snow fell as far south as the Tennessee Valley and freezing rain moved across northern New England. Cold rain was reported in parts of the Midwest, including the Ohio Valley and the lower Great Lakes.

Another storm system in the Northwest brought rain along coastal Oregon. More snow was forecast in the Cascade Range and in mountain passes in Montana and Wyoming.

There were just under 3,700 flights in the U.S. delayed as of Friday night, with another 162 canceled, according to the flight tracking service FlightAware.

The number of power outages, which peaked Thursday at more than 900,000 customers, fell to just under 200,000 by Saturday morning, according to utility tracker PowerOutage.us.

Bad weather in the East is taking its time to go

Conditions were expected to improve Friday across the entire eastern U.S., "but this huge system will take some time to weaken," the National Weather Service said on its website. Coastal flood warnings were posted from New Jersey to Virginia.

"A lot of standing water, tree branches, siding ripped off of houses and buildings," homeowner Chris Rizzo told CBS New York.

Waves crash against Virginia Beach Fishing Pier on Thanksgiving Day in Virginia Beach, Virginia, on Nov. 26, 2026. L. Todd Spencer/AP Photo

In Hampton, Virginia, the storm toppled a beloved landmark at Grandview Beach: a weathered, leafless tree known as the "Grieving Tree" or the "Shell Tree." Visitors regularly decorated its branches with seashells, and it became a popular subject for photographers.

After surviving many storms, the tree "may have finally met its match," local meteorologist Ricky Matthews wrote on Facebook, sharing a photograph.

Roofs in Ocean City and Rockville collapsed. In Norfolk, Virginia, crews rescued 39 people and two dogs, City Councilman Tommy Smigiel posted.

In Baltimore, the storm brought a record 3.04 inches of rain to BWI Thurgood Marshall Airport on Thursday, while high tide in Annapolis reached 4.48 feet that night, a level officials said was among the 10 highest on record.

Part of a fishing pier collapsed in Virginia Beach, Virginia, closing a 3-mile section of beach, including the boardwalk, "due to dangerous conditions," the city said.

Downtown merchants in Avalon, New Jersey, scrambled to pump out saltwater Friday after Thanksgiving brought some of the most significant tides in the seaside community's history. More than 1,100 people participated in a charity run, and Santa Claus was scheduled to arrive on a fire truck by evening to light the Christmas tree.

Conditions were a "million times better than they were 24 hours ago," borough business administrator Scott Wahl said.

Cheryl McKenna of Ocean City, New Jersey, said water flooded her garage and surrounded her property, keeping her family inside for six hours on the holiday. She said flooding has become more frequent since Superstorm Sandy in 2012.

A damaged traffic light pole lies across a flooded street in Ocean City, New Jersey, on Nov. 27, 2026, after heavy rain on Thursday. Allie Ippolito/AP Photo

"Our family has been here for 36 years," McKenna said. "But honestly, we're thinking, is this the right place for us to be? We're now retired, and we want to stay down here, but how often can we continue to do this."

Another round of rain and strong winds are expected to hit the East Coast by Sunday evening, potentially disrupting the Monday morning commute. Up to 2 inches of rain and wind gusts of 65 mph are possible in some areas, according to CBS News meteorologist Nikki Nolan.

Parts of South and Midwest see snow, while California contends with coastal flooding

Part of Tennessee was under a winter storm warning for up to an inch of snow Friday, after rain turned into light snow on Thanksgiving. Conditions were calmer for the Midwest, compared with Thanksgiving, when as much as 15 inches of snow fell in eastern Missouri.

The ice arena in Wentzville, Missouri, was empty when the roof caved in early Thursday.

Snow is expected to begin falling Saturday from Montana to Colorado, with accumulations of up to 10 to 18 inches in some areas, according to Nolan. The storm will then move into the Midwest and Gulf Coast on Sunday, bringing rain to cities including Chicago, St. Louis, Nashville and New Orleans.

A pedestrian is hit with water as a wave crashes into a seawall during inclement weather in Pacifica, California, on Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Jason Henry/Bloomberg via Getty Images

Waves driven by high tides caused flooding along the Pacific Coast and continued to affect train service Friday. Buses were pressed into service as Amtrak's Pacific Surfliner canceled or shortened more than a dozen trains between San Diego and Los Angeles.

Record tides along the California coast forced evacuations from Humboldt County in the far north to Ventura County near Los Angeles.

Heavy snow was expected in parts of Montana and Wyoming. A renewed surge of moisture associated with an atmospheric river across the Pacific Northwest moved toward the northern Rockies, the weather service said.

World.title: Gaza strike kills 2 MSF guards whom Israel claims were Hamas fighters
World.content:
Doctors Without Borders, also known by their French acronym MSF, said Friday night two of its staff who worked as guards were killed in an Israeli strike on a clinic in Gaza. The Israeli military accused the men of being Hamas fighters.

"We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen," the humanitarian organization said in a post on X. "This is a direct hit on MSF," it added.

In the statement, MSF also said its premises are marked with logos and its locations are communicated to the Israeli military.

"We stand in solidarity with the families and loved ones of our colleagues. We call for accountability," the statement said.

In response, the Israeli Defense Forces named the two men killed as Ahmed Sufyan Muhammad Ali Abu Hasira and Moaz Yousef Alitsbach, and claimed they were terrorists posing as humanitarian workers.

Palestinians attend the funeral ceremony of Ahmed Abu Hasira. Ali Jadallah/Getty Images

"While also serving as terrorists, the two worked as security guards at a clinic operated by Doctors Without Borders (MSF). This is another example of the Hamas terrorist organization embedding itself within international organizations," the IDF said in a statement released on Friday.

The Israeli military also disputed the claim that MSF facilities were targeted in the attack, claiming that no damage was caused to medical infrastructure. It added that it had used precision munitions and aerial surveillance to minimize "the expected harm to civilians."

MSF say the deaths bring the total number of their workers killed in Gaza to 17.

Mourners gathered Saturday for the two men's funeral prayers. Ahmad Abu Haseira, a relative of one of the killed men, said they were unarmed and wore MSF uniforms at the time of the attack.

A local MSF employee, Ahmad Shehada, said the two were making their rounds to check the clinic's facilities when a missile struck.

World.title: Spain's election could bring the far-right to power for 1st time in decades
World.content:
Spanish voters head to the polls on Sunday in a snap election that could see another major European country swing to the political right, as socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez battles to retain power amid mounting public discontent over housing, immigration and corruption.

Sánchez, one of Europe's most prominent left-wing leaders, has increasingly positioned himself as a political counterweight to President Trump on the world stage. He has defied Mr. Trump's demands over NATO defense spending, penned an opinion piece in The New York Times defending migration and denouncing "MAGA-style leaders" and cultivated ties with prominent figures on the American left, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

But at home, Sánchez faces a growing challenge from the center-right People's Party, led by Alberto Núñez Feijóo, and the nationalist, anti-immigration Vox party, led by Santiago Abascal, which could together form Spain's most right-wing government since the country returned to democracy following the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

Spain's Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez gives a speech in the Spanish city of Ceuta, following an attempted sea crossing by migrants from Morocco, on July 31, 2026. La Moncloa (Spanish Government)/Handout/Anadolu/Getty

A country divided

Housing has become a defining issue of the election, with soaring rents and property prices fueling widespread public anger.

On the same day Sánchez met Mamdani in New York City, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was forcibly removed from the Madrid apartment where she had lived for more than 70 years. Her landlord had sought to more than triple her monthly rent to $1,900, or 1,650 euros.

Her eviction – where she was carried out on a stretcher – sparked nationwide protests. Although her landlord subsequently agreed to let her return at a substantially lower rent, Abascal died in the hospital two weeks after her eviction, before she could sign the new lease. Her case became a symbol of Spain's housing crisis.

In response to the protests, Sánchez introduced emergency housing measures, including restrictions on rent increases. But the proposals were defeated in parliament, prompting Sánchez to call a snap election.

Demonstrators protest against evictions and the housing crisis in Madrid on September 26, 2026. Oscar DEL POZO /AFP via Getty Images

Sánchez has since sought to blame the PP and the far-right Vox for blocking protections for vulnerable tenants. The PP, meanwhile, argues that Sánchez has had eight years to address the housing crisis and has pledged to build one million homes.

The PP has made reducing the cost of living and tackling corruption central to its campaign.

Immigration has also become a particularly contentious election issue following the mass arrival of migrants in Ceuta, a Spanish territory on the northern coast of Africa, in July, and the Sánchez government's decision earlier this year to offer legal status to hundreds of thousands of undocumented migrants.

The far-right Vox party has sought to capitalize on public unease over immigration, calling for mass deportations and prioritizing Spanish nationals in access to public services.

Hugo Marcos-Marné, a political scientist at the University of Salamanca, told CBS News that the "electoral growth of Vox is multicausal," but perceptions of immigration, more than actual figures or changes in the country-wide objective situation, "is certainly behind" the party's rise.

Vox leader Santiago Abascal, prior to a between the candidates for Spanish Prime Minister. Alberto Ortega/Europa Press via Getty Images

The PP has also called for tightened immigration controls.

Corruption scandals involving Sánchez's political associates and members of his family have been a major feature of the election. Two deadly train crashes this year have also undermined confidence in his administration.

Vox has also been aided by "an anti-gender reaction, authoritarian nostalgia, and anti-elitism directed against mainstream parties and politicians," Marcos-Marné said.

Spain's far-right taboo

For decades, Spain was relatively resistant to the rise of far-right populism seen elsewhere in Europe, in part because of the country's experience of dictatorship under Franco.

Although the center-right PP is polling ahead of Sánchez's Socialists, polls suggest it could fall short of a parliamentary majority and need the support of Vox, which is polling at around 18%. Once reluctant to embrace the far-right party, the PP has increasingly shown a willingness to work with Vox, with the two parties having formed coalition governments at the regional level.

Alberto Nuñez Feijoo speaks during a campaign rally by the Spanish People's Party on November 25, 2026 in Madrid, Spain. Pablo Blazquez Dominguez / Getty Images

"Research shows that the radical-right was comparatively more stigmatized in Spain because of Franco dictatorship, but also that the Popular Party was a chameleonic party able to attract voters of the center-right and the radical-right," Marcos-Marné said.

Sánchez is hoping that the prospect of the far-right entering national government will galvanize progressive voters.

"The PP and Vox pose a real threat to many groups in our country," Sánchez wrote on X, accusing the parties of seeking to roll back the rights of women, workers and migrants. "Every seat that goes to the PP and Vox means taking a step backward."

The implications of Sunday's election extend well beyond Spain's borders.

With Spain the only large EU country currently governed by the left, Marcos-Marné said, the election is "certainly significant for the balance of forces at the EU level."

World.title: Iowa detonation did not increase levels of lead in water, EPA says
World.content:
The Environmental Protection Agency said Saturday the controlled detonation of a stockpile of degrading explosives in Iowa did not result in an increase of lead in water bodies that serve as a source of drinking water.

"EPA found no lead in the 38 water samples taken post-detonation at public water supplies, which included samples of finished treated drinking water and untreated water at the intake," the agency said in a press release.

"EPA sampled 35 drinking water sources across Iowa, Illinois, and Missouri before the controlled detonation to set a baseline," it added.

The EPA said it collected more than 1,632 air, water, soil and dust samples ahead of Wednesday's destruction of the lead azide stockpile, followed by 1,607 samples after the detonation, the agency said. Samples were sent to multiple EPA and private labs for testing.

"The agency is expecting to start receiving lab results on post-detonation sampling as early as tomorrow," the EPA said in a news release.

The EPA said it collected samples at more than 180 structures, including homes, schools, daycare centers and churches, as well as at parks, nearby farms, drinking water sources and the Mississippi River watershed.

The EPA said Friday that it had completed 88% of post-detonation sampling at homes that were sampled pre-detonation, and expected to finish the remainder Friday.

A contractor with the Environmental Protection Agency collects water in Augusta, Iowa, on Nov. 25, 2026. Austin Johnson/AP Photo

As of Thursday, no airborne lead had been detected throughout the region, the EPA said.

The agency said it is also testing for other compounds that may have been released during the detonation.

"The agency is testing for everything we were anticipating could potentially be released as a result of the controlled detonation," it said in Thursday's news release.

The Army on Wednesday detonated 5 tons of deteriorating explosives at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant located in the small community of Middletown, citing the risk of an unplanned explosion. Local residents and environmental groups had sought to block the detonation over concerns that a plume of toxic lead dust could threaten public health and agriculture.

EPA on-scene coordinator Sharon Kennedy, left, catalogs soil samples collected by her hired contractors in Augusta, Iowa, Wednesday, Nov. 25, 2026. Austin Johnson/AP Photo

The Middletown plant housed about 10,000 pounds of lead azide, which has been used in ammunition since World War I. The EPA said the lead azide had degraded over the last 20 years it had been in storage. It had undergone a recrystallization process that increased "the material's sensitivity to friction and shock" and made it more susceptible to the "risk of unintentional detonation," the EPA said.

The 8th Circuit Court of Appeals temporarily halted the detonation last week while it considered whether to impose a longer-lasting ruling. On Monday, the court said the environmental groups challenging the plan had failed to show they were likely to succeed.

The chaotic lead-up to the detonation reached the White House, prompting questions within the Trump administration about what went wrong and who was to blame for not elevating the matter to senior officials sooner, sources familiar with the matter told CBS News.

President Trump praised the detonation as having "exceeded expectations."

World.title: Perspective: A hero's name lives on
World.content:
Perspective: A hero's name lives on

toggle caption i Library of Congress

The ceremonial keel for the aircraft carrier USS Doris Miller will be laid next week.

CNN reported this summer that the Navy was considering naming the ship after President Trump instead. That brief controversy may have distracted from the personal courage of Doris Miller himself. And putting his name on an aircraft carrier is meant to memorialize his heroism.

Doris Miller, known to his shipmates as Dorie, was 22 years old when Japanese forces attacked the U.S. Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941. Miller was from a sharecropping family in Waco, Texas, hours away from any coast. But he wanted to see the world and send money to his family, so he enlisted in the Navy.

Sponsor Message

The U.S. Navy was segregated in those days, like all branches of the armed forces. Black sailors were assigned to custodial roles, in the kitchen and laundry.

Doris Miller became a cook and mess attendant aboard the USS West Virginia, and was in the laundry when bombs began to fall that Sunday morning. He leapt through flames and smoke to move wounded sailors to safer positions, including the ship's badly wounded captain.

Then Doris Miller made his way to a .50-calibre anti-aircraft gun. No Black crew members had been trained for combat duty. But Doris Miller fired that gun at the Japanese planes that were attacking the U.S. fleet, until he ran out of ammunition. And then he pulled men to safety from the oily water, until he was ordered to abandon ship.

More than 2400 Americans died in Pearl Harbor on that date that has lived in infamy. 106 were on the USS West Virginia.

Doris Miller received the Navy Cross for his heroism. It was personally presented by the commander of the US Pacific Fleet, and the citation reads, "for distinguished devotion to duty, extraordinary courage, and disregard for his own personal safety…"

Doris Miller would die in service two years later, in the fiery sinking of the USS Liscome Bay. His body was never recovered.

Sponsor Message

Seeing Doris Miller's name on an aircraft carrier may remind all of us that courage is not determined by rank or race. Doris Miller served a segregated Navy in a segregated America. He gave his country the highest order of heroism and sacrifice.

World.title: Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90
World.content:
Explosion at a school in eastern Afghanistan kills 7, wounds more than 90

toggle caption i AP Photo/AP

KABUL, Afghanistan — An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar Saturday killed seven people and wounded more than 90, the province's culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighboring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.

Up to 15 of the wounded remain in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.

Sponsor Message

Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.

Gemstone mining is on the rise in Kunar, with various companies extracting precious stones which are subsequently sold at auction.

In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children aged between 9 and 14.

World.title: New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system
World.content:
New wave of Democratic attorneys general may reshape the justice system

toggle caption i Eric Gay/AP

The nation's legal landscape is set for a major shift after voters elected Democrats to serve as attorney general in five formerly Republican-led states. That means a majority of states will soon have a Democrat serving as the top law enforcement officer.

Democratic candidates flipped attorneys general offices in Georgia, Iowa, Kansas, Ohio and Texas–and in Alaska, the incoming Democratic governor announced his pick for attorney general in a state previously run by Republicans.

The Democratic victories could have major effects for what alleged crimes are investigated, lawsuits filed and court cases heard across the U.S. State attorneys general typically have sweeping discretion in what legal challenges to bring or drop on behalf of their state's residents.

Sponsor Message

And with roughly seven in ten Americans set to live in a state with a Democratic attorney general, Democrats will be able to bring many more cases across the country that argue for their positions on the economy, environment, abortion, civil rights, and crime, rather than the Republican perspective.

"Voters picked AGs who will stand up and fight for them, whether that's taking on rising costs, pushing back against a lawless administration, or holding bad actors accountable. It's a time to celebrate, and also to get to work," Democratic Attorneys General Association President Sean Rankin said in a statement to NPR.

Conversely, the midterm election defeats for Republicans attorneys general candidates left the conservative legal movement reeling – and planning a comeback.

"There's no sugarcoating it, this was the worst election for Republicans since 1974," said Adam Piper, executive director of the Republican Attorneys General Association.

In an interview with NPR, Piper contended that Republican attorneys generals' policies are still broadly supported by voters, but were overshadowed by the unpopularity of the rest of the GOP. He noted that Republican attorneys general candidates ran ahead of GOP candidates for governor and U.S. Senate in some states.

Following the midterm results, Republican attorneys general convened for their fall meeting in Dallas, Texas, where the outgoing attorney general, Ken Paxton, lost his bid for Senate. He will soon be replaced by a Democrat, Nathan Johnson.

Sponsor Message

Piper said attendees grimly reflected on their challenges while also strategizing how to position Republican attorneys general to support the GOP as 2028 approaches. He added that the Republican Attorneys General Association are watching for potential "lawfare" by Democrats, including changing the number of Supreme Court justices or welcoming new states into the Union.

"We have to have better quality of candidates at the top of the ticket," Piper said. "We have to have better message discipline, and we need other committees in Washington to focus on what RAGA has done, and that is making sure we're good stewards of resources."

Democratic attorneys general held their own conference in Chicago, which some attendees said was both a celebration of the Democratic victories and an orientation for the incoming Democratic attorneys general.

"While a lot of the focus turns to what's next in Washington, we understand and we're not naive to the fact that we will continue to have a critical role in protecting our republic," said Illinois Attorney General Kwame Raoul during a Nov. 19 press briefing with other Democratic attorneys general.

Johnson, the incoming Texas attorney general, said at the same briefing that the wins for Democrats in the state house and governor's mansion could prompt Republicans to cooperate on a "cleansing" anti-corruption agenda. But he also signaled he'd support legislation and legal challenges to President Donald Trump's efforts to build a wall in Big Bend National Park on Texas' border with Mexico.

The Texas attorney general has traditionally brought cases on behalf conservative legal causes that had wide-ranging impacts across the country. The office also served as a training ground for Republican legal talent. U.S. Sen. John Cornyn and Texas Gov. Greg Abbott both served as attorney general before seeking higher office, while Sen. Ted Cruz served as solicitor general in the office before running for Congress. Other staffers have gone on to serve as judges, law clerks and prosecutors.

Sponsor Message

"Texas was a major intellectual force for the Republican attorneys general, and that's not going to be easily replaced," said James Tierney, a professor at Harvard Law School who has advised more than thirty attorneys general from both parties on staffing and legal philosophy.

"There are a lot of very smart, good lawyers in various AG offices who are very conservative," said Tierney. "But they don't have the heft and the size and the number of attorneys that Texas brings, and so for them, it's a very significant loss."

For Democrats, the recent wins could transform how the states enforce laws, bring legal cases, and support or hinder the Trump administration.

"These new attorneys general are not going to be particularly favorable towards the Trump administration, and will take an oppositional position in a number of different cases," said Anthony Michael Kreis, a constitutional law professor at Georgia State University. That may mean direct lawsuits against the administration in coalition with other attorneys general, Kreis said.

Many incoming Democratic attorneys general campaigned on bringing cases against alleged price gouging and digital surveillance by companies, as well as a tougher approach to antitrust concerns. But they will also face pressure to listen to their local business communities–including major multinational corporations.

"I think it's actually likely to increase bipartisan coalitions, particularly on economic issues," said Swain Wood, a partner at the law firm WilmerHale who now co-chairs the firm's practice advising clients on state attorneys general. Wood, who served as assistant attorney general to North Carolina Democratic Attorney General Josh Stein, cited past landmark settlements against tobacco and opioid distributors as cases where bipartisan groups of attorneys general found common ground.

World.title: Sudan's lost generation: War is stealing the childhood of millions
World.content:
Sudan's lost generation: War is stealing the childhood of millions

Three years of war have stolen childhood from millions of children in Sudan, leaving them displaced, hungry and fighting for survival instead of learning in a classroom.

Transcript

SCOTT DETROW, HOST:

For millions of children in Sudan, classrooms have been replaced by battlefields. Three years of civil war have left schools destroyed, families displaced and children exposed to drones, famine and forced marriage. Kate Bartlett reports.

(CROSSTALK)

KATE BARTLETT, BYLINE: The happy sounds of children playing belies their circumstances. These children are in a displacement camp in Tawila, in Sudan's North Darfur region.

SAM NUTT: If you ask the children how many of them were displaced by the war, every single hand goes up.

BARTLETT: Dr. Sam Nutt is the head of North American NGO War Child, which supports children in conflict zones with a particular focus on education. She's just returned from a trip to Sudan and described the capital Khartoum as, quote, "post-apocalyptic."

NUTT: If you ask the children one on one how many of them have witnessed someone who has been injured or killed as a result of the conflict, all of them say the same thing. Many of them lost one or both parents.

BARTLETT: Laura Mills from Amnesty International says this is just perpetuating the conflict.

LAURA MILLS: We spoke to many children in particular who told us that, you know, especially because they haven't been able to go to school for years, many of them saw their only option as going back to fight.

(SOUNDBITE OF EXPLOSIONS)

BARTLETT: The U.N. has called Sudan the world's worst humanitarian crisis. The conflict erupted in April 2023 when fighting broke out between Sudanese government troops and a paramilitary group called the Rapid Support Forces or RSF.

(SOUNDBITE OF EXPLOSIONS)

BARTLETT: Since then, the war has spread across the country, displacing millions and killing tens of thousands, according to the U.N. Both sides have committed atrocities, with the RSF accused of genocide in the remote western region of Darfur. And with almost 20 million Sudanese already facing acute hunger, U.N. agencies warn the super El Niño could exacerbate food shortages in the coming months. And while it might seem far away, the war in the strategically located mineral-rich country isn't happening in a vacuum, as Dr. Nutt explains.

NUTT: This conflict has significant global tentacles that are of interest to every single American.

BARTLETT: The conflict is not only impacting the surrounding countries, but is funded and supported by others much further away, from Iran and Russia to U.S. ally the United Arab Emirates, accused of backing the RSF, a charge it denies. Amnesty International's Mills again.

MILLS: Eventually, this is just going to lead to a more unstable world where we see the number of wars that are escalating by the day. And it will come back to haunt us.

BARTLETT: As for Sudan's children, there is one story in particular that has stayed with Dr. Nutt.

NUTT: There's one little girl who was 11-years-old in our class who wanted to be a doctor because she wanted to help keep people alive precisely because she had witnessed both of her parents being gunned down in front of her.

BARTLETT: The consequences of this war will also last long after the fighting stops.

Kate Bartlett, NPR News, Johannesburg.

World.title: Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels
World.content:
Thanksgiving storm batters East Coast. And, Black Friday sales to hit record levels

Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day.

Today's top stories

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

Hundreds of thousands of people are without power after a powerful storm swept through much of the East Coast and Midwest on Thanksgiving. Hundreds of flights were canceled and thousands were delayed during one of the busiest travel times of the year.



🎧 Flooding caused most of the damage and disruptions, NPR's Kat Lonsdorf tells Up First. Several bridges in New Jersey were shut down, and people were seen kayaking through usually busy streets in parts of coastal Virginia. Exceptionally high tides, known as the King Tides, have been battering the West Coast. Lonsdorf says there's still a lot of work to do before roads return to normal, but there is some hope. The storms should move out and the tides should recede heading into Saturday, as people begin their journeys home.

Despite inflation and concerns about the cost of living, Americans are expected to spend a record amount again this year for Black Friday. The National Retail Federation predicts a 4.2% increase in holiday retail sales this year compared with last year.



Sponsor Message

🎧 NPR's Alina Selyukh says surveys indicate people are cutting back on other spending to spend during the holiday season. She notes that while gas and housing costs have been big drivers of inflation, the prices of goods, including gifts, have not risen as dramatically. She also says she's watching a shift in the trend of how people are shopping. Although most people are doing their holiday shopping online, more are choosing to shop in person.

The Trump administration has banned asylum claims at the U.S.-Mexico border and canceled thousands of pending asylum applications over the past nearly two years. Critics say the sweeping immigration changes have all but shut down access to asylum. Soon, the Supreme Court will consider whether the president can circumvent Congress and existing federal immigration law and unilaterally suspend access to asylum protections. In December, Justices will also review the administration's strategy of deporting immigrants to third countries that have agreed to process asylum claims, even as some face human rights abuse allegations and cannot guarantee that the asylum-seeker won't be returned to their home nation.

Behind the story

toggle caption i Heather Diehl/Getty Images

This essay was written by Stephan Bisaha, NPR's personal finance correspondent

I was at a book club recently, chatting with a small group, when someone from another circle asked what we were discussing. Driven by an instinct to instigate (perhaps a side effect of our earlier heated book talk), I said the "benefits of AI."

Sponsor Message

After some anti-AI sighs, I told them about a source whose AI agent saved him $50 without him even asking. A friend uses Claude for her retirement funding decisions. Others are turning to AI for holiday shopping.

New AI agents can now help buy gifts, from brainstorming to checkout. Would I trust AI with my own shopping? Apparently not.

Those cheap acoustic panels AI recommended? Only a good deal if I ignored how tiny they were. The griddle it suggested? Too big. Then I started worrying about how much of my personal data my AI assistant was collecting and eventually asked it to forget everything about me.

Forrester principal analyst Emily Pfeiffer guided me through another attempt for my book club's gift exchange.

I gave Meta's new AI agent, Muse, my requirements: a $25 cap for a Gen Z crowd and something that makes noise, per the organizer's request (way to stereotype the radio reporter).

Muse's suggestions? A karaoke mic and a plastic, yodeling pickle. I wasn't sold on either.

Once again, my shopping cart is empty.

My next attempt with AI, though, might not be this holiday season. Instead I'm planning to buy a Tamagotchi for the gift exchange. Remember those virtual keychain pets from the '90s? A throwback to a time when you could take your digital companion shopping without worrying about your privacy.

Weekend picks

toggle caption i Getty Images/Bob Riha Jr.

Check out what NPR is watching, reading and listening to this weekend:

🍿 Movies: The holiday season is packed full of can't-miss films. These are 17 movies that you should see before the year ends.

📺 TV: Parks and Recreation star Amy Poehler and creator Michael Schur reunite for Dig, an ensemble comedy about a team of archaeologists caught up in a series of mysterious events after uncovering an ancient artifact in Greece.

📚 Books: Why settle for one book recommendation when you can get more than 300? Now's the time to browse this year's Books We Love.

Sponsor Message

🎵 Music: NPR Music's Stephen Thompson and Lars Gotrich join host All Songs Considered Robin Hilton to attempt to build a canon of music for giving thanks, spending time with loved ones and, of course, celebrating food. Check out their playlist here.

🍴 Food: A few years ago, Israeli American chef Alon Shaya spearheaded the Rescue Recipes initiative at the United States Holocaust Memorial Museum, exploring food's role in World War II. He has compiled his stories and dishes in a new cookbook, Memories of a Good Meal: Recipes of Resilience Inspired by Stories of World War II Survival.

3 things to know before you go

toggle caption i Steve Donahue for The National Dog Show.



Rocker the coonhound has won best in show at this year's National Dog Show. His glossy coat and big, floppy ears bested six other dogs that each won top honors in their groups. When Dungeons & Dragons came on the scene 50 years ago, some parents complained it kept their kids holed up inside. These days, the once-nerdy pastime is a screen-free parent's dream. Bakers across the country have taken inspiration from Little Free Libraries to offer free sweet treats to their neighbors.

This newsletter was edited by Majd Al-Waheidi.

World.title: French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault
World.content:
French cinema star Gérard Depardieu ordered to stand trial for rape and sexual assault

toggle caption i Aurelien Morissard/AP

PARIS — Gérard Depardieu, for decades one of France's most celebrated actors, has been ordered to stand trial on charges of raping and sexually assaulting a young actress, authorities said Thursday, less than two weeks after the cinema star abandoned his appeal of a sexual assault conviction in a separate case.

Actress Charlotte Arnould was 22 when she accused Depardieu in 2018 of raping her at his Paris home.

Eight years later, the Paris Court of Appeal ruled that the actor should face trial over allegations of rape and sexual assault on Aug. 7, 2018, while dismissing allegations relating to a second incident six days later.

Sponsor Message

Depardieu, 77, has denied the rape allegations. His lawyer, Delphine Meillet, told The Associated Press that he disputes Thursday's ruling, without specifying whether he would challenge it before France's highest court for civil and criminal cases.

The ruling upholds part of an investigating judge's August 2025 decision to send Depardieu to trial.

The case has become one of the most prominent in France's reckoning with sexual violence, as the #MeToo movement has faced resistance in the country, particularly in the arts.

A French cinema icon faces a #MeToo reckoning

With his hulking frame, crooked nose and commanding screen presence, Depardieu dominated French cinema for half a century.

He became one of the country's most recognizable cultural exports, earning an Oscar nomination for "Cyrano de Bergerac" and a Golden Globe for "Green Card."

But accusations of sexual misconduct and his subsequent conviction have increasingly overshadowed his cinematic legacy.

On Nov. 16, Depardieu abandoned his appeal against a conviction for sexually assaulting two women on a film set in 2021, accepting an 18-month suspended prison sentence and issuing a public apology that marked a departure from his earlier denials in that case.

"I therefore offer my deep and sincere apologies to those who may have suffered," he said in a written statement.

Sponsor Message

Depardieu was convicted in May 2025 of groping a set decorator and an assistant during the filming of "Les Volets Verts" ("The Green Shutters").

The court also ordered his name to be listed in France's national sex offender database.

"On film sets, I have long hidden behind provocation and crude humor. I believed my words and some of my actions had no consequences. But they did, particularly coming from someone who held as much power as I once did," Depardieu said.

Accusations against Depardieu sparked a national debate

The controversy surrounding Depardieu intensified in December 2023 after a television documentary showed him repeatedly making obscene remarks and gestures during a 2018 trip to North Korea.

Even French President Emmanuel Macron weighed in, drawing criticism from women's rights activists when he said the actor "makes France proud." Macron invoked the presumption of innocence and said he would not participate in a "manhunt."

The controversy exposed divisions in a country where some prominent cultural figures had pushed back against the #MeToo movement.

In 2018, actress Catherine Deneuve and 99 other women signed an open letter defending men's freedom to make advances toward women and warning against what they saw as the movement's excesses.

Born in 1948 into a working-class family in the central French city of Châteauroux, Depardieu overcame a speech impediment to become one of France's most prolific actors. His career spanned hundreds of films, from "The Last Metro" and "Jean de Florette" to the popular "Asterix" franchise.

His excesses off-screen also made international headlines, notably when he accepted a Russian passport from Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2013 amid a dispute over French taxes.

World.title: From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes
World.content:
From Thanksgiving blackouts to Black Friday, a holiday hit by wild weather and economic woes

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

A massive storm that stretched from the Midwest to Manhattan left almost a million people without power by Thanksgiving evening and disrupted holiday travel.

More than 400 flights were cancelled and more than two thousand were delayed around the country on Thursday during one of the busiest travel times of the year. Driving was also made difficult by either heavy rains or snow and ice. Some 81.5 million people were expected to travel for the holiday between Thursday and Monday, according to AAA .

Power was partially restored early Friday, but at the peak of the outage more than 980,000 people in New York, Pennsylvania, New Jersey and elsewhere were without electricity. Missouri also suffered blackouts after heavy snowfall.

toggle caption i Noah Berger/AP

Several areas were also hit by major flooding, including Old Town Alexandria, Virginia, and Atlantic City, New Jersey, where some low-lying areas had close to 2 to 3 feet of water, according to city authorities.

Sponsor Message

And there's more flooding forecast. The National Weather Service issued a coastal flood warning for the Washington DC area on Friday, saying the warning was in effect until 6 pm ET.

"The unprotected area on the Southwest Waterfront at the DC Seafood Market is expected to flood," the weather service said.

"Take the necessary actions to protect flood-prone property. If travel is required, do not drive around barricades or through water of unknown depth," the statement added.

On the other side of the country, the West Coast was hit by King Tides with strong waves battering the Bay Area in recent days. King Tides happen regularly, but they have been made worse by climate change and warming oceans, as well as a particularly strong El Niño.

Part of the Pacifica Pier south of San Francisco collapsed on Wednesday, roads saw some flooding and some homes along the coast have been affected.

toggle caption i Heather Diehl/AP

New York City's Central Park had its wettest Thanksgiving on record with 1.82 inches of rain. The city can expect strong winds on Friday, the weather service said, with gusts of up to 30 miles an hour.

Iconic Macy's parade postponed

Macy's annual Thanksgiving Day Parade in the city has been postponed for the first time in its history and will now take place on Saturday. While it's never been postponed before, it was cancelled altogether for several years during World War II.

Sponsor Message

Postponing it is causing major logistical problems, as there are around 11,000 participants in the parade, mostly volunteers, many of whom traveled in from out of state. But it's not safe to put up the iconic giant balloons the parade is known for during strong winds.

There have been incidents where those balloons hurt people in past parades, most notably in 1997 when high winds caused a Cat in the Hat balloon to hit a lamp post and then strike a woman in the crowd, leaving her critically injured. Weather grounded all of the balloons for the parade only once, back in 1971.

Saturday's parade will be Macy's 100th. To mark the milestone there will be 100 balloons, Will Coss, the parade's executive producer, told NPR's Morning Edition's host A Martinez.

"Our first parade in 1924 had live animals. But the animals unfortunately scared the children a bit more than our early parade producers anticipated," Coss said, explaining that was when they brought in balloons.

"Each balloon has its own level of complexity so a balloon from 'beginning to end' can take anywhere from 4 to 6 months," said Coss, noting they are all first hand-drawn.

toggle caption i Yuki Iwamura/AP

This year there will be eight new giant balloons including Bluey, Hello Kitty and Mickey Mouse from the Sorcerer's Apprentice.

Returning favorites include Spongebob Squarepants, Spider-Man –– and the balloon that made its debut in 1927 as the parade's first inflated character: Felix The Cat.

Black Friday kicks off

Americans are expected to spend more money today than on any other day of the year. But, amid inflation and high gas prices, a survey of almost 8,000 adult consumers found people are cutting back on other spending in order to prioritize expenses during the holiday season.

The National Retail Federation expects some 183 million shoppers to spend over $1 trillion in November/December holiday sales. Many surveyed said the high cost of living would affect how they shopped, with some planning to buy less expensive gifts for fewer people.

Sponsor Message

The majority of Americans would be shopping online, the Federation said, with 59% planning to use AI this year to help with recommendations, brainstorming gift ideas and scanning retailer sites to find the best prices.

The organization said the top three children's toys this year are LEGO, Hot Wheels and Barbie dolls.

Kat Lonsdorf and Alina Selyukh in Washington DC and Kate Bartlett contributed to reporting.

World.title: Can luxury save Macy's?
World.content:
Can luxury save Macy's?

toggle caption i Eugene Gologursky/Getty Images



Leaving the Macy's flagship store in New York, the Niesig family visiting from Germany sizes up their loot: a pair of sweatpants for mom, a Hurley jacket for dad, Ugg boots for their daughter. Son Mika, 16, is the only one empty-handed.

"I like zipper hoodies, and there was one zipper from Levi's that was pretty cool," he says. "But in the end, I didn't buy it because it was just a little boring."

Sponsor Message

As Macy's this week celebrates the 100th edition of its Thanksgiving Day Parade, the department store finds itself at a turning point. After years of questionable financial prospects, Macy's is trying to reinvent — as a luxury destination.

The retailer's gambit is to keep its old shoppers while also attracting new customers, who will perhaps pay more for real leather and upscale brands.

How Macy's got squeezed in the middle

Long before the pandemic, Macy's was grappling with America's shrinking middle class — and its own lack of fresh vision.

The department store business, to begin with, has become challenging. Big store space is expensive. Online competition is stiff. Shoppers are increasingly buying directly from their favorite brands.

And Macy's faces its own struggle. The chain is neither a discounter like Kohl's or T.J.Maxx, nor an upscale store like Bergdorf Goodman or Nordstrom. Macy's has languished in between.

"They were kind of like right in the middle," says Michael Prendergast, who advises retailers and brands at the consulting firm Alvarez & Marsal. "Now over time, that middle tier basically got crushed."

When the pandemic hit, store closures had Macy's forecasting an estimated $1.1 billion in losses. Its stock value dropped so low that the company was kicked off the big-league index, the S&P 500.

The way out is up

At one point, Macy's seemed to throw every other thing on discount just to get people buying something.

Sponsor Message

But it didn't work.

toggle caption i Michael M. Santiago/Getty Images

Stores looked disheveled and chaotic. Shoppers regularly noted a lack of workers to help on the floor. Over 2023, sales at Macy's dropped almost 7%.

Soaring inflation all but forced Macy's hand.

As the so-called K-shaped economy split the nation in recent years, folks with less money turned to Walmart or Target, which stepped up their game. Wealthier people continued to be the ones doing most of the spending, but also not at Macy's — leaning toward higher-end shops.

"For their size and scale the choice is almost made for them," says Prendergast, who's spent 20 years in the fashion business, including selling to Macy's at Tommy Hilfiger.

"If you're Macy's you say, 'We're still getting squeezed in the middle, our customer base in the U.S. is getting squeezed in the middle. Where can we go?' And really the only answer is to go up."

The new luxury vision

Luxury is now the big Macy's bet.

The retailer already owns the upscale Bloomingdale's, with its designer brands. Macy's also owns the luxury beauty chain Bluemercury.

In 2024, the head of Bloomingdale's took over the entire Macy's company and announced a turnaround plan, "A Bold New Chapter."

It included closing 150 stores and upgrading more than 300 others. Changes were proposed for the website and the staffing. Stores began to tackle clutter and add nicer items.

"We needed to remove the duplication, the redundancy," says Julie Walsh, senior vice president at Macy's whose team buys women's accessories and beauty products, including shoes, jewelry and makeup.

"When you come onto our floor now, it's a little bit lighter," she says. "So that the product that is on the floor shows up in a meaningful way."

Putting the higher prices to the test

In March, Macy's finally reported a year of growing sales.

The higher-end Bloomingdale's stores continued to drive much of the company's growth, but changes seemed to start paying off at Macy's, too.

Sponsor Message

Fancier options — like real leather instead of faux, brands like Ralph Lauren and Coach — have been raising the retailer's average selling price. It increased 9% in the latest quarter, executives said in September. They described shoppers' visits as "very steady and very significant."

toggle caption i Stephanie Scarbrough/AP

Barb Anderson-Kerlin, a loyal Macy's shopper checking out the retailer's flagship in New York, says she's noticed a difference at the chain, after years of finding stores that seemed to ramble in all directions.

"The department store was like bedding, towels, pots and pans, perfume," she says. "Because I'd go in and just be overwhelmed. But now it feels like it's easier to see where the brands are."

How far can luxury sales take Macy's?

Still, most shoppers at the flagship store appeared dubious of the image of Macy's as a high-end chain.

"If they want to be luxury," says Chelsea Bates, who is visiting from Tennessee, "I would say serve champagne." She laughs, but notes that other upscale rivals do offer lounges and refreshments, like coffee.

Macy's insists it's not turning away from the middle class — just striving for more. Not picking a whole new lane, but widening the road in a gamble for this bifurcated economy.

"Macy's strength is being able to service our customer across all different categories in all different price points, and we're not changing that," says Walsh.

"What we are doing is making sure that we've got the elevated product," she says. "So it's not to replace it, it's an additive."

One hurdle is just how long Macy's had spent building its middle-price reputation, says Prendergast. Breaking out of the mold is a tough climb.

But, he says, if anyone can do it, maybe it is Macy's — having outlived many rivals over its 168 years.

"They're really the last man standing in that range for a reason," says Prendergast. "Everybody likes to count Macy's down and out, and they continue to prove everybody wrong."

World.title: Canada is spending billions on defence. But is it getting ready for war?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Scary.

That's about the only way to describe the daily preoccupations of NATO military planners these days.

What is perhaps more unsettling is how NATO's deputy military commander, British Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer, described those concerns.

Being a military planner is at the best of times not a barrel of laughs, nor a job for the faint of heart given all of the grim scenarios and outcomes one must imagine.

Lately, it's not so much the routine prospect of a war with Russia, but rather the possibility that President Vladimir Putin, despite being consumed by his war of choice in Ukraine, might decide to have a go at one of the Western allies.

The distinction has profound implications for the way countries such as Canada prepare themselves militarily — and the speed with which they do it.

Throughout 2026, the warnings coming out of Europe have become more pointed and stark.

"Russia is a war economy now," Stringer said in an exclusive broadcast interview with CBC News, portions of which were aired on CBC Radio's The House on Saturday.

"Let's not dress it up any other way. It is."

The rate at which the Russians are producing everything from relatively unsophisticated drones to munitions to ballistic missiles far surpasses not only their pre-2022 production, but outstrips almost everything NATO is churning out, Stringer said.

WATCH | NATO's deputy commander on Canadian spending: Canada 'spending well' on NATO commitments: NATO's 2nd in command in Europe | Duration closed caption 1:16 Asked by CBC News about the Pentagon's assessment that Canada isn't pulling its weight on defence investment, NATO deputy commander Air Chief Marshal John Stringer said Canada is 'a nation that is recapitalizing its investments in its air forces and its land component, in maritime.'

And while the possibility of a direct military confrontation with NATO remains at the low end of the spectrum of potential outcomes, Stringer said the likelihood has increased.

The economic damage the Ukrainians have inflicted on Russia, notably on its oil industry, has heightened the possibility of recklessness on the part of Putin, he said.

Stringer said NATO's military planners concern themselves with possibilities, not probabilities.

It is an instructive lens through which to view a lot of what's happened recently in Ottawa as it relates to defence.

Cross Country Checkup is asking: What does an effective Canadian military look like to you? Leave your comment here and we may read it or call you back for Sunday's show

The federal government of Prime Minister Mark Carney has committed to the biggest sustained increase in defence spending in generations. Yet, the military is wrestling with budget restraint, curtailing some training activities and restructuring its reserve force.

The latest federal budget lays out an ambitious long-term spending trajectory, all of it calibrated to put Canada on track to spend five per cent of its gross domestic product on defence by 2035.

But the near-term funding picture for the Canadian Armed Forces is considerably less dramatic.

And the government is in the process of creating a powerful new Crown corporation to buy military equipment, an organization that will be expected to devote considerable energy to rebuilding the country's industrial base and fostering economic prosperity.

WATCH | Conservative defence critic on proposed Crown corp.: New defence bill is more paper-shuffling, bureaucracy: shadow minister | Duration closed caption 9:01 The newly designated Canadian Corporation for Defence Investment will operate at arm's-length from federal departments and have its own board of directors and CEO to speed up military procurement and investment decisions. But how is this latest move by the Liberals being received by the Opposition? Power & Politics hears from Conservative shadow minister for national defence James Bezan.

Taken individually, there are explanations — some of them perfectly reasonable — for each of those decisions.

Taken together, they invite a rather fundamental question, particularly in light of what the Europeans are saying.

Are we, or are we not, preparing for war?

The Carney government's own recent national security strategy spelled it out this way: Canada must "prepare for all contingencies up to and including war."

It is the "up to and including" part that has preoccupied the House of Commons defence committee as it studies Bill C-40, which converts the Defence Investment Agency into a Crown corporation.

But for retired Dutch admiral Rob Bauer, the former chair of NATO's military committee, it is the "including war" part on which he's fixated.

In a separate interview with CBC News chief correspondent Adrienne Arsenault, Bauer made the point that the Russians are rebuilding their military even as they are fighting in Ukraine.

"They're producing more weapons than they actually need in Ukraine," said Bauer.

The surplus equipment, he said, can be stockpiled or used to rebuild military formations elsewhere, including along the border with Finland, one of NATO's newest members.

And perhaps more importantly, the Russians are learning at enormous cost how to fight a modern, industrial-scale war.

For countries such as Canada, which have historically enjoyed the luxury of geography, Bauer had a particularly pointed observation.

"Your distance doesn't help you anymore. And basically, time is no longer our friend."

War of choice vs. defence

Much of the Western military establishment, including Canada's, was conditioned by the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq to think about military operations in terms of choices.

Governments decided whether to participate, how many troops to send, how long they would stay and what kind of equipment they would take with them.

There was generally time to train soldiers and, in Canada's case, buy equipment once it became apparent that what they had wasn't up to the job.

A war in defence of the Western alliance would be an altogether different proposition.

The enemy would have a considerable say in the timing, the duration and the scale of the commitment.

The time to buy equipment, stockpile ammunition and train soldiers would be before the shooting started.

It is worth noting that none of this is particularly at odds with the "more dangerous and divided world" Carney has articulated since he became prime minister.

What is less clear is the extent to which that assessment is driving the day-to-day decisions of the federal government.

The irony of the current budget restraint within National Defence is that it is taking place against the backdrop of what the Liberal government has characterized as a historic reinvestment in the military.

The department has been looking for hundreds of millions of dollars in savings in its operations and support budget.

Weekend training and competitions for military cadets have been suspended in various parts of the country until the end of the fiscal year.

More consequentially, the army's restructured reserve force is expected to result in the elimination of hundreds of full-time reservist positions.
