WATCH | More about cadet funding: 'It's heartbreaking': Parts of cadet programs on hold, for now, as national group reviews fiscal plan | Duration closed caption 1:58 Programming for national cadets and junior rangers programs across the country is changing — for now. Leaked emails reveal national defence budget constraints have forced a halt to parts of cadet training across the country. One former cadet from Newfoundland and Labrador disagrees with that decision, and has written a letter to the prime minister. The CBC's Madison Taylor reports.

There is a legitimate debate to be had about how many reservists should be employed in full-time administrative jobs and whether the money would be better spent getting part-time soldiers into the field.

But the reserve force, which in the event of a major war would be expected to provide much of the additional manpower, has historically been a convenient place for the Defence Department to find savings when money gets tight.

It is also the kind of institution that cannot be rebuilt overnight.

You could hear strains of that in the Pentagon's increasingly public, bellicose campaign to pressure the Carney government to meet the five per cent GDP NATO target before the end of the decade.

U.S. officials pointed to the low state of readiness of all three branches of the Canadian military.

And more pointedly, it accused Ottawa of prioritizing "parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization."

Given the enormous commercial stake in some of Canada's outstanding military equipment purchases, notably the F-35 fighter jet, the comments were taken in Ottawa with a giant heaping of salt.

But the temptation to dismiss the American criticism in its entirety because of the political and commercial motivations behind it obscures a rather uncomfortable reality.

"They're not wrong," was how Steve Saideman, a defence expert at Carleton University, described the Pentagon's criticism. "The key is that the Americans are upset that we're responding to their bullying by not giving in to them."

Much of the evidence the Pentagon marshalled in making its case was drawn from the Canadian Defence Department's own reporting.

The collision between industrial policy, nationalism and military necessity is not a new phenomenon. (Keito Newman/The Canadian Press)

And that leads us to a tiny — but important — moment of political theatre recently in front of the House of Commons defence committee.

Liberal MP Tim Watchorn read aloud a partial list of the military equipment and support contracts the federal government had signed since the newly minted Defence Investment Agency (DIA) was stood up in the fall of 2025.

Turning the agency into a Crown corporation means it will have substantial powers to sole-source military contracts but also invest in domestic arms companies.

In light of everything we're seeing in the world, Andrew Latham, a professor of international relations and political theory at Macalester College in Minnesota, offered the committee an important yardstick to evaluate the mandate of the agency.

"The overriding purpose of defence procurement is to ensure that the Canadian Armed Forces are equipped to fight and win in the conflicts they will actually be engaged in."

It is a debate that would have been familiar to several generations of Canadian politicians and military officers.

Perhaps the most notorious example of the collision between industrial policy, nationalism and military necessity was the controversy surrounding the Ross rifle in the early years of the First World War.

Canada's first domestically manufactured military rifle was championed by Sir Sam Hughes, the country's wartime minister of militia and defence. It was an exceptionally accurate weapon and represented the industrial ambitions of a young country that wanted to be something more than a customer of the British arms industry.

Unfortunately, the rifle proved unreliable under the conditions in which Canadian infantrymen found themselves fighting on the Western Front. Soldiers lost confidence in the weapon, some discarding it in favour of British Lee-Enfields. Hughes remained a stubborn defender of the Canadian rifle, blaming its shortcomings in part on British-manufactured ammunition. By 1916, the Ross had been withdrawn from front-line infantry service.

The significance of the Ross rifle controversy, more than a century later, is not that Canada was wrong to aspire to a degree of industrial independence. Rather, it is the extent to which the political investment in a domestic industrial undertaking made it difficult to acknowledge that the military's needs were not being adequately served.

Canadian history is littered with other examples, such as, in 1986, the Mulroney government passed over a cheaper, technically superior bid from Winnipeg's Bristol Aerospace for a lucrative CF-18 maintenance contract in favour of Montreal-based Canadair.

Pierre Trudeau's government opted for domestic production of the German-designed Iltis military jeep at considerably greater cost than importing it.

The Carney government will spend billions of dollars on defence over the next several years. There will be announcements about new weapons, new factories, new technologies and thousands of Canadian jobs.

What will be harder to discern amid all of that is how much more capable the Canadian military will be of fighting a war two or three years from now.

World.title: Melania Trump says she helped another group of children return to Ukraine. The reality is more complicated
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

When Alina Sydorenko woke up last week and discovered that drones and missiles had dealt a devastating blow to Russia's prized Kerch Bridge — causing a central section to collapse — it was the first time she felt annoyed by a Ukrainian win in the war against Russia.

Her mother was planning to cross the bridge from occupied Crimea into Russia to escort Sydorenko's eight-year-old son, Artem, out of their home in the southeastern port city of Berdyansk, which Russian troops seized during the early days of the war against Ukraine.

Sydorenko was in northern Ukraine when the full-scale invasion began in February 2022 and said she was separated from her only child for years.

While Ukraine says it has confirmed more than 20,000 cases of children being deported or forcibly transferred to Russia, thousands of others remain separated by the war — either trapped in occupied territory or in Russia because the relatives they were with at the start of the invasion fled there.

"The negotiations took a very long time," Sydorenko said in an interview with CBC News on Friday at a Ukrainian checkpoint a few kilometres from the border with Belarus.

"I can't even say how much stress and effort we went through to bring the child back here. It's terrifying to worry every single day about whether they are alive."

Artem and his grandmother ended up waiting a few days before taking a train to Russia. From there, they joined a larger group and travelled through Belarus as part of a humanitarian reunification mission secured in part with the help of U.S. first lady Melania Trump.

Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, who met with Melania in Washington, D.C . after she was credited with securing a ceasefire in the Russian-occupied community of Oleshky, even went so far as to say she is now their chief mediator when it comes to the return of children.

WATCH | Ukrainian families reunite after being torn apart by war: Families separated by war reunite at Ukraine-Belarus border | Duration 1:15 Separated Ukrainian families are reuniting at the Belarus border following the return of nine children and one vulnerable adult from Russia and Russian-controlled areas. Ukraine's human rights ombudsman, Dmytro Lubinets, says Melania Trump, the U.S. first lady, is the chief mediator and has helped to make these reunions happen.

Politics, public pressure play role in return

Before starting the long journey to reunite with their children, families face a mountain of paperwork and permissions. However, politics and public pressure are also factoring into how and when some of those who have been separated or forcibly deported to Russia are brought back to Ukraine.

The group that arrived on Friday included nine children and 29-year-old Anastasia (Nastia) Mamotiuk, who lives with a disability and has been in institutional group care since she was a young child.

She was one of more than 80 children and vulnerable young adults taken to Russia from the Oleshky Children’s Boarding School in southern Ukraine in the fall of 2022.

In recent months, the Emile Foundation, a humanitarian organization with offices in the Netherlands and Ukraine, has been able to track down more than 40 of the school's former residents. Bringing them back to Ukraine has been challenging due to medical needs, legal hurdles and the difficulty of locating individuals in the first place — especially as some have been shuffled between different care facilities.

Anastasia (Nastia) Mamotiuk, 29, arrives by ambulance at the Ukraine-Belarus border checkpoint on Friday. She had been placed at a facility in Russia. (Nicolas Hameon/CBC)

The foundation made contact with Mamotiuk in the spring and kept in touch on WhatsApp through messages and video calls.

"We were in touch with her all the time," said Mariam Lambert, co-founder and CEO of the Emile Foundation, who spoke to CBC News via Zoom. "There were good moments, there were really bad moments, there were moments where she was scared."

Mamotiuk was placed in a facility in Penza, Russia, a city about 500 kilometres southeast of Moscow. The home was managed by Sofia Lvova-Belova , the sister of Russia's children's commissioner, Maria Lvova-Belova, who is wanted by the International Criminal Court and accused of unlawfully deporting Ukrainian children to Russia.

Lambert said it was during their regular communication with Mamotiuk in May that she began expressing concern about being given more medication than she typically took.

A boy looks out from a bus transporting children from Belarus back to Ukraine on Friday. The children have been living away from home because of war with Russia. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

Then in the fall, she suddenly stopped communicating with those in Ukraine for several days. That prompted Lambert to go public with Mamotiuk’s case, speaking to the media and appealing to Melania Trump to intervene.

"We understand the political side of it, and this is why we made an appeal," Lambert said. "We were asking, of course, the international community to put pressure on Russia in order to return her."

A few days later, Mamotiuk was back in touch and was told arrangements were being made to get her a passport so she could travel.

CBC News reached out to the office of Russia’s children’s commissioner but has not received a response.

'Is it becoming a political game?'

While Lambert praised the International Committee of the Red Cross for helping arrange Mamotiuk's travel, she was dismayed by how much of her return to Ukraine unfolded. She said they first heard about the reunification from Melania, who posted about it on social media on Nov. 25.

In a press release, the White House stated that the latest agreement meant 43 children had now been "reunited through her humanitarian efforts."

The statement made it seem as though the children were already back with relatives, when in reality they were still in transit and had not yet reached Belarus — which they needed to pass through in order to cross into northern Ukraine.

Olha, right, who didn't want her last name published because of the high profile and sensitivity of the humanitarian mission in the midst of war, reunited with her nephew, Sasha. He had been living in occupied Kherson with his mother. When she died four months ago, he asked if he could leave and relocate to Kyiv to live with his aunt. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

After the announcement, the first lady reposted U.S. coverage of the reunification interspersed with posts promoting a new docuseries about her that's streaming on Amazon Prime.

Lambert only found out that Mamotiuk was arriving on Friday when the young woman got in touch herself.

"Is it really a humanitarian action, or is it becoming a political game?" she said.

Alevtyna Abibulaieva, left, kisses her niece, Valeriia Levchenko, 11, who crossed the border into Ukraine from Belarus by bus on Friday. (Evgeniy Maloletka/The Associated Press)

Bus arrives to waiting family, officials, media

Because they are not directly related, no one from the Emile Foundation was invited to the border checkpoint to welcome Mamotiuk — and neither was her closest contact, Viacheslav Shchyrskyi.

The 61-year-old had been in touch with Mamotiuk for more than a decade. He previously ran a small group home in Ukraine's Kherson region and was making arrangements to take her in before the war. But all of the legal paperwork was shelved after Russia's full-scale invasion began.

Shchyrskyi told CBC News that he spoke to Mamotiuk at the border as she was leaving Belarus.

"Finally, she's got what she wanted. She's been brought to Ukraine, but she's confused," he said in a phone interview with CBC News from Romania, where he currently lives. "Even though she's 29 years old, deep down she's still a child — a little girl who has been moved from one place to another, and then moved again."

The Emile Foundation's Maria Lebedieva, seen on a cellphone screen, speaks with Mamotiuk near the border checkpoint between Ukraine and Belarus on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

As the bus carrying the children arrived at the checkpoint on Friday afternoon, relatives, Ukrainian officials and a crush of cameras rushed toward the opening doors. Off to the side, an ambulance pulled up carrying Mamotiuk.

When CBC News entered the vehicle to greet her, she lay on a stretcher staring at the ceiling. She appeared quiet and unsure.

When we asked if she wanted to say hello to Maria Lebedieva, director of the Emile Foundation's Ukraine branch, who was waiting on the other side of the secured checkpoint, Mamotiuk's mood lifted.

Seeing a friendly face on a video call, a smile spread across her face. She said she hoped to see Lebedieva soon and wanted to know when she could see Shchyrskyi.

Sydorenko tightly hugs her son Artem after being reunited at a checkpoint about five kilometres from the Ukraine-Belarus border on Friday. (Briar Stewart/CBC)

Outside of the ambulance, some children got back on the bus with their relatives, while others, like Artem, got into vehicles to make the onward journey.

"I am even happier than I thought I would be," Sydorenko said as she prepared to leave with her son and head back to Kyiv.

As for Mamotiuk, a Ukrainian flag was placed over her legs like a blanket just before the ambulance carrying her pulled away toward a medical facility south of the capital.

World.title: Did that tip seem steep? The math might have included the tax
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

LISTEN | Doing the math when you leave a tip: Cost of Living 3:57 Why you should do the math why you leave a tip

You've heard of " tipflation " and " tip creep ."

But what may not be clear when you're prompted to tip your barista, hairdresser or even your mechanic is that you could be tipping on the total — tax included.

Back when leaving a tip meant having to do some mental or back-of-the-napkin math, the custom was to look at the subtotal before taxes and calculate from there.

But with point-of-sale terminals spitting out numbers lickety-split, it's hard to get a handle on how tipping equations are being run.

"In effect, a consumer has to take out their calculator to check if it was calculated before or after the tip, so it gets more difficult," said Sara Eve Levac, a lawyer for the Quebec-based non-profit Option Consommateurs, a consumer watchdog.

Sara Eve Levac of the Quebec-based non-profit consumer watchdog Option Consommateurs says the organization held discussion groups about tipping with consumers across Canada, and the findings were that 'people felt like it wasn't clear' if they included tax. (Maude Desbois Photographie)

In response to consumer feedback about the issue, Levac said their organization tested some restaurants and found cases where the tip was indeed calculated after the taxes.

Bonnie Simpson, a professor of consumer behaviour at Western University in London, Ont., said that in many places where we're being asked to tip these days, we often don't get itemized receipts with a clear delineation between total and subtotal.

"We get a tiny screen and it does not show us a breakdown," said Simpson, who has researched consumer attitudes toward tipping .

Sure, most sit-down restaurants still hand you a paper breakdown of everything you ordered, said Simpson, but it's straight to the point-of-sale terminal in a lot of other tipping contexts.

Even when there is a receipt that delineates the total before and after tax, it's often not obvious which is used to calculate the tip.

Levac said Option Consommateurs held discussion groups about tipping with consumers across Canada, and the findings were that "people felt like it wasn't clear."

In Quebec, new rules brought in with Bill 72 last year mean it's now against the rules for any establishment to prompt customers to tip on the tax-in total.

The Quebec government's consumer protection office told CBC in an email it has received 988 complaints and issued 389 notices since these provisions came into effect on May 7, 2025, and that the majority were for restaurants, bars and other food-related services.

It's the only province with clear rules on how tips are presented on pay machines.

WATCH | Quebec's effort to establish rules on how tips are calculated : Quebec moves to clamp down on growing ‘tip inflation’ at restaurants | Duration 1:41 Quebec’s justice minister has tabled a bill that would require restaurants to calculate tips on prices before taxes to protect cost-weary consumers from misleading tip recommendations.

Industry association Restaurants Canada said in a statement to CBC that it advises restaurants to "ensure automated tip suggestions on payment terminals are calculated on the pre-tax amount and presented in a clear, neutral way to ensure customers feel confident in making the best choice that reflects their experience."

Is the tech to blame?

Levac said she's read media reports in which merchants said it's difficult to change their payment terminal to calculate the tip before taxes.

But when the research team at Option Consommateurs looked at 12 common payment systems, Levac said they found it was "actually pretty easy for someone with minimal technical knowledge to be able to change the settings."

Moneris and Square are among the most used payment processors in Canada. They rent and sell the payment machines that are used by a lot of Canadian businesses.

In emails to CBC, both said their machines can be customized and it's up to businesses to decide how their tips are calculated and whether to include the tax or not.

Time for a new model?

In Edmonton, Sarah Burns said she feels privileged to be able to go out for coffees and the occasional dinner given the high cost of just about everything these days.

"But I do not like tipping on GST on my bill," she told Cost of Living.

"I would really prefer a European model where I believe servers are paid a living wage."

Western University Prof. Bonnie Simpson says tipping is a social contract we engage in as consumers and that it would take a lot of consumer pressure — and eventually legislation — to arrive at a new system. (Submitted by Bonnie Simpson)

Western University's Bonnie Simpson said tipping is a social contract we engage in as consumers and that it would take a lot of consumer pressure — and eventually legislation — to arrive at a new system.

"Somebody would need to study and propose an alternative that still allowed the hospitality industry success and still allowed the people working in it to make great wages. But it would be a huge change."

World.title: Would you use LinkedIn to find love?
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Savannah Giedroyc and Robert DeMichele had mutual friends when they started dating, but their love story didn't begin the way you'd expect.

Instead of approaching DeMichele through their social circle, the Toronto-based accountant decided to take matters into her own hands — and shoot her shot on LinkedIn.

"I decided to send him an invite and then he accepted. It's so cheesy, because he ended up viewing my profile," said Giedroyc. "So then I viewed his back so that he would get the alert that, like, I was also looking at his profile. Then about a month later, he actually messaged me back on Instagram, because we were mutual."

"He says if I didn't add him [on LinkedIn] and I didn't … clue into his profile, he would have never put two and two together."

Savannah Giedroyc and Robert DeMichele on their wedding day in Toronto in August 2026. (Submitted by Savannah Giedroyc)

LinkedIn is primarily used for professional networking and career development, and allows people in the job market to post their resumés and browse listings and gives employers an opportunity to potentially find hires. Many people also publish their thoughts on business trends on the site, although users have noticed an increased number of AI-generated posts.

Recently, it’s made headlines for misleading job postings that funnelled applicants to a multi-level marketing company that asked for money.

But amid a sea of job postings (both real and fake) and AI slop, could LinkedIn actually be an underrated dating app?

WATCH | Could you find your soulmate on LinkedIn?: Could you find your soulmate on LinkedIn? | Duration 2:21 Looking for your soulmate? Some say LinkedIn might be the answer. More users are turning to the app, and not just for career advancement, but for love. Experts say that although this holds potential for great connections, there should be professional boundaries in place to protect users from unwanted advances.

A way to find, research potential partners

A poll by Zety — a professional development site that provides resumé and cover letter building services — surveyed more than 1,000 U.S. employees and found one in eight people said they formed a romantic relationship that started on LinkedIn. Twenty-two per cent said they reached out to, or responded to, someone on LinkedIn with romantic intent.

Some say the app also shines in another way: one in five respondents admitted to using LinkedIn to research a potential romantic partner.

"You see, like, where they went to school, their job — it kind of answers some questions. If you have certain boxes that you want to tick, it's all listed there for you," said Giedroyc.

"I would be lying if I said I haven't done it," said Emily Durham, a Toronto-based recruiter and content creator. "Dating is such a personal experience. I've always just been interested to see what [potential partners are] interested in."

More people are moving away from traditional dating apps such as Tinder, Bumble and Hinge. The Harris Poll , a global market research firm, surveyed 2,177 Americans and found 56 per cent of respondents agree the app meetups are "cringe" and 72 per cent said these apps have made dating feel more "transactional" than "romantic."

Almost half of those surveyed said they find information on LinkedIn to be more trustworthy than on traditional dating apps. (Mauro Pimentel/AFP/Getty Images)

Meanwhile, 48 per cent of respondents to the Zety survey find information on LinkedIn to be more trustworthy compared to actual dating apps.

Advances must 'feel safe'

Durham cautions that these types of advances must be reciprocal, with respect and consent at the centre of it all.

"For many women, when we show up online to advance our careers, what we also get is an onslaught of romantic advancement and sexual harassment," said Durham. "I think it's really about understanding how to make [those approaches] happen in a way that they'll feel safe … in a situation where there is reciprocity and it's mutual."

Not everyone is up for LinkedIn becoming more personal. Sixty five per cent of respondents to the Zety survey said they believe using the site for dating could harm their reputation.

But proponents say LinkedIn could help you judge whether a potential love interest is a go-getter.

"I think career and ambition says a lot about someone," said Giedroyc. "It’s one of the most important factors of someone's life — you know, what they do in the day-to-day."

World.title: Trump has outsized influence in stock markets, but investors grow wary
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Stock markets wrapped up a head-spinning week of trading on a positive note Friday, with tech stocks rallying after taking a beating earlier on.

The Nasdaq had its best week in seven months. The Dow Jones Industrial Average and the S&P 500 both finished the session in positive territory.

When asked Thursday what he was most thankful for, U.S. President Donald Trump told American troops deployed abroad that stock markets have set records 88 times during his presidency.

"We have the highest stock markets in history," said Trump.

Markets have indeed performed incredibly well during Trump's tenure — and the president has played an outsized role in fuelling that rise.

Trump has repeatedly taken steps to boost the market, announcing deals, truces and agreements to move markets and push stocks higher. This week, he made one of his boldest moves yet, intervening to push the board of Nvidia to rehire Jensen Huang as CEO.

It led to one of the biggest one-day surges the Nasdaq has ever seen.

What is the 'Trump put?'

Traders call it the "Trump put," a belief that the president will intervene to push markets higher. Whether that's in announcing a deal or truce that may not be quite complete or backing off policies the markets dislike (as he did after the so-called Liberation Day tariffs caused a massive sell off in April 2025.)

But the Trump put was tested this week.

Nvidia lost much of the ground it regained on Monday. The company's stock price rallied briefly on the news that Huang would return to the corner office. But since then it resumed its fall. Since Nvidia peaked on Oct. 6, it has fallen nearly 31 per cent since.

The tech heavy Nasdaq is also down about 13 per cent in the same time period.

That slump has some wondering if Trump is reaching the limit of his ability to move markets.

"It's started to unwind," said Jim Thorne, the chief market strategist at Wellington-Altus Private Wealth.

WATCH | Nvidia CEO scandal reaches Trump's Commerce Department: Trump's Commerce Department under fire as Nvidia CEO scandal continues to rock markets | Duration closed caption 8:17 Both Democrats and Republicans are calling for answers over the Trump administration's apparent close ties to former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang. U.S. Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick is facing particular scrutiny. Huang's resignation following extramarital affairs has rattled the tech world — and stock markets.

Part of that is the sweeping Democrat victory in the midterm elections because, Thorne says, Trump moved away from the promises he made to his base.

"Let's be honest and clear about this, right? He screwed up. He lost in the midterms because he got away from the America first affordability crisis," said Thorne in an interview Friday.

But Thorne also says Americans and investors are wary of the way Trump involves himself in the markets.

"Is Trump losing his effect? Yes. People are tired," he said

Is Trump's stock market influence waning?

The whole basis for the Trump put is that investors believe him when he says something will happen. Or that it won't happen. This week he told markets Nvidia would be fine because Huang did nothing wrong.

At a fundamental level, that was hard to completely believe. Huang may not have broken any laws. He may not have known he was having an affair with an alleged Chinese spy or that his paramour's company was accused of illegally funnelling the best and most powerful American chips to Chinese companies with ties to the Chinese military.

Even with Huang back in the CEO's chair, the company will face increased scrutiny and tighter export regulations.

But Richard Dias, the global macro strategist at IceCap Asset Management, says there's a broader fatigue at play.

"Is the Trump thing getting exhausted? I think obviously, yes, I think everyone is exhausted. People who agree with him are exhausted," said Dias.

He says the idea that the president alone could move markets was always a bit of an embellishment.

"I think his weight and power in the markets, I think it's just massively, massively overstated. The markets are way smarter than you or me or any one man," Dias told CBC News in an interview.

Dias says markets were already looking for a reason to move against the broader AI trade. The circular financing agreements (under which NVIDIA would invest in AI companies provided they would in turn buy Nvidia chips) was raising alarm bells. And there were real questions about the sustainability of the AI buildout and focus on (wildly unpopular) data centres.

WATCH | Data centre backlash is a problem for Trump’s Republicans: Data centre backlash is a problem for Trump’s Republicans | Duration closed caption 9:52 Data centre development is exploding across Ohio, and it’s a growing problem for U.S. President Donald Trump and his Republican Party. For The National, CBC’s Katie Simpson goes to the crucial battleground state to find out more about how it could play out in the upcoming midterm elections.

Dias says humans love a narrative.

"The story that people will tell ourselves is, 'oh, Jensen Huang's infidelities and Trump meddling will be the cause of this tech sell-off,' when really there was a litany of ready-made examples and reasons why there was already loads of weakness."

There are still plenty of reasons the AI trade will rally.

There are still plenty of forces that may drive markets down — the Federal Reserve is eying more rate hikes before the end of the year that would dampen investor enthusiasm — and it would be folly to underestimate the power of any U.S. president to sway markets.

But there is a growing sentiment that this was the week that Trump began to see his impact tested and many, including the widely read Wall Street newsletter, The Kobeissi Letter, have declared an end to the "Trump put".

World.title: They gave birth in the south. Now, they're helping Inuit deliver closer to home
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Margaret Tukkiapik's hands are peppered with some of the accomplishments of her work.

Small circular tattoos line each one of her fingers — representing every umbilical cord she's cut in her time assisting labouring mothers.

"I'm missing a few dots," said Tukkiapik, holding up her hands proudly.

The midwife at the Ungava Tulattavik Health Centre's maternity ward, who has attended 95 births, jokes that the stick-and-poke tattoos can be quite painful.

In Inuit traditions, cutting the cord of a baby is an honour and a responsibility — marking the start of a special relationship with the child, who is referred to as the cord-cutter's arnaliaq, if the baby is a girl, or angusiaq, for a boy.

Tukkiapik has 10 of each.

Margaret Tukkiapik was a self-taught doula before starting to study as a midwife five years ago. She gets a marking on her fingers every time she cuts a baby's umbilical cord. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

"As they're cutting the cord, they will install values in the child," she said.

As they grow, the children present their accomplishments — their first sewing project, fish or caribou — back to the person who cut their cord, says Tukkiapik.

Tukkiapik's arnaliaqs and angusiaqs are part of what pushed her into midwifery in her home community of Kuujjuaq, Que.

She was a self-taught doula for years before she started studying through Puvirnituq's Inuulitsivik Health Centre midwifery program — now celebrating its 40th year in operation.

This month, Tukkiapik passed her exam after training for five years.

She joins the ranks of other Inuit midwives who have stepped up to provide safe options for pregnant Inuit who would otherwise have to fly south to deliver outside of their region, culture and language.

WATCH | Inside the northern maternity centre that welcomes 100 babies a year: Inside the northern maternity unit helping pregnant Inuit deliver close to home | Duration closed caption 3:03 Kuujjuaq's maternity centre sees an average of 100 births every year. Its Inuit midwives are among the team providing care for hose who would otherwise travel outside of their region, culture and language.

A 'night and day' difference

For Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, a midwife in training, this mission is personal.

She's edging closer to her due date with her second baby, and plans to deliver in Kuujjuaq. But she can't help but compare this pregnancy to her first — when she had most of her prenatal follow-ups and delivery in Montreal.

"There's really been a difference, like between night and day," she said.

"I'm able to be served in my language at home and not going into … a big crazy hospital that I'm not familiar with."

Kayla Annanack-Lauzon, left, will deliver her second child in December, in the same maternity ward where she currently works as a midwife. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

After studying nursing, Annanack-Lauzon began training with the Inuulitsivik midwifery program in May, and has attended four births. She says patients "always have something good to say about their experience when they compare it to the South."

But up north, there's no continuous monitoring, epidural or inductions, notes Tukkiapik. In cases of emergency, the doctors on staff in the hospital step in and transfer the patient to trauma rooms.

Some women have to be sent out of the community if it's medically necessary.

It's what happened to Tukkiapik during her first pregnancy.

Margaret Tukkiapik hopes each of the six other communities on the Ungava coast can have their own midwifery services. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

"I did not like that at all," she said.

"It's not how I was treated. It was just being away from home for so long, and then not knowing what to expect."

When she became pregnant with her daughter, in 2013, she said she took better care of herself — adamant that she wanted to stay home to deliver.

Doing things differently

Tukkiapik gave birth just down the hall from the current maternity ward, years before the unit created its own wing in the hospital.

Her daughter's birth was the first month Marilyn Mesher was on shift as a student, says Tukkiapik. Mesher later became the first Inuk from the Ungava coast to graduate from a midwifery program. She's now Tukkiapik's colleague.

"We're very proud," said Elena Mesher, Marilyn's sister.

Elena sat in a patient room in the maternity centre, holding her two-year-old son, Vincent — who was born at home, thanks to the help of the midwifery team, who also do house calls.

Elena Mesher delivered her son, Vincent, at home with the help of the midwives working in Kuujjuaq. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

"It's very important to have local midwives there with you because they understand what's going on," she said. "You can speak to them in your own language."

That's a sticking point for Tukkiapik.

Walking down the maternity ward's hallway, lined with parenting and newborn pamphlets, she pointed into some of the birthing rooms — whose doors have a notice posted on the outside: "Thank you for speaking Inuktitut or English in this room."

"Everyone's most comfortable in their first language," she said.

"If they don't understand, they will not ask you … But when you talk to them in their own language, they understand more and [are] able to ask for better care."

When appointments are done in Inuktitut, she says patients also have a better understanding of the level of care they should be receiving.

Piles of pamphlets are available at the maternity clinic, which is connected to Kuujjuaq's hospital centre. (Rachel Watts/CBC)

It's part of why both Tukkiapik and Annanack-Lauzon want to see their small ward expand.

Kuujjuaq's maternity centre began developing in the '80s. Decades later, they're still doing things differently.

In one of its two delivery rooms is a double bed — much bigger than a standard hospital bed, and made for women who want family members or partners close to them while they labour.

"We don't ask them to just be laying on their back as they're delivering. They can deliver in whatever position they're comfortable," said Tukkiapik.

Just to the right of the room is the centre's bulletin board, lined with babies' footprints, names and birth details — posted as a reminder of every child born in the ward in the calendar year.

"When it's a new year, we'll put them in a binder and start our new footprint collection," she said.

Talks of expansion

For over 40 years, the fertility rate in Nunavik has remained nearly twice as high as the Quebec average, according to a 2021 health profile of the region by the Nunavik Board of Health and Social Services.

In Kuujjuaq's maternity centre, deliveries over the past 10 to 15 years have also increased, and now the centre — consisting of the two birthing rooms and a few consultation rooms on the hospital's first floor — sees an average of 100 births every year, says Larry Watt, the executive director of the health centre.

"Our space … is very limited," said Watt.

Larry Watt, the executive director of the Ungava Tulattavik Health Centre, says there are plans to expand the midwifery building. (Josianne Letourneau/CBC)

But he says there's a plan to get a bigger facility in the next few years to offer more services, in part because the ward also takes on births, prenatal and postpartum care from neighbouring villages along the Ungava Coast.

Just next door to the maternity wing is the Maison de Transit, a temporary housing facility for the patients and family members from isolated communities who are flown in for care.

But for Tukkiapik, she dreams of a time when each of the 6 other communities on the Ungava coast have their own midwifery services.

"'Cause it makes a big difference," she said. "Each community must fight to have their own."

Annanack-Lauzon agreed, encouraging more Inuit to join.

"That's what we want," she said, cradling her baby bump. "It's really, really, awesome that we get to have this care."

World.title: Explosion at a middle school in Afghanistan kills at least 7, injures more than 90
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

An explosion at a school in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar killed seven people and wounded more than 90 on Saturday, the province’s culture and information director said, adding that the blast appeared to have originated in a neighbouring depot for explosives.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies. An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.

Up to 15 of the wounded remained in hospital, while the rest were discharged after treatment, he added.

Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10 a.m. at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building, part of which appeared to have collapsed.

Mining is a major industry in Afghanistan, a country that is rich in raw materials, including iron ore, copper, lead, zinc, gold, coal and precious stones. But safety standards at the mining companies are often poor, leading to accidents.

In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital, Kabul, wounded more than 40 children between 9 and 14 years old.

World.title: Legal wording once intimidated me. Now, it's becoming a language I can explain
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

This First Person article is the experience of Adu Asare, who lives in Scarborough, Ont. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ .

Two years after I arrived in Canada, I found myself holding a piece of paper containing legal jargon I did not understand.

Of course, I had questions. But I felt uncomfortable asking them.

So after the lawyer meant to help me with my Workplace Safety and Insurance Board Benefits asked me, I signed the document — without fully knowing its financial implications.

The document mentioned a contingency fee, which dictated my lawyer would retain a percentage of any settlement.

Now, I’m a paralegal student; at school, I’ve learned about contingency fees and the rest of what I was being asked to sign. But the experience in May 2023 taught me something else: that I want to help others make sense of the law.

A struggle for answers

My challenges with legal language began in my home country of Ghana.

Asare grew up in Ghana and immigrated to Canada in 2021. He had to navigate the legal paperwork of an asylum claim, seeking protection from threats, discrimination and the risk of harm if he returned to his home country. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

There, in 2019, I hired a lawyer to help with my divorce. I asked them questions, such as: What documents do I need to file? What are the legal grounds for divorce? How long will the process take? What are my rights and financial responsibilities?

The answers were often very technical, and I struggled to understand the practical implications and what I needed to do.

I faced that same sense of uncertainty when I immigrated to Canada in 2021 and had to navigate the legal paperwork of an asylum claim. I sought protection from threats to my safety, discrimination and the risk of harm if I returned to my home country.

I relied on an immigration consultant for help with my documents who, at times, did not offer the clarity I needed. That confusion made the process even more overwhelming.

How these experiences shaped me

These instances showed me that having access to a legal professional does not mean that a client feels comfortable asking questions or can make decisions with confidence — and that it can be even harder to know your legal rights when, like with my workplace accident, you are already going through a difficult time. I decided to learn about the law so that I can help others navigate legal challenges and make legal information easier to understand.

In January 2025, I enrolled in Centennial College’s Paralegal Court and Tribunal Agent program in Toronto. Learning the terminology did not change what happened in 2023, but it helped give me the confidence to ask questions.

It’s where I began to see that knowing legal terminology and explaining it clearly are two different skills. Plain language can help close that gap.

Asare is shown here in class at Centennial College. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

I put what I am learning into practice in my Ghanaian community. On one occasion, I helped someone understand an Ontario Works letter explaining that their assistance had stopped after they failed to tell their caseworker they had started a job. I have also helped people understand lawyers’ retainer agreements, sometimes explaining information in Twi, a dialect of our Akan language spoken in Ghana.

These conversations have shown me how everyday language can be used to help someone understand what a document says, and I always let them know that they can ask me any questions. Right now, I see my role as helping people understand the paperwork in front of them and to help them recognize when they need further assistance. (I am a student, not a licensed paralegal, and I know that explaining information in plain language is not a substitute for qualified legal advice.)

And I hope that by writing about legal issues, like in this essay, I can make the law and legal documents more accessible.

I am still learning how to communicate legal information accurately and responsibly. What I do know is that making the law easier to understand does not mean promising outcomes or pretending every issue has a simple answer. When I think about the person who signed that agreement in 2023, I do not see someone who lacked intelligence, I see someone trying to navigate an unfamiliar process without feeling equipped to ask the right questions.

Asare wants people to know they do not have to pretend to understand a document simply because they are afraid to ask questions. (Submitted by Adu Asare)

Looking back, I wish I had asked how the lawyer's fees would be calculated, what percentage would be deducted from any settlement and what services the agreement covered. I also wish I had asked whether the agreement could be explained to me in plain language before I signed it

I cannot change what I did not understand then. But I can use what I am learning now to help make the next person’s experience less confusing.

I want people to know they do not have to pretend to understand a document simply because they are afraid to ask. Sometimes, the first step toward making an informed decision is being able to say, “Can you explain that to me?” — and waiting for the thoughtful answer you deserve.

Do you have a compelling personal story that can bring understanding or help others? We want to hear from you. Here's more info on how to pitch to us.

World.title: The bizarre twists and turns of Colombia’s supermarket hostage siege
World.content:
Blackout drunk kidnappers, false statements by De La Espriella, and bogus accusations against hostages leave a trail of chaos and doubt.

Shortly after 76 hostages were liberated from the Exito Supermarket in Cartagena, Colombia, corporate media broadcast a video of two of the men they claimed were involved in the attack.

​The two men, Carlos Tapia and Daniel Díaz, appeared in handcuffs, being escorted by police from the scene of a tense 18-hour standoff between criminals and police.

The media, with information from President Abelardo de la Espriella, suggested that Tapia and Diaz were two of four surviving members of the gang that attacked the supermarket.

​De la Espriella praised the operation he said “came off perfectly,” and released a video of himself mocking two different men, who police say were the actual kidnappers, together with one more person who was killed in the operation.

The president also released a video of himself making demands into a walkie-talkie, falsely claiming that he was in charge of negotiations with the hostage-takers.

According to the indictment from the Prosecutor’s Office, all negotiations and communications with the three hostage takers were handled by Colombia’s anti-kidnapping police unit, the GAULA.

​Tapia and Díaz were released by police just a few hours later, and cleared of any wrongdoing after police confirmed the men were hostages rather than hostage-takers. De la Espriella confirmed shortly afterwards that the men were innocent of any crimes.

​The two men have since both spoken with Colombian media, in interviews in which both men claimed they were mocked by De la Espriella and treated badly by police before being cleared.

​A third man, Edgar Díaz, was also falsely accused by police. He released a video to social media as well, claiming that not only was he mocked and verbally abused by the President, but also robbed of a gold chain by police. Diaz says he was leaving a gym where he works as a personal trainer, in the same mall as the Exito, when he was grabbed by men who appeared to be armed.

The stories of the falsely accused hostages aren’t the only odd parts of the official story surrounding the stand-off between 3 nominally armed men and hundreds of marines, police, snipers, helicopters, and riot police in the city of Cali.

​One of the hostage-takers was killed by police when they entered the supermarket around 1 a.m., after the hostage-takers missed a deadline of 12:30 to release all hostages.

​According to police, the three men attempted to rob an armored car transporting money around 8 a.m., but the car had already left by the time the men arrived. For unclear reasons, the three decided to take nearly 100 people hostage in the Exito supermarket instead, which is part of the same “mega-mall” where the men allegedly intended to carry out the hijacking.

​Two of the men carried long guns that, again according to police, were “traumatic weapons” (similar to Airsoft rifles, the weapons fire foam bullets meant to be non-lethal), and one was armed with another that resembled a shotgun.

Early in the morning, before the men blocked windows in the supermarket, Colombian media captured one of the men from a distance clad in black tactical clothing, body armor, and what appeared to be a heavy steel helmet with a facemask.

​Many of those who were held hostage, speaking with media, said the men were drinking heavily throughout the day, with one witness going as far as to say they were “blind drunk” by the end of the day.

​Workers at the Éxito, who were also taken hostage, said the men set up large speakers, blasted music, and demanded to be given bottles of whisky.

​The two men who survived the police assault that liberated the hostages were asleep when police entered the Éxito, likely why they survived, according to multiple witnesses.

​Confusing matters even further, the wife of the man who was reportedly killed by police, Javier Humberto Muñetón Zapata, had spent the previous 14 hours speaking with local media in Cartagena, looking for her husband, who she believed to be among the hostages.

​She says they lived nearby and went to the mall every day, and that her husband had a membership at the same gym where Diaz works. She claims she began searching for her husband, who had promised to drive her to work and bring pastries from the supermarket, after he suddenly stopped replying to texts.

​She showed Blue Radio a text message at 8:12 a.m. from her husband that said, “Okay, I’m going to pop into Éxito, and I’ll pick you up right away.”

​She claims that her husband ran a small business, regularly drove her to work, and has no criminal record — a fact that has since been confirmed by Cartgena’s mayor. She has made multiple statements to the media asking for clarification and more information, claiming he could not have been involved in any crimes.

Early statements by police, shortly after the hostage situation began to unfold, put the number of hostages at 50. After two releases of hostages by the nominal gunmen, police stated they believed 20 hostages remained as evening approached.

​Shortly after the operation to enter the Éxito, police released details about their raid, claiming that they had “drilled holes in the walls and inserted cameras,” allowing them to identify the kidnappers and estimate the number of hostages.

​They also stated they had men on the roof, in the warehouse of the supermarket, and stationed at the interior entrance to the Éxito, which connects to the mega-mall.

​But more than 70 hostages remained when the raid was successfully carried out.

The attackers claimed in a letter to authorities that if the store was entered by police they would detonate explosives placed near the entrances, killing the hostages.

Police later revealed there were no explosives, and the men were bluffing.

​The two men who were captured alive (and reportedly asleep), Juan Camilo Torres Manco, 33, and Jhon Albeiro Mejía Blandón, 44, are both from Antioquia and have previous convictions for “violent” crimes, according to police.

​Both men appeared intoxicated in videos shortly after they were captured. De la Espriella released a video in which he berates the two men, telling them, “You thought you could just kidnap people and get away with it? Welcome to the miracle country.”

​The bizarre details of the event, as well as misreporting by the media, inaccurate and even contradictory statements by police throughout the day, and general confusion, led some critics of De le Espriella to claim the entire event was staged.

De la Espriella’s efforts to insert himself into the situation, and false claims made by the president, worsened that dynamic.

​There is no evidence currently to support those claims, but with a story that is just straight-up strange, we can see how some people came to that conclusion.

World.title: Colombia’s special forces liberate hostages from Cartagena supermarket
World.content:
Colombia’s security forces liberated some 20 people who were held hostage inside a supermarket in the northern city of Cartagena after a 15-hour stand-off.

The operation ended a tense situation that began around 8AM on Tuesday when the armed kidnappers entered the Exito supermarket in La Castellano, a residential neighborhood.

According to President Abelardo de la Espriella, who led the liberation operation, the kidnappers meant to rob an armored car that had already left with the proceeds of the day before.

The kidnappers subsequently kidnapped a group of 30 people, and demanded COP7billion ($2 million) and the possibility to escape the supermarket.

Throughout the day, at least five of the hostages were released from the supermarket cafeteria, whose windows had been covered with papers. One video showed a row of hostages sitting behind the window.

Riot police was deployed around midnight after family members and onlookers became restless.

The situation took a quick turn after 1PM when explosions were heard and special forces entered the building.

The security forces killed one of the kidnappers and detained the remaining four, De la Espriella said in a social media video.

Images that were shared on social media showed special police forces securing the Exito’s cafeteria and removing the paper from the windows.

De la Espriella said that all the hostages were released in an “extraordinary joint operation between the National Police and the military forces.”

One agent would have been injured in the rescue operation, reported Caracol Radio.

The kidnappers “were given the opportunity to surrender and release the hostages, but they rejected that opportunity, so we took decisive action,” said the president.

In the morning, the prosecution said the kidnappers’ arms and explosives were fake and former hostages said the hostage takers spent most of the day getting drunk.

World.title: 22 injured after car bomb strikes central Colombia governor’s office
World.content:
Twenty-two people were reportedly injured and more than 80 buildings were damaged in a car bomb attack on the Governor’s Office of Meta in Villavicencio, central Colombia.

According to Meta’s Security Secretary, Franklin Olivos, the car that exploded carried approximately 100 kilograms of explosives and caused damage to buildings that were located more than 100 meters away from the blast.

Among the injured are five private security guards. One of them needed surgery, according to his employer.

Olivos blamed the attack on the 39th Front, a unit of the FARC dissident group EMC, which has opposed the peace process that started 10 years ago on Tuesday and controls large swathes of jungle territory in the south of Colombia.

In an initial response, President Abelardo de la Espriella said that “narcoterrorism is desperate because we are confronting it head-on. It seeks to intimidate us and force us to back down so we seek another sham peace process.”

De la Espriella, an opponent of the peace process, has been advertising an “iron fist” policy against organized crime and illegal armed groups.

The president’s alleged offensive has failed to produce any results and guerrilla groups have continued to attack State security forces and infrastructure.

World.title: Colombia strips key critics of security details
World.content:
Colombia’s National Protection Unit (UNP) has withdrawn the security details of journalist Daniel Coronell, a major critic of President Abelardo de la Espriella, after vowing to protect the freedom of the press.

Coronell’s local security detail was removed because he lives in the United States, which would make it impossible for the UNP to reassess his protection plan.

The Miami-based journalist frequently travels to Colombia for his work and was in Bogota to receive a lifetime achievement award from the national journalism prize.

While receiving the prize, Coronell sharply criticized De la Espriella for promoting self-promotion over governance. using state resources to censor critics, restricting public information to “friendly media,” and leveraging a history of aggressive lawsuits against reporters.

The journalist’s criticism triggered a clash with Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez, who accused Coronell of being angry for having State subsidies pulled.

After press freedom foundation FLIP responded to defend Coronell, Ordoñez claimed that “the freedom of the press enjoys full protection and guarantees from the government.”

We value and defend freedom of the press as a cornerstone of democracy. The press is free, but it is also responsible. It is not a license to abuse, slander, defame, fabricate stories, spread misinformation, or engage in politics. Nor is it a license to destroy democracy or its institutions with lies. Interior Minister Alejandro Ordoñez

Coronell played a key role in Colombian journalism since the late 1980’s and was forced to flee Colombia in 2005 after reports on the ties of former President Alvaro Uribe and paramilitary groups escalated death threats.

The journalist currently works with Noticias Uno and Caracol Radio, and has more than 700,000 subscribers on YouTube.

The UNP previously stripped former President Gustavo Petro and former presidential candidate Claudia Lopez of their security details.

World.title: Illegal armed group carries out first urban drone attack: three injured in northeast Colombia
World.content:
A couple and their 18-month-old baby were injured in a drone attack on a police station in Cucuta, the first major city to be struck from the sky by guerrilla explosives.

The attack damaged more than 60 homes near the Norte de Santander Police Department in the Tasajero neighborhood in the north of the regional capital, the province’s security secretary, George Quintero, told press.

As of now, the situation is as follows: more than 60 damaged homes located just 20 meters from the police headquarters, and three people injured. Security secretary George Quintero

The homes were hit because the police department’s signal-jamming systems reportedly caused the drones to miss their target.

An unknown number of drones were able to reach the interior of the Police Department’s compound, leaving only minor damage.

Guerrilla group ELN has been carrying out multiple drone attacks in Catatumbo, a nearby region with major coca cultivations, and exercises control in the peripheral slums of Cucuta.

The group was accused of attacking the same police department with home-made mortars in August. This attack injured seven policemen.

In a response to the guerrilla attack, President Abelardo de la Espriella in October ordered the militarization of the border city, which has been struggling with security issues for years.

De la Espriella vowed that he “will not allow narco-terrorism to continue sowing fear and threatening families” in Cucuta and the surrounding Norte de Santander province.

According to the authorities, the militarization of the city sought to “strengthen territorial control, protect citizens, and confront” the illegal armed groups that operate in and around Cucuta.

The president’s offensive against illegal armed groups and organized crime has been hampered by an increase in the use of drones that are equipped with explosives.

All kinds of illegal armed groups use the relatively new technology to push back the authorities from areas under their control.

World.title: Colombia asks X to suspend Petro’s social media account
World.content:
Colombia’s communications ministry said Sunday that it had requested social media platform X to suspend former President Gustavo Petro for “possible incitement to violence.”

In a statement that was published of X, the ministry said it reported Petro’s account to X’s Public Affairs, Safety, and Rules Enforcement Team.

According to the statement, the request to suspend the leftist former president, who has more than 9 million followers, was due to a November 21 post in which Petro asked “the people of Colombia to demand Abelardo’s resignation now.”

Petro has been trying to promote popular opposition against De la Espriella, who he has called an illegitimate president.

According to the ministry, Petro’s call to “take action in the streets” could constitute a call for violence against the government.

In a response, the former president said the De la Espriella administration sought to impose censorship on him, which is “expressly prohibited by the Constitution.”

The ministry’s request “demonstrates the extent of the current government’s illegitimacy,” added Petro.

The former president is now the leader of the Historic Pact (PH) opposition party and has actively been promoting a general strike in response to his successor’s controversial policy decisions.

Petro is a member of the PH’s more radical wing and can still count on a significant following among Colombia’s population.

World.title: The deteriorating press freedom in Colombia and the Americas
World.content:
I sat down with Joshua Collins of Pirate Wire Services to discuss the deteriorating press freedom situation in Colombia and the rest of Latin America.
