World.title: Vast Majority of Women Suffer Violence Without Reporting It
World.content:
Actress Samantha Ruth Prabhu is participating in a campaign to end violence against women in India. Globally, only a very small percentage of women seek help or report the physical or sexual violence they have experienced to the authorities, and legal cases often fail to result in convictions or sentences. Image: UN Women India

By IPS Correspondent

HAVANA TIMES – Only seven percent of women who experience physical or sexual violence report it to the police, and barely 23 percent seek help from family members, their communities or authorities, according to a UN Women report released on Monday, November 23.

The study by the United Nations agency, based on data from 54 countries, estimated that worldwide, 840 million women and girls – nearly one in three – have experienced physical or sexual violence at some point in their lives.

Published ahead of the International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women, November 25, the report notes that even when women decide to come forward, justice is far from guaranteed.

Sexual violence crimes are among the least likely to result in a conviction.

Sima Bahous, executive director of UN Women, said that “too many justice systems around the world are failing women and girls who experience violence. Cases go unreported, trials fail to move forward, and rulings go unenforced.”

“Justice cannot be achieved when women and girls have no access to it or when the law fails to protect them. We must work to ensure that justice systems fulfill their fundamental responsibilities to protect survivors, uphold their rights and prosecute perpetrators,” she added.

The UN Women study reveals a system in which silence is the norm, accountability is the exception, and perpetrators are far more likely to go unpunished than women are to obtain justice.

Many women remain silent, not by choice, but to protect themselves from the risks associated with speaking out. That is why barely seven percent of victims report acts of physical or sexual violence to the police, despite it being one of the most widespread human rights violations.

Women who report abuse may lose their homes, their children and their income. They may face abandonment by their families, exclusion from their communities and threats from the perpetrators they identify.

When women decide to come forward – sometimes years after the crimes were committed – they are all too often punished for speaking out and blamed for having waited. Some are murdered by their abusers simply for seeking help.

The number of women survivors of violence seeking help is declining in most countries that track such data.

In Asia, according to UN Women, only 16 percent of survivors seek help. In Africa, the figure is 31 percent, and in Latin America and the Caribbean, 40 percent.

In European Union countries, while 64 percent of survivors speak about the assault with someone close to them, only 14 percent go to the police.

According to research cited in the report, between 63 and 97 percent of complaints worldwide do not result in a conviction. Cases get lost in the justice system; survivors are subjected to repeated questioning and intimidating situations, and perpetrators may never be brought to trial.

All too often, perpetrators in positions of power are never convicted of the crimes they commit, fostering a culture of impunity.

The same pattern is repeated in the digital sphere. Only 25 percent of women involved in public life who experienced online violence filed a complaint with the police.

It is not the perpetrators who are penalized, but the women, who are silenced and excluded from digital spaces and prevented from exercising their right to participate freely in public life.

Against this backdrop, Bahous stated that “progress is possible. Today there is greater recognition of violence against women and girls, more laws protecting survivors, and more perpetrators behind bars.”

She emphasized that “the protections women have today are the result of the struggles of generations who dared to speak out. Now we must honor their courage by delivering justice, ensuring that every law provides safety, every promise translates into protection, and every word into action.”

“Until every woman and every girl can live free from violence, without fear and without having to prove that she deserves to be believed,” the UN official added.

The theme of this year’s International Day for the Elimination of Violence against Women is “UNiTE to End Violence against Women and Girls.”

First published in Spanish by IPS and translated and posted in English by Havana Times.

Read more feature reports here on Havana Times.

World.title: Falklands Legislative Assembly welcomes tribunal decision: “A good day for the Falkland Islands”
World.content:
Falklands Legislative Assembly welcomes tribunal decision: “A good day for the Falkland Islands”

28th Saturday, November 2026 - 13:22 UTC Full article

“Argentina asked the Tribunal to stop the Sea Lion project, and it has failed,” Members of the Legislative Assembly said in a statement

The Falkland Islands Legislative Assembly on Saturday welcomed the International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea's decision to reject the provisional measures Argentina had sought to halt the Sea Lion oil project, and called on Buenos Aires to respect the “democratic wishes” of the islanders.

“Argentina asked the Tribunal to stop the Sea Lion project, and it has failed,” Members of the Legislative Assembly said in a statement, referring to the decision taken by 18 votes to 3. “This is a good day for the Falkland Islands. We can continue to exercise our right to develop our own natural resources and build our own future unimpeded.”

The lawmakers said Sea Lion “will transform our economy and give future generations a more secure and self-reliant Falklands”, and that it “will continue under our own legal and regulatory framework”.

The Assembly thanked the UK Government and the legal teams “who defended Islanders' interests and wishes so robustly in Hamburg”, as well as Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband “for their reassurances at the Joint Ministerial Council this week”, the annual forum between the UK Government and the Overseas Territories.

The lawmakers noted that the wider arbitration will continue and said they “will stay fully engaged in it”. “But our message to Argentina is simple: respect the democratic wishes of the Falkland Islanders and stop putting pressure on the businesses and people who work with us,” the statement concludes, in reference to Argentina's sanctions on companies linked to resource exploitation around the islands.

The tribunal concluded that it lacked prima facie jurisdiction because Argentina's claims would require a determination of sovereignty over the islands, and placed on record UK assurances that there will be no drilling before March 21, 2027, and no new licences. Javier Milei's government, for its part, stressed that the tribunal had recognised the existence of a sovereignty dispute and said it will seek new measures before the arbitral tribunal.

World.title: Law of the sea tribunal rejects Argentina's bid to halt Sea Lion, citing lack of jurisdiction over sovereignty
World.content:
Law of the sea tribunal rejects Argentina's bid to halt Sea Lion, citing lack of jurisdiction over sovereignty

28th Saturday, November 2026 - 13:20 UTC Full article

The tribunal recorded UK assurances: no drilling before March 21, 2027, no extraction before March 2028 and no new licences, as the licensing regime is suspended.

The International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea on Saturday rejected, by 18 votes to 3, Argentina's request for provisional measures to halt the Sea Lion oil project north of the Falklands, concluding that it lacked prima facie jurisdiction because Argentina's claims would require determining which state holds sovereignty over the islands, a question outside the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea.

The order, read in Hamburg by the tribunal's president, Judge Maurice Kamga, examines Argentina's four claims separately. On the first, based on the rights of the coastal state, the tribunal held that ruling on it ”requires the identification of the coastal State that has sovereignty over the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), and presupposes the determination of a question of territorial sovereignty“, which would mean applying ”not the Convention but other rules of international law“. It applied the same reasoning to the second claim, on the obligation to refrain from unilateral measures, and to the third, on protecting the marine environment. On the fourth, it concluded that the obligation to settle disputes peacefully and in good faith cannot by itself provide a basis for jurisdiction. Having found no jurisdiction, the tribunal did not examine urgency.

Judges Horinouchi, of Japan, and Patel, of India, and Argentina's judge ad hoc, Raúl Vinuesa, voted against the order. The 18 votes in favour included those of the UK's judge ad hoc, Vaughan Lowe, and Chilean judge María Teresa Infante Caffi.

The tribunal placed on record the assurances the United Kingdom gave at the hearing: drilling will not begin before March 21, 2027, extraction will not begin before March 2028, and ”no further licenses will be granted as the licensing regime is suspended“. It also stressed that ”the Convention is applicable in the maritime areas in dispute“ and that it expects the parties to act accordingly, and encouraged them to swiftly establish the arbitral tribunal that will rule on the merits. The order states that it does not prejudge that tribunal's jurisdiction or the merits of the case.

The Casa Rosada responded with a statement signed by Milei, saying the tribunal ”has recognised (in a non-unanimous vote) the existence of a sovereignty dispute“ and welcoming that ”recognition in the face of the United Kingdom's position“. It added that it does not share the conclusion on jurisdiction, that the decision does not ”legitimise“ hydrocarbon exploitation and that Argentina will move ”without delay” to constitute the arbitral tribunal, before which it will seek new measures.

https://t.co/M8LHss6CeT — Oficina del Presidente (@OPRArgentina) November 28, 2026

The British government, according to Clarín, welcomed the decision, which “confirms the strength of the UK's legal defence and strategy”. It said Argentina had tried “to prevent the Falkland Islanders from making their own sovereign decisions and failed”, and urged Buenos Aires to “end its wider policy of economic pressure against the islands”. “A good day for the Falklands,” said Stacy Bragger, a member of the islands' Legislative Assembly.

Sea Lion, operated by Israel's Navitas Petroleum, with 65%, and Britain's Rockhopper Exploration, with 35%, has estimated reserves of 1.7 billion barrels. The companies took the final investment decision in December 2025 and expect first oil in the first quarter of 2028.

World.title: Colombia's president backs Abascal: "Spain deserves a president like you"
World.content:
Colombia's president backs Abascal: “Spain deserves a president like you”

28th Saturday, November 2026 - 05:36 UTC Full article

Abascal and De la Espriella

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has backed Vox leader Santiago Abascal ahead of Sunday's general election in Spain, in a video Abascal himself shared on X on Friday, the last day of campaigning. “Dear friend, Spain deserves a president like you,” the Colombian president said.

Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has backed Vox leader Santiago Abascal ahead of Sunday's general election in Spain, in a video Abascal himself shared on X on Friday, the last day of campaigning. “Dear friend, Spain deserves a president like you,” the Colombian president said.

“To my friend Santiago Abascal, a man who defends founding principles and values, a man as consistent as they come, I wish the very best of luck this Sunday,” De la Espriella said from Bogotá. “Today more than ever I stand firm for Spain and firm for the homeland!” he concluded.

It is not the first time De la Espriella, elected in June, has intervened in foreign campaigns. He supported the candidacy of Keiko Fujimori, who won Peru's election; backed Flávio Bolsonaro before he lost to Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in Brazil; and campaigned alongside Republican congresswoman María Elvira Salazar ahead of the US midterm elections, prompting a protest from the Democratic Party. According to El País, after the Democrats' victory in those elections, the Colombian president has sought to reach out to the party to safeguard his country's alliance with Washington.

The relationship between the two leaders has been public since the start of the year. In January, while still a candidate, De la Espriella visited Madrid, met Abascal and signed a manifesto against the left that was also signed by, among others, Argentine President Javier Milei and Chilean President José Antonio Kast. Abascal, for his part, celebrated the Colombian's victory in June, saying his compatriots had “said enough to Petro's narco-socialism”.

At the other end of Colombia's political spectrum, former Liberal President Ernesto Samper, who governed from 1994 to 1998, recently expressed his support for Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, a Socialist. “Vox represents a dangerous move towards a non-ideological right, a de facto right that wants to reach power not to govern but to stay,” Samper told El País. Colombia's last three presidents, Iván Duque, Gustavo Petro and De la Espriella, have broken with the tradition of not intervening in other countries' election campaigns.

World.title: Spain wraps up its campaign: Sánchez appeals for a "progressive majority", Feijóo for "change"
World.content:
Spain wraps up its campaign: Sánchez appeals for a “progressive majority”, Feijóo for “change”

28th Saturday, November 2026 - 05:33 UTC Full article

Spain's general election

The main candidates in Spain's snap general election on Sunday closed their campaigns on Friday with packed rallies, at which Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez appealed for a “progressive majority” and People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo even asked left-wing voters to back “change”. The latest published polls gave the PP and Vox a combined majority.

The main candidates in Spain's snap general election on Sunday closed their campaigns on Friday with packed rallies, at which Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez appealed for a “progressive majority” and People's Party leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo even asked left-wing voters to back “change”. The latest published polls gave the PP and Vox a combined majority.

Sánchez closed his campaign at Madrid's Caja Mágica before more than 13,000 people, according to the Socialist Party. “They have tried to turn this election into a referendum against me, the evil Sánchez, and my family, but this election is not about me, it is about your rights, jobs and dignity,” he said. “The progressive majority is in sight, so let's row and vote to govern.” The prime minister also called on the PP to accept the result.

Feijóo closed his at Seville's Pabellón de la Navegación, alongside Andalusian regional president Juanma Moreno, before more than 9,000 people, according to his party, after a morning event in L'Hospitalet de Llobregat, near Barcelona. “I am not asking you to stop feeling left-wing,” he told disaffected Socialist voters, whom he asked for support to “change” the country. “This time, yes, we will not only win, we will govern,” he said. The PP leader promised to restore the prestige of high-speed rail after the Adamuz and Urda accidents, and summed up: “On Sunday we vote, on Monday we start.”

Vox leader Santiago Abascal closed his campaign at Valencia's bullring before more than 14,000 people, according to the party. “This is an existential election for Spain,” he said. Abascal defended “national priority” in access to public benefits and so-called “remigration”: “Let those who never should have left come back, and let those who don't know how to behave leave.” “On November 29, don't vote with fear, vote with courage,” he concluded.

Ada Colau, candidate for Frente Amplio, the coalition to the left of the Socialists, drew some 4,000 people to La Nave de Villaverde in Madrid, with about a thousand more outside, accompanied by Second Deputy Prime Minister Yolanda Díaz and several ministers. “Frente Amplio will never give up. On Sunday we will go out to vote, and we will not do it out of fear, we will do it with hope,” she said.

The closing rallies were shaped by Thursday's four-way debate, in which Feijóo told Colau “and you, keep quiet”, a remark the Socialists and Frente Amplio used to appeal to women voters. According to EFE, Feijóo said in the debate that he would resign if he fails to form a government.

The campaign has been marked by corruption cases involving former Socialist officials, the rail accidents and the lack of a budget during the legislature. A majority requires 176 seats. The latest poll by 40dB for El País and Cadena SER, published before the legal ban on releasing polls in the five days before the vote, put the PP and Vox above 190 seats, while the Centre for Sociological Research showed a Socialist recovery. Saturday is a day of reflection, with no campaigning.

World.title: Milei wins Senate approval to suspend primaries, with debates mandatory only in a run-off
World.content:
Milei wins Senate approval to suspend primaries, with debates mandatory only in a run-off

27th Friday, November 2026 - 17:21 UTC Full article

The government justifies suspending the primaries on cost grounds

Argentina's Senate on Thursday approved, by 43 votes to 29, the political reform promoted by Javier Milei's government that suspends the open, simultaneous and mandatory primary elections (PASO) ahead of the 2027 presidential election. The bill, which also limits mandatory presidential debates to a run-off, now goes to the Chamber of Deputies.

The ruling party secured 21 votes from La Libertad Avanza, 10 from the Radical Civic Union and three from PRO, joined by nine senators from provincial blocs and other parties, according to La Nación. Patricia Bullrich, the ruling party's Senate leader, who was tasked with securing the votes amid tensions with Milei, defended the savings of suspending the primaries. The economy, “which today is on a very important path of stability not achieved in many years, must be brought to every Argentine home,” she told the LN+ channel. “And to think some said we didn't have the votes to suspend the PASO in the Senate...,” cabinet chief Diego Santilli wrote on social media.

Besides suspending the primaries, the reform introduces the so-called “Clean Record” rule for candidacies, changes the financing of electoral advertising on radio and television and the election of Argentina's representatives to the Mercosur Parliament, and abolishes the pre-election campaign blackout. The presidential debate will be mandatory only in a possible run-off, and penalties for candidates who skip the first-round debate are removed.

The ruling party had initially sought to scrap mandatory debates altogether, but gave way on the run-off after 12 civil society organisations, including Cippec, Poder Ciudadano and the Argentine Journalism Forum, called for them to be kept. “The debate is a public good: it offers all candidates a common space to present their proposals and allows citizens to know and compare them,” they said.

The government justifies suspending the primaries on cost grounds. Its critics argue that it favours the ruling party, because without primaries the Peronist opposition, which lacks a common candidate, would find it harder to organise its electoral offer. Some allied lawmakers had also warned that Neuquén's decision to bring forward its provincial elections to February 14 meant changing the rules with the 2027 calendar already under way.

World.title: Argentina bans online betting advertising, including in football and on social media
World.content:
Argentina bans online betting advertising, including in football and on social media

27th Friday, November 2026 - 17:08 UTC Full article

Argentina's Senate during the debate on the betting law

Argentina's Senate unanimously passed, by 72 votes, a law to prevent gambling addiction and regulate online betting, banning gambling advertising in the media, on social media, in stadiums and on billboards, and requiring football clubs to review their sponsorship deals with betting firms. The law, approved on Thursday, had been pending in the upper house for more than two years.

Argentina's Senate unanimously passed, by 72 votes, a law to prevent gambling addiction and regulate online betting, banning gambling advertising in the media, on social media, in stadiums and on billboards, and requiring football clubs to review their sponsorship deals with betting firms. The law, approved on Thursday, had been pending in the upper house for more than two years.

The text was passed unchanged from the version the Chamber of Deputies approved in November 2024. It aims to limit children's and teenagers' exposure to betting and give the state tools to tackle compulsive gambling.

The law bans the advertising, promotion and sponsorship of betting on television, radio, print, the internet, social media, podcasts and billboards, as well as at stadiums, festivals and concerts, including covert advertising. The restrictions also apply to influencers, athletes and celebrities. The Argentine Football Association, the Professional League and clubs such as Boca Juniors, River Plate, Racing and Independiente will have to adjust their deals with betting companies, although the deadline will be set by the regulations, which the executive must issue within 120 days. The only exception is for licensed gaming halls and betting shops.

Under-18s will be banned from betting, and platforms must verify each user's identity and age through facial recognition linked to the national population register, not only when opening an account but at every login and when collecting a prize. Welcome bonuses and loyalty schemes are banned, and only debit cards or digital wallets with available funds may be used, with daily limits similar to those for cash machines. Credit cards and accounts receiving social benefits will not be accepted. A National Self-Exclusion Register is also created, to which close relatives can add a person.

The law sets heavy fines, 50% higher when minors are involved, and amends the Criminal Code to punish unlicensed gambling operations with three to eight years in prison. Judges will be able to order illegal sites to be blocked, and the Central Bank must prevent banks and wallets from processing payments to clandestine platforms.

The Catholic Church, which had called for the law's approval after Pope Leo XIV's recent visit, welcomed the decision. The Bishops' Commission for Social Pastoral Care received it with “deep gratitude” in a statement entitled “A step towards caring for our youth”.

World.title: US Air Force cloud platform hacked, Reuters reports
World.content:
US Air Force cloud platform hacked, Reuters reports

27th Friday, November 2026 - 17:06 UTC Full article

US Air Force

Cloud One, the US Air Force's cloud computing platform, suffered a computer intrusion that threatens the security of sensitive tactical, logistical and personnel data, three sources familiar with the incident told Reuters on Friday. It is the latest in a series of security breaches at US federal bodies.

Cloud One, the US Air Force's cloud computing platform, suffered a computer intrusion that threatens the security of sensitive tactical, logistical and personnel data, three sources familiar with the incident told Reuters on Friday. It is the latest in a series of security breaches at US federal bodies.

According to two of the sources, the intrusion was detected a month ago during system upgrade work and forced service interruptions on the platform. So far the attackers have not been identified, and the scope of the intrusion and whether information was stolen remain unknown.

Cloud One, launched in 2017, is one of the US military's largest cloud platforms, according to the sources, and combines resources from four providers: Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet. It supports numerous applications, including those handling personnel, payroll, logistics and maintenance data, the Air Force's cloud-based command and control system, which collects data from air defence radars across North America, and a system that tracks bombs and missiles at more than 200 Air Force installations worldwide. “A breach here is a very serious matter,” one of the sources said.

The Air Force declined to comment on its security, vulnerabilities or the operational status of its networks. “We continuously take prudent measures to protect the Department's information, systems and operational capabilities,” it said.

The revelation comes days after an intrusion was reported in an open-source intelligence analysis network of the CIA and the Office of the Director of National Intelligence, which exposed unclassified information, and following security breaches at the FBI and the Department of Agriculture. It also coincides with a series of failures that authorities attributed to technical causes rather than cyberattacks: the global Microsoft outage on November 12, the nationwide ground stop of all US flights for about four and a half hours on November 13, which the government blamed on outdated telecommunications equipment, and the outage of the National Security Agency's classified internal network on November 17.

World.title: Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time
World.content:
Earth exceeds 2C of warming for seven consecutive days for the first time

27th Friday, November 2026 - 04:35 UTC Full article

The record coincides with the failure of the UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya, which ended on November 22 without a main political agreement

The planet's average temperature exceeded pre-industrial levels by more than 2C for seven consecutive days, something that had never happened before, the Copernicus Climate Change Service, the European Earth observation programme, has confirmed. On Monday, November 23, the largest daily anomaly ever measured was also recorded: 2.25C above the 1850-1900 period.

The 2C threshold was reached on ten days in November — the 3rd, 4th, 13th and from the 18th to the 24th — seven of them consecutively. On November 23, the global average temperature was also 1.34C above the 1991-2020 average. These are not the highest absolute temperatures, which usually occur in July and August, but the largest deviation from normal for this time of year. Until now, 2C had been exceeded on only two days in November 2023 and four in February 2024. The data are preliminary, although Copernicus does not expect changes of more than 0.02C.

Exceeding that threshold for a few days is not the same as breaching the 2015 Paris Agreement, which aims to limit warming to 1.5C and keep it well below 2C, measured as an average over many years. “While this does not mean the long-term 2C threshold set by the Paris Agreement has been exceeded, it is a clear preview of where our climate is heading,” warned Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts. “El Niño is temporary; the underlying warming caused by greenhouse gas emissions will persist unless we reduce those emissions.”

Copernicus considers it very likely that 2026 will end as the second-warmest year on record, with a 20% chance of equalling or surpassing 2024, and expects it to be the second calendar year in which warming exceeds 1.5C. Its director, Carlo Buontempo, has warned that there is a fairly high chance of at least one year exceeding 2C before 2030.

The record coincides with the failure of the UN COP31 climate summit in the Turkish city of Antalya, which ended on November 22 without a main political agreement after several oil-producing countries refused to allow the final text to mention fossil fuels, the main cause of global warming.

World.title: New podcast episode: Is there such a thing as the ‘real Mexico’?
World.content:
What, exactly, is the “real Mexico”? That was the question I posed in a recent article, exploring why so many foreigners seem to want to point out that places they seem to think do not fall into the “real Mexico” category. To many of them, the most beautiful places — stunning beach towns, the colonial mountain Pueblo Mágicos, or the great neighborhoods of Mexico City — for some reason, aren’t the “real Mexico” in their minds.

I took issue with that sentiment in this recent article:

And in this week’s episode of MND’s “Confidently Wrong” podcast, George and I debate and discuss this whole concept of the “real Mexico” and what it means.

What do you think is the real Mexico? And is that even a concept that makes sense in such a diverse country?

World.title: Are you a tourist or a traveler? A perspective from our CEO
World.content:
A few weeks ago I took one of the more epic trips of my life, in the southern Mexican state of Oaxaca on the Camino Copalita trail. I had first heard of it from a Mexican friend who has done adventure travel around the world. “Camino Copalita is the best one, you have to do it!” she told my wife and I. We ourselves are not big adventure travelers, but we love nature and walking. This seemed to have plenty of both, so we went for it.

This was no ordinary vacation. To begin with, the website has a decidedly “non-touristy” vibe and very matter-of-factly outlines the basics of the trip. The schedule for days one through four described lots of walking starting at high altitude. Then on day five, we would be rafting down a river until reaching the ocean. Sounded pretty cool, and more importantly, sounded mostly downhill. Before we could sign up, the pre-trip process required a phone interview to make sure we knew what we were getting into and to ensure our physical health was good enough. I was able to quickly convince my wife to join (we had done the four-day Inca Trail together years ago and loved it), as well as three of my best friends, telling them this would be a trip of a lifetime. We apparently passed the phone interview with flying colors, were given the green light, and signed up for the walk.

I wasn’t sure it would actually be the trip of a lifetime. But I knew Oaxaca well, and in hearing how our friend had described the trip, I had a sense that it would be something very special. My wife and I spent a few months lightly training for the trip, as we would be starting at 11,600 feet of altitude and covering 100 kilometers over five days. That is not extreme, but it did require some preparation to make sure that pain or discomfort didn’t get in the way of enjoying things. The other thing (at least I) had to prepare for was the warning that there would be zero internet for the entire five days. Whoa!

How does one “train” for no internet access in today’s modern world? I have always been a bit more connected than I should be. In all honesty, buying an online news platform isn’t exactly good for your daily amount of screen time. In fact, I have gotten more and more connected over the past few years — nearly constantly checking our website, social media channels, YouTube channel and dozens of other news sites and channels. I tried to think of when I had last been totally “disconnected” for a full day. I couldn’t think of even one going back for more than a decade. How in the hell was I going to survive for five-plus days!?

As I told the MND leadership team that we would be out of contact for the week, I began to feel the anxiety creeping up inside of me. I felt like I was abandoning the business — abandoning my team. I had zero doubt that they would do absolutely fine (and likely enjoy my absence!), but it still wasn’t easy to get my head around being out of contact for so long. I began to have nightmares about what would happen if our site went down. I began to wonder what breaking news headlines I would miss, what the stock market would do, and how the Mexican peso-US dollar exchange rate might change in my absence.

But the time soon came for us to head to Oaxaca. That first morning, over breakfast at a small restaurant in Oaxaca City, our newly formed group of 14 hikers (both Mexican and foreign, young and old) was told: “Remember that on this trip, you will be travelers, not tourists.”

Consider for a moment the profound differences and implications that come with each of those words. I believe that modern society, myself very much included, has forgotten about the distinction. In fact, at the start of our trip, the difference didn’t mean much to me. But by the end of the journey, it had become a profoundly important concept that I find myself still reflecting on.

Think about modern-day tourism and travel. We often come with very high expectations derived from social media posts of places that must be seen, pictures that must be taken and things we must do. In some ways, I miss the days of travel guidebooks, when we would read about something and then have to wait and see what it would really be like in person. Social media now shows us everything in advance, and in perfect HD photos and 4K videos. Airbnb has built a massive business of cultivated, curated experiences that can be purchased in each city so that you don’t miss any of the important things to see or do. Our expectations have increased for everything. We expect fast, deferential service, even in France. We want the food and drinks that we have become accustomed to. We expect ice in our Coca Cola in Germany, Starbucks to taste the same in Japan, English to be spoken by our tour guide in Bali, Uber Eats to be available in Mozambique, and almond milk to be on the menu in Bolivia. And of course, we expect to be asked if we have a nut allergy before each meal.

So imagine, for a moment, a five-day trip in which NONE of those expectations apply:

– Wifi passcode? Um yeah, maybe in a week.

– Electricity? Nope.

– Running water? Nope, unless by “running,” you mean “dumped out of a bowl of river water.”

– Showers? But you just took one a few days ago … That’s what the river is for.

– Drinking water? Over there is the river and/or spring.

– Menu? Food choices? You eat what we eat.

– Cups to drink out of? Maybe on day three. In the meantime, here is a bowl.

– Lunch on today’s hike? Here is a banana if you want to take one.

– Trail mile markers? Elevation updates? … Why?

– Flushing toilets? Um, no.

– What time is it? Who cares?

– English? Maybe Spanish … maybe just the local Indigenous Zapotec language

What quickly became clear on this trip was that the real adventure was that we were not going to be treated like tourists — not for one minute! For those five days, we were mere travelers through the mountains of five rural Oaxacan villages. Villages that were kind enough to allow us to sleep on their land, walk on their trails, drink from their rivers, burn their wood for heat and cooking, and eat the food grown locally that they had prepared for us. They didn’t view us as tourists, and it quickly became clear that acting like one would have been absurd. We walked through 11 ecosystems, through pine forest and mountainous coffee and corn fields. We crossed rivers and passed massive ceiba, mango and palm trees.

For five days, the 14 of us roughed it — and roughed it hard! The first two nights were freezing, the last two nights were hot. There were times when I was really damn hungry. All of our bodies were hurting and aching to some extent. The first two evenings had no showers, two had “bucket showers” (literally a bucket with a bowl to pour water over your head), and for one, the “shower” was a river. We had to use only eco-banos for five days — enough said.

Despite the challenges, no one complained. Not once. About anything. On any “typical tourist” metric, we were living life far below what we were accustomed to, what we longed for, and even likely what most of us expected on this trip. And yet, here we were — totally out of our comfort zones, but in a state of complete bliss. I struggle to find the right word in a world of overused superlatives, but it was a truly magical experience.

I signed up for the trip expecting a great walk in beautiful mountains with my wife and friends. I also signed up to force upon myself a bit of healthy discomfort. We, of course, got that: The mountains were far more beautiful than I expected, the walk was awesome, and in countless ways I was far out of my comfort zone. What I didn’t expect was how calming, renewing, regenerating and truly impactful the experience was. The total disconnection from the chaos and overstimulation of our modern-day society turned out to be much easier (and more healing) than I expected. The fresh, local, organic food was simple yet full of flavor. The sustainable growing practices shared with us were educational. The fact that we created zero garbage over the course of a week was humbling. The warmth and welcoming attitude of each community was heartwarming. And the connection to the natural beauty around us and to my fellow walkers was incredibly powerful.

The trip ended on day five with a rafting trip down the Copalita River. As our boats stopped about a kilometer from the ocean, each of us stepped out and began walking for the final time of the trip. Each of us walked at our own pace, quietly, towards the beach. As we made the final river crossing right at the beach, our group spontaneously formed a circle, held hands, and shouted together “VIVA CAMINO COPALITA!” We began to hug each other, and many of us cried. I was one of them. Why? I still can’t put it into words. It was an exceptionally moving moment. We then walked for one last hour on the beach, our tired and bare feet welcoming the soft sand and warm ocean water. We walked towards the setting sun, to the end of the beach, where we would re-engage with the modern world again.

This trip is not for everyone. In fact, it’s not for most people. It’s not a group therapy trip. It’s not a motivational trip. It’s not meant to be a high-intensity workout trip. It’s not just another destination on a travel bucket list. It’s not a trip that is done for the epic selfies. It’s not a trip done for the bragging rights, as most certainly no one you talk to about it will have done it themselves, or even heard of it, for that matter.

The Camino Copalita isn’t something that you do, but rather a journey that can help you — if you are open to it — check in on yourself and on the life that you are living. It is an experience that, if you allow it to, can have a profound impact on you. As one of our local guides said to me before dinner on the second night, while looking out over the mountains after an exhausting day of hiking: “We have a first-class life here. We have clean air, we have clean water, we have fresh food. What more could we possibly need?”

An interesting perspective indeed as we face a world of ever-increasing consumerism, an epidemic of mental and physical health issues, and general anxiety about what the future of technology might bring.

If the idea of being a traveler appeals to you, and you want to learn more about the Camino Copalita, you can do so here: https://www.caminocopalita.com/.

Travis Bembenek is the CEO of Mexico News Daily and has been living, working or playing in Mexico for nearly 30 years.

World.title: Peso regains some ground after nearing 20 to the dollar in a week of losses
World.content:
After seven consecutive days of decline, the Mexican peso appreciated early on Friday, though trading volume is typically much lower on Black Friday than on a standard business day.

The peso fell to its worst level since April 2015 on Thursday, closing at 19.72 to the U.S. dollar, while depreciating 7.01% during the seven-day losing streak. It has fallen nearly 14% over the past three months and was down 9.54% on the year.

The peso initially climbed 0.64% to 19.57 shortly after opening, but had weakened to 19.657 by 5 p.m.

Banco Base expects the peso to end its losing streak and trade between 19.49 and 19.69 per dollar in a session of reduced liquidity, due to the partial reopening of U.S. capital and bond markets after the Thanksgiving holiday.

Mexico’s currency had not experienced such a prolonged negative stretch since the period from Aug. 31-Sept. 8, 2023, although the depreciation then was less severe (5.07%).

Analysts attribute the losing streak to investors unwinding carry-trade positions and shifting into safe-haven assets.

The carry-trade is a strategy where an investor borrows money at a low interest rate (in this case, the U.S. dollar) and invests it in an asset offering a higher rate of return (the Mexican peso), thus profiting from the interest rate gap.

However, Mexico’s central bank (Banxico) has embraced a policy of monetary easing. And when it cut its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 6.25% in early November just two months after the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its rate from 3.75% to 4%, the interest rate gap narrowed to 225 basis points, a historic low.

At the same time, markets are pricing in potential U.S. Federal Reserve hikes (it is widely expected to raise its rate again at its Dec. 8-9 meeting), expecting the yield cushion that made the peso attractive to narrow even further.

Meanwhile, persistent U.S. inflation, strong U.S. growth and broader risk-off sentiment have boosted demand for the U.S. dollar as a safe haven.

Some strategists expect elevated volatility heading into the Fed’s upcoming policy meeting and see potential for the peso exchange rate to surpass 20 to the dollar before stabilizing or drifting lower toward 18.50 in 2027.

However, headline inflation in Mexico neared 4.0% in the first half of November, which alongside tariff and trade uncertainty, complicates Banxico’s policy path, though it is not expected to lower its rate at its Dec. 17 meeting.

With reports from Reforma, El Financiero and La Jornada

World.title: Working poverty in Mexico hits its lowest level on record
World.content:
Listen to this article

Working poverty in Mexico fell to its lowest level since the indicator was first measured in 2005, thanks to wage recovery and steady economic growth.

Working poverty — defined as someone whose labor income is too low to buy a basic food basket, as determined by national statistics agency INEGI — decreased to 30.5% in the third quarter, a decline of 1.4 percentage points from the second quarter.

The 30.5% figure bettered the previous record low figure, which came in the first quarter of 2026, when it stood at 30.7%.

In year-on-year comparison, labor poverty — as it is also known — decreased by 3.9 percentage points, its largest drop since the third quarter of 2021, when it fell by 5.3 percentage points as the Mexican economy recovered from the COVID-19 pandemic.

Higher labor incomes supplied by a strong third-quarter economic performance helped improve working poverty, following a spike recorded in the second quarter.

In addition to the recovery of the Gross Domestic Product (GDP) in these two periods, the increase in the minimum wage mandated in January deserves credit for the improvement in INEGI’s Labor Poverty Trend Index (ITLP).

GDP grew 0.9% quarter-over-quarter and 3.3% year-over-year in the third quarter, the largest annual increase since the second quarter of 2023, while the minimum wage has increased by 154% since 2018.

In 2018 the percentage of the population in working poverty was at 40%. It has declined since then except for spikes in 2020 and 2021 during the COVID-19 pandemic.

Still, according to the economic observatory and research group “Mexico, ¿cómo vamos?,” the figures for working poverty indicate that 40.1 million people in Mexico live in households whose labor income is insufficient to purchase the basic food basket.

“It’s not something to celebrate just yet, because 30.5% of people don’t earn enough to eat,” says Rogelio Gómez Hermosillo, executive president of Citizen Action Against Poverty. “It’s good that it’s at the lowest point … but what more can we do?”

INEGI’s ITLP also breaks down the data by rural and urban populations.

While declining from a high of 62.6% in the third quarter of 2013, working poverty among rural residents was at 43.1% in Q3 2026. For urban residents, it was down from a COVID-induced high of 41.8% in Q3 2020 to 26.9% in the most recent report.

With reports from El Economista, Excelsior and La Jornada

World.title: Authorities rescue 4 Bengal tigers behind a former Mazatlán nightclub
World.content:
Authorities in Mazatlán found four Bengal tigers in a gated lot behind a former nightclub this week, marking the latest big-cat seizure in a country where wildlife trafficking persists.

Federal officers also seized four pavorreales (peacocks), five vehicles, a trailer and the property in the Francisco I. Madero neighborhood, an area that includes a zona de tolerancia (red-light district). It’s about six to eight kilometers inland from Mazatlán’s beachfront hotel zone.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by OstokSanctuary (@ostoksanctuary)

The operation began Monday when National Guard members in the state of Sinaloa received a citizen complaint about constant roars. After officers confirmed the roars as well as bird sounds, the area was secured and a federal prosecutor obtained a judicial warrant.

According to reports, the animals went to the Ostok Sanctuary, north of Mazatlán, at the request of the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa). Ostok used to have another site near Culiacán, the capital of Sinaloa, but it shut down last year and its roughly 700 animals were relocated because of nearby cartel violence.

This week’s transfer occurred Tuesday after the sanctuary’s team sedated the tigers: a white cub about 5 months old, a yellow cub about 7 months old and an adult pair.

All the animals were reportedly in good health.

Ostok Sanctuary President Ernesto Zazueta said the animals were found in “a place that they apparently used for experiments with animals or some kind of handling, because there was a wall full of photographs,” the news source EFE reported.

Prosecutors are investigating a possible crime against biodiversity, the newspaper El Debate Sinaloa reported. No reports mention arrests, and the tigers’ legal fate is undecided.

It was not Sinaloa’s first such case. In April 2025, Ostok rescued two Bengal tigers, a white tigress and a yellow tiger from an abandoned lot in the Golden Triangle, a mountainous region known for organized crime.

Wildlife trafficking is ‘out of control’ in Mexico

Throughout the country, animal trafficking remains widespread. A 2022 Center for Biological Diversity study concluded that “Wildlife trafficking in Mexico is out of control.”

Seizures include not only Bengal tigers, but many other animals, as well. Just this week, Profepa reported rescuing 70 turtles and a chameleon being moved illegally in Chihuahua state, 88.9 Noticias reported.

In Tlaxcala state, Profepa reported that police seized six wild birds and arrested two people for illegal possession of wildlife at a livestock market. The birds were two yellow-headed parrots, whose sale is prohibited, and four American kestrels; the vendors did not have documents proving the birds’ legal origin.

Profepa reported 1,119 Facebook and Instagram posts for possible illegal wildlife sales from May 2025 to June 2026, the agency said in a news release.

Titled “Profepa strengthens actions to detect and combat the illegal sale of wildlife on social media,” the release noted that Profepa worked with Meta — the platforms’ parent company — and that 640 of the posts, or 57%, were removed or resolved.

With reports from Ríodoce, El Debate Sinaloa and EFE

World.title: It’s confirmed: Gas stations and toll booths across Mexico will stop accepting cash
World.content:
As expected, the Finance Ministry (SHCP) has determined that gas stations and toll booths are the first segments of the economy that will be restricted to only accepting electronic payments.

The new Digital Economy Law required the SHCP to identify priority areas in which the use of cash would be eliminated, and it selected the two sectors that were already conducting pilot programs.

An SHCP directive published Friday defined the “strategic sectors” (hydrocarbons and infrastructure) and outlined the respective activities subject to the Digital Economy Law — sale to the public of gasoline and diesel, and collection of tolls.

The date that the new requirements will go into effect has yet to be announced. The publication of this order in the government’s Official Gazette gives these strategic sectors 15 business days to establish “the conditions, requirements, obligations and operations” for the receipt of digital and electronic means of payment.

According to the SHCP, digital and electronic means of payment are understood to be: QR codes and NFC devices; debit and credit cards; fund transfer orders (including direct debit); and any device, card or interface that allows the making of payments and transfers of resources.

The SHCP statement says the decision to declare gas stations a strategic sector is designed to discourage tax evasion and “tax-related fuel theft,” and close existing loopholes regarding the illegal sale of fuel.

The statement explains that handling cash makes it difficult to trace the true origin of fuel sold at retail. Electronic payments, on the other hand, leave a traceable footprint.

The government also believes that eliminating cash at public service stations can reduce the risks and costs associated with handling cash for the stations and station attendants.

With regard to toll booths, the SHCP said the transition to a digital economy will eliminate “operational frictions that translate into longer waiting times, traffic congestion and limitations in the capacity to process traffic flows, while also reducing crossing times and improving the efficiency of public transport service.”

For example, the SHCP cited a study that found that the average wait time at toll booths to enter Mexico City is nearly 15 minutes, a delay that would be reduced to 2.40 minutes by paying electronically.

With reports from El Economista, Informador and Forbes México

World.title: Sheinbaum to press US on SpaceX launches after Starship debris hits Tamaulipas beaches
World.content:
President Claudia Sheinbaum announced Thursday during her daily morning press conference that her administration intends to discuss with the United States the frequency of Elon Musk’s SpaceX launches from Texas, following complaints of their debris reaching the coasts of Tamaulipas.

The president said takeoffs from Starship, one of the company’s bases near the border with Tamaulipas, require the use of a portion of Mexican airspace, which needs clearance from the country’s aeronautical authority.

El 8 de octubre denunciamos a SpaceX por los daños ambientales que sus lanzamientos provocan en las costas de Tamaulipas. PROFEPA ya dio trámite a nuestra denuncia: exigimos que se investigue el impacto de estos residuos en el mar, la fauna y la pesca, ¡que SpaceX responda por los daños! — Jorge Álvarez Máynez (@AlvarezMaynez) November 27, 2026

Therefore, she said, Mexican authorities are looking for a diplomatic meeting between the aerospace authorities of both countries to “establish permission for the use of Mexican airspace including the frequency of such use, and, if necessary, to discuss the potential relocation of the launch site.”

Sheinbaum noted that, for now, the number of launches is low. However, she cited a future goal of up to 400 flights per year, which would necessitate determining the frequency with which Mexico might grant permits.

According to Sheinbaum, such an increase could affect air traffic due to the restrictions applied during each takeoff.

“What would this imply for Mexican airspace?,” she said.

Sheinbaum said that a meeting with the U.S. Embassy has already taken place, and clarified that these matters should be addressed with the U.S. government rather than with SpaceX, as the latter is a private company whose operations affect national airspace.

Sheinbaum clarified that the negotiations with the U.S. government are independent of the investigations into the waste on Mexico’s Gulf Coast, and that the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa) will determine any potential liability on the part of the company.

Meanwhile, SpaceX said last week that external partners indicated the small amount of debris discovered along the Tamaulipas shoreline is not directly linked to the company’s aerospace activities.

Regarding images that have circulated on social media showing suspected space debris on the coast of Tamaulipas, SpaceX said that most of the posts are “intentionally misleading.” It also added that independent tests conducted on the materials within Starship and the Super Heavy booster confirm that they “do not pose any chemical, biological, or toxicological risks.”

With reports from The Associated Press and El Financiero

World.title: A bitter indulgence: The reality of Mexico City’s street-cart potato chip vendors
World.content:
It’s a cloudy day, and sales have been very slow.

Elvia knows that with weather like this, it will be difficult to end her shift on a high note. At 32, she’s spent the last three years selling potato chips from a pushcart, a classic Mexico City street treat.

Although her stall sits on a bustling sidewalk along Parque México, in the heart of the capital’s affluent Condesa neighborhood, there hasn’t been much activity since lunchtime.

Competition is tough, particularly in tourist areas, where artisans, ice cream sellers, musicians and other street vendors all vie for relatively meager wages.

“It’s not like this in the summer,” Elvia says. “When it’s hot, people seem more inclined to buy potato chips.”

Elvia comes from a family of potato-chip street vendors — a trade that gained popularity in Mexico City during the 1940s and ’50s, and has since spread to the rest of the country.

An affordable indulgence

A “Mexicanized” take on U.S.-style French fries, this version consists of deep-fried julienned potatoes topped with a variety of hot sauces, chamoy, a sort of pickled pork skin known as cueritos and — for a more refined palate — bone marrow.

Three potato types are commonly used: Alpha, Atlantic and Fianna. Varieties like Atlantic and Fianna contain higher starch and less water, allowing them to crisp and brown properly when fried.

The potatoes are prepared using a double-frying method, which makes them crunchy on the outside and soft on the inside. As a result, they don’t taste like your average, mass-produced potato chips.

In addition to the traditional salt flavor, potato chips are also commonly found marinated, jalapeño-flavored or in mixed assortments. Generally, people order them with hot sauce, lime and salt.

Since street-cart potato chips and other classic fried snacks are so readily available, they punctuate many people’s childhood memories. You can easily find them outside subway stations, hospitals, parks, schools and government offices — essentially, anywhere with a high volume of foot traffic.

A complicated arrangement

At Mexico City’s Central de Abasto — where both small- and large-scale merchants purchase supplies for many businesses in Mexico City’s informal economy — potatoes start at just 12 pesos per kilogram, according to the Central de Abasto Price Monitor, which fluctuates daily.

On average, 1 kilogram yields 12 medium-sized bags. In Mexico City, small bags generally cost between 10 and 20 pesos, while large ones can go up to 50 pesos.

Taken at face value, owning a cart that sells potato chips (or other classic fried snacks found in Mexico City) can be a great business.

The profit, however, does not go to vendors like Elvia.

“The cart isn’t mine,” Elvia tells me. “It belongs to the man I work for.”

Unlike other vendors, she doesn’t have to purchase the supplies from Central de Abasto. They come with the cart, which Elvia rents and retrieves from a storage area every day.

This arrangement means vendors have to pay a percentage of sales to their employers. In Elvia’s case, she only keeps 25% of what she makes during an eight-hour workday.

When her shift ends, she’s not allowed to continue working. She must return the cart to the storage area until the next day, when she’ll retrieve it once again and bring it to the new location assigned to her.

In addition to the rental and supply fees, many street vendors face the daily burden of paying “piso,” “protection money” police officers and others demand in exchange for being allowed to work.

Elvia is one of the lucky ones. She hasn’t had to pay piso to operate. But given its nature, other potato vendors understandably did not want to grant us an interview.

One woman simply dismissed me, saying, “I’d rather not — customers keep coming, and we have to attend to them.” A logical explanation, of course. But her tone betrayed something more guarded, an impulse to protect herself.

A profession with a long tradition (and little legal protection)

When asked if she has an official permit, Elvia shrugged: “My boss handles that.”

In reality, street vendors in Mexico City are required to obtain a “Permit to Engage in Commerce on Public Thoroughfares” from the relevant borough authority.

The Mexico City government promoted these permits to regulate the industry and protect its employees, who are rarely covered by the law or supported by their employers.

However, vendors like Elvia don’t deal with the paperwork. That’s left to the person who assigns them the spots where they will operate for the day.

Elvia is not the only one facing this lack of state protection. Street vendors — selling fruit, aguas frescas, tamales and bread from baskets — work every day with few safeguards. Similarly, the capital’s other endemic trades contend with few labor protections, and some have even organized to demand greater protections from the state.

Elvia, however, has little faith that an advocacy group will organize on her behalf.

Since there is no union for street vendors in Mexico, “I can only rely on my family,” Elvia says. “My nieces and cousins also do this kind of work.”

For now, she’ll simply have to continue renting her cart, doling out the majority of her profits and hoping she’s never required to pay piso.

“It’s the only thing we have left,” Elvia says. “This is the only way we earn a living.”

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: South Africans to Spend Record US$18.8bn
World.content:
A record headline figure hides households that are cutting travel, barbecues and gifts to cover food and fuel.

South Africa: Consumers

South African households plan to spend a record R326 billion, in South African rand (about US$18.8 billion at about R17.37 to the dollar), this December, according to a survey released in late November 2026 by Wonga, a South African short-term lender. The average planned spend is R7,658 per person (about US$441), up 21% on last year.

Yet the same poll finds that nearly half of respondents feel financially worse off than a year ago. They rated the year 3.7 out of 10, the lowest score since 2020, when Covid hit.

Key Facts Who. Wonga, a South African short-term lender, polled more than 8,000 South African consumers.

What. Planned December spending hits a record R326 billion (about US$18.8 billion), a survey projection.

Where. South Africa, nationwide, with households cutting travel and gifts.

As of. 28 November 2026, 12:30 GMT.

A record headline figure hides households that are cutting travel, barbecues and gifts to cover food and fuel.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

Wonga’s ninth annual Summer Spending Survey covers more than 8,000 South African consumers across the country. Its previous edition, published on 8 December 2025 with just over 10,000 respondents, projected R289 billion (about US$16.6 billion at today’s rate) and an average of R6,299 (about US$363 at today’s rate).

The new total is therefore about 13% above last year’s projection, although both are one lender’s estimates rather than official statistics. Wonga polled fewer people this year than last, so the two totals are not like for like.

Food and drink take the biggest share, at an average of R3,225 per person (about US$186), according to the survey. Local travel and transport follow at R1,562 (about US$90), and for the first time they beat gifts at R1,465 (about US$84).

Fewer people are buying presents, as the share buying gifts for friends and family fell by 2 percentage points and 13% now buy gifts for nobody, up from 8%. Cash is the most wanted gift at 43%, and cash plus vouchers reach 78%, the highest since the survey began in 2018.

Only 23% plan to travel, down 4 points, and 53% will not travel at all because of cost. That includes 49% of those earning more than R50,000 a month (about US$2,880), who cite petrol and flight prices.

A braai, the South African barbecue, will be hosted by 39% of respondents, against an average of 49% in earlier years. Bryan Smith, Wonga’s spokesperson, suggested that higher meat and poultry prices play a part.

“Despite spending more, people are getting less,” Smith said. “People aren’t cancelling the festive season, but they are taking control of their spending by cutting back on luxuries, travel and additional spending to afford the basics.”

Some 28% plan to dip into savings, up 4 points, and 30% plan to use buy now, pay later services. Neil Roets, chief executive of Debt Rescue, a South African debt-counselling firm, warned against using emergency savings for festive spending.

“Higher expenditure should not be mistaken for economic optimism,” Roets said in a comment on the survey in November 2026. “When essential living costs absorb an increasing proportion of household income, even a modest festive celebration can require a considerably larger financial commitment than in previous years.”

Both voices point the same way: more money going out, less comfort at home. Our South Africa pages follow how households and shops cope.

Fuel Prices Squeeze Household Budgets

Official price data show where the pressure comes from. Statistics South Africa (Stats SA), the national statistics office, reported on Wednesday 18 November 2026 that consumer inflation rose to 5.2% in October from 4.5% in September, the highest since May 2024.

Annual fuel inflation reached 42.9% in October, against 27.9% in September and the highest since August 2022 (43.2%). An inland litre of 95-octane petrol cost R30.251 (about US$1.74) and diesel R35.622 (about US$2.05) that month.

Transport inflation of 15.2% contributed 2.1 percentage points to the 5.2% headline rate. Food and non-alcoholic drink inflation was only 1.4%, held down by cereals at minus 2.0% and meat at 0.2%.

File photo, 2015: a Shoprite supermarket on a street in Zeerust, a town in North West province. (Photo: South African Tourism, CC BY 2.0)

The Central Bank Pauses, With a Hike Possible

On Thursday 19 November 2026 the South African Reserve Bank, the central bank, held its repo rate, its key lending rate, at 7.25%, with the prime lending rate, which banks charge their best customers, at 10.75%. Four members of its Monetary Policy Committee, the panel that sets rates, preferred no change, while three favoured a 25 basis point (0.25 point) increase.

“After two policy adjustments this year, and with a moderately restrictive policy stance, we decided to pause for now,” Governor Lesetja Kganyago said. “We are mindful of risks, and will not hesitate to raise rates if needed, to return inflation to target over the policy horizon.”

Kganyago also said readings above 5% are expected to persist into early next year, and he voiced concern about the El Niño weather pattern, which can bring drought, and food prices. Stats SA is due to publish November inflation in mid-December, and the central bank’s next rate decision falls on Thursday 28 January 2027.

What Prediction Markets Say On Polymarket, a real-money prediction market, traders give a 25 basis point rate rise at the Reserve Bank’s January 2027 decision 54.5%, no change 31.0% and a 25 basis point cut 9.6%. About US$34,340 had been traded on the market by 7:52 a.m. ET on 28 November 2026, and these prices are bets, not polls or forecasts by the bank. Why we show this: prediction markets turn real-money bets into a live probability that moves within minutes of the news, which is why investors, campaigns and newsrooms in the United States now follow them closely. We show them next to polls and official results, never instead of them.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does record spending mean South Africans are confident?

Not according to the people surveyed or the debt counsellor quoted. Both describe households stretching budgets to cover essentials.

How reliable is the spending total?

It is a lender’s projection from a sample of respondents, not an official count or a sales figure. Read it as a guide to mood and intentions, not as a forecast of retail sales.

What happens next for interest rates?

The next signals are the November inflation figures from Statistics South Africa in mid-December and the central bank’s decision in late January. Both will show whether pressure on prices is easing.

World.title: Somali State Says Somaliland Backs Militias
World.content:
The claim is one side's account, with no casualty figures, no named armed groups and no reply yet from Somaliland.

Hargeisa, the capital of Somaliland, seen from a hillside in 2024. (Photo: Mheidegger, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons)

Somalia: Sanaag

The government of North Eastern State, a federal member state of Somalia, accused Somaliland of backing armed clan groups on Friday 27 November 2026. Its Ministry of Interior, Federal Affairs and Reconciliation said attacks by the militias originated in the Shidan area of Sanaag region, in northern Somalia.

Somaliland, the self-declared republic in northern Somalia that the Somali government does not recognise as a state, and which claims parts of Sanaag, had not publicly responded when the statement was reported on Saturday 28 November 2026 from Las Anod, the state’s seat. The allegation has not been independently verified.

Key Facts Who. North Eastern State, a Somali federal member state, accuses Somaliland, which claims parts of Sanaag.

What. Interior ministry says Somaliland-backed clan militias launched attacks from the Shidan area.

Where. Shidan, Sanaag region, northern Somalia. The state’s seat is Las Anod.

As of. 28 November 2026, 12:30 GMT.

The claim is one side’s account, with no casualty figures, no named armed groups and no reply yet from Somaliland.

The ministry’s statement, issued on Friday, said such actions “jeopardize peace, stability and the peaceful coexistence of the local community”. It urged Somaliland authorities to stop what it called interference and hostile activities against local communities immediately and unconditionally.

The ministry also warned against escalation that could force residents to flee. It said it would not tolerate attacks, outside interference or actions that threaten the safety of residents.

File photo, 27 November 2022: the seaport of Mogadishu, Somalia’s capital and its main gateway for imported goods. (Photo: African Union Transition Mission in Somalia, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons)

The statement gives no number of casualties and does not name the armed groups. It also does not say how far Somaliland’s alleged support goes.

North Eastern State was formed in late July 2025 from SSC-Khatumo, the interim regional administration that preceded it, according to the EU Agency for Asylum (EUAA), the European Union’s asylum agency. The EUAA traces the origin to protests in Las Anod in late 2022, followed by armed conflict between Somaliland forces and the newly formed SSC-Khatumo forces from February 2023.

In August 2023, the EUAA says, SSC-Khatumo consolidated control of Las Anod after Somaliland troops withdrew. Somaliland and North Eastern State still hold competing territorial claims in parts of northern Somalia.

The EUAA also reports that on 31 October 2025 fighting erupted in the Boocame area after forces of Puntland, a Somali federal member state in the north-east, allegedly attacked forces loyal to the new North Eastern State administration. Several people were reportedly injured.

In February 2026 the state’s administration accused Somaliland forces of attacking civilians in Waqdariya, in Lasqoray district of Sanaag. It alleged deaths and injuries but gave no official casualty figure.

In May 2026 Somaliland’s Interior Minister, Abdalle Mohamed Arab, known as Sandheere, called for an immediate end to deadly inter-clan fighting in the Erigavo area of Sanaag. Local reports at the time spoke of dozens of dead, with the cause given as disputes over grazing land and long-standing clan tensions.

Sanaag is contested, with Somaliland and the federal North Eastern State both claiming territory. The statement as reported does not say who controls Shidan.

No next step has been announced by either side. Our coverage of Somaliland politics and Somaliland rights issues follows any reply.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is North Eastern State?

It is a federal member state of Somalia, seated in Las Anod. It grew out of the SSC-Khatumo interim administration.

Has Somaliland answered the claim?

Not publicly, at the time the statement was reported on Saturday. Its authorities have not addressed the allegation.

Is the claim confirmed?

No. It is the ministry’s account, and it could not be independently verified.

World.title: Gambia Stops 203 Migrants, 92 Senegalese
World.content:
Senegalese made up just over half of those stopped in the immigration department’s count for 1 October to 2 November, which puts the new figure in context.

Painted fishing pirogues on the beach at Tanji, on The Gambia's Atlantic coast, in an earlier year. Photo: tjabeljan / Wikimedia Commons (CC BY 2.0)

Migration: Gambia and Senegal

Security forces in The Gambia intercepted 203 people preparing to leave the country irregularly on Friday 27 November 2026, according to a count published by a Senegalese news site on Saturday 28 November. They were stopped in Sotokoi and Faraba Sutu, two villages in the West Coast Region, on The Gambia’s Atlantic coast.

Earlier, on Saturday 14 November 2026, the GID and Spain’s national police intercepted 215 people in Banjul, Brufut, Ghana Town, Tujereng, Gunjur and Sareh Pateh. Senegalese and West African news sites relayed the GID figures: 154 Senegalese, 50 Gambians, 5 Malians, 5 Guineans and 1 from Guinea-Bissau, with two suspects arrested.

The GID published wider statistics on Tuesday 10 November 2026, as relayed by Senegalese news sites. Between 1 October and 2 November it carried out 45 operations and intercepted 1,786 migrants.

Senegalese were the largest group in that count, with 914 people or 51.2%, ahead of 740 Gambians (41.4%), 68 Guineans (3.8%), 36 Malians (2%) and 28 others (1.6%). More than 40 people suspected of smuggling were arrested in the same period.

All counts here are GID figures as relayed by Senegalese news sites. Gambia votes in its presidential election on Saturday 5 December 2026, according to the country’s Independent Electoral Commission.

Several points remain open: the GID has not published whether the 92 Senegalese will be returned to Senegal. It has also not said what happens to the others after processing.

Who ran the operation?

The Gambia Immigration Department led it with other local security units. Spain’s national police supported the work.

What happens to the people who were stopped?

They were taken to the Tanji migration centre for identification and processing. What comes next has not been published.

Is the count confirmed?

No second report was found. The count should be read as reported, not confirmed.

World.title: Uganda Truck Plunge Kills at Least 10
World.content:
A truck carrying cassava flour and passengers plunged off a narrow bridge in northern Uganda, and the Prime Minister has ordered a new crossing prioritised without giving a start date.

Photo: Jozef020, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0, taken 27 July 2018.

Road Safety: Uganda

A truck plunged off Nyagak Bridge into the River Nyagak in Zombo District, northern Uganda, on Thursday 26 November 2026, and the Uganda Police Force confirmed ten people dead. A later police update, reported on 28 November, raised the toll to 11 after an injured woman died in hospital.

The truck had left a market in northern Uganda on Wednesday 25 November, the police flash report said, and was carrying cassava flour and passengers when it fell. A Member of Parliament told the legislature on the same day that the narrow bridge puts road users at risk.

Key Facts Who. Passengers on a truck carrying cassava flour; the driver is among the dead.

What. A truck plunged off Nyagak Bridge in Zombo District; brake failure is the preliminary cause.

Toll. Ten confirmed dead on 26 November; a later update says 11.

As of. 28 November 2026, 12:50 GMT.

Africa Intelligence One email, every weekday morning. African markets, politics and business — filed from our newsroom in Rio. Yesterday’s subject line: “Congo halts cobalt, the metal in your battery” Get the brief

A truck carrying cassava flour and passengers plunged off a narrow bridge in northern Uganda, and the Prime Minister has ordered a new crossing prioritised without giving a start date.

Senior Superintendent of Police Josephine Angucia, the Uganda Police Force spokesperson for West Nile, the north-western region of Uganda, signed the police flash report of 26 November, which said the driver reportedly lost control. In later updates she said preliminary investigations pointed to brake failure.

Free daily brief — no card needed Get every Africa story in one morning email We build you a personalized brief around the topics you follow — free for 7 days. Love it? Your first month after that is US$1. Start my free brief Yes, email me my free daily brief — I can unsubscribe any time.

Angucia urged owners of commercial vehicles and drivers to service their vehicles, particularly the braking systems, before putting them on the road. Police said the driver is among the dead.

Grace Freedom Kwiocwiny, a Member of Parliament for Ora County, a constituency in Zombo, blamed the bridge itself. In a sitting of Parliament on Thursday 26 November she said she had told the Minister of Works and Transport in September to deal with bridge conditions along the Goli-Paidha-Zombo-Zeu road, a route in West Nile, before prioritising road construction.

She said the bridge’s narrow structure endangers road users, and she asked when government would start building a new one. Prime Minister Robinah Nabbanja directed the Minister of Works and Transport to prioritise the bridge and said in Parliament: “The Minister of Works has to work on that bridge so that our people can cross when they are safe.”

Nabbanja did not say when construction would begin. She said she would engage Kwiocwiny on the actual number of dead and on support for affected families.

The Toll Rose from Ten to 11

Zombo District traffic officer Simon Peter Komaketch confirmed the deaths, and police put the toll at ten on Thursday 26 November. Four people were seriously injured, two men and two women.

Angucia later confirmed that one of the injured, a woman of about 40, died in hospital on the evening of Thursday 26 November. That left three survivors, according to the police update reported on 28 November.

Divers resumed the search on Friday morning 27 November for people believed trapped in the river. They said they lacked supplies, including food, and appealed for help.

A relative of the missing said one relative and a baby were still unaccounted for. Officials have not stated how many people are missing.

Rio Times membership Read everything we publish for US$1 in the first month. Then US$8.99 a month. Cancel anytime. Start for US$1

The victims are not named here, out of respect for their families. Police have not said when a fuller report will follow.

File photo of the River Nile at Karuma in northern Uganda.

A Worsening National Record

The Uganda Police annual crime report 2025, presented on Monday 30 March 2026 by Lawrence Nuwabiine, the Traffic Police director, counted 26,044 road crashes in 2025, up 3.7% from 25,107 in 2024. It also recorded 4,602 fatal crashes.

The same report put road deaths at 5,383 in 2025, up 4.7% from 5,144 in 2024. By our calculation, that is about 15 deaths a day.

The river has drawn attention before: on Monday 23 February 2026 a taxi plunged into the River Nyagak in Zombo’s Abanga sub-county, and the Resident District Commissioner, the government’s local representative, said the driver lost control because of brake failure. At least seven people were missing and eight severely injured at the time.

A prime ministerial direction is a political instruction, not a funded contract, so the first real sign of action would be an announcement from the Works ministry. Until one comes, the brake-failure finding stays preliminary and the bridge stays as it is.

The immediate consequences are local: the families of the dead, the traders who use the Goli-Paidha-Zombo-Zeu road and the drivers who cross the Nyagak. No date has been announced for Nabbanja’s talks with Kwiocwiny or for any work on a new bridge.

Frequently Asked Questions

What caused the crash?

World.title: Sudan Fighting Pushes Families Over Border
World.content:
Local groups are counting new arrivals in Blue Nile, North Kordofan and South Sudan faster than UN tables can. Key claims about who holds the ground remain unverified.

Conflict: Sudan

Thousands of civilians fled fresh fighting in Sudan’s Blue Nile and Kordofan regions this week, local groups said on Friday 27 November 2026. They are heading for Ed Damazin, the Blue Nile state capital, and El Obeid, capital of North Kordofan, inside Sudan and, across the border, for South Sudan’s Upper Nile state.

The Sudanese army and the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), a paramilitary group, have fought each other since April 2023. The UN migration agency has counted only part of this wave, in West Kordofan, so local groups are the first to put numbers on Blue Nile and Renk.

What. Fighting in Blue Nile and Kordofan pushes families toward Ed Damazin, El Obeid and South Sudan.

Numbers. Sudan had 8,594,507 internally displaced people in October, 26% below the January 2025 peak.
