World.title: No need to hear from former PMs, says Senate president
World.content:
Opposition Senator Lambert Brown arguing in the Upper House on Friday for his fellow senators to accept an offer by former prime ministers Bruce Golding and PJ Patterson to mediate between both sides for a return of civility to the House of Representatives. Photo: Garfield Robinson

SENATE President Tom Tavares-Finson on Friday declared that he does not need to hear from former prime ministers Bruce Golding and PJ Patterson regarding the mediation role both men offered to play in a bid to bring civility back to the nation’s Parliament.

Tavares-Finson made the comment in a back-and-fourth argument with Opposition Senator Lambert Brown, who had appealed to his fellow senators to accept the offer while making his contribution to the debate on an amendment to the Financial Administration and Audit Act to suspend the fiscal rules for another year until March 31, 2028.

The amendment is being sought by the Government to create breathing room to continue recovery after the economic fallout caused by Hurricane Melissa, which hit sections of Jamaica on October 28, 2025.

There was bipartisan support for the suspension but Brown’s call was met with derision by Government senators. As far as Tavares-Finson is concerned, Opposition Leader Mark Golding’s lack of leadership is to be blamed for the breakdown of civility in the House of Representatives, and he alone needs to take action.

The former heads of government offered to intervene, if asked, after Jamaicans were left wondering if members of the governing Jamaica Labour Party (JLP), which Golding led, and the Opposition People’s National Party (PNP), which Patterson led, actually hate each other.

This, after the November 3 sitting of the House of Representatives descended into chaos when Opposition Member of Parliament Mikael Phillips got into a heated argument with Government member Desmond McKenzie. Phillips has since apologised for using an expletive during the argument and has been referred to Parliament’s Privileges Committee. He accused McKenzie of making a derogatory remark about his deceased mother, but McKenzie has denied doing so.

The dispute had spilled over from a heated debate on a censure motion brought by the Opposition against the Government over its abstention on a United Nations vote to lift the United States’s decades-old economic embargo on Cuba.

The Opposition’s complaint about Speaker Juliet Holness’s management of the sitting had also contributed to the uproar.

On Friday Brown, a firebrand senator who is often at odds with his Government counterparts, urged senators to accept the Patterson/Golding offer. He argued that fiscal discipline cannot be separated from the “discipline of decency”.

“I crave your indulgence, Mr President, to say, based on the privilege of my age and the benefit of hindsight, to make an appeal to all parliamentarians, all 84 of us. And it’s an appeal that starts by saying, ‘Let us heed the call of the two former prime ministers — PJ Patterson and Bruce Golding’.

“We need to have a reset in how we relate to each other in the Parliament. The other place [House of Representatives] in the public eye has descended from the decorum that the country desires of it,” Brown said.

“I’m not blaming he, she, or the old lady, I’m just simply saying at my age, my experience, with hindsight, we need to check ourselves,” he added.

An apparently impatient Tavares-Finson interrupted Brown, telling him, “I agree with you, enuh,” but quickly added, “Neither Mr Golding nor Mr Patterson can come here and tell me how to behave. The leaders of both parties know what to do and they’re not doing it.

“If you understand what I’m saying, none of those past prime ministers are in any position to tell the leader of the Opposition or the prime minister how to behave. The whole Jamaica see what the problem is and the leader [of the Opposition] is not addressing it,” Tavares-Finson added.

Brown attempted to continue but Tavares-Finson responded to what he determined was an offensive, off-microphone comment by Opposition Senator Cleveland Tomlinson directed at the Speaker of the House of Representatives.

“I hear that comment coming from you enuh Mr Tomlinson and it’s out a order enuh — mi a tell yuh dat enuh,” Tavares-Finson scolded Tomlinson.

Brown continued: “President, you and I have been around long enough to know that the course that we’re on as parliamentarians leads to one destination, and that destination is called regret. And as someone who has been there and seen where it has led to in the past, I’m making an appeal to all of us.”

But at this point Brown was cut off by a now very impatient Tavares-Finson.

“You need to direct your appeal to the leader of the Opposition, that’s where you need to send the appeal to,” he told Brown who hit back with, “Mr President, if you wish to be partisan, I wish to take the national [approach].”

But Tavares-Finson was not finished. “I’m taking the national opinion [into account] — and I really appreciate what you’re saying, enuh — [but] when one of your younger colleagues [Tomlinson] sit down behind you and passing remarks about the Speaker of the House [you said nothing],” the Senate president said, then made a quip about “the voice of Jacob and the hands of Esau” from Genesis 27:22 which describes a moment of deception and conflicting signals.

As a clear sign that tensions between the two political parties will continue to simmer, Tavares-Finson continued in a vein that is not customary for the person presiding in the chamber. He told Brown to “look at the latest outburst on social media from your colleague from Portland. Disgusting! And yuh come here and talking about taking a national approach? Tek a partisan approach an deal wid yuh party first”.

His reference was to comments made by the MP for Portland Eastern Isat Buchanan, which have been widely criticised for being crass, when he referred to a participant in a live chat as having a “stink mouth” while being disparaging to the person’s mother.

Government Senator Abka Fitz-Henley, who spoke immediately after Brown, said, “I find the member who preceded me quite ironic because moments after the member told a colleague to ‘Shut yuh mouth’ quite stridently, he called for a reset in how we relate to each other in the Parliament.

“I find that there’s a dissonance in terms of the Opposition’s posture — they will call for good behaviour while demonstrating the most insolent conduct inside and outside of the Parliament. But, of course, that speaks to a lack of leadership on their side,” Fitz-Henley said.

During crosstalk, while Fitz-Henley made his contribution to the debate, his fellow Government Senator Marlon Morgan was heard saying, “Do not bring the lower House to this dignified upper chamber. Leave the boogu yagga behaviour out by Angela Brown-Burke; don’t bring that boogu yagga behaviour up here.”

Brown was also interrupted twice on a point of order by Government Senator Sherene Golding-Campbell, daughter of former Prime Minister Bruce Golding, who told Brown in the first instance that, “I and other members have been quite patient listening to Senator Brown but …the fact is what he has embarked upon is completely irrelevant to the Bill before us.”

On the second occasion, as Brown continued, Golding-Campbell told him that he was showing indiscipline while calling on his colleagues to exercise discipline.

At the end of the debate Tavares-Finson appeared to mock Brown. “I commend all of the colleagues to pay attention to Senator Brown’s call for decorum in the Parliament,” he said while laughing, finishing afterwards with, “Aahhh bwoy.”

World.title: Bugle, Military Man draw attention to cost of living on new single
World.content:
Bugle

For many Jamaicans, payday has become less about celebrating a hard-earned salary and more about deciding which bills get paid first. Between rent, electricity, water, transportation, and the ever-increasing cost of groceries, making ends meet has become an exercise in financial gymnastics, with many households finding that their money runs out long before the month ends.

It is a familiar struggle that reggae artistes Military Man and Bugle have turned into music, using their collaboration, So Many Bills, to give voice to the financial pressures confronting working people.

Getting strong airplay locally, the track confronts the realities of an economic climate in which even those earning a regular income are finding it increasingly difficult to maintain a comfortable standard of living.

For Military Man, the inspiration was not particularly difficult to find. The everyday responsibility of keeping a household running, he explained, provided the foundation for the song.

“The pressure of the time. Rent, electricity and water were among the expenses weighing on my mind,” he said, describing the circumstances that inspired his writing. He went on to share that from its early emergence as a vehicle for social commentary, to its evolution into a globally celebrated genre, reggae has consistently provided a soundtrack for the struggles, aspirations, and resistance of ordinary people.

The song takes aim at rising prices and the burden they place on people with limited financial resources. Its lyrics include an appeal for the voices of poor people to be heard, reflecting a frustration that has become increasingly difficult to ignore.

For Bugle, the subject is one that extends beyond the recording studio. Through conversations with people who reach out to him for assistance, the artiste said he has encountered individuals who are employed but remain trapped in a ‘hand-to-mouth’ regimen.

Their circumstances, he suggested, speak to a larger problem that requires more than simply encouraging people to find work.

“We definitely need to focus on job creation, because people need work. But the problem goes beyond that. We need to find ways to make the salary match the financial struggles people face,” Bugle said. “People are working, but the money weh them a get at the end of the fortnight, at the end of the week, at the end of the month, it just not make no sense.”

The concerns are especially significant as Jamaica continues to recover from the devastating blows of Hurricane Melissa.

Bugle recalled seeing a woman on TikTok appealing for assistance following the storm. Rather than simply observing her circumstances, he decided to intervene, loading a vehicle with food supplies and personally delivering them to her home. That experience strengthened his call for greater accountability in the distribution of relief assistance, particularly as questions continue to surface about how donated food and other resources are reaching those most in need.

“We want some more accountability where them things is concerned, you know,” he said.

His comments come amid a wider public conversation about the management and allocation of Hurricane Melissa relief resources, including questions raised by fellow musicians about whether assistance is reaching affected Jamaicans. The resulting exchanges between public officials and members of the entertainment fraternity have also renewed discussion about the role of musicians in holding conversations around issues affecting the communities they represent.

So Many Bills was produced by Marvin “Skitta” Reid and is currently available for streaming on all digital platforms.

World.title: McKenzie targets year end handover of first Shrewsbury container homes
World.content:
Technical officer in the Ministry of Local Government and Community Development, Wray Mullings (left); contractor with CS Asphalting, Colin Johnson (second left); Minister of Local Government and Community Development Desmond McKenzie (second right); and executive director of the Social Development Commission Omar Frith examine a building plan. Anthony Lewis

SHREWSBURY, Westmoreland — Local Government Minister Desmond McKenzie is eyeing an end of year target to start getting Westmoreland residents whose homes were destroyed by Hurricane Melissa into container homes being built in Shrewsbury.

“Despite the mischief that is being made about the project, I am well pleased and satisfied about the pace of the project and what the outlook will be at the completion,” stated McKenzie.

“We’ll be working to see if by the end of December, we’ll be able to move the first set of families into these units. And then we will commence in early January the remaining units here [in the second phase],” added McKenzie during a tour of the relocation site on Thursday.

Work commenced in April, and the first 16 one-bedroom and four two-bedroom units are now almost ready under phase one. Another 36 units will be deployed in the complex for the build-out of the remaining community in the second phase.

“It’s a lot of work. They had to put in the lines, the water; they had to clear the lands and all that sort of thing. So, it took some time. But we are here where we are now, and we are far better than where we were in June,” McKenzie said in response to queries from the Jamaica Observer.

The minister noted that while the weather has impacted the timeline of the project, there will be no undue haste to make up the time if it means sacrificing the quality of work being done.

“[If] we rush it and it is not done properly, the same people who have been pressuring us will be the same ones to ask, ‘Where the money deh?’ I want them to see where the money is and how the money is spent. The contractor has been here [and] he has been faithful to the development,” argued McKenzie as he pointed to the measures being taken to provide a quality product.

“What we are putting down is not half-finished units. We are going to be putting in the fencing. The contract for the fence has been signed, and work will commence on that. The remaining units will be delivered next week by the Ministry of Economic Growth,” stated McKenzie.

He explained that in addition to the local government and economic growth ministries they have also partnered with the Ministry of Energy through Jamaica Social Investment Fund (JSIF), which has the responsibility of putting in the lighting system. The minister said JSIF will be putting in place a prepaid metering system and power can be purchased similar to the way in which credit can be supplied for phones.

“We’re not going to be worrying about theft, because there will be no opportunity for any individual here to steal JPS current,” McKenzie pointed out.

Turning to other utility infrastructure, the minister said potable water supply lines and individual sewage systems are in place.

“I want to commend the contractor because when you look at the quality of the sewerage system, each home has its own sewerage and its own water supply, so it means that this is a self-purpose-built community. The system that is in will provide a sense of relief to the residents,” stated McKenzie.

“If you look along the entire stretch of the development, you will see a paved road, kerb walls with a drainage system that leads to a major drain. We’re not just putting in the facility and leaving the community without the kind of infrastructure that is needed. At the completion of this, each driveway will be properly paved and then we’re going to be putting in a water storage tank for each unit,” the minister revealed, adding that each unit will also be provided with a small 200-watt solar generator.

McKenzie said the Government will continue to support people who are sheltered up to their time of departure.

“All that we have been doing in the shelters in providing the meals, all of that will continue. There are individuals who we are paying rent through the SDC; we will continue to take care of that. Once they occupy the units, then we will cease taking care of them,” he explained.

McKenzie told the Jamaica Observer that the housing complex is being developed on lands belonging to the Sugar Company of Jamaica Holdings Limited through a lease agreement.

“It is an all-of-Government approach: the Ministry of Agriculture through the Sugar Holdings, the Ministry of Local Government, the Ministry of Economic Growth and Infrastructure Development (MEGID), the National Water Commission, the Ministry of Energy, and the National Housing Trust (NHT),” stated McKenzie.

Principal director of projects and technical services in MEGID Kinson Case said units are being rolled out across the hardest-hit parishes of Westmoreland, St Elizabeth, Hanover, St James, and Trelawny. He added that efforts are ongoing to complete container units for individuals affected by the Category 5 storm that struck on October 28, 2025.

World.title: Big swings, bigger impact
World.content:
From Left: Lourdes Blanco, senior vice-president, finance & global treasurer, Unique Vacations; Andrew Blanco, chief operating officer, Unique Vacations; Heidi Clarke, executive director, Sandals Foundation; Iriela Garzia, data analyst, Unique Vacations; and Ingrid Mignot display the symbolic cheque for US$300,000 raised during the third annual Unique Vacations Golf Classic in Weston, Florida, towards Sandals Foundation education initiatives across the Caribbean.

ON November 16, more than 200 golfers came together for the third annual Unique Vacations Golf Classic in Weston, Florida. This year, teams swung into action, raising US$307,000 (approximately $48.5 million) to directly benefit education initiatives led by the Sandals Foundation across the Caribbean.

With 82 sponsors, funds raised from this year’s tournament will bolster education across the Caribbean, including schools along Jamaica’s West Coast affected by Hurricane Melissa, continuing to build resilient, safe and engaging learning environments for children.

Heidi Clarke, executive director at the Sandals Foundation, says the 2026 Golf Classic has been one of the foundation’s biggest fund-raisers for the year.

“This event is about giving children in the Caribbean the tools they need to gain opportunity to reach their full potential. We are beyond grateful to our partners at Unique Vacations for hosting this tournament, bringing together corporate and travel partners, as well as team members all for a wonderful cause.

“Together, we have been able to raise funds for our projects and programmes in the Caribbean. This year is especially critical as we continue to foster resilience among our schools. We are so pleased by the sponsors who have come on-board, not only to have fun, but to play with a purpose,” said Clarke.

Speaking at the tournament, chief operating officer at Unique Vacations Andrew Blanco said: “When I first envisioned hosting this tournament, my hope was that it would become something meaningful and lasting. Thanks to an extraordinary team and the generosity of our partners, it has. This year’s event raised over $300,000 for the Sandals Foundation, with momentum continuing to grow, and the energy throughout the day from everyone who attended was a true testament to what it has become.

“The Sandals Foundation team does the real work on the ground throughout the Caribbean, and it’s humbling to know our efforts help fuel it. It’s truly a privilege to watch a vision grow beyond expectations, and to see our partners connect with the foundation and become champions of its mission.”

Previously, funds raised by the Unique Vacations Golf Classic supported the installation of solar energy infrastructure within schools and community centres, bringing sustainable energy and uninterrupted digital learning to many.

World.title: THREEPEAT!
World.content:
Jamaica forward Jody Brown celebrates a goal against Costa Rica during the first half of their Concacaf W Championship quarter-finals at Texas Health Mansfield Stadium in Mansfield, Texas, on Friday.AFP

IN 2006, the Reggae Girlz missed out on qualification for the 2007 FIFA Women’s World Cup with the programme eventually being disbanded in 2011 following years of inactivity.

Twenty years later, they have rewritten their history, establishing Jamaica as a force in women’s football with a third-consecutive World Cup appearance.

The Reggae Girlz secured their place at next year’s World Cup in Brazil after a commanding 3-0 win over Costa Rica in the Concacaf W Championship quarter- final at the Texas Health Mansfield Stadium on Friday.

Both countries are assured of a place at the 2031 World Cup after being named co-hosts on Monday.

However, with just one spot available between them for the 2027 edition, the Jamaican women showed their determination to keep their record-breaking run alive.

Jody Brown made sure the Girlz’s first-half dominance was rewarded after slotting home from close range in the 16th minute.

Captain Khadija “Bunny” Shaw celebrated her 50th appearance for Jamaica with a decisive second-half performance.

The Manchester City forward set up Kiki Van Zanten in the 59th minute before finding the net herself six minutes later to score her 68th goal international goal and cap another memorable night for Jamaica.

The Reggae Girlz have now qualified for three-consecutive World Cups, following their appearances in France in 2019, and Australia and New Zealand in 2023.

They are also guaranteed a fourth-consecutive appearance after Jamaica secured co-hosting rights for the 2031 tournament.

Former national defender Sashana Campbell, who was a key player in the 2019 World Cup campaign, says the squad continues to show just how special its historic run has been.

“For us to be going to another World Cup a third time, it’s a big deal,” she told the Jamaica Observer.

“Especially that we’re going to host the co-hosting 2031 World Cup, we didn’t want to just go this year and then somebody’s going to say down the line that we got lucky because we’re co-hosting.

So I think tonight was a tremendous win for us and you can see that the girls have grown tremendously, really, together.” Despite a number of new faces joining the team since their debut appearance seven years ago, Campbell says the spirit of the team will always be key to their success.

“We’re one Jamaica, we’re one love, unity, strength.

Once you step in our clique, you’re just going to automatically vibe with us.

So when you go to the training ground, the vibe is already there.You just have to adjust and know that we are all here together and we just have to go out there and get the job done,” she said.

“The new players coming in and meshing with the old girls, I don’t think it was hard for them to gel together because the majority of the team has been playing together for a while.

The other players coming in, they knew what was at stake because I would assume they had been watching the team before they had joined the team.” Former Head Coach Charlie Edwards, who led the team before their World Cup qualification streak, says the Girlz’s achievements are a testament to their quality and determination.

“All of Jamaica right now is very excited about this one, especially after the failure of the Reggae Boyz who everybody thought would have made it through to the World Cup easily and somehow found a way to flop,” he told the Observer.

“So the Girlz now doing this is such an exciting moment for us.

“Even myself, I’m overwhelmed with it, I’m excited, I’m happy.

I watched the game, I was glued to the TV and it’s just a fantastic moment.

And it’s a threepeat — there was a time when nobody gave us a chance of making the World Cup and now, we have done three.” The Reggae Girlz return to Concacaf W Championship action on Tuesday when they contest the semi-finals, with a chance to make further history by qualifying for their first-ever Olympic Games.

World.title: KFC Jamaica partners with Marvel Studios for Avengers:Doomsday promotion
World.content:
KFC Jamaica is among the markets in more than 100 countries participating in the franchise’s biggest global collaboration to date, a blockbuster partnership with Marvel Studios, celebrating the highly anticipated film, Avengers:Doomsday, which will hit cinemas locally on December 16.

The campaign brings together two of the biggest globally recognised brands, connecting the excitement of the Marvel Cinematic Universe with the unmistakable KFC food and flavours that customers know and love.

Locally, the experience will extend to the big screen, with KFC Jamaica set to stage a viewing of Avengers:Doomsday at Carib 5 in Kingston.

Inspired by Doctor Doom, one of Marvel’s most iconic villains, the campaign will also introduce menu offerings designed to bring the excitement of the film to KFC customers islandwide.

Andrei Roper, marketing manager for KFC Jamaica, said the campaign offers an opportunity to bring together two brands with strong and very distinct connections to their audiences.

“Marvel Studios has built an incredible legacy, with stories and characters that resonate with audiences around the world, including right here in Jamaica,” said Roper.

“We’re excited to join forces with a brand of the calibre of Marvel, and bring some of that movie magic to our customers. It’s an opportunity to create something memorable that goes beyond the menu and gives Jamaicans another way to share in the excitement surrounding Avengers: Doomsday,” added Roper.

KFC Jamaica is introducing two limited-time, Doctor Doom-inspired offerings that put an exciting new spin on familiar finger lickin’ favourites.

First up is the Doom Zinger, which features the brand’s signature Spicy Zinger, complemented by smoky green mayo, cola BBQ sauce, pickles, cheese and lettuce, all served on a distinctive black sesame-seed bun.

Next are the Doom Loaded Fries, which combine crispy fries with KFC’s signature popcorn chicken, topped with smoky green mayo and cola BBQ sauce for a rich combination of flavours.

Both offerings will be available at KFC restaurants islandwide from November 26, accompanied by specially designed, limited-edition packaging inspired by the campaign.

“The Doom Menu brings a bold new twist to some of the favourites Jamaicans already enjoy.

“From the striking black bun to the smoky green mayo and cola BBQ sauce, there’s something very different and unique about these offerings, and we’re excited for customers to experience it first hand,” said Roper.

World.title: Greek junior minister resigns amid public contracts controversy
World.content:
“From the very first moment, I have stated that I have never had any involvement in my siblings’ professional activities and that there is no such thing as family responsibility,” he said. His sisters have not commented on the allegations.

The resignation is another blow to Mitsotakis’s center-right New Democracy party ahead of elections that have not been scheduled but are widely expected to take place next spring. While New Democracy is still the clear front-runner in the polls, current figures suggest it would not be able to form a majority government. Support has fallen sharply since the 2023 general election amid surging inflation and sweeping investigations into alleged fraud involving EU funds.

Liakos took office on Nov. 13, in a reshuffle triggered by Lazaros Tsavdaridis’s resignation after reports that his daughter was registered on a youth handball team to secure bonus points for her university entrance exams, without actually playing. Tsavdaridis denied any wrongdoing.

Prior to his resignation, Liakos argued that he was not linked to the companies and that his sisters’ businesses were flourishing because they are at “their most productive age.”

Opposition parties demanded his resignation, arguing that he “lacked the political and moral legitimacy to remain in the post” and accusing the government of turning the state “into a family business at the expense of the citizens.”

However, criticism also came from within the ruling New Democracy ranks with several of his colleagues arguing that he should make things easier for the government and step down.

World.title: Santiago Abascal: Spain’s far-right kingmaker
World.content:
That gives Abascal significant power as Spain’s kingmaker although, for now, he is keeping his cards close to his chest. He has yet to spell out whether he would enter a coalition as the PP’s junior partner, what ministries he might seek or what concessions he would demand from Feijóo.

His far-right agenda, however, is clear and would set the next Spanish government on a very different trajectory from Sánchez’s administration, which has prioritized multilateralism, the integration of migrants and the green economy.

By contrast, Abascal wants to lock in “national priority” policies granting Spaniards preferential access to public benefits, carry out mass deportations of immigrants, roll back labor regulations and scrap climate rules.

Even if he does formally join with the PP after Nov. 29, the big question is whether he will stay the course and keep the government stable. Feijóo casts himself as a moderate and sober manager, whereas Abascal is a fiery ideologue who has split from the PP in the past — both quitting the party personally, and pulling Vox out of regional coalitions with the center right.

At rallies during the current campaign, the Vox leader has described the general election as “existential” for Spain, insisting that “everything is at stake” and that it is “now or never.”

“This is the last opportunity for a vast majority of Spaniards, and we are not going to waste it,” he said at a rally in Madrid shortly after Sánchez called the snap election.

World.title: 9 things you need to read ahead of the Spanish election
World.content:
If a PP-Vox coalition comes to fruition, it’ll mark the first time the far right has governed in Spain since the death of dictator Francisco Franco in 1975.

From understanding the key political players and parties, to watching Sunday’s results like a pro, here’s everything you need to know. (Click on the headlines to read the full reports.)

Picture taken in 1936 of Spanish soldiers loyal to the young Republic acclaimed by the crowd as they arrive in Madrid from Vilcavaro to fight against the nationalist troops of General Franco. | AFP via Getty Images

Ninety years after the outbreak of the civil war, Spain’s campaign for the Nov. 29 election has unmistakable echoes of 1936.

Politicians are resurrecting the rhetoric of a conflict that still runs deep in the polarized national psyche, with Sánchez leading crowds in chants of “¡No pasarán!” (“They shall not pass!”), the slogan immortalized by the left-wing forces that resisted Franco’s three-year siege of Madrid.

Both far-right leader Santiago Abascal of Vox and Madrid’s regional President Isabel Díaz Ayuso of the PP have, in turn, referred to their left-wing opponents as the “Popular Front,” used by the coalition of communist, socialist and republican forces that governed Spain on the eve of the outbreak of the civil war.

The election is also set to reshape politics in the northern industrial region of the Basque Country, where the bitterly divisive question of independence is boiling up again.

World.title: ‘An advocate for Russia’: Kushner’s Putin comments spark outrage in Europe
World.content:
“This is extremely dangerous—not only for Ukraine but also for the security and national interests of the United States,” Oleksandr Merezhko, chair of the Ukrainian parliament’s foreign affairs committee and a lawmaker from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy’s Servant of the People party, told POLITICO.

The interview offered a rare window into Kushner’s thinking as he touched on his roles in Ukraine, Iran and Gaza and his belief that “America’s most valuable export is really capitalism.”

Kushner, who described Russian envoy Kirill Dmitriev in the interview as an “incredible friend,” was less complimentary toward Zelenskyy, saying he had “wrongly” attacked Trump in the past.

The remarks come at a fragile moment for Kyiv’s relations with the White House. Zelenskyy is still pressing for deliveries of U.S.-made Patriot interceptor missiles and U.S.-brokered peace talks in Abu Dhabi this month brought no breakthrough.

There have been persistent tensions between the U.S. and Ukrainian leaders, and Trump on Wednesday unilaterally tweaked a joint statement with NATO chief Mark Rutte to urge Ukraine, as well as Russia, to avoid expanding the war.

“I have long argued that Witkoff and Kushner need to be replaced,” Merezhko said, referring additionally to Steve Witkoff, Trump’s other peace envoy. “They view Ukraine not even as businessmen seeking deals with Russia, but through the eyes of Putin himself.”

World.title: We’d be ‘stupid’ not to: Poland defends $300M military AI deal with Palantir
World.content:
Maven uses AI to analyze military data, supporting everything from logistics to the identification of battlefield targets.

Palantir celebrated the deal on X, calling Maven “the vanguard of next-generation AI warfare” and saying it was proud to stand with Poland in defending a “sovereign Europe.”

The company, which has drawn criticism for its work with U.S. immigration authorities and the Israeli military, faced protests in Warsaw earlier this month over concerns about data security and technological independence.

“All the keys, servers and information are — and will remain — exclusively in the possession of the Polish Armed Forces,” Kosiniak-Kamysz said.

Defense authorities in Denmark, Finland, Italy, the Netherlands, Spain and Sweden already use Palantir software, though not all use Maven.

Some are seeking to reduce that dependence. The Dutch military said in late October it wanted a European alternative by 2028, while France and Germany agreed in July to explore developing their own defense software.

World.title: Meta’s UK rollout for Muse AI agent exposes it to more liability
World.content:
Muse, an AI agent that takes actions on users’ behalf, was introduced in the U.K. this week — several months after its launch in the U.S. — following talks with British regulators.

The Competition and Markets Authority, which enforces consumer law in the U.K., said Meta had made changes to Muse’s terms of service in the U.K. following “weeks” of engagement to “make them fairer for consumers” and ensure they reflect U.K. consumer law.

Meta declined to comment on detailed regulatory discussions. It says Muse can lend a “helping hand” on everything from chasing a refund and renewing car insurance to doing the Christmas shopping — but publicly acknowledges the tool “can and will still make mistakes.”

The AI agent, which is the first to be launched by a Big Tech company in the U.K., can also make payments on behalf of users with their approval.

The U.S. terms of service cap liability at $250 except for claims “arising from Meta’s gross negligence, willful misconduct or fraud.”

They absolve Meta of liability “to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law” for any losses or damages caused by Muse “taking any unintended, erroneous or unauthorized action.”

World.title: Asia-Pacific trade bloc opens accession talks with UAE, Philippines and Indonesia
World.content:
Accession talks with Uruguay, which have been running since early this year, are well advanced and could “potentially” be concluded early next year, a diplomat granted anonymity to discuss the plans told POLITICO.

Trade ministers are meeting in Hanoi, Vietnam, for the 11th CPTPP Commission meeting, hosted annually by a rotating chair.

The U.K. became the first country without a Pacific coastline to join the bloc in 2024. Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Canada, Mexico and Singapore were among its founding members in 2018. Decisions are taken by consensus.

The U.K. is expected to sign a trade deal soon with the Gulf Cooperation Council, which includes the UAE. But London has yet to strike trade deals with the fast-growing Indonesian and Philippine economies.

Negotiations with the three nations “are all complicated and will require serious effort to get across the line,” said Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation think tank. “This includes capacity building for some applicants to make certain that everyone is clear on what the CPTPP requires, as well as careful work to ensure that member concerns are addressed.”

The bloc is emerging as a “Plan B” as efforts to reform the World Trade Organization falter. China, Taiwan, Ecuador, Ukraine, Cambodia and Argentina have also applied to join.

World.title: The man who coined ‘Brexit’ likes the sound of ‘Breturn’ and ‘Brejoin’
World.content:
Since arriving in Downing Street, Burnham has argued that Brexit “has not worked” as he tees up tighter ties with the EU. He has said that he hopes to rejoin within his lifetime — but insisted Monday that it would be “unthinkable” to do so without a referendum.

“If you’re looking for something catchy, there’s a couple of options: Let’s Breturn or Brejoin,” Wilding said when asked what the moniker for a future campaign should be. “But really, Burnham doesn’t want to go back to the past, he wants to go to the future, and the faces and arguments of 2016 will be dumped.”

“There will be a tonal change where Burnham caters his argument towards the younger vote and the business vote — seizing these cohorts will be vital to electoral success,” the strategist added.

Wilding coined Brexit in 2012 when he penned an article on Britain’s place in Europe.

“Unless a clear view is pushed that Britain must lead in Europe at the very least to achieve the completion of the single market, then the portmanteau for Greek euro exit might be followed by another sad word, Brexit,” he wrote for news outlet Euractiv , now known as Rapporteur. His writing is cited as the earliest evidence of the word Brexit in the Oxford English Dictionary.

The term was subsequently adopted as the accepted shorthand for the U.K. leaving Europe and was plastered on buses and billboards during the 2016 referendum campaign on Britain’s membership.

World.title: Albania: Protesters call for PM resignation amid clashs
World.content:
Albanians from all across the country travelled to the capital, Tirana, on Saturday, for a rally where thousands of people called for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign.

 

Clashes broke out between protesters and police, who used tear gas and water cannons to push back protesters throwing rocks and using sticks to try and smash street cameras and government building windows. Police forces were deployed along main roads to conduct vehicle searches.

“We have come out to demand our rights. We have had enough. Life has become very difficult. We are calling for a change to the entire system,” said student Juna Vasili. Protesters chanted "Resignation!" while gathering in Tirana's main Skanderbeg Square.

The health ministry said eight people were injured, including a police officer and two journalists.

This protest coincides with the 114th anniversary of the country's independence, a public holiday usually dedicated to national celebrations.

This protest was part of a series of anti-government demonstrations that began in late May, initially sparked by the opposition to a major luxury tourism project on Albania's southern coast.

A project linked to an investment firm founded by Jared Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law.

'We are like stateless citizens'

Albanians also travelled from abroad to protest in Tirana: "I came here specifically for the protest," says Arian Lleshi, a 33-year-old living in the UK.

"Why? Because we have been suffering for far too long. We have spread ourselves across Europe and around the world, and it is almost as if we are citizens without a state. We are like stateless citizens."

For many like Lleshi, political parties that have emerged since the fall of communism in the 1990s "no longer represent anyone."

"They need to make way for a new generation of intellectuals and people who have a greater stake in the country’s future."

Suzana Gjeta, a retiree, was also out on the streets to support young people and those like herself "who are living on just 120 euros a month. We hope this system will go, that Edi Rama will go, and that this corruption will end."

The rallies took the name of the Flamingo movement and were soon joined by student demonstrations in September. In late October, the government set up fines of up to 500,000 leks (€5573) for violence, looting, or concealing one's identity during protests.

While many of these protests have turned violent, most of the demonstrators called for better education and living standards, and lately for Rama's resignation.

World.title: France's credit outlook cut to negative by S&P, economy minister calls it 'warning'
World.content:
"This shows that we are being watched, that the world is monitoring us": reaction from the French economy minister after the conclusions of the private ratings agency S&P Global.

 

Experts at the agency are keeping France's sovereign rating at A+, but are cutting the outlook attached to that rating from stable to negative.

"It is a warning", says minister Roland Lescure on France Info (source in French).

The economy minister is calling to "get back on track" and sees in S&P Global's analysis "a very clear signal that we need to have a budget".

The National Assembly has rejected the first part of the government's initial text for the 2027 Draft Budget Bill (PLF). The text has been sent to the Senate and discussions are continuing within the parliamentary shuttle process, with each chamber able to propose changes.

In Roland Lescure's view, the candidates in the 2027 presidential election must each be ready "in a credible way to restore the public finances".

"We can say that we are in a recession"

According to the latest figures from Insee, the National Institute of Statistics and Economic Studies, French gross domestic product fell by 0.2% in the third quarter. The head of Insee's National Accounts Department concludes that there is a "recession". In her view, "this does not really change" the overall picture of the French economy, "but indeed, we can say that we are in a recession".

In the absence of additional fiscal consolidation measures, the ratings agency S&P Global is forecasting a public deficit for France of 5.3% in 2027.

World.title: OpenAI and Apple accuse each other of committing trade secret theft, OpenAI countersues
World.content:
After a lawsuit from Apple in the summer, OpenAI strikes back with a countersuit, accusing Apple of committing trade secret theft.

 

The ChatGPT provider alleged that Apple was attempting to steal trade secrets through a former employee while also pressuring shared suppliers to impede OpenAI's entry into the connected devices market.

OpenAI filed the countersuit on Friday in a federal court in San Jose, California.

Apple denounced the filing as "a transparent attempt to distract from the substance" of its own lawsuit it had launched in July against OpenAI and two former Apple employees.

OpenAI's lawyers respond that Apple is seeking "to compete unfairly by any means available."

Both companies have been partnering since ChatGPT was integrated into Apple products in 2024. They are now set to become rivals as OpenAI is developing its first connected device designed for AI with Jony Ive, Apple's renowned former design chief.

Apple pressures suppliers

OpenAI's filing argues that Apple is pressuring suppliers to identify their projects with OpenAI and the employees assigned to them.

"Suppliers have expressed fear of losing Apple business and have moved or rescheduled meetings with OpenAI to avoid Apple seeing them," the filing says.

No suppliers were named, but the filing says one firm moved OpenAI's production to a night shift, while another dropped planned work with the tech company "because of threats from Apple."

A former Apple employee who worked at OpenAI before returning to the iPhone maker was accused of leaking "dozens of OpenAI documents" about a prototype to senior Apple staff in July "at Apple's request".

OpenAI lawyers challenged an Apple practice encouraging employees to mix work and personal files via their personal iCloud account. A practice, the lawyers say, allowing Apple to later accuse those who leave of theft.

"This case is about OpenAI employees deliberately stealing, accessing, and using Apple's secret and confidential information regarding our unreleased technologies, processes, and products — not about inadvertent retention of Apple information," an Apple spokesperson said.

OpenAI has pledged it wouldn't use information Apple claims to be trade secrets in response to the judge threatening to issue an order barring OpenAI from using it until trial.

World.title: US military denied any issues with computing platform after hack reported
World.content:
After media reports of a breach into the US Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, the US military issued a statement on Friday denying any issues with its computer security.

 

"The Department of War's systems are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world. We will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications," a Defence Department official said.

"As a matter of policy and operations security, the Department of War does not comment on the status of our networks," a Defence Department official said earlier on Friday.

Although the Pentagon did not specifically answer whether the Air Force's Cloud One platform had been hacked, sources told Reuters the Cloud One platform breach was discovered the past month.

Possible breach of 'sensitive military data'

This breach, which could jeopardise a swathe of sensitive tactical, personal and logistical data, led to disruption across the platform, according to these sources, quoted by Reuters.

"A breach here is a big deal," sources told Reuters.

The US Air Force's Cloud-Based Command and Control platform is used for air defence radar, data feeds from across North America and combat systems, which track bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world, according to Reuters.

NBC News reported on Friday that the cloud platform was hacked and that the attack "could have exposed sensitive military information." Federal News Network, a media covering US federal agencies, also reported the breach through a source "familiar with the incident."

Cloud One has been the target of hackers for a long time. In 2023, the platform's leadership boasted a "100% success rate" in beating attempts to breach the platform.

String of major outages in the US

In recent weeks, the CIA and FBI were also reportedly subject to hacks along with suppliers for major American financial institutions including JPMorgan Chase, Visa and Mastercard.

Microsoft Outlook, US air traffic control and a top-secret NSA network also suffered issues recently, with officials at pains to blame the outages on maintenance or defects — not intrusions.

But these tech outages are not limited to the US; the European Commission was cyberattacked in October by an AI-assisted hack.

World.title: Latest news bulletin | November 28th, 2026 – Midday
World.content: Catch up with the most important stories from around Europe and beyond in this Euronews news bulletin. In just a few minutes, our newsroom brings you the latest news and breaking news across world affairs, business, politics, culture, entertainment and travel, with the context you need to make sense of a fast-moving day. Reported with the independence and the European perspective that define Euronews, this regular round-up gives you a clear and reliable overview of the stories shaping our world right now, wherever you are watching from.

World.title: Australia's conservatives hope for victory in trendsetting state
World.content:
Australia's conservatives hope for victory as polls closed on Saturday for Victoria's state election in the region of Melbourne, the country's second-largest city.

 

The election was set to deal a potential blow to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's centre-left Labor party, which has been ruling the "Garden State" region for 12 years.

Recent opinion polls projected the Labour to be widely ousted by the state Liberal Party leader Jess Wilson, a 36-year-old first-term lawmaker who has vowed to restore fiscal discipline in the deeply indebted state.

If Wilson manages to unseat Labor incumbent Ben Carroll, she would become the first Liberal woman to take office as premier of the state — considered "Australia's toughest job" by the country's business newspaper, the Australian Financial Review.

Her main pledge is to reduce Victoria's debt — the highest in the country — through a total of Aus$20 billion (€12.2 billion) measures, including a controversial plan to privatise the sewerage system.

Labor defeat could be trendsetting

"I know there are a lot of polls, there are a lot of headlines, but this election is going to be closer than what people think," Wilson told Channel 7, one of Australia's major TV networks.

If Labor loses in Victoria, which is seen as a pacesetting state, it would pile even more pressure on Australia's PM, who has seen his approval ratings tumble to record lows due to discontent with the rising cost of living.

The country's central bank was again forced to raise interest rates to an 18-year high, citing the prolonged war in the Middle East and frequent inflationary pressures.

Far-right set to take seats in state parliament

The far-right anti-immigration One Nation party, led by Pauline Hanson, could pick up some seats in the state's parliament for the first time, according to polls.

Marginalised for years, One Nation has lately become one of Australia's most popular political parties, which could play a kingmaker role in the next Victoria government.

"We know that Labor's out of the state. Finished," Hanson told media, pre-emptively taking credit for Labor's defeat.

"They won't be in government, and that's where One Nation has played a big part in this," she said. "The Liberals could not have won it by themselves. No way in the wide world."

World.title: Putin unveils Russia's newest nuclear-powered submarine
World.content:
Russian President Vladimir Putin took part in a flag-raising ceremony for the country's newest nuclear-powered submarine, the Perm, in Severodvinsk on Friday. The Perm is the fifth Yasen-M class submarine to join Russia's fleet in six years.

 

Putin said Russia was among the few countries capable of building such powerful nuclear-powered submarines. He also announced that five missile-carrying submarines, including three Yasen-M class vessels, are scheduled to be delivered to the Navy by 2030.

World.title: US hotline to report cartel activities slammed as foreign interference by Mexico
World.content:
Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum lodged a formal complaint with the US for setting up a hotline dedicated to reporting drug cartel activities and corrupt officials in Mexico.

 

The US Drug Enforcement Administration said on Wednesday it would open channels for Mexican citizens to anonymously report individuals, public officials and money laundering networks linked to the Sinaloa cartel. The US has previously designated the Mexican cartel as a terrorist organisation.

The announcement stirred the ongoing struggle between the US and Mexico over who has the right to take action against cartels in Mexico.

"We have ​made it very clear that our relationship with the United States is one of coordination, not subordination," Sheinbaum said.

Sheinbaum said it had lodged a formal complaint with US Ambassador Ron Johnson, as she slams the hotline as a form of interference.

"We have to say what we are thinking, and furthermore it is an obligation to do so because we have to defend our sovereignty," she said in a news conference.

'We're all fed up'

Juan Manuel Partida Valdez, president of the Sinaloa Journalists Association, has welcomed this US hotline by being among the first to write to the tip line on Thursday.

He said he sent information about alleged ties between politicians from the Sinaloa region and criminal groups. Partida Valdez said that he got a quick response and that his move was motivated by the authorities' failure to put an end to violence and corruption in northern Mexican regions.

"I talk to so many people — in the streets, on social media, on WhatsApp and in chats — and you realise what people think: We’re all fed up," the 67-year-old journalist said on Friday. "We’re fed up with narco-governments."

In May, Sinaloa Governor Rubén Rocha Moya — a powerful figure of Sheinbaum's party — was forced to step down after he was indicted by the US on drug-trafficking charges. He returned to office in August to step down another time just a day after coming back.

This whole song and dance about sovereignty is just collusion with the politicians tied to drug trafficking who are being protected in our country Juan Manuel Partida Valdez President of the Sinaloa Journalists Association

For Partida Valdez, this case is one of the main reasons that led him to reach out to the tip line, saying it was a "very clear example of what we’re suffering because of these governments that do absolutely nothing but protect criminals."

"This whole song and dance about sovereignty is just collusion with the politicians tied to drug trafficking who are being protected in our country," he added.

While several warned of the dangers of the US DEA's strategy, some academics and politicians like Lilly Téllez, a senator for Mexico’s National Action Party, a weakened opposition party, have celebrated the line.

The politician from the US-Mexico border state of Sonora said on X that it was "a good way to cooperate against the common enemy of both countries" and strengthens efforts to combat cartels.

A balancing act for Sheinbaum

Despite the significant expansion of security cooperation between the two countries, US President Donald Trump's administration has continued putting intense pressure on Sheinbaum to crack down on her country's drug gangs.

Trump has repeatedly threatened to take unilateral action against Mexican cartels if Mexico didn't step up against organised crime.

A difficult position for Sheinbaum, as she wishes to extend a free-trade deal with the US and Canada, while staying firm on her country's sovereignty and security.

Last week, Mexico's military captured a drug lord named Fausto Isidro Meza alias Chapo Isidro, one of the FBI's most-wanted fugitives.

Sheinbaum's left-wing government has insisted on keeping the drug lord at home to judge him before considering a US extradition.

Homicide rates have plunged in Mexico as the government took out several top cartel bosses, often using US intelligence to do so.

World.title: Turkey pushes for Black Sea shipping deal as UN warns global food crisis looms
World.content:
Turkey is intensifying its diplomatic push to halt attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, where Russia’s war in Ukraine has all but frozen exports from a region that is a vital global breadbasket, prompting the United Nations to warn of a looming global food crisis.

Advertising

Ankara is rolling out a new maritime safety mechanism to guarantee safe passage for commercial vessels.

The move follows a UN Security Council briefing on Monday by World Food Program executive director Luke J. Lindberg, who described the Black Sea as the world's most perilous shipping route. He noted that more than 300 attacks have been recorded there this year.

Lindberg cautioned that 10 million metric tonnes of Russian and Ukrainian wheat exports, bound for vulnerable nations such as Somalia and Sudan, now hang in the balance.

Turkey, which has maintained ties with both Moscow and Kyiv since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, previously worked with the UN to broker the Black Sea Grain Initiative in 2022, a year-long safe passage deal.

While Ukraine has agreed to Turkey’s latest maritime proposal, Russia has pushed back.

However, Sinan Ulgen of the Istanbul-based Center for Economics and Foreign Policy Studies said Ankara’s leverage over Moscow could still tip the scales.

"Given that, since the start of the war, Turkey has had a balanced and calibrated approach towards Russia, Moscow values Turkey's current stance," Ulgen said, noting that Turkey has not joined European Union sanctions against Russia and has kept its air corridor open.

"Russia will want this opening to continue. It wouldn't want Turkey to turn more antagonistic towards Russia at a time when Russia is under considerable pressure. So that's the leverage Turkey has."

Shipping attacks threaten Turkey's resolve to keep warships out of Black Sea

'Ukraine is in a worse situation'

For now, Moscow is holding firm, insisting that any Black Sea deal be linked to a comprehensive peace agreement with Ukraine. US-brokered peace talks ended in a stalemate this month.

Russia’s refusal to halt attacks may stem from a belief that it holds the upper hand in the struggle to choke off grain exports.

Can Atbasoglu, a Turkey-based international grain dealer, said both countries are suffering – although Ukraine is bearing the brunt.

"[Exports] from Russia [are] continuing at a much slower pace from the Black Sea ports – it's not zero," Atbasoglu said, noting that traditional buyers such as Turkey, Egypt and Libya are still buying Russian grain.

"Ukraine is in a worse situation. Very rarely is a vessel moving from Odesa. So I think if you compare, in terms of the Black Sea Russia is affecting Ukraine's shipping more than Ukraine can affect Russia's."

To bypass the blockade, Ukraine is moving grain by truck and barge to Romanian and Bulgarian ports, or overland into Europe.

But Roman Grynyshyn, founder of World to Rebuild Rural Ukraine, a charity supporting small-scale farmers, warned that Ukrainian agriculture is teetering on the brink of collapse.

"The upcoming season is going to be the worst because the farmers were not able to sell commodities to supply their main needs before the closure of the ports happened," Grynyshyn said.

He added that currently only Ukrainian farmers located close to the border who can export their commodities with their own trucks are still able to make money from their yields.

Grynyshyn said depressed prices for spring crops such as sunflowers, corn and soybeans – a situation compounded by drought in Ukraine's most fertile regions – have backed growers into a financial corner.

"The prices for the spring crops... are way below their break-even point for them, and that's what has caused a lot of farmers to start selling their farms," he said. "They have not yet filed for bankruptcy, but they are at the edge. I'm hearing that from everywhere, from all the regions of Ukraine, even the ones with very, very fertile soils."

Fears of wheat price surge amid Ukraine-Russia clashes in the Black Sea

The breadbasket of Europe

Before Russia’s full-scale invasion, Ukrainian farms helped feed roughly 400 million people worldwide.

Global markets have avoided the extreme price spikes seen in 2022 because bumper harvests elsewhere have cushioned the shock – although European Union data shows global wheat prices are up roughly 15 percent from a year ago.

Joseph Glauber, an agricultural economist at the International Food Policy Research Institute, warned that food prices will rise even more sharply if high export costs persist.

"If farmers continue to face these very large costs of exporting, that means that over time, production will fall," Glauber said. "This is such an important region for the world that it is very critical to ensure that they're able to plant and market their crops."

At home, Turkish officials face mounting pressure to secure a breakthrough.

Black Sea hostilities have left much of Turkey's cargo fleet stranded, while Turkish consumers and businesses rely on affordable Russian and Ukrainian grain. But despite Ankara's diplomatic push, Moscow remains unmoved.
