World.title: Polish PM orders alternative financing channel for constitutional court after central bank freezes accounts
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Prime Minister Donald Tusk has issued an order for the National Development Bank (BGK) to provide financing for the Constitutional Tribunal (TK) after Poland’s central bank froze the TK’s accounts following a disputed takeover of the court by government-backed judges. The relevant funds for the TK to function will be allocated by the finance ministry, announced government spokesman Adam Szłapka on Thursday morning, a day after the cabinet approved a resolution authorising the move. However, the ousted chief justice of the court has condemned the government’s actions as “completely unlawful” and said that they make the court’s current leadership “directly subordinate” to the prime minister. Premier @DonaldTusk wydał dyspozycję, by Bank Gospodarstwa Krajowego zapewniał finansowanie Trybunału Konstytucyjnego, a środki na ten cel zabezpieczy minister finansów. Państwo musi działać. — Adam Szłapka (@adamSzlapka) November 26, 2026 The move marks the latest twist in a long-running battle for control over the TK, which dates back around a decade to the unlawful appointment to the court of three judges under the former national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) government. As a result, Tusk’s centrist government, which took power from PiS in 2023, had effectively ignored the court and its rulings until this year, when it began appointing new judges to fill a growing number of vacancies on the TK’s 15-person bench. Events came to a head on 30 October, when the eight judges appointed by Tusk’s majority in parliament – five of whom opposition-aligned President Karol Nawrocki has refused to swear in – seized control of the court. They announced that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, who was appointed under PiS, had been suspended. Święczkowski, backed by Nawrocki and PiS, rejected their actions as an illegal “coup d’état” and maintains he is the rightful head of the court. The disputed status of the TK’s leadership led the National Bank of Poland (NBP) to announce earlier this month that it had frozen all outgoing transfers from TK accounts. The central bank cited conflicting claims over who had the authority to manage the institution, saying it “has no authority to decide who is legally entitled to control the Constitutional Tribunal”. The NBP is led by Adam Glapiński, who was appointed under PiS and is a longtime associate of party leader Jarosław Kaczyński. Tusk’s government condemned the bank’s decision as politically motivated and pledged to find alternative ways of securing the tribunal’s finances. Meanwhile, both Święczkowski and Anna Korwin-Piątkowska, the government-backed judge who has assumed leadership of the court, each appealed to Glapiński to unblock the Constitutional Tribunal’s accounts and recognise their respective authority to manage the court’s funds. Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal, citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a takeover by a group of judges backed by the government https://t.co/ZYkzoneojO — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 17, 2026 On Wednesday, the government adopted a resolution “on taking measures necessary to prevent a crisis situation related to the functioning of the Constitutional Tribunal” due to the NBP’s decision to freeze its accounts. “At a time when, after many years, an opportunity has arisen to overcome the constitutional crisis, restricting the Constitutional Tribunal’s ability to exercise its constitutional powers will negatively affect the level of legal certainty for individuals, including citizens,” the resolution reads. It requires the prime minister and finance minister to take “appropriate measures to protect the interests of the State Treasury and to ensure the state’s internal security and public order.” Szłapka subsequently announced that Tusk had instructed BGK, a state-owned development bank, to provide financing to the tribunal. The dispute around Poland's constitutional court risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/mtgutqSTQh — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026 Jan Grabiec, head of the prime minister’s chancellery, on Thursday morning told broadcaster TVN24 that the tribunal had an “auxiliary account” at BGK. This would allow its day-to-day operations to be financed despite the NBP’s decision to block payment orders, he added. “It is not just a matter of ordinary tribunal staff potentially not receiving their salaries,” said Grabiec. “The State Treasury also bears responsibility for contracts entered into by the tribunal’s previous leadership that include specific payment deadlines.” “This creates a liability for damages, potentially amounting to losses of many millions of zloty,” he added. “We cannot allow the State Treasury to be exposed to losses resulting from such politically motivated decisions of the National Bank of Poland.” The International Commission of Jurists has criticised the takeover of Poland’s constitutional court, saying it “contravenes international standards on the independence of the judiciary” But it also criticised the president for refusing to swear in judges https://t.co/2kBv3GT20d — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 4, 2026 On Thursday, Święczkowski condemned the government’s decision to channel money to the TK through BGK, calling it “completely unlawful”, reports the Dziennik Gazeta Prawna daily. “If this usurper Anna Korwin-Piotrowska accepts money from Tusk’s government, it will mean she is directly subordinate to Tusk,” he added. At the time of writing, the NBP had not publicly commented on the government’s decision to channel funding to the tribunal through BGK. BGK, meanwhile, told PAP that it could not comment on the details of its arrangements with other parties, citing banking secrecy. World.title: Warsaw hospital accused of offering “VIP access” for politicians fined 2.3 million zloty

The Warsaw hospital at the heart of a recent scandal over allegations that politically connected patients were given preferential treatment has been fined 2.3 million zloty (€520,000) after an investigation found that it admitted patients out of turn and doctors were absent during scheduled shifts. The doctor at the centre of the scandal, who was a local councillor for Poland’s main ruling party, was charged with fraud in October and is now also facing disciplinary proceedings over alleged breaches of medical ethics and professional standards. Niestety – Dawid K. jednak nie posiadł daru bilokacji, cudu nie było. Z ustaleń kontrolerów Narodowego Funduszu Zdrowia wynika, że po prostu oszukiwał. Ale to nie jest tylko sprawa jednego młodego medyka z legitymacją Koalicji Obywatelskiej w torbie. Cały ten przypadek wiele… pic.twitter.com/DfC35LLUpo — OficjalneZero (@OficjalneZero) November 26, 2026 The audit was conducted by the National Health Fund (NFZ), which finances public healthcare in Poland. It was carried out following a series of revelations in June by media outlets about alleged irregularities at the hospital. Many of the claims centred around a young doctor, who can be identified only as Dawid K. under Polish privacy law due to the criminal proceedings against him. He served as coordinator of emergency services at the Southern Hospital. News outlet Zero.pl was the first to report that the doctor, who also served as a local politician for the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party that leads Poland’s ruling coalition, worked a seemingly impossible number of hours at four different hospitals and earned 1.6 million zloty last year alone. The website alleged that the doctor had declared shifts when he was actually not present and cited instances in which he reportedly appeared in local media during hours when he was officially listed as being on duty at the hospital. ❗️ Błyskawiczne przyjęcia, wykonywanie pakietów kilkunastu, a nawet kilkudziesięciu badań w bardzo krótkim czasie, możliwość przebywania w innym pomieszczeniu niż ogół pacjentów. W Warszawskim Szpitalu Południowym stworzono nieoficjalnie szybszą i bardziej komfortową ścieżkę… pic.twitter.com/3aanpRVeBu — Patryk Słowik (@PatrykSlowik) June 17, 2026 Over the following weeks, Zero.pl and two other news websites, Wirtualna Polska and Onet, revealed further alleged cases of huge salaries for some doctors and impropriety at the Southern Hospital, including preferential treatment for patients with political connections. This included claims that there was a “VIP lounge” in which patients with connections to KO were given more comfortable facilities than others and that such patients were often allowed to skip the queue and receive treatment more quickly. In its audit of the Southern Hospital, the NFZ found that certain patients had been admitted out of turn. Inspectors also identified cases in which patients in stable condition were admitted to the emergency department ahead of others whose health condition warranted more urgent attention. The NFZ also found that doctors were absent during scheduled shifts and and that medical services were sometimes provided by staff without the required qualifications. The audit raised further concerns about the appointment of an inexperienced doctor as the coordinator of the emergency department. In a statement published on Wednesday, the hospital acknowledged the NFZ’s fine but noted that it was a preliminary decision and that the hospital could submit objections. It said that its board was reviewing the details before deciding on its next steps. Poland’s health minister has unveiled a set of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in public hospitals following a series of reports about exorbitant pay for some doctors and that politically connected patients could skip queues and use a "VIP lounge" https://t.co/pidAHxohc4 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 8, 2026 After announcing the end of its audit, the NFZ noted that it would forward the findings to prosecutors who have been investigating reports of irregularities at Southern Hospital. Prosecutors last month charged Dawid K. with fraud, alleging that he submitted fraudulent or unreliable invoices to the hospital worth more than 583,000 zloty. He has pleaded not guilty. Prosecutors are also investigating other cases of alleged wrongdoing at the hospital. However, a spokesman last month said that the findings so far do not confirm reports of a “VIP lounge” at the hospital. Meanwhile, on Thursday, the spokesman for the National Chamber of Physicians (NIL), Poland’s medical professional body, announced that they had decided to bring disciplinary proceedings against Dawid K. The claims against him concern alleged improper performance of medical duties, breaches of professional ethics, and conduct that undermined public trust in the medical profession. Zgodnie z obietnicą przekazuję do wiadomości publicznej: Rzecznik Odpowiedzialności Zawodowej podjął decyzję o przedstawieniu zarzutów Dawidowi K. Dotyczą one rzetelności wykonywania zawodu, naruszenia etyki i podważenia zaufania do zawodu lekarza. Będziemy informować o… — Piotr Pisula (@PanPisula) November 26, 2026 In the wake of the allegations against him, Dawid K. resigned from his seat on the local council, left KO, and stopped working at the Southern Hospital. His former party also distanced itself from him. Jan Grabiec, the prime minister’s chief of staff and head of the KO in the Mazovia province, which includes Warsaw, told reporters in June that the scandal “has no connection to KO, but since he was a KO councillor, we will be all the more stringent in holding those responsible to account”. In July, the health minister, Jolanta Sobierańska-Grenda, unveiled a series of reforms intended to “rebuild trust” in the healthcare system. They include caps on doctors’ salaries, a requirement for them to work at least half their statutory working time at a designated hospital, and a new electronic waiting list system. Meanwhile, the mayor of Warsaw, Rafał Trzaskowski, who is also a deputy leader of KO, ordered a separate municipal audit of the hospital, which revealed a number of irregularities, including in relation to Dawid K.’s activities. It concluded with 44 recommendations that Trzaskowski said were being implemented. World.title: Poland plans no-fly zone on eastern border to aid downing of Russian missiles
World.content: Keep our news free from paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland’s defence ministry has announced plans to establish a no-fly zone along the country’s eastern border with the aim of making it easier to shoot down Russian missiles and drones that violate Polish airspace. Meanwhile, foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has again suggested that Poland should be allowed to shoot down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards the Polish border. However, the defence ministry acknowledged today that NATO is so far opposed to the idea. Wiceminister obrony Cezary Tomczyk zapowiedział wprowadzenie strefy zakazu lotów przy wschodniej granicy Polski. Jak poinformował minister Tomczyk, rozporządzenie trafiło do rządowego zespołu, strefa ma obejmować od kilkunastu do 50 kilometrów przy granicy wschodniej Polski i ma… pic.twitter.com/3xF68uNNRU — Dariusz Wiewiorka (@darekwiewiorka) November 25, 2026 Speaking on Wednesday at the opening of a new military satellite imaging centre, deputy defence minister Cezary Tomczyk announced that his department “will request the government to establish a no-fly zone on the country’s eastern border, to ensure Poland’s security”. Tomczyk acknowledged that, after three Russian missiles struck southeastearn Poland last Friday, NATO had offered support, including the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System (AWACS) to Poland. “But at the same time, the Polish military must do everything possible to protect our interests here and now,” he added. The defence ministry recently took one such step by allowing easier identification of objects that can be shot down, said Tomczyk. “The no-fly zone at the state border will be an additional factor supporting the operations of the Polish Air Force.” At a subsequent press briefing, Tomczyk provided more details of the plan. The proposed no-fly zone would stretch for a distance of between “a dozen or a few dozen kilometres from the border”, he said. “When a Polish fighter pilot knows that an aircraft is entering Polish airspace from Ukraine, is flying at a certain altitude and speed, is entering the no-fly zone and is detected on radar, this constitutes grounds for shooting down such an object…We will also urge NATO as a whole to establish such a rule on the eastern flank.” The deputy minister said that a relevant regulation had already been submitted and “will be processed in the coming weeks”. He expressed hope that the measures could be in place by the end of December or in early January. As well as last Friday’s missile strikes, on Monday this week a Russian drone entered Poland from Ukraine and spent a few minutes in Polish airspace. The Polish military had been authorised to fire upon it, but eventually did not do so after it turned back towards the border. Poland is changing the procedures under which its military can fire upon foreign aircraft, citing the "growing threat from Russia". Visual identification of targets will no longer be required, with other forms of data to be used instead https://t.co/foCWsBDazH — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 29, 2026 The government’s plans for a no-fly zone were, however, questioned by Mariusz Błaszczak, a former defence minister and now head of the parliamentary caucus of Law and Justice (PiS), the main opposition party. Błaszczak noted that current regulations already allow the introduction of a temporary no-fly zone. He suggested that what the government had announced was simply a “cosmetic measure” and asked what “real operational capabilities” it would provide to the military. Earlier on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported, based on unnamed sources, that Poland had, at a NATO meeting called on Monday to discuss last week’s Russian missile strikes in Poland, asked about the possibility of shooting down Russian missiles that are over Ukraine but heading towards NATO states. Asked about the issue, Tomczyk said that he could not confirm Bloomberg’s reporting, but noted that discussion of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukraine had been going on for months. “NATO is not in favour of this in any way,” said Tomczyk, quoted by broadcaster TVN. “If we want to make any decisions that concern the space over Ukraine, it must always be a decision of the entire NATO…Many months ago NATO decided that such a procedure was out of the question. And that’s where we stand now.” NATO has approved the deployment of an Airborne Warning and Control System to Poland in response to three Russian missiles striking Polish territory last week. Hours after the decision was announced, Poland’s airspace was again violated by a Russian drone https://t.co/gudQJsPlQ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 24, 2026 On Wednesday morning, before Bloomberg’s report had been published, Sikorski, the foreign minister, was asked during an interview with Polskie Radio about the idea of shooting down missiles over Ukraine before they reached Poland. “A missile or drone approaching our airspace already poses a direct threat to us, so I believe that shooting [it] down over Ukraine at Ukraine’s request would fall within the definition of self-defence,” said Sikorski. However, he acknowledged that any such policy would need to be agreed by NATO. As far back as 2024, Poland proposed the idea of shooting down Russian missiles over Ukrainian territory. But it was rejected by NATO, whose then-secretary general, Jens Stoltenberg, said that it would risk NATO “becoming part of the conflict”. World.title: Prague’s Christmas Garbage Trucks Return to the Streets on Sunday
World.content:
Prague’s decorated garbage trucks will return to the city center on Sunday, November 29, bringing thousands of lights to the streets as part of the capital’s Christmas season.

Two illuminated vehicles operated by Prague Services (Pražské služby) will work evening shifts until December 31. Their routes will cover both sides of the Vltava, with the trucks starting at 7 p.m.



The first vehicle will operate on the left bank, passing through the areas around Prague Castle, Hradčany and Malá Strana. The second will serve the right bank, including Betlémské náměstí, Uhelný trh, Ovocný trh and Mariánské náměstí.

The trucks are Mercedes-Benz 1830 GL models powered by natural gas. Their Christmas decorations were created in cooperation with the Prague municipal technology company Technologie hlavního města Prahy.

Together, the two vehicles feature more than 200 meters of lighting cables and approximately 4,400 LED lights.

The illuminated garbage trucks have become a seasonal attraction in Prague. This year marks the fifth time the company has sent them out in festive decoration. They first appeared on the city’s streets in 2021.

According to Prague Services chief executive Patrik Roman, the vehicles regularly attract attention from residents and visitors, who stop to take photographs and record videos for social media. The company is therefore continuing the tradition of sending two decorated trucks into the center, as it did last year.

Although their routes focus on the historic center, the vehicles may also be seen elsewhere in Prague. They remain part of the city’s regular waste collection service, transporting rubbish from black containers to the ZEVO Malešice waste-to-energy plant.

Prague Services has reminded the public that the illuminated vehicles are working garbage trucks, not parade vehicles. People are asked to keep a safe distance and avoid interfering with their operations.

World.title: How open communication and wellness habits are reshaping modern couples intimacy
World.content:
Modern couples are prioritizing open communication, stress reduction, and discreet non-medical wellness routines to nurture confidence and shared intimacy.

Balancing a demanding career with endless household responsibilities can easily push physical closeness to the bottom of your to-do list. When fatigue sets in, intimacy often starts to feel like another chore rather than a source of joy.

You do not need dramatic overhauls to bring warmth back into your relationship. Simple shifts toward open dialogue, shared relaxation, and discreet wellness tools help you build deeper emotional trust at your own pace.

Why Does Honest Dialogue Lower Performance Pressure?

Talking openly about comfort, pacing, and mutual expectations takes the guesswork out of the bedroom. When you share what feels good and what feels rushed, you replace silent assumptions with genuine curiosity.

Guidance from Harvard Health highlights that shifting attention toward broader physical affection and non-penetrative closeness delivers real pleasure while easing the performance anxiety that can dampen desire. You give yourselves permission to enjoy the moment when you stop treating intimacy like a test with a strict pass-or-fail grade.

Start these conversations outside the bedroom when both of you feel calm and rested. A quick check-in over weekend coffee keeps the tone light, supportive, and completely free of blame.

How Can You Reframe Daily Stress as a Team?

Work deadlines, family obligations, and unexpected bills drain your mental energy long before bedtime arrives. If you carry that tension into the evening, physical closeness naturally takes a back seat.

Research discussed in Psychology Today notes that viewing daily stress as a shared hurdle rather than a personal threat strengthens closeness and raises relationship satisfaction. You protect your bond when you tackle a rough week side by side instead of retreating into separate corners.

Set aside 15 minutes each evening to decompress together without screens. Taking a short walk, stretching, or sharing a quiet cup of tea signals to your nervous system that the workday has ended.

What Makes Modern Wellness Accessories Feel Approachable?

Discreet, non-medical wellness tools have moved far beyond outdated novelties into everyday self-care. Thoughtful couples now explore ergonomic, multi-mode vibrating cock rings and other body-safe designs to support mutual comfort and shared benefit without clinical pressure. These whisper-quiet, rechargeable accessories blend easily into a relaxed routine and keep the focus squarely on connection.

Modern designs prioritize simplicity, intuitive controls, and soft textures that feel natural against your skin. Because they operate quietly and charge via discreet USB cables, you can introduce them without interrupting the mood or feeling self-conscious.

How Do You Choose Materials That Prioritize Comfort?

Selecting the right materials protects your skin and keeps every session worry-free. Paying attention to 2 core details makes shopping straightforward.

Soft Hypoallergenic Silicone

Look for flexible, medical-grade silicone that warms quickly to your body temperature. Non-porous surfaces resist bacteria, clean up easily with warm water and mild soap, and stay gentle on sensitive skin.

Water-Based Lubrication

Pair silicone accessories exclusively with water-based lubricants. Silicone-based formulas can degrade soft silicone surfaces over time, whereas a clean, glycerin-free water-based option preserves the material and keeps movement smooth and comfortable.

Practical Habits for Unhurried Sessions

Small adjustments to your environment help you slow down and stay present with your partner. Try weaving these practical habits into your weekly routine:

Set a calm atmosphere: Dim the overhead lights, adjust the room temperature, and silence phone notifications to eliminate sudden distractions.

Keep pacing flexible: Check in with a gentle touch or a quick whisper so either partner can slow down or switch things up without awkwardness.

Prep your space early: Keep water-based lubricant, a clean towel, and fully charged accessories within easy reach so you never break the flow.

Prioritize post-session care: Rinse body-safe tools with mild soap right away and share a few minutes of quiet cuddling to reinforce emotional warmth.

Building Lasting Trust Outside the Bedroom

Physical intimacy thrives when emotional safety exists throughout the rest of the week. Small gestures – like listening without offering unsolicited fixes or taking a chore off your partner’s plate – build a steady foundation of goodwill.

When you feel heard and supported during ordinary Tuesday afternoons, opening up during intimate moments feels natural. Confidence grows steadily when both partners know their comfort always comes first. Even a brief daily ritual, like a genuine hug before parting for work or a few minutes of undistracted conversation at dinner, reinforces the sense that you are consistently on each other’s side.

Bringing open communication together with discreet, comfort-focused wellness accessories removes unnecessary pressure from your relationship. By slowing down, choosing body-safe materials, and treating stress as a shared challenge, you create space for a deeper, more relaxed connection that fits your real life.

World.title: Kampa Park Revitalization to Begin in March 2027, Main Work to Last Three Months
World.content:
The long-awaited revitalization of Kampa Park in Prague will begin in March 2027, with the main construction phase scheduled to last until the end of May.

Smaller-scale work will continue afterward, Prague 1 announced on Friday.

The park will remain open to pedestrians throughout the project, and access to local businesses and institutions will be maintained. However, the lawns and green areas will be temporarily closed and are expected to reopen once the main work is complete.



The project includes repairs to existing paths, the creation of new walkways, landscaping and the installation of new railings along the Čertovka stream. The park’s layout and character will remain unchanged.

Work will begin along the Čertovka stream, where surveys will be carried out to protect tree roots. The first phase will also include repairs to connecting paths and the walkway between Werich Villa and Sovovy Mlýny.

The contractor estimates this phase will take around 45 days.

Work on the main path is scheduled to begin in mid-April. Further improvements will include new street furniture and repairs to the children’s playground, with the detailed schedule still being finalized.

The park’s lighting is also being replaced with fixtures inspired by Prague’s traditional lanterns. Most of the work is expected to be completed this year, with some lamps near Sovovy Mlýny and in Odkolkovská Garden scheduled for replacement in 2027.

According to Prague 1 Councilor Kateřina Klasnová, up to 75 percent of the material from the existing paths could be reused in the new surfaces, reducing construction costs and the number of trucks transporting materials through the park.

The main paths and lawns are expected to be accessible again by the end of May 2027, allowing visitors to use the park during the summer.

World.title: Advent in Prague: Where to Order Festive Sweets, and Savor Mulled Wine
World.content:
From sweets to warming svařák and Christmas markets, the Czech capital offers many ways to embrace the holiday spirit.

Here’s a guide to help you savor the best of Advent in Prague this year.

Where to Order Luxury Christmas Sweets in Prague

If you’re not planning to bake this year but still want something special for your holiday table, Prague’s bakeries and cafés have you covered.



Myšák

For classic holiday sweets, Myšák’s e-shop (mysakdomu.cz) has you covered. Order a 500g box of traditional Christmas sweets for 1,445 CZK. You can also pair it with a Christmas cake, their signature Věneček egg liqueur, or a homemade syrup for mulled wine.

Known for its craftsmanship, Skála offers a 1kg assortment of 12 different Christmas sweets for 1,699 CZK. Pre-orders are available for specific dates, with slots still open during the festive season.

Etapa in Karlín

Etapa’s 450g Christmas box (1,050 CZK) combines Linzer cookies, caramel shortbread, chocolate hazelnut balls, and their signature beehives. A few holiday dates are still open, or you can stop by the café for extras.

Gluten-Free Christmas Sweets

For those avoiding gluten, Mezi Srnky provides both classic and gluten-free options. Their 400g boxes include gingerbread, rum balls, and Išelské cookies.

Where to Find the Best Mulled Wine and Eggnog in Prague

After sorting your sweets, take a walk through Prague and visit these places for warm drinks.

Mulled Wine Stops

Bjukitchen (City Center): Classic mulled wine alongside kid-friendly vanilla cocoa.

(City Center): Classic mulled wine alongside kid-friendly vanilla cocoa. Eska (Karlín): Known for its creative twist on Christmas drinks, including apple mulled wine.

(Karlín): Known for its creative twist on Christmas drinks, including apple mulled wine. Hrnek (Letná): Enjoy their secret recipe mulled wine served in a stylish onion-shaped mug.

Eggnog

Iveta Fabešová’s (Masaryčka building): Famous for her rich eggnog, available by the glass or bottle, making it a great gift option.

(Masaryčka building): Famous for her rich eggnog, available by the glass or bottle, making it a great gift option. Coffee Room (Vinohrady): try their seasonal eggnog-infused coffee, a must for coffee lovers.

Advent Markets in Prague: Intimate and Unique

Skip the crowded main squares and explore Prague’s smaller, cozier Christmas markets for a more relaxed holiday shopping experience.

The list of Prague cafés and bistros that invite you to a unique culinary experience would not be complete without Villa 63, which can be found on Hradešínská Street.

You can now also take a look at the neighboring property, which is named Zahrada 65.

World.title: Filmasia to Bring 16 Asian Films to Prague, Brno and České Budějovice
World.content:
The 22nd edition of the Filmasia Asian Film Festival will take place in Prague from December 3 to 13, bringing 16 films from Hong Kong, South Korea, Japan, Taiwan and Vietnam.

The festival will also welcome filmmakers from Hong Kong and South Korea before travelling to Brno and České Budějovice in January and February.

This year’s theme is “the thread of fate,” connecting established filmmakers with emerging artists.



The programme is divided into five sections, alongside a special retrospective dedicated to director Wong Kar Wai.

The festival will open on Friday, December 4, at 7 p.m. at Bio Oko with Good Trip, a Hong Kong comedy about a seriously ill father and his daughter embarking on a road trip. Directors Norris Wong and Wong Hoi will attend the screening.

The festival will also revisit four films by Wong Kar Wai in the In the Mood for Wong Kar Wai section. Audiences can see Chungking Express and Fallen Angels on Saturday, December 12, followed by Happy Together and In the Mood for Love on Sunday, December 13.

“We are delighted to welcome several prominent figures from Asian cinema to this year’s Filmasia. Meeting filmmakers in person is extremely important to us, as it allows our audiences to discover not only the films themselves but also the stories, experiences, and countries behind their creation,” said festival director Karla Stojáková.

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Filmasia (@filmasiafestival)

The festival will take place at Bio Oko in Prague from December 3 to 13, 2026.

Selected films will then be screened at Kino Art in Brno from January 6 to 23, 2027, and at Biograf Kotva in České Budějovice from January 27 to February 1, 2027.

All films will be screened in their original languages with Czech and English subtitles.

World.title: Prague Christmas Markets Reveal Prices for Mulled Wine, Sausages and More
World.content:
Prague’s main Christmas markets will open on Saturday, November 28, with mulled wine priced at 100 CZK and sausages costing 180 CZK.

Organizers say prices for several popular refreshments have remained unchanged, while the sausage is the main item to have become more expensive.



The markets on Old Town Square and Wenceslas Square will run until January 6, 2027, with stalls open daily from 10 a.m. to 10 p.m.

The company Taiko, which organizes the markets, says Prague remains among the most affordable Christmas market destinations in Europe for food and drinks.

The price of mulled wine has remained at 100 CZK since 2024. A hot apple drink will cost 70 CZK, the same as last year.

The price of sausages has increased, however. The item rose from 160 CZK to 180 CZK during the Easter markets and will remain at that level for the Christmas season.

The company also points to the ingredients used at its stalls. The sausages are made exclusively for the markets and contain up to 97 percent meat, while the mulled wine is produced from grapes supplied by the Moravian winery Chateau Valtice.

Prices at Prague’s main Christmas markets:

Mulled wine: 100 CZK

Hot apple drink: 70 CZK

Sausage: 180 CZK

Hot dog: 90 CZK

Sausage in a baguette: 180 CZK

Langoš with garlic, cheese and ketchup: 200 CZK

Draft Pilsner, 0.4 litre: 80 CZK

Hot chocolate: 130 CZK

Spiral potato: 100 CZK

French fries: 185 CZK

Record number of performers expected

The 2026 programme will feature a record 5,329 performers. Activities will include weekend workshops for children, a St. Nicholas Day event and the traditional Christmas Eve celebrations.

On December 24, festive soup will be served on Old Town Square from 11 a.m. A performance of the Czech Christmas Mass is scheduled for 9 p.m.

For safety reasons, the organizers have not announced the exact time of Saturday’s tree-lighting ceremony. They are also encouraging visitors to spread their first visits across the weekend and avoid bringing bulky luggage to the markets.

World.title: Expedia to Acquire Czech Flight Booking Company Kiwi.com
World.content:
American travel company Expedia Group has agreed to acquire Czech flight booking platform Kiwi.com, bringing a change of ownership to the Brno-based business.

The transaction is expected to be completed by the middle of 2027, although the companies have not disclosed its value.

The acquisition will see the departure of Kiwi.com’s current majority shareholder, US investment fund General Atlantic, which has controlled the company since 2019. Co-founder Oliver Dlouhý, who holds a minority stake, is also expected to exit.



Expedia said the deal would strengthen its technology and expand its position in the European air travel market. Kiwi.com generated approximately €227 million in revenue last year, equivalent to around CZK 5.6 billion.

Expedia said the acquisition would give travelers access to a wider selection of flights and provide new opportunities for growth across its brands, including Expedia, Hotels.com and Vrbo.

Kiwi.com was founded in Brno in 2012 by Dlouhý and his business partners. The company became known internationally for its search technology, which allowed it to combine flights from airlines that did not necessarily have direct partnerships with the platform.

The company has since developed into an international flight retailer, focusing on technology, automation and artificial intelligence to improve its operations.

The acquisition comes after several years of restructuring at Kiwi.com, which faced financial difficulties following the decline in air travel during the COVID-19 pandemic.

The company reduced its workforce by more than 200 employees in 2024. Earlier this year, it announced plans to cut approximately 250 jobs from a workforce of around 700.

Expedia Group was founded in 1996 as a division of Microsoft. It operates an online travel platform offering bookings for flights, accommodation, car rentals and activities, as well as technology services for corporate partners.

World.title: Christmas Trees You Can Replant After the Holidays Are Available in Prague
World.content:
Residents of Prague and Brno can choose a living Christmas tree this year and give it a chance to grow in the forest after the holidays.

Both cities are offering small potted firs that can be planted in spring with the help of foresters.

In Prague, the Forests of the Capital City of Prague are running their Christmas fir project for the tenth consecutive year. The initiative, known as A Christmas Fir with a Future, allows people to buy a young silver fir for 150 CZK.

The trees, approximately 50 centimeters tall, have been grown in a forest nursery in Čimický háj. Unlike cut Christmas trees, they retain their roots and can continue growing after Christmas.



The organizers acknowledge that the firs may not look like traditional Christmas trees. Their branches are often irregular, and each tree has its own shape.

The project also aims to support the return of silver fir to Czech forests. The native species (Abies alba) became scarce during the 20th century, partly because of air pollution, forestry practices and excessive numbers of wild animals.

Where to buy a living Christmas tree in Prague

The potted firs are available at several locations, including the Ďáblice Garden Center, the Prales eco-center and forest lodges in Hostivař, Chuchle, Šárka, Běchovice, Kunratice and Čimice.

How to care for a potted Christmas tree

A living Christmas tree needs more attention than a cut one. It should remain outdoors in a cool place, such as a balcony or garden, for as long as possible before being brought inside.

The tree should be gradually acclimatized to the warmer indoor temperature. The room should ideally stay below 20 degrees Celsius, and the soil needs regular watering. Spraying the needles with water can also help.

After Christmas, the tree should be moved back to a cooler environment gradually.

Even with careful handling, survival is not guaranteed. According to the Masaryk Forest Křtiny School Forest Enterprise, around 60 percent of the Christmas firs planted in previous years have successfully taken root.

World.title: The invisible hands keeping Budapest running
World.content:
Five workers in Budapest share the skills, challenges, and unexpected encounters behind their everyday professions.

At eight in the morning, Csenge Bujdosó begins her ten-hour working day at a small specialty coffee shop in Budapest. Less than an hour later, Andy Molnár arrives at Central Market Hall to check his stock and prepare for another day of welcoming visitors.

Across the Hungarian capital, similar routines unfold inside cafés, market stalls, shops, and restaurants. Delivery riders navigate the city’s streets, while business owners prepare their establishments for the day ahead. These are familiar sights to Budapest’s residents and visitors, but how much do they know about the people behind them?

Five workers share their experiences, the demands of their professions, and what their work has taught them about Budapest.

Different ambitions lead to different livelihoods

For Csenge, a barista at MTRM Roast, an interest in coffee developed during her time in the hospitality industry. She initially wanted to master latte art, but as she gained experience, she began to place greater importance on the quality and flavour of the drinks she prepared. After all, she explained, “A beautiful coffee that tastes bad kind of defeats its purpose.” Today, Csenge independently manages the café’s daily operations between 8 AM and 6 PM. Her responsibilities include preparing drinks, adjusting coffee settings, monitoring supplies, and maintaining equipment.

Source: Alina Hogertz, Jean Felix Muhire, Kate Berbano, Marla Enkhtaivan, and Sarah Salsabiila



For Andy Molnár, working at Budapest’s Central Market Hall was a decision influenced by his previous employment experiences. He moved to Budapest at 19 and initially worked in an office. Dissatisfied with the working conditions, he sought another opportunity and began working at the market at 21, where his ability to speak several languages proved useful.

A desire for better earning opportunities and greater independence led Raymond Arsene to become a Wolt delivery rider. Having previously worked in warehouses and restaurants, he now has the flexibility to organise his working hours around his university studies and other commitments.

For two other workers, personal interests eventually developed into business ventures. Niki Pás, the owner of Garden Rose, discovered her passion for floristry while working at a flower shop during university. She eventually established her own business, which now has locations on Paulay Ede utca and Teréz körút.

Meanwhile, Şükran Dalmış, the owner of Chimney Cake Point, developed an appreciation for Hungarian street food culture during her four years in Budapest. She was particularly drawn to kürtőskalács, or chimney cake, and decided to establish a business around the traditional dessert. “Chimney cake is such an iconic, warm, and joyful dessert here,” she said.

The work that goes into everyday conveniences

At Central Market Hall, Andy’s daily responsibilities include checking stock, attending to customers, and replenishing merchandise. He explained that spending nine hours on his feet without a break can be physically exhausting. Customer interactions also require patience, particularly when he encounters unpleasant behaviour or attempted theft.

Source: Alina Hogertz, Jean Felix Muhire, Kate Berbano, Marla Enkhtaivan, and Sarah Salsabiila

Physical endurance is equally important in floristry. At Garden Rose, Niki explained that assembling large bouquets requires considerable strength. Even routine tasks can be demanding when vases filled with flowers and water weigh between 10 and 15 kilograms. For her, however, the most challenging aspect of running a flower shop is the paperwork. Administrative responsibilities take up time that she would otherwise devote to floral arrangements.

Source: Alina Hogertz, Jean Felix Muhire, Kate Berbano, Marla Enkhtaivan, and Sarah Salsabiila

Şükran faces similar responsibilities as a business owner. Apart from preparing chimney cakes and attending to customers, she must coordinate staff schedules, manage daily operations, and maintain the quality of her products during busy periods. She also works with a team of students.

At MTRM Roast, Csenge believes that one of the most important skills a barista must develop is the ability to balance speed and precision. Specialty coffee requires an understanding of beans, equipment, and preparation techniques, even when customers expect their drinks to be ready within minutes.

For Raymond, efficiency requires careful judgement on the road. Delivery riders must navigate traffic, locate unfamiliar addresses, and ensure that orders reach the correct customers. “Delivery work requires considerable mental and physical effort,” he said. Raymond explained that an order may weigh approximately 12 kilograms, while his delivery backpack can add another seven kilograms. If a building’s lift is out of service, he may have to carry the load up several flights of stairs. He must also remain friendly and professional when interacting with customers, regardless of physical exhaustion or personal difficulties.

A finished bouquet, a cup of coffee, or a meal delivered to someone’s doorstep reveals relatively little about the expertise, preparation and judgement required to provide it.

The unexpected rewards of a working day

At Central Market Hall, Andy recalled meeting a group of tourists who happened to share his enthusiasm for one of his favourite singers. They ended up singing her songs together at the market. “The customers themselves make the day more interesting,” he said.

Csenge has also developed an appreciation for the relationships formed through everyday transactions. She notices when regular customers have not visited for several days and even remembers when their dogs arrive in new sweaters. Through her work, she has found that Budapest residents who initially appear reserved often become more open and friendly through conversation. For her, cafés provide a space for the genuine human interaction that people continue to seek.

Şükran’s chimney cake business has similarly become a place where Hungarian customers and international visitors can enjoy a local culinary tradition. Among her favourite experiences is seeing regular customers return with friends or family to introduce them to their favourite chimney cake. “Those genuine smiles and people telling us it was the best part of their day make all the hard work worthwhile!” she said.

Source: Alina Hogertz, Jean Felix Muhire, Kate Berbano, Marla Enkhtaivan, and Sarah Salsabiila

For Niki, some of her most memorable experiences reflect her development as a florist and entrepreneur. A video of one of her early large bouquets attracted more than a million views on TikTok. Another achievement involved creating a flower basket measuring 80 centimetres in diameter. Despite the effort that goes into these arrangements, she believes their temporary nature is precisely what makes them valuable. “Flowers don’t last forever, and I think that’s what makes them so special. Their beauty is temporary, which makes every moment with them even more precious,” she said.

Raymond, meanwhile, finds satisfaction in knowing that his work helps people receive a meal when they need it. Delivery work has also taught him patience, independence, and how to make decisions under pressure. His daily journeys have given him a greater appreciation of Budapest’s infrastructure, public transport, and the coordination necessary to support everyday life in the capital.

Source: Alina Hogertz, Jean Felix Muhire, Kate Berbano, Marla Enkhtaivan, and Sarah Salsabiila

A portrait of Budapest at work

The five workers’ stories form part of Invisible Hands of Budapest, a documentary photography project developed by five master’s students at Corvinus University of Budapest. Through 15 black-and-white photographs and personal reflections, the project seeks to recognise the skills, efforts and contributions of people whose work often goes unnoticed.

The complete series will be presented on 3 December 2026 at CAPTU[RED], the first Corvinus Digital Media Festival. Under the theme “Recognise. Engage. Direct.”, the festival examines how visual media can capture attention and influence what audiences notice and value.

Budapest’s architecture, history, and cultural heritage have long defined its international reputation, but the experiences of these five individuals reveal another dimension of the Hungarian capital. Their stories speak of professional expertise, personal ambitions, and the value of everyday human interactions.

As Raymond observed, “One of the biggest things I have learned is that a well-functioning city does not happen by accident. It is built through planning, organisation, and coordination.”

World.title: Dubai-Hungary business ties strengthen as 22 Dubai companies visit Budapest
World.content:
Dubai-Hungary business ties are gaining momentum as economic cooperation between the two markets continues to expand. A delegation of 22 Dubai-based companies recently visited Budapest to explore new trade and investment opportunities, establish business partnerships and strengthen bilateral economic relations. The visit also saw the signing of four cooperation agreements with prominent Hungarian business organisations.

Dubai-Hungary business ties enter a new phase

According to a press release issued by the Dubai International Chamber on 27 November, the business mission brought together government officials, business leaders and representatives of Hungarian and Dubai-based companies.

The delegation represented a wide range of industries, including agriculture, construction, cosmetics, electronics, environmental services, food and beverages, information and communication technology, pharmaceuticals, biotechnology, and fashion.

As part of the visit, the Dubai International Chamber organised the Dubai-Hungary Business Connect forum in Budapest, providing companies with an opportunity to participate in direct business negotiations and explore potential joint ventures.

The event was organised in cooperation with the United Arab Emirates’ embassy in Budapest, Hungarian government institutions and several national business organisations.

Among the speakers were Mohammad Ali Rashed Lootah, President and CEO of Dubai Chambers; Rashid Al Tunaiji, the UAE’s ambassador to Hungary; and Elek Nagy, President of the Hungarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry.

If you missed it: Flydubai resumes Budapest flights as airline expands network to more than 125 destinations!

Four agreements signed to boost economic cooperation

During the forum, Dubai Chambers signed four memoranda of understanding with Hungarian organisations:

Hungarian Chamber of Commerce and Industry (MKIK)

Hungarian Export Promotion Agency (HEPA)

National Association of Entrepreneurs and Employers (VOSZ)

National Association of Young Entrepreneurs (FIVOSZ)

The agreements aim to strengthen commercial relations, facilitate cooperation between businesses and create new opportunities for companies seeking to enter each other’s markets.

Dubai-Hungary business ties strengthen as 22 Dubai companies visit Budapest. Photo credit: Dubai International Chamber

Lootah highlighted the importance of developing partnerships in international markets with significant growth potential. He explained that the Hungarian business mission was designed to facilitate the expansion of Dubai-based companies into Hungary while encouraging Hungarian businesses and investors to establish a presence in Dubai.

Hungarian business presence in Dubai grows by 720%

The latest figures indicate that Dubai-Hungary business ties have strengthened considerably in recent years.

Non-oil bilateral trade between Hungary and Dubai exceeded HUF 267 billion (approximately EUR 717 million, or AED 2.9 billion) in 2025, representing a year-on-year increase of 12.6%.

Meanwhile, the number of active Hungarian member companies registered with the Dubai Chamber of Commerce increased from just 30 at the end of 2020 to 246 by the end of 2025, marking a remarkable 720% increase over five years.

The upward trend continued in 2026, with a further 42 Hungarian companies joining the chamber during the first nine months of the year.

Another important milestone was the establishment of the Hungarian Business Council in March 2025 under the umbrella of the Dubai Chamber of Commerce. The organisation provides a platform for knowledge sharing, professional networking and the development of cross-border business partnerships.

Hungary and Dubai offer gateways to international markets

The Budapest forum also highlighted the strategic advantages both markets can offer international businesses.

Salem AlShamsi, Executive Vice President of International Relations at Dubai Chambers, presented Dubai’s competitive advantages and its extensive network of international business connections.

Dubai-Hungary business ties strengthen as 22 Dubai companies visit Budapest. Photo credit: Dubai International Chamber

As one of the United Arab Emirates’ major commercial hubs, Dubai can serve as a gateway for Hungarian companies seeking to expand into the Middle East, Africa and Asia.

Conversely, Hungary’s membership of the European Union and its location in Central Europe make it a potential entry point for Emirati businesses looking to establish operations within the European market.

Marcell Németh, Deputy CEO of the Hungarian Investment Promotion Agency (HIPA), outlined Hungary’s economic strengths, growing industries, investment incentives and strategic support mechanisms available to companies from the UAE.

Dubai has ambitious economic plans for 2033

The expansion of Dubai-Hungary business ties also aligns with Dubai’s broader economic development strategy.

The Dubai International Chamber, one of three chambers operating under Dubai Chambers, supports the objectives of the Dubai Economic Agenda (D33). The strategy aims to double the size of Dubai’s economy by 2033 and position the emirate among the world’s top three global cities.

Dubai-Hungary business ties strengthen as 22 Dubai companies visit Budapest. Photo credit: Dubai International Chamber

While the Budapest forum did not disclose specific investment commitments or the financial value of potential projects, the growing number of Hungarian companies operating in Dubai, rising bilateral trade and newly signed cooperation agreements point to increasingly close economic relations between the two markets.

World.title: Hungarian MÁV launches Advent Express trains for one-day Christmas market trips to European cities
World.content:
Hungarian State Railways (MÁV) is once again running its Advent Express special trains, offering passengers the chance to visit Christmas markets in neighbouring European countries and return home on the same day, without needing to book accommodation.

This year’s programme includes direct services to Olomouc in the Czech Republic and Zagreb in Croatia. The trains feature first- and second-class compartments, as well as a dining car operated by MÁV’s Utasellátó catering service, with seasonal food and drinks available on board.

The first journey departs Budapest’s Déli railway station for Olomouc on Saturday, 28 November, at 5.45am. Travelling via western Hungary, the train is scheduled to arrive at 11.31am. Passengers will have several hours to explore the city’s Christmas market, held in its Upper and Lower Squares, before the return departure at 5pm. The train is due back in Budapest at 11.34pm.

Olomouc offers more than festive stalls selling local food and crafts. Visitors can also see its UNESCO-listed Holy Trinity Column and the astronomical clock on the historic town hall.

Zagreb trips in December

The next MÁV Advent Express destination is Zagreb, with a special train from Budapest on 5 December. It will depart at 5.45am, travelling along the southern shore of Lake Balaton and through southern Zala County, before reaching the Croatian capital at 12.02pm. The return journey leaves Zagreb at 5.15pm, arriving in Budapest at 11.49pm.

A second Zagreb service will depart from Pécs on 12 December at 6.01am, reaching the city at 10.39am. It will leave Zagreb at 5.15pm and return to Pécs at 11pm.

Zagreb Christmas market. Photo: MÁV

Zagreb’s Advent celebrations spread across several central locations, including Ban Jelačić Square, Zrinjevac Park and King Tomislav Square, where a large outdoor ice rink is a major attraction. Visitors can also sample fritule, small doughnut-like pastries popular in Croatia.

Tickets include seat reservations and are available only as return journeys. Second-class adult fares start at €59, while children’s tickets cost from €44. First-class fares start at around HUF 29,000 (EUR 79) for adults and HUF 20,000 (EUR 54) for children. Tickets can be purchased through MÁV’s website or at railway ticket offices.

World.title: Hungary’s most expensive and cheapest streets revealed — with a 210-fold price gap
World.content:
Last year, average prices in Budapest’s Vérhalom Street exceeded HUF 3 million (EUR 8,120) per square metre, while homes in the cheapest streets sold for just HUF 34,000 (EUR 92). This year, nine of the 20 most expensive streets are around Lake Balaton.

Hungary’s most expensive residential streets saw prices of HUF 2–3 million per square metre in 2025, with the country’s priciest street breaking the HUF 3 million mark. Elsewhere, homes in some streets sold for only a few tens of thousands of forints per square metre.

The figures come from a new analysis by property website ingatlan.com, based on the Hungarian Central Statistical Office’s (KSH) latest property database for 2025 and ingatlan.com’s own listing data for this year.

The rising threshold for making the top 20 reflects how quickly prices increased. In 2024, an average price of HUF 1.89 million per square metre was enough to make the list. In 2025, the twentieth-ranked street, Napkelte Street in Budapest’s District XI, had an average price of more than HUF 2.2 million — an increase of over 17 per cent in a year, according to László Balogh, ingatlan.com’s chief economic expert.

Buda streets top last year’s rankings

According to KSH transaction data, Vérhalom Street in Budapest’s District II was Hungary’s most expensive street in 2025. Based on six sales, its average price exceeded HUF 3 million per square metre.

Kútvölgyi Road in District XII ranked second, at more than HUF 2.8 million, followed by Orom Street in District I, where the average exceeded HUF 2.6 million.

The top ten also included Muraközi Street and Budakeszi Road in District II, Bíró László József Boulevard in District XI, Széchenyi Street and Sas Street in central Pest, and Országház Street in the Buda Castle District. Average prices on these streets ranged from HUF 2.29 million to HUF 2.58 million per square metre.

The only location outside Budapest to make the top ten was Clementis László Street in Budaörs, with an average of HUF 2.405 million. No street around Lake Balaton made the top ten in 2025, unlike the previous year, when Balatonfüred was represented.

Buda Castle District. Budapest, Hungary. Photo by Unsplash

The cheapest streets had prices below HUF 50,000

The cheapest streets in 2025 were Orczy Street in Jánoshalma, Bács-Kiskun County, and Kossuth Lajos Street in Kisbér, Komárom-Esztergom County. Both recorded an average of HUF 34,000 per square metre.

Kossuth Street in Csanádpalota, Csongrád-Csanád County, ranked third at HUF 35,000. Each of the three streets had three sales behind its average.

The country’s ten cheapest streets also included locations in Ózd, Putnok, Salgótarján, Bátonyterenye, Gyöngyös, Mezőhegyes and Orosháza. Their average prices ranged from HUF 38,000 to HUF 49,000 per square metre.

Although the most expensive street reached a new record, the gap between the two extremes narrowed in 2025. In 2024, the average price in Levél Street in District II was almost 112 times that of Kölcsey Ferenc Street in Borsodnádasd. Last year, the difference between the most and least expensive streets was 88-fold.

There were also substantial price differences within Budapest. Csepel’s Vasas Street was the capital’s cheapest street in 2025, at HUF 438,000 per square metre. It was followed by Köztársaság Square in District XX, at HUF 537,000, and Mansfeld Péter Street in District XXI, at HUF 540,000. The gap between the most and least expensive streets in the capital was nearly sevenfold.

Lake Balaton dominates this year’s expensive-street list

For its 2026 ranking, ingatlan.com analysed residential property listings that had been removed from its website by 25 November. Unlike the 2025 list, which is based on completed sales and average prices, this ranking uses the median price per square metre of advertised properties.

The lakeside resort area features prominently: nine of the 20 most expensive streets are around Lake Balaton.

The national ranking is led by Pisky Promenade in Tihany, with a median price of HUF 5.25 million per square metre. March 15 Square in Budapest’s District V is second at HUF 4.43 million, followed by Árpád Part in Fonyód at HUF 4.37 million.

The top ten also includes Kitaibel Pál Street and Bolyai Street in Budapest’s District II, and Dobsinai Street in District XII. Lake Balaton is further represented by Széchenyi Square in Balatonfüred, Cserhegy in Tihany, Vasút Street in Ábrahámhegy and Szentmihályi Street in Balatonboglár. Median prices on these streets range from HUF 3.73 million to HUF 3.98 million per square metre. Six of this year’s ten most expensive streets are around the lake, and four are in Budapest.

The cheapest street this year is in Kövegy

At the other end of the 2026 ranking, Kossuth Lajos Street in Kövegy, Csongrád-Csanád County, has a median price of HUF 25,000 per square metre. Rákóczi Road in Tornaszentjakab, Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County, ranks second at HUF 27,000, followed by Széchenyi Street in Köröstarcsa, Békés County, at HUF 28,000.

Other streets among the cheapest include locations in Etes, Tiszalúc, Nagyér, Ambrózfalva, Kunmadaras, Katymár, Ecsegfalva and Nagybánhegyes. Their median prices range from HUF 32,000 to HUF 40,000 per square metre.

The difference between the most expensive and cheapest streets in this year’s listing is therefore 210-fold.

Csepel again has Budapest’s cheapest streets: median prices are HUF 407,000 per square metre in Liget Street and HUF 409,000 in Klapka Street.

Balogh said the regional disparities were also clear in the proportion of streets priced above the national average. In Budapest, 97 per cent of streets are above that level, while in some counties there are almost none. Within the capital, every street in District V is more expensive than the citywide average, while no street in Districts XXI and XXIII reaches it.

World.title: Hungary lifts entry ban on Ukrainian drone commander Robert “Magyar” Brovdi
World.content:
The three-year ban on the Ukrainian military commander, who is of Hungarian origin, has been removed from the immigration authority’s records.

Hungary has lifted the entry and residence ban on Robert Brovdi, a senior Ukrainian drone commander whose military callsign is “Magyar”, the Hungarian outlet Magyar Hang reported. The National Directorate-General for Aliens Policing (NDGAP) has deleted the ban from its system, according to the report.

Brovdi is the highest-ranking soldier of Hungarian origin serving in Ukraine’s armed forces. He was sentenced to life imprisonment in absentia by a Russian court.

The ban was announced in August 2025 by then Foreign Minister Péter Szijjártó, following attacks on the Druzhba oil pipeline. At the time, Szijjártó said the commander of the military unit responsible for the attacks would be barred from Hungary and the entire Schengen Area.

Brovdi responded angrily, telling Szijjártó to “shove” the sanctions, and accusing him of protecting his own interests rather than Hungarian sovereignty. He also alleged that Hungarian officials were benefiting from cheap raw materials subject to sanctions.

If you missed it: Hungary bans Transcarpathian Hungarian commander responsible for attack on Druzhba pipeline

How the ban was lifted

Magyar Hang contacted several ministries for an explanation and received a response from the Interior Ministry. The ministry said the Constitution Protection Office (AH) can propose imposing an independent entry and residence ban, and can also initiate its withdrawal if the national security risk no longer exists.

The process requires an opinion from the Information Office. If the relevant circumstances have significantly changed, the immigration authority may withdraw the ban or shorten its duration.

The NDGAP published a notice about Brovdi’s case on 18 November. It stated that the independent three-year entry and residence ban imposed on the Ukrainian citizen had been cancelled, and that the related warning had been removed from the immigration register.

Magyar Hang noted that the decision was made before Prime Minister Péter Magyar met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Transcarpathia earlier this week.

World.title: A country came together to save her: Young woman dies after being dragged by train at station
World.content:
The 18-year-old, who suffered life-threatening injuries in the incident on 24 November, died in hospital despite doctors’ efforts to save her.

The young woman who was dragged by a train at Mezőkövesd station on 24 November has died, the Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County Hospital announced on Friday afternoon.

In a statement, the hospital said she had died despite “all efforts made to aid her recovery, careful treatment and the full use of available therapeutic options”. It also thanked those who donated blood and offered help, and expressed its condolences to her family.

The woman, identified as Viviána in public statements, was taken to hospital in Miskolc with life-threatening injuries. Her condition was still critical on Friday morning, according to earlier reports.

Health Minister Zsolt Hegedűs expressed his condolences to the family, saying medical staff had fought heroically to save the young woman’s life. Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy also spoke by phone with her father, offering condolences on his own behalf and that of the MÁV Group. He urged people to refrain from political debate and allow the family to grieve.

Prime Minister Péter Magyar had also expressed his sympathy on Thursday, when the young woman was still in critical condition, and wished her a recovery. He said the National Blood Supply Service had confirmed that enough blood had been made available through targeted donations.

Investigation into the circumstances continues

According to preliminary information, the woman’s bag may have become caught in the doors of an InterCity train as she was getting off, and the train then dragged her along. Police in Borsod-Abaúj-Zemplén County told Telex they were investigating the incident as an offence involving the endangerment of railway transport. The circumstances are still being established.

Police in Mezőkövesd and the county issued a public appeal on Thursday, asking witnesses to come forward. They said several people who were at the station may have seen what happened.

Station cameras reportedly recorded the incident

Earlier accounts suggested that cameras on the train and at the station were not working, but that footage from a Volán bus had captured the incident. MÁV later confirmed that station surveillance cameras had recorded it.

According to a report by 24.hu, which obtained a MÁV report, three surveillance cameras captured the incident. The outlet’s account of the footage said the train doors appeared to reopen after the train had begun moving. It reported that one passenger had initially got off the train and walked towards the bus station, after which the doors closed around 18–19 seconds later.

The report said ticket inspectors, having seen no passengers boarding or leaving, gave the departure signal and returned to the train. Footage reportedly showed the door-warning light flashing for three seconds before a person ran through the carriage towards the rear door.

According to 24.hu, people on the platform noticed what was happening, but by the time the signal was changed to red and the driver was contacted, the train had already accelerated to around 100 km/h. Telex said a source familiar with the matter confirmed that the footage showed the sequence described by the outlet.

Vitézy has also said the incident highlights the need to renew Hungary’s railway fleet. He noted that, although the train was operating as an InterCity service, it included an older carriage that could not check whether its doors were closed in the same way as newer vehicles or prevent departure until they were shut.

Several other politicians and public officials, including the Speaker of the National Assembly, members of the Tisza parliamentary group, ministers and MÁV Group chief executive Zsolt Hegyi, have also expressed their condolences to the family.

World.title: Budapest shopping centre passage closed overnight? Corvin Plaza says corridor remains available via security intercom
World.content:
The shopping centre’s operator says pedestrians can still pass between Kisfaludy and Futó streets at night by contacting security through a dedicated intercom. The clarification follows a report about a customer who was unable to reach the underground car park.

Corvin Plaza’s operator, Indotek Group, has disputed claims that the Budapest shopping centre is closed to pedestrians overnight, saying that passage remains available outside regular opening hours with the assistance of security staff.

In a statement sent to our editorial team, the company said people wishing to cross between Kisfaludy and Futó streets at night can use a dedicated intercom to contact the shopping centre’s security team. Security personnel then open the doors and supervise their passage through the building.

The operator also stressed that the underground car park remains accessible 24 hours a day. If necessary, security staff personally accompany customers to the parking facilities.

Operator says reported incident involved a misunderstanding

The clarification follows a report by Józsefváros Újság about a customer who was unable to access the underground car park early in the morning. According to the account, the woman was told there was a power outage and subsequently faced additional costs after having to take a taxi. Her request for reimbursement was reportedly rejected.

Indotek Group said the incident resulted from a misunderstanding: the customer had contacted the intercom of the neighbouring office building rather than the one used to reach Corvin Plaza’s security team. The operator emphasised that the office building’s staff are not responsible for providing overnight access to the shopping centre’s underground car park.

However, the company also acknowledged that the customer was not told she had contacted the wrong facility and was not directed to the appropriate intercom. Indotek Group said it regretted the inconvenience caused.

If you missed it: Budapest’s festive light tram fleet brings Christmas to the streets

Municipality previously referred to 24-hour access obligation

The issue also concerns an agreement between the shopping centre’s operator and the local municipality. According to the municipality, the agreement requires the passage between Kisfaludy and Futó streets to remain accessible around the clock. The local authority said it would call on the operator to comply with this obligation.

In its latest statement, Indotek Group maintains that overnight pedestrian access is provided, but requires visitors to contact security through the designated intercom.

The reported incident and the operator’s explanation point to a practical issue that visitors should be aware of: anyone wishing to pass through the shopping centre or reach its underground car park at night should contact Corvin Plaza’s own security team, rather than the neighbouring office building.

World.title: Tisza’s lead over Fidesz widens as poll finds opposition party in deep crisis
World.content:
The Republikon Institute’s November poll puts Tisza ahead of Fidesz-KDNP by 67 to 23 per cent among decided voters who say they will vote, while two-thirds of respondents doubt Fidesz-KDNP can recover.

The gap between Tisza and Fidesz-KDNP widened in November, according to a new poll by the Republikon Institute, commissioned by Kontroll.hu. Tisza gained two percentage points and Fidesz-KDNP lost two among the general population, putting the parties at 56 and 20 per cent respectively.

Among decided voters who say they will vote, Tisza leads 67 to 23 per cent. The institute estimates that Tisza has around 4.25 million supporters, compared with approximately 1.5 million for Fidesz-KDNP.

The representative survey was conducted with 1,000 respondents. Republikon said Fidesz-KDNP’s current support amounts to around two-thirds of its share of the domestic party-list vote in the April election, while Tisza’s support has risen sharply since then.

Two-thirds doubt Fidesz-KDNP can recover

The poll also asked respondents whether Fidesz-KDNP could recover from its current low level of support. Around two-thirds said a comeback was impossible or unlikely, while only a quarter believed the party alliance could regain strength.

Even among Fidesz-KDNP supporters, only a quarter were confident that the party could recover, according to the survey.

Republikon argued that, six months after the election, Tisza would have a two-thirds majority even under a fully proportional electoral system. The institute described Fidesz-KDNP as being in a “crisis” and said the election result represented more than a temporary setback.

Photo: MTI/Máthé Zoltán

Most respondents see corruption as systemic

The survey also asked whether recent corruption cases that received significant media attention were isolated actions by individual politicians or part of systemic corruption within Fidesz-KDNP.

Sixty per cent of respondents said they reflected systemic corruption, while 22 per cent viewed them as isolated cases.

Opinions were sharply divided along party lines. Among Tisza supporters, 88 per cent said the cases were part of systemic corruption. By contrast, 57 per cent of Fidesz-KDNP supporters considered them isolated incidents.

Mi Hazánk loses support

Mi Hazánk lost one percentage point across each of the poll’s voter categories compared with October. It stood at 6 per cent among the general population and 7 per cent among both party voters and decided voters who say they will vote.

Other parties were supported by 3 per cent of the general population and 4 per cent of decided voters who say they will vote. The share of undecided respondents remained unchanged at 15 per cent.

World.title: Week in Review: Between Transformation and Evolution
World.content:
As Serbian citizens and regional observers watch for signs of what to expect from the Student List as it assumes power in Belgrade, one important piece of the jigsaw remains the new government’s approach to Kosovo. During the campaign, the student movement made repeated references to Serbia’s constitutional claim to Kosovo.

Ian Bancroft tackles the question of what to expect. He cautions against expectations of radical transformation and believes space exists either for an improvement in relations, or for even more gridlock. Which path will be taken?
