World.title: €100 Million Investment for New Jadrolinija Fleet Launched
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – A €100 euro investment for a new Jadrolinija fleet has now been launched, with 10 brand new vessels planned.

Part of the tenders for the construction of new ships has already been published and is in the implementation phase. Sinisa Malus reports for Poslovni that the Minister of Maritime Affaits, Transport and Infrastructure Oleg Butković stated this week that the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija is now ready. He added that the accompanying contracts will soon be signed for the implementation of the shore power supply system for ships at the Brajdica and Zagrebačka obala container terminals in Rijeka.

fleet modernisation

“Jadrolinija is going into recapitalisation, that is ready. We are going in two directions – with the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija and with the World Bank. Part of the tenders for the construction of new ships has already been published and is in the implementation phase, so Jadrolinija expects to sign contracts for the construction of new ships next year,” Butković revealed. Unofficially, it has been learn edthat the recapitalisation of Jadrolinija should be worth up to €100 million. It is closely linked to modernisation and should secure Jadrolinija’s financial position until 2043. It is a combination of different sources. Jadrolinija Management Board President Robert Blažinović revealed to us that the tenders should be published by the end of November.

“I think that within the next ten days or so we will also proceed to contracting the construction of the first ship,” Blažinović told us. This was preceded by a competitive procedure with negotiations for construction and design. Jadrolinija’s strategy of building ships with alternative propulsion and electric propulsion is well known, and the locations where they will sail have been determined in advance – the Šibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik areas. The ships with alternative and electric propulsion will sail in the waters around Šibenik, Zadar and Dubrovnik.

alternative fuel vessels

Blažinović revealed that the Ministry of Transport has established very active cooperation with the World Bank and the International Finance Corporation (IFC). It has been known for some time that the company has a mandate letter with the IFC, which is working with Jadrolinija on preparing a sustainable financing model for the fleet renewal programme, as well as on assessing projects from the financial, technical, environmental and organisational aspects. We’re talking about a programme that can cover up to ten new ships and represents one of the largest investment phases in the recent history of this state-owned company. At the same time, the possibility of co-financing from EU funds in the segment of green technologies is also opening up, where maximum co-financing can be secured.

“The new ships should bring greater energy efficiency, reliability and comfort, with capacities adapted to the needs of individual lines. At the same time, we must continue investing in the existing fleet, digitalisation and the knowledge of our employees in order to maintain a leading position in maritime passenger transport and continue building the trust of passengers that we have been gaining for eight decades. The greatest challenge will be to align the scope of the necessary investments with the financial sustainability of operations. The green transition requires significant capital, but its implementation also depends on the availability of alternative fuels and the development of appropriate infrastructure. Jadrolinija must be business-efficient and competitive while at the same time ensuring the connectivity on which the daily life of islanders, the local economy and tourism depend. Our transformation is therefore part of a broader development strategy,” Robert Blažinović concluded.

World.title: New Pension Increases Announced for Croatian Retirees in 2027
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – Further pension increases have been announced for Croatian retirees in 2027, commenting on their previous growth and on the economy.

Prime Minister Andrej Plenković commented on the growth of pensions and the societal position of pensioners, emphasising that both wages and pensions have risen in the recent period, and announced additional changes that come into force from 2027. Poslovni reports that Croatia will apparently achieve economic growth of around 2.4 percent this year. During the terms of the current Government, absolute GDP has increased from €47 billion to €101 billion. Today, 1.76 million people are employed in Croatia, while the number of unemployed is around 70,000.

Plenković emphasised that as of the 1st of January 2027, the payment of income tax by pensioners is being abolished, which will further increase pensions for more than 540,000 pensioners. In November, 571,945 pensioners paid almost €20 million in tax into the budgets of cities and municipalities, or an average of €34.62 per pensioner. The opposition has warned that by tax relief for some pensioners the Croatian Government will shift the cost onto local budgets.

The state budget for 2027, presented in the Croatian Parliament, according to the Prime Minister’s words also has an important role in preserving social cohesion. The Government plans to allocate around €11 billion for pensions, which is €875 million more than this year.

wage growth will be reflected in pension growth

Plenković recalled that in recent years, Croatia has faced major external shocks and crises, as well as the devastating earthquakes in Zagreb and Banovina. €5.3 billion has so far been allocated for reconstruction. Croatia has recorded 22 consecutive quarters of economic growth, and projections for next year envisage growth of 2.1 percent. A budget deficit of 2.9 percent and a slowdown in inflation to 2.7 percent on an annual basis are also expected. Such trends should enable further growth in the wages of employees in public services, agreed with the trade unions. The wage base will increase by three percent as of the 1st of January 2027, and as of the 1st of April a meal allowance of €30 is being introduced. This will be followed by an additional one-percent increase in the base from 1 August and an increase in the meal allowance by a further €20 as of the 1st of October. Wage growth in the public sector will also be reflected in pensions through their regular adjustment.

World.title: Croatia Can Expect €15.9 Billion in Revenue From Tourism
World.content:
November the 27th, 2026 – Croatia can expect to bring in €15.9 billion in revenue from tourism alone, with the prime minister discussing the second most important visitors.

Croatia should finish this year with slightly better tourism results than it recorded last year, and the value of fiscalised invoices is growing significantly faster than the number of invoices issued. Croatia should end 2026 with approximately €15.9 billion in tourism revenue, around 22 million tourist arrivals and 110 million overnight stays, Prime Minister Andrej Plenković stated on this week at a government session.

Reflecting on the results presented during last week’s Days of Croatian Tourism (Dani hrvatskog turizma) in Poreč, the Prime Minister emphasised that positive movements were recorded this year both in arrivals and overnight stays, as well as in the value of tourist spending. According to the data presented at that event, during the first ten months 21.3 million arrivals and 109 million overnight stays were recorded, representing growth of two percent in arrivals and one percent in overnight stays compared with the same period last year.

an 18% increase in fiscalised invoices in tourism

Particularly notable is the growth in the value of fiscalised invoices in the tourism sector. In the first ten months of the year, invoices worth approximately €8.6 billion were fiscalised, which is 18 percent more than in the same period of 2025. At the same time, around 410.4 million invoices were issued, or six percent more than last year. The value of invoices is thus growing significantly faster than their number, which points to an increase in the average fiscalised amount. A distinction should be made here between fiscalised turnover and revenue from foreign tourists, which is recorded separately in the statistics of the Croatian National Bank.

croatian tourists are now right behind the germans

Plenković particularly singled out the importance of domestic guests for Croatian tourism. According to him, Croatian tourists occupy second place among the most important tourist markets, right behind guests from Germany. Data presented at the Days of Croatian Tourism show that domestic guests recorded approximately 3.1 million arrivals and 13.6 million overnight stays this year. The Prime Minister also emphasised the importance of further investments in the development of continental tourism, especially projects that connect healthcare services, rehabilitation and the tourist offer. The government expects the continuation of positive trends during the post-season as well, along with preparations for the next tourist year. Although the final financial result for 2026 still needs to be confirmed, the indicators so far point to another year of growth for Croatian tourism.

World.title: Professor: Bad experiences with the system fuel belief in conspiracy theories
World.content:
Conspiracy theories spread easily during crises, and officials should admit when they do not have all the answers, says University of Tartu folklorist Anastasiya Astapova.

Astapova, recently appointed professor of folklore studies at the university, notes that personal anecdotes from acquaintances can often outweigh hard science and can also stem from poorly felt interactions with the state.

People who believe in conspiracy theories are more likely to have had a bad experience with the education, healthcare, or another state system.

Anyone who already believes one conspiracy theory is likely to be credulous of many more.

The state and public authorities should have the courage during a crisis to admit honestly when they, too, are in the dark.

Even the most solidly grounded science-based information always competes in people's minds with personal anecdotes from the people they know.

Folklore studies as a discipline can help states combat disinformation, by studying how rumors and conspiracy theories propagate.

People's actual behavior during a crisis can be predicted by studying the views circulating among the public.

At the end of October, as a newly appointed professor of folklore studies, you delivered your inaugural lecture on the links between folklore and security. Congratulations on that. What does becoming a professor mean to you personally, and what doors does it open?

That is a very good question. We always have fantasies on the one hand and reality on the other. The reality in this new post does not change, and it does not mean there are suddenly many more opportunities. Even as a professor, everything depends on how hard you push: how much work you do, how many projects you apply for, and how many of those projects you win. A professor's workload can even be heavier.

In fact, it makes you think about what is coming next. Let's be honest: you cannot go much further than professor, and that makes you look for what else is viable. Which projects have you still not won, and which collaborations have you still not done? There is a lot you can do, so what do you choose and why? It is somewhat of an existential question.

Turning to the substance of your lecture and your broader research, you primarily study conspiracy theories. Is their emergence in society inevitable? If rumors arise because people are trying to make sense of the world but with limited information, isn't it much the same case with conspiracy theories?

Both rumors and conspiracy theories are actually a paradoxical phenomenon. I once studied both in the context of Chernobyl, for example. There, everything was very simple: there was no information at all. The state shared nothing whatsoever, so people looked for answers about what was happening and how to cope on their own. That is how rumors and conspiracy theories emerged there.

Today, however, it is interesting because the reverse is true: there is so much information. Yet in this environment, both rumors and conspiracy theories are arguably even more popular than before. So it does not depend on whether there is too little or too much information. I like to say that they are the fairy tales of our time, so to speak. That is the genre of our era.

University of Tartu Professor of folklore studies Anastasiya Astapova. Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

If it is not due to a lack of information, why do conspiracy theories still emerge? Are certain groups in society just somehow more susceptible to them?

In my view, it is a myth that some people believe them more than others — especially when it comes to education level. It may seem to us that people with lower levels of education believe conspiracy theories much more readily than those with stronger analytical thinking. That is not always the case, however, and it depends heavily on the area. For instance, certain conspiracy theories appeal even to people with PhDs — such as those related to vaccinations.

"Personally, I would say that belief [in conspiracy theories] is always linked to some kind of bad experience."

From a gender perspective, it is the same story: there is a widespread myth that believers in conspiracy theories are mostly men at lower education levels. In reality, that may not be the case. More and more studies show that women play a major role here too. Those same vaccine-related theories, for example, are definitely more of a female genre.

So none of this is black and white, and every academic discipline weighs in from its own angle. Psychologists, for instance, say narcissistic people believe conspiracy theories more often: they think along the lines of, "I am the chosen one and nobody else gets what is going on." Others point out that very smart people believe conspiracies because they know how to construct a system and have a mindset conducive to belief.

Personally, I would say that such belief is always linked to some kind of negative experience. If a person has had an unpleasant encounter with a system — the healthcare system, the education system, state authorities, whatever it may be — they are more likely to start believing them. Research has shown that once they believe them, that belief grows stronger over time.

Take, for example, someone who denies that humans ever really landed on the moon. It seems harmless — let them believe it, it's no big deal, it doesn't affect anything. Yet it is not that straightforward: such a person will certainly believe other things as well, and over time they accumulate more and more conspiracy theories.

Let's think back to the crises that have hit Estonia, Europe, and the world over the past decade. We already mentioned the coronavirus pandemic and vaccination indirectly, but which crises caused conspiracy theories to flourish most?

The pandemic was of course the biggest explosion. As I can clearly see from my own research, Russia's war against Ukraine immediately came to the fore as well.

I had a research project examining how people behaved during the pandemic and how conspiracy theories shaped their behavior. In March 2022, I began interviewing people who had chosen not to get vaccinated. They immediately told me: hold on, vaccination is important of course, but that is not all — it is part of a larger plan. That the war is also part of that plan, and the pandemic was merely the initial experiment on humanity.

According to this theory, the organizers of that experiment are observing, to see whether we behave as expected. If they tell us to put on a mask, do we put it on? If they tell us to support the Ukrainian people, do we support them? Whatever crisis comes along, it is all connected.

Looking back, can we say the crisis communication was poor? With the benefit of hindsight, could anything have been done differently to stop these theories from spreading like that?

In Estonia, communication during the coronavirus pandemic was very straightforward and clear, in my opinion. I also liked that it was very simple — there was no superfluous information. Sometimes, less is more.

Perhaps both in Estonia and in science more broadly, it would be good to show how we sometimes do not know things. We should say so honestly, rather than asserting with certainty that this is what the virus is like and this is what we are going to do. We should admit honestly that we do not know 100 percent what is going on. When the state or any institution speaks honestly about this, there may be a bit more trust. Unfortunately, there is no single recipe here.

Anastasiya Astapova. Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

As you pointed out, the next major crisis after the pandemic was the war in Ukraine. You have studied Estonia's Russian-speaking community in connection with this. To what extent did the war provide fertile ground for conspiracy theories among them?

At first, their belief in various theories was quite strong, as my research demonstrated. Nowadays I can no longer say anything. I had recruited participants for this study, but they will no longer speak to me because they are afraid. In one way or another, it became an embarrassing and painful topic. Perhaps they are also accompanied by a fear that they are not allowed to say what they really think. I will say honestly that I no longer have access to that community, and the situation is ethically very complex. I also published an article about this in the journal Baltic Worlds, where I state openly that as researchers, we do not know.

In a way, their silence is not a bad thing either. If this talk is not as public as it used to be, perhaps it will not spread further.

In your inaugural lecture, you also highlighted the espionage case a couple of years ago involving former University of Tartu professor Vyacheslav Morozov. How did that come onto your radar, and what conspiracy theories did it spark?

I didn't even hear about it from the news. I hadn't even opened the news yet when a Russian-speaking scholar working at a Western university wrote to me saying something like: "What is going on at the University of Tartu, have you gone crazy? He is a big-name professor — what do you mean, in prison?"

Facebook's algorithm immediately began serving me posts from academics with a similar profile asking the exact same thing. They claimed it was Russophobia and asked why Morozov had been fired when he had not yet been officially found guilty: where was the presumption of innocence? In fact, that happened specifically because the University of Tartu failed to mention in its press release that Morozov himself had submitted a letter of resignation.

"Perhaps both in Estonia and in science more broadly, it would be good to show how we sometimes do not know things."

The University of Tartu did correct this later, by the way, but nobody reads corrections anymore. What sticks in people's minds is what was there at the beginning. Or else people start wondering: where did that correction come from? That must mean something really was wrong. That is how the idea takes hold that this is Russophobia and a witch hunt, and that the man was imprisoned simply because he is Russian-speaking. After all, he is a scholar and was a major authority. To my knowledge, Morozov and I have never met in our lives, yet I think even my own first reaction was denial — how could it be?

After that, I monitored social media on both Facebook and Twitter. One scholar from Georgia wrote on Twitter that a spy does not hand you a business card listing "spy" as their profession. Perhaps that is precisely what makes a good spy — someone nobody suspects at all.

It was an interesting case because some of the posts were outright classically imperialist. People who proclaim themselves liberals and say Russia's actions in Ukraine are completely wrong expressed very bitter views about Estonia in their posts.

Whether it is a pandemic, a war, or an espionage case, the question remains: who do people trust amid information confusion? Does the word of a neighbor, a TV host from a neighboring country, or the prime minister, carry more weight?

Great question. If we think about those same vaccination rumors or conspiracy theories, you can have any statistics and science you want at your fingertips. Suppose, however, that at the same time you have an acquaintance who in turn has an acquaintance whose child spoke wonderfully at age two, like a three-year-old. Then the child got a shot, and all of that disappeared: the child no longer speaks at all and became autistic. Such an emotional, personal story will carry far more impact than any science. You may not even know the person, but if it happened to a friend of a friend, it has a 100 percent impact.

A situation like that certainly makes crisis communication harder. How can folkloristics, classically a text-centered branch of the humanities, help policymakers or public authorities here?

Quite a bit has already been done in this area, though much more remains to be done. In my lecture, I also spoke about the University of Tartu's first professor of folklore, Walter Anderson. He conducted an experiment on the transmission of rumors, looking at what stays and what disappears.

His results were interesting, and social psychologists have done a great deal of similar work since. Yet we could go further and examine the spread of stories from the very beginning in a real-world context. What happens, for example, in Estonia as a country that fears war? What happens in Finland, where constant preparations and waiting are underway? When a rumor emerges, what becomes of it?

"In my view, we folklorists are major players on the topic of disinformation — researchers studying misinformation around the world welcome us very warmly."

Even more importantly, what happens if someone intervenes? What happens when a story is reframed — for instance, if someone makes a joke about it? How does it depend on who exactly deals with the rumor? If the state says something to counter a rumor, does it actually work? In other words, the idea would be to examine the exact life cycle of a rumor against the backdrop of what is done to counter it.

Very little of this has been done, and it could be studied in contexts like Estonia or Ukraine as well as in an academic context, which is supposedly the domain of experts. Can academics tell what is a rumor and what is not? My research shows that we, too, are only human.

Rumor studies can also be conducted in the lab, so that transmission is not tied to any specific context. You could take six people, for example, who pass rumors to one another, and then introduce interventions: say, someone makes a joke about the rumor. How do they react then?

Anastasiya Astapova Source: Airika Harrik/ERR

So, figuratively speaking, we are talking about laboratory folkloristics.

Yes, exactly. Walter Anderson actually did just that — perhaps not directly in a lab; using students instead, but he did it as best he could, a hundred years ago, at the University of Tartu. Today, it is studied in laboratories though.

I think a folkloristic approach to the spread of rumors and conspiracy theories would be quite useful, because we have extensive experience and these topics are being studied more and more within folklore studies. In my view, we folklorists are major players when it comes to the topic of disinformation — researchers studying misinformation around the world tend to welcome us very warmly.

So far we have been focusing on conspiracy theories, yet you are also a humor researcher. If the public's reaction to a crisis were a coin with conspiracy theories on one side, would we find a flood of memes on the other, brighter side?

Yes, when there is a crisis, as we saw during the pandemic, conspiracy theories spread on one side and memes on the other. Sometimes they are intertwined: people poke fun at conspiracy theorists, and conspiracy theorists fire back — it can become a debate in its own right.

"When there is a crisis, as we saw during the pandemic, conspiracy theories spread on one side and memes on the other."

Right now, together with our Nordic colleagues, we are starting to edit a book titled "Conspiracy Theories and Humor." For years, several people have told me that the two are strongly connected and wondered why nothing has been written about it yet. Now we are taking it on.

The book's authors will thoroughly investigate whether humor actually helps against disinformation or not. Once again, it is very context-dependent: everything depends on the people involved and whether humor is being used for prevention or rebuttal. Why do we run so many media literacy training sessions in schools, for example? That is prevention, and using humor there is very helpful. When dealing with someone who already believes a conspiracy, however, joking is very risky — humor is tricky in that situation and can spark bigger conflicts.

What is the psychological function of crisis humor? How much does it differ between countries with different political systems, such as democratic Estonia and authoritarian Belarus?

That function is very different. There are many theories here, and none of them explains every context. For instance, George Orwell said that every joke is a tiny revolution. Yet that is only one theory trying to explain why jokes are told. We know of no event in the world where a real revolution broke out because of a joke or humor.

Others, following Sigmund Freud, say that in a joke we say what we dare not say in any other way. Yet why say it at all if you could be punished for it? Why not say something else that is not so problematic?

Then there is the null hypothesis, which holds that it makes no difference whether we sing or tell a joke, because we simply want to express ourselves through some narrative and genre. Again: why not sing something less problematic, then? Why specifically tell a joke?

"The problem with conspiracy theories is precisely that nobody listens to the people who believe them."

In my own research, I have also shown how the function of humor in Belarus can be completely different. I demonstrated how humor that may appear anti-dictatorship actually reinforces that dictatorship. In such cases, the joke serves as a constant reminder to people that the situation is frightening — you may tell a joke, sure, but you have to keep your mouth shut.

I don't know how things are in Belarus right now, of course, since I haven't been there in a long time. When I did visit and conduct research, however, alongside regular jokes I heard jokes about fear and even jokes about jokes. There were so many of them that a kind of meta-level emerged.

One illuminating joke that I also told in my lecture dates back to the Soviet Union, yet still circulates in Belarus today. Someone calls the KGB and hurls all kinds of insults at them because they are so fed up with the whole situation. They end the call by saying: "And you don't know how to do your job at all!" As soon as they hang up, someone taps them on the shoulder and says: "We do the best we can." What else is such a joke if not a reminder that you are always being watched?

We already touched on crisis communication, but as a folklore researcher, do you have any more advice for decision-makers, politicians, or society at large on coping with such tense times?

I think we folklorists have a very long history of listening to people: we go around, sit down, and record interviews. Sometimes these are elderly people who talk for hours and hours. Yet we stay there and transcribe everything very carefully in order to hear what people are saying — especially now that transcription has become so easy.

I would recommend the same approach to decision-makers, politicians, and institutions. You shouldn't rely solely on questionnaires with "yes," "no," "I don't know," or "I'm not sure" answers, because that doesn't help all that much. What matters more are personal stories, which vary greatly from person to person. Those stories could also be published in some way so that all kinds of people in Estonia are heard. On television, for example, you could show how different people live and what their concerns are.

The problem with conspiracy theories is precisely that nobody listens to the people who believe them. Why was it so easy for me to record interviews about vaccine skepticism? Because I was perhaps the first person willing to listen. Even those people's relatives may not have wanted to hear it or talk about it, or they may have overreacted. It then turned out that every single one of them had some very sad experience that nobody wanted to know anything about.

I understand that listening like that takes a great deal of energy. Today, however, we live in the age of artificial intelligence, where — while of course complying with data protection rules and anonymizing data beforehand using specialized software where necessary — observations can be systematized and summarized more easily, tracked and compiled without having to read an entire interview, for example. Different perspectives emerge from people's stories. In folklore studies, we have historically listened to marginalized people as well, such as minorities or those who believe UFOs exist. We still recorded their stories, looked at them, and asked why things were that way — others can do the same.

Now that your professorship has officially begun, what do you plan to research next? What is currently underway, and what else would you like to find out?

First, I am currently writing a major ERC project proposal related to rumors: tracking rumors both in the laboratory and in real life.

My second plan involves gendered conspiracy theories. Historically, the world still pays more attention to men. At the same time, there are many things related to women that we do not know about. In the Estonian context, for example, Triin Laisk, who researches endometriosis and hormones, is doing wonderful pioneering work. We know very little about women's health, and historically all those hormones were dismissed as some kind of "crazy woman" issue.

"The way people behave in a crisis depends on the public's perspective."

Yet I am interested not only in how and what women themselves believe, but also in how they cope in situations where, say, men believe conspiracy theories and go down the rabbit hole, figuratively speaking. Often it is the woman who keeps the peace in the family when an uncle, husband, or father believes something like that. In fact, some studies have shown that when someone in a family goes down the rabbit hole, their family members experience symptoms similar to post-traumatic stress disorder. I am interested in how women cope with that.

My third endeavor is about listening to people. Security experts have mostly focused on the elite — what politicians think will happen. I, however, am interested specifically in the people's perspective. For example, if a crisis occurs in Estonia, it is great if the Estonian state delivers a very clear message, but what do people actually believe? Perhaps what their neighbor says — which direction the Russians are coming from or which way they will move, compared to what the state tells them.

In academic literature, this is called the vernacular or people's perspective. It is actually the most important factor, because the way people behave in a crisis depends on the public's perspective. We saw this in Ukraine too, when experts said Kyiv would fall in three days, yet people are still holding out today. Nobody could foresee that precisely because the people's perspective was unfamiliar to them.

World.title: Elections chief: Mobile voting still possible in future despite court ban
World.content:
Lede: Mobile voting will not be available in next spring's Riigikogu elections, though development will continue and voters will eventually be able to cast ballots via the app, State Electoral Office head Arne Koitmäe told ETV.

The Supreme Court on Friday overturned a National Electoral Committee (VVK) decision that would have permitted mobile voting for the first time in next spring's Riigikogu elections, ruling that relying on foreign-owned app stores to distribute voting software is unlawful.

Preparations for mobile voting are complete. Will all that work now go to waste?

A lot of work has gone into this, and it was necessary to ensure all the systems we use in elections are secure and up to date. We designed the mobile voting app to meet legal requirements and to be secure and reliable. In its ruling today, however, the Supreme Court found that distribution must also be entirely under our control. That is impossible with Apple's and Google's app stores as they currently operate.

Did that come as a surprise, or was there work left undone? How do you see it?

App stores, app downloads, and updates have been in focus for several years. We audited the apps and found that their integrity can be verified and is being maintained, though verifying it is far from straightforward. As we see it, we need to pause and pick this up after the election.

Does that mean you'll still move ahead with mobile voting? Do you think it's possible to address the Supreme Court's concern that distributing the app through Apple and Google is risky or beyond your control?

We'll definitely be looking into it. It is hard for me to say now what the answer will be. Technology is constantly evolving, and changes or updates come out every day.

Do you think people will be able to vote on a smart device in the future?

I surely do. Mobile phones have become an everyday tool that people use for important tasks, and in that sense there are no fundamental barriers. The mobile app works exactly the same way as the desktop app. We'll come back to it later.

So voting in the March election will work as it always has done?

Yes. People will be able to vote electronically or by paper ballot. You can mark down March 1–7.

Background:

In partly upholding a complaint filed by election observer Märt Põder and NGO Ausad Valimised, the Supreme Court found that distributing voting applications via Google Play and Apple's App Store under their standard terms would leave critical election infrastructure outside Estonia's legal oversight. While the ruling blocks voting via Android and iOS devices, traditional computer-based online voting — as well as mobile vote-verification apps — remains permitted. Estonia's next Riigikogu elections are scheduled to take place from March 1, when advance voting commences, with polling day to follow on Sunday, March 7, 2027.

World.title: Mystery object that sparked Pärnu bomb squad alert turns out to be research balloon
World.content:
Emergency services temporarily closed a stretch of road in Pärnu on Friday after a suspicious white balloon came down near the Papiniidu Bridge, Pärnu Postimees reported .

However, the falling object, whose response also led to the halting of nearby ongoing construction work, later turning out to be a harmless research balloon belonging to an Estonian tech firm

The Emergency Response Center received a report at a little before 2 p.m. on Friday, November 27, that an unidentified balloon had landed beside Liivi tee in the eastern edge of Pärnu, Rescue Center spokesperson Anu Paumer told the paper.

Rescue crews, explosive ordnance disposal technicians, and police responded to the scene, with roughly a dozen emergency vehicles deployed. While bomb disposal specialists worked to identify the object, authorities closed Liivi tee to both motor vehicles and pedestrians and diverted traffic via Riia mnt. and the Papiniidu intersection.

Work was also temporarily suspended at the nearby Rail Baltica railway bridge construction site, according to the paper.

Around two hours later, authorities confirmed that the 1.5-meter-diameter balloon belonged to an Estonian technology company and was being used for research and development when it made an unscheduled landing in the area, Russian-language "Aktuaalne kaamera" reported. "This balloon posed no danger to the public," Paumer added.

The original Pärnu Postimees piece is here.

World.title: Kersti Kaljulaid: It is possible to give up violence
World.content:
For many, the process of healing begins simply with recognizing that certain patterns of behavior, some dating back to their own childhood, are manipulative and abusive, writes Kersti Kaljulaid.

November 25 was the International Day for the Elimination of Violence Against Women, but there is only so much you can accomplish in a day. That is why, for us at the President Kaljulaid Foundation, this date marked the beginning of the Orange Weeks. This is now the fourth year we have held them. The color orange symbolizes hope and a future free from violence.

The Orange Weeks are no longer just our initiative; they belong to a great many people. This year, participants range from the Ministry of the Interior to the Von Krahl Theater. All members of our Violence-Free initiative for Estonian businesses are also taking part. These are companies that understood the nature of the problem even before the publication of recent statistics by the Riigikogu's Foresight Center: Violence comes at a cost to society as a whole, including employers. Politicians, journalists and other opinion leaders have also been invited to reflect on the issue.

Over the years, it has been through our cooperation with businesses — and companies in our network now employ 5 percent of Estonia's workforce — that we have seen firsthand just how true the central findings of intimate partner violence researchers are. Violence really does know no boundaries, whether educational, socioeconomic or ethnic.

There is not a single company where violence awareness training has not marked the beginning of someone's journey toward a better life. Often, in the safe environment these training sessions provide, people come to the conclusion that it is worth sharing their story. That it is worth involving their employer in their recovery. Employers can then provide help and support to ensure that journey is successful. At one company, the first employee came forward seeking help just five minutes after their employer announced it was joining the Violence-Free initiative.

Those who have experienced abuse come forward, but so do those who, during the training itself, have begun to consider whether some of their own tendencies in managing anger or communicating at home might constitute abusive behavior.

Of course, we are not talking about pathological batterers or tormentors. They know perfectly well what they are doing, even if they invariably blame their victims for their behavior. It is ordinary people who come forward, people who have begun to realize that they could make life better for themselves and their families by giving up abusive behavior, whether directed at their partners or their children.

Our usual thinking is: What's the problem? Punish those who beat others and put killers behind bars. Violence has nothing to do with the rest of us. Our thinking changes when we realize that abuse can be psychological or economic and that even yelling or throwing a plate against a wall — rather than at another person — is in fact a form of violence that victimizes our loved ones. It is probably safe to say that one in two of us has personally experienced violence at home, whether in our own intimate relationships or during childhood.

When a problem is this widespread, prison is certainly not the solution. Giving up abusive behavior would help. But how do we go about doing that?

Estonia has exactly five positions for professionals whose job it is to help people who have behaved violently get back on the right track. Only three of those positions are currently filled. The vast majority of clients seen by the Social Insurance Board's violence prevention counselors are referred by the police or the Prosecutor's Office. Very few seek help on their own initiative. If more did, the counselors would no longer be able to cope with their workload.

There would be less violence in Estonian homes if far more people sought help voluntarily. We therefore need to change the way we think about violence and responsibility.

Surely the person who strikes the blow bears responsibility? Or do they?

For some reason, victims of violence must not only convince society that they are victims in the first place, but also take responsibility for resolving the situation. The responsibility for ending the relationship with the support of victim support services and other organizations, and for enduring the financial and other hardships that often accompany that decision, falls entirely on the victim. Why?

"A great many people prone to abusive behavior need practical skills for building healthy and safe relationships."

It is possible to break away from violent behavior. For many, the process of healing begins simply with recognizing that certain patterns of behavior, some dating back to their own childhood, are manipulative and abusive. Sometimes, all it takes is a desire to be better toward one's children, for example. A great many people prone to abusive behavior need practical skills for building healthy and safe relationships.

It is the person who strikes the blow who also bears responsibility for ensuring it never happens again and that their loved ones are not hurt. Alongside victim support, we need to foster a stronger culture of abandoning abusive behavior, starting with the understanding that no one other than the person behaving violently is responsible for the violence and that the responsibility for changing that behavior is theirs alone. No one else's. Certainly not the victim's. Those who commit violence must seek and receive help because we cannot build a safer society through the efforts of victims alone.

We spend a total of €3.6 million in public funds on victim support, support centers and prevention. Around €350,000 of that is allocated to helping people give up abusive behavior. Meanwhile, a full 75 percent of people in Estonia recognize that the system for supporting people in giving up abusive behavior both needs and deserves further development.

So, political parties, here is one way to make Estonia a better place in the way voters want. Those who have committed violence must take responsibility and learn to communicate without violence going forward. Bring the orange mindset into your election platforms!

World.title: Woman in Lääne County loses €22,000 to scammers
World.content:
Scammers convinced a local woman to invest in cryptocurrency and, through various pretexts, extracted a total of €21,900 from her.

The victim saw a Facebook  promoting an opportunity to earn money through a cryptocurrency platform and registered on it, said the Lääne Police Prefecture.

After registering, she received a call from a Russian-speaking person who assured her that she needed to invest €150 to begin. The woman transferred the money and confirmed the payment using her PIN codes.

She was later contacted by another Russian-speaking individual who continued communicating with her through WhatsApp over the following months.

At the scammers' instruction, the woman installed the remote-access program AnyDesk on her phone, as well as the cryptocurrency applications Bitcoin and Blockchain.

After the initial payment, the woman was repeatedly asked to make additional transfers, both for further "investments" and for various fees and charges that were supposedly required to recover her previously invested funds.

Yielding to the pressure, the woman took out loans from Swedbank, Svea Finance AS and Bondora. She also used money withdrawn from Estonia's mandatory funded pension.

World.title: Owners seeking buyers and tenants for historic nightclub venue in central Tallinn
World.content:
The former Hollywood nightclub premises in Tallinn's Sõprus cinema building have stood vacant for five months, and the owners are looking for a new use for the space.

"We are currently holding discussions with both potential tenants and prospective buyers. We welcome tenants and partners who have both the interest and a vision for making meaningful use of these historic spaces," said Alis Möll, property manager of the Sõprus cinema building at Vana-Posti 8 in central Tallinn.

Neither the building managers nor the owners want to leave valuable downtown premises empty. The managers are also hoping for the city's involvement in shaping the building's future.

They are actively exploring opportunities for the future use and want the Sõprus building to continue hosting diverse cultural and event activities.

Sõprus Cinema building in central Tallinn. Source: Tallinna Strategy Center.

Vana-Posti 8 is owned by Prospicio Invest OÜ, whose owners are Tatjana Birjukova and Pavel Solomatin. The building is managed by Zenith Property Management, part of asset management company Zenith Family Office. Half of Zenith Property Management is owned by Möll, who serves as the building's property manager.

"The Sõprus cinema building is one of the historic buildings in downtown Tallinn, holding a special place in the city's cultural history and in the personal memories of many Tallinn residents," Möll explained.

"We fully understand that a situation where a major entertainment venue has disappeared from the city center and the premises remain unused is not good for any party involved. At the same time, decisions regarding the future of such a historic and unique building are not simply a question of leasing the space as quickly as possible. It is important to find a solution that is economically sustainable, takes the building's unique characteristics into account, and helps ensure that it remains a lively and accessible place in the heart of Tallinn in the future," she added.

World.title: Snow cannons fired up in Otepää as winter sports season gets underway
World.content:
With major international competitions ahead this season, the Tehvandi Sports Center, just outside the Valga County town, is firing up 10 snow cannons alongside a specialized container unit that works above freezing.

Not willing to leave ski tracks and tubing hills to the mercy of unpredictable winter weather, operators in Otepää launched artificial snowmaking as soon as temperatures dipped a few degrees below zero.

Such is the importance of winter sports to the area, snow is referred to colloquially as "white gold" in and around Otepää. However, since natural snowfalls cannot always be relied on, the Tehvandi Sports Center is putting its 10 snow cannons into operation. Even these require chilly temperatures.

Since the major events scheduled this winter require thorough preparation, Tehvandi has already been producing snow for several days, using a specialized machine built for the still relatively mild conditions.

"When the weather gods were not so kind to us back in 2020 and didn't give us any freezing temperatures, meaning a competition had to be canceled due to a lack of snow — or rather postponed to another location — we afterwards acquired a snow container that makes it possible to produce snow even in temperatures above zero. This is a highly energy-intensive production, though when there are no other options, it is a big help," Tehvandi snowmaker Tiit Tammemäe told "Aktuaalne kaamera".

The snow cannon were first switched on at full blast on Thursday at Otepää's snow tubing hill, to take full advantage of every sub-zero spell.

"Now we have the first decent sub-zero temperatures. What matters is having below-freezing temperatures around the clock so we don't have to shut the cannons down in between. We need to make 15 million liters of snow. Roughly speaking, if it's minus 10 outside, we can get that done in four to five days and nights. But if it's minus three or minus four, it might take us two weeks. The colder it is, the better the output, the faster we can make snow, and the less energy it uses too," Otepää snowmaker Siim Kalda explained of the logistics.

Last winter proved unpredictable for Estonia's winter capital. While snow cannon were similarly activated in late November 2025, warmer weather meant Otepää was almost entirely snowless as late on as Christmastime, when it was officially proclaimed winter capital for the 2025–2026 season. The sustained sub-zero temperatures arrived shortly afterwards, however, with a roughly two-month stretch of subzero conditions affecting the whole of Estonia that time.

Preparations carry extra weight this season as Tehvandi Sports Center gears up to host the FIS Nordic Combined World Cup Stage in mid-January. Even more critical is the 2027 IBU Biathlon World Championships, taking place in Otepää a month later, from February 9–21. Last winter's World Cup test event in Otepää had to be staged under difficult snow conditions, making early stockpiling critical.

World.title: Conservation of Enn Põldroos tapestry named heritage achievement of the year
World.content:
On Thursday, the National Heritage Board presented awards to last year's outstanding preservers and promoters of historical heritage.

The rescue conservation and digitization of "Inimeste elu" ("The Life of People"), a tapestry created by Enn Põldroos for Tallinn's Linnahall, was named Heritage Achievement of the Year.

Awards for outstanding restoration of historic buildings and interior details went to the teams that restored a mural in the main building of Laimjala Manor and the altarpiece of Vastseliina St. Catherine's Church, as well as the restorers of the Patarei Memorial Museum of the Victims of Communism and the Ukuaru Music House in Rakvere.

Awards were also presented to people who promote, preserve and research cultural heritage. The Agne Trummal Young Heritage Conservationist Award was presented to Britta Karin Arnover. Lifetime achievement awards went to Eva Mölder and Ülle Tamla.

"We see a very diverse picture. We see people who have done something for their communities, as well as major construction projects. We had 16 nominations and more than 70 nominees, and I am very pleased that even in economically difficult and uncertain times, there are people among us who remain willing to invest both their time and money in preserving heritage. That is truly wonderful," said Marilin Mihkelson, director general of the National Heritage Board.

World.title: Iraq Stars League round 15 continues Saturday with three fixtures
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Action in Round 15 of the Iraq Stars League continues on Saturday, November 28, 2026, with three key fixtures scheduled across stadiums in Baghdad, Diyala, and Sulaymaniyah as clubs battle to climb the domestic standings.

Saturday’s matchday lineup features three staggered kickoffs (all times Baghdad local time, GMT+3):

World.title: Oil Minister pledges 80% of BP jobs to Kirkuk residents
World.content:
Kirkuk (IraqiNews.com) – Kirkuk Governor Qahtan Al-Wandawi announced on Friday, November 27, 2026, that Oil Minister Basim Al-Abadi pledged during an official visit to the governorate to allocate at least 80% of upcoming employment positions with British energy major BP to Kirkuk residents, while confirming that crude oil exports through the Iraq–Turkey pipeline have resumed at 300,000 barrels per day (bpd) and are projected to climb to 500,000 bpd within the next few days.

In a recorded video address following meetings at the Kirkuk Governorate headquarters, Al-Wandawi commended Ministry of Oil personnel for restarting flows along the northern export pipeline, noting the economic significance of the 500,000 bpd ramp-up for both Iraq and Kirkuk.

Addressing local labor concerns, the governor clarified that BP has not yet commenced its recruitment drive, while reiterating the minister’s commitment to reserving a minimum 80% hiring quota for local youth once hiring opens.

Beyond oil exports and BP hiring quotas, Al-Wandawi detailed several service and economic agreements reached with the visiting ministerial delegation:

Fuel Allocations: Both sides discussed increasing Kirkuk’s quotas of gasoline and kerosene, alongside accelerating fuel allocation increases for private neighborhood generator operators across the city.

Local Business Priority: Officials emphasized granting the majority share of service contracts and joint-venture opportunities to Kirkuk-based companies and local contractors to stimulate domestic job creation.

Social Benefit Funds: The governorate and the Ministry of Oil agreed to allocate dedicated social benefit revenues to Kirkuk for direct investment in education, healthcare, municipal services, and environmental projects.

Al-Wandawi confirmed that continuous coordination will proceed over the coming days between the Kirkuk provincial administration, the Minister of Oil, and the Director-General of the North Oil Company to finalize implementation.

World.title: Nasiriyah International Airport airside reaches 100% completion ahead of navigation system checks
World.content:
Nasiriyah (IraqiNews.com) – Nasiriyah International Airport Director Ali Al-Gharabi announced on Friday, November 27, 2026, that construction on the airport’s airside infrastructure has reached 100% completion, while infrastructure works and the dedicated airport access highway have achieved advanced completion rates amid ongoing federal and provincial efforts to accelerate the facility’s opening.

Speaking to the Iraqi News Agency (INA), Al-Gharabi noted that the project is progressing steadily under direct follow-up from the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport, and the Secretary-General of the Council of Ministers to overcome operational hurdles.

He confirmed that the fully completed airside section encompasses the main runway, taxiways, and aircraft parking apron, adding that a specialized technical committee is scheduled to depart soon to conduct factory acceptance testing for the airport’s air navigation systems.

Alongside terminal and utility construction, Al-Gharabi reported substantial progress on the parallel Nasiriyah International Airport Road project, which stretches from the city center to the international highway to connect Dhi Qar’s urban landmarks directly with the airport.

Once operational, the airport will feature an annual capacity of 750,000 passengers alongside a dedicated air cargo terminal—providing a major transit and economic hub for Dhi Qar Governorate and its archaeological heritage sites.

World.title: Zaidi orders flat 5% import tariff and doubles traveler dollar quotas to 12 trips annually
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Faleh Al-Zaidi issued sweeping economic directives on Friday, November 27, 2026, establishing a unified 5% customs tariff across all imported goods and doubling the annual foreign currency cash allowance for Iraqi travelers through the Central Bank of Iraq (CBI).

According to a statement from the Prime Minister’s Media Office received by the Iraqi News Agency (INA), the measures form part of a broader government drive to bolster macroeconomic stability and streamline trade and monetary policy:

Unified 5% Customs Tariff: Effective December 1, 2026, customs duties on all imported goods will be standardized at a flat rate of 5%, replacing tiered tariff schedules to curb customs evasion and simplify border clearance.

Doubled Traveler Dollar Quotas: Under parallel monetary adjustments executed by the Central Bank of Iraq, citizens traveling abroad are now entitled to receive 12 foreign currency cash allocations per year—up from the previous cap of six—at $3,000 per trip (raising the maximum annual traveler allowance from $18,000 to $36,000).

The dual fiscal and monetary package aims to expand citizens’ access to foreign currency at the official exchange rate of 1,520 IQD per dollar while easing upward pressure on parallel cash markets ahead of the new year.

World.title: Iraq seizes smuggled oil bound for Sulaymaniyah as Baghdad tightens control
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi security forces intercepted a truck carrying smuggled oil at the Chimen checkpoint in Kirkuk on Friday as Baghdad steps up efforts to fight oil smuggling and reinforce federal authority across the nation.

According to Iraq’s Security Media Cell, which reports to the Prime Minister’s Office, forces from the Kirkuk Operations Command seized a vehicle traveling from Basra to Sulaymaniyah, which was carrying a container labeled as plumbing materials and protected with customs seals.

Security staff got suspicious of the package and ran a scan, which revealed hidden oil.

The driver was apprehended, and the truck was confiscated for further investigation and legal action.

The seizure comes as Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi pushes for more federal supervision of border crossings in Iraq’s Kurdistan Region and oilfields in disputed territory as part of larger measures to curb smuggling and defend Iraq’s national resources.

On Friday, US President Donald Trump voiced support for Al-Zaidi’s efforts to establish state authority across Iraq, curb oil smuggling, battle corruption, and place all weaponry under government control.

The operation comes as Baghdad steps up its attempts to improve government management of transportation routes, border crossings, and the country’s oil resources.

World.title: Trump backs Baghdad’s push to assert federal authority across Iraq
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – US President Donald Trump pledged support for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali Al-Zaidi’s attempts to establish federal authority throughout the country on Friday, as Baghdad prepares to place border crossings in the Kurdistan Region and numerous oilfields in disputed territory under federal control.

In a post on Truth Social, Trump praised Al-Zaidi’s efforts to fight oil smuggling, battle corruption, and place all weaponry under state control.

“We support Prime Minister Al-Zaidi’s efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions,” Trump said.

Washington’s backing is a diplomatic setback for the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), which has sought international support against Baghdad’s aspirations to strengthen federal authority over border crossings and oil resources.

Iraqi Kurdish officials have aggressively criticized Al-Zaidi’s decree, claiming it breaches the region’s constitutional rights and weakens Iraq’s federal structure.

Iraqi Kurdish Prime Minister Masrour Barzani urged the international community to protect the region’s constitutional rights. In contrast, Trump’s speech expressly supported Baghdad’s attempts to impose state authority throughout the country.

The support also indicates the improved ties between Washington and Baghdad under Al-Zaidi’s leadership.

A national conversation is set for December 1 to resolve remaining conflicts between Baghdad and Erbil in line with the Iraqi constitution.

The advances occur as Baghdad works to consolidate state power, establish national sovereignty, and create a unified Iraq that serves all residents, regardless of race, religion, or sectarian affiliation.

World.title: Under-attack Palestinians find unlikely ally in Israeli retired general
World.content:
As Sawiyah – The four Israeli soldiers stepped out of their car in the occupied West Bank, their faces masked, their uniforms unmarked and automatic weapons strapped across their shoulders.

They had entered a Palestinian olive grove but, little did they expect, the person there planning to tell them to leave could have once been issuing them orders.

A retired Israeli general, Eyal Ben Reuven, had come that day to the Palestinian town of As Sawiyah, on a mission to prevent some of the rampant violence against Palestinians by extremist Israeli settlers.

For the 72-year-old, joined by fellow battle-hardened veterans of the Israeli military, the violence is a stain on the institution in which they once served.

“I’ve fought in a number of wars. And unfortunately, I have reached the point where I have seen an evolution,” said the former military man with piercing eyes, who spent much of his career driving tanks.

The army is failing to act, he said, even when the violence has reached a level “I never could have imagined”.

Unrest has soared in the West Bank since the unprecedented October 7, 2023 attack by Hamas on Israel, which responded with a massive military campaign in the Gaza Strip.

More than 1,100 Palestinians have been killed by the army or settlers in the West Bank since then. More than 50 Israelis have died in the same time in the territory, which Israel captured in 1967.

The olive harvest has become a flashpoint, with settlers attacking or stealing from Palestinian farmers on a nearly daily basis.

With the other former soldiers, Ben Reuven has set up a protective presence, a tactic more common among leftist activists who put themselves in the way in a bid to stop attacks against Palestinians.

– Army intervenes in harvest –

Clad in comfortable hiking attire and carrying walking sticks, it is difficult to imagine that some of the greying volunteers fought in intense combat.

Like good soldiers, they review instructions upon going out — they are there to assist the olive harvest, not to confront the settlers, and they will obey the army’s instructions.

A Palestinian human rights activist, Arafat Abu Ras, led the military men to a small olive grove. An old Palestinian woman was waiting to guide them and the soldiers, more accustomed to the battlefield than to farming, used sticks and small rakes to start knocking the olives off the trees, volunteering to do the work on the Palestinians’ behalf.

Almost immediately a military vehicle arrived. Under the humming of a drone, one of the serving soldiers shoved aside an AFP team to prevent filming, while another checked Abu Ras’s identity papers and ordered everyone to leave.

Abu Ras said that the olive farmers had coordinated with the army, which insists that Palestinians receive approval for their harvests in the occupied West Bank, arguing that it is for safety reasons.

“They say, ‘yes, yes’, and then the next day they come and force us to leave,” Abu Ras said.

After the serving soldiers arrived, a second vehicle came, this time with Israeli settlers. An official from a neighbouring settlement also ordered the olive pickers out, with troops saying it was a “closed military zone”.

The Israeli veterans, in line with their guidance, complied. They instead moved elsewhere with the farmers, hoping to prevent attacks on them.

“Our army is a joke,” fumed Yoel Feldschuh, a 77-year-old former air force brigadier general.

“Is it its role to shut an olive grove? What does the military have to do with that?”

Feldschuh made headlines when he was handcuffed and taken away by police in a similar action a month earlier.

Changing the behaviour of the military, he said, “will take a generation”.

– Rampant violence –

COGAT, the Israeli body responsible for civil affairs in the Palestinian territories, maintains that “security forces are deployed to ensure a safe olive harvest”.

But since September, the harvest has been marked by nearly 500 attacks, some of them fatal, according to the Israeli human rights organisation Yesh Din.

Amram Mitzna, an 81-year-old retired general, attributes the army’s inaction to the young ages of the soldiers, who have grown up under now-caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving leader.

“They consider every Arab an enemy who must be treated as such,” said Mitzna, who has also served as mayor of Haifa, Israel’s third largest city.

Netanyahu has allied himself with the far-right and championed a rapid growth of West Bank settlements, which are considered illegal under international law.

Netanyahu is fighting for political survival after losing ground in elections. Gadi Eisenkot, a former general seeking to succeed him, supports many of Netanyahu’s security policies but accuses him of yielding to “Jewish terrorism” in the West Bank and vowed to crack down on extremist settlers.

In As Sawiyah, the former soldiers eventually finished harvesting the olives in a nearby area alongside a school, putting them in bags to be taken by Palestinian villagers.

While no one was injured, Ben Reuven remained deeply disturbed by how the young soldier acted during the altercation.

“When I saw him arrive, masked, shouting, kicking sacks of olives, I was ashamed.”

World.title: BP eyes deeper energy ties with Iraq as CEO visits Baghdad
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – British energy giant BP has reaffirmed its commitment to expanding operations in Iraq following CEO Meg O’Neill’s first visit to the country and meeting with Prime Minister Ali Falih Al-Zaidi in Baghdad.

According to the Prime Minister’s office, talks centered on developing oilfields and boosting exploration efforts, notably at Rumaila in Basra, Eridu in Dhi Qar, and Kirkuk, as Iraq aims to produce 10 million barrels of oil per day by 2032.

To reach output objectives, Al-Zaidi advocated for faster development, intensified field activities, and longer working hours.

Iraq’s Prime Minister also emphasized the need for collecting related gas and decreasing waste to improve domestic energy supply.

O’Neill reaffirmed BP’s commitment to expanding its activities in Iraq, utilizing sophisticated technology and technical experience to boost production and develop the country’s oilfields.

Following the meeting, O’Neill lauded Iraq’s objectives, workforce, and energy potential on LinkedIn, stressing prospects to enhance the company’s collaboration with Baghdad.

Along with its partners and the Iraqi operator, BP plays a critical role in Rumaila, Iraq’s biggest producing oilfield, providing technical knowledge to boost production and maximize resource recovery.

In Kirkuk, BP is engaging in a large rebuilding program involving oil, gas, electricity, and water infrastructure, with the first phase covering resources amounting to more than three billion barrels of oil.

The company’s growing presence is especially important as Iraq pursues foreign investment, modernizes its energy infrastructure, reduces gas flaring, and expands its oil production capacity.

O’Neill emphasized that combining Iraq’s immense natural resources and indigenous knowledge with BP’s technology and worldwide experience may provide significant benefits for both parties.

The visit highlights Iraq’s strategic significance to BP, as well as the company’s long-term engagement in growing the country’s oil industry.

World.title: ‘Final call in day or two’: India-bloc ally JMM to decide stand on delimitation, women's quota Bills after assessing impact on Jharkhand
World.content:
JMM to decide stand on delimitation, women's quota Bills after examining impact on Jharkhand

Revised Bills propose 50% increase in seats

Opposition raises concerns over social justice

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: India-bloc ally Jharkhand Mukti Morcha (JMM) will announce its position on the proposed delimitation and women's reservation Bills in a day or two after examining their provisions and assessing their impact on the state, the party said on Saturday.The decision was taken at a meeting of JMM MPs chaired by chief minister Hemant Soren at his official residence in Ranchi."We received copies of the bills on Friday night. The chief minister asked all party MPs to study the bills properly to find out whether they are favourable to Jharkhand. The CM will also seek expert opinions. After the study, a final call will be taken in a day or two," Rajya Sabha MP Mahua Maji told reporters.The party is particularly examining whether the proposed changes would lead to a proportionate increase in seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes (STs) in Jharkhand."If the tribal seats increase proportionately, then it is fine, and we will consider it," Lok Sabha MP Nalin Soren said.Rajya Sabha MP Sarfraz Ahmad said the Bills did not clearly specify the extent to which seats reserved for Scheduled Tribes, Scheduled Castes (SCs) and Other Backward Classes (OBCs) would increase.Rajya Sabha MPs Sarfraz Ahmad and Baidyanath Ram, and Lok Sabha MPs Vijay Hansdak, Joba Manjhi and Nalin Soren attended the meeting, along with Maji.The JMM's decision comes amid differing positions among opposition parties, with INDIA bloc ally NCP (Sharadchandra Pawar) extending support to the proposed delimitation Bill. Another key regional party, the DMK, may also back the legislation if certain conditions are met.The Centre is set to introduce a fresh Constitution amendment Bill in the Lok Sabha on Monday as part of a revised legislative package aimed at implementing 33 per cent reservation for women in Parliament and state legislatures.The package proposes increasing the allocation of Lok Sabha and Assembly seats in every state and Union Territory by 50 per cent. It also provides for redrawing constituency boundaries using the 2011 Census figures, while keeping the distribution of seats among states frozen until 2051.The proposed changes are intended to facilitate the implementation of the women's quota ahead of the 2029 general elections.The Union Cabinet has approved three draft legislations: the Constitution (132nd Amendment) Bill, 2026, the Delimitation (Second) Bill, 2026, and the accompanying Union Territories Laws Amendment Bill. The revised proposals are expected to replace the Bills introduced in April, which failed to pass the Lok Sabha.The Congress has opposed linking women's reservation with the delimitation exercise and has called for the quota to be implemented within the existing strength of 543 Lok Sabha seats.Addressing a press conference on Saturday, leader of opposition in Lok Sabha, Rahul Gandhi, accused the government of undermining social justice by relying on the 2011 Census and keeping the distribution of seats frozen until 2051."The caste census has been put aside, and the 2027 Census has been rendered irrelevant. Why? Because it is going to show some very inconvenient facts, which the BJP does not appreciate. So they are going to use the 2011 Census, and everything is going to be frozen till 2051. Means for 40 years, you can forget social justice. They're undermining the rights of SC, ST, OBC, disempowering minorities," he said.Rahul also argued that the share of seats reserved for SCs and STs would remain unchanged despite changes in their population. He called for a bipartisan Delimitation Commission and demanded an OBC sub-quota within women's reservation.Meanwhile, some regional parties and NDA allies have expressed support for the revised package. JD(U) national working president Sanjay Jha argued that delimitation was necessary because constituency population figures were outdated. The BRS also said its Rajya Sabha MPs would support the legislation, citing the proposed protection of states' relative share of seats until 2051.The JMM, however, has said it will take a final position only after studying the provisions and assessing their implications for Jharkhand.

World.title: From Dali to Picasso, a 23-year-old's mission to bring European art to India
World.content:
Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

Surrealist master Salvador Dali treated his painting titles like poetry. Sometimes they worked like a literary mirror of his visual aesthetic---and political obsessions. One 1945 oil-on-canvas is titled 'Napoleon's nose, transformed into a pregnant woman, strolling his shadow with melancholia amongst original ruins'. As the viewer would have already guessed, the painting shows exactly that. The rocky profile of French emperor Napoleon Bonaparte emerges from the landscape. On closer inspection, his massive nose and chin have transformed into the curved belly and robes of a pregnant woman amidst cracked architecture, crumbling walls and barren plains. It is supposed to convey themes of the fall of empires and rebirth after war.While one has to go to the DalÃ­ Theatre-Museum in Catalonia in Spain to see this curious painting in its original form, art lovers in Delhi were treated to a 'granolithograph' of the same in a recent exhibition. Called 'Visions of Modernity', it featured works of the greatest masters of modernism and surrealism---Salvador DalÃ­, Pablo Picasso and Marc Chagall---under one roof. There were etchings, aquatints, lithographs---and granolithographs.For instance, the psychological edge of the pregnant nose of Napoleon softened into quiet domestic intimacy with Picassoâthe towering figure of Cubismâwhose 'Les Repas des Enfants' placed vividly rendered children around a table beneath the protective presence of a maternal figure. Chagall, the Belarusian-French pioneer celebrated as modernismâs great poet of colour and folklore, suspended the viewer in a lyrical Parisian night with 'Le Quai de Bercy', dissolving the Bercy Bridge and the Seine into a strange, luminous reverie. While Dali's paintings dominate art history textbooks and museum collections, his sculptures are not so easy to find. But three of his bronze sculptures also made it to this exhibition at India Habitat Centre this month, including 'Lady Godiva with Butterflies' where an Anglo-Saxon noblewoman is shown riding naked on horseback through the streets of Coventry to protest the crushing taxes of her husband.But more interestingly, it was a 23-year-old who made this exhibition in Delhi happen. Aarohi Garg, founder and curator of Studio Verasa, is the exclusive representative of DalÃ­ Universe in India and the brains behind the exhibition which features works from its collectionDalÃ­ Universe has works assembled over nearly five decades by Italian art dealer and collector Beniamino Levi, whose association with DalÃ­ began in the 1960s. Levi, now 98 years old and former director of Galleria Levi in Milan, exhibited and traded works by some of the leading artists of modernism, including Picasso, MirÃ³, Magritte, and Kandinsky. His close association with DalÃ­ eventually led him to commission and publish bronze sculptural editions based on the artist's paintings, bringing a lesser-known, three-dimensional facet of DalÃ­'s practice to audiences. The collection, now among the world's foremost private collections of DalÃ­ sculptures and three-dimensional works, has travelled across continents, appearing in museums, cultural institutions and public spaces. "Mr Levi has the largest collection of Dali's work and I am really hoping to bring that to India," says Garg whose own interest in art began in Madrid, where she spent four years studying behavioural sciences. "But mostly I would skip my class to go to museums and galleries. That's when I knew I wanted to do something in the arts," she says, recalling afternoons spent looking at works by Spanish artists like DalÃ­, Sorolla, MirÃ³ and VelÃ¡zquez. That fascination eventually took her to Sotheby's in London, where she completed a short course and learnt from art dealers and educators. After returning to India and working with galleries, she decided to build her own platform and launched Studio Verasa this year'Visions of Modernity' is Verasa's first exhibition which Garg says came together in just 24 days. But it is part of a longer-term partnership with DalÃ­ Universe. " My end goal is to bring original pieces and set up a museum much like Levi and his team have built in Montepulciano in Tuscany---a hybrid cultural space which is half-museum, half-gallery showcasing contemporary art," says Garg about her plans to offer Indian audiences a chance to encounter European art beyond reproductions and familiar names on textbooks.Many lithographs and engravings in the collection were produced in standard limited editions of 500, meaning individual prints are numbered out of 500 (e.g., 500/500). One such print numbered '500/500' in the exhibition belongs to a lithograph of Picasso's 'Femme accoudÃ©e Ã sa fenÃªtre' (Woman Leaning at Her Window). "It's the last piece in the world. After this, there won't be any left," says Garg with pride.

World.title: Police use water cannon on Congress workers protesting outside Meta office
World.content:
The protest, led by the Congress youth wing, is part of a growing confrontation between the opposition party and Meta
