World.title: Buklod: Songs of an unfinished struggle
World.content:
Forty years after the EDSA Revolution, the music of folk group Buklod remains a haunting reminder of a promise left unfulfilled — and a fight that is far from over

To be an activist in the years immediately after the 1986 EDSA Revolution meant sailing against the optimistic tide that swept the nation following the ouster of the Marcos dictatorship. Democracy had been restored, Cory Aquino was president, and the mood was blazing yellow. Everyone, it seemed, wanted to move on and celebrate.

And to be a protest musician at a time when vacuous pop, delivered by singers and bands with gelled hair and shoulder pads, ruled the airwaves meant strumming an acoustic guitar in the middle of Euphoria: nobody could hear you, and those who did wished you weren’t there.

They played on anyway.

Protest musicians of the post-EDSA years did not come out of nowhere. They followed a tradition of protest artists from the ’70s and early ’80s whose songs were in the form and vernacular of folk and folk-rock: Jess Santiago, Paul Galang, Susan Fernandez, Pancho Lara, Gary Granada; folk groups like Pahayagan and Sinaglahi. Asin and Heber Bartolome’s Banyuhay carried it into the mainstream, proving that a song about the environment, or the daily struggles of working people could sell records.

The folk group Buklod was that period’s best-kept secret.

Noel Cabangon, Romeo Dongeto, and Rene Boncocan sang at political gatherings long before anyone thought of them as recording artists. Their first album, Bukid at Buhay, came out in 1988 as a trio; Boncocan left the following year, and Cabangon and Dongeto carried on as a duo in “Tatsulok” (1991) and “Sa Kandungan ng Kalikasan” (1992).

Buklod’s songs found a home in mainstream compilation albums such as Karapatang Pantao and Dear Cory, masterminded by maverick producer Ed Formoso, known for the psychedelic-folk group Dinosaur, a trio with Boy Camara and Jett Montelibano, and for birthing the supergroup Lokal Brown.

It wasn’t until “Kanlungan” was used in a burger commercial, and “Tatsulok” was covered by Bamboo many years later, that the secret was out.

“Kanlungan” became the song everyone requested from Cabangon, by then an established solo recording artist. It didn’t matter, of course, that a song about longing and the passing of time performed by activists became a jingle for an American fast food chain. Or that “Tatsulok,” an indictment of oppressive class structures, became a rock anthem for a generation largely spared from a policeman’s truncheon. By then, Buklod had long disbanded.

Buklod would jam occasionally, but there was never a full reunion or a new album. Not until 2018, 30 years after their first record, when the three went back to the studio for 3 Dekada: Ang Muling Pag-awit.

The comeback, the urge to make their voices, now older, heard again, was triggered by the brazen extra-judicial killings and rights violations under the then two-year old regime of now detained former president Rodrigo Duterte. Three decades on, the old songs still resonated and it was the trio’s way of joining the outrage.

A few nights ago, they reunited again, this time for a fund-raiser for ailing painter Federico “Boy” Dominguez, known in activist and art circles as BoyD. In the crowd were battle-hardened activists, finding comfort in familiar songs.

Forty years after EDSA, Buklod’s songs still carry the same weight as the day they were first sung. The promise of the EDSA Revolution has since soured: old and new elites, despots who use the rhetoric of democracy to undermine its values, disenchantment with its failure to lift people from chronic hunger and poverty, activists who dared to protest treated with the same iron fist as Marcos the father. And Marcos the son is back in Malacañang.

Buklod and the other post-EDSA protest artists were right all along: The revolution left too much undone. In the face of public indifference, they still said it and sang about it, even if it meant preaching to the converted, dodging bullets at rallies, raising families on a folk singer’s income, or enduring years of separation over ideological and political disagreements.

In the end, it is the songs that outlast the quarrels. Songs that bring old friends and comrades together and remind them, and the rest of us, that the fight they sang about was never finished. – Rappler.com

World.title: Will Sara Duterte finally attend her impeachment trial?
World.content:
YEAREND PRESSCON. Vice President Sara Duterte answers questions from the media during the Office of the Vice President's thanksgiving event in Mandaluyong City on November 27, 2026.

Vice President Sara Duterte says she had repeatedly told her defense lawyer, Michael Poa, 'Allow me to lawyer for myself and stand there as a lawyer'

Will Vice President Sara Duterte ever show up at her impeachment trial?

That question has persisted since Day 1 of the trial on July 6, amid mounting calls for the Vice President to appear in court and personally respond to the allegations against her.

Duterte has visited the Senate on at least two occasions outside her trial. The first was on July 7, when she met with her defense team and delivered a one-sentence statement to the media, “In this bloodbath and bludgeoning, I will be bloodied but unbowed.”

She left the Senate before the trial could resume.

On November 26, Duterte returned to the chamber while the trial was suspended to attend plenary deliberations on her office’s proposed P785.2 million budget for 2027.

She exchanged pleasantries with some of the senators serving as judges in her trial. But when the media asked questions, including whether she will attend her trial, she only responded with “Merry Christmas.”

Duterte’s defense team has repeatedly said her attendance would depend on how the trial unfolds, stressing that her physical appearance is not required because she is fully represented by counsel.

Duterte herself said in August that the participation of her lawyers was “sufficient” and tantamount to her attending the impeachment proceedings.

But in a rare, nearly hour-long press conference at the Office of the Vice President central office in Mandaluyong City on Friday, November 27, Duterte claimed that she had long wanted to attend her trial. It could be recalled that the Vice President herself had repeatedly questioned the impeachment proceeding itself, describing it as “political theater” in the guise of accountability.

On Friday, Duterte said that her defense lawyer and former spokesperson, Michael Poa, ignored her whenever she raised the possibility of her appearance at her trial.

“Ilang beses na ako nagsabi sa kanya: ‘Michael Poa, allow me to enter my appearance for myself. Allow me to lawyer for myself and stand there as a lawyer.’ Hindi niya talaga ako pinapansin at all. Somehow, nililihis niya ‘yung usapan,” Duterte said at her latest press conference.

(I’ve told him several times, “Michael Poa, allow me to enter my appearance for myself. Allow me to represent myself and stand there as a lawyer.” He really didn’t pay attention to me at all. Somehow, he keeps steering the conversation away from the subject.)

Poa, defense spokesperson, has yet to respond to requests for comment.

Asked whether she could still be presented as a witness at this point, with the defense nearing the end of its presentation, Duterte said she had yet to discuss the matter with her lawyers. “We are not there yet but sabi kasi nila tapos na sila this week e. So hindi pa namin napag-uusapan kung a-attend ako as witness o hindi,” Duterte said.

(We are not there yet but they said they will be done this week. So we have not discussed yet if I will attend as a witness or not.)

The defense team is set to present two witnesses when the trial resumes next week. Both are expected to testify in relation to Cale88 Foods Corporation, a company at the center of allegations of unexplained wealth against Duterte.

Will Duterte at least be present when the impeachment court hands down its decision? The court targets a ruling by December 18. The Vice President indicated that this event, which her political fate hinges on, is not a priority.

“If I’m in Davao, then no. Because we have a series of activities for Davao thanksgiving for December,” she said in response.

Duterte also said her office is “preparing for the worst” and that she would accept the court’s decision. However, she cautioned that removing an elected vice president would have “consequences,” pointing to possible negative public reaction.

Play Video

Meanwhile, the Vice President said she would not fly to The Hague for the trial of former president Rodrigo Duterte for a crimes against humanity case before the International Criminal Court beginning November 30. She said it would be a “waste of money” as visits to her father would not be allowed during the trial.

She shared that she owed friends at least P5 million which helped cover for her trip to The Hague last year, as well as legal expenses for her impeachment trial and her father’s case. She said she planned to sell properties to repay her debt.

Duterte is facing one remaining allegation in her impeachment case: unexplained wealth. The House prosecution panel dropped the three other articles of impeachment, which involved grave threats, misuse of confidential funds, and bribery. – Rappler.com

World.title: What are AI chips, and what’s so special about Nvidia’s?
World.content:
How Nvidia’s GPUs evolved from powering video games to becoming the backbone of the global AI race

The commotion around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s ouster and reinstatement, the central role of Nvidia in the U.S.-China AI competition, and the U.S. economy’s reliance on the AI boom might leave you asking: What’s so special about Nvidia’s chips?

The answer comes down to graphics processing units, or GPUs, and how far they’ve come from their humble beginnings as sidekicks to computers’ main chips: central processing units, or CPUs.

GPUs now power the most visible advances in generative artificial intelligence, but they began as modestly priced add-on cards for video games and video rendering.

As a researcher of high-performance computing and computer processors, I see three factors that explain how GPUs have become so important to the modern economy and how Nvidia became their dominant supplier: software that made GPUs useful beyond graphics, a research breakthrough that showed what they could do for AI, and a global commercial and political race to build ever-larger AI models.

GPUs vs. CPUs

The CPU is built to handle a wide variety of complicated tasks quickly, a few at a time. In contrast, a GPU typically operates on simpler mathematical tasks, such as multiplying two sets of numbers, but it can perform many of these simpler operations in parallel.

A GPU’s design turns out to be ideal for AI. Training a neural network, the kind of AI model behind today’s chatbots and image generators, comes down mostly to multiplying enormous grids of numbers, over and over. Today’s top AI GPUs can perform more than a quadrillion, or thousand trillion, of these operations every second.

From pretty pictures to AI data centers

Early GPUs could only draw graphics. Programmers controlled them with small programs called shaders, which calculate things such as the color of each pixel and which can be repeated across millions of pixels in parallel. Nvidia dominated the market for graphics chips in the late 1990s and 2000s.

In the early 2000s, Stanford University researchers built software tools that let programmers use this hardware for other kinds of calculations. That work provided the basis for Nvidia’s Compute Unified Device Architecture, or CUDA, which was released in 2007. CUDA allowed scientists and engineers to run scientific and more general purpose programs using the GPU’s parallel execution model.

The second major shift occurred when AlexNet, a neural network model developed and trained on GPUs, won the 2012 ImageNet challenge, an annual competition to see which software could most accurately identify objects in a set of photographs. AlexNet was trained on two Nvidia GPUs, and it made far fewer mistakes than any competitor. The result showed that GPUs made it practical to train neural networks big enough to beat the older techniques, and AI researchers quickly adopted them for their work.

Because Nvidia had spent years building CUDA and the software around it, it was positioned to benefit more than anyone. Competitors, including AMD, which also makes GPUs, and Google, which designs its own AI chips, called tensor processing units, have since built strong alternatives.

Nvidia and other chipmakers then began redesigning GPUs for AI with specific features. These include adding hardware specialized for the matrix multiplication math that neural networks rely on, using reduced precision numbers to improve the speed of neural network training and adding larger amounts of fast memory to keep these chips supplied with data for AI workloads.

AI takes off

In 2017, Google researchers introduced the transformer, a neural network design originally built to translate between languages. Transformers turned out to perform remarkably well in terms of accuracy as the model and dataset size grew, and this design became the foundation of today’s chatbots and many other generative AI systems.

The growth of these new transformer models has also led to the current boom of generative AI companies, including U.S.-based companies OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, Google and xAI, as well as Chinese companies such as DeepSeek, Alibaba and Baidu. Each of these companies is actively focused on building large data centers composed of high-end GPUs to train next-generation foundation models.

These foundation models, exemplified by Google’s Gemini, Anthropic’s Claude Fable and OpenAI’s GPT Astra, are very large neural networks that can reason, write software code and analyze information in response to plain language instructions. The companies working on foundation model training are betting that the best models will automate much of the world’s information work and generate enormous economic returns.

Nvidia’s GPUs dominate the AI market, but rival companies developing other chips are trying to knock Nvidia off its throne.

AI ‘arms race’

Nvidia trains some AI models of its own, but most of its profit comes from selling the chips and software that other companies use to build theirs. This AI boom has led to record profits for Nvidia, but it has also drawn attention from the U.S. government, which has debated how far to restrict sales of advanced chips to China. The Trump administration tightened its export controls for advanced GPUs in the immediate aftermath of the scandal involving Huang’s relationship with an alleged Chinese spy.

Demand for AI chips looks likely to keep growing as the leading AI companies compete to build more capable models, but the boom faces real limits. AI data centers require enormous amounts of electricity, raising questions about the power costs and environmental impacts to local communities.

The most advanced AI chips, including Nvidia’s, are fabricated largely by one company, Taiwanese chip giant Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., known as TSMC. Demand for AI hardware has also strained supplies of memory chips, creating shortages that reach gaming graphics cards and smartphones.

Nvidia also faces direct competition from AMD, cloud companies designing their own chips, and startups, all promising to run AI more cheaply and with less power. Whether Nvidia’s software and hardware advantages can hold off these challengers is one of the biggest open questions in the industry. – Rappler.com

This article first appeared on The Conversation.

Jeffrey Young, Principal Research Scientist, Partnership for an Advanced Computing Environment, Georgia Institute of Technology

World.title: Hackers breach US Air Force flagship Cloud One computing platform
World.content:
Hacker code is seen in this illustration taken October 30, 2026.

The breach of Cloud One, a one-stop shop for the US Air Force's IT needs, raises concerns over sensitive military data security and operational disruptions

WASHINGTON DC, US – Hackers have breached the US Air Force’s flagship cloud computing platform, three people familiar with the matter told Reuters, in a development that could jeopardize a vast swathe of sensitive tactical, personnel and logistics data.

The intrusion at Cloud One was discovered within the past month or so during work to upgrade the system, two of the people said, adding that the discovery has led to disruption across the platform. Reuters could not establish the identity of the hackers, the full scope of the intrusion or whether any data had been stolen.

In a statement to Reuters, the Air Force said it “does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities or operational status of specific networks and systems. We continuously take prudent measures to protect Department (of the Air Force) information, systems and mission capabilities.”

A one-stop shop

Initiated in 2017, Cloud One was meant to serve as a one-stop shop for the Air Force’s IT needs, combining the resources of four operators — Microsoft, Amazon, Oracle and Alphabet — to power scores of applications including ones that manage personnel data and pay or logistics and maintenance.

Among them are the Air Force’s Cloud-Based Command and Control, which collates air defense radar and other data feeds from across North America, and the Theater Integrated Combat Munitions System, which tracks bombs and missiles across more than 200 US Air Force locations around the world.

SAIC was the prime contractor for Cloud One until 2026, when Leidos took over. SAIC did not respond to a request seeking comment. Leidos referred questions to the Air Force.

Cloud One is among the US military’s biggest cloud platforms, according to two of the sources.

“A breach here is a big deal,” one of the sources said.

Investigators have called in Cyber Command, the US military’s cyber force, to assess the damage, one of the sources said.

Cyber Command did not respond to requests for comment.

A range of disruption

The discovery of the hack led to a range of disruption. Two of the sources, along with a fourth person familiar with the matter, said that efforts to migrate back-office applications to Cloud One, a longstanding military priority, have been paused.

Updates to applications already running on Cloud One were blocked, leaving Air Force personnel unable to apply fixes just as a new batch of serious software vulnerabilities has been disclosed across the technology industry. A fifth source said that some users had their administrator rights revoked.

All five sources spoke on condition of anonymity.

One source said that the cyber intruders exploited a software vulnerability to reach the control plane. That person likened the control plane to a universal remote, as intruders in theory could leverage their access to check the operational status of military aircraft or the movement of spare parts, though it was unclear whether the hackers did so in this case.

Reuters could not identify the specific vulnerability exploited by the hackers.

String of hacks

News of the breach comes amid heightened anxiety over AI-powered intrusions, a particularly serious problem for cloud-based networks because of the ability of AI models to swiftly detect weaknesses across wide surface areas.

The US government already has been dealing with the fallout from at least six other recently disclosed cyber incidents, including two at the FBI, a previous hack of Pentagon data, a recent leak of Department of Homeland Security personnel information, a breach affecting at least two spy agencies and a hack at the Treasury Department.

Cloud One has long been in the crosshairs of hackers.

In a 2023 commentary carried by the online publication FedScoop, Cloud One’s leadership touted what they called a “100% success rate” in beating back what they said was a “staggering” number of attempts to penetrate the platform.

“There is no room for error when it comes to security,” Cloud One’s leadership wrote. – Rappler.com

World.title: In ‘Shux,’ Bicol band Kilyab calls out ‘ayuda’ politics, climate neglect
World.content:
GRASSROOTS MUSIC. Kilyab performs in the streets and at venues across Naga City and the Bicol region.

Drawn from a Gen Z expression of disappointment, the track urges voters in Camarines Sur and across Bicol to look beyond band-aid relief efforts

ALBAY, Philippines – Bicol pop band Kilyab isn’t just singing about change — they’re marching for it in the streets, too. With their new single, “Shux,” the band pushes back against the idea that climate suffering is unavoidable, blaming decades of systemic neglect for the ongoing struggles in their community.

“Drawing inspiration from Camarines Sur, we saw how even delivering ayuda (relief aid) is being used to mind-condition voters instead of really solving the issues that worsen climate change,” songwriter and lead vocalist Karl Ramirez said.

“If we don’t talk and do something about it, most of our fellow citizens will continue to fall prey to the same system,” he added.

PROTEST. Kilyab’s lead vocalist Karl Ramirez speaks on the importance of socially relevant songs during a rally against Pax Silica in Naga on November 17, 2026. Photo by Jascyl Jee Hugo Sayson

The band emphasized that voters are often left with almost no real alternatives when choosing their leaders, trapping them in a recurring cycle: enduring calamities while politicians exploit those same disasters for self-promotion.

“These politicians don’t even hide it anymore — they even post videos on their social media accounts showing them handing out money disguised as prizes during their relief operations,” Ramirez said.

For Ramirez, “Shux” reflects the band’s firm belief in using socially relevant music to awaken their fellow citizens — and help end the cycles of neglect in their province and the wider Bicol region.

“Now and any time is the right time to sing songs that reflect the hardship and condition of our nation, and inspire all of us to continue taking a stand against corruption and imperialism,” he noted.

Verna Velasco, Kilyab’s keyboardist and a Bicol Pop mentor who coined the song’s title, said the word comes from a Gen Z expression.

“Shux” is a shortened version of “shucks,” used to convey disdain or disappointment.

“Using the ‘shux’ expression feels like a call for the youth and their communities to be more vigilant, starting with reflecting on why we vote for the people we put into power,” Velasco said.

“Like what the lyrics ask, ‘Ba’t ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo?’ (Why did you vote for them in the first place?), the song explains to us that we also have a shared responsibility for the neglect happening now amid the sufferings and issues we face,” she added.

CIVIC ADVOCACY. Bicol Pop band Kilyab performs its original hits in Naga City at major gatherings advocating for youth empowerment and anti-corruption accountability.

In a world quick to move past pressing issues, Velasco hopes the song will help people remember — especially when selecting new leaders.

That call for electoral reflection lands in a province long shaped by entrenched political power. Camarines Sur has been dominated by the Villafuerte dynasty for nearly 40 years.

In the 2025 midterm elections, the family maintained its grip on the province as Luis Raymund “LRay” Villafuerte reclaimed the gubernatorial seat, while his sons, Migz and Luigi, also secured seats in Congress. (READ: Iriga City bet decries harassment, vote buying in Camarines Sur).

Water crisis

Ramirez told Rappler that the song’s lyrics were written in one sitting during a songwriting class with Bicol Pop students back in April.

Set against soaring oil prices and looming warnings of a Super El Niño, the track was sparked by growing frustration over the government’s failure to step up.

“Our government can do major things regarding the climate crisis, or at least to ease the suffering of those affected. But instead of helping, we still allow some of our local watersheds — like Mount Isarog in Camarines Sur — to be destroyed,” Ramirez said.

That environmental vulnerability is already playing out on the ground. In 2025, San Jose Mayor Jerold Peña pointed out that rampant quarrying near the Rangas River had accelerated erosion within the Mount Isarog watershed and worsened flooding.

“What we are witnessing is not only the force of nature, but also the consequence of human actions — rampant quarrying and a widespread lack of understanding of the natural dynamics of the Rangas River,” Peña said at the time.

SOCIAL RELEVANCE. Kilyab recorded its new single, ‘Shux,’ to reflect issues surrounding El Niño and inflation caused by bad governance.

A year later, in preparation for El Niño, the mayor assured residents that the local government had formed a task force to monitor the watershed and secure community water supplies, though he acknowledged that meeting agricultural demands during the dry season would remain a steep challenge.

For Kilyab, the strain on Mount Isarog and Bicol’s watersheds highlights a stark disconnect between what local leaders prioritize and what communities actually need to survive worsening climate impacts.

Rather than treating floods and dry spells as mere acts of nature, the band argues that years of unchecked quarrying, weak environmental enforcement, and band-aid relief operations are the real drivers of the region’s recurring crises — the exact cycle of neglect that “Shux” wants to expose.

Rooted in their environmental protection advocacy, Kilyab cuts straight to the heart of political accountability with the song’s biting line: “Bakit ba kasi sila ang binoto niyo? Oh ayan, naghihirap tayo (Why did you vote for them in the first place? Look now, we’re suffering).” – Rappler.com

World.title: Food for feed: The price paid beyond the plate
World.content:
IMPACT. An anchovy purse seine fishing vessel, docked at a harbor in Chile, in 2021. The industry faces declining stocks and pressure from the fishmeal sector that depends on them.

Much of the fishmeal and fish oil that support imported farmed seafood consumed in the Philippines comes from global supply chains linked to pollution, labor abuses, overfishing, and food insecurity in other countries

In May 2025, a regional office of the Philippines’ fisheries agency in Visayas announced an initiative that would invite fishers to government meetings held to expand fish farming in the region.

Officials would introduce the fishers to ongoing fish breeding, processing, and distribution projects as part of a push to transform the local economy “from fish hunting to fish farming.” They emphasized that this transformation would ease stress on the ecosystem.

“Instead of constantly taking from the sea, let’s try to cultivate fish and give the ocean a chance to recover,” said community development officer Joel Lutao.

But critics worldwide have questioned whether the practice of catching and reducing whole, fresh fish to grow more seafood can ever be considered sustainable. The most popular types of farmed seafood — milkfish, tilapia, salmon, shrimp, and trout — are fed the kinds of wild fish that aquaculture claims to be saving, thereby accelerating ocean depletion, not slowing it.

Two-thirds of global aquaculture grows species that are fed fishmeal and fish oil. Before it reaches market, a farmed salmon, for instance, eats at some farms more than six times its weight in wild-caught fish.

The concerns about aquaculture extend far beyond the fate of the oceans. The feed that powers most of this industry comes with a huge variety of other hidden costs, according to a wide-reaching investigation by The Outlaw Ocean Project, a news organization based in Washington, DC.

These costs include the loss of artisanal fishing jobs, chronic chemical exposure, avoidable worker deaths, violent protests typically spurred by the horrid smell from fishmeal factories, and escalating geopolitical tensions as countries compete for scarce sources of protein.

‘There’s no fish left here’

What economists often call “externalities,” these social and environmental impacts exact a price primarily paid by the poorer countries where the feed ingredient is harvested and processed, far from where the resulting luxury seafood is eaten.

In The Gambia and Mauritania, the investigation documented how the industry drives food insecurity, as fish that once sustained local communities are increasingly being diverted into fishmeal factories for export.

In remote islands in Russia’s far east and in China’s Xinjiang region, the reporting detailed the use of forced labor on ships, at farms, and in factories.

In other countries, including India and Peru, this industry was tied to at least 80 incidents of civil unrest, some of them violent, usually in the form of labor strikes and community protests sparked by the water pollution or stench from factories cooking thousands of tons of decomposing fish, according to Bait to Plate, an online tool that tracks the fishing and seafood industries.

WORK. Workers offload catch at a fishmeal plant in Ullal. Photo courtesy of Changing Markets Foundation

In Senegal, fishmeal has put local fishers out of work, so increasingly they are selling — or repurposing — their boats to flee to Europe, typically taking the roughly 930-mile sea journey to Spain’s Canary Islands, a route that claimed more than 3,000 lives in 2025.

“We’re fishermen, but there’s no fish left here, so we left,” said Cheikhou Omar, a 21-year-old fisher, in September 2024 as he sat on a beach in Senegal, rescued after the fishing boat he took trying to get to Spain capsized, killing two dozen.

The five-year investigation mapped roughly the entire global fishmeal industry, including more than 1,400 fishmeal factories across 64 countries, tracing supply chains from fishing vessels to processing plants, feed mills, fish farms, and seafood retailers. The reporting effort involved dozens of journalists from as many countries, visiting factories and farms and boarding fishmeal ships at sea.

Unsustainable fishing

The oceans bear an especially heavy and largely invisible burden of the fishmeal and fish oil industry. More than a fifth of wild-caught fish around the world is used for non-human consumption, especially as feed for fish, but also chickens and pigs.

The investigation assessed more than 2,400 ships tied to fishmeal production, operating in the waters of at least 30 countries. It found that most of these ships do not fully comply with the Global Charter for Fisheries Transparency, a guide created by leading ocean-focused civil society groups detailing accountability standards for industrial fishing fleets.

For example, less than 30% of the fleet had publicly available location information, and under 25% had a unique vessel identification number, or ship license plate. Such opacity makes the fleet difficult to police.

Scientific studies classified at least half of the species landed by the assessed fishmeal vessels as “overexploited” or worse. Most of the ships in this fleet are purse seiners or trawlers, which deploy vast nets to capture dense schools of fish. Both gear types are associated with high levels of waste, routinely hauling in large volumes of bycatch and non-target species.

At least 165 of the ships in the global fishmeal fleet were bottom trawlers, conducting a particularly destructive form of fishing that uses weighted nets that scrape the ocean floor, destroying virtually everything in their paths.

The problem of unsustainable fishing is compounded by heavy government subsidies that keep too many vessels operating, accelerating pressure on already stressed fisheries.

“Any accounting of the true impact of aquaculture has to start not with the farm, but with the feed,” said Daniel Pauly, project director of the Sea Around Us initiative at University of British Columbia. “And that kind of accounting offers a very different picture than the industry offers.”

The problem with fishmeal

As commodities, fishmeal and fish oil promise to grow in international importance.

Starting in 2022, more than half of the seafood eaten globally came from fish farms rather than wild catch. Aquaculture is a $313-billion industry and the fastest-growing segment of global food production. Most of these fish farms are powered by fishmeal and fish oil.

Fishmeal processing in the Philippines is concentrated in three cities. The first is the port city of Navotas, known as the country’s “fishing capital.” Located in Metro Manila on the island of Luzon, it has at least one fishmeal plant.

The second is Zamboanga, a city on the island of Mindanao regarded as the Philippines’ “sardine capital,” home to half a dozen fishmeal plants. The third is General Santos. The national “tuna capital,” it lies in Mindanao and hosts four fishmeal plants.

Many of these plants focus primarily on processing seafood for human consumption, but they also redirect inedible offcuts into fishmeal. This practice is widely cited as sustainable and socially beneficial, since it uses materials that would otherwise be thrown away.

Therefore, fishmeal production in the Philippines is less of a driver of food insecurity than it is in other countries that use whole edible fish. However, the Philippines suffers from severe food insecurity because of general overfishing and the export of most catch, be it small anchovies or larger species like tuna.

The far greater burden of food insecurity, social unrest, and air and water pollution is borne by the poorer countries that produce the fishmeal or fishmeal-fed seafood the Philippines imports. The country imported more seafood than it produced as of 2023.

Half of all seafood globally is farmed, and most of that is fed fishmeal. The fish farms in several of the countries that export the most seafood to the Philippines — including China, Vietnam, Papua New Guinea, Chile, and Japan — have ties to severe problems caused by fishmeal production, according to the investigation.

Hidden costs

The investigation revealed a surprising diversity of hidden costs in the global feed industry.

In Senegal, fishmeal production accelerated overfishing, eroding traditional fishing grounds and contributing to thousands of young men attempting deadly and desperate voyages at sea to Europe.

In Russia, fishmeal workers were held captive in secluded company towns in remote parts of the country, or stuck on ships far from shore.

“People have nowhere to go, no money,” one worker said in a plea to Russian President Vladimir Putin, who participated in an episode of a call-in television show about the fishmeal plant. “Please, help us,” a second worker said.

In Chile, several hundred protesters burned tires and blocked coastal highways and railway tracks, demonstrating against the early closure of the fishing season, a move partly driven by overfishing tied to fishmeal.

The investigation also unveiled the hidden role of forced labor and land appropriation in China’s growing aquaculture industry. (To be continued) – Rappler.com

The reporting for this story was part of a larger investigation conducted by an international team of journalists based at The Outlaw Ocean Project.

World.title: Gatchalian ensures fairness of Senate impeachment court in VP’s trial
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian. INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Saturday ensured that the Senate impeachment court will uphold fairness in the ongoing trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.

Gatchalian was asked to comment on the statement of Duterte on Friday that she is “preparing for the worst” on the verdict of the impeachment court on her trial.

“Makakaasa naman ang taumbayan na magiging patas ang impeachment court at magiging fair ang impeachment court lalo na pagdating sa ebidensya at pagtanggap ng ebidensya,” Gatchalian said in an interview with DWIZ.

Article continues after this 

(The people can expect that the impeachment court will be fair, especially when it comes to assessing evidence.)

“Ito nasabi ko na nung una, ang puno’t dulo nito ay yung ebidensya. At kung paano ma-present ng prosecution at paano rin ma-disprove o ma-counter ng defense. So iyan yan ang pinakamahalaga,” he added.

(This is what I have been saying before, the end goal of this is the evidence. And how the prosecution presents their evidence and how the defense disproves and counters them. That is the most important.)

READ: Sara Duterte ‘prepared for worst’ as trial nears decision

Speaking in a press conference on Friday, Duterte said that her office and staff will continue implementing projects if her camp secures a verdict of acquittal. However, if she is convicted, she said that several employees of the Office of the Vice President (OVP) will lose their jobs as they are co-terminus with her as vice president.

Article continues after this 

She added that OVP employees would have to move out from its central office in Mandaluyong as she wanted to retain the building, which used to be her campaign headquarters during the 2022 elections.

Meanwhile, when asked if he is confident that the trial will be finished before the year ends, Gatchalian answered: “Sa takbo, mukhang kakayanin bago mag-end of the year. Ang qualification ko lang, marami kong beses sinasabi ito, hindi ako tumatama. Pero sa mukha naman sa number of witnesses na binigay na ng defense, mukha naman aabot.”

Article continues after this 

(By the looks of it, this may be done before the year ends. My qualification is, like I always say before, I don’t get it right. But with the number of witnesses presented by the defense, I think it’s possible.)

READ: VP Sara Duterte’s dentist expected as next defense witness

Duterte’s defense team has so far presented nine witnesses since November 9 against the allegations of her unexplained wealth, failure to truthfully declare her assets and liabilities, and failure to divest herself of business interests while serving as vice president.

World.title: Senators unite vs proposed coffee tax, say it would burden poor
World.content:
Senator Panfilo Lacson.

MANILA, Philippines — Senators have closed ranks against a proposed tax on coffee products, warning that it would burden poor consumers, hurt local farmers and make an everyday staple more expensive.

Sen. Panfilo “Ping” Lacson on Saturday said his colleagues were nearly unanimous in considering the proposal anti-poor, noting that some Filipinos, particularly those in rural communities, could barely afford more than coffee and pandesal for breakfast.

“Halos nagkakaisa ang sentimyento ng senador diyan na parang napaka-anti-poor kasi ang mga kababayan natin, lalo sa malayong lugar sa bukid, talagang halos ang iba kahit pandesal na lang ang kinakain,” Lacson said in an interview with DZRH radio.

Article continues after this 

(We in the Senate are almost one in considering the coffee tax as anti-poor. Many Filipinos especially in rural areas have only coffee and pandesal for breakfast)

“So, para pang-almusal, para buwisan pa natin ang kape, parang anti-poor,” added Lacson of the Senate majority bloc.

(So, for the government to potentially tax even coffee, that is anti-poor)

Palace also cold

Malacañang also rejected the proposal, with Presidential Legislative Liaison Office Secretary Joey Salceda saying that Filipinos shifting from alcohol to coffee was a positive development.

Article continues after this 

“We oppose taxing coffee itself. If more Filipinos are drinking coffee instead of alcohol, that is a good thing. It means that sin taxes on alcohol are working as designed,” Salceda said.

“Simply put, you can drive after drinking coffee. You should not drive after drinking alcohol. The distinction is that simple,” he added.

Article continues after this 

Salceda said excise taxes were designed to discourage socially undesirable behavior, not to make up for declining revenues from other sin taxes.

He, however, distinguished the proposed coffee tax from proposals to expand the coverage of the sweetened beverage tax to include sweetened coffee products, such as 3-in-1 mixes.

“There may be legitimate public health reasons for considering such measures, particularly excessive sugar content. But these proposals should be evaluated on their own merits, not on the basis of declining alcohol tax revenues,” he explained.

READ: Coffee tax proposal fails to perk up senators

Other senators earlier rejected the proposal to tax coffee, which was floated by a liquor industry representative during a House hearing on Wednesday as an alternative to higher taxes on alcoholic beverages.

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said taxing coffee was not a good idea, pointing out that Filipinos had developed a strong coffee-drinking culture and that many workers and drivers relied on the beverage to stay awake during overtime work.

He also called for sensitivity toward the country’s farmers and fishermen, whose products deserve government support.

Sen. Pia Cayetano of the minority bloc who raised the issue during Friday’s Senate deliberations on the proposed 2027 budget of the Department of Health, said the proposal would no longer move forward after House ways and means committee chair Miro Quimbo declared it “dead on arrival” at the lower chamber.

Cayetano also stressed that coffee was a product whose farmers the government should help, adding that she was not aware of any harm from drinking it unless consumed in excessive amounts.

Senate Deputy Majority Floor Leader Joel Villanueva, meanwhile, joked that discussing a coffee tax could lead to a messy situation.

“Maghahalo ang balat sa tinalupan,” he said, prompting laughter during the budget deliberations.

(The skin will mix with the peeled one.)

READ: Proposed coffee tax gets cold before it can brew at House

Senate Minority Leader Alan Peter Cayetano had also dismissed the proposal, saying senators were not seriously considering it.

The suggestion to tax coffee came from Olivia Limpe-Aw, president of the Distilled Spirits Association of the Philippines, who argued during the House hearing that younger consumers were shifting from liquor to coffee.

She cited declining liquor sales, attributing the trend to higher prices and changing consumer preferences, including younger Filipinos’ preference for coffee.

World.title: Bantug: VP Duterte’s whole-day impeachment trial to resume next week
World.content:
Senate Secretary and Impeachment Clerk of Court Renato Bantug Jr. presides over the pre-trial conference for the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte on Monday, June 22, 2026. — Photo from Senate of the Philippines/Facebook

MANILA, Philippines — The whole-day impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte will resume next week, December 1-4, according to Senate secretary Renato Bantug.

The impeachment trial was suspended this week to give way to the marathon plenary deliberations of the proposed P7.2-trillion national budget for fiscal year 2027.

READ: VP Duterte faces Senate on OVP budget, dodges impeach questions

Article continues after this 

“The Impeachment Court, upon the instruction of the Presiding Officer, hereby advises all concerned that whole-day trial will be conducted on December 1, 2, 3, and 4, 2026 (Tuesday to Friday), 10:00 a.m. onwards,” Bantug said in an advisory.

Duterte’s defense team earlier asked the Senate impeachment court to subpoena Dr. Lourdes Lebosada, Duterte’s dentist and said to be a former co-owner of controversial banana chips company Cale88 Foods Corp., and Bureau of Customs Deputy Commissioner Agaton Teodoro Uvero to take the witness stand. They are expected to testify between December 1 and 4.

READ: VP Sara Duterte’s dentist expected as next defense witness

Meanwhile, in a press conference on Friday, Duterte said that she still has not discussed with her team if she will be testifying as a witness in her own trial. She noted that her team said that the presentation of witnesses may be finished next week.

Her defense team has so far presented nine witnesses since November 9 against the allegations of her unexplained wealth, failure to truthfully declare her assets and liabilities, and failure to divest herself of business interests while serving as vice president. /ms

World.title: Man hacks brother over land dispute in Bukidnon
World.content:
A 58-year-old man is confined at the Quezon Health Infirmary Hospital in Quezon, Bukidnon, after sustaining a hack wound to the left side of his body when his 51-year-old brother allegedly attacked him with a bolo during an intoxicated argument over their parents’ land in Barangay 9, Poblacion, on November 27, 2026. Photo courtesy of Quezon PNP

QUEZON, Bukidnon — A 51-year-old man was arrested by police after he allegedly hacked his 58-year-old brother with a bolo during a heated argument over family land in Barangay 9 Poblacion here on Friday morning, November 27.

According to the Quezon Municipal Police Station (MPS), authorities received a cellphone report from a concerned citizen regarding the hacking incident at around 10:30 a.m.

Responding officers immediately proceeded to the scene and launched a hot pursuit operation, resulting in the arrest of the suspect.

Article continues after this 

Initial investigation revealed that the brothers were having a drinking spree with a neighbor before the attack.

After consuming alcohol, the two got into a heated argument over land owned by their parents.

During the altercation, the 51-year-old suspect went inside his house, grabbed a bolo, and hacked his older brother once on the left side of his body.

The 58-year-old victim sustained a single hack wound and was rushed to the Quezon Health Infirmary Hospital for medical treatment.

The suspect is currently detained at the Quezon MPS custodial facility for proper disposition and the filing of appropriate charges. /ms

World.title: Poe wants proposed AI authority placed under DOST, not DICT
World.content:
Rep. Brian Poe delivers his address at the Media People’s Choice Awards 2026 on Thursday, Nov. 11, 2026. —Photo from his office

MANILA, Philippines — A lawmaker pushing for a national framework on artificial intelligence (AI) wants a proposed agency overseeing the technology’s development placed under the Department of Science and Technology (DOST), saying the department is better equipped to drive research and innovation than the Department of Information and Communications Technology (DICT).

FPJ Panday Bayanihan Rep. Brian Poe Llamanzares said the DICT already has its hands full overseeing telecommunications, social media data and other digital concerns, and should not be burdened with the additional responsibility of leading the country’s AI development.

“I don’t want to bog down the DICT. I see how much they have to handle telecommunications, social media data… and then you’re going to stack on top of it this monumental problem of artificial intelligence. I feel like it’s too much,” he said.

Article continues after this 

Llamanzares made the remarks during the 2026 Asean-ROK AI+ Connectivity Forum organized by the Stratbase Institute and the South Korean Embassy in the Philippines last Thursday.

The lawmaker proposes the creation of an AI development authority (Aida), which would formulate the country’s AI strategy and coordinate initiatives among government agencies, industries and other sectors.

“The DICT is more regulatory in nature. [You] should put it in an agency whose sole purpose is to advance innovation… give it to an agency that hasn’t been given as much importance or attention as it should be,” he said.

Llamanzares argued that placing the proposed authority under the DOST could also help address the country’s longstanding underinvestment in research and development (R&D).

READ: AI needs citizen representation

Article continues after this 

Compared with other countries, he said, the Philippines continues to lag in research and development partly because of insufficient government attention and funding for the sector.

“We don’t give enough attention to the DOST,” he said, adding that placing the AI body under the department could encourage fiscal managers to allocate more resources to R&D.

Article continues after this 

He also said the proposed authority could encourage more graduates in science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) to pursue careers in government research and innovation.

Since 2024, the DOST has been pushing for the National AI Strategy for the Philippines (NAIS-PH) to guide AI’s development and deployment through 2028.

The government approved NAIS-PH in May 2025 to serve as the strategic direction for the development and adoption of Al in the country.

Llamanzares also discussed his proposed AI Governance Act, filed under House Bill No. 1196, which seeks to establish a regulatory framework for the use and development of AI in the country.

The measure is among 27 AI-related bills being consolidated in the House of Representatives.

He said his original proposal was patterned after the European Union’s risk-based regulatory framework, which classifies AI applications according to the potential risks they pose to users and the public.

Earlier this month, President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. signed Executive Order No. 131, creating the National AI Council (Naic), an interagency body responsible for coordinating, facilitating and monitoring the implementation of the national Al framework.

The council is chaired by the Executive Secretary and brings together key government agencies and private sector representation.

READ: Marcos EO sets up national council on AI development

Beyond domestic regulation, Llamanzares also pushed for closer regional cooperation in AI governance, citing discussions within the Asean Inter-Parliamentary Assembly on establishing an Asean AI center.

The proposed center would help investors navigate the different AI regulatory frameworks across Southeast Asian countries by providing information on their respective rules and requirements.This, he said, could make it easier for companies to expand and distribute their AI operations across the region. /ms

World.title: Gatchalian: Amendments on P7.2-T budget bill set on Dec. 4
World.content:
Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian INQUIRER PHOTO / NIÑO JESUS ORBETA

MANILA, Philippines — Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Saturday said that the proposed P7.2-trillion budget bill for 2027 will enter its period of amendments in the Senate on Friday, December 4, after the upper chamber wrapped up its plenary deliberations on the proposed budget for next year.

The Senate began its marathon debates on the proposed budget last Monday, November 23, and concluded them early Saturday, November 28.

“So magkakaroon kami ng period of amendments on Friday at iku-close na on second reading para ma-review ng mga senators natin over the weekend yung budget,” Gatchalian said in an interview with DWIZ.

Article continues after this 

(So we will have a period of amendments on Friday and we will close it on second reading so the senators can review the budget over the weekend.)

READ: VP Duterte faces Senate on OVP budget, dodges impeach questions

He also said that the Senate aims to hold the third and final reading for the proposed budget bill by Monday, December 7.

“Hindi ito certified as urgent para mabigyan ng panahon ang mga senators na i-review pa, basahin over the weekend yung budget,” he added.

(This is not certified as urgent so the senators can have enough time to review the budget over the weekend.)

Article continues after this 

He then shared that several senators have submitted their preliminary amendments for the proposed budget. However, he ensured that their amendments will still be discussed next Friday.

He added that the senators are required to use their official letterhead in filing their amendments and that the amendments made must be uploaded on the Senate’s official website.

Article continues after this 

READ: Lacson flags unequal distribution of P760-B multi-purpose buildings

What amendments to advance

When asked what kind of amendments he will be pushing for, Gatchalian said that he will focus on three things: safeguarding provisions, augmentation for the education sector; and the continuation of implementation of foreign-assisted projects.

“Unang-una yung safeguards na na-emphasize ni Sen. Ping [Lacson] na hindi pwedeng generic yung pangalan. At so isa yan sa mga mahigpit namin i-monitor at sisiguraduhin sa budget, yung safeguards at of course yung supporting documents,” he added.

(First of these are the safeguards emphasized by Sen. Ping [Lacson] that the names of projects cannot be generic. That will be one of the things we will closely monitor in the budget, and the supporting documents.)

During the last day of the plenary debates, Lacson questioned the unequal distribution of multi-purpose building projects among local governments as he noted that most of them are built in high-income cities and municipalities.

World.title: New classroom gives over 100 Albay students safe place to learn
World.content:
More than 100 students in Manito, Albay, now have a safe and permanent place to learn after Grab Philippines and HOPE turned over a new classroom to Inang Maharang Elementary School. The P1.4-million project, funded through the Grab HOPE Hour initiative, also provided laptops and school supplies to support teaching and learning. (Photos courtesy of Grab Philippines and HOPE)

LEGAZPI CITY — More than 100 students in Manito, Albay, who had been holding classes in makeshift spaces after Super Typhoon Uwan (international name: Fung-wong) struck, now have a permanent classroom following its turnover to Inang Maharang Elementary School.

The 7-by-9-meter classroom was built through a partnership between Grab Philippines and HOPE, which raised about P1.4 million through the Grab HOPE Hour initiative.

The campaign encouraged Grab users to donate GrabCoins and book eligible GrabCar rides and GrabFood orders, with their contributions supporting the construction of classrooms for Filipino students.

Article continues after this 

The classroom, turned over on Nov. 10, is equipped with electrical and lighting systems, a restroom, a teacher’s desk and a chalkboard. Laptops and school supplies were also provided to support teachers and students.

“Last year, we committed to moving malasakit into action. Today, that commitment has become a classroom,” Grab Philippines Country Managing Director CJ Lacsican said in a statement on Saturday.

School head Salvacion A. Dazal said the new facility fulfilled the school community’s dream of providing learners with a safe and conducive place to study.

HOPE founder and executive chairperson Nanette Medved-Po said the project demonstrated how small contributions could be turned into lasting benefits for communities.

Grab Philippines and HOPE are set to launch Grab HOPE Choice Meals in December. Under the initiative, participating GrabFood merchants may nominate menu items, with every purchase generating a fixed donation to HOPE’s classroom-building program. /ms

World.title: Criminal cases filed vs Italian entrepreneur, co-accused junked
World.content:
INQUIRER.net stock images

MANILA, Philippines — A string of criminal charges filed against an Italian entrepreneur and other individuals over alleged human trafficking and other illegal acts have been dismissed by trial courts and the Department of Justice (DOJ).

Italian entrepreneur Adel En Nouri and several foreign and Filipino individuals faced non-bailable cases such as qualified trafficking in person, large scale illegal recruitment, and serious illegal detention.

READ: DOJ to start handling ‘syndicate-level’ drug cases only

Article continues after this 

Last October 16, the Pasay City Regional Trial Court (RTC) junked the qualified trafficking charge against Nouri, Centvin Menez, and an unidentified “Mami Jhane” as it found that the prosecution failed to present sufficient evidence against the accused individuals.

The case stemmed from complaints of two Filipino women who accused Nouri and Menez of allegedly forcing them to do online sexual shows for foreign clients.

The court said that the allegations of the complainants were based “almost entirely on their own uncorroborated narration” adding that their statements “are highly suspect, internally vulnerable, and laden with circumstances that cast serious doubt on their credibility and motivation.”

It added that the prosecution failed to prove that the accused committed trafficking and that the conclusion that they are criminally liable as “end-users” is unsupported by proof of a participation in a trafficking scheme as distinguished by allegations of online interaction.

Article continues after this 

“Taken together, the record reveals a prosecution case built not on solid evidence, but on conjecture, inference, and the bare assertions of complainants whose credibility is materially compromised by their own admissions and motivations. To require the accused to undergo the rigors of a full-blown criminal trial under these circumstances would be a violation of their constitutional right to due process and the presumption of innocence,” the court wrote.

In a separate decision issued by Bacoor City RTC last November 12, the court also dismissed illegal detention charges against Nouri, and co-accused John Gabriel Siopongco and Bueno Caesar Baldado as the prosecution failed to provide sufficient evidence.

Article continues after this 

“Thus, in the absence of evidence presented by the prosecution to support the charges and considering the private complainants’ sworn clarification as to the circumstances that led to the filing thereof, the Court finds no sufficient justification to require the accused to stand trial for charges whose factual basis has been seriously put into doubt,” it said.

The court also recalled the arrest warrants issued against Nouri and Baldado dated April 10, 2026.

The Tanauan City RTC also junked the illegal recruitment charge against Nouri, Mohammed En Nouri and Myrna Paterno and recalled the arrest warrants issued against them. It also lifted the hold departure order issued against Nouri last August 3.

The court noted the private complainant’s lack of interest to prosecute the case against the accused individuals.

“With this development, the court finds merit in the prosecution’s contention that it has been deprived of the witnesses required to prove the charges beyond reasonable doubt. Allowing the cases to remain pending would only result in unnecessary clogging of the court’s docket, which would ultimately be in vain considering the lack of vital prosecution witnesses. Relatedly, crucial to the dispensation of justice is the nipping of untenable cases as soon as their baselessness is discernible,” it ruled.

The court also dismissed the same case filed against En Nouri’s co-accused Raffaela Razon, Krizia Ann Loyang, Joshua Lim, and Ricardo Evangelista due to the complainant-witness’ repeated failure to attend the hearings.

Likewise, the Tanauan City RTC granted the motion filed by complainants to withdraw the large-scale illegal recruitment complaint filed against Nouri, Narwani Ricky Ravin, Prerna Giani, Nisha Deepak Khemlani, Clarence Co Quinlop, Brian James De Jesus So, Michelangelo Tang Co, Jacqueline Sio, Krizzia Ann Geronda Loyang.

“The complainants alleged that after a mere thorough and careful evaluation of the facts and circumstances surrounding the case, they have come to realize that there was a misapprehension and/or misappreciation of the material facts which led to the filing of the instant complaint,” the court said.

The DOJ-Office of the Prosecutor in Lipa City also junked the qualified trafficking in person, illegal recruitment, and serious detention cases filed against Nouri and his co-accused Norminda Esperilla, Angelito Sayco, Yuness En Nouri, Mohammed En Nouri, and Fatima Arfaque.

World.title: More Multinationals Exit Myanmar as Economic Turmoil Deepens
World.content:
At least four more international brands announced their withdrawal from Myanmar this month, as deepening post-coup turmoil triggers a fresh exodus of foreign investment.

They joined a broader retreat of multinational businesses since the 2021 military takeover, driven by regime import and currency controls, soaring production costs, power outages, and international sanctions.

On Thursday, Singapore-based Pezzo Pizza announced it would close all branches in Myanmar starting today (Nov. 27), ending 10 years of operations. The company entered the market in 2016, operating five branches across Yangon and Mandalay.

The announcement came a day after The Manhattan Fish Market shuttered its last Yangon outlet, at Myanmar Plaza, ending the Malaysia-based seafood chain’s 12-year presence.

On Nov. 13, Japanese automaker Isuzu announced it had ended Myanmar repair and maintenance operations after liquidating its local service unit.

Meanwhile, British consumer goods giant Unilever will exit Myanmar after 16 years by selling its shares to Centig Holding, a subsidiary of local partner Europe and Asia Commercial (EAC), with the deal expected to close in 2027.

While the four companies gave no reason for their exit, the World Bank 2026 report notes that Myanmar’s private sector is operating in “a highly challenging and uncertain environment” driven by conflict, macroeconomic pressures, policy reversal and weakening state capacity. It adds that firms are facing “higher cost, greater compliance risks, [and] weaker incentives to invest, expand and innovate.”

According to a Myanmar Peace Monitor report released on Nov. 27, the post-coup flight of foreign investment encompasses nearly 40 multinational companies across 16 countries ranging from neighboring Thailand, Malaysia and India to the U.S., UK, Spain, Germany, Austria, Italy and Norway. It said the withdrawals were being driven by the spread of armed conflict and a collapsing business environment.

The departing businesses span major sectors such as oil and gas, mining, banking, telecommunications, real estate, and manufacturing, including 12 global clothing brands whose exit has dealt a severe blow to local garment workers.

“More companies are monitoring the situation and planning exit strategies,” a Myanmar policy analyst told The Irrawaddy, blaming currency controls and raw material shortages triggered by regime import controls.

“Foreign investors can’t endure these losses any longer,” he said, adding that he expects the situation to worsen amid rising unemployment, soaring inflation and shortages of basic goods.

World.title: Beijing Shields Myanmar Regime After Genocide Ruling, Naypyitaw Begs for Energy Investment, and More
World.content:
Myanmar seeks more Chinese energy investment at Belt and Road forum

Naypyitaw’s reliance on China for energy investment, fuel supplies and electricity infrastructure is deepening all the time, with Energy Minister Ko Ko Lwin using his latest trip to China to seek yet more investment across the sector.

At the Fourth Belt and Road Energy Ministers’ Conference in Qingdao on Nov. 25-26, Ko Ko Lwin met officials from China’s National Energy Administration (NEA), urging them to help Myanmar meet its electricity and energy needs. Discussions covered new offshore gas exploration, hydropower projects, cross-border power lines, solar and wind projects, and energy storage batteries.

Much the same topics were on the agenda when Ko Ko Lwin traveled to Kunming and Beijing in April to secure lower rates for fuel imports from a number of Chinese firms. Myanmar relies on imports for 97 percent of its gasoline and diesel needs, a dependence that had already taken a serious toll on the cash-strapped regime before the Middle East crisis triggered shortages and price hikes.

Regime officials are also asking Chinese state enterprises to invest in refinery projects linked to the Myanmar–China oil pipeline network. In April the regime signed a deal with China’s North Petro-Chem to increase production at the Htaukshabin-Kanni oil field in Magwe Region’s Minbu.

It has also revived the Thanlyin No. 1 Oil Refinery near Yangon with Chinese assistance, potentially enabling it to bypass jet-fuel sanctions and sustain air operations. The facility’s expected output of up to 150,000 metric tons of jet fuel annually roughly matching Myanmar’s imports last year.

China defends Myanmar regime after ICJ genocide ruling

China has publicly defended Myanmar after the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s landmark ruling that the country committed genocide against the Rohingya.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing “noted” the ruling but argued that the Rakhine issue should be handled cautiously given its “complex historical, ethnic and religious dimensions.” He urged the international community to avoid “complicating” the issue and reiterated China’s support for dialogue and the repatriation of displaced Rohingya.

China also raised concerns about what it called judicial “overreach” and questions of jurisdiction by international courts.

The ruling stems from a case brought by the Gambia over the Myanmar military’s 2017 clearance operations in northern Rakhine State, which drove more than 700,000 Rohingya into neighboring Bangladesh.

Guo also defended the Chinese judge on the ICJ, Xue Hanqin, who voted in Myanmar’s favor, saying she had “acted independently in her personal capacity.”

As a permanent member of the UN Security Council, China has consistently pushed back against international pressure on Myanmar over the Rohingya crisis, arguing that it should be resolved through dialogue and cooperation between Myanmar and Bangladesh rather than external intervention.

However, the ruling, the first finding of state responsibility for genocide in the ICJ’s 81-year history, places China in an awkward position while it continues to shield Naypyitaw from international pressure and deepens ties with a military regime now found guilty of one of the world’s worst atrocities in recent decades.

China drawn deeper into Myanmar–Thai river pollution dispute

China has promised to dispatch experts to help investigate river pollution affecting Mekong tributaries in Thailand due to unregulated Chinese-invested mining across the border in Myanmar.

The announcement came after a meeting in Bangkok on Tuesday where Thailand urged China to help halt mining operations in Shan State for at least six months as the Kok, Sai, Ruak and Mekong rivers flowing into northern Thailand are contaminated, threatening human health and livelihoods.

Thailand’s Pollution Control Department has repeatedly found arsenic, lead, cadmium and other heavy metals above safety limits in the rivers, tracing the pollution to unregulated gold and rare-earth mines in Shan State. Most of them are run by Chinese people in areas controlled by China-linked armed groups like the United Wa State Army (UWSA).

Thailand and Myanmar agreed to conduct their first joint testing of the Kok and Sai next month. But while pledging to participate in the investigation, Beijing stopped short of agreeing to the proposed shutdown and cautioned against drawing “premature conclusions.”

Instead, the Foreign Ministry spokesman claimed Chinese companies operating overseas are required to comply with local laws and environmental regulations—except that these are non-existent in the lawless borderlands of Myanmar.

Still, China seems to feel it can no longer completely dodge the issue as Thailand has brought it up at every high-level meeting, no matter how amiable, in recent weeks amid growing outrage and protests at home.

Chinese scammers move with the times

Shaken up by major crackdowns on Myanmar’s border scam hubs, online fraud networks now infest other parts of the country, from upscale condominiums in the commercial capital Yangon to remote corners of Shan State.

Since mid-November, the military regime has reported a series of raids that netted more than 570 suspected online scammers and gambling operators, over 400 of them Chinese.

In Yangon, the raids in Yankin, Mayangone and Thaketa townships resulted in nearly 230 arrests. Nearly half of them were Myanmar nationals who reportedly worked voluntarily for their Chinese bosses. In Thaketa, arrests included a Chinese ringleader wanted by China’s Public Security Ministry, but in Yankin the boss escaped, throwing his workers under the bus.

In southern Shan around the same time, some 330 Chinese scammers and around 20 Myanmar women were arrested in Kyethi and Mong Kung townships. In Kyethi, they were nabbed with a cache of rifles and pistols.

Now some major border scam centers have been dismantled under pressure from Beijing, operators appear to have dispersed across the country, running smaller, more mobile operations. But in Myawaddy near the Thai border, big compounds still thrive under the protection of regime-aligned ethnic militias.

Compiled by Thurein Lynn

World.title: Myanmar Garment Sector Braces for EU Bombshell After Genocide Verdict
World.content:
International labor unions’ calls for the European Union to strip Myanmar of its duty-free trade privileges after the International Court of Justice’s genocide ruling have sent shockwaves through local export industry. Operators warn that withdrawing benefits would have severe impacts on the country’s garment industry and hundreds of thousands of workers.

In a Nov. 24 letter to EU leaders, IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union called on Brussels to withdraw Myanmar’s Everything But Arms (EBA) trade preferences and terminate the EU-funded MADE in Myanmar program.

IndustriALL Europe and IndustriALL Global Union represent over 50 million industrial and garment workers in more than 140 countries. Both have pressed for stronger action against Myanmar’s military regime over labor rights abuses since the 2021 coup.

The EBA grants tariff-free entry to European markets for all exports — barring weapons and ammunition — from least-developed countries, including Myanmar. The scheme underpins Myanmar’s US$ 3-billion annual garment export trade with Europe. MADE in Myanmar, meanwhile, is an EU-backed initiative aimed at improving labor standards and working conditions in the country’s garment industry.

Local garment manufacturers said international labor groups have pushed for withdrawal of Myanmar’s EBA privileges for years, but warned the move could devastate an industry on which hundreds of thousands depend.

“If the EU decides to suspend the scheme, we will have to find alternative markets. We can no longer rely on a single export destination,” one garment operator told The Irrawaddy.

Labor organizations argue that EBA and MADE in Myanmar help channel revenue into the coffers of an illegitimate military regime and should therefore be withdrawn. The EU has yet to respond their calls.

Local factory owners, however, say the industry’s difficulties stem more from domestic challenges since the coup — including foreign-exchange controls, rising production costs, shortages of raw materials, and financial transaction difficulties after Myanmar’s inclusion on the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) blacklist.

The garment industry targeted $5 billion in export earnings for the 2026-27 fiscal year ending March, but industry sources say that goal is increasingly out of reach.

“With just a few months left, we have barely achieved half the target ,” said a Yangon-based garment business owner in Yangon.

Myanmar’s garment sector employs 450,000 to 500,000 workers, mostly women, and relies heavily on the Cut-Make-Pack (CMP) model, under which foreign brands pay factories to process their raw materials. Most exports go to Japan and the EU.

Before the 2021 coup, more than 70 percent of Myanmar’s garment exports went to the EU. That share has since fallen to around 50 percent after manufacturers began shifting production to other countries.

Industry sources say more than 20 manufacturers, including suppliers for major international brands such as H&M, have either closed or plan to leave Myanmar this year.

The Myanmar Garment Manufacturers Association (MGMA) has urged the EU to consider the potential impact on workers before making any decision, warning that broader trade restrictions could further weaken the export sector and threaten jobs across the industry.

World.title: Thailand Tests Find High Lead, Arsenic in River Shellfish
World.content:
BANGKOK—Thai authorities have found dangerous levels of arsenic and lead in shellfish and other species in rivers contaminated by suspected mining pollution from neighboring Myanmar, an official said Thursday.

The findings, from nearly two years of testing, prompted authorities to urge residents to avoid eating 10 species including shellfish and river snails.

The warning came earlier this week, but with no details of the contamination levels found or the testing processes.

An official from Thailand’s Fisheries Department, speaking on condition of anonymity as they were not authorized to talk to media, told AFP that over 500 samples were taken from five rivers, and 18 had heavy metals at levels over safety limits.

The details came as Thai officials held talks in Bangkok to try to address growing public fears about river contamination from mining operations in war-torn Myanmar.

Heavy metals including mercury, lead, cadmium and arsenic were found at levels exceeding safety standards in 10 species, the Fisheries Department official said.

In some, arsenic was detected at nearly four times the permitted limit and lead at nearly six times the limit.

The affected species include freshwater shrimp, river snails, freshwater mussels and horse mussels, as well as local fish that feed on them, the official said.

The official said the tests involved samples from the Mekong and Salween rivers, which flow through Thailand and Myanmar, and three other rivers in Thailand’s north, the Sai, Kok and Ruak.

No contamination was found in farmed aquatic species, the official added.

Local residents in Thailand’s north and northeast have for months complained about river contamination from mines in Myanmar, but the issue has gathered growing public attention in recent weeks.

Tap water supplies to 14 villages in Mae Sai district near the Myanmar border were suspended this month after officials found arsenic levels in the local waterworks to be 30 times higher than safe limits.

Campaigners, experts and politicians trace the pollution back to mining in Myanmar, where the long-running civil war has led to unregulated exploitation of natural resources.

In a bid to spur action, residents this week prepared traditional dishes with locally caught food from affected areas and invited politicians, attempting to highlight the risks they now face.

There are fears contamination could spread further down the Mekong, which supports millions of people across several countries.

“Fish are harder to find and even if you find, people won’t buy it,” said Saengwaree Suvirakan, a farmer from Chiang Mai, who joined a protest in Bangkok this week.

World.title: Myanmar’s Putschist President Shrugs at ICJ Genocide Verdict
World.content:
Myanmar’s putschist president, Min Aung Hlaing, hit back at the International Court of Justice (ICJ)’s genocide ruling on Wednesday, telling his cabinet that the regime will not implement “unacceptable” measures.

“As a responsible country, we will carry out measures we consider necessary but will not comply with those that should not be followed,” he said.

The World Court ordered Myanmar to implement several measures after ruling on Nov. 19 that it committed genocide against the Rohingya during military operations in Rakhine in 2016-17: Prosecute the perpetrators, provide reparations, ensure safe repatriation, guarantee non-repetition, and pass laws criminalizing genocide.

The junta chief claimed the ruling had damaged Myanmar’s national dignity, dismissing the case brought by the Gambia as a one-sided accusation.

“I will not accept anything that harms the country,” said the self-appointed president, who as military chief oversaw the 2016-17 Rakhine “clearance operations” now ruled as genocide. He also stands accused of war crimes and crimes against humanity following the coup he staged in 2021.

Legal experts noted that the ICJ ruling is legally binding, meaning the losing party cannot selectively choose which parts of the judgment to accept or reject.

“It was a final judgement from the international court — not a statement, recommendation or instruction,” human rights lawyer Zar Li Aye told The Irrawaddy.

“As per UN charter 94 (1), every member state is legally obliged to comply with orders from the International Court of Justice,” she stressed.

She added that Myanmar risked being found guilty of violating additional international laws if it failed to comply with the ICJ’s decision.

The ruling has drawn widespread international backing from Western and regional governments, the EU, UN officials, and major human rights organizations, which welcomed the landmark decision as a decisive step toward accountability for the Rohingya community.

Permanent members France and the UK requested a closed-door UN Security Council meeting on Wednesday to press members on Myanmar’s compliance with the ruling. The outcome of the meeting remains unknown.

Meanwhile, the judgement has triggered a chorus of denial from the regime and its allies. The Ministry of Foreign Affairs rejected it as “a great disappointment delivered with dissenting opinions” and “not decided unanimously by judges,” referring to the 9-6 ruling.

However, it remains unclear what effect the judgement will have on the regime’s international standing.

“We may see no direct impact from the ICJ’s decision in the short term,” Myanmar political researcher Sai Kyi Zin Soe told The Irrawaddy.

“We expect to see different responses from different countries, depending on how Myanmar responds and to what extent it complies with the court’s decision,” he said.

World.title: Myanmar’s Economy Reeling as Kyat Nosedives
World.content:
The rapid depreciation of the kyat is tearing across Myanmar’s economy, disrupting imports, driving up production costs and raising fears of further economic shocks.

The kyat market rate steadily weakened since last month before nosediving to reach over 5,400 kyats to the dollar on Thursday.

Exporters as well as importers say their businesses are increasingly unprofitable, exacerbated by regime restrictions.

One exporter told The Irrawaddy that although businesses are officially allowed to exchange 85 percent of their export earnings at market rates, banks are often unable to offer them, plus the regime requires the remaining 15 percent to be converted at the fixed rate of 2,100 kyats per dollar, resulting in significant losses.

Rising operating costs and volatile exchange rates are forcing some exporters to scale back overseas shipments. Traders are also struggling to determine how to price imported goods as foreign-currency costs fluctuate sharply.
