“Importers are finding it difficult to set prices because the dollar rate is so unstable. This problem needs to be resolved immediately or domestic consumption will also be affected,” said a trader.

The latest decline is due to several factors, not least that the regime has announced it will borrow over 2 trillion kyats from the Central Bank to pay plug the hole in its budget—essentially telling the bank to print money. The rubberstamp Parliament has already approved an additional budget for the Central Bank to churn out fresh banknotes.

At the same time, the regime recently issued new import licenses, driving up demand for dollars. Another factor at play is planned salary increases for civil servants in the next fiscal year.

The regime also relaxed the fixed exchange rate for remittances from overseas workers from 3,600 kyats per dollar to 4,600 kyats in a bid to encourage them to go through official banking channels—but that backfired and was read as a sign of weakness by the market.

Other currencies have soared apace, with 100,000 kyats falling from 700 Thai baht earlier this month to around 600 baht.

That is bound to make Thai consumer goods and clothing forbiddingly expensive, to say nothing of imported medicines, cooking oil and industrial raw materials.

As usual when the situation runs away from it, the regime is targeting currency traders to try and frighten the market into submission. Yangon money traders say officers from the Bureau of Special Investigation are roaming the markets in search of anyone to fine and arrest.

World.title: Myanmar’s Democratic Opposition Urges ASEAN to Shun ‘Genocidal’ Junta Leaders
World.content:
Myanmar’s democratic opposition has urged ASEAN not to reintegrate regime leaders accused of war crimes and responsible for genocide, following an ASEAN-backed stakeholders’ dialogue in the Philippines.

The two-day meeting, hosted by the ASEAN chair in Tagaytay on Nov. 22-23, brought together representatives from the National League for Democracy (NLD), the Committee Representing Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (CRPH), the Steering Council for the Emergence of a Federal Democratic Union (SCEF), resistance organizations and civil society groups.

CRPH spokesperson Sithu Maung said participants warned against any ASEAN move to recognize Myanmar’s de facto military regime.

“We reiterated that ASEAN should no longer provide space for military leaders who have committed war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide,” he said, referring to recent remarks by Min Aung Hlaing that his administration is reconsidering ‌the country’s relationship with the regional bloc. The putschist president spoke out after ASEAN leaders at last week’s Manila summit reaffirmed the ban on regime leaders attending high-level regional meetings.

Singapore, which will assume the ASEAN chair next year, attended the stakeholders’ dialogue as an observer. Delegations from both the Philippines and Singapore received the SCEF’s policy paper on Myanmar during the meeting.

Also in attendance were representatives from Chin resistance forces, the All Burma Students’ Democratic Front (ABSDF), elected lawmakers and other stakeholders. Discussions focused on the military situation, obstacles to delivery of humanitarian aid, implications of the Rohingya genocide ruling by the International Court of Justice (ICJ), and the regime’s escalating airstrikes against civilians.

SCEF said last week’s genocide ruling should spur stronger efforts to enforce accountability for the regime’s past atrocities and ongoing crimes in Myanmar. It urged the international community not to shield military leaders from responsibility or enable further violence.

Then-military chief Min Aung Hlaing oversaw the 2017 “clearance operations” against the Rohingya in northern Rakhine that the World Court said amounted to genocide.

The regime rejected the ICJ ruling as “unfair” and stated its repatriation of Rohingya refugees would continue on its own terms, ignoring UN calls to grant them citizenship rights.

The democratic opposition’s appeal comes amid growing debate over ASEAN’s approach to Myanmar. While the bloc continues to exclude Min Aung Hlaing and his leadership from top-level meetings, members including Thailand, Malaysia, the Philippines, Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia have expanded bilateral engagement with the regime in recent months.

World.title: Myanmar Records Worst Landmine Casualties in the World for 3rd Year
World.content:
Myanmar recorded the highest number of casualties from landmines and unexploded ordnance in the world last year with nearly 1,900, according to the Landmine Monitor report released Tuesday.

The group’s research shows that Myanmar was the country worst affected by deaths from landmines and so-called “explosive remnants of war” for the third year running.

Worldwide, some 6,929 casualties were recorded in 2025, counting both civilians and military personnel. Myanmar accounted for a massive proportion of over 27 percent or nearly one-third with 1,891.

The military has regularly used antipersonnel mines since 1999 and increased their use notably after the coup in February 2021, the report pointed out.

Casualties soared as a result, from just 368 in 2021 to 1,003 in 2023 before doubling to 2,029 the following year.

They are regularly planted around military bases and outposts as well as mobile phone towers, mining operations and fuel pipelines.

One regime combat engineer reported that he was ordered to plant mines in Kachin and Rakhine states near populated areas, marked only by “Danger Do Not Enter” signs without mentioning mines.

“Often there are no signs,” said Thet Oo of the resistance Yinmabin–Salingyi Strike Committee in heavily mined Sagaing Region.

He said the regime frequently plants landmines when launching offensives or raiding villages, placing them at the entrance of houses.

They are designed to sever legs.

He admitted that the heartland resistance People’s Defense Forces (PDF) also used remote-controlled handmade landmines across the country after the coup. But when resistance governing bodies were formed, they banned mines near settled areas except for military purposes that require their authorization.

“The mines are meant to injure or delay the enemy,” he added. But he claimed they are always cleared before residents return.

The report says ethnic armed organizations reported seizing regime landmines almost every month between January 2022 and this September 2026, showing how prevalent their use is.

Regime-aligned ethnic Border Guard Forces (BGF) and the militias under the regime’s command also use landmines, it says.

“We urge all states to reject the production and use of antipersonnel mines, by any actor, under any circumstances,” Tamar Gabelnick, director of the International Campaign to Ban Landmines (ICBL) told AFP.

Syria was the second-most affected country with an equally massive 1,602 casualties, trailed at a substantial distance by Afghanistan with 497.

World.title: Kazakhstan’s Cinemas Top 1 Million Screenings for First Time
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan’s cinemas held more than one million screenings in 2025 for the first time, according to Energyprom.kz analytical website.

Screenings rose 18.3% last year to nearly 1.1 million, up from 927,500 in 2024. Audiences grew as well. Cinemas had 27 million visitors in 2025, a 16.2% increase from 23.3 million the year before.

The new record ends years of uneven recovery. In 2019, before the pandemic, Kazakhstan held 962,300 screenings. When theaters closed in 2020, the number fell to 292,400. It climbed back to 985,500 in 2022, passing the pre-pandemic level, stayed roughly the same in 2023 and dipped in 2024. Twenty years ago the market was much smaller: in 2005, the country held only 111,000 screenings, nearly ten times fewer than last year.

The industry remains concentrated in the largest cities. Kazakhstan had 118 cinemas in 2025, and 21 of them were in Almaty. Astana had 11, the Mangystau Region nine, and the Karagandy and Zhambyl regions and Shymkent seven each.

Almaty alone accounted for 374,600 screenings, or 34.1% of the national total. Astana followed with 153,600 and Shymkent with 79,800. Together, the three cities held 55.4% of all screenings. Among the regions, the Pavlodar Region led with 48,300 thousand, ahead of the East Kazakhstan Region with 46,500 and Kostanai with 40,200.

The number of cinemas in a region does not always match how many films they show. The East Kazakhstan Region has only two cinemas but held 46,500 screenings, while the Mangystau Region, with nine cinemas, held 39,500.

Attendance shows the same concentration. Almaty cinemas drew 9.1 million viewers, Astana 4.8 million and Shymkent 2.2 million. Together, the three cities accounted for almost 60% of all cinema visits in the country.

Revenue grew faster than attendance. Cinema services brought in 62.5 billion tenge (US$136.8 million), up 74.7% from 35.8 billion tenge (US$78.4 million) in 2024. This figure covers more than ticket sales: it also includes other services and events, such as arcade games. Analysts say the gap between revenue and attendance growth may come from higher prices and a wider range of services, not only from more viewers.

Prices have also gone up. Cinema services nationwide increased by 10.1% in cost over the past year. In Almaty, they rose 28.8%, in the Aktobe Region 16.2% and in the Mangystau Region 12.4%. In Astana, prices rose 1.1%.

In October, the average cinema ticket in Kazakhstan cost 2,600 tenge (US$5.7). Tickets were most expensive in Ust-Kamenogorsk, at 3,300 tenge (US$7.2), followed by Atyrau and Almaty at 2,900 tenge (US$6.35) each. Semei had the cheapest tickets at 1,700 tenge (US$1.72), while Taraz, Petropavl and Taldykorgan averaged around 1,900 tenge (US$4.16).

World.title: Astana Opera Brings Legendary Queen Tomyris to Ballet Stage
World.content:
ASTANA – More than two millennia after her legendary confrontation with Persian King Cyrus, Tomyris, the queen of the Massagetae, came to the ballet stage in a new production by Astana Opera. The two-act production premiered on Nov. 26, bringing the story of the ancient ruler to life through classical ballet, contemporary choreography and traditional Kazakh music. A second performance followed on Nov. 27.

Created to mark the 35th anniversary of Kazakhstan’s independence, the ballet brought together Astana Opera’s own creative team, including choreographer Sultanbek Gumar, composer Khamit Shangaliyev and librettist Yermek Amanshayev.

During a press conference ahead of the premiere, Astana Opera Director Alexander Sovostyanov highlighted the significance of the production as an example of Kazakhstan’s growing creative capacity.

“We are proud that this production was born entirely in Kazakhstan, through the efforts and talent of our own creative people,” he said.

He also highlighted the contribution of the theater’s artistic team, including costume designer Dariga Taishykova, and the importance of mentorship in developing a new generation of Kazakh ballet professionals.

Bringing the story of Tomyris to the stage

Set in the sixth century B.C., the ballet draws on historical accounts and ancient legends surrounding Tomyris, the queen of the Massagetae, and her confrontation with Persian King Cyrus. The story follows Tomyris, her son Spargapises and Arnava, leader of the Amazons and Spargapises’ beloved.

When Spargapises sets out to defend their homeland, Tomyris faces betrayal, his capture and the loss of many warriors. Following her son’s death, she gathers her people for a decisive battle against the Persian forces.

For librettist Yermek Amanshayev, the story of Tomyris reflects the deep historical roots of Kazakh statehood and the legacy of the great steppe.

“Our statehood has a history spanning centuries. It did not emerge overnight or take shape in a short period of time. The great steppe has its own great historical figures, and Queen Tomyris is among the most sacred and significant of them,” he said.

Amanshayev also compared Tomyris’ confrontation with Cyrus to the Battle of Thermopylae, a historical episode familiar to international audiences. He stressed that Tomyris was not merely a regional ruler but a figure whose actions carried broader geopolitical significance. In his interpretation, her victory halted Persian ambitions toward Greece for nearly half a century.

A collaboration between music and movement

For Gumar, working on “Tomyris” was a new challenge. Unlike several previous national ballet productions at Astana Opera, which were staged by foreign choreographers, this time the theater turned to one of its own artists.

“Previously, many of the national ballets at our theater were staged by foreign specialists. This time, the responsibility was given to someone who had developed professionally within the theater. We therefore sought to meet that responsibility to the highest standard,” Gumar said.

Music and choreography developed side by side, with Gumar and Shangaliyev shaping the production through a close creative collaboration.

“We worked with Khamit almost around the clock in the studio. When I danced, he would translate my movements into music,” Gumar said.

The creative team initially considered using a symphony orchestra but eventually incorporated traditional Kazakh instruments, including the dombra, sazsyrnai and sybyzgy, to reflect the ballet’s Kazakh identity.

“Since this is a national ballet, we decided to use our traditional instruments. They gave us greater freedom to convey ideas through movement,” he said.

Shangaliyev described the production as a collaborative effort in which music, choreography and visual elements had to come together like pieces of a mosaic.

One of the main challenges, he said, was recreating the sound and atmosphere of the Saka period through music.

The composer said the true success of a ballet could not be judged on its premiere night alone.

“If a ballet continues to live on stage for decades, only then can we say that the work has truly succeeded,” Shangaliyev said.

A queen beyond the battlefield

Costume design also played an important role in shaping the production’s interpretation of Tomyris. According to Taishykova, the characters’ inner transformations and personalities were reflected in their stage appearance.

“This production can be described as a tribute to Tomyris. We wanted to portray her as a mother, a woman, a source of inspiration, a warrior and a defender of her people,” she said.

The title role of Tomyris was performed by Sofiya Adilkhanova and Torgyn Leben. Doskhan Zaidin and Islam Kaipbai portrayed Spargapises, while Aidan Kalzhan and Zhaksylyk Saukymbekov appeared as Cyrus. The role of Arnava was performed by Alina Zyryanova and Limara Aidarova.

The ballet combines contemporary choreography with elements of Kazakh and classical dance, bringing together large ensemble scenes and more intimate moments that explore the characters’ personal experiences.

Alongside the warrior and ruler, audiences see a mother facing the loss of her son and the difficult choices that come with defending her people. This balance between personal tragedy and the fate of an entire nation gives the story a more emotional dimension.

With its blend of historical storytelling, contemporary choreography and traditional Kazakh musical elements, “Tomyris” offers a new stage interpretation of one of the most recognizable female figures associated with the great steppe. For Astana Opera, the ballet is also an opportunity to bring a story rooted in the region’s history to a new generation of audiences, while giving Kazakhstan’s composers and choreographers the space to tell it in their own way.

World.title: Kazakhstan Sees Unusually Warm November, Winter Forecast to Be Milder Than Usual
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan has experienced unusually warm weather this November, with average temperatures in Astana and Almaty exceeding climatic norms, while the upcoming winter is also expected to be warmer than usual.

During the first 20 days of November, Astana recorded an average temperature of 1.3 degrees Celsius, five degrees above the climatic norm. In Almaty, the average reached 7.2 degrees, 3.1 degrees above the norm, according to climate experts cited by Kazinform on Nov. 25.

On Nov. 6, temperatures in Astana reached 13.5 degrees, while Almaty recorded 22.3 degrees on Nov. 9, setting new daily records.

Experts from the Center for Ecology and Climate Monitoring attributed the warm weather partly to atmospheric circulation patterns that brought warm air from Iran and the Arabian Peninsula into northern Kazakhstan, while limiting the movement of cold air masses from the Arctic.

They also highlighted the broader impact of global warming. Between 1950 and 2025, average November temperatures increased by 0.63 degrees per decade in Astana and 0.52 degrees in Almaty.

November 2025 was the warmest on record in Kazakhstan, with the country’s average temperature exceeding the climatic norm by 8.74 degrees. Monthly temperature records were also updated at 193 weather stations.

Winter forecast

According to the preliminary Kazhydromet forecast, the winter of 2026-2027 is expected to be warmer than usual.

December temperatures could exceed the climatic norm by two degrees, while January may be 1-2 degrees warmer and February 1-3 degrees warmer than average.

Some regions are also expected to see higher-than-usual precipitation in December and February.

Experts also noted that El Niño, a natural climate pattern characterized by unusually warm surface waters in the tropical Pacific Ocean, may influence precipitation patterns in Kazakhstan during winter and spring, notably in the southern and southeastern regions.

The winter forecast remains preliminary, and actual weather conditions may differ from projections.

World.title: Kazakhstan Votes for Local Councils: What Maslikhat Elections are All About
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan votes on Nov. 29 to replace every local council in the country, more than a year ahead of schedule, marking the final step in rebuilding the political system from the ground up after this year’s constitutional overhaul.

Nearly 11,000 candidates are running for 3,447 seats in 228 maslikhats, the elected assemblies that work alongside regional, city and district governments. President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev dissolved the maslikhats on Oct. 12.

The maslikhats approve the budgets that pay for roads, heating, schools and water pipes, and they can vote no confidence in akims, the appointed governors and mayors. Whether Sunday produces livelier councils or simply relabels the old ones will shape how much say people have over that money.

What a maslikhat does

A maslikhat is the elected council of a region, city or district, and the main voice voters have in local government. While the akims run the administration, the maslikhats are the elected check on them.

There are three tiers: 20 regional councils, 38 city councils and 170 district councils.

Their core powers include approving local budgets, proposing amendments, approving plans for a region, city or district, which decide, for example, where schools are built and which roads and utility networks get fixed. In cases set by law, deputies can start a no-confidence vote against an akim.

How the vote works

Deputies are elected for five years by secret ballot. Vote for maslikhats in the capital, the regions and cities of national significance, which are Astana, Almaty and Shymkent, mix party lists with constituency races, while districts and towns elect only individual candidates.

Of the 3,447 seats, 334 will be filled from party lists and 3,113 in single-member districts.

“In 20 regions, 97 party slates have been registered for 334 seats. These slates include 1,160 candidates. Thus, there are an average of three to four candidates per seat,” said Azamat Aimanakumov, a member of the Central Election Commission, at a Nov. 27 briefing in Astana.

Candidates are nominated by parties, in some cases by public associations, or by themselves in single-member races.

Seven parties are on the ballot: Auyl, the National Social Democratic Party, the People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Respublica, Aq Jol, the Baytaq Green Party and Adilet. Each party may register only one list per region, and women and young people together must make up at least 30% of it.

In single-member districts, 9,422 candidates are on the ballot. Any citizen aged 20 or older can run, except people a court has declared legally incapable, those serving prison sentences, and those with a criminal record or a corruption conviction. No one may run in more than one district.

“The fiercest competition is in the Turkistan Region, where there are up to five candidates vying for a single seat. In another 121 districts, four candidates are running for each seat. This represents the highest level of competition,” said Aimanakumov. “There are also regions with the least competition, where two candidates are vying for a single seat. Specifically, in 11 regions across 44 districts, two people are vying for a single seat,” he added.

Overall, 12,679,459 people are on the voter list. On Nov. 29, 10,338 polling stations will open: 101 at 6 a.m. and the rest at 7 a.m. Voting ends at 8 p.m. People with no permanent registration who were never on a voter list can register on the day at 218 designated polling stations.

Alongside digital outreach, precinct commission members went door to door with personal invitations to vote, said Mukhtar Yerman, the CEC’s deputy chairman.

“We see the task not just as reaching people with information, but as creating conditions in which every voter can easily get what they need to know and exercise their constitutional right on Nov. 29,” he said.

Some 258 public associations and nonprofit groups have accredited observers, 13 with the CEC and 245 with territorial commissions. O

Why now?

The maslikhats elected in March 2023 were not due to face voters until 2028. Their early end follows a year of rapid change at the national level. In March, a referendum approved a new Constitution that replaced the two-chamber parliament, the Senate and Mazhilis, with a single chamber, the Kurultai. It took effect July 1.

In June, Amanat, the former Nur Otan party built by first president Nursultan Nazarbayev, voted to merge itself into Adilet, a pro-presidential party registered in June. In August, Adilet won 71.17% of the parliamentary vote and 110 of Kurultai’s 145 seats. Its leader Aibek Dadebay, a former head of the presidential administration, became the chamber’s chairman.

In October, after consulting Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov and Kurultai Chairman Aibek Dadebay, as the Constitution requires, President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev signed the decree ending all maslikhat mandates.

World.title: Kazakhstan Brings Together Global Sports Leaders to Strengthen Anti-Doping Efforts
World.content:
ASTANA – Kazakhstan hosted a meeting of the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) Foundation Board on Nov. 26 in Astana, bringing together representatives of more than 50 countries to discuss global anti-doping policies, athlete protection and international cooperation.

The meeting was attended by WADA President Witold Bańka, Director General Olivier Niggli, Kazakh Tourism and Sports Minister Yerbol Myrzabossynov, representatives of the International Olympic Committee and International Paralympic Committee, and heads of national anti-doping organizations, the ministry reported.

Discussions focused on implementing the World Anti-Doping Code, strengthening safeguards for clean sport, expanding educational and scientific programs, and improving international cooperation.

Kazakhstan highlights clean sport priorities

Addressing the meeting, Myrzabossynov said Kazakhstan views clean sport as a matter of fairness and equal opportunities, emphasizing that athletes should win through honest effort.

He reaffirmed the country’s commitment to strengthening its national anti-doping system, aligning it with international standards and promoting anti-doping awareness among young athletes.

“Every athlete should achieve victory through honest work. Our common goal is to protect athletes’ rights, create equal conditions for everyone and preserve trust in sport,” he said.

Expanding cooperation with WADA

Cooperation between Kazakhstan and WADA gained momentum following Bańka’s visit to Kazakhstan in October 2025.

Earlier this year, Myrzabossynov and Bańka signed a memorandum of understanding to expand cooperation in anti-doping education, prevention of anti-doping rule violations, scientific research and international knowledge-sharing.

The WADA Foundation Board is the agency’s highest governing body, comprising representatives of the international sports movement and governments. It plays a central role in shaping global anti-doping policy.

World.title: Hong Kong Sees Kazakhstan as Promising Tourism Market Ahead of Direct Flight Launch
World.content:
ALMATY – Hong Kong is looking to strengthen tourism ties with Kazakhstan and expand its presence in Central Asia ahead of the launch of direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong in January 2027, Hong Kong Tourism Board (HKTB) Executive Director Anthony Lau said at the travel mission presentation in Almaty on Nov. 27.

“The future has never looked brighter for tourism between Hong Kong and Kazakhstan,” Lau said in his welcoming remarks at the event.

Cathay Pacific plans to launch direct flights between Almaty and Hong Kong on Jan. 9, 2027 with flights departing every Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday from Almaty.

The new route is expected to facilitate not only leisure travel but business exchanges. Forty representatives from Hong Kong’s tourism industry traveled to Kazakhstan to discuss opportunities for cooperation with local companies and industries.

“This enhanced connectivity will bring our cities closer than ever before and open up exciting new opportunities for tourism exchange and business cooperation in the years ahead,” Lau told The Astana Times.

Lau said the HKTB seeks to build long-term partnerships in Central Asia as part of their strategy. Tourism is not an exchange of residence, it is about exchange of culture, and friendship, and long-term business partnerships.

The mission also included a meeting between Lau and Galiya Tokseitova, Department of Tourism of Almaty City, to strengthen tourism exchanges.

“The world has changed, and for us, those developed markets are developed,” Lau said.

“We are looking for new sources of tourism growth. Our next phase of growth will be very much along the Belt and Road countries. We are picking different Belt and Road countries which we believe have potential for tourism growth. One factor in facilitating tourism exchange between two destinations would be air connectivity. There is really no point if there is no connection between one place and another. We think it is the right time for us to come to Almaty, to come to Kazakhstan, to understand the market,” he explained.

One of the main benefits is that Hong Kong offers 14-day visa-free entry for Kazakhstan passport holders, making it easier to plan visits.

“As of this moment, it is only three flights a week. Hopefully, if the business comes along, the number of flights will expand to daily, or even twice daily. We are also looking at possible connections with Chinese airlines. For example, from Almaty to Guangzhou or Shenzhen, you can take a fast 45-minute train ride to Hong Kong. You can spend a couple of days in Guangzhou, come to Hong Kong, and then return to Almaty,” said Lau.

Lau highlighted Hong Kong’s combination of urban attractions, natural landscapes, gastronomy and cultural experiences as part of its appeal to visitors. Visitors can travel from the city’s iconic skyline to its beaches in around 20 minutes. Its culinary scene ranges from Michelin-starred restaurants to local specialties, alongside a growing selection of halal-certified dining options.

Lau described Hong Kong as both a destination and a gateway to wider journeys across mainland China.

Cathay Pacific offers a 10% discount on the base fare for bookings made by Dec. 31, 2026, for travel to Hong Kong by March 31, 2027, and other options available on the company’s website.

“As Cathay Pacific’s very first destination in Central Asia, we look forward to welcoming customers onboard our non-stop flights connecting Almaty and Hong Kong. Whether traveling for business or leisure, customers can enjoy our signature hospitality, from our award-winning cabin crew services and lounges, Asia Pacific’s largest inflight entertainment selection, to Hong Kong-inspired dining and international flavors,” said Cathay Chief Customer and Commercial Officer Lavinia Lau.

World.title: Enjoy Final Days of Fall With Music and More
World.content:
ASTANA – As November comes to a close, the cities offer plenty of ways to enjoy the weekend. From ballet and classical music to theater performance and concerts, The Astana Times editorial team has curated a list of events to explore with friends and family.

Astana

“Golden Centaurs” excursion, Nov. 28

Discover the military traditions of the Golden Horde through a guided museum tour featuring historical weapons, armour and interactive displays. Visitors can learn about the equipment used by medieval warriors and explore the history of nomadic military art.

Venue: National Museum of Kazakhstan; 54 Tauelsizdik Avenue. Tickets are available here.

Freedom Festival, Nov. 29

The internationally renowned London City Ballet will perform as part of the Freedom Festival, bringing together dancers from leading ballet companies. The programme features works by celebrated choreographers, including John Neumeier, Kenneth MacMillan and Ashley Page, offering audiences an evening of classical and contemporary ballet.

Venue: Astana Opera; 1 Konayev Street. Tickets are available here.

Symphony concert, Nov. 28

South Korean violinist Lim Ji-young will perform a classical music program. Enjoy beautiful melodies and experience the magic of live music.

Venue: Astana Ballet; 43 Uly Dala Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Musical Heritage of Western Kazakhstan” concert, Nov. 28

Celebrate the musical traditions of western Kazakhstan through an evening of traditional songs and kuis. The program features works by renowned Kazakh composers and performers, including Mukhit Meraliuly and Garifolla Kurmangaliyev, highlighting the region’s rich musical heritage.

Venue: Qazaqconcert; 10/1 Mangilik El Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Dürer. Metamorphoses of Alchemy” exhibition, Nov. 27 – Jan. 24

Explore the artistic and intellectual world of the Renaissance through an exhibition dedicated to German artist Albrecht Dürer. The collection brings together engravings, historical books, geometric studies and alchemical texts, offering a closer look at the connection between art, science and philosophy.

Venue: LM Lulanshi Art; 22A Amanzholov Street. Tickets are available here.

Almaty

Oyu gala concert, Nov. 28

Celebrate five years of Oyu live with a concert bringing together popular performers. For the first time in the project’s history, familiar songs by artists including Sadraddin, Ayau, ALEM, Yenlik and dudeontheguitar will be performed with a symphony orchestra, offering a new interpretation of contemporary music.

Venue: Almaty Theater; 30 Al-Farabi Avenue. Tickets are available here.

“Kanysh” performance, Nov. 28

The theatrical production tells the story of Kanysh Satpayev, one of Kazakhstan’s most prominent scientists and the founder of Kazakh geology. Through scenes from his life and scientific journey, the play explores his dedication to knowledge, his contribution to national science and his service to the country.

Venue: Alatau Theater; 6 Nurkent microdistrict. Tickets are available here.

Night at the Museum, Nov. 28

What happens when a museum comes to life after closing time? This ballet production follows a young guide who discovers that museum exhibits have come alive. Combining traditional Korean dances, historical characters, humour and modern K-pop rhythms, the performance takes audiences on a journey through Korean culture.

Venue: Korean Theater of Musical Academy; 158 Bogenbay Batyr. Tickets are available here.

Kaleo concert, Nov. 29

The anniversary tour celebrates 10 years since the release of the album A/B. Fans can enjoy live performances of the band’s popular songs, including “Way Down We Go,” “All the Pretty Girls” and “No Good.”

Venue: Baluan Sholak Arena; 44 Abay Avenue. Tickets are available here.

World.title: Baiterek Holding to Expand Investment Support for Kazakhstan’s Economy in 2027
World.content:
ASTANA – Baiterek National Investment Holding plans to provide 8 trillion tenge (US$17.5 billion) in economic support in 2027, focusing on boosting investment, expanding industrial capacity and supporting businesses, following a meeting of its Board of Directors chaired by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov on Nov. 27.

The board approved the holding’s annual budget and key performance indicators for its chairman and management board members for 2027, according to the Prime Minister’s press service.

The holding’s performance targets will reflect the country’s priorities, notably improving investment efficiency and developing the real sector of the economy. Key indicators will include fixed-capital investment, revenue generated by supported enterprises and their export sales.

Of the planned support, investments in fixed capital across manufacturing, infrastructure and the agro-industrial sector are expected to reach 1.17 trillion tenge (US$2.6 billion). With the holding’s participation, approximately 2.7 million square meters of housing are also expected to be commissioned in 2027.

To finance these projects, Baiterek will continue raising funds on the market. Non-government sources are projected to account for 54% of the holding’s total borrowing next year. The holding will also assess the participation of second-tier banks in business financing through state support instruments.

The plans are based on the holding’s updated Development Plan through 2033, which its Board of Directors approved in August. One priority is to expand financing opportunities for businesses launching new production facilities or increasing the capacity of existing ones. Baiterek plans to involve commercial banks and private investors in financing these projects.

Bektenov also emphasized the need to improve the effectiveness of the holding’s anti-corruption compliance, internal audit and procurement control services. He called for concrete measures to prevent corruption risks and urged the holding to move beyond formal approaches to its responsibilities, focusing instead on practical proposals to improve performance.

World.title: How man who knew nothing about fine fragrances became perfumer: a video story
World.content:
How to become a perfumer: the story of Levon Ghazaryan

It turns out that anyone can become a perfumer, even someone who has never taken an interest in fragrances and cannot tell one scent from another.

We tell the story of 23-year-old Levon Ghazaryan, who suddenly became so fascinated by fragrances that he now blends them with scientific precision and an artist’s imagination, creating his own distinctive style.

The moment you enter the perfumer’s “workspace”, you find yourself surrounded by fragrances. The air is filled with all kinds of scents: floral, citrus and woody. After a while, you begin to distinguish them as they emerge one by one, seemingly competing to see which will prove the most alluring.

The room is filled with glass bottles, flasks and test tubes of all shapes and sizes. Each little vial holds its own secret. Some contain clear liquids; others hold oils in golden, amber or almost colourless shades. Pipettes, measuring vessels and containers of fragrance blends are everywhere. Some blends have already become perfumes, but have yet to receive a name.

Perfumer Levon Kazaryan is in his element. Completely focused, he combines fragrances and inhales them as if waiting for a miracle. He opens one bottle after another and brings it to his nose. He pauses for a moment, then makes a note. Sometimes he spends a long time thinking; at other times, he adds a new ingredient without hesitation. Yet he pours each component into a glass vessel on the scales with the utmost care. Even a single tiny drop can completely change the character of a fragrance.

Levon admits that he never dreamed of becoming a perfumer as a child.

His interest in fragrances began in his teens, when people started giving him perfumes.

“When someone gave me perfume or bought it for me, they would say, ‘This is a good perfume.’ But I couldn’t understand the difference between a good fragrance and a bad one. I started taking an interest and trying to figure it out. Eventually, I wanted to create perfumes myself. The artist in me came alive. It was as if someone inside me had awakened — someone who wanted to mix ingredients, create and experiment,” he says.

Levon says his path to becoming a perfumer was difficult because Armenia has no school where he could learn the basics. He therefore had to master the craft on his own and find a way to achieve results.

“For a whole year, I couldn’t get anything right. There are so many secrets in this field. Every perfumer has their own secret formulas. There are plenty of tutorials online, but they seem to leave something out. You simply cannot create anything worthwhile using those formulas. I searched for different sources, collected recipes for 2,000 well-known fragrances and began analysing them one by one. I studied exactly which molecules the perfumers had used and how they combined them.

This process is not simply about mixing scents. You can create a fragrance, but it might not last on the skin. It might have no sillage and fail to ‘speak’ in the air around you. It could end up smelling like soap: you notice it for a moment, and then it disappears. You need to know the ‘secrets’ that make a fragrance last,” Levon explains.

He believes he has already developed a style of his own.

He is also convinced that even if someone got hold of his formulas, they would not be able to reproduce his fragrances. He has also developed a unique technique for blending oils.

The young perfumer says he enjoys working with fragrances that “unfold” when combined. He believes they have an invisible connection that only the right combination can bring out.

Levon took a difficult path before becoming a perfumer. That experience inspired him to establish the Armenian Association of Perfumers. He wants to bring together fragrance enthusiasts and aspiring professionals, helping them source the ingredients they need and create their own perfumes.

Alongside people interested in ready-made fragrances, Levon also welcomes clients who want to commission a perfume of their own. Tourists often visit him, too. They like to take fragrances home as souvenirs from their travels. A scent created especially for them can serve as a reminder of Yerevan.

But in the evening, Levon closes his door to visitors. That is when he turns to creating, searching for new combinations of fragrances.

How to become a perfumer: the story of Levon Kazaryan

World.title: ‘The entire logic of how power operates needs to change’: views on electoral reform in Abkhazia
World.content:
Heated debate has erupted in Abkhazia over electoral reform ahead of parliamentary elections scheduled for 2027.

The reform would replace the majoritarian system with a mixed electoral system. Yet supporters of both approaches agree on one point: both systems are too vulnerable to offer much hope of significantly improving the “quality” of the elected parliament.

Prominent Abkhaz public figure and former MP Ilya Gunia proposes considering a model of governance in which the election of MPs and the president would be entirely independent of local or party interests.

What Ilya Gunia proposes

Abolishing territorial constituencies in parliamentary elections

“Parliament is a national legislative body, not a local self-government institution. Therefore, citizens across the republic should be able to vote for individual candidates, regardless of where they live.

Under a nationwide vote, the first 35 or 45 candidates who receive the most votes would win parliamentary seats,” Gunia believes.

In his view, this model would shift the focus from local election campaigns to nationwide competition. It would also give people with a public profile across the republic, rather than just in individual districts, a chance to enter parliament.

Changing the way the president is elected

As an alternative to direct presidential elections, Gunia proposes that parliament elect the president:

“This would reduce the financial and political burden on society, eliminate the need for a separate large-scale presidential election campaign, and make MPs responsible for choosing the head of state.”

He stresses that the president’s powers must be clearly defined. The country must also establish safeguards for parliamentary independence and mechanisms to oversee the executive branch.

Redistributing powers and establishing a system of checks and balances

“The most important thing is to review the current system of relations between the branches of government. The Constitution must clearly define their powers, establish mechanisms for mutual oversight and accountability, and provide safeguards against the concentration of power in one person’s hands,” Ilya Gunia believes.

In his view, the relationship between the branches of government must be legally synchronised. If the president becomes unable to perform his duties and resigns before the end of his term, parliament should automatically dissolve. This would force the legislative and executive branches to work closely together, share responsibility to the public and spare Abkhazia from an endless cycle of elections.

The former MP says his proposal aims to create a system in which no branch of government can shift responsibility onto another without facing consequences.

*“Abkhazia does not simply need a new electoral system. We need to change the very logic of how power operates, put an end to recurring political crises and build institutions that function regardless of who occupies the presidential office or which political forces hold seats in parliament.

In my view, this should be the main goal of genuine political reform,”* Ilya Gunia says.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian deputy foreign minister announces new restrictions on Georgian companies
World.content:
Meeting between Russian and Georgian diplomats

The first meeting as part of the resumed dialogue between Georgia and Russia did not result in the lifting of restrictions on Georgian beverage exports. Giorgi Zurabashvili, the Georgian prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia, said that, on the contrary, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin had announced plans to impose sanctions on two more Georgian wine producers during their meeting in Minsk on 19 November.

Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze also confirmed the information, suggesting that a “deep state” might be behind Russia’s decision and could have bribed mid-level Russian officials.

What did Galuzin tell Zurabashvili?

Zurabashvili is Georgia’s first deputy foreign minister. Since October, he has also served as the prime minister’s special representative for relations with Russia. On 19 November, he met the Russian deputy foreign minister in Minsk. It was his first meeting in this capacity.

Zurabashvili first disclosed details of the meeting on 25 November on pro-government Imedi TV. According to him, the Georgian side’s main objective was to restore Georgian wine producers’ access to the Russian market.

● Moscow and Tbilisi prepare to resume dialogue

● Russia signals new opportunities for closer ties with Georgia

● ‘Moscow is ready to restore diplomatic relations with Georgia’ — Russian Foreign Ministry

● Kremlin message to Tbilisi: diplomatic ties with Russia would bring greater economic benefits

In October, Russia restricted imports of products from seven Georgian producers. Four of them are wine producers: Teliani Valley, Tbilvino, Vineni and Askaneli Brothers. The list also included beer produced by Georgian Beer Company, as well as Coca-Cola beverages and Nabeghlavi mineral water bottled in Georgia.

According to Zurabashvili, Galuzin cited three reasons for imposing the restrictions: product quality, allegations that the companies were funding the war in Ukraine, and “anti-Russian rhetoric”. Zurabashvili rejected all three accusations. His hopes that the restrictions would be lifted immediately did not materialise, with new announcements following instead.

“Naturally, I was surprised and stunned by this news, since nothing of the sort is happening,” Zurabashvili said, adding that Galuzin had not provided a single fact to substantiate his claims. “Therefore, these are political assertions that have absolutely no basis.”

According to Zurabashvili, the Georgian side raised a number of technical issues, while the Russian side put forward around 10 proposals, predominantly of a humanitarian nature. As an example, he cited an initiative to establish a partnership between a university in Russia’s Don region and a Georgian state university. In Zurabashvili’s view, these proposals were aimed against the Georgian Dream government and sought to strengthen the opposition’s position. He did not mention any other topics.

Who warned Zurabashvili?

Mamuka Pipia, international secretary of the pro-Russian Solidarity for Peace party, claimed that Zurabashvili had been warned while still in Tbilisi that the Russian ban would be extended to two more companies. According to Pipia, the companies in question are Winiveria and Chateau Mukhrani. This information has not been corroborated by other sources.

Kobakhidze confirmed that Yury Balashov, head of the Russian-Georgian Business Council, had visited Tbilisi ahead of the meeting in Minsk. According to the prime minister, Balashov had promised that all companies would be removed from the list by the end of the year but subsequently changed his position. Kobakhidze noted that Galuzin had expressed the same position.

‘Deep state’ – now in Moscow too

Kobakhidze described Galuzin’s arguments as absurd, noting that Tbilisi had expected all existing restrictions to be lifted. He compared Russia’s actions to the behaviour of the European bureaucracy, which, he claimed, had been “bought” by a “deep state” and was acting against the interests of its own countries.

The prime minister did not name any specific individuals. He expressed hope that the issue would be discussed at the highest level of the Russian leadership and added that the dialogue should continue.

In Moscow, Tbilisi – or nowhere at all

Six days after the meeting, on 25 November, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov welcomed remarks made by Georgian Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili.

Bochorishvili had called for overcoming the fear of engaging in dialogue with Russia. Meanwhile, according to Russian state news agency TASS, Belarusian Foreign Minister Maxim Ryzhenkov said the sides had made significant progress in building mutual trust and that the talks could be moved to their respective capitals.

Bochorishvili denied this, saying that no proposals had been made or decisions taken regarding meetings in Moscow or Tbilisi. She noted that Belarus was not a party to the negotiations and had no information about their outcome.

The following day, Kobakhidze suggested that meetings could be held alternately in Moscow and Tbilisi. The prime minister insisted that neither this nor the presence of national flags posed a threat to Georgia’s policy of non-recognition of the occupied territories.

Parliament Speaker Shalva Papuashvili said the prime minister would decide when and where the meetings would take place. He added that seeing the Georgian flag in Russia would be a source of pride. Papuashvili also stressed that the issue of occupation must be part of the negotiations.

“Do you really think the special representative would attend a meeting, talk about wine and herbs, and not even touch upon the main problem in relations with Russia?” he asked.

In his interview with Imedi TV, Zurabashvili also noted that dialogue was necessary to discuss issues of sovereignty and de-occupation. The informal dialogue format between Georgia and Russia was established in 2012 and initially focused exclusively on trade, economic and humanitarian issues. It is known as the Zurab Abashidze-Grigory Karasin format. Before Zurabashvili’s appointment, the post of special representative for relations with Russia had been vacant since December 2025.

‘Communication failure’: Reactions

Former Foreign Minister Irakli Menagarishvili told Radio Liberty that although dialogue with Russia was necessary, he saw no grounds for optimism. He urged caution.

Berdia Sichinava, one of the leaders of the Gakharia for Georgia party, described the meeting as a “disaster”. According to him, Minsk cannot be regarded as a neutral venue. He questioned Zurabashvili’s competence and highlighted Galuzin’s diplomatic experience, including his tenure as ambassador to Japan.

Nika Gvaramia, leader of the Coalition for Change, told TV Pirveli that a Georgian official’s visit to Belarus contradicted the government’s own rhetoric about pursuing peace. “This is not about striving for peace but, on the contrary, about indirectly participating on Russia’s side,” he said. Gvaramia called on the government to inform the public about what had been discussed in Minsk.

Khatia Dekanoidze, one of the leaders of the Unity – National Movement party, argued that moving the negotiations to Moscow would constitute a diplomatic disaster.

“It is important to understand that all this is happening behind closed doors,” she said. Dekanoidze suggested that Zurabashvili had agreed to a visit by Galuzin to Tbilisi, although this information has not been confirmed.

Grigol Gegelia, a leader of the Lelo – Strong Georgia party, believes that the government is preparing a “new stage of capitulation”. According to him, Georgian Dream has increased the country’s economic dependence on Russia, effectively giving Moscow leverage to blackmail Georgia.

Imprisoned former President Mikheil Saakashvili wrote: “We have been left completely defenceless and vulnerable in the face of an enraged Russia – entirely deprived of support from America or Europe.”

Salome Zurabishvili’s meeting with EU ambassador

On 26 November, the European Parliament adopted a strongly critical resolution on Georgia.

According to TV Pirveli, 441 MEPs voted in favour of the document. The resolution calls for the immediate release of Paata Burchuladze, Irakli Nadiradze and Paata Manjgaladze. It also calls for sanctions against Bidzina Ivanishvili, Irakli Kobakhidze, Shalva Papuashvili, Kakha Kaladze and other officials.

On the same day, Salome Zurabishvili met EU Ambassador Pawel Herczynski. According to the Foreign Ministry, she described the resolution as an attempt to spread “false narratives” about the country. Zurabishvili also asked EU representatives to clarify whom exactly they considered to be arbitrarily detained.

Commenting on the meeting, Irakli Kobakhidze said: “In this case, the European Parliament has reached the point of absurdity.” Shalva Papuashvili, in turn, described the European Parliament as a “reincarnation” of the Soviet-era Congress of People’s Deputies.

World.title: Besiktas football match in Batumi sparks political tensions between Georgia and Turkey
World.content:
Besiktas match in Batumi

A Europa League match in Batumi between Turkish club Besiktas and Israeli club Hapoel Be’er Sheva has sparked political tensions between Georgia and Turkey. The Turkish authorities reacted strongly to clashes between Turkish football fans and Georgian police. Just hours after the clashes in the stands, three Turkish ministers contacted their Georgian counterparts. The actions of Georgian police were condemned by the Turkish presidential administration, the sports minister and the ruling party.

According to Georgia’s Interior Ministry, Besiktas fans instigated the disturbances. The ministry said three police officers had been injured and 16 people detained.

What happened?

Tensions arose even before the start of the match, on the city streets where Besiktas fans were holding a march. According to InterPressNews, participants failed to comply with police demands and began throwing various objects at law enforcement officers. Police responded by using pepper spray.

The match kicked off at Batumi Arena at 21:45. Footage from Turkish TV channel TRT Spor, cited by Radio Liberty, shows police officers approaching two fans holding a Palestinian flag in the stands and confiscating it. A scuffle ensued.

Fans began breaking seats in the stands. Police again used pepper spray, and the clashes spilled onto the pitch. The match was suspended for about half an hour during the first half and resumed at 22:45.

How did Ankara respond?

According to Turkish media reports, Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan held a telephone conversation with his Georgian counterpart, Maka Bochorishvili. The Anadolu news agency, citing diplomatic sources, reported that representatives of the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi and the consulate-general in Batumi were present at the stadium.

Interior Minister Mustafa Ciftci contacted his Georgian counterpart, Sulkhan Tamazashvili. According to the Turkish side, Ciftci expressed dissatisfaction over the use of disproportionate force against Turkish fans and demanded that their safe return to Turkey be ensured.

Turkish Justice Minister Yilmaz Tunc, following a conversation with Georgian Justice Minister Paata Salia, said he expected the detained Turkish citizens to be released immediately. He also called for those responsible for the incident to be held accountable.

The strongest condemnation came from the administration of Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. Presidential communications director Burhanettin Duran said:

“I strongly condemn the disproportionate police intervention targeting our fans during the match between Besiktas and Hapoel Be’er Sheva in Batumi.”

According to Duran, peaceful expressions of solidarity with the Palestinian people cannot justify violence or the use of force.

● “President Erdogan’s leadership is an example for all of us,” – Georgia PM

● “Batumi flag-bearer” Temur Katamadze deported from Georgia to Turkey

Youth and Sports Minister Osman Askin Bak condemned the “disproportionate actions” of security forces. Omer Celik, spokesman for the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP), said the use of force against fans for displaying a banner and flag in support of Palestine was unacceptable. Celik also accused the Israeli team of “simulation” (feigning injury) on the pitch.

In a statement, Besiktas said it had contacted the Turkish consulate-general in Batumi and Uefa over the incident. According to the club, President Erdogan informed Besiktas chairman Serdal Adali that he was closely monitoring the situation. The Anadolu news agency reported that six other Turkish clubs, including Fenerbahce, Galatasaray and Trabzonspor, had expressed solidarity with Besiktas.

Georgian Interior Ministry: Clashes began before flag incident

According to Georgia’s Interior Ministry, some Turkish fans had already displayed aggressive behaviour during their march from Europe Square to Batumi Arena.

The ministry said they had disturbed public order by shouting obscenities and throwing various objects, refused to comply with police demands and engaged in physical clashes with law enforcement officers.

At the stadium, fans broke seats and threw them at police officers. Police used special means to bring the situation under control.

The ministry denied foreign media reports that force had been used because of the display of flags and banners in support of Palestine.

According to the ministry, aggressive behaviour and clashes with police began during the march, well before these symbols were displayed. The ministry also stressed that Georgian law applied to everyone, regardless of citizenship or nationality.

Footage from Turkish TV channel TRT Spor, cited by Radio Liberty, shows police officers approaching two fans holding a Palestinian flag in the stands and confiscating it.

A scuffle broke out immediately afterwards. According to the Turkish Interior Ministry, Tamazashvili told Ciftci that the flags had been confiscated by Uefa representatives rather than Georgian government officials. He also said he had dispatched his deputy to the stadium. The Georgian side has not released its own account of the conversation.

Match results and detentions

The match was suspended for approximately half an hour during the first half and resumed at 22:45. Besiktas secured a 2-1 victory.

According to Turkish media reports, almost all detained Turkish citizens were released following the intervention of the Turkish embassy in Tbilisi. The same sources reported that two fans who had been hospitalised were discharged in the presence of consular officials. The Georgian side has yet to confirm the release of those detained.

Why was the match played in Batumi?

The match was originally scheduled to take place in Istanbul, but the Turkish authorities informed Uefa that this was not possible due to security concerns. On 30 October, Uefa announced that the match would be played in Batumi with spectators in attendance.

Relations between Turkey and Israel have deteriorated sharply over the war in the Gaza Strip. In November 2024, a match between Besiktas and Maccabi Tel Aviv was moved to Hungary and played behind closed doors.

World.title: Why Temu’s low prices are seen as a violation in Azerbaijan
World.content:
Investigation into Temu in Azerbaijan

Azerbaijan’s State Agency for Antimonopoly Control and Consumer Market Supervision under the president has completed its investigation into the Chinese online shopping platform Temu. According to information released by the agency on 25 November, signs of violations of Azerbaijan‘s competition legislation were identified in the operations of PDD Holdings, which owns the platform. A special commission has been established to decide whether to initiate proceedings.

However, the nature of the allegations is unusual for antimonopoly investigations. The agency suspects Temu not of inflating prices but of selling goods at excessively low prices, including below cost. This raises the following question:

Whose interests is the state protecting by taking action against low prices: those of consumers or local retailers?

When do low prices become a violation of the law?

The agency announced the launch of its investigation in mid-July. At the time, it said the investigation had been prompted by a complaint it had received. It did not disclose who had submitted the complaint.

The agency cited three provisions of the Competition Code, each concerning the abuse of a dominant market position:

16.2.1: setting monopolistically low or high prices;

setting monopolistically low or high prices; 16.2.7: setting low prices that restrict competition or prices that prevent competitors from maintaining sustainable profitability;

setting low prices that restrict competition or prices that prevent competitors from maintaining sustainable profitability; 16.2.8: selling goods below cost without economic or technological justification.

For these provisions to apply, it must also be established that Temu holds a dominant position in the Azerbaijani market. According to guidance published on the agency’s website, a company may be deemed to hold a dominant position if its share of the relevant market exceeds 35%. However, the agency has not specified which market segment is concerned or what share Temu holds in it.

If the violations are confirmed, the company could face significant sanctions. According to the Axar.az news website, citing the Competition Code, the commission could order the company to change its pricing policy, impose a fine equivalent to 10% of its annual turnover in Azerbaijan or impose a financial penalty amounting to half of its unlawfully obtained revenue.

Who is complaining and who is concerned?

Although it remains unclear who filed the complaint, dissatisfaction with Temu’s operations emerged long before the investigation was completed. In July, Haqqin.az reported that local entrepreneurs had been complaining on social media about declining sales and a drop in the number of shops operating in shopping centres. They proposed introducing taxes or restrictions on purchases made through the platform, or even blocking the app in Azerbaijan.

However, several economists who commented on the situation in the media took a different view. Former MP and economist Vahid Ahmadov told Haqqin.az that Temu offered an alternative to well-known brand stores for middle- and low-income consumers. In his view, the antimonopoly watchdog should combat monopolies rather than restrict access to affordable goods. Complaints about product quality, meanwhile, fall within the remit of other government agencies.

Economist Rauf Garayev suggested in the same article that the pressure on the platform came not from manufacturers but from retailers operating in shopping centres such as Bina and Sadarak. According to Garayev, unlike Turkey, Azerbaijan has virtually no domestic production of consumer goods. Imposing restrictions on foreign shopping platforms would therefore only limit consumer choice.

Meanwhile, one of Temu’s competitors had previously spoken in favour of competition. In October 2024, at the opening of Turkish online shopping platform Trendyol’s Baku office, the head of its Azerbaijani division, Irem Cagri Yilandil, said in response to a question about Temu: “Competition always benefits consumers.”

Consumers have also expressed concern. According to Axar.az, since the launch of the investigation, there has been an increase in social media posts reporting rising prices on Temu.

What happened at customs?

Temu has no official representative office in Azerbaijan. Orders are delivered from overseas warehouses through transport companies. This year, delays occurred in the customs clearance of parcels ordered through the platform.

State Customs Committee Chairman Shahin Bagirov explained the reasons for the delays on 29 April at a meeting of one of the committees of the Milli Majlis (Azerbaijani parliament). According to him, the volume of shipments from Temu had increased sharply, with goods arriving at the airport without customs authorities being notified electronically in advance. This resulted in delays of approximately two weeks. The State Customs Committee therefore required Temu to provide shipment details in advance.

At the same meeting, Bagirov said that more than one million people in the country shopped online and that the number of customs declarations submitted had reached 18 million. He noted that a revision of the $300 duty-free import threshold was not currently under consideration, but pointed out that similar exemptions had already been abolished in neighbouring countries. Since 2020, goods imported into Azerbaijan by an individual within a 30-day period by post or through transport companies have been exempt from customs duties, provided their total value does not exceed $300.

What measures have other countries taken against Temu?

In Turkey, which Bagirov cited as an example, the simplified customs clearance procedure for overseas parcels worth up to 30 euros was abolished on 1 February. Earlier, on 21 January, Turkey’s competition watchdog conducted an on-site inspection of the platform’s Istanbul office. In late January, Temu suspended deliveries of goods from abroad to Turkey.

Other countries have also taken measures against the platform, although on different grounds:

European Union. In May, the European Commission fined Temu 200m euros for failing to adequately assess the risks associated with the sale of dangerous and illegal products on the platform. The company disagreed with the decision.

In May, the European Commission fined Temu 200m euros for failing to adequately assess the risks associated with the sale of dangerous and illegal products on the platform. The company disagreed with the decision. Uzbekistan. In March 2025, access to the platform was restricted. The authorities cited non-compliance with legislation on e-commerce, consumer protection and personal data protection, as well as outstanding tax liabilities.

In March 2025, access to the platform was restricted. The authorities cited non-compliance with legislation on e-commerce, consumer protection and personal data protection, as well as outstanding tax liabilities. Vietnam. In December 2024, Temu’s operations in the country were suspended over its failure to complete mandatory registration.

In December 2024, Temu’s operations in the country were suspended over its failure to complete mandatory registration. Indonesia. In 2024, the government called for the app to be blocked to protect the interests of local small businesses.

In the EU, Uzbekistan and Vietnam, the main concerns regarding the platform centred on product safety, compliance with registration requirements and tax legislation. The situation in Indonesia most closely resembles that in Azerbaijan, with the Indonesian authorities justifying their actions by citing the need to protect local retailers.

What happens next?

The competition commission must now decide whether there are grounds for initiating proceedings. If no violation is established, the matter may be dropped.

Economist Khalid Karimli believes that the platform is unlikely to be blocked in the near future. According to him, initial measures could include issuing a warning, imposing a fine and giving the company a deadline to rectify the violation. The company could also challenge the commission’s decision in court. Karimli noted that stricter measures could only be taken if the company continued to violate the law and failed to comply with the authorities’ requirements.

It remains unclear how the commission’s decisions would be enforced against a company with no official representative office in Azerbaijan. Temu has yet to comment publicly on the investigation.

World.title: Flurry of diplomatic visits to Baku fuels speculation over Azerbaijan’s OSCE chairmanship bid
World.content:
Diplomatic visits to Baku and OSCE

Between 17 and 26 November, Azerbaijan received visits from the foreign ministers of Germany, Italy, Georgia and Lithuania, the prime minister of Montenegro and the US secretary of homeland security. Estonia’s foreign minister is also expected to visit Baku on 27 November.

According to official statements, the main topics of discussion were energy, the development of the Middle Corridor and the peace process between Azerbaijan and Armenia.

However, these visits coincided with a decisive stage in another diplomatic process. On 19 November, Azerbaijan announced in Vienna its readiness to chair the OSCE. The issue of the organisation’s chairmanship for 2027–2029 will be discussed at a meeting of the OSCE Ministerial Council, scheduled to take place on 3–4 December in the Swiss city of Lugano. This raises the following question:

What are the objectives of these numerous visits by foreign officials to Baku, and are they linked to Azerbaijan’s bid for the OSCE chairmanship?

Who visited and why?

According to official statements, the main topics of the visits were as follows:

Germany, 17–18 November. During a meeting between President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, discussions focused on Azerbaijani gas supplies to Germany, which began this year, the development of the Middle Corridor and “cooperation within international organisations”. Wadephul travelled to Yerevan after visiting Baku.

During a meeting between President Ilham Aliyev and Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul, discussions focused on Azerbaijani gas supplies to Germany, which began this year, the development of the Middle Corridor and “cooperation within international organisations”. Wadephul travelled to Yerevan after visiting Baku. US, 22 November. Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin discussed the TRIPP transport route, which will pass through Armenian territory, during his meeting with Aliyev. The launch of the project’s implementation was announced the following day.

Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin discussed the TRIPP transport route, which will pass through Armenian territory, during his meeting with Aliyev. The launch of the project’s implementation was announced the following day. Italy, 22–23 November. According to the Italian Foreign Ministry, Azerbaijan is the country’s second-largest oil supplier and third-largest gas supplier. The ministry stressed that, against the backdrop of the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, Azerbaijan was a “strategic and reliable partner” in ensuring Italy’s energy security. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani also attended a business forum featuring representatives of more than 240 companies.

According to the Italian Foreign Ministry, Azerbaijan is the country’s second-largest oil supplier and third-largest gas supplier. The ministry stressed that, against the backdrop of the crisis in the Strait of Hormuz, Azerbaijan was a “strategic and reliable partner” in ensuring Italy’s energy security. Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani also attended a business forum featuring representatives of more than 240 companies. Montenegro, 24 November. Prime Minister Milojko Spajic spoke about Azerbaijani investment in Montenegro’s economy.

Prime Minister Milojko Spajic spoke about Azerbaijani investment in Montenegro’s economy. Georgia, 24 November. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and Georgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili discussed the development of the Middle Corridor and the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway.

Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov and Georgian Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Maka Bochorishvili discussed the development of the Middle Corridor and the Baku-Tbilisi-Kars railway. Lithuania, 25–26 November. Foreign Minister Kestutis Budrys said that once Lithuania assumed the presidency of the Council of the EU in January 2027, Vilnius intended to initiate the process of easing visa requirements for Azerbaijani citizens. During his meeting with Aliyev, Budrys also announced the forthcoming signing of a joint declaration on strategic partnership between the two countries.

None of the official statements issued by the parties mentioned Azerbaijan’s bid for the OSCE chairmanship.

What is at stake at the OSCE?

Switzerland currently holds the OSCE chairmanship. On 19 November in Vienna, Swiss Foreign Minister Ignazio Cassis proposed adopting a single decision on which countries would chair the organisation over the next three years. Switzerland believes that such an approach would ensure continuity in the organisation’s work and regional balance. According to the OSCE, Azerbaijan, Armenia, Austria and Norway expressed their readiness to assume the chairmanship during the meeting. Cyprus and Georgia reaffirmed their candidacies, although consensus on either has yet to be reached.

The decision requires consensus among all 57 OSCE participating states. This means that any of them, including Armenia, can block any candidacy. No agreement has yet been reached on the chairmanship for 2027. The foreign minister of Georgia, whose candidacy has also failed to secure unanimous support among participating states, visited Baku that same week. However, neither side mentioned the OSCE chairmanship in its official statements.

Relations between Baku and the OSCE have been strained for many years. In 2015, the Azerbaijani government terminated its memorandum of understanding with the OSCE Project Co-ordinator in Baku and ended the operations of its office. The OSCE Minsk Process, which facilitated mediation efforts to resolve the Karabakh conflict, was terminated in September 2025 by a decision of the OSCE Ministerial Council following a joint request from Baku and Yerevan. Azerbaijan is now seeking the chairmanship of the organisation.

All countries whose representatives visited Baku are OSCE participating states. Some carry particular political weight in the context of the forthcoming decision: Italy and Germany are among the EU’s largest member states, Lithuania will assume the presidency of the Council of the EU in January, and the US is acting as a mediator in the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan.

Who opposes Azerbaijan’s bid?

Civil society representatives were the first to openly oppose Azerbaijan’s candidacy. A joint appeal published on 23 November on the website of the human rights organisation Human Rights House Foundation was signed by 46 organisations, including the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), the US-based Freedom Now, the Human Rights Centre of Azerbaijan and the Network of Independent Lawyers.

The signatories called on OSCE participating states not to support Azerbaijan’s bid to chair the organisation. They cited a report by the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe (PACE), published in May 2026, according to which Azerbaijan had 328 political prisoners, including 31 journalists. The appeal also noted that Azerbaijan was among the countries with the highest number of unimplemented judgments of the European Court of Human Rights (ECtHR).

The Azerbaijani government has yet to make any public statements regarding either the appeal by human rights organisations or its bid for the OSCE chairmanship.

Possible pardons and other explanations

The increase in diplomatic visits to Baku caught the attention of Ilgar Mammadov, former chairman of the REAL party and now a member of its political committee. In a Facebook post, he suggested that one of the reasons behind the intensified diplomatic contacts could be Azerbaijan’s bid for the OSCE chairmanship:

“If this is the reason, then the possibility of releasing some political prisoners through presidential pardons at the end of the year is also being discussed, so that participating states can justify their support for Azerbaijan’s chairmanship to international human rights organisations.”

Mammadov did not rule out other explanations. In his view, if the visits were linked to rising tensions surrounding Iran, this would be accompanied by an increase in oil prices, which has not materialised. The politician argued that the prospect of rising gas prices better explained the geographical pattern of the visits, but did not provide a complete picture either.

There has been no official information about possible pardons so far. Mammadov himself presented this as just one of several possible scenarios.

What to expect from the Lugano meeting?

The final decision on the OSCE chairmanship is expected to be taken by consensus in Lugano. Switzerland said consultations would continue until the meeting of the organisation’s Ministerial Council.

However, Baku’s diplomatic agenda extends beyond this issue. Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov believes that Lithuania’s presidency of the Council of the EU, which begins in January, will provide a good opportunity to advance the visa liberalisation agenda in the first half of 2027. Bayramov stressed, however, that decisions on visa policy are taken at EU level.

Estonia’s foreign minister is expected to visit Baku on 27 November, with just a week to go before the OSCE Ministerial Council meeting in Lugano.

World.title: ‘Not tailored to one person’: Pashinyan on Armenia’s new Constitution and its controversial provisions
World.content:
Pashinyan proposed that the opposition vote to put the draft Constitution to a referendum. He promised to resign if voters rejected it and not to stand for prime minister in the next election if they approved it. The opposition factions Armenia and Strong Armenia rejected his proposal. The parliamentary opposition calls the new Constitution “Aliyev’s Constitution”. Opposition politicians claim that the government is amending the country’s fundamental law at Azerbaijan’s request. Azerbaijan refuses to sign a peace treaty until Armenia amends its Constitution. Baku considers the reference in the preamble to the Declaration of Independence problematic. The declaration calls for the reunification of Armenia and Nagorno-Karabakh. The new draft removes this reference. Parliament must first approve the proposal to put the new Constitution to a referendum. Two-thirds of MPs must vote in favour. The ruling Civil Contract party does not have enough seats and needs six more votes.

According to Pashinyan, “institutional peace is now entirely achievable — indeed, it is already within arm’s reach; all we need to do is reach out and grasp it”. He believes that adopting a new Constitution is the way to achieve this.

“This is exclusively our domestic agenda, but it will clearly have regional and international consequences as well,” he said.

During the briefing, Pashinyan also discussed some of the changes to the draft Constitution. In particular, he addressed provisions on judicial reform and possible changes to the state symbols. He stressed that discussions on the draft had only just begun and that dialogue with the opposition and society would continue. He said the ruling party was ready to consider any facts and arguments: “Every issue is open for discussion. But that does not mean we will accept every proposal.”

The following sections contain the prime minister’s comments and explanations of the changes to the draft Constitution.

Changes to the judicial system are “fundamentally important”

The prime minister said that the proposed changes to the judicial system were fundamentally important.

“We face criticism both for the possibility of vetting judges and for the possibility of not doing so. We must decide which of these critical positions carries more weight for us. This is a political choice.”

According to Pashinyan, adopting a new Constitution should resolve the problem of public trust in the judicial system.

“The louder the judicial system protests against these changes, the stronger public consensus will become around the text of the new Constitution,” he said, commenting on a statement by the Union of Judges.

Under the draft Constitution, more than 300 Armenian judges will become acting judges. Authorities will then assess their professional competence, conduct and the legality of their income. The assessment will also cover their compliance with codes of conduct and conflict-of-interest rules over the five years following the Constitution’s entry into force.

A five-member commission, elected by MPs, will assess the judges. The commission will issue either a positive or a negative assessment. Judges who receive a negative assessment will not be reappointed.

Judges will have no right to challenge the commission’s assessments in court.
