The Union of Judges issued a statement condemning the draft Constitution. The judges argued that official discussions and consideration of its provisions could undermine the independence and authority of the judiciary.

“Constitutional guarantees of judicial tenure and judicial independence must not become casualties of political expediency. Nor can the need for constitutional reform justify any restrictions on these guarantees,” the statement said.

The Union of Judges also called on the Supreme Judicial Council — the constitutional body that safeguards the independence of courts and judges — to demand the removal of the provisions concerning the judiciary from the draft Constitution.

According to the prime minister, problems in the judicial system require fundamental solutions, including a new Constitution and the introduction of jury trials.

One of the changes proposed in the draft Constitution is the introduction of jury trials. A separate law will determine the categories of cases in which citizens can serve as jurors, as well as the procedures governing their participation.

Speaking about the problems in the judicial system, Pashinyan cited the cases against former president Robert Kocharyan. In particular, he referred to the fact that Kocharyan remained free and put a question to journalists:

“Do you think Robert Kocharyan should be free? I believe he should not be free. I have said so openly. I made that statement in Republic Square in front of tens of thousands of people. And tens of thousands of people applauded this position.”

The prime minister is convinced that the people themselves should make decisions about all aspects of the “life of the state”.

New constitutional provision on revoking citizenship is “a preventive measure”

Journalists asked Pashinyan whether the new constitutional provisions allowing the authorities to revoke citizenship could become an instrument of political pressure.

The prime minister replied that the most reliable way to neutralise this risk was to have an independent judiciary that “would guarantee that this cannot happen”.

“As for other cases — for example, if a person with dual citizenship is convicted of espionage — why should we preserve and protect their citizenship and continue to grant them civil rights?”

According to Pashinyan, the state must protect itself, particularly given the existence of dual citizenship.

“Imagine a situation in which a person with dual citizenship is caught acting as an agent of a foreign intelligence service and is subsequently convicted. Why should we not empower a court to revoke that person’s citizenship? This would serve as an additional preventive measure against treason or espionage.”

Article 24 of the draft Constitution provides that a person may lose their citizenship by court order in certain circumstances, including crimes against the foundations of the constitutional order or state security. The current Constitution does not allow the authorities to revoke citizenship on these grounds. Moreover, it explicitly states that the Republic of Armenia cannot deprive a citizen of their citizenship.

Citizens should decide on changes to state symbols in a referendum

Addressing the absence of descriptions of Armenia’s state symbols in the draft Constitution, Pashinyan said that a law would define them and that voters would approve it in a referendum.

“We have no specific proposal. We are saying that this law will be adopted in a referendum. Citizens themselves must decide what they consider to be their flag, coat of arms and national anthem.”

The prime minister believes that the authorities must do everything possible to ensure that citizens feel an organic connection with the state and its symbols.

One journalist asked: “Are you going to say now that if we do not remove Mount Ararat from the coat of arms, war will break out?”

“No, I will not threaten anyone,” Nikol Pashinyan replied.

The current Constitution describes the colours of the Armenian flag and their order, as well as the main elements of the coat of arms. The draft Constitution contains no descriptions of the flag or coat of arms. It states that the symbols of the Republic of Armenia are its coat of arms, flag and national anthem. A law, which voters will approve in a referendum, will define their descriptions or lyrics.

Pashinyan on Armenia’s new Constitution

World.title: Abkhazia introduces law to curb dumping by Russian tour operators
World.content:
The authorities in Abkhazia plan to introduce an anti-dumping law aimed at protecting small hotels from organised price-cutting by large Russian tour operators.

Abkhazia’s parliament has already passed the bill, titled “On Amendments to Certain Legislative Acts of the Republic of Abkhazia to Prevent the Monopolisation of the Tourist Accommodation Services Market”, in its first reading.

For several years, a trend has emerged in which large Russian tour operators buy up hotel rooms in Abkhazia at low prices ahead of the tourist season. They then sell them to tourists at even lower rates, offsetting the losses through other services.

The tour operators themselves describe this kind of dumping — offering a hotel room with three meals a day for 200 roubles ($2–3) — as a “special offer” designed to attract tourists to Abkhazia.

Small hotels suffer the most. They cannot afford to adopt such pricing policies and find themselves at a competitive disadvantage. As a result, they incur losses, and some even go bankrupt, selling their properties or renting them out to the same large tour operators.

Under the new bill:

Hotels will have to register contracts containing fixed room quotas with the Ministry of Tourism.

The register will record the number of rooms and the purchase price.

If a tour operator sells a room for more than 30% below its purchase price, the Ministry of Tourism will be able to issue a formal complaint.

If the violation is not rectified, sales may be suspended or the contract terminated.

The bill also introduces the concept of a “high season”, covering the period from 1 June to 1 September, during which all promotional discounts will be prohibited.

Abkhazia’s Tourism Minister Astamur Logua stressed that the aim was not to ban discounts, but to prevent dumping and market monopolisation.

If passed, the new rules could come into force on 1 January 2027.

World.title: Rotana signs deal to manage Samarkand hotel – Tourism Committee
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Rotana Hotel Management Corporation PJSC has signed an agreement with Uzbekistan’s Universal Building LLC to manage a new hotel in Samarkand under the Rotana brand, marking the international hospitality group’s entry into Uzbekistan’s hotel market.

The agreement was signed on November 28 following the 31st Tashkent International Tourism Fair, “Tourism on the Silk Road,” according to Uzbekistan’s Tourism Committee. It followed a meeting between the committee’s Chairman, Abdulaziz Akkulov, and Amna Al Nowais, director of strategy at Rotana Hotel Management Corporation.

Rotana has become the 35th international hotel brand to enter Uzbekistan’s hospitality market, the committee said.

During the meeting, the parties discussed developments in Uzbekistan’s tourism sector, the expansion of hotel infrastructure and investment opportunities for international hospitality groups.

Al Nowais welcomed the progress of Uzbekistan’s tourism industry and said Rotana was exploring opportunities to introduce several of its brands to the market. These include the five-star Rotana Hotels & Resorts brand, targeting the premium hospitality segment; the four-star Edge by Rotana; and the three-star Centro Hotels by Rotana, which focuses on modern accommodation. The entry of international hotel operators is expected to broaden accommodation options, introduce international service standards, and support the growth of inbound tourism.

Separately, agreements were signed during the tourism fair with international hotel brands for the management of 18 hotels across Uzbekistan. These arrangements cover both the management of existing properties and partnerships to develop new hotel projects.

International hotel chains are also expanding beyond Tashkent, with projects underway or planned in major tourism destinations, including Bukhara, Samarkand, Nukus, Chimgan and Beldersay.

The expansion reflects Uzbekistan’s efforts to attract international hospitality operators, increase hotel capacity, and strengthen its position as a regional tourism destination.

World.title: Turkmenistan, Türkiye discuss cooperation on migration issues
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, November 28. Turkmenistan and Türkiye have discussed ways to strengthen bilateral cooperation in migration during a meeting between officials in Ankara, according to the press service of the Turkmen government.

Turkmen Ambassador to Türkiye Mekan Ishanguliyev met with Muhammet Selami Yazıcı, head of the Turkish Presidency of Migration Management under the Ministry of Interior.

The two sides reviewed current migration-related cooperation, exchanged views on matters of mutual interest and emphasized the importance of maintaining regular working contacts between their respective agencies.

They also discussed cooperation within international organizations and reaffirmed their commitment to further strengthening the bilateral partnership.

Turkmenistan and Türkiye established diplomatic relations shortly after Turkmenistan gained independence. Türkiye was the first country to recognize Turkmenistan, on October 27, 1991, and opened its embassy in Ashgabat in February 1992. The countries cooperate in the political, economic, cultural and educational spheres, while Türkiye supports Turkmenistan's policy of permanent neutrality.

Economic ties remain an important component of bilateral relations. According to Türkiye's Foreign Ministry, bilateral trade reached $2.2 billion in 2025, comprising $1.3 billion in Turkish exports to Turkmenistan and $860 million in imports from Turkmenistan. The presidents of the two countries have set a target of increasing bilateral trade to $5 billion in the near term.

Turkish companies have also been active in Turkmenistan's construction and industrial sectors. Since Turkmenistan gained independence, they have completed more than 1,000 projects worth over $54 billion.

World.title: Taiwan elections: Candidate criticised by China concedes Taipei mayoral race
World.content:
Taiwan's ruling party candidate has conceded defeat in the Taipei mayoral election as results emerged from local elections across the island's 22 cities and counties.

Democratic Progressive Party candidate Puma Shen mounted a strong challenge to incumbent Mayor Chiang Wan-an but fell short of returning the city to DPP control for the first time since 1994.

"I know there's many people crying here. I want to thank every person who voted for me," Mr Shen told thousands of supporters after conceding.

What are Taiwan's nine-in-one elections? Analysts say the elections will be watched closely by Beijing, while Taiwan has warned against possible Chinese interference.

Mr Shen, whom Beijing has labelled a separatist, said he had called Mr Chiang to congratulate him.

With votes from 1,606 of 1,790 polling stations counted — or almost 90 per cent — Mr Chiang had about 53.8 per cent of the vote to Mr Shen's 45.6 per cent, according to the electoral authorities.

The capital has traditionally been a stronghold of the opposition Nationalist Party, also known as the Kuomintang or KMT, which favours closer ties with China.

The elections featured candidates mostly from the DPP or the KMT.

Traditionally, the KMT has performed well in local elections. In 2022, the DPP won in only five of 22 localities.

Taiwan's President Lai Ching-te campaigned for DPP candidates, appearing on Thursday night to support his party's mayoral candidate in Taoyuan City.

China looms despite focus on local concerns

DPP candidate Puma Shen on stage after losing his bid to win the Taipei mayorship in Taipei. (Reuters: Ann Wang)

Unlike presidential elections — when relations with China and Beijing's pressure on the self-ruled island are major issues — Saturday's vote focused more on local concerns, including social welfare benefits and other livelihood issues.

But China has not been entirely absent from the debate.

Initially viewed as a long shot, Mr Shen was known for his work organising civil defence courses.

He gained attention and support while campaigning on issues such as planting more trees and making city government more responsive.

His campaign unfolded under pressure from Beijing, which imposed sanctions on him and launched an investigation into his activities.

The Chinese government claims Taiwan as its territory and has not ruled out force to annex it.

Taiwanese authorities have accused Beijing of attempting to sow distrust in the island's electoral system, allegations that Chinese authorities have rejected.

Taiwan's Ministry of National Defense reported about 33 sorties by Chinese warplanes, including bombers and fighter jets, toward the island between Friday and Saturday.

Nuclear power, economy among key issues

Chiang Wan-an (centre), of the opposition party KMT, at his campaign headquarters. (Reuters: Yu Chih Wei)

As well as electing local leaders, voters also cast their ballots in a referendum to overturn a policy that banned nuclear power.

The proposal calls for using nuclear energy to boost the economy.

Supporters say additional energy sources are needed to meet the artificial intelligence industry's growing demand for electricity.

Voter Chang Li-fen said the economy was her foremost concern, but declined to say whom she had voted for.

"If the Taiwan economy is good, only then will people be able to live well," she said.

"In France and in Italy, people are protesting because of energy costs, which raised the cost of living, so I think the economy is most important."

Candidates held rallies on Friday in a last-minute bid for votes.

Mr Shen travelled in a motorcade across the city, stopping for 15 minutes at a time to greet the crowds of supporters.

Chiang held a Friday night rally with other KMT city council members, with supporters waving balloons, flags and light-up sticks to cheer him on.

AP

World.title: One Nation finds its base in regional Victoria
World.content:
Shortly before the election polls closed on Saturday, Chris Burson was standing with a trio of his fellow One Nation candidates outside a Geelong polling booth.

The team was excited to see just how well they would do in the count, particularly following pre-election polling predicting the rise of One Nation.

They were equal parts confident and circumspect. A primary vote explosion seemed likely, but so too did difficult preference flows.

One Nation enjoyed a surge in voter support in regional Victoria on election day. (ABC News: Jeremy Story Carter)

Victoria election 2026 live updates: The Coalition has been swept into power in Victoria, ending 12 years of Labor rule. Look back on how election night unfolded in our live blog.

"I think there's a real vibe that things are going to change in not just Victoria, but Geelong," Mr Burson, the party's lead candidate for Western Victoria, said.

"It's really exciting," he said. "I mean, this is history, really."

As one of the slowest, and most complicated election night counts neared midnight on Saturday, it would appear Mr Burson was right.

One Nation had asserted itself as the most disruptive force ever seen in a Victorian election, largely driven by its rise in the regions.

Numbers will fluctuate as vote counting continues on Sunday and into the next week, but the proportion of One Nation voters in regional Victoria compared to Melbourne early in the count is extremely telling.

One Nation has found its heartland in regional Victoria. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A snapshot of the count at 9:15pm on Saturday had One Nation holding 15.7 per cent of the total primary vote count in metropolitan Victoria, compared to 32.3 per cent of the vote in the regions.

The question now will be how that vote translates to lower or upper house seats in the regions.

On Saturday evening, One Nation's Eureka candidate Paul Ballinger said he was not getting ahead of himself, despite a strong start in the polls.

"There is still an awful long way to go," Mr Ballinger said.

He said the rise of One Nation was simple: voters were sick of "professional politicians".

"They've never actually been out in the real world," Mr Ballinger said.

Despite the huge primary vote trickling in throughout Saturday evening, the orange wave faced complicated preference flows which could dampen the surge in votes.

Prior to election day, Narracan, Morwell and Murray Plains were all seen as seats One Nation had a strong chance of taking.

Member for Narracan Wayne Farnham looks like he may hold off a One Nation surge (ABC News: Madeleine Stuchbery)

But — with more counting to come — taking more than 40 per cent of primary votes in all three seats as of 11pm on Saturday had not translated to wins for One Nation.

Counting and preferences made the seats near impossible to call on Saturday night, but all three looked on track to be won by the Coalition.

As vote counting closed on Saturday evening, the Coalition seemed poised to convert a strong primary and favourable preferences to winning seats across the regions.

As her own seat hung in the balance on Saturday evening, Labor Wendouree MP Juliana Addison said it had been an "extraordinary day for democracy".

"We have seen the emergence of One Nation, we've seen a huge Greens vote — this has really shaken everything up," Ms Addison said.

She also voiced her disappointment that Premier Ben Carroll lost his seat of Niddrie, in what was a catastrophic election for Labor.

"I'm sad for Ben. He's given so much to the Labor Party, but I'll have to process that," she said.

One Nation well placed in upper house

While a slow and complicated vote count continues to play out in coming days, One Nation is already looking toward the more favourable expected preference flows of the upper house, where they hope to see votes translate to One Nation MPs.

Ben Carroll conceded defeat at the Victorian state election, also losing his seat. (ABC News: James Oaten)

"We're more likely to have success in the upper house than the lower house, as we've talked about before, because of those preferences," Pauline Hanson's chief of staff Chris Taylor said.

"But they're building, they're building."

One Nation leader Pauline Hanson addressed an adoring crowd on Saturday evening, announcing the party's mission to disrupt Victoria's political status quo was already a success.

"One Nation is snapping at the heels of the political establishment, Labor and Liberal both, and they know it," she said.

World.title: Labor MPs are in 'disbelief' after electoral annihilation in Victoria
World.content:
Victorian Labor will have at least a handful of seats.

"At least a Tarago, maybe three Camrys," one outgoing Labor MP teased.

Tonight's results represent electoral annihilation of the party in Victoria.

"We [Labor] need a fresh start," said another MP, who should narrowly hold on, in an apparent nod to Liberal leader Jess Wilson's commanding campaign.

Not long ago, Labor seemed to be the natural owners of the state's politics.

Tonight Labor candidates and senior party figures barely had the words to explain how they had fallen from the 56-seat highs they experienced only last election under Daniel Andrews.

It was, invariably, "bad", "not good", "disbelief".

Labor's longstanding so-called red wall in the north and west of Melbourne didn't just lose a brick, it took out the premier.

Ben Carroll lost his own seat of Niddrie.

Sydenham will fall. Sunbury. Point Cook. Possibly Greenvale, Kalkallo, Werribee, St Albans, Tarneit, Essendon.

The red wall could look more like a letterbox.

For 123 days, Ben Carroll walked in the shadow of his predecessors While he had promised a new direction for Labor, Victorians tonight decided they wanted a fresh start — including in Ben Carroll's own seat of Niddrie.

In a gracious concession speech, Carroll listed off Labor achievements during 12 years in government — and there are many.

He spruiked Labor policies he was proud of from major infrastructure projects such as the Metro Tunnel and level crossing removals to free TAFE, teacher pay deals and voluntary assisted dying.

He pointed to Labor's decade of work to deliver of a Treaty with Victoria's First Peoples.

"Because it was the right thing to do," Carroll said.

For the first time since taking the leadership, Carroll seemed to say Daniel Andrews' and Jacinta Allan's names with ease on Saturday night.

Who becomes the next Victorian Labor leader, responsible for rebuilding, will depend on who is left. (AAP: Con Chronis)

For some in Labor, the campaign was so conscious of avoiding its ghosts — like corruption on its transformative infrastructure projects — that it erased its victories from the narrative entirely.

An autopsy will look at what went wrong.

Some party figures have been taking notes for months.

Deputy leader Gabrielle Williams said Labor failed to learn from hits to its primary vote in its heartland in 2022 and at last year's Werribee byelection.

"It's quite clear we didn't heed the warnings," she said.

"There were many inflection points that should have given us cause to listen or, more importantly, to respond."

Deputy Labor leader Gabrielle Williams on election night. (ABC News: Alonso Gajardo)

Outgoing MP Gary Maas, who leaves the parliament after deciding not to recontest in Narre Warren South, told the ABC that Labor forgot who it represented.

"Labor's primary rightfully bottomed," said Maas, who has Sri Lankan heritage.

"We traditionally rely on our multicultural and multi-faith communities yet our multicultural and multi-faith communities aren't reflected as actual MPs in Labor governments.

" When South Asian communities are voting for One Nation, this should be a huge wake-up call. "

Outgoing MP Sonja Terpstra had a few choice words.

"Standing in the middle trying to straddle things meant standing for nothing," she wrote on social media.

The party had been "trading values to quell front pages instead of holding the line", Terpstra said.

Labor's primary vote plummeted by more than 20 per cent in Sydenham.

What's the result in your electorate? Explore the results across Melbourne and regional Victoria with these maps.

Two elections ago, the party won on first preferences.

"We need to assess why working class people abandoned us in this election and work hard to win them back," Sydenham candidate Uroš Rasic told the ABC.

"Labor needs to take a good look at itself and rebuild trust with Victorians."

In the eastern suburbs, Labor won't make the two-party preferred result in seats the party held a day ago.

Not that this was ever Labor territory, but the party bet big under Daniel Andrews.

Once the final preferences are distributed, Victoria's 61st parliament will likely include just 15 Labor MPs in an 88 seat house.

Who becomes the next Victorian Labor leader, responsible for rebuilding, will depend on who is left.

World.title: Explosion at Afghanistan school kills seven students, wounds 97 people
World.content:
An explosion at a school in Afghanistan has killed seven students and wounded more than 90, officials say.

The blast appeared to have originated in a neighbouring depot for explosives in the eastern Afghan province of Kunar on Saturday, the province's culture and information director said.

Kunar province, which borders Pakistan, is home to a number of mining operations.

Sami ul Haq Bayan said initial information indicated the blast at the school on the outskirts of the provincial capital, Asadabad, occurred due to negligence at the depot storing explosives belonging to mining companies.

An investigation into the incident was underway, he said.

Up to 15 of the wounded are in hospital, while the rest have been discharged after treatment, he added.

Earlier, Kunar Provincial Police Headquarters spokesperson Farid Dehqan said the explosion occurred at 10am local time at a school in the Andar Ser area on the outskirts of Asadabad.

Footage posted on social media showed cars bringing wounded children to the emergency department of a hospital in Asadabad, as well as images of the school building — part of which appeared to have collapsed.

In August, a hand grenade attack at a school complex in the Afghan capital of Kabul wounded more than 40 children aged between nine and 14.

AP/Reuters

World.title: School camp staffer fired after reports of inappropriate touching
World.content:
A school camp staff member on the NSW Mid North Coast has been stood down amid allegations of inappropriate touching involving students.

The Great Aussie Bush camp is a well-known rite of passage for thousands of students, with seven camp sites located across New South Wales, Queensland, and Victoria.

The ABC understands an allegation has been made that at least three primary school children were touched by a staff member at the Tea Gardens facility while on camp.

A spokesperson from New South Wales Police says a report was made by the school to the child protection hotline.

A spokesperson from the Great Aussie Bush Camp said it places the utmost importance on safety, wellbeing and dignity of children at the centre of its operations.

"The Great Aussie Bush Camp is aware of an incident that happened this week at its Tea Gardens camp," the statement said.

"The [staffer] involved was immediately stood down pending investigation.

"As the incident is under investigation by the appropriate authorities, we are unable to comment further," the statement read.

New South Wales Police have told the ABC they will attend a school in the New England North West region on Monday to investigate and talk to students who attended the camp.

"Police are aware of the report and are conducting inquiries into the matter," the statement said.

No charges have been laid and the incident remains under investigation.

In a statement, a spokesperson from the Department of Education said staff immediately reported the allegations and notified families.

"The safety and welfare of students is the Department's highest priority."

World.title: Election day rescue of hikers trapped in floodwaters at Lerderderg Gorge
World.content:
Search crews have rescued a group of hikers who got caught in rising floodwaters in Lerderderg Gorge in central Victoria.

Victoria Police said 11 hikers were in the gorge when rising waters prevented them from hiking out about 10:30am.

They had set out on the hike amid significant rain across the state.

The gorge is a popular attraction within the 44,000-hectare Wombat-Lerderderg National Park.

The Victoria Police helicopter was called in to help find the hikers who had to be guided to safety along a high ridge line.

The State Emergency Service Bacchus Marsh Unit has urged hikers to avoid the Werribee and Lerderderg Gorge until floodwaters recede.

Victoria Police said no-one was injured.

World.title: For 123 days, Ben Carroll walked in the shadow of his predecessors
World.content:
He was the premier for 123 days.

It was by no means the shortest time in leadership for a Victorian premier. It was also not the easiest.

Labor had plunged in the polls after 12 years in government and Ben Carroll walked in the shadow of two controversial leaders.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: The Coalition has been swept into power in Victoria, ending 12 years of Labor rule. Look back on how election night unfolded in our live blog.

Ben Carroll with then-opposition leader Daniel Andrews at Essendon Keilor College in 2014. (Facebook: Ben Carroll MP)

Daniel Andrews ordered one of the world's longest COVID lockdowns and kicked off Victoria's Big Build infrastructure boom, which was also under the remit of Jacinta Allan when she was public transport infrastructure minister then premier.

The project is now the subject of a royal commission into alleged crime and corruption on building sites, which was called by Mr Carroll after he took the leadership from Ms Allan.

While Mr Carroll promised a new direction for Labor, Victorians tonight decided they wanted a fresh start — including in his own seat of Niddrie.

"We are part of the longest serving Labor government in Victoria's history," Mr Carroll said during his concession speech on election night.

"We ran a strong campaign, but you can't outrun time."

Deputy Labor leader Gabrielle Williams said Mr Carroll's exit was a "huge loss" for the party and that he was "one of the most decent human beings" she had encountered in politics.

From working class to political class

Ben Carroll was born into a working class family in the northern Melbourne suburb of Airport West in 1975.

His mother was a school teacher and his father was an electrician.

Mr Carroll was elected as the member of Niddrie in 2012. (Facebook: Ben Carroll MP)

Mr Carroll often spoke of growing up under the flight path, getting an after-school job at Kmart at the age of 14 and watching his father run a small business.

He studied law at university and later spent time as a volunteer lawyer at a community legal service.

He landed a job as a political advisor in 1999 to then-Labor premier Steve Bracks.

"In those early years, I had the honour of working in his office and saw up close how he brought people together as we travelled right across the state," Mr Carroll wrote in a social media post.

Mr Carroll crossed over to parliament after standing for pre-selection for the seat of Niddrie in 2012 against future cabinet colleague Jaclyn Symes.

Ben Carroll has said he has enormous respect for former premier Steve Bracks. (Facebook: Ben Carroll MP)

He then won the seat in a by-election after the resignation of Rob Hulls.

He started his maiden speech to state parliament by telling the story of his ancestor Michael Carroll leaving Ireland in 1840 during the potato famine and arriving on a boat in Australia.

"The reason I tell this story is to illustrate the power of opportunity: that a descendant of a labourer from Tipperary, Ireland, can now stand before you in this special place, this great chamber of history and achievement, due to the opportunity provided by a young nation to a young Irishman more than 170 years ago," he said in April 2012.

In 2014, Carroll was appointed as the Parliamentary Secretary for Justice. (Facebook: Ben Carroll MP)

During more than 5,300 days in parliament, Mr Carroll has held 16 portfolios in a range of areas, from two stints as the minister for medical research to WorkSafe and the Transport Accident Commission, manufacturing and crime prevention.

He was the minister for education when Victorian state school teachers held their first mass strikes in 13 years and during years of blunders with VCE exams, including the leaking of exam questions, typos and errors in exams and some students being given the wrong paper.

Carroll paints a sound wall on Fullarton Road in Airport West in 2015. (Facebook: Ben Carroll MP)

Mr Carroll was elevated to the position of deputy premier when Dan Andrews quit as premier in 2023, handing the leadership over to Ms Allan.

In July, as Labor's popularity nosedived in the months before the state election, rumblings of a leadership challenge grew.

Ben Carroll at state parliament in 2015. (Facebook: Ben Carroll MP)

After assuring he was standing by Ms Allan as leader, Mr Carroll announced he would nominate for the position.

He said the change of heart came after he was visited by a delegation of Labor MPs.

"It is clear that the premier has lost the majority of our caucus," he said.

"As such, I have visited the premier to inform her that I will be nominating for the leadership of the Labor Party."

In the end, he did not have to challenge Ms Allan.

Ben Carroll with Jacinta Allan and Jaclyn Symes at the new Parkville railway station in 2025. (AAP Image: Joel Carrett)

Ms Allan announced she was not only stepping down as premier but would quit politics at the state election.

However, Mr Carroll still had to face a Labor caucus meeting, which descended into chaos and yelling when Allan loyalist Sonya Kilkenny made a surprise run for the leadership — with Ms Allan adding her signature to the nomination.

Inside the Labor leadership battle Ben Carroll emerged from a meeting of the Labor caucus on Tuesday as the party's new leader, but what the public did not see was a two-hour fight behind closed doors to decide who would run the state.

In the end, Ms Kilkenny pulled out of the race to avoid a leadership battle that could have lasted weeks due to Labor's requirement that it be put to a full vote of party members.

Mr Carroll was sworn in as Victoria's 50th premier, with his first move being to call the royal commission into the Big Build.

"I am honoured and humbled to be elected unanimously as the new leader of the Victorian Labor Party," he told his first press conference as the state's leader.

"This was not an easy decision, but the stakes at this election are too high."

Loading Instagram content

He also used his first day in office to telephone Victoria Police Chief Commissioner Mike Bush to discuss crime and community safety.

Mr Carroll also had another big statement to make that day in his first press conference as premier.

" Let me make one thing very clear: I am not Daniel Andrews, I am not Jacinta Allan. "

In his short time in the job, he cut the number of ministers in cabinet, promised Victoria would meet its school funding obligations under the former Gonski plan and announced $2 billion worth of cuts to the Suburban Rail Loop.

Mr Carroll has described himself as relatable and hard-working.

His list of priorities on his official parliamentary biography are heavily focused on education.

He also stated that he wanted Victoria to become a world leader in mental health support and to take strong action on climate change, with a vision for the state to become a global leader in the creation of a zero-emissions, renewable workforce.

Ben Carroll announces a royal commission immediately after taking the role of premier. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

A week before the election, Mr Carroll told the ABC's state political reporter Richard Willingham he was feeling positive.

"Victoria is the best state in the greatest nation on earth," he said.

World.title: The meteoric rise of Victoria's new millennial premier Jess Wilson
World.content:
Less than four years ago, 32-year-old Jess Wilson, freshly elected member for Kew, stepped up to make her maiden speech in parliament.

There are hints of the politician that is to come in that speech, but Ms Wilson is young.

Victoria election 2026 live updates: The Coalition has been swept into power in Victoria, ending 12 years of Labor rule. Look back on how election night unfolded in our live blog.

She speaks quickly. Takes little breaths.

Early career media appearances suggest a hint of nervousness rarely glimpsed during the final stretch of Ms Wilson's historic campaign to become Victoria's first elected female premier.

Now the 36-year-old speaks more slowly and pauses for effect.

Ms Wilson has gone from president of the Victorian Young Liberals to Victorian premier in just 10 years.

When being grilled on commercial radio on her millennial tendencies this year (yes, she does like Harry Potter and smashed avocado) she admitted sharing her generation's inclination to text rather that call.

"It can be very efficient," she said.

Her meteoric rise to the top job — leading a campaign to topple a 12-year-old Labor government that won office when Ms Wilson was still at university — was very efficient.

She went from first-term MP to opposition leader in three years.

Jess Wilson, a first-term MP, was elected as the Liberal party leader in November 2025. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Her victory, delivered by a campaign sold firmly on her image, marks a serious turnaround of a state Liberal division that proved unelectable for a decade as it struggled to unite on a direction or a leader.

Finally the Victorian Liberals presented a united front under their millennial leader — the first of her generation to become a state premier in Australia.

Ms Wilson has led the Coalition out of 12 years in political opposition. (ABC News: Danielle Bonica)

Critics have hinted that as the daughter of a former state Liberal politician, Ms Wilson's pathway into politics was expected rather than earnt, a suggestion that those close to her firmly reject.

What is clear is that she had something of a head start, telling parliament in her maiden speech:

"Mum and Dad ensured that I was baptised into the three great faiths: the Catholic Church, the Liberal Party and the Collingwood Football Club," she said.

Who is Jess Wilson?

Jess Wilson was born in 1990.

Her father Ron Wilson was a Liberal MP for the now abolished seat of Bennetswood in Melbourne's eastern suburbs and in Ms Wilson's own words, her "first political hero".

Victorian Liberal leader Jess Wilson (left) was born and raised in Melbourne's eastern suburbs. (Instagram: Jess Wilson MP)

Karina Klonis, her close friend and bridesmaid, has known her since they were in year 7 at Strathcona Girls Grammar School, when they bonded over their shared love of Boost Juice (the flavour was all berry bang, for those wondering).

Ms Klonis said Ms Wilson's political streak wasn't so obvious at school, but her work ethic was.

"I don't know anyone who works harder than her," Ms Klonis said.

She described Ms Wilson as "a natural leader, very sure of herself and really decisive".

Ms Wilson was an excellent student, a hockey player and prefect "fondly recalled" by those in the school community according to current Strathcona principal Lorna Beegan.

High school friends Karina Klonis and Jess Wilson ended up studying at university together. (Supplied: Karina Klonis)

"At Strathcona, we believe girls are unstoppable, and Jess's journey shows what can happen when young women are given the confidence, skills, and encouragement to lead," she said in a statement.

Ms Wilson's old school is one of about 60 high-fee independent schools which stand to benefit from their alumnus's ascension to government, via a Liberal election promise to remove payroll tax.

The plan to scrap Labor's private school tax changes is estimated to cost the state government $1.8 billion in revenue over 10 years, according to the independent Parliamentary Budget Office.

From law student to Young Liberal president

Ms Wilson went on to study Arts/Law at Monash University, where she further developed her political nous.

She joined the Liberal Party at 19, becoming Monash Liberal president and then Victoria's Young Liberal president.

The party's youth wing was where she met her husband Aaron Lane, a barrister and one-time state Liberal candidate who was stood down in 2014 over homophobic tweets.

Jess Wilson pictured with former MP for Kew Tim Smith (left), Georgina Downer and federal MP Josh Frydenberg at a Victorian Young Liberal event in 2016. (Facebook)

Photos from that time show a grinning younger Ms Wilson, pictured alongside Liberal Party figures like then-state MP Tim Smith, fellow young Liberal and daughter of former foreign minister Alexander Downer, Georgina Downer, and federal Liberal minister Josh Frydenberg.

She went on to work in Mr Frydenberg's office as an advisor when he was environment minister, as well as in consulting and policy in the private sector.

Jess Wilson's career: KPMG consultant (2014 — 2016)

Federal government advisor (2016 — 2017)

Business Council of Australia policy advisor (2018 — 2022)

Member for Kew (since 2022)

Victorian Liberal leader (since 2024)

Ms Wilson was later pre-selected for Mr Smith's seat of Kew in state parliament, after his resignation following a drink-driving incident.

She was elected as the member for Kew in 2022, to another Liberal defeat in Victoria which triggered the resignation of leader Matthew Guy.

The party's new leader John Pesutto, promoted Ms Wilson into the shadow ministry straight away, bestowing her with responsibility for Finance, Economic Reform, Home Ownership and Housing Affordability.

Jess Wilson shakes hands with former Prime Minister John Howard during her first campaign for the seat of Kew in 2022. (Instagram: Jess Wilson MP)

By December 2024, John Pessuto had lost the leadership, resulting in the promotion of Brad Battin, who was then rolled after less than a year in the top job.

In November 2025, Ms Wilson, still a first-term MP, was elected unopposed as leader.

Ms Wilson stepped into the role with a strong team by her side.

She has been supported on her campaign by federal Liberal senator James Paterson, who is also a godparent to her young son Patrick, who was born in 2024.

Victorian Liberal senator James Paterson on the hustings with Jess Wilson during a visit to an early voting centre. (AAP: CON CHRONIS)

In Ms Wilson, the Victorian Liberals finally had a young, female leader with cut through on social media.

For many, it was the "fresh start" the party needed to provide a credible alternative government in Australia's most progressive state.

New look Liberal backed by old guard

Ms Wilson has described her political leanings as "classic Liberal".

She campaigned hard on crime, potholes, economic reform and the need for a change of government.

Her move to match, rather than politicise, Labor's election pledge to offer free abortions, hinted at a decisive and modern approach to Liberal leadership.

She was the only state Liberal to vote yes in the Voice to Parliament referendum.

During her maiden speech to parliament she acknowledged the Aboriginal traditional owners of her electorate.

But her leadership role has been backed by conservative Liberal MPs, including those with an active role in leadership spills of recent years.

Jess Wilson has been backed by party figures including conservative powerbroker MP Bev McArthur. (AAP: Joel Carrett)

Ms Wilson's commitment to scrapping Victoria's Treaty, a policy estimated to save more than a billion dollars over 10 years, has devastated members of the Aboriginal community.

Political commentator George Megalogenis has described her as an "insider presenting as an agent of change".

As noted by ABC Insiders host David Speers, her last-minute reveal of a plan to privatise Melbourne's sewerage network, a proposal the Liberals had taken to the last two state elections, proved she was "a fresh young face … still capable of the dirty old political trick".

The question will be whether her unprecedented ability to unite the Coalition can continue in the face of a potentially chaotic upper house.

Jess Wilson raises a glass at the Victorian Young Liberals ball in 2015, when she was president of the party's youth wing. (Facebook)

When Ms Wilson was Young Liberals president, her leadership was challenged by a group of self-described "small L liberals", concerned with the direction of the party and the influence of the conservative right.

She survived that revolt.

Her former challenger, fellow young Liberal and now high school teacher Luke Corcoran, said he admired her recent campaign and her way of "bringing the party together".

"Jess was always exceptionally skilled. She has only improved," he said.

Her old friend, Karina Klonis, has no doubts. She said Jess Wilson would be the one to make the changes Victoria needed and stay the course.

World.title: The seats that changed hands: Premier ousted, ministers wiped out in historic Labor rout
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election The seats that changed hands: Premier ousted, ministers wiped out in historic Labor rout James Costa November 29, 2026 — 12:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.08 % counted LNP 57 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 17 seats remaining

After 12 years in power, the unprecedented rejection of the Labor Party has been characterised by the loss of about a dozen previously safe seats, and significant losses in other marginal electorates. But while the upstart One Nation was meant to clean up, this masthead has so far not called any seats for the party, leaving the Victorian leader Warren Pickering without a seat. Loading In one of the most significant swings and in a shattering defeat, the outgoing Premier Ben Carroll has lost his seat of Niddrie with a swing of more than 18 per cent to the Liberal Party’s Samantha Byrne. “This is a significant loss for Labor,” Carroll said of the loss of government in his concession speech. “As leader of the party, I take full responsibility.”



A sitting premier losing their seat is a feat that, in recent history at least, has only been accomplished by 51-day Victorian premier Ian MacFarlan, the member for Brighton in 1945. The reason behind MacFarlan’s short premiership is a bit confusing: he was expelled from the Liberal Party for striking a deal with the Country Party to form a stop-gap government to secure a supply bill in October 1945, making him a premier without a party. In the November election of that year, MacFarlan lost his seat. It has not been a good night in the seats of two other former Labor premiers, either. Carroll was only premier for four months, replacing Jacinta Allan. The former premier opted not to contest her Bendigo East seat, held by Labor since 1999, and it was won by Nationals candidate Andrew Lethlean.



Labor has also lost former premier Daniel Andrews’ seat of Mulgrave to the Liberals’ Charles Tran. It’s a little reminiscent of the 2025 federal election, when former Greens leader Adam Bandt lost his supposedly safe seat of Melbourne to Labor, and when former Liberal Party MP and opposition leader Peter Dutton was rejected not only as the alternative prime minister but also as the member for Dickson in Queensland. The Coalition hadn’t won a seat north or west of the Yarra since 1996. That drought has ended, with the Liberals gaining Yan Yean, Sydenham, Bundoora, and Macedon among others. Elsewhere, the Liberals have picked up Frankston, Mordialloc, Carrum and Bentleigh, unseating four senior Labor ministers: Paul Edbrooke, Tim Richardson, Sonya Kilkenny and Nick Staikos. Here are the changing seats The Age has called in the 2026 Victorian election so far.

The Greens have claimed victory in what was previously Labor heartland of Footscray, catapulting Elena Pereya into parliament.

Pereya took to the stage at 11.30pm at the Greens election party to huge applause.

Supporters celebrate at the election night event for The Greens. Elke Meitzel

“Footscray has been the dumping ground for Labor’s worst ideas,” Pereya said, in what was likely a reference to the construction of data centres in the area.

“For a long time, it’s been a cautionary tale of what you don’t do everywhere else, and now it’s a cautionary tale for Labor to not take people for granted because they have chosen hope and prosperity and a hopeful future.”

With 58 per cent of votes counted, Elena Pereyra had polled 62.1 per cent of the two-candidate-preferred vote, ahead of Labor’s Katie Hall on 37.9 per cent. That represents a 16.4 per cent swing towards the Greens.

Pereya said she was proud to be the next Green MP for Footscray and thanked the many people who had worked on her campaign. She said key issues for the electorate had been data centres, housing, transport, cycling infrastructure and air quality.

World.title: The overlooked corner of New Zealand that deserves a detour
World.content:
InspirationNew Zealand The overlooked corner of New Zealand that deserves a detour Rob McFarland November 29, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Given all the uncertainty in the world, you’d think that New Zealand would be a safe bet for a holiday: stable government, no snakes, decent coffee. However, it still has weather, and halfway through a six-day Adventure South cycle trip on the North Island, the storm gods throw a tantrum, unleashing 170 millimetres of rain and 130km/h winds. Not ideal for biking. Crossing the Bridge to Nowhere in Whanganui National Park. Until then, things had been going swimmingly. After meeting in Taupo, our group of nine cyclists and two guides, one of whom is a retired meteorologist (a good omen, surely?), drives two hours south to the small town of Taihape. Taihape is known as the Gumboot Capital of New Zealand, a title it has earned thanks to its annual gumboot throwing competition in March. Naturally, this is something we need to try, particularly when our lead guide, Robyn Marchant, tells us that on last year’s tour, a woman managed 22 metres using a bright pink Barbie boot.



I have many excuses as to why I only manage a paltry 17 metres, but more impressive is that the Taihape record is a frankly staggering 48.65 metres, held by New Zealand’s undisputed gumboot hurling king, Kieran Fowler from Dunedin. 



Our base for the next two nights is the lovely Powderhorn Chateau, a wood-panelled, chalet-style property in Ohakune. A popular winter base for the ski fields at nearby Mount Ruapehu, the town’s other claim to fame is that it is New Zealand’s Carrot Capital, a self-bestowed title in honour of its prodigious carrot production. Not to be outdone by the giant corrugated iron gumboot that welcomes visitors to Taihape, Ohakune has not only erected a 7.5m-high carrot (voted New Zealand’s 2023 Landmark of the Year), but also created an adorable vegetable-themed sculpture park featuring, among others, a supersized Brussels sprout called Sir Lancelot. From pedal to paddle power on the Whanganui River. The following day, we ditch the bikes to explore one of the region’s natural and historical treasures – the Whanganui River. In 2017, it famously became the world’s first river to be granted legal personhood, recognising its deep spiritual significance for the region’s Maori, who regard it as an ancestor. After driving to the small riverside settlement of Pipiriki, our adventure begins with an exhilarating 32km blast upstream in a jetboat. Along the way, our driver points out the remains of steel traps that local Maori once used to catch native longfin eels. Harder to spot are the holes gouged into the moss-covered gorge walls that were used as pivot points to haul their wooden canoes upstream.



After being dropped at Mangapurua Landing, we follow a 2.7km track through thick native bush to the much-photographed Bridge to Nowhere, a 40m-long concrete bridge built in the mid-1930s. Intended to provide better access for the returning World War I soldiers and their families trying to settle in the valley, the road project was abandoned in 1942 after most pioneers gave up due to the region’s remoteness and unforgiving terrain. By comparison, our return journey is a joy – a short jetboat ride followed by a 12km downstream kayak trip. Snaking through fern-draped mudstone gorges, we paddle past swallows, hawks and the occasional startled goat. During the trip expect to be serenaded by a chorus of moos, bleats and baas. There’s a sense of deja vu when we return to Pipiriki the following day. However, this time we’ve come armed with bikes. The plan is to ride south along the Whanganui River Road, an undulating sealed road that promises sweeping views of the river and the surrounding bush-covered hills. Unfortunately, the weather has other ideas – a strong headwind, persistent rain and several testing ascents make it a slog, even for those of us on e-bikes.



Although the grey skies mar the vistas, there are less grandiose distractions, such as the St Joseph’s Convent in the settlement of Jerusalem, whose wooden mailbox simply reads “The Sisters”, plus a remote property whose apt moniker is “Middla Nowhere”. Our destination is Whanganui, a coastal city that flies under the tourist radar despite being New Zealand’s only UNESCO City of Design – a designation it earned in 2021 for its thriving creative community. The itinerary only has us staying here one night, but it turns into two because of the ferocious storm that hits the North Island that night, triggering a state of emergency. Although the guides make a spirited attempt to drive us to the next accommodation, we’re eventually foiled by fallen trees and have to turn back. Meal stops are a highlight and an opportunity to fuel up for the next cycling stage. While Adventure South’s back-office team scrambles to find us alternative digs, we explore Whanganui’s many cultural delights, which include the excellent Te Whare o Rehua Sarjeant Gallery and the nearby Whanganui Regional Museum. Both are so compelling that the guides will recommend including them on future departures.



When we wake the following day to bright sunshine and blue skies, it’s as if it was all just a bad dream. We’re back on track – sort of. Road closures mean we can’t cycle the original route, but the guides pivot admirably and find us a scenic 36km alternative between the villages of Kiwitea and Kimbolton. Kimbolton’s noteworthy distinction is that it claims to have New Zealand’s smallest public library – a humble weatherboard shack so diminutive that at first I struggle to find it. From here we push on to our next accommodation, the gorgeous Makoura Lodge, a high country station the same family has owned for more than 125 years. When we arrive, there’s no power thanks to last night’s storm, but our hosts limp on with generators and still produce a sensational dinner of tender lamb shank followed by a lavish dessert platter of mini brownies, meringues and cheesecakes. Related Article New Zealand Most people do this NZ trip for the views. I had a different motive Our last day is a cracker – a delightful romp on quiet country lanes through a rumpled landscape of plunging valleys and grassy knolls. We cycle through pungent clouds of eau de farmyard, watch butterflies pirouette across our handlebars, and are frequently serenaded by a chorus of moos, bleats and baas. After rendezvousing with the support van for morning tea – a sumptuous roadside picnic of fruit, nuts and camembert shared with three inquisitive chickens – we turn on to a deserted gravel track for the final 11km push to Mangaweka, from where we’ll drive back to Taupo.



All in all, it’s been a fascinating trip, not just because it explored a lesser-known region that deserves much more attention, but also because it took on an unexpectedly intrepid, expedition-like quality. At times like this, being on a guided tour with expert leaders and diligent back-office staff really pays off. And while the cycling was enjoyable (when we could do it), my abiding memories will be of the quirky rural communities that are so often bypassed for better-known destinations. Like Ohakune with its giant carrot and Kimbolton with its tiny library. And, of course, let’s not forget Taihape, which one day I will return to with the lightest, sleekest, most aerodynamic gumboot I can find. DETAILS Adventure South’s six-day Mt Ruapehu & the Three Rivers trip begins and ends in Taupo, from $NZ3895 ($3212) a person; you can bring your own bike or hire one for $NZ180 ($148); $NZ600 ($495) for an e-bike. See adventuresouth.co.nz; Air New Zealand flies to Taupo via Auckland. See airnewzealand.com.au; newzealand.com The writer was a guest of Tourism New Zealand and Adventure South
