World.title: ‘Jess we can’: Inside the room where Wilson made history
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Jess we can’: Inside the room where Wilson made history Annika Smethurst and Michael Bachelard November 28, 2026 — 11:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.08 % counted LNP 57 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 17 seats remaining

To ecstatic chants of “Jess we can,” Jess Wilson was greeted like a rock star when she descended into the ballroom of the Park Hyatt hotel to accept the accolades of party members and Melbourne’s business elite as premier elect of Victoria. The state’s first elected female leader and first millennial premier, Wilson chose the 1997 dance hit Sunchyme, to accompany her to the stage (lyrics: Hey mamama [hey]). Hundreds of the Liberal faithful pulled out their smartphones to film the moment. Liberal leader Jess Wilson celebrates an historic win with her husband Aaron Lane. Jason South Dressed in a cornflower blue blazer – a slight change-up from her usual royal blue – Wilson scored her biggest cheer when she declared Victoria was “back open for business”.



Melbourne’s business elites, out in big numbers for the return of the Liberals, were rapt. Related Article Victorian election Victorian election 2026 as it happened: Ben Carroll concedes as Labor’s vote collapses; Jess Wilson to become Victoria’s first elected female premier Spied in the crowd were retail titan Solomon Lew, former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg, long-time mining industry figure and former Reserve Bank member Hugh Morgan, businessman and philanthropist Ian Carson, Nina Kirby Aberdeen from the Village Roadshow family, and Melbourne-based financial executive Marcus Freeman. They were joined by business executive Jennifer Westacott – a former boss of Wilson – JB Hi-Fi chief executive Richard Murray and Jeff Kennett’s treasurer, Alan Stockdale. Late into the night, comedian and late-career anti-Labor figure Dave Hughes also slipped into the room. In a gesture to the 12, dark years in opposition, Wilson thanked each of her predecessors as opposition leader one by one. Brad Battin, Michael O’Brien, John Pesutto and Matthew Guy all received a shout-out to huge applause from the Liberal faithful.



Battin, on the panel for the Nine coverage, had tears in his eyes as he revealed how he pledged his allegiance to Wilson after she took the leadership from him a year ago. “I’ll do everything right,” Battin revealed he’d told her at the time. “I genuinely call Jess a friend. I’m so proud to see what she’s done … I can’t wait to work with her over the next four years.” Loading The catalogue of former Liberal leaders, more than anything else, was a reminder of the long, dark years under Daniel Andrews when it seemed they might never make it back into power. On Saturday night, Wilson breathed out and consigned that period decisively to history. “A lot has been said about the future of the Liberal Party,” she said. “Tonight we showed that those last rites were premature.”



The room breathed out with her. Editor's pick Analysis

Victorian election Labor’s faithful tried to tell the party it had lost its way. At this election, they stopped trying She promised to repay the trust invested in her – both by those who habitually voted Liberal and those who were doing it for the first time – with “the truth”. She wanted to be “the kind of premier who is honest from day one,” she said, to more applause. Earlier, the crowd had booed Senator Pauline Hanson as her speech was broadcast into the room, and there was also a ripple of boos when outgoing premier Ben Carroll recognised the traditional owners of the land he spoke from in his concession speech. The Liberal Party has vowed to abolish the Treaty negotiated by Labor with the state’s First Nations people. When Carroll congratulated Wilson on her victory at about 8.40pm, however, the boos turned to cheers. At around the same time, federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, made his appearance in the Hyatt hotel party.



The mood had been building since 7.40pm, when television networks started calling Coalition victories in multiple seats, and then overall. More than 300 people had poured into the Liberal Party’s city celebration by then, with the main ballroom erupting in cheers as large Liberal swings were shown on the screens. Deputy premier elect David Southwick celebrating the Coalition’s return to power on Saturday night at the Park Hyatt. Jason South The volume went up on the favoured TV coverage – provided by News24, the channel formerly known as Rupert Murdoch’s Sky News – and people started watching in earnest. The sense of inevitability about a Wilson election victory had infected the state on Saturday, and attendees at the East Melbourne party caught the bug. One Liberal elder – a former state minister who did not want to be identified – told The Age Wilson’s campaign had been perfect. He had been around booths during the day and that “on the ground, it was marvellous,” he said, because he was around “people who’ve made their mind up”.



“Very few people looked like they were still thinking about it … I just think there’s an overwhelming mood for change, and Jess has been such a cohesive and strong worker.” Related Article Victorian hot seats Victorian hot seats: ‘We beat them’: Shepparton mayor beats off One Nation threat A year ago, the 16 seats required to win majority government seemed almost insurmountable. By the time the Liberal faithful started watching the numbers fall their way, for the first time in a dozen years, that number suddenly started to feel insubstantial. The last time the Liberal Party won an election in this state it was 2010 – 16 years ago – and the leader was Ted Baillieu. His government lasted just one term. This time, under Wilson, hopes of much more have started to stir. And inside this ballroom in East Melbourne, this Liberal crowd could not be happier.

World.title: ‘Cult of the leader’: Labor powerbrokers sheet home disaster to one man – and it’s not Ben Carroll
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Cult of the leader’: Labor powerbrokers sheet home disaster to one man – and it’s not Ben Carroll Kieran Rooney November 28, 2026 — 11:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 58 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 16 seats remaining

Before the sun had set, Labor leaders were already reflecting on where the party had gone so wrong as the election was called for the Coalition within two hours of polls closing. Even though less than 30 per cent of the vote was counted in many seats by midnight, Premier Ben Carroll had already conceded the election to Liberal leader Jess Wilson by 8.30pm. Ben Carroll has conceded the Labor Party has a lot of listening to do. Luis Enrique Ascui He addressed the Labor faithful about 8.40pm. “Tonight has not been the night we were working towards,” he said. “I’ll always love our great state, no matter who leads it. Friends, this is a significant loss for Labor. It’s not the result we wanted, but it is the result we accept. As leader of the party, I take full responsibility. “Democracy is both beautiful and brutal,” he said. “Victorians have spoken, and their message is clear. They want change.”



Standing in the crowd, his emotional parents, Greg and Kay, watched as their son bade farewell to 12 years of Labor in devastating circumstances. Towards the end, his mother moved closer to the stage and looking proudly up at her son as he spoke, putting herself as close as possible in one of his most challenging moments. Ben Carroll’s parents, Greg and Kay, watched their son bow out graciously. Luis Enrique Ascui Even while projected to lose his own seat of Niddrie, Carroll made a final plea for party unity. “To the Victorians who did not vote Labor, we’ll spend the next four years working to rebuild your trust,” he said. “That starts with listening. There will be a lot of talking after this result, but right now, Labor needs to listen, and we need to listen as a united team, not a divided one.”



Most in the room had already resigned themselves to a Labor defeat, but in the front row, people still held back tears, particularly as Carroll spoke about Labor’s achievements for the Indigenous community, including signing a historic Treaty with Victoria’s First Peoples. One staffer, Lily, misty-eyed, told The Age she was inspired by his comments. “I’m thinking of all my colleagues and our friends across the state who have worked really, really hard, and it is not easy,” she said. “We are keeping our head high.” Labor supporters held back tears as the departing premier addressed them for the last time. Luis Enrique Ascui Although Carroll was true to form and spoke haltingly at times, the crowd burst into laughter when he let his personality shine through – making fun of his own love of books about US political figures and talking with adoration about his wife Fiona and daughter Madeleine. The Buckley Park Bowls Club was largely full of local branch members, including staunch diehards also draped in Essendon gear. One member yelled out “thank you, Ben” with genuine gratitude as he spoke about his local achievements.



Always nearby were close confidants Bassel Tallal, Mounir Kiwan, Phil Dalidakis, Ari Suss and former Bracks speechwriter Joel Deane. Related Article Victorian election The seats that changed hands: Premier ousted, ministers wiped out in historic Labor rout Even before Carroll took to the podium, current and former MPs were also conceding publicly they had been seriously punished by the Victorian public and needed to do some serious soul-searching. “These sorts of results I think send a clear message, and they also give us cause to reflect on the lessons perhaps we should have taken from the 2022 result,” Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams said on the ABC. “I think there’s been a significant, entrenched erosion of the Labor vote for a significantly longer time.”



Amid a surging One Nation vote, Williams said Labor had assumed they could bank on the migrant vote, despite past stigmas surrounding One Nation. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election Labor’s faithful tried to tell the party it had lost its way. At this election, they stopped trying “There was certainly cohorts within our migrant communities that were definitely compelled by One Nation, and that was quite visible,” she said. “In my areas, I noticed it among established communities ... the older Greek and Italian communities, eastern European communities, there was a visible vote there.” She noted Carroll was set to lose his seat in parliament.



“From a personal perspective, I feel for Ben,” Williams said. “He’s one of the most decent human beings I’ve ever known in my life. I’ve known Ben for over 20 years.” Former federal opposition leader Bill Shorten was less diplomatic on Channel Seven. He labelled the government under Dan Andrews’ leadership a “Stalinist outfit”. “If you wanted to disagree with the leader, you were put in the freezer,” Shorten said.



“The reality is, where you have a political party where we’ve got this cult of the leader, and the rank and file get ignored, and you don’t have preselections, and everything’s done through a deal, the danger you create is that if the leader makes the wrong call, there’s no one to tell them they’re wrong.” “All political parties have suffered from it, but for me, what’s important is the Labor Party tomorrow morning says we’re going to go back to listening to the people rather than top-down dictatorships.” Minister for Jobs, Industry and Advanced Manufacturing Melissa Horne defended Andrews, saying that while he had a “very strong, domineering personality”, Victoria needed “that sort of leadership during the pandemic because it was unprecedented times”. Steve Dimopoulos, who until Saturday was Victoria’s Sports Minister, apologised to Victoria.



“I’m sorry we weren’t good enough for you to vote for us, that’s a sincere apology,” he said, his voice breaking. Loading “I was very concerned and upset and hurt that often second-generation Greek migrants weren’t taking Labor, they were taking One Nation or Liberal,” he said. He added: “The reality is, I don’t think we clearly offered a package, platform or pathway, for these people, that they found compelling to re-elect us.” He briefly mentioned tax settings and small business.



“This is a terrible result for Labor. It’s heart-wrenching for our volunteers, members. We clearly did not address what they wanted, not just in our campaign but also our term.” The initially upbeat atmosphere at the election night party plunged dramatically as the ABC called the election for the Coalition. While few in the room were expecting Labor to win, the reality of the loss sunk in as the result was called, and the music was turned down and the chatter subsided. Some volunteers in red shirts hugged each other as they gathered around the TV – but the drinks kept flowing and the crowd largely appeared to have accepted the result ahead of time. Most people had left 20 minutes after Carroll finished speaking. In stark contrast to the Coalition’s more glamorous event at the Park Hyatt, a dozen bowls regulars were still finishing off their mid-strength beers in the adjoining room before heading home as red-shirted Labor faithful filed in. One exiting patron remarked to a security guard, “You’re in for an interesting night, and potentially a very lonely one.”

World.title: One Nation defiant, ebullient, but lower house seats still a tall order
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election One Nation defiant, ebullient, but lower house seats still a tall order Stephen Brook November 28, 2026 — 11:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 58 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 16 seats remaining

One Nation began its celebratory speeches at its election night party with an attack on The Age, after this newspaper urged readers to vote against the conservative party. “To the editor of The Age – you can go and get stuffed,” said One Nation upper house candidate Mark Nicholson, who also creates the party’s controversial cartoons. One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering celebrates the party’s strong performance with Senator Pauline Hanson. Joe Armao He had just read out part of The Age’s editorial column in scathing tones.“If you are tempted to support One Nation on Saturday, The Age urges you to reconsider your vote,” the editorial read. One Nation federal leader Pauline Hanson entered to cheers from supporters and to the strains of Thunderstruck by AC/DC along with state president Warren Pickering, Liberal Party defector Colleen Harkin and federal MP Barnaby Joyce.



“I’ve had some very proud moments in my life, but I don’t think there’s ever anything that has surpassed this,” Hanson said. Loading She praised Pickering for taking the leadership role and alluded to the allegations from his ex-partner that led him to admit previous drug and alcohol abuse. “I’ve seen him grow over a period of time. And the media were like a pack of wolves, ready to tear him down,” Hanson said as she was drowned out by cheers. Hanson acknowledged the many multicultural supporters in the crowd.



“Those people who have chosen to make Australia their home, we welcome you with open arms so long as you respect and love this nation. Related Article Victorian election ‘Most of the Sri Lankan community are for One Nation’: The unlikely voters supporting Hanson “This nation is about bringing Australians together, that’s what it is all about.” Sri Lankan One Nation supporter Lalin De Silva, whom The Age previously profiled, said at the party he was feeling “very invigorated”. “This is a platform we have laid to win the federal election,” he said. “We have come second today. There is no reason we cannot come first in 2028.”



As early poll results suggested a strong showing for One Nation, Pickering was ebullient – but not counting his chickens just yet. At about 8pm, chants of “Aussie Aussie Aussie, oi oi oi” rang out, after Pickering told supporters at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre: “Let’s watch this state get taken back into the hands of the conservatives, whatever the disposition of parliament.” Warren Pickering was ebullient but careful not to pre-empt results. Joe Armao Although multiple lower house seats were three-cornered contests that were too close to call, including his own seat of Pakenham, Pickering’s party was on a 22 per cent primary vote overall. “Whatever the outcome tonight, One Nation Victoria is part of the permanent political landscape,” he told his supporters. “And this is another step on the road to New South Wales and the orange wave that is going to sweep federal parliament.”



One unexpected federal parliamentarian attending the party was Ralph Babet, federal senator for the United Australia Party. His presence sparked immediate speculation the senator for Clive Palmer’s party was thinking about defecting to Pauline Hanson’s party. “I support One Nation, I love what they are doing,” said Babet, who previously announced that he would not recontest the next federal election. My values are very much aligned to One Nation – that is Australia first, that is looking after the people or our country before any other country. That is limited government, that is free speech. That is fiscal responsibility. The Liberal Party pretends it is those things, but it is not.” But Babet, accompanied by his brother, confirmed he intended to leave parliament at the next federal election. “There are no plans at all for me to move across to One Nation.” Guests listened to a string of retro top-40 hits, including Kylie Minogue and The Human League, enjoying a free bar and catering, including duck spring rolls.



Federal director James Ashby said he had flown in on One Nation’s aircraft at 2.30am on Saturday morning. He arrived accompanying recently defected Liberal federal senator Leah Blyth. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election The Coalition’s historic win is one of width – not depth One Nation lower house MP Barnaby Joyce said Labor’s failings in Victoria had led to this result. “It is the worst government in the 60,000 years of human habitation on the Australian continent,” he said, pointing out the difficulty that presented itself to the conservative party in the vote count. “Labor doing poorly in the primary helps the Liberal Party massively.” As for federal implications, the former Nationals MP said the result pointed to unpredictability. “It will reinforce the febrile nature of politics in Australia. There’s more people on the charcuterie board than there was before. And people are going to eat all sorts of things.”



Less than one hour later, a One Nation supporter was thrown to the ground after becoming unruly. A bald, bearded man had his orange One Nation T-shirt ripped off and was thrown to the ground in the foyer outside the function room by a man in a tan suit jacket before he helped to escort him from the centre. Loading Earlier in the day, Pickering acknowledged he had to secure the highest primary vote in Pakenham, otherwise the accumulation of preferences from the Greens, Labor, and the Liberal Party would be hard to beat. “As for the rest of the state, I know a lot of these three-way contests won’t go our way,” he said.



“I think there will definitely be some seats where One Nation’s leading on primary, but still doesn’t secure the seat.” One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering at a Pakenham polling centre with his daughter, Jhett. Joe Armao Handing out One Nation how-to-vote cards was Pickering’s daughter, Jhett. She rose to prominence after a press conference in September when the pair responded to allegations of drug and alcohol use made by Pickering’s former partner and Jhett’s mother, Jo Scott. “It was a bit weird,” said Jhett, a mechanical engineering student. “Honestly, all it did for me was make me feel disheartened for the media that put us in the position in the first place.”



Jhett said support for the party at the polling centre had been “massive”. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election Straightforward win or One Nation shock? The federal stakes in Victoria’s vote On Friday, party founder and federal senator Pauline Hanson toured Victorian Labor electorates, including Mill Park in Melbourne’s north, aboard a chartered bus that was painted in the party colours of orange and emblazoned with the slogan, “Labor’s Farewell Tour”, which turned out to be prescient. The party promised to recreate an online real-time government expenditure tracker to monitor government spending but refused to allow its policies to be budgeted by the Parliamentary Budget Office. The party claimed “the books are cooked” and said accurate costings would only be possible after the election when the true state of the budget became known.

World.title: ‘It’s a Green wave baby!’: Could the Greens form opposition?
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘It’s a Green wave baby!’: Could the Greens form opposition? Angus Delaney and Cara Waters November 28, 2026 — 10:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 58 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 16 seats remaining

The Greens have made major gains and are likely to win a swag of seats across the inner city, riding a wave of anti-Labor sentiment and giving themselves a chance to form opposition in the next parliament. At about 10pm, Nine had called five seats for the Greens, and the party had established a strong position in other seats once considered safe Labor territory. With nearly a quarter of all votes counted, the Greens recorded a 15.7 per cent primary vote, up 4.2 percentage points on their 2022 result. Greens leader Ellen Sandell speaks to attendees at the party’s post-election function. Elke Meitzel Speaking to the party faithful at an election event in Docklands, Greens leader Ellen Sandell said “this is a turning point”. “We have at least doubled our numbers in the parliament,” she said. “This is a turning point in the Green movement and in politics as a result. What we have seen tonight here in Victoria is the crumbling of the two-party system.



“We have won more seats than One Nation. It is wild the number of seats we are still in the hunt for.” Greens candidate Campbell Gome unseated Labor incumbent Kat Theophanous in Northcote, polling 64.6 per cent of the two-party-preferred vote shortly before 10pm. Labor clung to the seat in 2022 by less than 200 votes, and it was one of the first seats to fall on Saturday night. In Pascoe Vale, former local mayor Angelica Panopoulos unseated incumbent Anthony Cianflone, recording a two-party-preferred vote of 55.3 per cent by 10pm. In Footscray, Greens candidate Elena Pereyra beat Labor incumbent Katie Hall. Pereyra, a former councillor who contested the seat in 2022, campaigned on a cost of living, climate and anti-data centre platform.



The count in Footscray, which Labor has held for 99 years, will be complicated, with 15 candidates on the ballot paper and preferences set to play a major role. The Greens are also in a strong position in Richmond – which it won in 2022 – and is a chance in Preston and Prahran. The 23 per cent of votes counted so far do not include postal votes, which tend to skew conservative and could threaten the Greens’ early success. But with Labor suffering a 19.4 per cent hit to its primary vote, it raises the prospect of the Greens forming the next opposition. Greens leader Ellen Sandell votes in Kensington. Ruby Alexander



“It’s possible,” said federal Greens senator Barbara Pocock. She said the Victorian election was a “disaster” for Labor, and the Greens were ready to step up. “I have real, real confidence,” she said. “We’ll possibly have some significant increase in numbers and some new people who aren’t experienced, but that’s exciting, and I think our policy offering was really clear, and people have responded to hope and a progressive vision.” Deputy leader of the Victorian Greens Sarah Mansfield wouldn’t be drawn on the prospect of forming opposition when pressed on the ABC. “Let’s see what happens,” she said. Former Victorian Greens upper house MP and political consultant Nina Springle said it was too early to tell, but “if it continues on the trajectory that is has been all evening, [forming opposition is] absolutely possible”.



But Springle said if the Greens wanted to be a “real replacement for Labor” they needed to broaden their appeal to voters outside the inner city by listening to suburban voters. Related Article Victorian election The accidental leader who negotiates with the premier and nude toddlers “To be a true opposition they’d definitely need to look to having a strong presence in the suburbs in a more substantial and enduring way.” City of Yarra Greens councillor Sophie Wade said the party was a strong contender to forming the new opposition instead of Labor. “We’ve got Ellen Sandell as a leader,” Wade said. “We saw what she could do the other night on the debate stage. She is absolutely up for being leader of the opposition, much more so than who we’ve seen recently.”



Wade said seats were in contention for the Greens that had never been on the radar before like Bellarine, near Geelong. “I can’t wait to see the world where Ellen is the leader of the opposition,” Wade said. “I think that’s really exciting, I would welcome Victorians having a Green opposition.” Stephen Donnelly, former assistant secretary for Victorian Labor, said the shifting demographics of inner-city voters would threaten Labor’s hold, including in seats like Preston. “The Greens are putting up a serious challenge. They are upbeat about winning the electorate,” Donnelly said on the pro-Labor Socially Democratic podcast live show. “But [suburbs] like Preston and Thornbury are also gentrifying … therefore making it far more challenging for Labor to hold the seat of Preston.”



Earlier on Saturday night Sandell said winning five lower house seats and making gains in the upper house would “be a record for the Greens”. “It’s pretty extraordinary to even have the Greens competitive in places that are further out from the city, but we’ll just have to see what happens tonight.” There was a festive atmosphere at the Greens election party at the Mission for Seafarers in Docklands, with volunteers and party members clad in various permutations of green. “It’s a Green wave baby,” one volunteer said as positive results trickled in.



Sandell said despite the election of a conservative, Coalition government, the result was not an endorsement of the Liberals’ plans. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Nearly half a million voters abandon Labor as party’s support crashes to new low “I think it’s more a rejection of Labor that’s moved away from their values, and a rejection of politics in general that hasn’t been working for people,” she says. “The Greens will be more important than ever if there is a Liberal government. We will be a very strong opposition to some of their worst plans to sell off our sewerage, to rip up treaty, to rip up renewable energy, to cut jobs, and I hope that we will be that bright spark of hope in the parliament for progressives and that strong opposition.” Sandell also had to address an awkward moment when casting her vote on Saturday morning. Sandell posed for photos while making her vote, displaying her ballot paper which showed the Greens leader went against the party’s own how-to-vote card.



Sandell had preferenced the Animal Justice Party’s Naomi Jones third, despite her how-to-vote cards instructing voters to place independent Mohamed Yusuf in that position. The ballot she cast on Saturday also had Labor’s Davydd Griffiths in fourth, while her how-to-vote card had him further down the ticket at fifth. Sandell said she preferenced the Animal Justice party higher than they were on the Greens how to vote cards because they aligned with her values. “I was trying to wrangle my four-year-old, and I probably should have actually folded it [my paper] up, but look, we always tell people to preference according to their values,” Sandell says. Read more on the Victorian election: Analysis: Labor’s faithful tried to tell the party it had lost its way. At this election, they stopped trying

World.title: The seats that changed hands: Premier ousted, ministers wiped out in historic Labor rout
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election The seats that changed hands: Premier ousted, ministers wiped out in historic Labor rout James Costa November 29, 2026 — 12:16am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 57 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 17 seats remaining

After 12 years in power, the unprecedented rejection of the Labor Party has been characterised by the loss of about a dozen previously safe seats, and significant losses in other marginal electorates. But while the upstart One Nation was meant to clean up, this masthead has so far not called any seats for the party, leaving the Victorian leader Warren Pickering without a seat. Loading In one of the most significant swings and in a shattering defeat, the outgoing Premier Ben Carroll has lost his seat of Niddrie with a swing of more than 18 per cent to the Liberal Party’s Samantha Byrne. “This is a significant loss for Labor,” Carroll said of the loss of government in his concession speech. “As leader of the party, I take full responsibility.”



A sitting premier losing their seat is a feat that, in recent history at least, has only been accomplished by 51-day Victorian premier Ian MacFarlan, the member for Brighton in 1945. The reason behind MacFarlan’s short premiership is a bit confusing: he was expelled from the Liberal Party for striking a deal with the Country Party to form a stop-gap government to secure a supply bill in October 1945, making him a premier without a party. In the November election of that year, MacFarlan lost his seat. It has not been a good night in the seats of two other former Labor premiers, either. Carroll was only premier for four months, replacing Jacinta Allan. The former premier opted not to contest her Bendigo East seat, held by Labor since 1999, and it was won by Nationals candidate Andrew Lethlean.



Labor has also lost former premier Daniel Andrews’ seat of Mulgrave to the Liberals’ Charles Tran. It’s a little reminiscent of the 2025 federal election, when former Greens leader Adam Bandt lost his supposedly safe seat of Melbourne to Labor, and when former Liberal Party MP and opposition leader Peter Dutton was rejected not only as the alternative prime minister but also as the member for Dickson in Queensland. The Coalition hadn’t won a seat north or west of the Yarra since 1996. That drought has ended, with the Liberals gaining Yan Yean, Sydenham, Bundoora, and Macedon among others. Elsewhere, the Liberals have picked up Frankston, Mordialloc, Carrum and Bentleigh, unseating four senior Labor ministers: Paul Edbrooke, Tim Richardson, Sonya Kilkenny and Nick Staikos. Here are the changing seats The Age has called in the 2026 Victorian election so far.

The Greens have claimed victory in what was previously Labor heartland of Footscray, catapulting Elena Pereya into parliament.

Pereya took to the stage at 11.30pm at the Greens election party to huge applause.

Supporters celebrate at the election night event for The Greens. Elke Meitzel

“Footscray has been the dumping ground for Labor’s worst ideas,” Pereya said, in what was likely a reference to the construction of data centres in the area.

“For a long time, it’s been a cautionary tale of what you don’t do everywhere else, and now it’s a cautionary tale for Labor to not take people for granted because they have chosen hope and prosperity and a hopeful future.”

With 58 per cent of votes counted, Elena Pereyra had polled 62.1 per cent of the two-candidate-preferred vote, ahead of Labor’s Katie Hall on 37.9 per cent. That represents a 16.4 per cent swing towards the Greens.

Pereya said she was proud to be the next Green MP for Footscray and thanked the many people who had worked on her campaign. She said key issues for the electorate had been data centres, housing, transport, cycling infrastructure and air quality.

World.title: The overlooked corner of New Zealand that deserves a detour
World.content:
InspirationNew Zealand The overlooked corner of New Zealand that deserves a detour Rob McFarland November 29, 2026 — 12:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Given all the uncertainty in the world, you’d think that New Zealand would be a safe bet for a holiday: stable government, no snakes, decent coffee. However, it still has weather, and halfway through a six-day Adventure South cycle trip on the North Island, the storm gods throw a tantrum, unleashing 170 millimetres of rain and 130km/h winds. Not ideal for biking. Crossing the Bridge to Nowhere in Whanganui National Park. Until then, things had been going swimmingly. After meeting in Taupo, our group of nine cyclists and two guides, one of whom is a retired meteorologist (a good omen, surely?), drives two hours south to the small town of Taihape. Taihape is known as the Gumboot Capital of New Zealand, a title it has earned thanks to its annual gumboot throwing competition in March. Naturally, this is something we need to try, particularly when our lead guide, Robyn Marchant, tells us that on last year’s tour, a woman managed 22 metres using a bright pink Barbie boot.



I have many excuses as to why I only manage a paltry 17 metres, but more impressive is that the Taihape record is a frankly staggering 48.65 metres, held by New Zealand’s undisputed gumboot hurling king, Kieran Fowler from Dunedin. 



Our base for the next two nights is the lovely Powderhorn Chateau, a wood-panelled, chalet-style property in Ohakune. A popular winter base for the ski fields at nearby Mount Ruapehu, the town’s other claim to fame is that it is New Zealand’s Carrot Capital, a self-bestowed title in honour of its prodigious carrot production. Not to be outdone by the giant corrugated iron gumboot that welcomes visitors to Taihape, Ohakune has not only erected a 7.5m-high carrot (voted New Zealand’s 2023 Landmark of the Year), but also created an adorable vegetable-themed sculpture park featuring, among others, a supersized Brussels sprout called Sir Lancelot. From pedal to paddle power on the Whanganui River. The following day, we ditch the bikes to explore one of the region’s natural and historical treasures – the Whanganui River. In 2017, it famously became the world’s first river to be granted legal personhood, recognising its deep spiritual significance for the region’s Maori, who regard it as an ancestor. After driving to the small riverside settlement of Pipiriki, our adventure begins with an exhilarating 32km blast upstream in a jetboat. Along the way, our driver points out the remains of steel traps that local Maori once used to catch native longfin eels. Harder to spot are the holes gouged into the moss-covered gorge walls that were used as pivot points to haul their wooden canoes upstream.



After being dropped at Mangapurua Landing, we follow a 2.7km track through thick native bush to the much-photographed Bridge to Nowhere, a 40m-long concrete bridge built in the mid-1930s. Intended to provide better access for the returning World War I soldiers and their families trying to settle in the valley, the road project was abandoned in 1942 after most pioneers gave up due to the region’s remoteness and unforgiving terrain. By comparison, our return journey is a joy – a short jetboat ride followed by a 12km downstream kayak trip. Snaking through fern-draped mudstone gorges, we paddle past swallows, hawks and the occasional startled goat. During the trip expect to be serenaded by a chorus of moos, bleats and baas. There’s a sense of deja vu when we return to Pipiriki the following day. However, this time we’ve come armed with bikes. The plan is to ride south along the Whanganui River Road, an undulating sealed road that promises sweeping views of the river and the surrounding bush-covered hills. Unfortunately, the weather has other ideas – a strong headwind, persistent rain and several testing ascents make it a slog, even for those of us on e-bikes.



Although the grey skies mar the vistas, there are less grandiose distractions, such as the St Joseph’s Convent in the settlement of Jerusalem, whose wooden mailbox simply reads “The Sisters”, plus a remote property whose apt moniker is “Middla Nowhere”. Our destination is Whanganui, a coastal city that flies under the tourist radar despite being New Zealand’s only UNESCO City of Design – a designation it earned in 2021 for its thriving creative community. The itinerary only has us staying here one night, but it turns into two because of the ferocious storm that hits the North Island that night, triggering a state of emergency. Although the guides make a spirited attempt to drive us to the next accommodation, we’re eventually foiled by fallen trees and have to turn back. Meal stops are a highlight and an opportunity to fuel up for the next cycling stage. While Adventure South’s back-office team scrambles to find us alternative digs, we explore Whanganui’s many cultural delights, which include the excellent Te Whare o Rehua Sarjeant Gallery and the nearby Whanganui Regional Museum. Both are so compelling that the guides will recommend including them on future departures.



When we wake the following day to bright sunshine and blue skies, it’s as if it was all just a bad dream. We’re back on track – sort of. Road closures mean we can’t cycle the original route, but the guides pivot admirably and find us a scenic 36km alternative between the villages of Kiwitea and Kimbolton. Kimbolton’s noteworthy distinction is that it claims to have New Zealand’s smallest public library – a humble weatherboard shack so diminutive that at first I struggle to find it. From here we push on to our next accommodation, the gorgeous Makoura Lodge, a high country station the same family has owned for more than 125 years. When we arrive, there’s no power thanks to last night’s storm, but our hosts limp on with generators and still produce a sensational dinner of tender lamb shank followed by a lavish dessert platter of mini brownies, meringues and cheesecakes. Related Article New Zealand Most people do this NZ trip for the views. I had a different motive Our last day is a cracker – a delightful romp on quiet country lanes through a rumpled landscape of plunging valleys and grassy knolls. We cycle through pungent clouds of eau de farmyard, watch butterflies pirouette across our handlebars, and are frequently serenaded by a chorus of moos, bleats and baas. After rendezvousing with the support van for morning tea – a sumptuous roadside picnic of fruit, nuts and camembert shared with three inquisitive chickens – we turn on to a deserted gravel track for the final 11km push to Mangaweka, from where we’ll drive back to Taupo.



All in all, it’s been a fascinating trip, not just because it explored a lesser-known region that deserves much more attention, but also because it took on an unexpectedly intrepid, expedition-like quality. At times like this, being on a guided tour with expert leaders and diligent back-office staff really pays off. And while the cycling was enjoyable (when we could do it), my abiding memories will be of the quirky rural communities that are so often bypassed for better-known destinations. Like Ohakune with its giant carrot and Kimbolton with its tiny library. And, of course, let’s not forget Taihape, which one day I will return to with the lightest, sleekest, most aerodynamic gumboot I can find. DETAILS Adventure South’s six-day Mt Ruapehu & the Three Rivers trip begins and ends in Taupo, from $NZ3895 ($3212) a person; you can bring your own bike or hire one for $NZ180 ($148); $NZ600 ($495) for an e-bike. See adventuresouth.co.nz; Air New Zealand flies to Taupo via Auckland. See airnewzealand.com.au; newzealand.com The writer was a guest of Tourism New Zealand and Adventure South

World.title: ‘Jess we can’: Inside the room where Wilson made history
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Jess we can’: Inside the room where Wilson made history Annika Smethurst and Michael Bachelard November 28, 2026 — 11:37pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 58 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 16 seats remaining

To ecstatic chants of “Jess we can,” Jess Wilson was greeted like a rock star when she descended into the ballroom of the Park Hyatt hotel to accept the accolades of party members and Melbourne’s business elite as premier elect of Victoria. The state’s first elected female leader and first millennial premier, Wilson chose the 1997 dance hit Sunchyme, to accompany her to the stage (lyrics: Hey mamama [hey]). Hundreds of the Liberal faithful pulled out their smartphones to film the moment. Liberal leader Jess Wilson celebrates an historic win with her husband Aaron Lane. Jason South Dressed in a cornflower blue blazer – a slight change-up from her usual royal blue – Wilson scored her biggest cheer when she declared Victoria was “back open for business”.



Melbourne’s business elites, out in big numbers for the return of the Liberals, were rapt. Related Article Victorian election Victorian election 2026 as it happened: Ben Carroll concedes as Labor’s vote collapses; Jess Wilson to become Victoria’s first elected female premier Spied in the crowd were retail titan Solomon Lew, former federal treasurer Josh Frydenberg, long-time mining industry figure and former Reserve Bank member Hugh Morgan, businessman and philanthropist Ian Carson, Nina Kirby Aberdeen from the Village Roadshow family, and Melbourne-based financial executive Marcus Freeman. They were joined by business executive Jennifer Westacott – a former boss of Wilson – JB Hi-Fi chief executive Richard Murray and Jeff Kennett’s treasurer, Alan Stockdale. Late into the night, comedian and late-career anti-Labor figure Dave Hughes also slipped into the room. In a gesture to the 12, dark years in opposition, Wilson thanked each of her predecessors as opposition leader one by one. Brad Battin, Michael O’Brien, John Pesutto and Matthew Guy all received a shout-out to huge applause from the Liberal faithful.



Battin, on the panel for the Nine coverage, had tears in his eyes as he revealed how he pledged his allegiance to Wilson after she took the leadership from him a year ago. “I’ll do everything right,” Battin revealed he’d told her at the time. “I genuinely call Jess a friend. I’m so proud to see what she’s done … I can’t wait to work with her over the next four years.” Loading The catalogue of former Liberal leaders, more than anything else, was a reminder of the long, dark years under Daniel Andrews when it seemed they might never make it back into power. On Saturday night, Wilson breathed out and consigned that period decisively to history. “A lot has been said about the future of the Liberal Party,” she said. “Tonight we showed that those last rites were premature.”



The room breathed out with her. Editor's pick Analysis

Victorian election Labor’s faithful tried to tell the party it had lost its way. At this election, they stopped trying She promised to repay the trust invested in her – both by those who habitually voted Liberal and those who were doing it for the first time – with “the truth”. She wanted to be “the kind of premier who is honest from day one,” she said, to more applause. Earlier, the crowd had booed Senator Pauline Hanson as her speech was broadcast into the room, and there was also a ripple of boos when outgoing premier Ben Carroll recognised the traditional owners of the land he spoke from in his concession speech. The Liberal Party has vowed to abolish the Treaty negotiated by Labor with the state’s First Nations people. When Carroll congratulated Wilson on her victory at about 8.40pm, however, the boos turned to cheers. At around the same time, federal Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, made his appearance in the Hyatt hotel party.



The mood had been building since 7.40pm, when television networks started calling Coalition victories in multiple seats, and then overall. More than 300 people had poured into the Liberal Party’s city celebration by then, with the main ballroom erupting in cheers as large Liberal swings were shown on the screens. Deputy premier elect David Southwick celebrating the Coalition’s return to power on Saturday night at the Park Hyatt. Jason South The volume went up on the favoured TV coverage – provided by News24, the channel formerly known as Rupert Murdoch’s Sky News – and people started watching in earnest. The sense of inevitability about a Wilson election victory had infected the state on Saturday, and attendees at the East Melbourne party caught the bug. One Liberal elder – a former state minister who did not want to be identified – told The Age Wilson’s campaign had been perfect. He had been around booths during the day and that “on the ground, it was marvellous,” he said, because he was around “people who’ve made their mind up”.



“Very few people looked like they were still thinking about it … I just think there’s an overwhelming mood for change, and Jess has been such a cohesive and strong worker.” Related Article Victorian hot seats Victorian hot seats: ‘We beat them’: Shepparton mayor beats off One Nation threat A year ago, the 16 seats required to win majority government seemed almost insurmountable. By the time the Liberal faithful started watching the numbers fall their way, for the first time in a dozen years, that number suddenly started to feel insubstantial. The last time the Liberal Party won an election in this state it was 2010 – 16 years ago – and the leader was Ted Baillieu. His government lasted just one term. This time, under Wilson, hopes of much more have started to stir. And inside this ballroom in East Melbourne, this Liberal crowd could not be happier.

World.title: ‘Cult of the leader’: Labor powerbrokers sheet home disaster to one man – and it’s not Ben Carroll
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘Cult of the leader’: Labor powerbrokers sheet home disaster to one man – and it’s not Ben Carroll Kieran Rooney November 28, 2026 — 11:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 58 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 16 seats remaining

Before the sun had set, Labor leaders were already reflecting on where the party had gone so wrong as the election was called for the Coalition within two hours of polls closing. Even though less than 30 per cent of the vote was counted in many seats by midnight, Premier Ben Carroll had already conceded the election to Liberal leader Jess Wilson by 8.30pm. Ben Carroll has conceded the Labor Party has a lot of listening to do. Luis Enrique Ascui He addressed the Labor faithful about 8.40pm. “Tonight has not been the night we were working towards,” he said. “I’ll always love our great state, no matter who leads it. Friends, this is a significant loss for Labor. It’s not the result we wanted, but it is the result we accept. As leader of the party, I take full responsibility. “Democracy is both beautiful and brutal,” he said. “Victorians have spoken, and their message is clear. They want change.”



Standing in the crowd, his emotional parents, Greg and Kay, watched as their son bade farewell to 12 years of Labor in devastating circumstances. Towards the end, his mother moved closer to the stage and looking proudly up at her son as he spoke, putting herself as close as possible in one of his most challenging moments. Ben Carroll’s parents, Greg and Kay, watched their son bow out graciously. Luis Enrique Ascui Even while projected to lose his own seat of Niddrie, Carroll made a final plea for party unity. “To the Victorians who did not vote Labor, we’ll spend the next four years working to rebuild your trust,” he said. “That starts with listening. There will be a lot of talking after this result, but right now, Labor needs to listen, and we need to listen as a united team, not a divided one.”



Most in the room had already resigned themselves to a Labor defeat, but in the front row, people still held back tears, particularly as Carroll spoke about Labor’s achievements for the Indigenous community, including signing a historic Treaty with Victoria’s First Peoples. One staffer, Lily, misty-eyed, told The Age she was inspired by his comments. “I’m thinking of all my colleagues and our friends across the state who have worked really, really hard, and it is not easy,” she said. “We are keeping our head high.” Labor supporters held back tears as the departing premier addressed them for the last time. Luis Enrique Ascui Although Carroll was true to form and spoke haltingly at times, the crowd burst into laughter when he let his personality shine through – making fun of his own love of books about US political figures and talking with adoration about his wife Fiona and daughter Madeleine. The Buckley Park Bowls Club was largely full of local branch members, including staunch diehards also draped in Essendon gear. One member yelled out “thank you, Ben” with genuine gratitude as he spoke about his local achievements.



Always nearby were close confidants Bassel Tallal, Mounir Kiwan, Phil Dalidakis, Ari Suss and former Bracks speechwriter Joel Deane. Related Article Victorian election The seats that changed hands: Premier ousted, ministers wiped out in historic Labor rout Even before Carroll took to the podium, current and former MPs were also conceding publicly they had been seriously punished by the Victorian public and needed to do some serious soul-searching. “These sorts of results I think send a clear message, and they also give us cause to reflect on the lessons perhaps we should have taken from the 2022 result,” Deputy Premier Gabrielle Williams said on the ABC. “I think there’s been a significant, entrenched erosion of the Labor vote for a significantly longer time.”



Amid a surging One Nation vote, Williams said Labor had assumed they could bank on the migrant vote, despite past stigmas surrounding One Nation. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election Labor’s faithful tried to tell the party it had lost its way. At this election, they stopped trying “There was certainly cohorts within our migrant communities that were definitely compelled by One Nation, and that was quite visible,” she said. “In my areas, I noticed it among established communities ... the older Greek and Italian communities, eastern European communities, there was a visible vote there.” She noted Carroll was set to lose his seat in parliament.



“From a personal perspective, I feel for Ben,” Williams said. “He’s one of the most decent human beings I’ve ever known in my life. I’ve known Ben for over 20 years.” Former federal opposition leader Bill Shorten was less diplomatic on Channel Seven. He labelled the government under Dan Andrews’ leadership a “Stalinist outfit”. “If you wanted to disagree with the leader, you were put in the freezer,” Shorten said.



“The reality is, where you have a political party where we’ve got this cult of the leader, and the rank and file get ignored, and you don’t have preselections, and everything’s done through a deal, the danger you create is that if the leader makes the wrong call, there’s no one to tell them they’re wrong.” “All political parties have suffered from it, but for me, what’s important is the Labor Party tomorrow morning says we’re going to go back to listening to the people rather than top-down dictatorships.” Minister for Jobs, Industry and Advanced Manufacturing Melissa Horne defended Andrews, saying that while he had a “very strong, domineering personality”, Victoria needed “that sort of leadership during the pandemic because it was unprecedented times”. Steve Dimopoulos, who until Saturday was Victoria’s Sports Minister, apologised to Victoria.



“I’m sorry we weren’t good enough for you to vote for us, that’s a sincere apology,” he said, his voice breaking. Loading “I was very concerned and upset and hurt that often second-generation Greek migrants weren’t taking Labor, they were taking One Nation or Liberal,” he said. He added: “The reality is, I don’t think we clearly offered a package, platform or pathway, for these people, that they found compelling to re-elect us.” He briefly mentioned tax settings and small business.



“This is a terrible result for Labor. It’s heart-wrenching for our volunteers, members. We clearly did not address what they wanted, not just in our campaign but also our term.” The initially upbeat atmosphere at the election night party plunged dramatically as the ABC called the election for the Coalition. While few in the room were expecting Labor to win, the reality of the loss sunk in as the result was called, and the music was turned down and the chatter subsided. Some volunteers in red shirts hugged each other as they gathered around the TV – but the drinks kept flowing and the crowd largely appeared to have accepted the result ahead of time. Most people had left 20 minutes after Carroll finished speaking. In stark contrast to the Coalition’s more glamorous event at the Park Hyatt, a dozen bowls regulars were still finishing off their mid-strength beers in the adjoining room before heading home as red-shirted Labor faithful filed in. One exiting patron remarked to a security guard, “You’re in for an interesting night, and potentially a very lonely one.”

World.title: One Nation defiant, ebullient, but lower house seats still a tall order
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election One Nation defiant, ebullient, but lower house seats still a tall order Stephen Brook November 28, 2026 — 11:26pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.73 % counted LNP 58 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 16 seats remaining

One Nation began its celebratory speeches at its election night party with an attack on The Age, after this newspaper urged readers to vote against the conservative party. “To the editor of The Age – you can go and get stuffed,” said One Nation upper house candidate Mark Nicholson, who also creates the party’s controversial cartoons. One Nation Victorian leader Warren Pickering celebrates the party’s strong performance with Senator Pauline Hanson. Joe Armao He had just read out part of The Age’s editorial column in scathing tones.“If you are tempted to support One Nation on Saturday, The Age urges you to reconsider your vote,” the editorial read. One Nation federal leader Pauline Hanson entered to cheers from supporters and to the strains of Thunderstruck by AC/DC along with state president Warren Pickering, Liberal Party defector Colleen Harkin and federal MP Barnaby Joyce.



“I’ve had some very proud moments in my life, but I don’t think there’s ever anything that has surpassed this,” Hanson said. Loading She praised Pickering for taking the leadership role and alluded to the allegations from his ex-partner that led him to admit previous drug and alcohol abuse. “I’ve seen him grow over a period of time. And the media were like a pack of wolves, ready to tear him down,” Hanson said as she was drowned out by cheers. Hanson acknowledged the many multicultural supporters in the crowd.



“Those people who have chosen to make Australia their home, we welcome you with open arms so long as you respect and love this nation. Related Article Victorian election ‘Most of the Sri Lankan community are for One Nation’: The unlikely voters supporting Hanson “This nation is about bringing Australians together, that’s what it is all about.” Sri Lankan One Nation supporter Lalin De Silva, whom The Age previously profiled, said at the party he was feeling “very invigorated”. “This is a platform we have laid to win the federal election,” he said. “We have come second today. There is no reason we cannot come first in 2028.”



As early poll results suggested a strong showing for One Nation, Pickering was ebullient – but not counting his chickens just yet. At about 8pm, chants of “Aussie Aussie Aussie, oi oi oi” rang out, after Pickering told supporters at the Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre: “Let’s watch this state get taken back into the hands of the conservatives, whatever the disposition of parliament.” Warren Pickering was ebullient but careful not to pre-empt results. Joe Armao Although multiple lower house seats were three-cornered contests that were too close to call, including his own seat of Pakenham, Pickering’s party was on a 22 per cent primary vote overall. “Whatever the outcome tonight, One Nation Victoria is part of the permanent political landscape,” he told his supporters. “And this is another step on the road to New South Wales and the orange wave that is going to sweep federal parliament.”



One unexpected federal parliamentarian attending the party was Ralph Babet, federal senator for the United Australia Party. His presence sparked immediate speculation the senator for Clive Palmer’s party was thinking about defecting to Pauline Hanson’s party. “I support One Nation, I love what they are doing,” said Babet, who previously announced that he would not recontest the next federal election. My values are very much aligned to One Nation – that is Australia first, that is looking after the people or our country before any other country. That is limited government, that is free speech. That is fiscal responsibility. The Liberal Party pretends it is those things, but it is not.” But Babet, accompanied by his brother, confirmed he intended to leave parliament at the next federal election. “There are no plans at all for me to move across to One Nation.” Guests listened to a string of retro top-40 hits, including Kylie Minogue and The Human League, enjoying a free bar and catering, including duck spring rolls.



Federal director James Ashby said he had flown in on One Nation’s aircraft at 2.30am on Saturday morning. He arrived accompanying recently defected Liberal federal senator Leah Blyth. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election The Coalition’s historic win is one of width – not depth One Nation lower house MP Barnaby Joyce said Labor’s failings in Victoria had led to this result. “It is the worst government in the 60,000 years of human habitation on the Australian continent,” he said, pointing out the difficulty that presented itself to the conservative party in the vote count. “Labor doing poorly in the primary helps the Liberal Party massively.” As for federal implications, the former Nationals MP said the result pointed to unpredictability. “It will reinforce the febrile nature of politics in Australia. There’s more people on the charcuterie board than there was before. And people are going to eat all sorts of things.”



Less than one hour later, a One Nation supporter was thrown to the ground after becoming unruly. A bald, bearded man had his orange One Nation T-shirt ripped off and was thrown to the ground in the foyer outside the function room by a man in a tan suit jacket before he helped to escort him from the centre. Loading Earlier in the day, Pickering acknowledged he had to secure the highest primary vote in Pakenham, otherwise the accumulation of preferences from the Greens, Labor, and the Liberal Party would be hard to beat. “As for the rest of the state, I know a lot of these three-way contests won’t go our way,” he said.



“I think there will definitely be some seats where One Nation’s leading on primary, but still doesn’t secure the seat.” One Nation’s Victorian leader Warren Pickering at a Pakenham polling centre with his daughter, Jhett. Joe Armao Handing out One Nation how-to-vote cards was Pickering’s daughter, Jhett. She rose to prominence after a press conference in September when the pair responded to allegations of drug and alcohol use made by Pickering’s former partner and Jhett’s mother, Jo Scott. “It was a bit weird,” said Jhett, a mechanical engineering student. “Honestly, all it did for me was make me feel disheartened for the media that put us in the position in the first place.”



Jhett said support for the party at the polling centre had been “massive”. Related Article Analysis

Victorian election Straightforward win or One Nation shock? The federal stakes in Victoria’s vote On Friday, party founder and federal senator Pauline Hanson toured Victorian Labor electorates, including Mill Park in Melbourne’s north, aboard a chartered bus that was painted in the party colours of orange and emblazoned with the slogan, “Labor’s Farewell Tour”, which turned out to be prescient. The party promised to recreate an online real-time government expenditure tracker to monitor government spending but refused to allow its policies to be budgeted by the Parliamentary Budget Office. The party claimed “the books are cooked” and said accurate costings would only be possible after the election when the true state of the budget became known.

World.title: ‘It’s a Green wave baby!’: Could the Greens form opposition?
World.content:
PoliticsVictoriaVictorian election ‘It’s a Green wave baby!’: Could the Greens form opposition? Angus Delaney and Cara Waters November 28, 2026 — 10:45pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

VIC election 2026 Full election results 48.08 % counted LNP 57 Tick ALP 7 GRN 6 IND 1 ON 0 OTH 0 45 seats needed for a majority Hemicycle 17 seats remaining

The Greens have made major gains and are likely to win a swag of seats across the inner city, riding a wave of anti-Labor sentiment and giving themselves a chance to form opposition in the next parliament. At about 10pm, Nine had called five seats for the Greens, and the party had established a strong position in other seats once considered safe Labor territory. With nearly a quarter of all votes counted, the Greens recorded a 15.7 per cent primary vote, up 4.2 percentage points on their 2022 result. Greens leader Ellen Sandell speaks to attendees at the party’s post-election function. Elke Meitzel Speaking to the party faithful at an election event in Docklands, Greens leader Ellen Sandell said “this is a turning point”. “We have at least doubled our numbers in the parliament,” she said. “This is a turning point in the Green movement and in politics as a result. What we have seen tonight here in Victoria is the crumbling of the two-party system.



“We have won more seats than One Nation. It is wild the number of seats we are still in the hunt for.” Greens candidate Campbell Gome unseated Labor incumbent Kat Theophanous in Northcote, polling 64.6 per cent of the two-party-preferred vote shortly before 10pm. Labor clung to the seat in 2022 by less than 200 votes, and it was one of the first seats to fall on Saturday night. In Pascoe Vale, former local mayor Angelica Panopoulos unseated incumbent Anthony Cianflone, recording a two-party-preferred vote of 55.3 per cent by 10pm. In Footscray, Greens candidate Elena Pereyra beat Labor incumbent Katie Hall. Pereyra, a former councillor who contested the seat in 2022, campaigned on a cost of living, climate and anti-data centre platform.



The count in Footscray, which Labor has held for 99 years, will be complicated, with 15 candidates on the ballot paper and preferences set to play a major role. The Greens are also in a strong position in Richmond – which it won in 2022 – and is a chance in Preston and Prahran. The 23 per cent of votes counted so far do not include postal votes, which tend to skew conservative and could threaten the Greens’ early success. But with Labor suffering a 19.4 per cent hit to its primary vote, it raises the prospect of the Greens forming the next opposition. Greens leader Ellen Sandell votes in Kensington. Ruby Alexander



“It’s possible,” said federal Greens senator Barbara Pocock. She said the Victorian election was a “disaster” for Labor, and the Greens were ready to step up. “I have real, real confidence,” she said. “We’ll possibly have some significant increase in numbers and some new people who aren’t experienced, but that’s exciting, and I think our policy offering was really clear, and people have responded to hope and a progressive vision.” Deputy leader of the Victorian Greens Sarah Mansfield wouldn’t be drawn on the prospect of forming opposition when pressed on the ABC. “Let’s see what happens,” she said. Former Victorian Greens upper house MP and political consultant Nina Springle said it was too early to tell, but “if it continues on the trajectory that is has been all evening, [forming opposition is] absolutely possible”.



But Springle said if the Greens wanted to be a “real replacement for Labor” they needed to broaden their appeal to voters outside the inner city by listening to suburban voters. Related Article Victorian election The accidental leader who negotiates with the premier and nude toddlers “To be a true opposition they’d definitely need to look to having a strong presence in the suburbs in a more substantial and enduring way.” City of Yarra Greens councillor Sophie Wade said the party was a strong contender to forming the new opposition instead of Labor. “We’ve got Ellen Sandell as a leader,” Wade said. “We saw what she could do the other night on the debate stage. She is absolutely up for being leader of the opposition, much more so than who we’ve seen recently.”



Wade said seats were in contention for the Greens that had never been on the radar before like Bellarine, near Geelong. “I can’t wait to see the world where Ellen is the leader of the opposition,” Wade said. “I think that’s really exciting, I would welcome Victorians having a Green opposition.” Stephen Donnelly, former assistant secretary for Victorian Labor, said the shifting demographics of inner-city voters would threaten Labor’s hold, including in seats like Preston. “The Greens are putting up a serious challenge. They are upbeat about winning the electorate,” Donnelly said on the pro-Labor Socially Democratic podcast live show. “But [suburbs] like Preston and Thornbury are also gentrifying … therefore making it far more challenging for Labor to hold the seat of Preston.”



Earlier on Saturday night Sandell said winning five lower house seats and making gains in the upper house would “be a record for the Greens”. “It’s pretty extraordinary to even have the Greens competitive in places that are further out from the city, but we’ll just have to see what happens tonight.” There was a festive atmosphere at the Greens election party at the Mission for Seafarers in Docklands, with volunteers and party members clad in various permutations of green. “It’s a Green wave baby,” one volunteer said as positive results trickled in.



Sandell said despite the election of a conservative, Coalition government, the result was not an endorsement of the Liberals’ plans. Related Article Exclusive

Victorian election Nearly half a million voters abandon Labor as party’s support crashes to new low “I think it’s more a rejection of Labor that’s moved away from their values, and a rejection of politics in general that hasn’t been working for people,” she says. “The Greens will be more important than ever if there is a Liberal government. We will be a very strong opposition to some of their worst plans to sell off our sewerage, to rip up treaty, to rip up renewable energy, to cut jobs, and I hope that we will be that bright spark of hope in the parliament for progressives and that strong opposition.” Sandell also had to address an awkward moment when casting her vote on Saturday morning. Sandell posed for photos while making her vote, displaying her ballot paper which showed the Greens leader went against the party’s own how-to-vote card.



Sandell had preferenced the Animal Justice Party’s Naomi Jones third, despite her how-to-vote cards instructing voters to place independent Mohamed Yusuf in that position. The ballot she cast on Saturday also had Labor’s Davydd Griffiths in fourth, while her how-to-vote card had him further down the ticket at fifth. Sandell said she preferenced the Animal Justice party higher than they were on the Greens how to vote cards because they aligned with her values. “I was trying to wrangle my four-year-old, and I probably should have actually folded it [my paper] up, but look, we always tell people to preference according to their values,” Sandell says.
