World.title: Inside the NZ genebank sending seeds to the Arctic Circle doomsday vault
World.content:
New Zealand is marking 10 years of contributing to Norway's Svalbard Global Seed Vault - also known as the doomsday vault - by sending 300 seed samples to the Arctic Circle.

These come from the Margot Forde Genebank in Palmerston North, where director Kioumars Ghamkhar showed RNZ around this week.

From the outside, it's a nondescript 1960s-era building across the road from Massey University, but inside its refrigerated walls are tens of thousands of packets of seeds from all over New Zealand and beyond.

"You can't tell what's in there, but it's actually 180,000 packets of seeds, each one genetically unique."

After 12 years as director, Ghamkhar said helooked forward to its pending move to a more modern facility, expected to open in March.

The genebank is named after one of his predecessors.

The collection started in the 1930s and 1940s, but the genebank in its present form began in the 1980s.

Video player removed for printing https://players.brightcove.net/6093072280001/default_default/index.html?videoId=6408899016112

It acts as a form of insurance against crop destruction.

The bank itself has a vault-like entrance, with a reminder note saying at least 150 seed samples of each variety must remain.

The collection continues to expand, especially since the creation of the Bioeconomy Science Institute, where it is sited, formed by combining Crown entities such as AgResearch, and Plant and Food.

"I've already received huge batches and 10,000 accessions of pine tree seeds are coming our way," Ghamkhar said. "We've received some of them already.

"We're going to be New Zealand's national genebank, no matter what. There can be pine trees, which are also important for the economy.

"There's going to be crops. We're going to have wheat and canola,"

"Generally speaking, the biggest contribution to our economy is from grasses, and the top of them is perennial ryegrass and the second one is a clover."

The genebank has some native species too, but that's not its main focus. It also picks up donations from the likes of retired scientists or breeders.

Kioumars Ghamkhar says the new facility, opening in March, will have an improved cooling system. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

Visitors inside the current vault need to put on thick jackets to view the shelves, which are packed to the rafters with seeds. It is chilled to about 0-4 degrees Celsius, with a smaller vault at -20C.

The packets have QR codes on them and are all numbered, so they can be found. They're also colour-coded.

"When it's green, it means it's OK, it can be grown in this country," Ghamkhar said. "There are different colours.

"Black is okay, but in transition, but when we have red, you can't grow this thing in New Zealand."

Inside, we find facility manager Michelle Williamson, a 30-year veteran of the genebank.

"We receive seeds from people, and we document it and then store it in here," she said. "We also get requests from people, so we get the seed out and send it to people - plant breeders, universities in New Zealand and around the world, and researchers.

"We wear winter clothes all year round, because we're working at low temperature. On a 30C day, it's very nice in here.

"In the middle of winter, less so."

Michelle Williamson has worked at the genebank for more than 30 years. RNZ/Jimmy Ellingham

We make our way back out into the warmer workspace.

Ghamkhar said the current facility's cooling system dated from the 1980s, while the new one would have more flexibility with temperature control.

"We have six units there - six vaults," he said. Most of these things will move to -20C to last longer.

"If you keep them in -20C, they can be alive from between 50-100 years."

The genebank doesn't have the resources to test seed viability at the moment, but was getting technology to allow for this.

An external estimate showed the bank had contributed about $1 billion to the economy over 20-25 years, Ghamkhar said.

World.title: Police responding to vessel in 'difficulty' in Mount Maunganui
World.content:
Police have responded to a water incident near Mount Maunganui, following reports of a vessel getting into difficulty.

Coastguard National Operations Centre was notified by police at around 3pm of a vessel sinking on the Mount Maunganui side of the Tauranga Harbour entrance.

Coastguard Tauranga volunteers responded with their rescue vessel TECT Rescue.

Hato Hone St John dispatched three ambulances, one rapid response unit and one manager to the scene.

A helicopter located the individuals in the water, and six people - three adults and three children - were recovered and dropped ashore to be checked over by ambulance personnel.

Police described the incident as a "near tragedy", with the boat not carrying enough lifejackets for all the occupants.

"At that point, we were extremely concerned and we had no idea where they were," said Inspector Tristan Murray. "When you know there are people somewhere out to sea, treading choppy water in waterlogged clothes, with no floatation support at all, you start expecting the worst.

"The reality is they are in a perilous position and it becomes a race against time to find them, before they can't keep their head above the waves."

One of those rescued was in a serious condition and all were transported to Tauranga hospital.

Murray praised the efforts of police, Coastguard, and Mount Maunganui and Omanu surf lifesaving clubs.

"This is as close as it gets, it's a miracle nobody died," he said. "Everyone involved in this rescue should feel proud of themselves - they've saved lives today.

"Every person who's going out in a boat has a responsibility to learn from this. If something goes wrong, you may not have time to react.

"A life jacket can't help you, if you're not wearing it."

While this rescue took place, local responder faced another along Mount Maunganui beach, where three people were caught in a rip.

All were quickly brought ashore, one in serious conditions.

"We have wonderful beaches and great swimming spots in the Bay of Plenty, but we want people to stay safe," Murray said. "If you're swimming, please do it between the flags and be mindful of hazards like rips.

World.title: Black Caps hold upper hand over India after day two of Christchurch test
World.content:
The Black Caps hold the strong upper hand over India after the second day of the second cricket test at Hagley Oval, Christchurch.

Starting the day at 246/5, the Black Caps added another 110 runs, before being dismissed in the second session, and then had India reeling at 116/6 at stumps, still 240 runs in arrears.

New Zealand scored 356, with wicketkeeper Tom Blundell leading the way with 89, before he was the ninth batter out, as he hit out at the Indian bowling attack.

He struck 10 boundaries in his 211-ball innings and had solid support down the order from Glenn Phillips, who was out early on Saturday for 36, Nathan Smith, Kyle Jamieson and Matt Henry.

Akash Deep took his fifth wicket for the day, when Henry was last man out for 19.

Henry was straight back into the action, snaring Indian opener Yashasvi Jaiswal for a duck with the last ball of the first over of India's innings.

Jamieson followed up soon after, having Devdutt Padikkal caught behind by Blundell for 21, and India, who racked up 720/9 in their first innings of the drawn test in Wellington, looked much shakier.

Jamieson boosted the Black Caps further, tempting India captain Shubman Gill into an edge that Tom Latham gratefully snaffled at second slip.

That left India 59/3 at tea, but with dangerman Rishabh Pant at the crease. The Wellington centurion had scored 23, when he tried to slog Jacob Duffy out of the park, but was caught by Jamieson.

Duffy claimed the fifth wicket, when opener KL Rahul speared a ball to Devon Conway at point.

Then just before stumps, Washington Sundar edged one to Latham, leaving his team in big trouble, as the Kiwi pace bowlers starred with a sterling performance.

Duffy took 2/21, a welcome rebound, after he became the first New Zealand bowler to concede 200-plus runs in a single test innings at the Basin Reserve last week.

He said he really enjoyed the crowd supporting the bowlers on Saturday.

"The first half was really good to get to a competitive total, on the back of Tommy's [Blundell's] bat," he told Sky Sport.

Then, when the New Zealanders were bowling, the Canterbury crowd got behind them.

"They had a few beers by the end of it and they were getting pretty rowdy. It was good fun."

Duffy, who was named today in the New Zealand squad for the four-test series against Australia, said he had battling a few demons with his bowling action lately.

"So to get a bit of luck go your way, it's actually quite nice."

World.title: Law expert Andrew Geddis calls for review of overhang seat rules
World.content:
An electoral law expert says New Zealand's overhang seat rules must be reviewed to prevent political parties from influencing future election outcomes.

University of Otago law professor Andrew Geddis said the 2026 election highlighted how overhang seats could affect the proportionality of the Mixed Member Proportional system.

The election resulted in Parliament expanding to 130 MPs, with National gaining six seats and Te Pāti Māori four.

Geddis said the overhang had distorted the possible outcomes of the election by limiting the combination of parties that could form the government.

"If the seats were allocated based purely on the party vote, then the Opportunity Party would be an actual kingmaker able to go for either a left-wing or a right-wing coalition."

He said the overhang had left only one path to power, with the existing coalition needing the Opportunity Party's support to form a government.

Geddis warned parties could focus on engineering election outcomes through methods like tactical voting or split voting, rather than seeking support for their policies.

"I think that would be harmful for future elections."

He said the overhang also threatened the principle of proportional representation that MMP was all about.

"MMP, if we want it to work like it should, requires proportionality, and the overhang threatens that and needs revisited."

He said campaigns focused on tactical voting could undermine public confidence in the electoral system.

World.title: Why is my gas so expensive? Ask Susan
World.content:
Got questions? RNZ has a podcast, 'No Stupid Questions', with Susan Edmunds.

We'd love to hear more of your questions about money and the economy. You can send through written questions, like these ones, but even better, you can drop us a voice memo to our email questions@rnz.co.nz.

You can also sign up to RNZ's new money newsletter, 'Money with Susan Edmunds'.

For several years now, I have been battling the principle behind Genesis Energy requiring every residential LPG customer to rent two 45kg cylinders, however little gas they use. Genesis makes no exceptions. For careful, low-use households, that means paying more per kilogram to rent the cylinders than to buy the gas, at around $179 a bottle. I know of no other household service that makes customers pay for more than they know they need: for example no one is made to rent a second fibre line.

The policy treats low-use customers' properties as a storage facility for unwanted empty cylinders, while charging them monthly rent for the privilege. It leaves frontline complaints teams reciting the rulebook, with no apparent mandate to question whether the policy is fair.

As a semi-retired person living alone, one cylinder lasts me about 18 months. I have an open fire and electricity for other heating and cooking. I use LPG mainly for a gas hob; it is also connected to a gas fireplace in a separate room that I use once or twice a year. I pay $138 a year to rent the two cylinders and use about 30kg of gas a year, so the rental alone costs me about $4.60 for every kilogram of gas I use. A household using 10 bottles a year (450kg) pays exactly the same $138, which works out at about 31 cents a kilogram. My second cylinder has been empty since late 2022. Genesis refused to collect it in 2023, and this month confirmed in writing that rental applies "regardless of whether both cylinders are actively being used". When I challenged it, I was told I was free to go elsewhere.

I thought it sounded very odd that you're in this situation so I approached Genesis.

A spokesperson told me that the company is sorry that this has taken so long to resolve.

"We too often explained our standard product and the reasons for it without properly considering whether it was suitable for [the customer's] needs."

It said its standard LPG service used two 45kg cylinders to offer continuity of supply, so a customer could use one cylinder while arranging a replacement for the other.

"This reduces the risk of a customer running out of gas when they need it most. Changing an existing installation to use one cylinder isn't as simple as disconnecting the second; it needs to be assessed to ensure it remains safe and suitable.

"We don't have a final solution for [the customer] today, but we're continuing to work through her situation. [She] has kindly agreed to share her perspective with our product team, which will directly inform our review of how we support low-use customers and how clearly we explain who our standard service suits. We're also looking at how we can improve the way we listen to customers' individual circumstances and use their feedback to identify opportunities to improve our products and services."

I know that your concern is primarily with the principle of the issue but I think in this instance it could be that the most useful solution is to take up the suggestion to go elsewhere for your gas.

Paul Fuge, who is general manager of Powerswitch, says most people who are using gas only for cooking can switch to a barbecue-style gas bottle that they can then manage themselves. He said the alternative would be to try to get off gas completely, although that is not practical in some cases.

I've just bought Allbirds in their Black Friday sale. I've had several pairs before, same style, and bought the same size. These ones are slightly different and are too big! But their website says all Black Friday sales are final sale and can't be refunded or exchanged. Is that fair?

Consumer NZ says, under the Consumer Guarantees Act, a retailer isn't obliged to provide a refund or exchange if a consumer changes their mind after they've purchased a product. However, a retailer still has to provide a remedy when a product is not of acceptable quality or isn't fit for purpose, including products that are on sale.

"This is a particularly interesting one because if the size and style has been purchased previously then the person who's bought them could reasonably expect a new pair in the same size and style will fit. We recommend they reach out to Allbirds and explain the situation - see if they'll offer an exchange of size."

My question relates to New Zealand Post and stamps. I had assumed stamps were legal tender. Having bought a birthday card a little late, I wanted to get it couriered. I knew this would cost more, so I placed two stamps ($3.60 each) on the card, then went to the NZ Post Outlet where I live, and asked to pay the difference to have the card couriered. The courier was to be $9.20 they told me. The difference would then be $2. However, they refused. Can NZ Post legally refuse to accept stamps as payment?

NZ Post says whether stamps can be used as a payment for its services depends on the type of service being purchased and whether the NZ Post outlet has the technology required to issue a tracking barcode.

"In this specific case, we would need more information about the service the customer was trying to purchase and the location they visited to understand why they were unable to use stamps as payment."

World.title: A day in the life of NZ's 'chicken whisperer'
World.content:
Audio player for " How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._v4.laWzzQVil69j0DGqQk4Ywh3JMAvc5jXoA1Fn8ldP8DY/business/2856939%2Fa-day-in-the-life-of-nz-s-chicken-whisperer

How do I tell a scam from a real bank call? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 15m

Nathan Williams describes himself as a "chicken whisperer".

While he runs the company, the chief executive and founder of eg. Free Range Eggs is also out in the shed every night, lifting each bird up to its spot in the bird aviary, so no-one sleeps on the floor.

"You can pet them and they'll all talk to each other, and the whole shed will go dead quiet and they all go to sleep, and the lights go off," he said. "We treat them like pets.

"Someone is in the shed 16 hours a day. A human is in there with them, picking up eggs or any injured birds, checking feed and water, ventilation and lighting.

"There's always something to do."

He said the industry perception was that free-range farming was harder than cage farming.

"They do go outside, you've got to get them all back. There are hawks and wild cats or whatever outside.

"To get them back inside and up on to the bird aviaries, what I do is create their daily routine in where they lay eggs, where they eat, where they sleep.

"Where they sleep every night is where they'll stay for the rest of their life cycle. If I go into the shed at 9.30 tonight, the lights go out and I might be lucky to find 10 chickens on the floor.

"They all do it themselves now."

Chicken whisperers - and chicken chasers - are some of the unusual roles that Kathleen Webber, founder of salary benchmarking platform LiveRem, has noticed among the salary data.

Others include a thinner - who picks fruit off trees so the rest grow bigger - a poultry boner, hatchery driver, cheese quality controller, water spider - who keeps a factoryline stocked - and bingo co-ordinator.

"When someone says they're a water spider or a chicken chaser, you naturally want to know more," she said.

Nathan Williams runs the largest free-range farm in the country. He plans to triple in size. EG. FREE RANGE EGGS

"The names are memorable, but behind each one is a practical job that an employer needs done. Most of us experience these jobs through the end result - food on the supermarket shelf, electricity at home or a production line running smoothly.

"We rarely think about all the different people and roles that make that possible.

"One of the fascinating things about working with pay data is seeing the sheer variety of work people do. Even within a familiar industry, there are specialist roles many of us have never heard of.

"There's a useful careers lesson here - don't judge a job by its title. Look at what the person actually does, the skills involved and where that experience could take you.

"You might never have considered becoming a cheese quality controller or a drone pilot asset inspector. Sometimes, discovering that a job exists is the first step towards finding work that interests you."

Williams said finding staff was hard, with a lack of training available, which made it a hard industry to break into.

"It is very labour intensive, and not many people like being dirty and sweaty, and scratched by chickens all day. A lot of people have a fear of chickens as well, especially when you see 30,000 in the shed.

"It's not for everybody. Chickens originate from dinosaurs, they're like T-rexes.

"They are very temperamental, and they'll get a read on your body language or your heartrate. If you're panicking, they all start panicking.

"If I'm calm and relaxed, then they all are. You can't cause them any stress, because they're birds, and they'll start flying and smashing into everything."

Williams said he could not imagine doing anything else.

"I have 120,000 chickens, the largest free-range farm in the country, and I plan to be three times the size in the next 3-4 years. It is a seven-day-a-week operation from 5.30 in the morning until 11 o'clock at night.

"You get a hundred thousand eggs the next day, no matter what, it doesn't stop. There's no getting out of it.

"It's a lifestyle I chose for myself, unfortunately... but I love it. Challenging though.

"Every day, I'm like, 'Why am I doing this to myself?', but then I get back up the next day and go again."

World.title: Amount of wastewater overflow not known after issue at Wellington treatment plant
World.content:
This story has been updated after Tiaki Wai provided more accurate information

Wellington's water authority says a recent wastewater overflow was caused by a problem with the water treatment plant's UV disinfection system.

The failure occurred at the Wellington Wastewater Treatment Plant at about 3am Saturday morning and led to a discharge of treated wastewater that emerged near the mouth of Karori Stream.

The authority, Tiaki Wai, said the plant was now operating as normal and it was working to establish the cause.

There was also a failure at the Western UV Weir Gate on Friday afternoon led to partially treated water being discharged in the Karori Stream between 12:40pm and 4:37pm.

Tiaki Wai said it did not yet know the volume of wastewater discharged in either event.

People are being advised to stay out of the water in the immediate vicinity of the Karori Stream outfall pipe into Cook Strait - four kilometres northwest of Red Rocks, over the weekend.

World.title: Motorbike rider left with serious injuries after Canterbury crash
World.content:
A motorbike rider has been left with serious injuries after a crash in Prebbleton.

Police were called to the crash at the intersection of Shands Road and Robinsons Road, involving a car and a motorbike, at about 9:30am.

A St John spokesperson said the motorbike rider was taken to Christchurch Hospital in a serious condition.

Police are urging any witnesses to come forward or anyone with dashcam or CCTV footage from the crash or around the area at that time.

World.title: Matildas salute in style for Catley's 150th milestone match
World.content:
Steph Catley celebrated her 150th appearance for Australia in style, playing a key role in the Matildas' go-ahead goal as they kicked away in the second half to secure a 3-1 win over Colombia.

After Alanna Kennedy and Linda Caicedo netted inside the opening 15 minutes, Catley’s 59th-minute corner ricocheted off Daniela Arias's back to put Australia into the ascendancy, before Caitlin Foord struck three minutes later to secure a match-winning cushion.

The defender had donned the armband for her milestone appearance at a wet GIO Stadium on Saturday night, with Joe Montemurro also fielding the returning Mary Fowler and Kyra Cooney-Cross in his XI — the latter making her first Matildas appearance in 252 days.

Alanna Kennedy scored the opening goal against Colombia in Canberra. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Chasing continuity and insight ahead of the Women’s World Cup next June, the coach will get another chance to look at his side — and chase a final win in 2026 — next Wednesday, when the two sides meet in Geelong.

Every time 21-year-old Caicedo got near the ball, alarm bells rang for the Matildas, with her combination of pace, close control and positional nous leaving defenders scrambling.

But Montemurro’s adjustments at half-time, which saw Kerr withdrawn for Hayley Raso, put the clamps on the South Americans, who didn’t produce another shot until Manuela Vanegas’s 94th-minute header.

The match heated up between the sides in the final 10 minutes. (Getty Images: Cameron Spencer)

Catley’s set piece and Foord’s strike — the latter the result of class build-up from Fowler and Cooney-Cross — then served to secure an assured result.

Catch up on all the action through our live blog below.

World.title: North Melbourne AFLW duo announce retirement after historic three-peat
World.content:
Inaugural AFLW North Melbourne captain and eight-time All Australian Emma Kearney has announced her retirement following the Kangaroos' third straight premiership victory.

Kearney joined North Melbourne in 2019 after two years at the Western Bulldogs, where she also won a flag.

She led the Kangaroos for six seasons before handing over the captaincy to Jasmine Garner before the 2025 campaign, having steered the club to its maiden AFLW premiership in 2024.

Her teammate, three-time premiership player, inaugural player and long-time partner, Kate Shierlaw, also announced her retirement.

The pair told teammates today they would both be hanging up their boots.

(From left) Emma Kearney, Kangaroos coach Darren Crocker, and Kate Shierlaw, who says the third flag was the most emotional of the lot. (Getty: Morgan Hancock/AFL Photos)

“This club means the world to me, and I couldn’t be prouder of everything we’ve built and achieved together” Kearney said.

"Getting the opportunity to join North Melbourne ahead of our inaugural season in 2019 was so special, and watching this program grow into what it is today has been the greatest privilege of my career.

“The thing I’ll miss the most is simply being around this group every single day. Walking away from that daily environment is the hardest part.

“I’m so grateful to Crock (coach Darren Crocker) for the belief, guidance and care he has shown me and the entire group.

“Finally, a massive thank you to the North Melbourne fans. Your passion and loyalty through all the highs and lows has meant everything to us, and sharing these moments with you is something I’ll cherish forever.”

North Melbourne three-peat North Melbourne claims a historic three-peat after a near flawless but challenging season.

Following the premiership win over Melbourne last night at Princes Park, Crocker said Kearney had "left a legacy for our football club".

"She has really set the standards, when a lot of players actually didn't understand what it looked like," he told reporters post win.

Garner, who asked Kearney on stage to lift the cup beside her, said she was "an amazing player but also an amazing person".

"I looked up to her. A lot of us didn't really know what it looked like to have really high standards and work hard and be a team-first player," Garner said.

"I feel like she helped guide us through that.

"Not sure what she's going to do, but it was just really nice to have her up there (on stage)."

Shierlaw, an inaugural player for Carlton and co-captain for St Kilda before joining North, told ABC Sport the third flag was the most emotional win of the lot.

"I'm very overwhelmed with emotions. Relief, excited," Shierlaw said.

"It's just like a lot of hard work over four or five years … just Kearns and I having a great time out here, living our dreams. Three in a row."

World.title: The tactics that secured North Melbourne's third AFLW premiership
World.content:
As rain bucketed down, North Melbourne confirmed its AFLW dynasty with an historic third consecutive premiership.

While it may seem repetitive to talk about the Roos' record-breaking run, what they had to compete with in 2026 makes this third flag that little bit more special.

For the first time since 2023 they lost a game, and challengers consistently came closer than in the previous two years.

The looming feeling that senior players could potentially hang up their boots also added a sense of occasion to the victory.

And then the weather showed up. The rain was going to be the great equaliser, allowing fellow grand finalist Melbourne to gather some confidence.

But by dominating three specific phases of the game, North Melbourne made history on Friday night, securing a three-peat.

The fast start that set up the victory

Throughout 2026, North Melbourne hasn't been an overly strong first-quarter team.

Generally, the opening terms were largely arm wrestles, almost like the Roos were playing with the opposition, giving them hope, before taking it away.

Roos are 'finally able to say' the words they have refused all season North Melbourne claims a historic three-peat after a near flawless but challenging season.

But on Friday night, the fast start was necessary. With rain already falling, and more on the radar, any early lead was going to be seriously valuable, so the Roos ensured they were the team in front.

Tess Craven knocked through the first goal of the game within 21 seconds, and captain Jasmine Garner kicked a second six minutes in. They went direct, gained ground with kicks, and got deep entries to unsettle Melbourne's typically staunch defence.

Both goals for the Roos came from stoppage, which was a worrying sign for Melbourne so early on. Last time these sides met, it was off turnover — not stoppage — that North Melbourne had set itself apart.

But this time around, the Roos tipped those scales in their favour.

Score sources North Melbourne Melbourne Points from intercept 15 13 Points from stoppage 29 5

Best on ground medallist Garner set the tone early in the piece. In the first quarter alone, Garner's stats included seven disposals, four inside 50s, and the goal, laying the foundations for how North Melbourne was going to attack the game.

While it took Melbourne some time to adapt to what the game was throwing up, North Melbourne just got to work.

The Demons over-possessed the footy in slippery conditions, opting for the handball too often, instead of getting boot to ball to win all-important territory.

Holding steady as the Dees fought back

Once Melbourne managed to get into the game, the Roos had to simply batten down the hatches and absorb the blows being thrown their way.

But crucially, just as in the first quarter, North Melbourne had already taken advantage of its early momentum on the scoreboard, with a classy Eilish Sheerin goal 39 seconds into the next term.

The Demons shifted to more of a kicking game in the second quarter, got into more dangerous positions, and Tayla Harris's contested marking reared its head. With this shift, they kicked what would be their only two goals of the match.

Quarter Kicks, handballs, tackles North Melbourne Melbourne Quarter 1 Kicks 46 40 Handballs 24 36 Tackles 17 23 Quarter 2 Kicks 35 39 Handballs 34 14 Tackles 17 19 Quarter 3 Kicks 48 36 Handballs 21 36 Tackles 18 24 Quarter 4 Kicks 43 38 Handballs 17 18 Tackles 15 18

That shift in style was borne out in the stats, with Melbourne's ratio of 39 kicks to 14 handballs in the second quarter helping to throw North Melbourne's movement out of whack.

While the second quarter was Melbourne's lowest-disposal quarter of the match, it was the side's most effective. Notably, both of the goals came from intercepts.

Roos create AFLW history with three-peat North Melbourne defeats Melbourne by 26 points in the grand final to claim a historic third consecutive AFLW premiership.

Pressure was also a major consideration in the second term, with Melbourne recording a pressure factor of 2.30 across the quarter — a rate at the upper end of the elite category — which rose to 2.38 in the third term.

But, crucially for the Roos, they maintained a lead even when the Demons threw their best at them. And the third quarter became a stalemate, in which North Melbourne maintained its arm's-length lead. The Roos' deep defence was staunch, repelling repeated forward entries and preventing Melbourne from scoring further goals.

Midfielders Garner (eight intercepts) and Ash Riddell (seven) were important in this respect, sliding behind the ball post-stoppage, while winger Amy Gavin Mangan, half-forward Jenna Bruton, and half-back Eliza Shannon (all six intercepts) got busy defensively.

In doing so, they lulled the Demons back into over-possession of the footy, taking their kick rate way back down to 50 per cent.

Essentially, the middle two quarters were a tale of the Roos just taking the hits and remaining on their feet.

Five-minute burst seals the premiership

While the game largely felt like it was in the balance for the duration, a five-minute patch in the last quarter turned a six-point lead into a 26-point victory for North Melbourne. It was a classic demonstration of the Roos' brand, taking the game away in a flash.

Melbourne controlled territory for the bulk of that term, attempting to break through the numbers in its attacking arc but unable to convert for the major that would have really rattled the Roos.

Instead, North Melbourne again absorbed the blows — and then the fast break happened. A long rebounding kick unlocked the Roos' speed, which had been a worry for Melbourne all evening and in the end proved the difference.

It allowed the Roos to set up an attack once again, create a stoppage inside 50, and secure a crucial goal off the boot of Bella Eddey.

And that goal was the dam wall breaking. It put the Roos up by 13 points, and opened the floodgates for two more goals via Blaithin Bogue, taking the game from a thrilling nailbiter to a comprehensive North Melbourne victory.

This is the Roos' style: absorb, absorb, absorb — then land the felling blow.

Throughout the season they have consistently dominated late in games.

They kicked the last three goals in their preliminary final, and continued the trend by kicking the last three goals in the grand final.

Prior to the game, one question for Melbourne was whether it could prevent that final flurry and hold on.

On Friday night, North Melbourne provided an emphatic answer.

World.title: High-heel skipping and handbag throwing: Perth's queer sports history uncovered
World.content:
Competitive handbag throwing and high-heel skipping were once acts of political defiance in Perth.

Both disciplines featured in what was originally known as the city's 'Gay Olympics', which ran annually from 1979 to 1999 to raise money for gay and lesbian charities.

They event also pushed for law reform at a time when consensual homosexual sex between men was still illegal in Western Australia; the decriminalisation of which only began in 1990.

The games were a colourful way of bringing the LGBTQIA+ community together. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

Volunteers at the West Pride Archives have been sifting the event's history ahead of Perth hosting the 2030 International Gay Games.

Jo Darbyshire, co-convenor of West Pride Archives said Perth's original games had a strong political edge.

"Being visible out in the community and not being shamed was a huge element to (them)," she said.

Australia's longest-running gay nightclub, Connections, had a team base at the games. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

"We were still fighting for gay law reform, for gay men in particular to be able to have sex with other men without being harassed by the police or charged or considered dirty and deviant."

Marches and colourful floats were part of the parade. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

The games galvanised the community, but fundraising was also a key part with money going towards things including the telephone bill for the Gay Lesbian Counselling Service.

The games were held in Perth from 1979 until 1999. (Supplied: Tim Grant/ State Library of WA)

"That sort of power over helping our own communities enabled us to have the courage to really push for gay law reform and equality in the law," she said.

" We refused to just roll over and die. "

'Winners with Muscles' receiving an award from Holly Wood at the McGillivray Oval in1983. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

Tim Grant photographed the event in the 1980s, and said it was a unique chance to document his community, as it was forbidden to take photos inside bars and clubs at the time.

"It was safe and one the few large-scale spectaculars that my local community could ever have at the time," he said.

Costumes and fashion played a big role in the games and the community. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

"I felt I had no restraints on what I could photograph on the day, as I was a known face and just a part of the scenery."

The Girls of Head Office Women’s Team #2 at the Opening Parade in 1982. (Supplied: Tim Grant/State Library of WA)

International Gay Games

Ray Currell, 78, said the local event was "very important" for the community.

"It was great, we had high-heel skip, the handbag throw and then there were some serious events," he said,

" [The games] meant freedom. I've always been gay, I've never hidden the fact. "

West Pride Archives volunteer Sophie Herbert and Ray Currell hold his badges from international Gay Games. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Currell also helped organise the first Perth team of around 30 members to participate in the New York Gay Games in 1994, which coincided with the 25th anniversary of the Stonewall Riots.

Team Perth went to New York for the Gay Games in the 1990s. (Supplied: West Pride Archives)

The Gay Games do not require any qualifications for participants.

"As long as you could afford to get there and compete, they let you," Currell said.

Held every four years, Currell competed in five Gay Games and said he would still compete if his body allowed him.

Team Perth participated at the Sydney Gay Games in 2002. (Supplied: Adrian Lily and Ray Currell)

Perth to hold 2030 Gay Games

Perth will host the international Gay Games for the first time in 2030, which is expected to attract thousands of people.

At the 2026 Valencia Gay Games, more than 50 Western Australia participants formed the Australian contingent.

It is expected to be far larger when it's Perth's turn to host.

Ray Currell participated in five international Gay Games for bowling. (ABC News: Mietta Adams)

Sophie Herbert, volunteer at West Pride Archives, said it was "heartwarming and inspiring" to discover the light side of Perth's LGBTQIA+ history.

"They were very brave in the way that it was just people existing and going out and having fun — but just by doing that was an act of protest in itself," they said.

"Although there was so much awful stuff happening at that time, people were resisting in their own way and that's really inspiring."

They said they hoped the Gay Games caused the local event to be resurrected, and they encouraged people to donate their photos and medals to the West Pride Archives ahead of the 2030 Games.

World.title: Nathan Lyon axed as Australia names Test squad
World.content:
Corey Rocchiccioli has ended Nathan Lyon's 13-year reign as Australia's first-choice spinner, with the veteran tweaker one of three players axed for the Test series against New Zealand.

Selectors on Saturday unveiled a 13-man squad for the home summer, with spinner Rocchiccioli and Queensland batter Jack Clayton named in their first Test squads.

Lyon, Cooper Connolly and Marnus Labuschagne are all gone from the team that lost a series decider to South Africa in Cape Town just four weeks ago.

Steve Smith is fit again and will return.

Australia Test squad vs New Zealand Pat Cummins (captain), Scott Boland, Alex Carey, Jack Clayton, Cameron Green, Josh Hazlewood, Travis Head, Josh Inglis, Michael Neser, Matthew Renshaw, Corey Rocchiccioli, Steve Smith, Mitchell Starc

Beau Webster's future also appears clouded, missing out on the squad entirely after being dropped for the Cape Town loss after playing Australia's previous five Tests.

The omission of Connolly and Webster means Clayton is every chance of debuting in a reconfigured top seven, after averaging 74.83 in the Sheffield Shield this season.

Selectors have left the door open for another player to come into the group, with Cricket Australia confirming a 14th man will be added after next weekend's Sheffield Shield round.

There is also nothing stopping selectors changing their squad between Tests, given it is a home summer.

But still the most seismic decision of all comes with Rocchiccioli's selection ahead of Lyon, the nation's second leading wicket-taker of all time.

Lyon has been Australia's first-choice spinner since being recalled to the Test side midway through the 2013 Ashes, after briefly being dropped for Ashton Agar.

He has also formed part of every Australian Test squad since his debut tour of Sri Lanka midway through 2011.

At age 39, there are now serious questions over his future in the Test side.

Jack Clayton drawing on AFL experience Jack Clayton says missing out on the AFL draft has taught him how to deal with the pressure of chasing a Test cricket debut for Australia.

Lyon has made clear he wants to play in next year's tours of India and England, and as it stands he remains determined to fight back into the side.

He took six wickets at an average of 43.67 in Australia's most recent series loss to South Africa, where he was left out for the second Test in Gqeberha.

The 145-Test veteran has since returned to the Sheffield Shield and taken seven wickets 43.28 for NSW across two matches.

"Nathan has not quite had the impact we would like with the ball in recent matches," chief selector George Bailey said.

"We also know he has an extraordinary record and his experience, knowledge and skill can still be valuable to the program we have moving forward."

Lyon's axing also calls into question whether Test cricket's most successful bowling quartet in history will take to the field together again, alongside Pat Cummins, Josh Hazlewood and Mitchell Starc.

Rocchiccioli, meanwhile, has been on the fringe of Australia's squads in recent years.

The 29-year-old has taken 18 wickets at 33.88 for Western Australia this summer, and showed his all-round ability with a century against Tasmania last week.

Whether he debuts in Perth remains to be seen, with Australia every chance of playing Scott Boland as one of four quicks.

"Corey has been a strong performer in domestic cricket for the past few seasons and has traits that are well suited to Australian conditions," Bailey said.

AAP

World.title: MotoGP world champion Marquez announces shock retirement
World.content:
Marc Marquez will take his final bow in Valencia after the eight-time MotoGP champion announced on Friday that he would retire following the 2026 season finale, ending one of motorcycle racing's greatest careers.

The Spaniard made the announcement days after wrapping up a record-equalling eighth premier-class title in Portugal, drawing him level with Giacomo Agostini.

"Thank you to everyone who's been part of the journey. I hope you've enjoyed it as much as I have. This will be my last race in MotoGP. We made history," Marquez said in a video recorded in the Valencia garage.

Loading Instagram content

The announcement came as a surprise after Marquez, who won six MotoGP titles with Honda before joining Ducati, signed a contract extension with the Italian team earlier this year that was due to run until 2028.

The 33-year-old said he decided to retire at last month's Japanese Grand Prix after the physical and mental toll of repeated injuries and operations began to weigh heavily on him.

"Sometimes you need to understand the situation, but it's true that the situation this year was on the limit," Marquez said.

"When I signed the contract in March, as always, I was super optimistic and I didn't know that I would have another surgery on my right shoulder (in May)."

Marquez said he had begun to "feel the fear" despite remaining determined to compete and had also been troubled by brief recurrences of double vision after the Indonesian and French grands prix.

He recovered within days on both occasions but said the episodes made him more cautious.

"It was one of the main reasons why I controlled the risk and why I crashed less this second part of the season," he added.

Marquez had been expected to lead MotoGP into its new 850cc era, with compatriot Pedro Acosta's arrival at the factory Ducati team viewed as a symbolic passing of the torch.

There were tears in the Ducati garage and among the crowd when fans at the Circuit Ricardo Tormo were told the Spaniard would be competing in his final race this weekend.

Jorge Martin, his main rival for the 2026 title, appeared stunned, while Marquez's brother Alex, who had been told of the decision during the Japanese Grand Prix, watched with a sombre expression.

From rookie champion to all-time great

Marquez swept into MotoGP in 2013 and won the title at his first attempt, becoming the youngest premier-class world champion at the age of 20.

By 2019, he had amassed six championships with Honda and appeared virtually unbeatable, a blur of orange and red tearing through the field.

Everything changed at the opening race of the 2020 season in Jerez, where he crashed and broke his arm.

The injury began the darkest period of his career. Marquez underwent four operations, abandoned several comeback attempts and suffered blurred vision, all while trying to push an underperforming Honda bike far beyond its limits.

He later spoke of wondering whether continuing was worth the pain as speculation about his retirement intensified.

Instead, Marquez took the decision to leave Honda and make the switch to Gresini Racing, which was using year-old Ducati machinery.

He slowly rediscovered his belief, ending a 1,043-day wait for victory in Aragon before securing the factory Ducati seat that would change everything.

"I had my second life (after leaving Honda), and I enjoyed my second life in MotoGP," Marquez said.

In 2025, Marquez claimed his seventh MotoGP crown in Japan, a feat Acosta likened to basketball great Michael Jordan's return from baseball to lead the Chicago Bulls to another NBA title.

Erasing a 102-point deficit

What followed in 2026 was perhaps even more extraordinary as Marquez overturned a 102-point deficit to retain the championship.

After failing to win early in the season and then crashing in France, he underwent surgery on his shoulder and a fractured foot, missing his home grand prix while his rivals collected victories and points.

He sat eighth in the standings but won six of the next nine rounds, as Aprilia rivals Martin and Marco Bezzecchi faltered, before sealing the title in Portugal with a round to spare.

If his seventh championship was his most emotional, the eighth cemented his place among the sport's greats and was marked by a celebration rich in symbolism.

Marquez climbed a staircase as the silhouette of a goat, shorthand for "greatest of all time", appeared on a screen behind him before Agostini presented him with a commemorative golden helmet.

Reuters

World.title: Wallabies end 2026 with massive loss to Ireland in London
World.content:
Wallabies coach Les Kiss admits his side has "work to do" after finishing their 2026 campaign with a 38-14 defeat to Ireland in the Nations Championship at Twickenham.

With the Rugby World Cup in Australia less than 12 months away, the result in London saw the Wallabies end the Test season with a 6-7-1 (win-loss-draw) record.

They finished sixth in the Nations Championship, one spot behind Ireland.

Trailing 17-7 at half-time, the Wallabies were made to pay for several wasted attacking opportunities when camped in Ireland's territory.

They earned repeated entries inside the Irish 22, but a Kalani Thomas try was all they could show for their efforts in the second half.

Ireland, on the other hand, crossed for three second-half tries, a tally which included a double to reserve forward James McNabney.

The Wallabies, ranked seventh in the world, lost five of their last six Tests for the year.

A win over world champions South Africa in September was a rare highlight for Kiss's troops.

"Every team above us [on the world rankings], bar one, we haven't been able to beat," Kiss told Stan Sport.

"We've got work to do."

Irish reserve James McNabney scored a late double in the win over the Wallabies. (Getty Images: Seb Daly)

The Wallabies opened the scoring against Ireland in the 21st minute following Jeremy Williams's converted try.

World number two Ireland, who was coming off a 20-17 win over the Springboks in Dublin, replied on the scoreboard with tries to Robbie Henshaw and Nick Timoney.

Sam Prendergast converted both and added a penalty goal on the stroke of half-time to establish Ireland's 10-point lead at the break.

Robert Baloucoune scored Ireland's third straight try early in the second half and following Prendergast's conversion, the Wallabies were trailing 24-7.

Thomas's try, and Carter Gordon's conversion, closed the gap, but McNabney's brace inside the final 10 minutes of the match helped ice Ireland's winning margin.

Look back at how the action unfolded in our live blog.

World.title: Roos are 'finally able to say' the words they have refused all season
World.content:
All season the North Melbourne AFLW side was not allowed to use the word "three-peat".

The team came into the year as back-to-back premiers and outright favourites for the flag. They started the finals series as minor premiers, having lost just one game (to Hawthorn), their first defeat in three years.

Roos create AFLW history with three-peat North Melbourne defeats Melbourne by 26 points in the grand final to claim a historic third consecutive AFLW premiership.

For the duration of the year, the AFLW world was talking about the Kangaroos' incoming third consecutive flag. But not the Roos themselves.

As Jasmine Garner said post-game, it's a cliche as old as football, but one that's tried and tested: treat the season as one game at a time.

Then the siren sounded. They had defeated Melbourne by 26 points under lights at Princes Park after beating Brisbane the two years prior.

And they let the emotions overrun them.

North Melbourne is the first side in AFLW history to claim three consecutive premierships. (Getty: Kelly Defina)

All Australian Erika O'Shea said it was one of "the best moments of my life, 100 per cent".

"Oh my god, it's the most surreal feeling,"O'Shea told ABC Sport.

"Nothing will ever feel like this. I started crying instantly when I heard that siren.

"I think a sigh of relief, but also just all the hard work that we've done during the year, and yeah … three-peat. I can't believe it.

"To finally be able to say it with a smile is the best thing ever."

Head coach Darren Crocker said it was up to the AFLW community and media to decide whether the side was a dynasty or not, but he was pretty sure the consecutive flags made for one.

He said the 2024 flag — the first AFLW cup for North Melbourne — meant a lot. The second broke new ground when the first side became the first to go back-to-back in AFLW history.

And the three-peat felt pretty good.

Even opposition captain Kate Hore said "we'll talking about this team forever".

Jasmine Garner won her second best-on-ground medal on Friday night. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

Garner said this year was more difficult than last.

"I always had the belief that we were good enough to do it, but you know, this year, it hasn't been perfect," she said.

"We've lost one game in 42, but we've been challenged. We've had injuries. We've had different hurdles pop up along the way.

"But we felt this year we were kind of building slowly and we kept our best footy to the finals. I think that's what got us over, our experience and our calmness.

"I reckon this final series has been the best it's ever been, but it's just so good for women's footy. Just really proud of the group."

The players were finally able to let the emotions flow after a challenging but near flawless season. (Getty: Daniel Pockett/AFL Photos)

Kangaroos forward Kate Shierlaw said this win made her the most emotional of the three.

"I'm very overwhelmed with emotions. Relief, excited," Shierlaw said.

"It's just like a lot of hard work over four or five years … just Kearns [Emma Kearney, North Melbourne stalwart defender and Shierlaw's partner] and I having a great time out here, living our dreams. Three in a row."

Shierlaw and Kearney hinted at possible retirement. Shierlaw said she would "talk to the club" and Kearney told the broadcast she may have played her last game.

Tech.title: Here’s how to make that new Black Friday TV look its best
Tech.content:
is a senior reviewer covering TVs and audio. He has over 20 years experience in AV, and has previously been on staff at Digital Trends and Reviewed.

It’s the season of great deals on TVs. But once you get a new one home and set it up in your living room, it might not meet expectations when you turn it on. Maybe it’s overly bright, or things just look… off. Luckily, there are some easy tweaks you can make so that new, expensive purchase looks its best.

It seems counterintuitive, but the default mode for most TVs out of the box isn’t accurate and can include lots of extra processing that makes the image look artificially detailed or overly smooth. The mode is usually called something like Eco or Energy Saving and is used to meet energy consumption requirements. But it also negatively affects picture quality.

The easiest way to make the biggest positive change to your TV’s image is by changing out of this picture mode. Using Filmmaker, Movie, Cinema, or Professional picture mode (each company uses different names) will make the color temperature more accurate — it will look more red in comparison to the very blue Eco mode, but trust me, it’s far more realistic — and will either turn off extra processing or, at the very least, tone it down. Also, avoid Vivid and Dynamic modes, which are only there to blast brightness and make the image incredibly blue.

Another setting you should immediately turn off is the ambient light sensor. The idea behind it is solid — it adjusts the picture brightness and color temperature based on the ambient light in the room — but I have yet to find one that doesn’t make distracting brightness adjustments while I’m watching TV. This option can also be called Brightness Optimization, Ambient Light Detection, Intelligent Mode, or Energy Saving Step, and it’s usually not in the picture settings menu. Instead, look for it under General settings in a power-saving menu and switch it off.

The best picture settings aren’t always under the Picture menu.

After the ambient light sensor is off, you can adjust the brightness based on how much light is in your room. This can be done with the brightness or backlight slider, whichever one looks like it changes the brightness across the entire screen. Having the brightness pumped up in the middle of the day can be great to combat sunlight streaming through the windows, but can be overbearing once the sun goes down. Adjusting it to taste can be the difference between an immersive movie experience and a headache two hours later.

Of course, the one setting everyone thinks about when it comes to TVs is motion smoothing. I’ve made it a personal mission to turn it off on any TV I have access to, be it in a waiting room, a hotel room, or my parents’ living room. It uses a process called frame interpolation to create extra frames between existing ones to smooth out motion. It’s quite often referred to as the “soap opera effect” because it makes movies look like afternoon TV dramas. Using Filmmaker mode will generally turn this and other extraneous processing off, but it’s still best to double-check.

As with the ambient light sensor, the idea behind motion smoothing is good, and for some programs with fast motion, like sports, it can actually do a solid job depending on the TV manufacturer (Sony’s Motionflow on its lowest setting can be decent).

If you plan on gaming, using Gaming mode will turn off some of that extra processing to reduce input lag as much as possible, and to make high refresh rate modes available. I recommend looking for the color temperature setting and switching it to something with “warm” in the title, as that will move the color temp toward something more natural.

Finally, if you have anything connected to your TV via HDMI (especially a gaming console), make sure the HDMI settings are set to Enhanced instead of Standard. This will expand the bandwidth to the port’s full capability. As with the power settings, HDMI settings are usually found in a General menu and can be called HDMI signal format or External Device Manager.

Getting a new TV is a big investment, and one that should last you a few years at least. And while most TVs today can perform incredibly well, they still need a bit of a nudge to get all the performance you paid for. Making these tweaks will do exactly that and lead to years of enjoyment.

Photography by John Higgins / The Verge

Tech.title: The M5 MacBook Air just got its biggest discount since Apple raised the price
Tech.content:
If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June, you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.

The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount, is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.

Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model, the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display, or one of the M6-powered machines. A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

Tech.title: This purple electric Chinese minivan can go up to 559 miles on a charge
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Electric minivans could be the ultimate in utility, with room for passengers, gear, and huge batteries. While VW’s ID Buzz only gave us 200 miles of real-world driving on a charge in 2023, China’s BYD has just announced a flagship purple peoplemover that can go an estimated 559 miles (900 km) on electricity.

It’s called the BYD Whale, and some back-of-the-napkin math suggests it lives up to the name. The van would be bigger than a Honda Odyssey, bigger than a Chrysler Pacifica, and bigger than a Toyota Sienna, at 17.3 feet (5,270mm) long, 6.5 feet (1,996mm) wide, 6 feet (1,815mm) tall, and with a 123-inch (3,130mm) wheelbase.

Image: BYD via Autohome Image: BYD via Autohome

According to an auto-translated press release, the vehicle should have room for seven passengers and seven suitcases at a time, not that the company has shown off its interior yet. You can see a prominent sensor cluster on its forehead, though, and it’ll come equipped with LiDAR for advanced hands-free driving.

Photo: 车若初见 (Weibo) Photo: 车若初见 (Weibo)

CarNewsChina points out it’s actually not the first with 900 km of CLTC battery range on board — Geely’s all electric Zeekr 009 minivan also claims to offer up to 900 km of range in one configuration. But BYD’s also claiming the can charge its battery from 10 percent to 97 percent in just nine minutes, and it get you from 10 percent to 70 percent in five minutes, according to Electrek.

The Whale will also come in a 248-mile (400 km) plug-in hybrid version as well, and the company’s planning to ship it in China in Q1 of 2027 for around 300,000 yuan. That’s roughly $45,000. As we’ve reported, Chinese cars are becoming quite competitive. Will they make it to the US?
